### [1] [HierBias: Context-Conditioned Hierarchical Media Bias Detection with Multi-Task Type Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26100)
*Kaining Li,Ruichen Yan,Yuxin Dong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: HierBias is a hierarchical media bias detector that leverages inter-sentence document context via a RoBERTa encoder and cross-sentence Transformer aggregator. It introduces context-conditioned bias probability, proves context reduces Bayes error, and achieves SOTA on BABE and BASIL (0.853 F1, 0.723 MCC).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing sentence-level media bias detection methods classify sentences independently, ignoring inter-sentence contextual signals that human annotators naturally exploit. This limitation motivates a hierarchical, context-conditioned approach that formally models document context to improve bias prediction accuracy.

Method: HierBias introduces: (1) a formal definition of context-conditioned bias probability with theoretical proof that document context strictly reduces the Bayes error when inter-sentence mutual information is non-zero; (2) a multi-task generalization bound showing joint training of binary bias detection and fine-grained bias type classification improves sample efficiency; (3) an architecture pairing a sentence-level RoBERTa encoder with a cross-sentence Transformer aggregator and dual output heads (binary detection + four-class type classification).

Result: On BABE and BASIL benchmarks, HierBias achieves 0.853 F1 and 0.723 MCC, outperforming the prior SOTA bias-detector by +2.6% F1 and +4.3% MCC (McNemar's test, p < 0.05). Ablation studies confirm each theoretical component contributes independently and consistently.

Conclusion: Leveraging inter-sentence document context via a theoretically grounded hierarchical architecture significantly improves media bias detection. The combination of context-conditioned modeling and multi-task learning yields robust gains, validated by both empirical results and formal generalization bounds.

Abstract: Media bias detection is a critical task for ensuring fair and balanced information dissemination, yet existing sentence-level approaches classify each sentence independently, ignoring inter-sentence contextual signals that human annotators naturally exploit. We present \textbf{HierBias}, a hierarchical context-conditioned media bias detector that formally models document context in bias prediction. We introduce the \emph{context-conditioned bias probability} and prove theoretically that leveraging document context strictly reduces the Bayes error of sentence-level classification when inter-sentence mutual information is non-zero. A multi-task generalization bound further establishes that jointly training binary bias detection and fine-grained bias type classification improves sample efficiency on small annotated corpora. Architecturally, HierBias pairs a sentence-level RoBERTa encoder with a cross-sentence Transformer aggregator and dual output heads for binary detection and four-class type classification. Evaluated on BABE and BASIL, HierBias achieves 0.853 F1 and 0.723 MCC, surpassing the state-of-the-art bias-detector by $+2.6\%$ F1 and $+4.3\%$ MCC (McNemar's test, $p < 0.05$). Ablation experiments confirm that each theoretical component contributes independently and consistently.

</details>


### [2] [Know2Guess: A Contamination-Aware Multi-Zone Benchmark for Knowledge-Boundary Evaluation in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26101)
*Renwei Meng,Bowen Zhang,Jian Wang,Xican Wang,Haoyi Wu,Xuanyan Qiu,Shengan Yang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Presents Know2Guess, a contamination-aware multi-zone benchmark with 1,200 items across five domains for evaluating LLMs' ability to distinguish answerable questions from unknowns. Evaluates FLAN-T5, Qwen2.5-Instruct, and Llama-3-Instruct, finding Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct achieves best reliability but persistent calibration and refusal issues. Provides a reproducible protocol auditing answerability, abstention, refusal, and contamination as distinct reliability dimensions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM evaluation conflates supported answering with unsupported guessing, and fails to separate these from confounds like data contamination, prompt idiosyncrasy, and generic refusal behavior. A benchmark is needed that isolates the transition from answerable knowledge to abstention-expected unknowns under controlled, contamination-aware conditions.

Method: The authors construct a 1,200-item benchmark across five domains with: (1) explicit abstention expectations, (2) contamination-risk metadata, (3) frozen build-time labels, and (4) dual parsing (official strict + normalized robustness). They evaluate FLAN-T5, Qwen2.5-Instruct, and Llama-3-Instruct using locked answer-or-abstain prompts, answer-only controls, and prompt-template variants to isolate answering vs. abstention behavior.

Result: FLAN baselines show weak productive abstention. Stronger instruction-tuned models exhibit a selective but incomplete transition from answering to abstaining. Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct achieves best overall reliability, yet answer-expected zones remain difficult, calibration is poor, and benign-item refusal persists. Prompt and parser robustness analyses preserve the main ranking and qualitative conclusions.

Conclusion: Know2Guess provides a reproducible protocol for auditing answerability, abstention, refusal, and contamination as distinct but interacting dimensions of LLM reliability. The benchmark is not trivially solved by generic non-answer behavior, and results highlight that even the best models struggle with calibration and selective abstention.

Abstract: Reliable evaluation of large language models should separate supported answering from unsupported guessing without conflating either with data contamination, prompt idiosyncrasy, or generic refusal behavior. We present a contamination-aware, multi-zone benchmark for measuring the transition from answerable knowledge to abstention-expected unknowns under frozen build-time labels. The benchmark contains 1,200 items across five domains, explicit abstention expectations, contamination-risk metadata, and dual parsing with an official strict parser plus a normalized robustness parser. We evaluate FLAN-T5, Qwen2.5-Instruct, and Llama-3-Instruct models under locked answer-or-abstain prompts, answer-only controls, and prompt-template variants. The benchmark is not solved by generic non-answer behavior: FLAN baselines remain weak on productive abstention, while stronger instruction-tuned models expose a selective but incomplete transition from answering to abstaining. Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct achieves the best overall reliability, but answer-expected zones remain difficult, calibration remains poor, and benign-item refusal persists. Prompt and parser robustness analyses preserve the main ranking and qualitative conclusions. The benchmark therefore provides a reproducible protocol for auditing answerability, abstention, refusal, and contamination as distinct but interacting dimensions of LLM reliability.The dataset is publicly available at https://github.com/renweimeng/Know2Guess-A-Contamination-Aware-Multi-Zone-Benchmark.

</details>


### [3] [Helpfulness Hurts: Domain-Dependent Degradation of Mid-Trained Compassion Values Under Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26102)
*Jasmine Brazilek,Juliana Seawell*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Post-training a Llama 3.1 8B model on helpfulness data significantly degrades animal compassion values (vs. coding-domain training), and this degradation affects general moral reasoning in English but does not transfer cross-lingually — whereas compassion values from mid-training do transfer across languages, suggesting values are more deeply encoded than domain-specific reasoning improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard post-training pipelines (SFT + RL) aim to make LLMs helpful but may inadvertently erode values instilled during pre-training or mid-training. The authors investigate whether the domain of post-training data differentially affects the retention of specific values — in this case, animal compassion — and whether such effects generalize across moral reasoning and across languages.

Method: A Llama 3.1 8B model was first mid-trained on compassion-oriented synthetic data. Then two post-training paradigms were compared: SFT (Dolly-15k for helpfulness vs. Magicoder-110K for coding) and GRPO (RLHFlow for helpfulness vs. Magicoder for coding). Evaluation used the Animal Harm Benchmark (AHB 2.2) and the MORU benchmark (Moral Reasoning Under Uncertainty), with both English and multilingual components.

Result: Helpfulness training significantly degraded animal compassion relative to coding training on AHB (SFT: 35.7% vs. 65.2%; GRPO: 18.7% vs. 32.0%). On English MORU, helpfulness training reduced moral reasoning by 25.5 pp (46.4% vs. 71.9%). However, on multilingual MORU, the domain effect disappeared (SFT: 52.3% vs. 51.2%). Conversely, the animal compassion effect transferred cross-lingually, with Magicoder's AHB gain over the base model 4.5× larger on non-English items than English items.

Conclusion: Values instilled through mid-training are encoded more deeply and cross-lingually than reasoning improvements from domain-specific post-training. For labs building on value-laden mid-training, coding-domain post-training may better preserve mid-trained values than helpfulness post-training, without harming general reasoning capabilities.

Abstract: Standard post-training pipelines apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) to make language models helpful, but these processes may inadvertently degrade values instilled during pre-training. We investigate whether the domain of post-training data differentially affects the retention of animal compassion values in a Llama 3.1 8B model mid-trained on compassion-oriented synthetic data, using both SFT (helpfulness via Dolly-15k vs. coding via Magicoder-110K) and GRPO (helpfulness via RLHFlow vs. coding via Magicoder), evaluated on the Animal Harm Benchmark (AHB 2.2) and MORU benchmark (Moral Reasoning Under Uncertainty). Helpfulness training significantly degrades animal compassion relative to coding training on AHB (SFT: 35.7% vs. 65.2%; GRPO: 18.7% vs. 32.0%), replicating across two independent helpfulness datasets and two training paradigms. On English MORU items, helpfulness training degrades general moral reasoning by 25.5 percentage points (46.4% vs. 71.9%), a striking gap that rivals the compassion effect in magnitude. However, this effect does not transfer cross-lingually: on the multilingual MORU benchmark, the domain effect disappears (SFT: 52.3% vs. 51.2%). In contrast, the animal compassion effect transfers consistently across languages, with Magicoder's AHB percentage-point gain over the base model 4.5 times larger on non-English items than English items. This divergence suggests that values instilled through mid-training are encoded more deeply and cross-lingually than reasoning improvements from domain-specific post-training. These results suggest that, for labs building on value-laden mid-training, coding-domain post-training may better preserve mid-trained values than helpfulness post-training without harming general reasoning capabilities.

</details>


### [4] [Investigating LLM's Problem Solving Capability -- a Study on Statics Questions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26103)
*Tanner Culleton,Hung-Fu Chang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This study evaluates LLM performance on statics problems using a model distillation approach, revealing that while LLMs handle text-only problems well, accuracy drops significantly with diagrams due to multi-step reasoning difficulties rather than image recognition limitations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior LLM education studies rely on public datasets and lack topic-specific analysis, particularly in mechanical engineering statics. A systematic investigation is needed to understand how LLMs perform on domain-specific problem types, especially when visual elements are involved.

Method: A model distillation process was used to extract 25 text-only statics questions from ChatGPT. Two additional datasets were constructed by (1) adding diagrams and (2) modifying numerical values. LLM performance was then evaluated across these three dataset variants to isolate the effects of visual information and reasoning complexity.

Result: LLMs perform well on text-only statics problems. Accuracy decreases when diagrams are added and problems require multi-step reasoning. The performance drop is attributed primarily to difficulties in multi-step reasoning and consistent application of extracted visual information, not to image recognition failures.

Conclusion: LLMs' main weakness in solving statics problems lies in multi-step reasoning with visual context rather than in image recognition. This has implications for how LLMs should be integrated into engineering education and highlights areas needing improvement.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly influenced many aspects of society, particularly education, due to their demonstrated ability to complete assignments and examinations across a wide range of subjects. Although prior studies have examined the educational impact of LLMs, much of the existing work relies on public or open problem datasets and lacks topic-specific analysis. In engineering education, especially within mechanical engineering, systematic investigations of LLM performance on specific problem types remain limited. Instead of using traditional methods that directly ask textbook questions to an LLM tool, our study adopts a model distillation process to evaluate LLM capabilities in solving statics problems. By distilling ChatGPT, we extracted 25 text-only statics questions and further constructed two additional datasets by adding diagrams and modifying their numerical values. Experimental results show that while LLMs perform well on text-only statics problems, their accuracy decreases when diagrams are introduced and the problems require multi-step reasoning. Further analysis suggests that this performance drop is not primarily caused by limitations in image recognition, but rather by difficulties in multi-step reasoning and in consistently applying extracted visual information across successive solution stages.

</details>


### [5] [Assert, don't describe: Linguistic features that shift LLM reasoning about animal welfare](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26104)
*Jasmine Brazilek,Harper Dunn*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The study measures how ten linguistic features in fine-tuning data shift Llama-3.2-1B's stance on animal welfare. Seven features (assertive certainty, moral vocabulary, emotion words, evaluative claims, narrative structure, harm severity, immediate temporal framing) strengthen pro-animal-welfare reasoning; two (hedged language, concrete sensory description) dilute it; first-person perspective has no effect. Key takeaway: make the writer's position explicit rather than describing neutrally.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Animal-welfare advocates generate substantial written content that increasingly enters LLM training corpora, and millions of people query these models about animal welfare topics. The authors aim to empirically identify which linguistic features in that writing most effectively shift model reasoning toward a pro-animal-welfare stance, providing actionable, evidence-based guidance for advocates rather than relying on intuition.

Method: The authors use vocabulary-matched stance-contrast probes on a held-out animal-welfare benchmark. They fine-tune Llama-3.2-1B on texts systematically varying across ten linguistic features (assertive certainty, explicit moral vocabulary, emotion words, evaluative claims, narrative structure, depicted harm severity, immediate temporal framing, hedged language, concrete sensory description, first-person perspective) and measure the resulting shift in the model's preference for pro-animal-welfare reasoning.

Result: Eight of ten features produce statistically significant shifts. Seven strengthen pro-animal-welfare reasoning: assertive certainty, explicit moral vocabulary, emotion words, evaluative claims, narrative structure, depicted harm severity, and immediate temporal framing. Two dilute the pro-animal-welfare stance: hedged language and concrete sensory description. First-person perspective shows no statistically significant effect.

Conclusion: The practical implication is that writers of animal-welfare texts destined for LLM training data should assert a clear position rather than describe scenes neutrally. Features that make the writer's stance explicit shift models toward pro-animal-welfare reasoning; features that present animal-welfare content while withholding or softening stance dilute it. This provides evidence-based rhetorical strategy for advocates concerned with AI-mediated discourse.

Abstract: Animal-welfare advocates produce a lot of writing, and increasingly that writing trains the language models that millions of people then ask about animal welfare. Using vocabulary-matched stance-contrast probes on a held-out animal-welfare benchmark, we measure how each of ten linguistic features changes Llama-3.2-1B's preference for pro-animal-welfare reasoning when used as fine-tuning data. Eight of the ten features produce statistically significant shifts. Seven move the model toward stronger pro-animal-welfare reasoning: assertive certainty, explicit moral vocabulary, emotion words, evaluative claims, narrative structure, depicted harm severity, and immediate temporal framing. Two move it the other way: hedged language and concrete sensory description both dilute the pro-animal-welfare stance. First-person perspective has no statistically significant effect. The practical recommendation for anyone writing animal-welfare text that may end up in LLM training corpora: assert a position rather than describe a scene neutrally. The features that shift the model are the ones that make the writer's position explicit; the features that dilute it hold animal-welfare content but withhold stance.

</details>


### [6] [Context Recycling for Long-Horizon LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26105)
*Derek Thomas*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ContextForge recycles task-relevant information across multi-turn conversations via structured queries, external memory, and controlled synthesis, reducing token overhead while maintaining accuracy without full context replay.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs perform well in short contexts but degrade over long conversational horizons due to context window limits and inefficient token usage. Full context replay is costly; larger windows or retraining are impractical solutions.

Method: ContextForge combines three components: (1) structured query generation to extract salient information from prior turns, (2) external memory retrieval to store and access relevant context, and (3) controlled synthesis to integrate retrieved information into responses. Evaluated on a 15-turn conversational benchmark with healthcare queries testing multi-turn reasoning, back-references, and domain shifts.

Result: Compared to an identical-model baseline agent, ContextForge achieved improved consistency, reduced token consumption, and comparable response accuracy over 15-turn conversations.

Conclusion: Context recycling is a practical strategy for extending LLM capabilities in long-horizon tasks without requiring larger context windows or model retraining.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong capabilities in short-context reasoning but degrade in performance over long conversational horizons due to context window limitations and inefficient token usage. We introduce ContextForge, a system for context recycling that maintains task-relevant information across turns by combining structured query generation, external memory retrieval, and controlled synthesis. The system enables efficient reuse of prior computation without relying on full context replay, reducing token overhead while preserving answer quality. We evaluate ContextForge using a 15-turn conversational benchmark that tests multi-turn reasoning, back-references, and domain shifts across structured healthcare queries. Compared to a baseline agent using identical underlying models, ContextForge demonstrates improved consistency and reduced token consumption, while maintaining comparable response accuracy. These results suggest that context recycling provides a practical approach for extending LLM capabilities in long-horizon tasks without requiring larger context windows or model retraining. Code and evaluation artifacts are available at https://github.com/Betanu701/ContextForge.

</details>


### [7] [Reducing Conversational Escalation in Large Language Model Dialogue with Nonviolent Communication Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26106)
*Zhixing Sun,Shenghe Xu,Tao Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether lightweight, prompt-level constraints based on Nonviolent Communication (NVC) principles can guide LLMs toward de-escalating conversational behavior. Using dual-agent simulations, the authors find NVC-constrained prompting consistently reduces escalation and stabilizes interactions with resistant users.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in emotionally charged contexts (interpersonal conflict, distress), yet prior safety research focuses on preventing explicit toxic outputs rather than unintentional conversational escalation. There is a gap in understanding how to shape LLM dialogue behavior to be de-escalating rather than inflammatory in conflict-prone settings.

Method: The authors reformulate Nonviolent Communication (NVC) principles as process-oriented prompt-level guidelines (discouraging blame attribution, emphasizing emotional experience, encouraging clarification before advice). They evaluate these constraints using a dual-agent simulation framework across multiple instruction-tuned models under varying levels of user resistance, measuring conversational escalation as the primary outcome.

Result: NVC-constrained prompting consistently reduces conversational escalation across models. The approach also stabilizes interactions with highly resistant users, suggesting that lightweight communication constraints can meaningfully improve LLM trustworthiness in conflict-prone dialogues.

Conclusion: Simple, prompt-level communication constraints derived from NVC can effectively reduce escalation in LLM-mediated conflict conversations. This offers a practical, low-cost method for improving the safety and trustworthiness of LLM dialogue beyond traditional toxic-content filtering.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in emotionally charged situations involving interpersonal conflict, frustration, and distress. While prior safety research has focused on preventing explicit harms such as toxic or policy-violating content, less attention has been paid to conversational behaviors that may unintentionally escalate conflict. In this paper, we investigate whether LLMs can be guided toward more de-escalating dialogue behavior through lightweight prompt-level constraints derived from Nonviolent Communication (NVC). We reformulate NVC principles as process-oriented guidelines that discourage blame attribution, emphasize attention to users' emotional experiences, and encourage clarification before advice. Using a dual-agent simulation framework across multiple instruction-tuned models and user resistance levels, we show that NVC-constrained prompting consistently reduces conversational escalation and stabilizes interactions with highly resistant users. These results suggest that simple communication constraints can meaningfully improve the trustworthiness of LLM dialogue in conflict-prone settings.

</details>


### [8] [Low Resource Multimodal Translation of Nepali Spoken Words into Emotion-Conditioned Sign Language Avatars](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26107)
*Jatin Bhusal,Salma Tamang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: NEST-V1 is a lightweight multimodal framework that generates emotion-conditioned Nepali Sign Language avatars from spoken input, achieving ~80% accuracy on both ASR and emotion recognition with 22.1M parameters, demonstrating feasibility for low-resource, edge-deployable sign language systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sign language communication systems that integrate emotional expression are underexplored, especially for low-resource languages like Nepali. Existing systems lack emotion-aware translation, and there is a need for lightweight, edge-deployable architectures suitable for resource-constrained settings.

Method: A proof-of-concept multimodal framework using a shared acoustic encoder for simultaneous Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and emotion classification. The system was evaluated on four Nepali words ("thank you", "hello", "house", "me") across three emotional states (happy, neutral, sad), using 600 labeled audio samples from 50 speakers. Parameter sharing yields 37% efficiency gains over separate models.

Result: The system achieved 81.1% ASR accuracy and 79.21% emotion recognition accuracy with only 22.1M parameters. It demonstrated 37% parameter efficiency compared to separate model architectures, confirming viability for edge deployment.

Conclusion: NEST-V1 establishes a viable technical foundation for emotion-aware sign language translation in low-resource settings. The lightweight, scalable framework shows promise for real-time, emotionally expressive communication and provides a clear pathway for expansion to larger vocabularies and more diverse emotional expressions.

Abstract: Sign language communication systems, that integrate emotional expression remain underexplored, particularly for low-resource languages. This pilot study presents NEST-V1 (Nepali Emotion and Speech Transformer - Version 1), a proof-of-concept multimodal framework that demonstrates the feasibility of generating emotion-conditioned Nepali Sign Language avatars from spoken input. As a preliminary investigation, we focus on four common Nepali words ("thank you", "hello", "house", "me") across three emotional states (happy, neutral, sad) to validate our core technical approach. Our lightweight architecture employs a shared acoustic encoder for simultaneous Automatic Speech Recognition and emotion classification, achieving 81.1% ASR accuracy and 79.21% emotion recognition accuracy on a dataset of 600 labeled audio samples from 50 speakers. The system demonstrates 37% parameter efficiency compared to separate model architectures while maintaining a lightweight footprint with only 22.1M parameters suitable for edge deployment. This pilot work establishes the technical foundation for emotion-aware sign language translation in low-resource settings and provides a scalable framework for future expansion to larger vocabularies and more diverse emotional expressions. Our preliminary results indicate the viability of real-time, emotionally expressive sign language communication systems for the hearing-impaired community, with clear pathways for enhancement in subsequent development phases.

</details>


### [9] [Where Larger Models Excel: The Primacy of Constraint-Guided Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26108)
*Guan-Yi Lin,Hen-Hsen Huang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Larger language models outperform smaller ones on reasoning benchmarks by 6-7%. The authors develop AdvCluster, an automated framework to identify and categorize where larger models gain their advantage, finding that "Constraint-Guided Reasoning" — the ability to identify, structure, and verify constraints — is the recurring theme behind these gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While it is well-documented that larger LLMs outperform smaller ones on reasoning tasks, the specific reasoning behaviors and mechanisms underlying this performance gap remain underexplored. The authors aim to move beyond aggregate scores to understand *how* larger models reason differently.

Method: The authors propose AdvCluster, an automated framework with three stages: (1) identifying questions where the larger model shows a stable, statistically significant advantage; (2) extracting fine-grained advantage descriptions from paired reasoning traces (comparing larger vs. smaller model outputs on the same question); and (3) performing semantic clustering of these descriptions, with quantitative evaluation and selection of clusters guided by a reviewer model, yielding a systematic taxonomy.

Result: The framework produces a systematic taxonomy of reasoning advantages. These span both common advantages recurring across domains (math, physics, chemistry, programming) and specialized advantages tied to specific domains. The central recurring theme is "Constraint-Guided Reasoning": larger models excel at identifying explicit and implicit constraints, organizing them into structured reasoning, and using constraints to prune infeasible paths and verify intermediate steps.

Conclusion: The performance gap between larger and smaller models is not merely quantitative but qualitative in nature. Larger models reason fundamentally differently by leveraging constraint-guided reasoning. This taxonomy provides a fine-grained understanding of where and why scale improves reasoning, offering insights for model development and evaluation.

Abstract: Larger language models consistently outperform smaller ones on reasoning benchmarks, yet the reasoning differences underlying this gap remain underexplored. Across benchmarks in mathematics, physics, chemistry, and programming, we observe stable performance gaps: averaged over datasets, Qwen3-32B outperforms Qwen3-8B by 6.43%, while GPT-OSS-120B exceeds GPT-OSS-20B by 7.38%. To study the reasoning differences behind these gains, we develop AdvCluster, an automated framework that identifies questions where the larger model shows a stable advantage, extracts fine-grained advantage descriptions from paired reasoning traces produced by larger and smaller models, and organizes them through semantic clustering with quantitative evaluation and selection guided by a reviewer model. Our analysis yields a systematic taxonomy of larger model reasoning advantages, spanning both common advantages that recur across domains and specialized advantages associated with particular domains. Across these patterns, a recurring theme is Constraint-Guided Reasoning: larger models are better at identifying explicit and implicit constraints, organizing them into structured reasoning, and using them to rule out infeasible paths and verify intermediate steps.

</details>


### [10] [From Lexicon to AI: A Structured-Data Pipeline for Specialized Conversational Systems in Low-Resource Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26112)
*Siddhant Hitesh Mantri,Dhara Gorasiya,Malhar Kulkarni,Pushpak Bhattacharya*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents a methodology for converting structured lexical databases (Hindi WordNet) into instruction-response pairs to fine-tune a 12B-parameter LLM via quantized LoRA, yielding a Hindi learning chatbot that outperforms general-purpose models (91.0 vs. 79.4–83.6) while offering a scalable blueprint for low-resource languages with WordNet resources.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Low-resource languages lack massive training corpora needed for building specialized conversational AI systems. The authors aim to bridge this gap by leveraging existing structured linguistic resources (WordNet) as an alternative to corpus-intensive approaches, thereby democratizing AI accessibility for hundreds of low-resource languages.

Method: The methodology consists of three stages: (1) systematic transformation of Hindi WordNet into 1.25 million diverse instruction-response pairs; (2) fine-tuning a 12B-parameter language model using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) with 4-bit quantization for resource efficiency; (3) evaluation via a Hindi language learning chatbot benchmark, comparing against general-purpose models on pedagogical effectiveness and semantic performance.

Result: The structured-knowledge-based system achieved 91.0 on pedagogical effectiveness, significantly surpassing general-purpose models (79.4–83.6). It also maintained competitive semantic performance and demonstrated exceptional consistency, validating that expert-curated lexical databases can serve as effective foundations for specialized conversational AI.

Conclusion: The work establishes a proof-of-concept that structured linguistic resources like WordNet can substitute for massive corpora in developing specialized AI systems for low-resource languages. The pipeline is generalizable to hundreds of languages with existing WordNet resources, offering a practical path to closing the AI accessibility gap.

Abstract: Low-resource languages face a critical challenge in AI development: creating specialized conversational systems without access to massive training corpora. We present a systematic methodology for transforming structured linguistic resources into specialized AI systems, demonstrating that expert-curated lexical databases can serve as effective foundations for conversational AI development. Our approach converts Hindi WordNet into 1.25 million diverse instruction-response pairs, fine-tunes a 12B-parameter language model using resource-efficient LoRA with 4-bit quantization. Evaluation through a Hindi language learning chatbot demonstrates that structured-knowledge-based systems achieve superior pedagogical effectiveness (91.0 vs. 79.4-83.6 for general-purpose models) while maintaining competitive semantic performance and exceptional consistency. The complete pipeline demonstrates a proof-of-concept methodology using Hindi for developing specialized AI systems for any languages with WordNet resources. This work addresses the critical gap in AI accessibility for low-resource languages, offering a practical alternative to corpus-intensive approaches and potentially enabling specialized AI development for the hundreds of languages with existing WordNet resources.

</details>


### [11] [ProvenAI: Provenance-Native Traces of Evidence in Generated Answers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26449)
*Mohammad Faizan,Dalal Alharthi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ProvenAI introduces a three-layer transparency framework for retrieval-augmented QA, separately measuring answer correctness, citation fidelity, and per-document influence via ablation. Evaluated on HotpotQA (7,405 examples, 509K passages), it achieves 53.53% accuracy and 71.55% citation fidelity, and reveals a "citation-influence gap" where cited sources may exert weak behavioral influence while uncited sources demonstrably shift outputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing retrieval-augmented systems present citations without confirming whether cited sources meaningfully shaped the generated answer. There is no established framework for independently measuring and verifying the actual influence of cited (versus uncited) documents on multi-hop QA outputs, creating a transparency deficit that ProvenAI aims to address.

Method: ProvenAI implements a seven-stage pipeline: (1) data normalisation, (2) retrieval indexing, (3) citation-aware answer generation, (4) attribution auditing, (5) ablation-based influence estimation via leave-one-resource-out intervention, (6) batch evaluation, and (7) interactive inspection. The framework decomposes transparency into three independently measurable layers — answer correctness, citation fidelity (against benchmark supporting evidence), and per-document behavioural influence. It grounds these measurements in causal-mediation analysis and database-provenance theory, and formalizes the relationship between the surface proxy and a token-level KL-divergence target through a stated faithfulness condition.

Result: Evaluated on 7,405 HotpotQA distractor validation examples drawn from 509,300 passages: answer accuracy of 53.53%, mean citation-fidelity score of 71.55%. A worked example surfaces the "citation-influence gap": a clean citation audit co-occurs with a profile where one cited source registers only weak influence while seven uncited sources demonstrably shift the output.

Conclusion: Meaningful transparency in retrieval-grounded QA requires traceable links across retrieved, cited, and behaviourally influential evidence as three distinct, independently measured layers. ProvenAI establishes this layered framework and demonstrates that citations alone are insufficient proxies for actual document influence, with implications for integration with cryptographic provenance architectures in autonomous scientific discovery.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented systems routinely present citations alongside generated answers, yet a citation does not confirm that the corresponding source meaningfully shaped the output. This paper introduces ProvenAI, a framework that decomposes transparency in multi-hop question answering into three independently measurable layers: answer correctness, citation fidelity against benchmark supporting evidence, and per-document influence under leave-one-resource-out intervention. Targeting the HotpotQA distractor benchmark through a seven-stage pipeline covering data normalisation, retrieval indexing, citation-aware answer generation, attribution auditing, ablation-based influence estimation, batch evaluation, and interactive inspection, ProvenAI evaluates 7,405 validation examples drawn from a canonical corpus of 509,300 passages. The system achieves 53.53% answer accuracy alongside a mean citation-fidelity score of 71.55%, and a worked example surfaces what we call the citation-influence gap: a clean citation audit co-occurring with a profile in which one cited source registers only weak influence while seven uncited sources demonstrably shift the output. We formalise the relationship between the implemented surface proxy and a token-level KL-divergence target through a stated faithfulness condition, ground the framework in causal-mediation analysis and database-provenance theory, and discuss how the three measurement layers compose with cryptographic provenance architectures emerging in autonomous scientific discovery. ProvenAI establishes that meaningful transparency in retrieval-grounded QA requires traceable links across retrieved, cited, and behaviourally influential evidence as three distinct, independently measured layers.

</details>


### [12] [Dynamic-dLLM: Dynamic Cache-Budget and Adaptive Parallel Decoding for Training-Free Acceleration of Diffusion LLM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26120)
*Tianyi Wu,Xiaoxi Sun,Yanhua Jiao,Yulin Li,Yixin Chen,YunHao Cao,YiQi Hu,Zhuotao Tian*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Dynamic-dLLM is a training-free inference acceleration framework for diffusion LLMs that uses Dynamic Cache Updating and Adaptive Parallel Decoding to achieve >3× speedup without performance loss, addressing the O(L³) complexity challenge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion LLMs suffer from O(L³) computational complexity with sequence length, making them impractical for long-sequence and real-time applications. Existing acceleration methods (static caching, parallel decoding) ignore the dynamic behavior of token properties across layers and decoding steps, limiting their effectiveness.

Method: Dynamic-dLLM introduces two training-free components: (1) Dynamic Cache Updating (DCU), which adaptively allocates cache-update budgets based on layer-wise token dynamics rather than using static caching; (2) Adaptive Parallel Decoding (APD), which dynamically calibrates decoding thresholds to balance generation quality and efficiency during denoising.

Result: Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct, LLaDA-1.5, and Dream-v0-7B-Instruct across MMLU, GSM8K, and HumanEval benchmarks show Dynamic-dLLM achieves an average speedup exceeding 3× while maintaining performance, outperforming state-of-the-art acceleration methods.

Conclusion: Dynamic-dLLM provides an effective plug-and-play solution for efficient dLLM deployment, demonstrating that dynamic, adaptive strategies for caching and parallel decoding significantly outperform static approaches without requiring retraining or compromising generation quality.

Abstract: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) offer a promising alternative to autoregressive models, excelling in text generation tasks due to their bidirectional attention mechanisms. However, their computational complexity scales on the order of L cubed with the sequence length L. This poses significant challenges for long-sequence and real-time applications, primarily due to the lack of compatibility with key-value caching and the non-autoregressive nature of denoising steps. Existing acceleration methods rely on static caching or parallel decoding strategies, which fail to account for the dynamic behavior of token properties across layers and decoding steps. We propose Dynamic-dLLM, a training-free framework that enhances dLLM inference efficiency through two components: Dynamic Cache Updating (DCU), which adaptively allocates cache-update budgets based on layer-wise token dynamics, and Adaptive Parallel Decoding (APD), which dynamically calibrates decoding thresholds to balance generation quality and efficiency. Extensive experiments on models like LLaDA-8B-Instruct, LLaDA-1.5, and Dream-v0-7B-Instruct across benchmarks such as MMLU, GSM8K, and HumanEval demonstrate that Dynamic-dLLM significantly improves inference speed. It attains an average speedup exceeding 3 times while maintaining performance. Dynamic-dLLM outperforms state-of-the-art acceleration methods and provides a plug-and-play solution for efficient dLLM deployment without compromising performance. The code is available at https://github.com/TianyiWu233/DYNAMIC-DLLM.

</details>


### [13] [Extracting Problem and Method Sentence from Scientific Papers: A Context-enhanced Transformer Using Formulaic Expression Desensitization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26481)
*Yingyi Zhang,Chengzhi Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper tackles the problem of extracting problem and method sentences from scientific papers. To overcome limitations of small-scale annotated datasets, the authors propose: (1) formulaic expression (FE) desensitization data augmenters to generate synthetic data and reduce model reliance on surface forms, and (2) a context-enhanced transformer that leverages surrounding context to weigh word importance and filter noise. Experiments show 3.71% and 2.67% macro F1 improvements over baselines, while LLM-based in-context learning proves unsuitable for this task.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scientific paper understanding requires identifying problem and method sentences, but manual annotation is expensive and yields small datasets. Models trained on such limited data overfit to formulaic expressions (stereotyped phrasing patterns), severely reducing generalization to unseen papers.

Method: Three-pronged approach: (1) Formulaic Expression (FE) desensitization — a data augmentation technique that identifies and neutralizes stereotyped patterns to generate diverse synthetic training instances and reduce model dependence on surface forms. (2) A context-enhanced transformer that uses surrounding context to re-weight word importance in target sentences and attenuate contextual noise. (3) Evaluation of LLM-based in-context learning (ICL) for comparison.

Result: The proposed models achieve macro F1 improvements of 3.71% and 2.67% over baselines on two scientific paper datasets. LLM-based ICL methods are shown to be unsuitable for problem and method extraction.

Conclusion: Addressing small-scale dataset limitations through FE desensitization data augmentation and context-enhanced modeling yields significant gains in scientific paper sentence extraction. LLM-based ICL, however, is not a viable alternative for this specific task.

Abstract: Billions of scientific papers lead to the need to identify essential parts from the massive text. Scientific research is an activity from putting forward problems to using methods. To learn the main idea from scientific papers, we focus on extracting problem and method sentences. Annotating sentences within scientific papers is labor-intensive, resulting in small-scale datasets that limit the amount of information models can learn. This limited information leads models to rely heavily on specific forms, which in turn reduces their generalization capabilities. This paper addresses the problems caused by small-scale datasets from three perspectives: increasing dataset scale, reducing dependence on specific forms, and enriching the information within sentences. To implement the first two ideas, we introduce the concept of formulaic expression (FE) desensitization and propose FE desensitization-based data augmenters to generate synthetic data and reduce models' reliance on FEs. For the third idea, we propose a context-enhanced transformer that utilizes context to measure the importance of words in target sentences and to reduce noise in the context. Furthermore, this paper conducts experiments using large language model (LLM) based in-context learning (ICL) methods. Quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that our proposed models achieve a higher macro F1 score compared to the baseline models on two scientific paper datasets, with improvements of 3.71% and 2.67%, respectively. The LLM based ICL methods are found to be not suitable for the task of problem and method extraction.

</details>


### [14] [Thinking Like a Scientist? A Structural Study of LLM-Generated Research Methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26130)
*Francesca Carlon,Brecht Verbeken,Vincent Ginis,Andres Algaba*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper investigates how LLMs (GPT-5.1, Gemini 3 Pro, DeepSeek-V3.2) suggest research methodologies when given only a research question, compared against actual methods in 1,000 arXiv CS papers. LLMs converge on a far narrower set of methods (59-96 effective model entities vs. 1,232 in papers), with the strongest bias in provider choice (JSD 3-5x larger than other dimensions). LLMs agree more with each other (ρ=0.55-0.68) than with papers (ρ=0.33-0.56), revealing shared, query-specific but concentrated defaults that risk narrowing researchers' methodological search space.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used to guide research methodology, but their default methodological tendencies under minimal prompting are unknown. Understanding these biases is critical to assess whether LLMs inadvertently narrow the methodological diversity of research.

Method: The authors prompt three LLMs (GPT-5.1, Gemini 3 Pro, DeepSeek-V3.2) with LLM-extracted research questions from 1,000 recent arXiv CS papers. They extract structured method features (model provider, dataset task type, evaluation metric type) from both LLM suggestions and paper-derived experimental inventories, map them into a shared taxonomy, and quantify divergence using Jensen-Shannon divergence, effective number of entities, rank correlations (inter-LLM vs. LLM-to-paper), popularity baselines, BM25 retrieval calibration, and paper-level similarity tests.

Result: Provider choice shows the strongest imbalance (JSD 3-5x larger than other taxonomy dimensions). Other/Academic single-occurrence models are underrepresented by 23-24 pp, while reused academic/community models are slightly overrepresented (4-6 pp). LLMs contract the effective number of model entities from 1,232 to 59-96. Inter-LLM rank correlations (0.55-0.68) exceed LLM-to-paper correlations (0.33-0.56), indicating shared distortions. Controls confirm outputs are query-specific but filtered through a narrower option set.

Conclusion: LLMs exhibit a strong, shared tendency to concentrate methodological suggestions toward popular, familiar choices, particularly in model provider selection. Researchers using LLMs for methodology guidance without cross-checking risk substantially narrowing their design space, reinforcing dominant paradigms at the expense of less-visible alternatives.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to guide research methodology, yet their default methodological tendencies under minimal prompting remain unclear. Here, we prompt GPT-5.1, Gemini 3 Pro, and DeepSeek-V3.2 with an LLM-extracted research question from each of 1,000 recent arXiv computer-science papers and compare the resulting methodology suggestions against a paper-derived experimental inventory. Since we provide only the research question, the differences we measure reflect initial suggestions and not how optimal those suggestions are. We extract structured method features from both sources, map them into a shared taxonomy, and quantify divergence across multiple taxonomy dimensions including model provider, dataset task type, and evaluation metric type. The strongest imbalance appears in provider choice, with Jensen-Shannon divergence about 3-5x larger than any other taxonomy dimension. Other/Academic single-occurrence models are underrepresented by 23-24 percentage points, while reused academic/community models are slightly overrepresented (4-6pp). LLMs also suggest a much narrower range of methods overall: the effective number of model entities contracts from 1,232 to 59-96, and inter-LLM rank correlations (0.55-0.68) generally exceed LLM-to-paper correlations (0.33-0.56), so the distortions are largely shared across models. Popularity baselines, BM25 retrieval calibration, and paper-level similarity tests confirm that the outputs are query-specific responses, but filtered through a narrower set of options. Researchers who rely on LLM suggestions without cross-checking therefore risk narrowing their methodological search space toward a more concentrated default.

</details>


### [15] [Utilizing Cognitive Signals Generated during Human Reading to Enhance Keyphrase Extraction from Microblogs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26485)
*Xinyi Yan,Yingyi Zhang,Chengzhi Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: EEG signals complement eye-tracking for automatic keyphrase extraction from microblogs, with EEG features yielding the largest performance gains. Combining both signal types shows partial complementarity but also redundancy, suggesting multimodal cognitive signals warrant further study.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Microblog-based AKE is challenging due to short, noisy, dispersed text. Eye-tracking has been used to capture readers' attention to salient words, but it suffers from physiological, acquisition, and feature-decoding limitations. The authors explore whether EEG signals can overcome these limitations and complement eye-tracking.

Method: Using the ZuCo corpus, 8 EEG and 17 eye-tracking features were selected and injected into AKE models at two points: the soft-attention layer input and the self-attention layer query vectors. Different feature combinations and model architectures were systematically evaluated.

Result: Cognitive signals consistently improved AKE performance across all feature combinations and architectures. EEG features provided the largest gains. Combining EEG and eye-tracking yielded performance intermediate between the two individual modalities, indicating partial complementarity but also redundancy/noise.

Conclusion: EEG signals offer valuable cognitive evidence for microblog AKE. Multimodal cognitive signal integration is a promising direction, but naive combination may introduce redundancy; more sophisticated fusion strategies are needed.

Abstract: Microblogging platforms generate massive amounts of short, noisy, and dispersed user content, making automatic keyphrase extraction (AKE) an important but challenging task. Prior studies have used eye-tracking signals to improve microblog-based AKE because such signals reflect readers' attention to salient words. However, eye tracking alone is limited by physiological, acquisition, and feature-decoding constraints. To address this issue, we investigate whether electroencephalogram (EEG) signals can complement eye-tracking signals for AKE. Using the ZuCo cognitive language processing corpus, we select 8 EEG features and 17 eye-tracking features and incorporate them into microblog-based AKE models. To reduce possible distortion of cognitive signals by model structures, we inject these features into the input of the soft-attention layer and the query vectors of the self-attention layer. We then evaluate different combinations of cognitive signals across AKE models. The results show that cognitive signals produced during reading consistently improve AKE performance, regardless of feature combinations and model architectures. EEG features bring the largest gains, while combining EEG and eye-tracking features yields performance between the two individual signal types, suggesting partial complementarity but also possible redundancy or noise. These findings indicate that EEG signals provide useful cognitive evidence for microblog-based AKE and that multimodal cognitive signals deserve further investigation.

</details>


### [16] [From Structure to Synergy: A Survey of Vision-Language Perception Paradigm Evolution in Multimodal Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26196)
*Haoxiang Sun,Tao Wang,Li Yuan,Jian Zhao,Jiancheng Lv*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Presents the first systematic survey that treats multimodal large language model (MLLM) perception as a unified, inseparable vision-language capability, introducing a five-stage evolutionary taxonomy, surveying milestones at each phase, and outlining challenges toward artificial general intelligence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MLLM surveys are fragmented — they examine vision or language separately and fail to capture the cross-modal, integrated evolution of perception. There is a need for a unified perspective that treats vision and language as an inseparable modality, analogous to human innate perception.

Method: The authors conduct a systematic literature survey with three contributions: (1) formalizing MLLM perception as an intrinsic unified vision-language capability, (2) proposing a five-stage taxonomy that traces the paradigm evolution of MLLM perception, and (3) surveying representative methods and milestones at each evolutionary phase.

Result: The survey delivers a structured five-stage taxonomy of MLLM perception evolution, catalogs key methods and milestones per stage, identifies open challenges, and proposes research directions for advancing unified multimodal intelligence toward AGI.

Conclusion: Treating vision and language as an inseparable modality provides a more coherent framework for understanding MLLM perception. The five-stage taxonomy offers both foundational understanding and an actionable roadmap, aiming to guide future research toward truly general, unified multimodal intelligence.

Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have recently made remarkable progress in unifying vision-language understanding and reasoning, especially following the introduction of models such as OpenAI's O-series and DeepSeek's R-series, which have driven a paradigm shift toward perception-centric intelligence. However, there remains a lack of systematic surveys that examine perception from a truly unified vision-language perspective -- one that treats vision and language as an inseparable modality. Existing reviews are often fragmented, focusing separately on either vision or language, and thus rarely capture the cross-modal evolution of perception as an integrated capability. To bridge this gap, we present the first systematic survey of unified vision-language perception in MLLMs. Specifically, we (1) formalize MLLM perception as an intrinsic, unified vision-language capability analogous to human innate perception, (2) introduce a five-stage taxonomy tracing the paradigm evolution of MLLM perception and survey representative methods and milestones at each phase, and (3) identify open challenges and outline promising research directions toward truly general, unified multimodal intelligence. We hope our study will provide both a foundational understanding and an actionable roadmap to foster further innovation on the path toward artificial general intelligence (AGI).

</details>


### [17] [SocialPersona: Benchmarking Personalized Profiling and Response with Multimodal Social-Media Context](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26654)
*Qinkai Zhang,Yanyan Zhao,Xin Lu,Yulin Hu,Pengtao Han,Bing Qin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SocialPersona is a benchmark that evaluates whether multimodal LLMs can infer user preferences from longitudinal social-media timelines (text, images, timestamps) and use those inferred preferences to personalize dialogue, revealing that models struggle with fine-grained and recent interests despite identifying broad domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current personalization evaluation focuses narrowly on explicit memory recall, but true personalization requires inferring users' latent preferences from naturally occurring multimodal traces — a significantly harder and underexplored capability.

Method: The authors construct SocialPersona from 171 non-promotional social-media users' longitudinal timelines, containing text, images, timestamps, and 2,597 human-verified preference tags across seven interest domains (separating stable vs. recent interests). Two tasks are defined: (1) constructing structured user profiles from multimodal context, and (2) generating dialogue responses aligned with inferred profiles. Both proprietary and open-weight MLLMs are evaluated.

Result: Models can identify broad interest domains but performance degrades on fine-grained and recent interests, and further drops when inferred profiles must be used to personalize dialogue. Text and images provide complementary preference signals.

Conclusion: Robust cross-modal, long-horizon user modeling remains a key challenge. SocialPersona provides a rigorous testbed for advancing assistants capable of inferring and acting on revealed preferences.

Abstract: Personalized language-model assistants are often evaluated through a memory lens: can a model recall preferences users have explicitly stated in dialogue? More comprehensive personalization demands a harder capability -- inferring what users care about from the multimodal traces they naturally leave behind. We introduce SocialPersona, a benchmark for evaluating whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can recover revealed preferences from longitudinal social-media timelines and use them in dialogue. Built from longitudinal timelines of 171 everyday, non-promotional social-media users, SocialPersona contains text, images, timestamps, and 2,597 human-verified preference tags across seven interest domains, separating stable interests from recent interests. It supports two tasks: constructing structured user profiles from multimodal context and generating responses aligned with inferred profiles. Experiments with proprietary and open-weight MLLMs show that models can identify broad interest domains, yet their performance drops on fine-grained and recent interests and degrades further when inferred profiles must be used to personalize dialogue. Together with evidence that text and images provide complementary preference signals, these results indicate that robust cross-modal, long-horizon user modeling remains a key challenge, and that SocialPersona can help measure and advance progress toward assistants that infer and act on revealed preferences.

</details>


### [18] [Phonetic and semantic analyses of spoken corpora of Beijing and Taiwan Mandarin indicate that the neutral tone is a lexical tone](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26360)
*Yuxin Lu,Zhexuan Li,R. Harald Baayen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A corpus-based study of spontaneous Beijing and Taiwan Mandarin reveals that the neutral tone possesses its own tonal target, exhibits word-specific pitch signatures predictable from contextualized embeddings, and should be reclassified as a lexical tone rather than a toneless or reduced tone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The neutral (floating) tone of Mandarin Chinese has ambiguous phonological status — variably described as reduced, lexically fixed, or toneless. The authors aim to resolve this ambiguity by empirically investigating whether the neutral tone behaves phonetically like the four canonical lexical tones.

Method: Corpus-based phonetic analysis of spontaneous conversational speech from Beijing Mandarin and Taiwan Mandarin corpora, examining pitch contours of disyllabic words with neutral tones, comparing tonal targets, word-specific pitch signatures, and using contextualized embeddings to predict pitch signatures and account for cross-varietal differences.

Result: The neutral tone has its own distinct tonal target. Disyllabic words with neutral tone show pitch contours dependent on the first syllable's tone, mirroring lexical-tone disyllables. Word-specific pitch signatures exist for neutral-tone words and are partially predictable from contextualized embeddings. Cross-varietal differences partly reflect semantic usage differences in the corpora.

Conclusion: The neutral tone is in fact a lexical tone in both Taiwan Mandarin and Beijing Mandarin, supported by its possession of a tonal target, word-specific pitch signatures predictable from embeddings, and parallels with lexical tone behavior.

Abstract: The neutral, or floating, tone of Mandarin Chinese is a tone with an enigmatic set of properties. It has been described as a reduced tone, or as a tone that sometimes is lexically fixed but that can also be toneless. In two-syllable words, it is found only on the second syllable, but single-syllable words can also have the neutral tone. We present a corpus-based study of the phonetic realization of the neutral tone in spontaneous conversational speech corpora of Beijing Mandarin and Taiwan Mandarin. We show that the neutral tone has its own tonal target, just as the four lexical tones of Mandarin. We also show that disyllabic words with a neutral tone have pitch contours that have a pitch component that depends on the tone on the first syllable, just as has been observed for two-syllable words with a lexical tone on the second syllable (Chuang et al., 2026). Furthermore, words with a floating tone have word-specific pitch signatures, which have also been documented for single-syllable words (Jin et al., 2026) as well as two-syllable words (Lu et al., 2026b). These word-specific pitch signatures are shown to be predictable to some extent from words' contextualized embeddings, as previously reported for lexical tones (Chuang et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026b). As there is also considerable variability in the realization of lexical tones, we propose that the neutral tone is, in fact, a lexical tone in both Taiwan Mandarin and Beijing Mandarin. We document both similarities and differences in the realization of the floating tone in these two varieties and provide evidence, using contextualized embeddings, that some of the observed differences may arise from differences in the meanings of the words as used in the two corpora.

</details>


### [19] [ConvMemory v3: A Validity Context Layer for Conversational Memory via Target-Conditioned Relation Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26753)
*Taiheng Pan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ConvMemory v3 introduces a validity context layer that detects outdated/superseded memories via a dual-evidence gate, achieving 90.12% accuracy on synthetic benchmarks and 98.8% transfer accuracy to real data without target labels, while preserving retrieval by default with an opt-in demote mode that boosts current-active H@1 from 45.1% to 95.7%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Retrieved conversational memories can be both relevant and outdated — later turns may update, correct, or supersede earlier ones. Prior ConvMemory versions lack a mechanism to detect this validity decay, motivating a layer that surfaces update evidence without disrupting the existing retrieval pipeline.

Method: ConvMemory v3 adds a validity context layer after the v1/v2 retrieval path. The core is a dual-evidence gate that conditions relation judgments on a specific target proposition: it scores (target, source) pairs via the product of a MiniLM slot head and a DeBERTa-v3 slot head, gated by conservative event/operation evidence. The layer operates in two modes: (1) a default context mode that attaches structured validity metadata while preserving candidate set and rank order, and (2) an explicit opt-in query-conditioned demote mode for dense current-state workloads. Training uses synthetic pairs exclusively, with a real-data feedback loop mining failure patterns. The system enforces six machine-verifiable safety contracts. Multi-hop graph propagation is validated, but fully automatic strict prerequisite edge construction is characterized as a boundary due to counterfactual world knowledge requirements.

Result: The dual-evidence gate achieves 90.12% ± 1.73 accuracy on a synthetic multi-hop validity benchmark. Through real-data feedback (trained only on synthetic pairs), the verifier transfers to Memora role binding with zero target-side labels, reaching 98.8% ± 0.9 group-all-correct. The demote mode raises current-active H@1 from 45.1% (never-demote baseline) to 95.7% ± 1.2, while protecting non-superseded memories at 99.4% recall.

Conclusion: A validity context layer can be effectively retrofitted onto an existing conversational memory retrieval system. Synthetic-only training with real-data feedback loops enables strong zero-shot transfer. Default-preserving architecture design (context mode as default, demote as opt-in) balances safety with utility. Multi-hop propagation is validated, but strict prerequisite edge construction remains an open boundary requiring counterfactual reasoning.

Abstract: Conversational memory retrieval optimizes relevance, yet a retrieved memory can be relevant and simultaneously outdated: a later turn updates, corrects, or supersedes it. ConvMemory v3 adds a validity context layer that detects and surfaces this update evidence through target-conditioned relation verification, sitting after the v1/v2 retrieval path. The core mechanism is a dual-evidence gate that conditions a relation judgment on the specific target proposition, scoring a (target, source) pair through the product of a MiniLM slot head and a DeBERTa-v3 slot head and gating it by conservative event/operation evidence. On a synthetic multi-hop validity benchmark the gate reaches 90.12% +/- 1.73 accuracy; through a real-data feedback loop that mines failure patterns but trains on synthetic pairs only, the verifier transfers to Memora role binding with zero target-side labels, reaching 98.8% +/- 0.9 group-all-correct. The deployed layer preserves retrieval by default: a context mode attaches structured validity metadata while keeping the candidate set and rank order fixed, and a query-conditioned demote mode is an explicit opt-in for dense current-state workloads, where it raises current-active H@1 from a never-demote baseline of 45.1% to 95.7% +/- 1.2 while protecting non-superseded memories at 99.4% recall. Six machine-verifiable safety contracts pin the layer's behavior. Multi-hop graph propagation is validated as a mechanism; fully automatic construction of strict prerequisite edges is characterized as a boundary, since strict necessity requires counterfactual world knowledge. This report extends ConvMemory v1 (arXiv:2605.28062) and v2 (arXiv:2606.10842).

</details>


### [20] [Charting the Growth of Social-Physical HRI (spHRI): A Systematic Review Pipeline Augmented by Small Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26382)
*Mayumi Mohan,Ju-Hung Chen,Alexis E. Block*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Small language models (SLMs <1.5B parameters), while not matching human reviewer accuracy, can substantially augment systematic literature screening by identifying missed papers and operating orders of magnitude faster locally, making large-scale reviews more accessible.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The field of social-physical human-robot interaction (spHRI) suffers from fragmented terminology and inconsistent methodologies, hindering systematic synthesis. Scalable review practices are needed, prompting investigation into whether SLMs can assist with title and abstract screening for large-scale systematic reviews.

Method: The authors evaluated the performance of small language models (SLMs with <1.5B parameters) on title and abstract screening for a large spHRI systematic review. They compared SLM performance against human reviewers and tested an SLM ensemble approach to identify papers for inclusion.

Result: No individual SLM matched human reviewer performance. However, SLMs operated locally and screened papers orders of magnitude faster than humans. The combined SLM ensemble identified 39 papers that human reviewers missed, representing 10.29% of the final relevant dataset.

Conclusion: SLMs can augment, not replace, expert reviewers in systematic literature reviews, making large-scale screening more accessible, sustainable, and effective by catching papers humans may overlook.

Abstract: Social-physical human-robot interaction (spHRI) has grown rapidly across robotics, human-computer interaction, human-robot interaction, and haptics. Yet, fragmented terminology and inconsistent methodologies make systematic synthesis difficult. To support scalable review practices, we evaluated the extent to which small language models (SLMs; < 1.5B parameters) can assist with title and abstract screening for a large spHRI systematic review. While no SLMs matched human reviewers' performance, the models operated locally and screened papers orders of magnitude faster. The combined SLM ensemble identified 39 papers reviewers missed, representing 10.29% of the final relevant dataset. These results demonstrate that SLMs can augment, rather than replace, expert reviewers and make large-scale literature reviews accessible and sustainable.

</details>


### [21] [From Vajrayana Tara to Bengali Baul: A Computational Study of Lexical Transmission Across Buddhist, Shakta, and Vaishnava Traditions in Bengal](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26803)
*Joy Bose*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A computational corpus study of 75 Bengali and Sanskrit devotional texts (8th–19th c.) using TF-IDF character n-gram vectorization and cosine similarity demonstrates that Buddhist Vajrayana vocabulary was absorbed into the Shakta Tantra tradition post-Pāla collapse, with strong specificity (Gitagovinda: 0.0 similarity to Shakta Kali vs. Bridge Tara texts: 0.54), providing the first quantitative evidence for Buddhist-Shakta syncretism in Bengal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To empirically test the long-standing but previously unquantified historical claim that Buddhist Vajrayana vocabulary survived the collapse of the Pāla monasteries and was absorbed into Bengal's Shakta Tantra tradition, using computational text analysis across eight tradition layers.

Method: A corpus of 75 texts spanning eight tradition layers (Buddhist Vajrayana, Shakta Tantra, Vaishnava, Baul) from the 8th–19th centuries was vectorized using TF-IDF on character n-grams, with inter-text relationships measured via cosine similarity. Vocabulary transmission chains were assessed by comparing similarity scores across traditions, languages, and centuries, including a key controlled contrast between two 12th-century Sanskrit texts.

Result: The Gitagovinda (Vaishnava Sanskrit) has zero cosine similarity to Shakta Kali texts, while Bridge Tara texts (Buddhist-Shakta transitional) score 0.54 — an 8.5-fold contrast demonstrating specificity to the Buddhist-Shakta chain. Three Brihannilatantra Tara texts show Shakta-to-Buddhist vocabulary ratios of 2.0–4.0. Ramprasad Sen's 18th-century Bengali Kali songs contain 56 occurrences of "Tara" alongside 103 of "Kali." The Vaishnava-to-Baul chain (similarity 0.29) parallels but is slightly weaker than the Buddhist Sahajiya-to-Baul chain via Charyapada (0.31).

Conclusion: The study provides first quantitative, multi-tradition corroboration that Buddhist-Shakta vocabulary syncretism in Bengal is a specific historical transmission phenomenon, not a generic property of Sanskrit devotional literature, validated through controlled comparisons and measurable lexical transition ratios.

Abstract: We present a computational corpus study of vocabulary relationships across eight tradition layers of Bengali and Sanskrit devotional literature spanning the 8th to 19th centuries, encompassing Buddhist Vajrayana, Shakta Tantra, Vaishnava, and Baul traditions. Using a corpus of 75 texts and TF-IDF character n-gram vectorization with cosine similarity analysis, we address the historically argued but previously unquantified claim that Buddhist Vajrayana vocabulary survived the collapse of the Pala monasteries and was absorbed into the Shakta Tantra tradition of Bengal. The central finding is a specificity result: the Gitagovinda (Vaishnava Sanskrit, 12th century) has zero cosine similarity to Shakta Kali texts, while Bridge Tara texts (Buddhist-Shakta transitional, same century, same language) have cosine similarity 0.54 to Shakta Kali. This 8.5-fold contrast between two Sanskrit traditions from the same century demonstrates that the Buddhist-Shakta vocabulary overlap is not a generic property of Sanskrit devotional literature but is specific to the Buddhist-Shakta transmission chain. Three Brihannilatantra Tara texts show Shakta-to-Buddhist vocabulary ratios of 2.0 to 4.0, constituting measurable evidence of lexical transition within that chain. Ramprasad Sen's 18th-century Bengali Kali songs preserve Buddhist vocabulary residue including 56 occurrences of Tara alongside 103 occurrences of Kali. The Vaishnava Bengali tradition contributes a parallel chain to modern Baul vocabulary (similarity 0.29), slightly weaker than the Buddhist Sahajiya chain via Charyapada (0.31). These results provide the first quantitative multi-tradition corroboration of historically argued Buddhist-Shakta syncretism in Bengal.

</details>


### [22] [ProfileFoundry: A Synthetic Person-Object Substrate for Privacy, Memory, and Tool-Use Evaluation in LLM Agent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26403)
*Sriram Selvam,Anneswa Ghosh*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PROFILEFOUNDRY is a deterministic synthetic data generator releasing 100,000 adult Person Objects with rich relational and temporal structure, designed as a responsible, inspectable source layer for foundation-model evaluations involving memory, privacy, document understanding, and agent state.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Foundation-model research requires realistic personal data (user state, histories, relationships, documents) for controlled evaluation, but real user data poses sharing, privacy, and audit challenges. Independently generated fake data lacks the cross-field and temporal consistency needed for meaningful benchmarks. A responsible, consistent synthetic source is needed.

Method: PROFILEFOUNDRY is a deterministic generator producing 100,000 synthetic adult Person Objects across eight locales. Each object includes a typed current snapshot, household/family/employer links, snapshot-aligned events, normalized relational views, and generation provenance. The release comprises 709,228 events, 40,338 households, 52,491 employers, and 518,564 directed relationship edges. Evaluation uses population-marginal comparisons, per-object invariant checks, referential and temporal closure tests, and coincidence/provenance screens.

Result: The release successfully generates a large-scale, internally consistent synthetic population with verifiable cross-field and temporal integrity. Evidence is reported across four categories: population-marginal alignment, per-object invariants, release-wide referential/temporal closure, and provenance traceability. The output is not a population-fidelity model, a rendered-text corpus, or a formal privacy mechanism.

Conclusion: PROFILEFOUNDRY fills a gap between real (hard-to-share) and naive synthetic (inconsistent) data by providing a deterministic, inspectable, and relationally coherent synthetic source. It enables responsible construction of foundation-model evaluations while maintaining transparency about each synthetic person's provenance.

Abstract: Foundation-model research increasingly needs data about people: user state, personal histories, relationships, contact-like fields, documents, and longitudinal updates. Real user data is difficult to share, perturb, audit, or redistribute responsibly, while independently generated fake fields rarely preserve the cross-field and temporal consistency needed for controlled evaluation. We present PROFILEFOUNDRY, a deterministic generator and fixed reference release of 100,000 adult synthetic Person Objects across eight locales. Each object combines a typed current snapshot, household, family, and employer links, snapshot-aligned events, normalized relational views, and generation provenance. The release contains 709,228 events, 40,338 households, 52,491 employers, and 518,564 directed relationship edges. We report evidence in separate categories: selected population-marginal comparisons, per-object invariant checks, release-wide referential and temporal closure, and coincidence/provenance screens. PROFILEFOUNDRY is not a population-fidelity model, a rendered-text corpus, or a formal privacy mechanism. Instead, it is a responsible synthetic source layer for constructing downstream foundation-model evaluations involving memory, privacy, document understanding, record linkage, and agent state while keeping the synthetic person behind each artifact inspectable

</details>


### [23] [ConflictScore: Identifying and Measuring How Language Models Handle Conflicting Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26437)
*Siyi Liu,Aaron Halfaker,Dan Roth,Patrick Xia*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ConflictScore is a new metric that evaluates whether a model's response acknowledges conflicting evidence in grounding documents, decomposing answers into atomic claims and measuring both the proportion of conflicting claims (CS-C) and the balance of supporting vs. contradicting evidence (CS-R). The authors also introduce ConflictBench for systematic evaluation and demonstrate ConflictScore's utility in improving TruthfulQA performance via corrective feedback.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing factuality and faithfulness metrics only assess whether an answer is supported or contradicted by grounding documents, but fail to capture scenarios where both supporting and contradicting evidence coexist. This gap means models can produce overconfident, one-sided answers even when evidence is ambiguous or mixed.
