Method: The ConflictScore framework works in three stages: (1) decompose responses into atomic claims, (2) label each claim against each grounding document as supporting, contradicting, or neutral, and (3) aggregate labels into two metrics — ConflictScore-Count (CS-C), the proportion of claims exhibiting conflicts, and ConflictScore-Ratio (CS-R), which measures the balance between supporting and contradicting evidence. The authors also construct ConflictBench, a benchmark spanning ambiguity, contradiction, and divergent opinion conflicts.

Result: Experiments demonstrate that ConflictScore effectively detects overconfident claims across diverse domains. Furthermore, ConflictScore can be used as a corrective feedback mechanism that improves truthfulness on the TruthfulQA benchmark.

Conclusion: ConflictScore fills a critical gap in evaluation by quantifying a model's ability to acknowledge conflicting evidence, moving beyond binary supported/contradicted judgments. It serves both as a diagnostic metric and as actionable feedback for improving model truthfulness.

Abstract: Existing metrics for factuality and faithfulness evaluate whether an answer is supported or contradicted by its grounding documents, but they fail to capture when both supporting and contradicting evidence coexist. We introduce ConflictScore, a novel metric that quantifies how well a model's response acknowledges conflicting evidence in its grounding documents. Our framework decomposes responses into atomic claims, labels each claim against each grounding document, and then aggregates these labels into two complementary measures: ConflictScore-Count (CS-C), the proportion of claims exhibiting conflicts, and ConflictScore-Ratio (CS-R), the balance between supporting and contradicting evidence. We develop ConflictBench, a benchmark covering diverse forms of conflicts such as ambiguity, contradiction, and divergent opinions, to systematically evaluate our metric. Experiments show that ConflictScore effectively detects overconfident claims across domains and can serve as a corrective feedback mechanism that improves truthfulness on TruthfulQA.

</details>


### [24] [AnySimLite: A Lightweight Few-Shot Similarity Encoder for On-Device Speech-Adjacent Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26452)
*Sourav Ghosh,Yash Bhatia,Keshav Goyal,Sahil Singh Bagri,Mohamed Akram Ulla Shariff,Saravana Balaji Shanmugam*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: AnySimLite is a lightweight similarity encoder using word- and character-level channels that solves multiple speech-adjacent classification tasks via text similarity, achieving SOTA-competitive few-shot performance with under 1/250th the size of a 7B-parameter LLM baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deploying multiple specialized on-device models for natural language classification on edge devices creates memory footprint challenges. The authors investigate whether a single lightweight architecture can handle multiple speech-adjacent classification tasks by reformulating them as text similarity problems.

Method: AnySimLite is a lightweight similarity encoder combining word-level and character-level channels. It is paired with a dataset transformation strategy that reduces diverse speech-adjacent classification tasks to a nuanced text similarity formulation, enabling a single model to serve multiple tasks.

Result: AnySimLite achieves SOTA or SOTA-competitive performance in few-shot settings across multiple speech-adjacent classification tasks. In the worst case, performance drops below 7% while using less than 1/250th the model size of the qLLaMA_LoRA-7B baseline.

Conclusion: A single lightweight similarity encoder can effectively replace multiple specialized models for speech-adjacent NLP tasks, offering a practical memory-efficient solution for on-device deployment with minimal accuracy trade-offs.

Abstract: To minimize privacy concerns and inference latency on edge devices like smartphones, lightweight on-device models remain important for end-user applications. Many of these applications involve natural language classification, but deploying multiple specialized models creates a memory footprint challenge. We investigate: Can a single lightweight architecture solve multiple Speech-Adjacent (SA) classification tasks through reduction to a nuanced text similarity formulation? We propose AnySimLite, a lightweight similarity encoder that combines word-level and character-level channels. Together with a dataset transformation strategy, we evaluate AnySimLite across multiple SA classification tasks and show that it consistently achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) or SOTA-competitive performance in few-shot settings while maintaining a low memory footprint. Even in the worst case, the performance drop remains below 7% while using $<\frac{1}{250}^{\mathrm{th}}$ of the model size of the SOTA qLLaMA_LoRA-7B baseline.

</details>


### [25] [Soft Token Alignment for Cross-Lingual Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26466)
*Jiayi He,Jungsoo Park,Wei Xu,Alan Ritter*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: SOLAR introduces an auxiliary training objective that aligns soft-token (probability-weighted vocabulary mixture) representations across languages using English as a pivot, improving multilingual reasoning consistency and accuracy, especially for low-resource languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multilingual LLMs produce divergent reasoning across semantically equivalent prompts in different languages because discrete token generation forces language-specific lexical choices. Prior work shows intermediate representations are relatively language-agnostic, but final-layer outputs diverge. The authors seek a cross-lingual alignment signal decoupled from any specific vocabulary item or script.

Method: SOLAR is an auxiliary supervised fine-tuning objective that aligns soft-token representations cross-lingually. Soft tokens are defined as probability-weighted mixtures over vocabulary embeddings, producing continuous representations that aggregate semantically related tokens across languages. Using English as a pivot, each non-English soft-token summary is aligned to its English counterpart in the shared embedding space.

Result: Across four multilingual reasoning benchmarks, SOLAR achieves up to +17.7 accuracy points over the base model and +3.8 over standard supervised fine-tuning, with the largest gains on low-resource languages. It also increases final-layer cross-lingual similarity and substantially reduces language-cluster separability.

Conclusion: Aligning soft-token representations during fine-tuning preserves shared semantic structure across languages, mitigating reasoning divergence and improving multilingual performance, particularly benefiting low-resource languages.

Abstract: Multilingual large language models often produce inconsistent reasoning and answers for semantically equivalent prompts in different languages. Prior work suggests that intermediate representations can be relatively language-agnostic, but generation becomes increasingly language-specific as models commit to discrete output tokens. This is problematic because language-specific lexical choices can cause semantically equivalent reasoning paths to diverge across languages. These divergences motivate searching for a cross-lingual alignment signal that is less tied to any single vocabulary item or script. We propose SOLAR, an auxiliary objective for supervised fine-tuning that aligns soft-token representations across languages, using English as a pivot. Soft tokens are probability-weighted mixtures over the vocabulary embeddings, yielding continuous representations that can aggregate information from semantically related tokens across languages. We then align each non-English soft-token summary to its English counterpart in the shared embedding space. Across four multilingual reasoning benchmarks, SOLAR improves accuracy by up to +17.7 points over the base model and +3.8 over standard supervised fine-tuning, with the largest gains on low-resource languages. SOLAR also strengthens final-layer cross-lingual similarity and substantially reduces language-cluster separability, suggesting that aligning soft-token representations helps preserve shared semantic structure during multilingual reasoning.

</details>


### [26] [Agent Capsules: Quality-Gated Granularity Control for Multi-Agent LLM Pipelines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.00410)
*Aninda Ray*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Agent Capsules is an adaptive runtime that optimizes multi-agent LLM pipelines by selectively merging agent calls when quality constraints allow, using a three-tier escalation ladder with quality-gated mode switching. It achieves 42-68% token savings while maintaining or improving output quality, without per-model configuration or per-pipeline engineering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-agent pipelines issue N LLM calls per run, incurring high token costs. Merging agents into fewer calls ("compound execution") can save tokens, but naive merging degrades quality through tool loss and prompt compression artifacts. The core insight: injecting more context into merged calls worsens compression rather than relieving it, so quality recovery requires moving back toward per-agent dispatch rather than rewriting merged prompts.

Method: Agent Capsules frames multi-agent execution as a constrained optimization problem. The runtime: (1) instruments coordination overhead per agent group, (2) scores composition opportunity, (3) selects among three compound execution strategies (standard compound, two-phase, sequential), and (4) gates every mode switch on rolling-mean output quality. The escalation ladder recovers quality by reverting toward per-agent dispatch when compound execution fails quality thresholds. The framework also delivers pre-compound efficiencies via automatic policy resolution, cache-aligned prompts, and topology-aware context injection.

Result: Against a 14-agent LangGraph competitive intelligence pipeline: 51% fewer fine-mode input tokens, 42% fewer compound-mode input tokens, with +0.020 and +0.017 quality respectively. Against a 5-agent DSPy due diligence pipeline: 19% fewer tokens than uncompiled DSPy at quality parity, 68% fewer tokens than MIPROv2 at +0.052 quality. The controller matched a hand-tuned oracle on every measured (model, group, mode) cell without per-model configuration.

Conclusion: Compound execution is viable and efficient when gated by empirical quality constraints with an escalation ladder. The negative result — that adding context to merged calls worsens compression — is critical, as it justifies the ladder approach over prompt engineering. The framework generalizes across models and pipelines without training data, making adaptive multi-agent execution practical.

Abstract: A multi-agent pipeline with N agents typically issues N LLM calls per run. Merging agents into fewer calls (compound execution) promises token savings, but naively merged calls silently degrade quality through tool loss and prompt compression. We present Agent Capsules, an adaptive execution runtime that treats multi-agent pipeline execution as an optimization problem with empirical quality constraints. The runtime instruments coordination overhead per group, scores composition opportunity, selects among three compound execution strategies, and gates every mode switch on rolling-mean output quality. A controlled negative result confirms that injecting more context into a merged call worsens compression rather than relieving it, so the framework's escalation ladder (standard, then two-phase, then sequential) recovers quality by moving toward per-agent dispatch rather than by rewriting merged prompts. On LLM-judged quality, the controller matches a hand-tuned oracle on every measured (model, group, mode) cell: routing compound whenever the oracle would, and reverting to fine whenever quality would fail the floor, without per-model configuration. Against a hand-crafted LangGraph implementation of a 14-agent competitive intelligence pipeline, Agent Capsules uses 51% fewer fine-mode input tokens and 42% fewer compound-mode input tokens, at +0.020 and +0.017 quality respectively. Against a DSPy implementation of a 5-agent due diligence pipeline, the framework uses 19% fewer tokens than uncompiled DSPy at quality parity, and 68% fewer tokens than MIPROv2 at +0.052 quality. Even before compound mode fires, the runtime delivers efficiency through automatic policy resolution, cache-aligned prompts, and topology-aware context injection, matching both hand-tuned and compile-time baselines without training data or per-pipeline engineering.

</details>


### [27] [Speaking Numbers to LLMs: Multi-Wavelet Number Embeddings for Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26487)
*Defu Cao,Zijie Lei,Muyan Weng,Jiao Sun,Yan Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: TempoWave proposes a plug-and-play temporal wavelet digit interface that maps scalar time series values into multi-wavelet, multi-scale digit-wise embeddings, enabling LLMs to better handle continuous numerical data for context-aware forecasting while preserving numerical ordering and precision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are attractive for context-aware time series forecasting due to their ability to integrate heterogeneous textual signals, but their discrete, language-oriented tokenization and embedding interfaces are fundamentally misaligned with continuous numerical values. This misalignment harms numerical ordering, forecasting reliability, and precision. Existing numeric tokenization approaches fail to adequately capture both fine-grained local fluctuations and macro-level global structures in time series data.

Method: TempoWave introduces a temporal wavelet digit interface that: (1) maps each scalar observation into digit-wise embeddings using multi-wavelet, multi-scale coefficients; (2) directly overrides standard token representations in a transformer-compatible form; (3) preserves precise numerical formatting, distinct digit identity, and robustness to common normalization operations throughout the LLM pipeline; and (4) operates as a plug-and-play module requiring no architectural changes to the underlying LLM.

Result: Experiments across five context-enriched forecasting benchmarks show that TempoWave consistently improves LLM-based forecasters over standard numeric tokenization and alternative embedding interfaces, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

Conclusion: The numeric interface is a critical bottleneck in LLM-based time series forecasting. Principled multi-resolution embeddings, such as TempoWave's wavelet-based approach, can better couple LLMs' contextual reasoning capabilities with precise numerical forecasting, offering a promising direction for future research.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are attractive for context-aware time series forecasting because they can integrate heterogeneous textual signals, yet their discrete, language-oriented tokenization and embedding interfaces are misaligned with continuous numerical values, often harming numerical ordering and forecasting reliability. We propose TempoWave, a plug-and-play temporal wavelet digit interface that maps each scalar observation into digit-wise embeddings constructed from multi-wavelet, multi-scale coefficients. By directly overriding standard token representations, TempoWave seamlessly exposes both fine-grained local fluctuations and macro global structures in a transformer-compatible form, ensuring that precise numerical formatting, distinct digit identity, and robustness to common normalization operations are maintained throughout the LLM pipeline. Experiments across five context-enriched forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that TempoWave consistently improves LLM-based forecasters over standard numeric tokenization and alternative embedding interfaces, achieving a new state-of-the-art. These results highlight the numeric interface as a key bottleneck and suggest that principled multi-resolution embeddings can better couple LLMs' contextual reasoning with precise forecasting. Our code is available at https://github.com/DC-research/TempoWAVE and our model can be accessed at https://huggingface.co/Melady/TempoWAVE.

</details>


### [28] [Comparing BERT Sentence-Pair Classification and Few-Shot LLM Prompting for Detecting Threat and Solution Framing in German Climate News](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26489)
*Raven Adam,David Maier,Marie Kogler*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Comparison of few-shot LLM prompting (Llama 4 Maverick) vs. fine-tuned German BERT (gbert-large) for sentence-level classification of threat and solution framing in German-language climate news, finding BERT outperforms LLM (F1 0.83 vs 0.78), with context from preceding sentences significantly boosting BERT performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: News media shape public perceptions of climate change, and threat vs. solution framing affects audience engagement and policy support. Manual coding of framing patterns at scale is infeasible, motivating automated sentence-level classification to enable large-corpus analysis in computational social science.

Method: Two approaches are systematically compared on 440 manually coded Austrian newspaper articles: (1) few-shot prompting with Llama 4 Maverick using chain-of-thought reasoning and structured confidence-scored output; (2) fine-tuned deepset/gbert-large for sentence-pair classification where the preceding sentence provides context. Both implement two independent binary classifiers (threat vs. solution). An ablation study tests the contribution of preceding-sentence context.

Result: Fine-tuned BERT achieves F1 scores of 0.83 for both threat and solution classification tasks. The LLM-based approach reaches F1 of 0.78. The ablation study confirms that providing preceding-sentence context substantially improves BERT performance over single-sentence input.

Conclusion: Fine-tuned encoder models outperform prompted generative LLMs for this sentence-level framing classification task, and contextual information from adjacent sentences is critical for accurate frame detection. The work contributes to the broader comparison of these two paradigms for text classification in computational social science.

Abstract: News media play a central role in shaping public perceptions of climate change, and whether coverage emphasizes threats or solutions has measurable effects on audience engagement and policy support. Automated detection of these framing patterns at the sentence level would allow researchers to analyze large corpora that are infeasible to code manually. We present a systematic comparison of two approaches for classifying sentences from German-language climate news articles as threat-oriented, solution-oriented, both, or neither. The first approach uses few-shot prompting with an open-weights large language model (Llama 4 Maverick), employing chain-of-thought reasoning and structured output with confidence scoring. The second approach fine-tunes a German BERT model (deepset/gbert-large) for sentence-pair classification, where the preceding sentence provides contextual information for the target sentence. Both approaches implement two independent binary classifiers, one for threat framing and one for solution framing. We evaluate both methods on a corpus of 440 Austrian newspaper articles that were manually coded following a detailed coding scheme developed with domain experts. The fine-tuned BERT classifiers achieve an F1 score of 0.83 for both the threat and solution tasks, while the LLM-based classifiers reach an F1 of 0.78. An ablation study confirms that providing the preceding sentence as context improves BERT classification performance substantially compared to single-sentence input. These results contribute to the growing body of work comparing fine-tuned encoder models with prompted generative models for text classification in computational social science.

</details>


### [29] [Nemotron-TwoTower: Diffusion Language Modeling with Pretrained Autoregressive Context](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26493)
*Fitsum Reda,John Kamalu,Roger Waleffe,Mostofa Patwary,Mohammad Shoeybi,Bryan Catanzaro*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: TwoTower decouples diffusion language models into a frozen AR context tower and a trainable diffusion denoiser tower, achieving 2.42× generation throughput while retaining 98.7% of baseline quality on a 30B MoE model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing diffusion language models use a single network for both context representation and iterative denoising, which forces one model to handle both tasks and limits capacity for either. This motivates decoupling these roles to improve efficiency while maintaining generation quality.

Method: TwoTower separates generation into two components: (1) a frozen autoregressive (AR) context tower based on Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B (a 30B hybrid Mamba-Transformer Mixture-of-Experts model) that causally processes clean tokens to produce context representations; (2) a trainable diffusion denoiser tower with bidirectional block attention that refines noisy blocks via cross-attention to the frozen context. Training uses block-wise autoregressive diffusion on approximately 2.1T tokens.

Result: Nemotron-TwoTower retains 98.7% of the autoregressive baseline's generation quality while achieving 2.42× higher wall-clock generation throughput. Code and model weights are publicly released.

Conclusion: Decoupling context representation and denoising into separate towers enables significant throughput gains with minimal quality degradation, demonstrating that diffusion language models can be made practical for large-scale deployment without sacrificing the benefits of autoregressive quality.

Abstract: Diffusion language models offer a promising alternative to autoregressive models due to their potential for parallel and iterative generation. However, existing approaches use a single network for both context representation and iterative denoising, forcing one model to serve both roles and limiting its capacity for either role. We propose TwoTower, a block-wise autoregressive diffusion model that decouples these roles into two towers: a frozen AR context tower that causally processes clean tokens, and a trainable diffusion denoiser tower with bidirectional block attention that refines noisy blocks via cross-attention to the context. Built on Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B, an open-weight 30B hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE model, and trained on approximately 2.1T tokens, Nemotron-TwoTower retains 98.7% of the autoregressive baseline's quality while offering 2.42X higher wall-clock generation throughput. We release the code and model weights at https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/nemotron-twotower.

</details>


### [30] [Temporal Validity in Retrieval Memory: Eliminating Stale-Fact Errors for AI Agents over Evolving Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26511)
*Neeraj Yadav*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) fails at handling evolving knowledge because cosine similarity cannot distinguish contradicted (stale) facts from duplicated ones. MemStrata introduces a bi-temporal ledger with a deterministic supersession rule that retires stale facts without LLM calls, achieving near-perfect accuracy on evolving knowledge and eliminating stale-fact errors, while matching RAG on static knowledge and maintaining fast retrieval latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RAG systems lack a model of time, so when facts change (e.g., renamed functions, restructured APIs), semantically similar stale and current values coexist in the retrieval corpus. Cosine similarity fails to discriminate between contradicted and duplicated facts (AUROC 0.59, near chance), causing agents to serve superseded information or abstain. This is a structural limitation that cannot be resolved by better embeddings alone.

Method: MemStrata stores facts in a bi-temporal ledger where each fact is a (subject, relation, object) triple. When a new fact contradicts an existing one (same subject and relation, different object), a deterministic supersession rule automatically retires the stale value — no similarity threshold and no LLM call required. Static recall is preserved by retaining non-contradicted facts. The system uses a 7B model for evaluation across six benchmarks.

Result: MemStrata ties RAG on static knowledge benchmarks. On evolving knowledge tasks, it achieves 0.95–1.00 accuracy versus RAG's 0.20–0.47. The stale-fact-error rate drops from 15–40% (RAG) to approximately 0%. Retrieval latency is ~2.1s for MemStrata versus ~16–18s for LLM-reranking baselines.

Conclusion: MemStrata demonstrates that a deterministic temporal ledger with supersession rules effectively solves the stale-fact problem in RAG, eliminating a failure class that embedding-based retrieval cannot address. The approach is both more accurate and more efficient than LLM-reranking alternatives for knowledge evolution scenarios.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) gives agents access to accumulated knowledge, but has no model of time. When a fact changes (e.g., a function is renamed or API restructured), RAG retrieves both the stale and current value with near-identical embedding similarity. The agent then either abstains or serves the superseded fact. We show this is a structural problem: on a calibrated dataset, cosine similarity distinguishes a contradicted fact from a duplicated one with AUROC 0.59 (near chance), as contradictions are often more embedding-similar to the original than rephrased duplicates.
  We present MemStrata, a retrieval memory maintaining temporal validity. It stores facts like RAG, preserving static recall, but when a fact's value is contradicted, a deterministic (subject, relation, object) supersession rule retires the stale value in a bi-temporal ledger - with no similarity threshold and no LLM call. Across six benchmarks run locally with a 7B model, MemStrata ties RAG on static knowledge and reaches 0.95-1.00 accuracy on evolving knowledge (where RAG reaches 0.20-0.47). The central result is the stale-fact-error rate: when required to answer, RAG serves superseded values 15-40% of the time; MemStrata drives this to ~0%, a failure class RAG cannot avoid. MemStrata achieves this at retrieval latency (~2.1s) versus ~16-18s for LLM-reranking baselines. We release the harness, datasets, and a marker-free evaluation protocol for memory under knowledge evolution.

</details>


### [31] [Assessing Post-Reform Changes in Risk Disclosure Quality with a Multidimensional Text Analysis Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26522)
*Nobuhiro Aikawa,Mitsuo Yoshida*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper proposes a longitudinal text analysis framework combining Japanese NLP metrics with paired testing, shift functions, and inter-metric correlations to evaluate qualitative changes in corporate narratives. Applied to Japan's 2019 disclosure reforms across 19,770 firm-year observations (FY2015–2024), the approach reveals that increased disclosure volume came at the cost of reduced readability, and while information structure improved, specific descriptive quality stagnated, with uneven adaptation across market segments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Corporate narrative disclosures are inherently multidimensional — improvements in one textual dimension often coincide with changes in others. Conventional single-indicator methods mask these complex, joint dynamics, making comprehensive evaluation of qualitative changes over time (e.g., post-regulatory reforms) difficult.

Method: The authors propose a longitudinal text analysis framework that combines: (1) Japanese-language NLP metric extraction, (2) paired testing, (3) shift function analysis, and (4) inter-metric correlation analysis. They extend prior indicator sets with a novel cross-section relevance indicator measuring topical alignment between risk disclosures and management strategies. The framework is applied to 19,770 firm-year observations spanning FY2015–FY2024 to evaluate Japan's 2019 disclosure reforms.

Result: The joint analysis reveals complex disclosure pattern shifts masked by conventional methods: (1) disclosure volume increased substantially but readability declined; (2) overall information structure improved, yet specific descriptive quality stagnated; (3) the degree of adaptation varied significantly across market segments.

Conclusion: Evaluating narrative disclosure reforms requires a multidimensional, joint-analysis approach rather than single-indicator methods. Japan's 2019 reforms produced mixed outcomes — gains in volume and structure were offset by losses in readability and stagnant descriptive quality, with heterogeneous effects across market segments — underscoring the importance of the proposed framework for policy evaluation.

Abstract: While corporate narrative disclosures provide crucial information to capital markets, comprehensively evaluating their qualitative changes over time remains challenging. Narrative text is inherently multidimensional, meaning that an improvement in one textual dimension often occurs alongside changes in others. To capture these underlying dynamics, we propose a longitudinal text analysis approach combining Japanese-language NLP metric extraction with paired testing, shift function analysis, and inter-metric correlation. Our framework extends prior indicator sets by incorporating a cross-section relevance indicator to measure topical alignment between risk disclosures and management strategies. Applying this approach to evaluate Japan's 2019 disclosure reforms, we analyze 19,770 firm-year observations over a 10-year period (FY2015-FY2024). The joint analysis reveals complex shifts in disclosure patterns that are frequently masked by conventional single-indicator methods. Specifically, we find that while disclosure volume increased substantially, it was accompanied by a decline in readability. Furthermore, although the overall information structure improved, specific descriptive quality stagnated, and the degree of adaptation varied across market segments.

</details>


### [32] [The Inattentional Gap: Task-Conditioned Language and Vision Models Omit the Safety-Critical Signals They Can Otherwise Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26529)
*Kwan Soo Shin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Models conditioned on a narrow task suppress reporting of co-present but unspecified safety-critical signals—a phenomenon the authors term the "Inattentional Gap." This occurs across language and vision models regardless of scale, persists in reasoning models, and decouples benchmark safety from real-world safety.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI safety evaluation typically measures how well a model detects specified hazards, but real-world accidents often stem from hazards that were never specified. The authors investigate whether task-conditioning causes models to overlook co-present safety-critical signals they could otherwise detect, drawing a parallel to human inattentional blindness.

Method: The authors designed experiments across radiology and driving text scenarios, as well as chest-radiograph vision tasks. They compared model performance in reporting safety-critical signals when constrained to a narrow task versus when unconstrained, testing multiple model families, scales, and a reasoning model to measure the suppression effect.

Result: Suppression appeared in every model tested, did not diminish with increasing model scale, persisted even in a reasoning model, and varied more by model family than by size. Unconstrained models reported the same safety-critical signals at substantially higher rates.

Conclusion: The Inattentional Gap decouples measured benchmark safety from real-world safety: a system can achieve near-perfect scores on specified hazard evaluations while remaining blind to unspecified hazards that cause actual harm.

Abstract: AI safety is evaluated by how reliably a model detects the hazards it is told to find, yet accidents often arise from the hazard no one specified. We show that conditioning a language or vision model on a narrow task suppresses its reporting of co-present, safety-critical signals it can otherwise report, a machine analogue of human inattentional blindness arising from a different mechanism. Across radiology and driving text scenarios and chest-radiograph vision tasks, suppression appeared in every model tested, did not diminish with scale, persisted in a reasoning model, and varied more by model family than by size, while the same models reported these signals at substantially higher rates when unconstrained. We name this dissociation the Inattentional Gap and argue that it decouples measured benchmark safety from real-world safety: a system can score near-perfectly on the hazards an evaluation specifies while remaining blind to those that cause harm.

</details>


### [33] [\textsc{DiARC}: Distinguishing Positive and Negative Samples Helps Improving ARC-like Reasoning Ability of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26530)
*Yuxuan Yang,Feiyang Li,Yile Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: DiARC introduces preference alignment for ARC-like reasoning tasks by constructing negative samples (via visual transformations, DSL rule inversion, and rule editing) to help models distinguish correct from near-miss solutions, consistently improving performance over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current open-source LLM approaches for ARC tasks yield unsatisfactory results, while closed-source methods are too costly. Existing efforts focus on positive-sample supervised fine-tuning but overlook the value of learning from negative samples to improve reasoning discrimination.

Method: DiARC applies preference alignment by constructing preference pairs with negative samples, using three strategies: (1) output-level visual transformations, (2) DSL-level rule inversion, and (3) task-specific rule editing. These generate near-miss alternatives while preserving the original input demonstrations.

Result: Experimental results across multiple ARC-like benchmarks demonstrate that DiARC consistently improves performance over baseline models.

Conclusion: Solving ARC-like problems benefits from both positive supervision and the ability to distinguish negative samples; preference alignment with carefully constructed negative samples is an effective and consistent method for improving model reasoning on such tasks.

Abstract: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC;~\citealp{chollet2019measure}) contains tasks that require summarizing patterns from limited grid samples and predicting output grids. Recently, many large language model based approaches have attempted to transform it into a text-based reasoning task. However, methods based on open-source models have generally yielded unsatisfactory results, while those relying on closed-source models are too costly. Current efforts mainly focus on data augmentation, constructing ARC-like data for more comprehensive supervised fine-tuning. In this work, we argue that solving ARC-like problems requires not only \textit{positive} sample supervision but also the ability to improve model reasoning by distinguishing \textit{negative} samples. To this end, we draw on the idea of preference alignment and propose \textsc{DiARC}, a method that constructs preference pairs to enable the model to distinguish between them. Specifically, we propose three ways to construct negative samples, including output-level visual transformations, DSL-level rule inversion, and task-specific rule editing. The resulting negative samples provide informative near-miss alternatives while keeping the observed demonstrations unchanged. Experimental results across multiple ARC-like benchmarks show that \textsc{DiARC} consistently improves performance over baseline models. The code is released at https://github.com/szu-tera/DiARC.

</details>


### [34] [Erase-then-Delta Attention: Decoupling Erase and Write Addresses in Delta-Rule Linear Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26560)
*Xiao Li,Chengruidong Zhang,Hao Luo,Xi Lin,Zekun Wang,Zihan Qiu,Yunfei Mao,Langshi Chen,Man Yuan,Minmin Sun,Huiqiang Jiang,Siqi Zhang,Rui Men,Wei Hu,Gong Cheng,Bo Zheng,Dayiheng Liu,Jingren Zhou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: EDA extends delta-rule linear attention by adding a decoupled erase step that selectively suppresses stale memory at an independently chosen address before performing the standard corrective write, improving language model performance across dense and MoE architectures up to 128k context lengths.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard delta-rule linear attention only corrects memory at the current write address, leaving stale information at other addresses unaddressed. This limits the memory-management capacity of recurrent models, as outdated content persists passively unless overwritten.

Method: EDA introduces a two-step memory update: (1) a targeted erase step along a learned erase direction at an independently chosen address, followed by (2) the standard delta-rule corrective write. The erase and write addresses are decoupled, and the model learns when and where to erase through a gating mechanism. EDA retains the corrective behavior of delta-rule while adding an active cleanup pathway.

Result: EDA achieves the best performance in language-model pretraining across dense 2.5B and MoE 25B-A2.8B models. Gains persist after 80B-token long-context midtraining on MoE models, with EDA outperforming baselines on long-context evaluations from 4k to 128k tokens. Memory-state probing shows EDA's erase mechanism is most active when passive decay is weak, validating the decoupled cleanup hypothesis.

Conclusion: Recurrent memory models benefit from explicitly deciding not only what to write but also what stale information to erase and where. EDA demonstrates that decoupling erase and write operations enhances memory-management capacity, yielding consistent gains across model scales and context lengths.

Abstract: Delta-rule linear attention improves recurrent memory updates by correcting what is already stored at the current write address before writing new content. However, the active correction is still anchored to that same write address. As a result, stale information stored at a different address cannot be actively removed before new content is written elsewhere. We propose Erase-then-Delta Attention (EDA), a memory update rule that decouples where to erase from where to write. The key insight is that recurrent memory models should not only correct the current write, but also selectively suppress outdated memory at an independently chosen address. Concretely, our method first applies a targeted erase step along a learned erase direction, and then performs the standard delta-style corrective write along the current write direction. This preserves the corrective behavior of delta-rule updates while expanding their memory-management capacity. Language-model pretraining experiments across dense 2.5B and MoE 25B-A2.8B model families show that EDA performs best in both settings. The gain persists after 80B-token long-context midtraining of the MoE models, where EDA also performs best in long-context evaluations from 4k to 128k contexts. A compact update analysis and memory-state probes suggest why: EDA keeps the delta-rule corrective write intact while allocating an additional cleanup path most strongly when passive decay is weak. These results suggest that recurrent memory models should decide not only what to write, but also what stale information to erase and where.

</details>


### [35] [Zero-shot Tweet-Level Stance Detection Enhanced by External Knowledge and Reflective Chain-of-Thought Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26571)
*Yiju Huang,Wenxian Wang,Lijun Zhou,Rui Tang,Xiao Lan,Tao Zhang,Haizhou Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: KIRP is a zero-shot stance detection framework that combines external knowledge graphs with entity reorganization, reflective Chain-of-Thought reasoning, and stance-aware contrastive learning with a three-layer iterative prototype network to address context sparsity, implicit target relevance, and the neutral-vs-irrelevant confusion problem, achieving SOTA on SemEval-2016, WT-WT, and the newly constructed Japanese KIRP-D dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Zero-shot tweet-level stance detection suffers from (1) context sparsity in short texts, (2) difficulty linking implicit targets to textual content, and (3) the inability of current models to reliably distinguish "neutral" from "irrelevant" labels. Existing methods over-rely on external knowledge while ignoring intrinsic semantic cues within key intra-textual entities.

Method: The authors (1) construct KIRP-D, the first Japanese four-class, multi-topic tweet stance detection dataset; (2) propose KIRP, which uses knowledge graphs for entity supplementation and reorganization as data augmentation, reflective Chain-of-Thought reasoning to extract and validate implicit targets, stance-aware contrastive learning for discriminative feature learning, and a three-layer iterative prototype network for fine-grained four-class classification.

Result: KIRP achieves SOTA: 84.05% F1 (three-class) on SemEval-2016, 84.99% F1 (four-class) on WT-WT, and 79.18% F1 (four-class) on KIRP-D.

Conclusion: Integrating external knowledge with intra-textual entity reorganization, reflective CoT reasoning, and prototype-based contrastive learning effectively addresses the key challenges in zero-shot stance detection, particularly the neutral-irrelevant distinction, and extends to multilingual settings including Japanese.

Abstract: Zero-shot tweet-level stance detection confronts two primary challenges: (1) mitigating the context sparsity inherent in short texts, and (2) establishing the relevance between implicit targets and textual content. While existing methods primarily focus on incorporating external knowledge, they neglect the intrinsic semantic cues embedded within key intra-textual entities. Furthermore, current models exhibit limited capability in determining the relevance of unseen targets to the given text, thereby struggling to differentiate between "neutral" and "irrelevant" stance labels. To address these issues, we first construct a four-class, multi-topic Japanese tweet dataset. To our knowledge, this is the first Japanese tweet-level dataset for stance detection. We then propose KIRP, a zero-shot stance detection framework. It integrates external knowledge with entity reorganization for data augmentation and employs prompt chaining for reasoning. Specifically, the framework incorporates knowledge graphs to supplement and reorganize key textual entities, while reflective Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning extracts and validates implicit targets. To better distinguish "neutral" from "irrelevant" labels, we adopt stance-aware contrastive learning to capture discriminative features and design a three-layer iterative prototype network for fine-grained classification. Experimental results on SemEval-2016, WT-WT, and KIRP-D show that KIRP achieves state-of-the-art performance. KIRP obtains F1 scores of 84.05% (three-class) on SemEval-2016, and 84.99% and 79.18% (four-class) on WT-WT and KIRP-D, respectively.

</details>


### [36] [Closing the Quality Gap in Low-Resource Text-to-Speech: LoRA Fine-Tuning of VoxCPM2 for Khmer and Korean](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26618)
*Phannet Pov,Sovandara Chhoun,Hyun Woo Park,Wan-Sup Cho,Saksonita Khoeurn*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A 2.4B-parameter TTS model (VoxCPM2) is adapted to low-resource Khmer and high-resource Korean using LoRA. For Khmer, where the base model is weak, adaptation significantly boosts MOS (3.85→4.23). For Korean, already well-handled, adaptation yields no benefit and even degrades quality at higher ranks. Validation loss and human ratings disagree on optimal rank.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large pretrained TTS models perform poorly on languages underrepresented in training data. The authors aim to study and mitigate this quality gap for Khmer (a low-resource language) versus Korean (a well-resourced language) using parameter-efficient adaptation.

Method: VoxCPM2, a 2.4B-parameter tokenizer-free TTS model combining a MiniCPM-4 language-model backbone with a flow-matching diffusion decoder, is adapted via a single LoRA adapter trained on a shared, language-tagged 26-hour corpus covering both Khmer and Korean. The adapter is zero-initialized (preserving the zero-shot baseline at training start) and applied to both the LM and decoder. Ranks 64 and 128 are evaluated, affecting 0.19%–3.03% of parameters.

Result: For Khmer, MOS improves from 3.85 (zero-shot) to 4.23 (rank-64 LoRA), a significant gain (p<0.001, paired Wilcoxon). Validation loss is lowest at rank 128, but MOS peaks at rank 64, revealing a mismatch between automatic and human evaluation. For Korean, the adapter yields no improvement, and high-rank adaptation degrades quality.

Conclusion: Parameter-efficient LoRA adaptation substantially benefits low-resource TTS where the base model is genuinely weak, but provides no gain—and can even harm—languages already well-modeled. Automatic loss metrics do not reliably predict human-perceived quality, underscoring the need for native-speaker listening tests in TTS evaluation.

Abstract: Large pretrained text-to-speech (TTS) models sound almost human for well-resourced languages, but much worse for languages that are rare in their training data. We study this quality gap for Khmer and Korean using VoxCPM2, a 2.4B-parameter, tokenizer-free TTS model that joins a MiniCPM-4 language-model backbone with a flow-matching diffusion decoder. We build one shared, language-tagged corpus of about 26 hours and adapt VoxCPM2 with a single Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapter, trained on both languages at once and added to both the language model and the decoder. The adapter is zero-initialized, so training starts exactly at the original (zero-shot) model. In native-speaker listening tests, the Khmer Mean Opinion Score (MOS) rises from 3.85 to 4.23 with the best adapter (rank 64), a highly significant gain (paired Wilcoxon test, p<0.001), while training only 0.19 to 3.03 percent of the parameters. The automatic loss and the human ratings, however, disagree on the best rank: validation loss is lowest at rank 128, yet MOS peaks at rank 64. The same adapter brings no gain for Korean, a language the base model already handles well, and at a high rank it even degrades quality. Adaptation therefore helps mainly where the base model is genuinely weak.

</details>


### [37] [CAT-Q: Cost-efficient and Accurate Ternary Quantization for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26650)
*Shigeng Wang,Chao Li,Yangyuxuan Kang,Jiawei Fan,Anbang Yao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CAT-Q is a post-training ternary quantization method for LLMs that uses learnable modulation and softened ternarization to efficiently compress models (1.7B–235B parameters) into ternary precision with only 512 calibration samples, outperforming BitNet models trained on 100B tokens while requiring ~100,000× fewer training tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing state-of-the-art ternary quantization methods depend on costly, data-intensive quantization-aware training to mitigate performance degradation. There is a need for an efficient post-training quantization scheme that can compress and accelerate LLMs of diverse architectures and sizes without such heavy training overhead.

Method: CAT-Q is a post-training quantization scheme with two coupled components: (1) Learnable Modulation (LM), which uses learnable factors to modulate pre-trained weight distributions and the ternary threshold to reduce sensitivity to ternarization; (2) Softened Ternarization (ST), which employs a differentiable transition function to guide ternarization toward stable convergence. The method operates with only 512 calibration samples.

Result: On LLMs with 1.7B–8B parameters, CAT-Q achieves superior performance compared to BitNet 1.58-bit v1 and v2 families (1.3B–7B parameters) trained on 100B tokens, representing a ~100,000× reduction in training tokens. For larger models (14B–235B parameters), CAT-Q produces leading ternary models within 8–60 hours on 8 A100-80GB GPUs — a first-time demonstration at this scale.

Conclusion: CAT-Q demonstrates that high-quality ternary quantization of LLMs is achievable via efficient post-training quantization without expensive quantization-aware training, enabling practical compression and acceleration across a wide range of model scales, from 1.7B to 235B parameters.

Abstract: In this paper, we present CAT-Q, Cost-efficient and Accurate Ternary Quantization, for compressing and accelerating LLMs. Unlike existing state-of-the-art ternary quantization methods that rely on data-intensive and costly quantization-aware training to mitigate severe performance degradation, CAT-Q is a simple yet effective post-training quantization scheme that is readily applicable to LLMs with diverse architectures and model sizes. It has two key components, learnable modulation (LM) and softened ternarization (ST), which are coupled from an optimization perspective. LM leverages a composition of learnable factors to modulate the distribution of pre-trained high-precision weights and the ternary threshold, making them less sensitive to ternarization. ST further introduces a differentiable transition function to guide the ternarization process toward stable convergence. We show that, for pre-trained LLMs with 1.7B to 8B parameters, CAT-Q can efficiently quantize them into ternary models using only 512 calibration samples, while achieving superior performance than the seminal BitNet 1.58-bit v1 and v2 families (with 1.3B to 7B parameters) trained with 100B tokens, yielding about a 100,000X reduction in training tokens. Moreover, we show for the first time that CAT-Q can quantize much larger pre-trained LLMs having 14B to 235B parameters into leading ternary models within just 8 to 60 hours on 8 A100-80GB GPUs. Code is available at https://github.com/IntelChina-AI/BitTern.

</details>


### [38] [Beyond Logical Forms: LLM-Extracted Patterns for Fallacy Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26698)
*Eleni Papadopulos,Firoj Alam,Giovanni Da San Martino*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper proposes a framework that uses LLMs to inductively extract abstract logical patterns from fallacious reasoning examples and their explanations, then combines these patterns with linguistic cues for improved fallacy classification, demonstrating significant gains over zero-shot baselines and competing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Logical fallacies often appear in subtle, nuanced forms that make automated classification difficult. Existing approaches may lack the abstract logical structure needed to reliably detect these defective reasoning patterns, motivating an investigation into whether merging abstract logical structures with surface-level linguistic cues enhances classification performance.

Method: The authors develop a framework that inductively extracts abstract logical patterns from fallacious examples and their associated explanations using Large Language Models (LLMs). These extracted patterns are then integrated with context-level linguistic cues to form richer representations for fallacy classification. The framework is evaluated in both zero-shot and one-shot configurations across multiple LLMs.

Result: The proposed pattern-enhanced approach yields statistically significant improvements over zero-shot baselines and outperforms competing approaches. Cross-dataset experiments further validate the generalization capability of the method, confirming that data-driven pattern extraction is an effective strategy for generating logical representations.

Conclusion: Merging inductively extracted abstract logical patterns with linguistic cues substantially improves fallacy classification. Data-driven pattern extraction via LLMs offers a robust, generalizable method for constructing logical representations, advancing automated reasoning flaw detection.

Abstract: In today's fast-paced information era, logical fallacies, defined as defective patterns of reasoning, inevitably contribute to the growth of information disorder. However, often fallacies appear in nuanced forms that complicate automated classification. In this study, we investigate whether merging abstract logical structures with context-level linguistic cues proves beneficial for fallacy classification, developing a framework that inductively extracts such patterns from fallacious examples and their explanations using Large Language Models (LLMs). We evaluate the impact of these patterns across different LLMs and experimental zero- and one-shot configurations, showing statistically significant improvements over zero-shot baselines and outperforming competing approaches. Cross-dataset experiments validate generalization, establishing data-driven pattern extraction as an effective method for generating logical representations.

</details>


### [39] [Evaluation Pitfalls and Challenges in Multimedia Event Extraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26775)
*Philipp Seeberger,Steffen Freisinger,Tobias Bocklet,Korbinian Riedhammer*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper presents the first systematic analysis of evaluation pitfalls in multimedia event extraction, identifying three major sources of issues — inconsistent data processing, inconsistent task assumptions, and overly relaxed evaluation settings — and demonstrates through controlled experiments that minor evaluation choices can cause large performance variations and overestimate model capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite steady progress in multimedia event extraction (jointly identifying events and arguments across text and images), the reliability and comparability of reported results are questionable. No prior work has systematically examined how evaluation choices affect performance estimates, creating a need for rigorous analysis of evaluation pitfalls that may lead to overestimated model abilities.

Method: The authors conduct a systematic analysis under a strict evaluation framework, running controlled experiments to isolate the effects of three categories of evaluation issues: (1) inconsistent data processing pipelines, (2) inconsistent task assumptions across studies, and (3) overly relaxed or lenient evaluation settings. They quantify how these variations impact performance metrics.

Result: Minor evaluation choices produce large performance variations and systematically lead to overestimation of a model's true cross-modal event grounding ability. The findings reveal that current evaluation practices lack the rigor needed for reliable benchmarking.

Conclusion: The field urgently needs comparable, standardized evaluation protocols. The authors call for a shift toward more rigorous evaluation standards in multimedia event extraction to ensure reported progress reflects genuine improvements in cross-modal event understanding rather than artifacts of evaluation design.

Abstract: Multimedia event extraction aims to jointly identify events and their arguments across multiple modalities, such as text and images, to support more comprehensive event understanding. While recent work reports steady and substantial progress, the reliability and comparability of these results critically depend on consistent and rigorous evaluation. In this work, we present the first systematic analysis of evaluation pitfalls in multimedia event extraction and identify three major sources of issues: inconsistent data processing, inconsistent task assumptions, and overly relaxed evaluation settings. We demonstrate, through a series of controlled experiments under a strict evaluation framework, that minor evaluation choices can cause large performance variations and lead to overestimation of a model's ability to ground real-world events across modalities. Our findings highlight the need for comparable evaluation standards and encourage a shift toward more rigorous evaluation in multimedia event extraction.

</details>


### [40] [OPID: On-Policy Skill Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26790)
*Shuo Yang,Jinyang Wu,Zhengxi Lu,Yuhao Shen,Fan Zhang,Lang Feng,Shuai Zhang,Haoran Luo,Zheng Lian,Zhengqi Wen,Jianhua Tao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: OPID proposes on-policy skill distillation that extracts hierarchical skills (episode-level and step-level) from completed trajectories, uses a critical-first router to inject skills into context, and derives token-level self-distillation advantages from log-probability shifts — improving language agent RL without external skill memories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Outcome-based RL for language agents suffers from sparse trajectory-level rewards that fail to guide intermediate decisions. Existing skill-conditioned self-distillation methods address this but rely on external skill memories or retrieved privileged context, which are costly to maintain and suffer from distribution mismatch with the current policy in multi-turn interactions.

Method: OPID (On-Policy Skill Distillation) extracts skill supervision directly from completed on-policy trajectories. It represents trajectory hindsight as two-level hierarchical skills: episode-level (global workflows, failure-avoidance rules) and step-level (local decision knowledge at critical timesteps). A critical-first routing mechanism selects step-level skills for critical decisions and falls back to episode-level skills otherwise. The selected skill is injected into interaction history, and the old policy re-scores the same response under both original and skill-augmented contexts. The log-probability shift yields a token-level self-distillation advantage, combined with the outcome advantage for policy optimization.

Result: Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-based QA demonstrate that OPID generally improves agent performance, sample efficiency, and robustness over outcome-only RL and existing skill-distillation baselines.

Conclusion: OPID preserves RL as the primary training objective while introducing dense, distribution-matched hindsight supervision, effectively addressing the sparsity of outcome-based RL without the maintenance cost and distribution mismatch issues of external skill memories.

Abstract: Outcome-based reinforcement learning provides a stable optimization backbone for language agents, but its sparse trajectory-level rewards provide little guidance on which intermediate decisions should be reinforced or suppressed. On-policy self-distillation offers dense token-level supervision, yet existing skill-conditioned variants often rely on external skill memories or retrieved privileged context, which are costly to maintain and can be mismatched with the state distribution induced by the current policy in multi-turn interaction. We propose \textbf{OPID} (\textbf{O}n-\textbf{P}olicy Sk\textbf{i}ll \textbf{D}istillation), a framework that extracts skill supervision directly from completed on-policy trajectories. OPID represents trajectory hindsight as hierarchical skills: episode-level skills capture global workflows or failure-avoidance rules, while step-level skills capture local decision knowledge at critical timesteps. A critical-first routing mechanism uses step-level skills when critical decisions are identified and falls back to episode-level skills as default guidance otherwise. The selected skill is injected into the interaction history, allowing the old policy to re-score the same sampled response under both original and skill-augmented contexts. The resulting log-probability shift yields a token-level self-distillation advantage, which is combined with the outcome advantage for policy optimization. OPID thus preserves RL as the primary training objective while introducing dense, distribution-matched hindsight supervision. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop and Search-based QA demonstrate that OPID generally improves agent performance, sample efficiency, and robustness over outcome-only RL and existing skill-distillation baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/jinyangwu/OPID/tree/main.

</details>


### [41] [FBK's Long-form SpeechLLMs for IWSLT 2026 Instruction Following](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26819)
*Zhihang Xie,Marco Gaido,Sara Papi,Matteo Negri,Luisa Bentivogli*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Submission to IWSLT 2026 on speech instruction following. For short-form, achieves SIFS 2.0708 on MCIF. For long-form, fixed 30-second segmentation yields best HIFS of 2.0663. Hallucination appears as repetitive insertions, impacting ASR and SSUM; short-form abilities are preserved after long-form extension.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Develop SpeechLLMs for both short-form and long-form speech instruction following under constrained settings, and address the challenge of unstable long-form generation.

Method: For the short track, direct evaluation using the MCIF benchmark. For the long track, three speech segmentation methods are explored. A new metric, HIFS, is introduced to account for unstable long-form generation. The winning approach uses fixed 30-second segmentation.

Result: Short track: SIFS score of 2.0708. Long track: fixed 30-second segmentation achieves the highest HIFS score of 2.0663. Hallucination primarily manifests as repetitive insertions, significantly affecting ASR and SSUM performance, while short-form capabilities are largely retained after long-form extension.

Conclusion: Fixed 30-second segmentation provides the most robust long-form performance. Hallucination remains a key challenge in long-form generation, particularly through repetitive insertions, but the underlying short-form capabilities are preserved.

Abstract: This paper describes our submission to the IWSLT 2026 Instruction Following shared task. SpeechLLMs are developed for both short-form and long-form speech instruction following under constrained settings. For the short track, strong performance is achieved on MCIF, with a SIFS score of 2.0708. For the long track, three speech segmentation methods are explored, and the HIFS score is introduced to account for unstable long-form generation. Experimental results show that fixed 30-second segmentation provides the most robust long-form performance, achieving the highest HIFS score of 2.0663. Further analysis shows that hallucination mainly manifests as repetitive insertions in generated outputs, substantially affecting ASR and SSUM, while short-form capabilities are largely retained after long-form extension.

</details>


### [42] [Cascaded Multi-Granularity Pruning for On-Device LLM Inference in Industrial IoT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26861)
*Jinghan Wang,Yanjun Chen,Wei Zhang,Xiaotong Huang,Tianchen Liu,Gaoliang Peng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A cascaded multi-granularity pruning framework with low-rank inter-stage recovery achieves up to 13.8× compression on LLMs for IIoT edge deployment; a formal Structural Independence Assumption (SIA) predicts when pruning criteria are reliable, exposing a ~74pp accuracy collapse on architectures that violate it.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing structured pruning methods for LLMs fail at high compression ratios due to one-shot importance estimation and exhibit unpredictable cross-architecture behavior, limiting deployment on resource-constrained IIoT edge devices.

Method: A cascaded multi-granularity pruning framework operating in coarse-to-fine order: layers → attention heads → feed-forward channels. Lightweight low-rank recovery is inserted between stages to re-estimate component importance. The Structural Independence Assumption (SIA) is formalized as a checkable condition to predict pruning criterion reliability across architectures (MHA+GELU vs. GQA+SwiGLU).

Result: On bearing fault diagnosis (88M–6.25B parameters): MHA+GELU architectures achieve 13.8× compression with 83.82% accuracy (+3.70pp over strongest baseline). GQA+SwiGLU architectures suffer ~74pp accuracy collapse, consistent with SIA violation predictions. On NVIDIA DGX Spark, compressed models reduce inference latency by up to 67.2% and peak memory by 62.5%.

Conclusion: The framework enables viable LLM deployment on IIoT edge devices for architectures satisfying SIA (MHA+GELU). The SIA provides a principled tool for predicting pruning reliability. GQA+SwiGLU architectures are fundamentally harder to prune reliably, indicating a need for new pruning paradigms tailored to modern LLM designs.

Abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) on Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) edge devices demands extreme compression, yet existing structured pruning methods collapse at high compression ratios due to one-shot importance estimation, and their cross-architecture behavior remains unpredictable. This article presents a cascaded multi-granularity pruning framework that removes layers, attention heads, and feed-forward channels in coarse-to-fine order, with lightweight low-rank recovery between stages to re-estimate component importance. An information-theoretic analysis motivates this ordering, and the Structural Independence Assumption (SIA) is formalized as a checkable condition predicting whether per-component pruning criteria are reliable for a given architecture: Multi-Head Attention (MHA)+GELU designs satisfy the SIA, whereas Grouped Query Attention (GQA)+SwiGLU designs violate it. On bearing fault diagnosis spanning 88M to 6.25B-parameter models, the framework extends achievable compression to 13.8 times on MHA+GELU architectures with 83.82% accuracy (+3.70 percentage points (pp) over the strongest baseline), while exposing a ~74pp accuracy collapse on GQA+SwiGLU architectures that violate the SIA. Deployed on an industrial slewing bearing fault diagnosis platform with NVIDIA DGX Spark, compressed models reduce inference latency by up to 67.2% and peak memory by 62.5%, demonstrating viability for IIoT edge inference.

</details>


### [43] [Information-Aware KV Cache Compression for Long Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26875)
*Jushi Kai,Zhuiri Xiao,Alexandra Birch,Zhouhan Lin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes InfoKV, an entropy-aware KV cache compression framework that combines attention scores with information-theoretic signals (predictive uncertainty and layer-wise representation evolution) to better identify important tokens. The key insight is that attention-selected tokens influence nearby contexts, while tokens with high predictive uncertainty strongly influence distant future contexts, leading to superior performance on long-context reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing KV cache compression methods rely solely on attention weights to estimate token importance, overlooking complementary information-theoretic signals such as predictive uncertainty and token informativeness. This leads to suboptimal token retention, especially for tokens critical to distant future reasoning steps.

Method: The authors introduce "Forward Influence," a metric measuring how compressed tokens affect future contexts. They observe an influence-distance dichotomy: attention-selected tokens affect nearby contexts, while high-uncertainty tokens affect distant contexts. Based on this, InfoKV integrates (1) token-level predictive entropy and (2) layer-wise representation evolution into entropy scores, which are combined with attention scores to guide KV cache compression during both prefilling and decoding stages.

Result: Experiments on long-context reasoning benchmarks using Llama-3.1, Llama-3.2, and DeepSeek-R1 demonstrate that InfoKV consistently outperforms existing attention-based KV cache compression methods in both long prefilling and decoding scenarios.

Conclusion: Incorporating information-theoretic signals (predictive uncertainty) alongside attention scores yields more effective KV cache compression. The forward-looking perspective reveals that high-uncertainty tokens play a crucial role in distant reasoning contexts, a factor that attention-only methods systematically miss.

Abstract: Reasoning capability has advanced rapidly in large language models (LLMs), leading to an increasing size of key-value (KV) cache in both prefilling and decoding stages. Existing KV cache compression methods mainly rely on attention weights to estimate token importance. While attention effectively captures contextual relevance, it overlooks complementary information-theoretic signals related to predictive uncertainty and token informativeness. In this paper, we revisit token importance from a forward-looking perspective and introduce \textit{Forward Influence}, a metric that measures how compressed tokens affect future contexts. Our analysis reveals that tokens selected by attention scores mainly influence nearby contexts, whereas tokens associated with high predictive uncertainty exhibit substantially stronger influence on distant future contexts. Based on the observation, we propose \textbf{InfoKV}, an entropy-aware KV cache compression framework that incorporates information-theoretic signals. It combines token-level predictive uncertainty with layer-wise representation evolution and integrates the resulting entropy scores with attention scores during reasoning. Experiments on long-context reasoning benchmarks with Llama-3.1, Llama-3.2, and DeepSeek-R1 demonstrate that InfoKV consistently outperforms existing attention-based KV compression methods in both long prefilling and decoding scenarios.

</details>


### [44] [Heterogeneous Neural Predictivity from Language Models During Naturalistic Comprehension](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26880)
*Xiao Jia*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This study demonstrates that language model representations can predict neural activity during naturalistic speech and text comprehension, but emphasizes that predictive utility should be distinguished from claims about shared neural organization or computational mechanisms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To rigorously evaluate whether language model-derived features serve as informative neural predictors during natural language comprehension, while controlling for confounds such as temporal structure, acoustic features, and representation capacity, and to separate mere predictive usefulness from stronger claims about neural-computational alignment.

Method: The authors analyzed three neural datasets (Brain Treebank, MEG-MASC, Podcast ECoG) using eight frozen language models with blocked encoding models. They employed matched temporal, nuisance, and representation-capacity controls, along with feature ablation experiments. Strict controlled predictive-only criteria were applied (67 of 432 evaluable rows met this standard). Control analyses included brain-derived, timing-linked, acoustic, and implanted-signal controls to verify component-level sensitivity.

Result: Widespread positive held-out prediction and gains over low-level baselines were observed in source-level summaries. However, participant-level matched-control advantages were localized rather than uniform. Response-profile and feature-specificity contrasts placed boundaries on representational or computational interpretations. Only 67 of 432 evaluable rows met the controlled predictive-only criterion, indicating that many apparent prediction effects may be driven by confounds.

Conclusion: Language model features are useful neural predictors, but predictive usefulness alone does not warrant claims about shared neural organization or common language-processing computations. Complete co-indexed integrated interpretation will require future jointly indexed coverage across modalities and datasets.

Abstract: Language-model representations provide structured, high-dimensional annotations of naturalistic language stimuli and can serve as informative neural predictors during comprehension. We analyzed locked derived data from Brain Treebank, MEG-MASC, and Podcast ECoG with eight frozen language models, blocked encoding models, and matched temporal, nuisance, and representation-capacity controls. Positive held-out prediction and gains over low-level baselines were widespread in source-level summaries. Across Brain Treebank and Podcast ECoG, 67 of 432 evaluable rows met a controlled predictive-only criterion, and model-side feature ablations changed prediction scores in most evaluable source rows. Brain-derived, timing-linked, acoustic, and implanted-signal controls confirmed component-level sensitivity of the analysis pipeline. These findings show that language-model-derived quantities can annotate neural activity during natural speech and text comprehension. Participant-level matched-control advantages were localized rather than uniform, response-profile and feature-specificity contrasts bounded representational or computational interpretations, and complete co-indexed integrated interpretation will require future jointly indexed coverage. Together, the analyses identify language-model features as useful neural predictors and separate predictive usefulness from claims about shared neural organization or language-processing computations.

</details>


### [45] [SamaVaani: Auditing and Debiasing Multilingual Clinical ASR for Indian Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26901)
*Subham Kumar,Prakrithi Shivaprakash,Abhishek Manoharan,Astut Kurariya,Diptadhi Mukherjee,Prabhat Chand,Pratima Murthy,Koustav Rudra,Lekhansh Shukla,Animesh Mukherjee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: An audit of ASR systems on multilingual Indian psychiatric interviews reveals significant performance disparities across languages, speaker roles, and gender. The authors propose SamaVaani, a fairness-aware fine-tuning technique that jointly improves transcription accuracy and demographic equity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ASR is increasingly deployed in clinical documentation, but its reliability across India's multilingual, demographically diverse healthcare settings is unknown. Existing models may exhibit systematic biases tied to language, gender, and speaker role, raising concerns about equitable clinical deployment.

Method: The authors audit eight state-of-the-art ASR models (IndicWhisper, WhisperLargeV3, Sarvam, GoogleS2T, Gemma3n, OmniLingual, Vaani, Gemini) on real psychiatric interviews in Kannada, Hindi, and Indian English. They then fine-tune the two best open-source models (Gemma3n, OmniLingual) using various methods, analyze performance gaps by speaker role and gender, and propose SamaVaani, a unified debiasing technique for simultaneous ASR improvement and fairness enhancement.

Result: Substantial variability was found across models and languages; some systems performed well in Indian English but poorly on regional languages. Systematic performance gaps by speaker role and gender were uncovered. Fairness-aware fine-tuning via SamaVaani mitigated these disparities while improving overall ASR performance.

Conclusion: Deploying ASR in multilingual clinical contexts without auditing for demographic fairness risks exacerbating healthcare inequities. SamaVaani offers a practical solution by jointly optimizing for accuracy and fairness across linguistic and demographic groups.

Abstract: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) is increasingly used to document clinical encounters, yet its reliability in multilingual and demographically diverse Indian healthcare context remains largely unknown. In this study, we first conduct the systematic audit of ASR performance on real-world psychiatric interview data spanning Kannada, Hindi and Indian English, comparing eight state-of-the-art models including IndicWhisper, WhisperLargeV3, Sarvam, GoogleS2T, Gemma3n, OmniLingual, Vaani, and Gemini. Our results reveal substantial variability across models and languages, with some systems performing competitively in Indian English but failing in regional speech. We further fine-tune two of the best performing opensource models, i.e., Gemma3n and OmniLingual, using various methods. With this, we uncover systematic performance gaps tied to speaker role and gender, raising concerns about equitable deployment in clinical settings, which are further mitigated by fairness-aware fine-tuning. To this end, we propose SamaVaani, a unified debiasing technique that simultaneously improves ASR performance and improves fairness across demographic groups.

</details>


### [46] [GAVEL: Grounded Caption Error Verification and Localization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26923)
*Zixian Gao,Atsushi Hashimoto,Kuniaki Saito*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: GAVEL introduces a unified task for verifying, explaining, and localizing misalignments in image-text pairs, along with a benchmark dataset. Even strong VLMs struggle, but supervised training on human annotations yields consistent improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-language models frequently hallucinate or produce outputs where text and images are misaligned. Existing work lacks a unified framework that jointly addresses detecting misalignment, explaining the discrepancy, and localizing visual evidence. GAVEL fills this gap by introducing a composite task and benchmark.

Method: The authors propose GAVEL (Grounded Caption Error Verification and Localization), a task combining three sub-tasks: verification (detecting misalignment), explanation (describing the discrepancy), and localization (grounding evidence in the image). They construct a human-annotated dataset with a training split and evaluate both closed-source VLMs and a supervised baseline trained on these annotations.

Result: Strong closed-source VLMs perform poorly on the GAVEL benchmark. The supervised baseline, trained on human-annotated data, achieves consistent improvements across both grounding and explanation metrics, demonstrating that the task provides learnable supervision.

Conclusion: GAVEL is a challenging and learnable task that combines verification, explanation, and localization of image-text misalignments, offering a useful benchmark for improving VLM faithfulness.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) often produce hallucinated or inconsistent outputs, where text and images are not properly aligned. Addressing this issue requires not only detecting misalignment but also explaining the discrepancy and localizing its visual evidence. We introduce GAVEL (Grounded Caption Error Verification and Localization), a task that jointly addresses verification, explanation, and localization for image-text pairs. To support systematic evaluation, we also present a corresponding dataset and benchmark. We further train a supervised baseline on the human-annotated training split to assess whether GAVEL provides learnable supervision for these abilities. Experiments show that even strong closed-source models struggle on GAVEL, while the supervised baseline yields consistent improvements across grounding and explanation metrics.

</details>


### [47] [Term-Centric Hierarchy Induction from Heterogeneous Corpora](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26963)
