*Elena Senger,Yuri Campbell,Jan-Peter Bergmann,Rob van der Goot,Barbara Plank*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A term-centric framework is proposed for inducing hierarchical taxonomies from large-scale, heterogeneous document corpora. By extracting terms rather than using whole-document representations, the method achieves better cross-source alignment and produces interpretable hierarchies, outperforming text- and summary-based baselines on a million-document bilingual benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing taxonomy induction methods use document-level representations that capture entire documents instead of specific domain concepts. This limits generalization across heterogeneous sources. A scalable, term-centric approach is needed to organize knowledge from diverse text sources into interpretable hierarchies for applications like policy analysis, innovation monitoring, and domain mapping.

Method: A term-centric framework that (1) maps documents from diverse sources into a shared representation space using automatic term extraction, enabling robust cross-source alignment, and (2) constructs interpretable hierarchies by integrating domain priors with data-driven clustering. The method scales to massive document collections.

Result: Experiments on a novel English and German multi-source benchmark of over one million documents show improved cross-source coherence and hierarchy quality over text- and summary-based baselines. A case study on German regional innovation analysis demonstrates practical utility for technology landscape mapping.

Conclusion: Shifting from document-level to term-centric representations significantly improves taxonomy induction from heterogeneous corpora. The approach scales effectively and provides practical value for real-world knowledge organization tasks, such as mapping regional innovation landscapes.

Abstract: Organizing knowledge from diverse text sources into interpretable hierarchies is crucial for tasks such as policy analysis, innovation monitoring, and exploratory domain mapping. Existing taxonomy induction methods typically rely on document-level representations that capture entire documents rather than the specific domain concepts relevant for knowledge organization, limiting their ability to generalize across heterogeneous sources. We propose a term-centric framework for inducing hierarchical taxonomies from heterogeneous corpora that scales to massive document collections. Our approach maps documents from diverse sources into a shared representation space using automatic term extraction, enabling robust cross-source alignment. Based on these representations, we construct interpretable hierarchies that integrate domain priors with datadriven clustering. Experiments on a novel English and German multi-source benchmark of over one million documents demonstrate that our method improves cross-source coherence and hierarchy quality over text- and summarybased baselines. A case study on German regional innovation analysis further demonstrates its practical utility for technology landscape mapping.

</details>


### [48] [RedVox: Safety and Fairness Gaps in Speech Models Across Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26968)
*Beatrice Savoldi,Sara Papi,Wafa Aissa,Matteo Negri,Luisa Bentivogli*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RedVox is a multilingual safety and fairness benchmark for speech models covering five languages. The authors find only 8% of model releases document multilingual safety analysis, that vulnerabilities worsen in non-English languages and with spoken input, and highlight unique privacy challenges in collecting speech safety data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Speech-capable AI models are increasingly deployed across languages, yet safety and fairness evaluations beyond English and under naturalistic (spoken) conditions are severely understudied. Only 8% of state-of-the-art model releases provide any multilingual safety documentation, creating a critical gap in understanding model vulnerabilities in real-world, cross-lingual settings.

Method: The authors introduce RedVox, a multilingual safety and fairness benchmark built on real human voices, covering unsafe and unfair stereotypical requests across five languages (English, French, Italian, Spanish, German). They evaluate eight state-of-the-art speech models under non-adversarial conditions, comparing text-based vs. spoken input across languages. Additionally, they survey the human participants who contributed voice data to document the personal and privacy challenges inherent in naturalistic speech data collection.

Result: Key findings: (1) vulnerabilities persist even under non-adversarial conditions; (2) safety failures are amplified in non-English languages compared to English; (3) spoken input exacerbates vulnerabilities relative to text input; (4) collecting speech data from human participants introduces unique personal and privacy challenges that pose broader sociotechnical barriers to naturalistic speech safety research.

Conclusion: The work reveals a significant gap in multilingual safety evaluation for speech models and demonstrates that current safeguards are brittle across languages and modalities. RedVox serves as both a benchmark and a call to action for more inclusive, naturalistic safety assessment practices, while also highlighting the underappreciated ethical complexities of building such resources with real human voices.

Abstract: Speech-capable models are increasingly deployed in real-world applications across languages. Yet their safety and fairness beyond English settings and under naturalistic conditions remain understudied. We survey safety reporting practices across state-of-the-art speech model releases, finding that only 8% document any multilingual analysis. To address this gap, we introduce RedVox, a multilingual safety and fairness benchmark for audio and speech built on real voices, covering unsafe and unfair stereotypical requests across five languages (English, French, Italian, Spanish, and German). Evaluating eight state-of-the-art models, we find that vulnerabilities persist even under non-adversarial conditions, worsen in non-English languages, and are amplified when the request comes from a spoken input. Finally, by surveying the participants who contributed to RedVox, we document the unique personal and privacy challenges of collecting speech data with human participants, pointing to broader sociotechnical challenges in naturalistic speech safety research.

</details>


### [49] [Auditing Framing-Sensitive Behavioral Instability in Large Language Models for Mental Health Interactions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26982)
*Abla Bedoui,Ashley L. Greene,Mohammed Cherkaoui*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Semantically similar mental health prompts with different contextual framings systematically alter LLM responses. Probing reveals framing information is decodable throughout transformer layers, and activation steering can partially modulate these behavioral effects. Robustness to contextual variation is crucial for trustworthy mental health AI.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in mental health support, where behavioral stability is critical. However, semantically equivalent concerns can be framed differently (contextual variation), potentially yielding inconsistent responses. While behavioral-level framing effects have been studied, little is known about how these variations manifest in the internal representations of aligned LLMs.

Method: Controlled matched-prompt experiments across multiple contextual framing conditions and several instruction-tuned model families. Layer-wise probing analyses to decode behavior-associated information through transformer depth. Held-out framing probes with strong lexical baselines. Activation steering experiments to test whether framing-associated representational directions can causally modulate downstream behavioral outcomes.

Result: Framing systematically alters interpretive response tendencies across architectures. Behavior-associated information remains decodable throughout transformer depth, with architecture-dependent variation in decoding strength. Held-out framing probes remain above chance across all architectures, even against strong lexical baselines. Activation steering partially modulates behavioral outcomes along framing-associated directions.

Conclusion: Robustness to contextual variation represents an important, underexamined dimension of consistency and trustworthiness in conversational AI systems deployed for mental health applications. The representational-level findings provide mechanistic insight into how framing effects manifest in aligned LLMs.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into mental health support tools and other psychologically sensitive conversational applications. In such settings, behavioral stability and consistency are important for trustworthy human-AI interaction. However, semantically similar concerns can be presented through different contextual framings, potentially eliciting different model responses. Such framing-sensitive variability may challenge user expectations regarding system behavior and complicate the assessment of AI reliability. While prior studies have primarily examined such effects at the behavioral level, less is known about how framing-related variation is reflected in the internal representations of aligned language models. In this work, we investigate these effects using controlled matched prompts spanning multiple contextual framing conditions across several instruction-tuned model families. Across architectures, framing systematically alters interpretive response tendencies. Layer-wise probing analyses show that behavior-associated information remains decodable throughout transformer depth, with architecture-dependent variation in decoding strength. Moreover, held-out framing probes remained consistently above chance across architectures despite strong lexical baselines. Activation steering experiments further suggest that framing-associated representational directions can partially modulate downstream behavioral outcomes. Finally, these findings indicate that robustness to contextual variation may represent an important consideration when evaluating the consistency and trustworthiness of conversational AI systems deployed in mental-health-oriented interactions.

</details>


### [50] [ReaORE: Reasoning-Guided Progressive Open Relation Extraction Empowered by Large Reasoning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26986)
*Xin Lin,Liang Zhang,Guoqi Ma,Hongyao Tu,Jinsong Su*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ReaORE is a two-stage OpenRE framework that uses coarse-to-fine reasoning — first filtering candidate relations via multi-aspect reasoning and embedding similarity, then performing fine-grained comparative reasoning to distinguish confused relations — outperforming existing methods on benchmark datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing OpenRE methods fall into two camps: clustering approaches that cannot generate explicit relation labels and generalize poorly, and LLM-based direct generation approaches that lack discriminative power for distinguishing easily confused relations. A method is needed that combines reliable generalization with fine-grained discriminative capacity.

Method: ReaORE employs a progressive, coarse-to-fine reasoning framework with two stages: (1) Relation Filtering — multi-aspect reasoning over relations and instances yields an initial candidate relation set, which is then augmented and filtered via embedding-based similarity to ensure target relation coverage; (2) Relation Prediction — fine-grained comparative reasoning over the filtered set to accurately select the target relation, specifically addressing easily confused relations.

Result: Extensive experiments on two widely-used OpenRE datasets show that ReaORE outperforms all existing baselines.

Conclusion: ReaORE effectively addresses the generalization and discrimination challenges in OpenRE by decomposing the task into progressive reasoning stages, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

Abstract: Open Relation Extraction (OpenRE) requires a model to extract unseen relations between head and tail entities from unstructured text for real-world applications. The core challenge of OpenRE lies in achieving reliable generalization to unseen relation types. Current OpenRE approaches either employ clustering techniques, which cannot generate relation labels and suffer from poor generalization, or rely on direct relation label generation via Large Language Models (LLMs), which lack sufficient discriminative capacity to distinguish easily confused relations. To address these limitations, we propose Reasoning-guided progressive OpenRE (ReaORE), a framework for performing relation extraction through coarse-to-fine relation reasoning. Specifically, ReaORE consists of two key stages: (i) relation filtering, which reasons over multiple aspects to understand relations and instances, yielding an initial relation set, and further supplements and filters relations via embedding-based similarity to ensure the target relation is included; (ii) relation prediction, which aims to predict the target relations from the above set via fine-grained comparative reasoning to better distinguish easily confused relations. Extensive experiments on two widely used OpenRE datasets demonstrate that ReaORE outperforms existing baselines.

</details>


### [51] [Where Do Models Find Happiness? Emotion Vectors in Open-Source LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26987)
*Sinie van der Ben,Raphaël Baur,Yannick Metz,Mennatallah El-Assady*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper replicates findings of emotion vectors (originally discovered in Claude Sonnet 4.5) in two open-weight models, confirming valence geometry generalizes across architectures, while revealing model-specific differences in how valence emerges across layers and finding that arousal encoding depends on the extraction corpus.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test the generality of emotion vectors — internal representations encoding emotion concepts with causal behavioral influence and psychologically-structured geometry — beyond proprietary Claude Sonnet 4.5 to open-weight models.

Method: Extracted emotion contrast vectors across all layers from Apertus-8B-Instruct-2509 and Gemma-4-E4B-it using two model-generated text corpora; measured PC1–valence and PC2–arousal correlations via PCA on these vectors.

Result: Both models recovered valence geometry (PC1–valence: r=0.76 and r=0.83, approaching Claude's r=0.81). Gemma encodes valence strongly in early layers (collapsing later), while Apertus shows the reverse (absent early, emerging mid-depth). Arousal encoding (PC2) was corpus-sensitive: stronger with Gemma-generated stories (r up to 0.45) than Apertus-generated ones (r ≤ 0.21).

Conclusion: Emotion vectors generalize across model architectures, confirming valence as a robust representational primitive, but their layer-wise emergence and arousal sensitivity to corpus highlight important architectural and methodological factors for interpreting emotion representations in language models.

Abstract: Recent work identified emotion vectors in Claude Sonnet 4.5, which are internal representations that encode emotion concepts, causally influence behavior, and exhibit geometry mirroring human psychological structure. We test the generality of these findings in two open-weight models, Apertus-8B-Instruct-2509 and Gemma-4-E4B-it, extracting emotion contrast vectors across all layers, using two model-generated corpora. We recover valence geometry for both models, with peak PC1--valence correlations of $r = 0.76$ and $r = 0.83$, approaching the $r = 0.81$ reported for Claude.Beyond replication, we observe notable differences in how valence representations emerge across model depth. In Gemma-4-E4B-it, valence is strongly encoded in early layers but collapses towards later layers, whereas Apertus-8B-Instruct-2509 exhibits the opposite pattern, with valence representations absent in early layers, but emerging at mid depths. Arousal encoding, in contrast, is sensitive to the extraction corpus: both models show stronger PC2--arousal alignment with Gemma-generated stories ($r$ up to $0.45$) than Apertus-generated ones ($r \leq 0.21$), suggesting arousal-relevant cues are unevenly distributed across generated corpora. We open-source our experiment code and dataset for reproducible investigation of emotion representations across language model architectures.

</details>


### [52] [MinGram: A Minimalist Unigram Tokenizer with High Compression and Competitive Morphological Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27019)
*Sander Land*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MinGram simplifies Unigram tokenizer training by replacing complex components (suffix arrays, forward-backward, iterative pruning) with BPE-seeded vocabulary, Hard EM on minimum-token paths, and single-step score pruning, achieving better compression than BPE and standard Unigram while maintaining morphological alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard Unigram tokenizers have elegant vocabulary representation but suffer from heavy, complex training involving suffix arrays, forward-backward passes, and iterative pruning. The authors aim to simplify this while preserving Unigram's advantages.

Method: MinGram uses three key simplifications: (1) a BPE-derived seed vocabulary instead of suffix-array-based seeding, (2) Hard EM optimization on a minimum-token path rather than soft forward-backward, and (3) a single flat score-pruning step replacing iterative prune loops. Token count serves as the primary objective with Unigram scores used only for tiebreaking.

Result: Across six languages, MinGram compresses better than both BPE and standard Unigram. A compression-oriented variant matches the strongest token-count compressors while retaining higher morphological alignment. In downstream LM training, Unigram-family tokenizers (MinGram among the best) consistently beat BPE in bits-per-byte.

Conclusion: MinGram demonstrates that Unigram's training complexity is unnecessary — a minimalist approach using BPE seeding, Hard EM, and single-step pruning achieves superior compression and downstream performance, making Unigram-family tokenizers a compelling alternative to BPE.

Abstract: The Unigram tokenizer uses an elegant representation which makes it straightforward to edit vocabularies, but its training is comparatively heavy and complex. We introduce MinGram (Minimalist Unigram), which keeps the token-list representation but simplifies training using a BPE-derived seed vocabulary, Hard EM on a minimum-token path, and a single flat score-pruning step. This removes the suffix array, the forward-backward pass, and the iterative prune loop, leaving a procedure that requires little beyond tokenizer inference itself. By making token count the primary objective and using a Unigram score only as a tiebreak, MinGram keeps the compression of pure token-count methods while retaining much of the morphological alignment and downstream quality of probabilistic ones. Across six languages, MinGram compresses better than both BPE and standard Unigram, and a compression-oriented variant matches the strongest token-count compressors while retaining substantially higher morphological alignment. In controlled downstream language-model training, Unigram-family tokenizers, with MinGram among the best, consistently beat BPE in bits-per-byte.

</details>


### [53] [Improving General Role-Playing Agents via Psychology-Grounded Reasoning and Role-Aware Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27025)
*Zhenhua Xu,Dongsheng Chen,Jian Li,Yitong Lin,Zhebo Wang,Jiafu Wu,Yizhang Jin,Chengjie Wang,Meng Han,Yabiao Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces Psy-CoT, a psychology-grounded chain-of-thought framework for role-playing agents that decomposes reasoning into three steps (Interaction Perception, Psychological Empathy, Logical Construction), and RAPO, a reinforcement learning method using profile–token mutual information to asymmetrically weight gradients, preventing reward model hacking. Both methods outperform existing approaches on role-playing benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Supervised fine-tuning for role-playing agents produces shallow behavioral mimicry without deep internal reasoning, leading to poor out-of-distribution generalization. Additionally, LLM-based reward models in RL training fail to distinguish between generic phrases that hack the reward and genuinely role-specific phrases, causing both to receive identical gradient signals and degrading character fidelity over training.

Method: (1) Psy-CoT: a chain-of-thought framework that structures pre-response reasoning into three sequential steps — Interaction Perception (interpreting user input in context), Psychological Empathy (modeling the character's inner state), and Logical Construction (formulating a coherent, in-character response). (2) RAPO (Role-Aware Policy Optimization): a reinforcement learning method that computes profile–token mutual information to asymmetrically weight policy gradients — amplifying role-specific tokens under positive advantage and attenuating them under negative advantage, thereby preventing reward hacking.

Result: Psy-CoT outperforms existing role-playing CoT methods on CoSER, CharacterBench, and CharacterEval benchmarks. RAPO consistently surpasses GRPO across multiple model scales.

Conclusion: Structured psychological reasoning (Psy-CoT) combined with role-aware gradient weighting (RAPO) provides a more faithful and generalizable approach to building character-consistent role-playing agents, addressing both the shallow mimicry problem of SFT and the reward hacking problem in RL-based alignment.

Abstract: Building general-purpose role-playing agents that faithfully portray any character from a natural-language profile remains challenging. The dominant paradigm -- supervised fine-tuning -- encourages behavioral mimicry without deep, human-like internal thought processes, resulting in poor out-of-distribution generalization. Therefore, we propose \textbf{Psy-CoT}, a psychology-grounded chain-of-thought framework that decomposes pre-response reasoning into three role-specific steps -- \emph{Interaction Perception}, \emph{Psychological Empathy}, and \emph{Logical Construction} -- so that the model \emph{thinks dynamically} from the profile rather than merely mimicking surface patterns. While structured reasoning provides a foundation, it alone is insufficient; reinforcement learning is essential to further align the model with character fidelity. However, we observe that under LLM-based reward models, both generic phrases that hack the reward model and genuinely role-specific phrases receive identical gradient signals -- this hacking accumulates over training, misleading the model into treating both as equally optimal choices. To address this, we propose \textbf{Role-Aware Policy Optimization (RAPO)}, which uses profile--token mutual information to weight gradients asymmetrically -- amplifying role-specific tokens under positive advantage while attenuating them under negative advantage. Experiments on CoSER, CharacterBench, and CharacterEval demonstrate that Psy-CoT outperforms existing role-playing CoT methods, and RAPO consistently surpasses GRPO across multiple model scales.

</details>


### [54] [NuclearQAv2: A Structured Benchmark for Evaluating Domain-Science Competence in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27047)
*Henry Shaowu Yuchi,Michal Kucer,Benjamin H. Sims,Selma Peterson,Emily Taylor*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: NuclearQAv2 is a benchmark of ~1,240 QA pairs for evaluating LLMs on nuclear engineering, revealing that while models handle factual questions well, quantitative reasoning and conceptual understanding remain challenging.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs perform well broadly but lack systematic evaluation in highly technical domains like nuclear engineering, which demands factual knowledge, quantitative reasoning, and conceptual understanding.

Method: NuclearQAv2 is built via a hybrid pipeline combining expert-authored questions, existing datasets, and LLM-assisted generation from domain-specific technical corpora. It spans boolean, numeric, and verbal question types. Structured prompting is used for both automated generation and evaluation, enabling scalability.

Result: Evaluation across diverse LLMs shows strong performance on factual (boolean) questions, but substantially weaker results on quantitative reasoning and conceptual understanding tasks.

Conclusion: Multi-faceted evaluation frameworks are essential for technical domains; NuclearQAv2 serves as a scalable benchmark that exposes critical gaps in LLMs' quantitative and conceptual reasoning in nuclear engineering.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of tasks, but ensuring their reliability in highly technical domains remains a significant challenge. In nuclear engineering, problem solving often requires not only factual knowledge but also quantitative reasoning and conceptual understanding. To address the need for systematic evaluation in this domain, we introduce NuclearQAv2, a benchmark for assessing LLMs on nuclear engineering knowledge. The benchmark comprises approximately 1,240 question-answer pairs spanning three categories: boolean, numeric, and verbal. NuclearQAv2 is constructed using a hybrid pipeline that combines expert-authored questions, existing datasets, and LLM-assisted generation from domain-specific technical corpora. By leveraging structured prompting for both automated question generation and response evaluation, the proposed framework enables scalable benchmark construction and evaluation. We evaluate a diverse set of LLMs using NuclearQAv2 and observe substantial performance differences across task types. While the models generally perform well on factual questions, quantitative reasoning and conceptual understanding remain considerably more challenging. These results highlight the importance of multi-faceted evaluation frameworks and establish NuclearQAv2 as a scalable benchmark for assessing LLM capabilities in technical domains.

</details>


### [55] [Towards Explainable Adjudicative Variance: Quantifying Judicial Discretion via Gated Multi-Task Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27069)
*Stanisław Sójka,Felix Steffek,Matthias Grabmair*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper proposes a Judge-Aware Gated Multi-Task Learning architecture that disentangles factual evidence from judicial discretion in legal outcome prediction. Using a fine-grained outcome taxonomy and a gated fusion mechanism, the model dynamically modulates reliance on judge identity. Evaluated on 13,937 UK Employment Tribunal decisions, the structured LoRA-adapted approach outperforms generative SFT baselines (Gemma-4 26B-A4B) with far fewer parameters, especially on rare and ambiguous outcomes, while offering interpretability through learned judge embeddings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Legal outcome prediction requires separating objective case facts from adjudicative context (judicial discretion). Existing approaches that inject judge identity and outcome taxonomy as prompt tokens or autoregressive targets into a single generative model fail to compose these signals effectively. The authors argue that the conditioning interface—structured, differentiable composition versus prompt-based composition—dominates model scale for this task.

Method: The authors propose a Judge-Aware Gated Multi-Task Learning architecture. A LoRA-adapted Gemma-4 encoder produces representations supervised by a fine-grained outcome taxonomy, enforcing structural regularization that disentangles semantic pathways. A Gated Fusion mechanism then dynamically modulates reliance on judge identity embeddings. This is benchmarked against supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of Gemma-4 26B-A4B where judge identity and taxonomy are injected as prompt tokens or autoregressive output targets.

Result: The proposed architecture achieves state-of-the-art performance on the 13,937-case UK Employment Tribunal benchmark, with gains concentrated on the most ambiguous and rarest outcome classes. It requires an order of magnitude fewer trainable parameters than generative SFT baselines. Learned judge embeddings and calibration profiles localize cases where adjudicative context drives predictions, demonstrating interpretability.

Conclusion: For identity-conditioned classification of legal outcomes, the choice of conditioning interface dominates scale: differentiable structured composition yields more accurate, more parameter-efficient models than prompt-based composition over substantially larger backbones.

Abstract: Legal outcome prediction must disentangle objective case facts from adjudicative context. Merit-based rulings rely on factual evidence while technical disposals may hinge on judicial discretion. We propose a Judge-Aware Gated Multi-Task Learning architecture that explicitly models this distinction. We introduce a fine-grained outcome taxonomy to supervise the encoder, enforcing a structural regularization that disentangles distinct semantic pathways. This granular legal curriculum enables our Gated Fusion mechanism to dynamically modulate reliance on judge identity. We evaluate our approach on 13,937 UK Employment Tribunal decisions. We benchmark our design against supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of a Gemma-4 26B-A4B backbone, in which judge identity and the taxonomy are injected as prompt tokens or autoregressive output targets. The two contextual signals compose only weakly when forced through a single autoregressive channel. In contrast, coupling a LoRA-adapted Gemma-4 encoder with our gated architecture defines a new state of the art on this benchmark while requiring an order of magnitude fewer trainable parameters than the generative SFT baselines, with gains concentrated on the most ambiguous and rarest outcome classes. Beyond accuracy, the architecture is interpretable; learned judge embeddings and calibration profiles localize the cases where adjudicative context drives the prediction. These results indicate that, for identity-conditioned classification of legal outcomes, the choice of conditioning interface dominates scale: differentiable structured composition yields more accurate, more parameter-efficient models than prompt-based composition over a substantially larger backbone.

</details>


### [56] [The Riddle Riddle: Testing Flexible Reasoning in Large Language Models and Humans](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27103)
*Bella Fascendini,Kathryn McGregor,Max D. Gupta,Thomas L. Griffiths*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper introduces the "riddle riddle" paradigm to test whether LLMs genuinely reason flexibly or merely pattern-match. LLMs excel at genuine riddles but fail on riddle riddles (which only need literal answers) by over-applying inventive reasoning, while humans show the opposite pattern. The findings suggest LLM performance on reasoning tasks may reflect memory retrieval rather than true flexible reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether LLMs' strong performance on cognitive tasks stems from flexible reasoning or from superficial pattern matching against training data, and to reveal the risk of conflating reasoning-like outputs with genuine reasoning.

Method: The authors designed the "riddle riddle" paradigm: word problems mimicking the surface structure of popular riddles but altered so that correct answers require only literal interpretation. Nine state-of-the-art LLMs and 100 human participants were tested across two experiments on both genuine riddles and riddle riddles, with error analysis categorizing failure modes as either overextending inventive reasoning or overextending literal reasoning.

Result: LLMs achieved 84.9% accuracy on genuine riddles but only 50.7% on riddle riddles; humans showed the reverse (50.5% vs. 80.5%). Error analysis revealed 90.8% of LLM errors on riddle riddles came from inappropriately applying inventive reasoning, versus only 57.6% of human errors on genuine riddles from overextending literal reasoning — indicating LLMs make reasoning mistakes more frequently than humans.

Conclusion: LLMs' success on genuine riddles likely reflects memory retrieval from training data rather than flexible, context-sensitive strategy selection. Without carefully controlled stimuli like riddle riddles, it is easy to mistake pattern-matched outputs for genuine reasoning.

Abstract: Humans flexibly adapt their reasoning strategies to the requirements of a given problem. Large language models (LLMs) have performed well on many cognitive tasks, however, it is unclear whether this accuracy is a result of pattern matching from training data or flexible reasoning. Here, we introduce a novel paradigm to test this question: the riddle riddle paradigm. Riddle riddles are word problems written to mimic popular riddles, but altered so their answers only require literal interpretations. Identifying correct answers requires looking past the structure of each question and flexibly apply different reasoning strategies based on the content. If LLMs respond to surface features, such as form, a riddle-like structure should cause models to use an inventive reasoning strategy even when a literal interpretation suffices. Alternatively, if LLMs reason based on content, they should flexibly switch strategies when appropriate. Across two experiments with nine state-of-the-art LLMs and 100 human participants, we show humans and LLMs fail on this paradigm in opposite directions. LLMs were far more accurate on genuine riddles than on riddle riddles (84.9% vs. 50.7%); whereas humans showed the reverse effect (50.5% vs. 80.5%). Error analysis shows that 90.8% of LLM errors on riddle riddles (the condition where they show diminished performance) were due to inappropriate use of inventive reasoning while only 57.6% of human errors on genuine riddles were due to overextending literal reasoning. Thus, while both groups make mistakes, reasoning mistakes are made more often by LLMs than by humans. Overall, LLMs' strong performance on genuine riddles may reflect memory retrieval rather than flexible strategy selection, and without stimuli designed to elicit this contrast, it becomes easy to conflate LLM-generated outputs that look like reasoning with genuine reasoning.

</details>


### [57] [Forecasting With LLMs: Improved Generalization Through Feature Steering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27199)
*Humzah Merchant,Bradford Levy*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper uses sparse autoencoders to identify interpretable temporal features in LLMs applied to forecasting tasks, finding that amplifying "time-awareness" features causally reduces look-ahead bias, while directly steering "look-ahead-bias" features has no effect.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs exhibit look-ahead bias in forecasting — leveraging future knowledge that would not have been available at the time of prediction. The authors aim to understand the internal mechanisms behind this bias and explore whether interpretable features can be causally manipulated to produce more historically grounded reasoning.

Method: The authors apply LLMs to forecasting tasks and inspect internal representations using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to discover features. They identify features linked to (1) time-aware reasoning and (2) look-ahead-biased reasoning. They then perform cross-domain feature intervention experiments — amplifying time-awareness features and steering look-ahead-bias features — to test causal effects on forecasting behavior.

Result: Amplifying time-awareness features significantly reduces look-ahead bias on forecasting prompts while preserving general reasoning performance. In contrast, directly steering candidate look-ahead-bias features does not produce a measurable effect, suggesting an asymmetric causal relationship between these feature types.

Conclusion: Interpretable temporal features discovered via SAEs can be causally manipulated to shift LLMs toward more historically grounded forecasting. The findings demonstrate a practical application of mechanistic interpretability for debiasing, and the asymmetry in intervention effects suggests that promoting correct reasoning may be more effective than directly suppressing biased reasoning.

Abstract: Successful forecasting involves identifying patterns between historical and future states of the world which generalize to future observations. We apply LLMs to a variety of forecasting tasks and inspect their internal states using sparse autoencoders to understand whether they appear to rely on time-specific pieces of knowledge versus generalizable patterns. Our analyses identify features associated with both time-aware reasoning and look-ahead-biased reasoning. We then apply the LLMs to an entirely different domain and intervene on these features. We find that amplifying time-awareness features substantially reduces look-ahead bias on forecasting prompts while preserving general reasoning performance. In contrast, steering the candidate look-ahead-bias features does not produce an effect. These results suggest that interpretable temporal features can be used to causally shift LLMs toward more historically grounded reasoning.

</details>


### [58] [Syntactic Belief Update as the Driver of Garden Path Processing Difficulty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27206)
*Alan Zhou,Miloš Stanojević,John T. Hale*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Garden path sentences challenge standard lexical surprisal models of sentence processing. The authors propose a Syntactic Belief Update metric—based on Rényi divergence between syntactic probability distributions before and after each word—that better predicts human reading times at disambiguation points, suggesting a non-lexical alternative to surprisal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Lexical surprisal, a dominant measure in psycholinguistics for predicting processing difficulty, fails to account for the processing disruption observed at the critical disambiguation point in garden path sentences. This gap motivates the search for a metric that captures structural reanalysis difficulty independent of lexical probabilities.

Method: The authors model a processor that maintains a probability distribution over syntactic trees (a "syntactic belief") and incrementally updates this distribution after each word. The magnitude of belief revision at each word is quantified using a generalized Rényi divergence between the prior and posterior syntactic distributions. This Syntactic Belief Update metric depends only on syntactic structure, not lexical item probability.

Result: The Syntactic Belief Update metric provides a better fit to human reading time data on garden path sentences compared to lexical surprisal.

Conclusion: The findings suggest that purely syntactic, non-lexical metrics like Syntactic Belief Update represent a promising new research direction for modeling human sentence processing, moving beyond surprisal-based accounts.

Abstract: Garden path sentences present a processing difficulty for humans -- the sentence prefix leads the listener towards one interpretation, until the listener hears a critical word that shows that the initial interpretation was wrong. Lexical surprisal, a measure that usually predicts sentence processing difficulty quite well, fails to provide good predictions for garden path sentences.
  We propose an alternative that actively predicts a probability distribution over syntactic trees (its syntactic belief) and updates that distribution after each new word. If a processor is led down a garden path, syntactic beliefs will be wrong and will require a large update at the critical word. The magnitude of the update is measured with a generalized Rényi divergence. Crucially, this metric is dependent on lexical items, but is fully independent of the probability of lexical items. This Syntactic Belief Update provides a better fit to the human reading time data on garden path sentences. This suggests a new research direction examining purely non-lexical alternatives to surprisal for psycholinguistics.

</details>


### [59] [Paved with True Intents: Intent-Aware Training Improves LLM Safety Classification Across Training Regimes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27210)
*Jeremias Ferrao,Niclas Müller-Hof,Iustin Sîrbu,Traian Rebedea,Yftah Ziser*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: AIMS, a dataset of 1,724 safety prompts annotated with user intent and harm labels, demonstrates that explicitly modeling user intent improves safety classifiers. Intent-aware training—especially GRPO-based reinforcement learning—achieves state-of-the-art performance and establishes the latency-F1 Pareto frontier across five external benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current safety classifiers typically predict harm labels directly from prompts, ignoring the intermediate signal of user intent. The authors argue that modeling intent explicitly can improve robustness, but no dataset or training framework previously existed to test this hypothesis systematically.

Method: The authors introduce AIMS, a human-annotated dataset of 1,724 difficult safety prompts with intent descriptions and harm labels. They evaluate four intent-aware training paradigms: supervised fine-tuning (SFT), preference learning (DPO), reasoning distillation, and reinforcement learning (GRPO). GRPO directly rewards intent faithfulness; DPO leverages model-generated intent errors; and intent-conditioned distillation compares against reasoning-only baselines.

Result: DPO from intent errors outperforms SFT. Intent-conditioned distillation beats reasoning-only distillation in most teacher-student pairs. GRPO yields the strongest average performance across five external safety benchmarks. Intent-aware models also form the inference latency-F1 Pareto frontier.

Conclusion: Faithful intent modeling provides a compact, high-quality supervision signal that yields more robust safety classifiers, with GRPO-based intent reward demonstrating the most consistent gains.

Abstract: We argue that safety classifiers should model user intent as an explicit signal between the prompt and the final label. To study this, we introduce AIMS, a human-annotated dataset of 1,724 difficult safety prompts, each paired with an intent description and harm label. We use AIMS to evaluate intent-aware training across supervised fine-tuning, preference learning, reasoning distillation, and reinforcement learning. Despite its size, AIMS enables competitive safety classifiers across training regimes: DPO from model-generated intent errors improves over SFT, and intent-conditioned distillation outperforms reasoning-only distillation in most teacher-student pairs. Most notably, directly rewarding intent faithfulness with GRPO yields the strongest average performance across five external safety benchmarks, while our intent-aware models form the inference latency-F1 Pareto frontier. These results show that faithful intent modeling is a compact, high-quality supervision signal for more robust safety classifiers.

</details>


### [60] [Compositionality and the lexicon in evolutionary semantics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27228)
*Fausto Carcassi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A framework is introduced where lexical meanings and a composition function co-evolve under pressures for simplicity and communicative accuracy. Applied to quantifiers, it shows that the semantic universal of conservativity emerges as an efficient abstraction on the Pareto frontier, reconciling formal semantics with evolutionary modeling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evolutionary models of semantic universals either model lexicons with fixed signal structures or holistic composition without interpretable lexical parts. They fail to incorporate the formal semantics insight that sentence meanings arise from recursively composing lexical meanings. This gap limits the ability to explain universals like conservativity that involve syntactic structure and compositional meaning.

Method: The authors introduce an evolutionary framework where lexical meanings and a composition function co-evolve under two competing pressures: conceptual simplicity and communicative accuracy. The framework is applied specifically to quantificational meaning, and results are analyzed via the Pareto frontier to identify optimal trade-offs between these pressures.

Result: Conservativity—the most well-known semantic universal for quantifiers—emerges naturally as an efficient, system-wide abstraction on the Pareto frontier. The account is sensitive to syntactic structure and helps reconcile tensions between empirical learnability evidence and prior evolutionary models.

Conclusion: The picture of sentential meaning from formal semantics can be productively integrated with evolutionary modeling. The framework provides a template for studying universals involving global compression within grammatical categories, semantic specialization of syntactic arguments, and co-evolution of lexical and compositional meaning.

Abstract: Formal semantics has shown that sentence meanings arise by recursively composing lexical meanings, yet much of the literature on semantic universals models either lexicons with fixed signal structures or holistic composition without interpretable lexical parts. We introduce a framework that integrates this fundamental insight of formal semantics in evolutionary modeling, by allowing lexical meanings and a composition function to co-evolve under pressures for conceptual simplicity and communicative accuracy. We apply this framework to the evolution of quantificational meaning. Analyzing the Pareto frontier, we find that the most well-known semantic universal, conservativity, emerges as an efficient system-wide abstraction. The account is sensitive to syntactic structure and helps reconcile tensions between empirical evidence on quantifier learnability and prior evolutionary models. More broadly, the results demonstrate that the picture of sentential meaning developed in formal semantics can be productively combined with evolutionary modeling. The framework offers a template for studying universals that involve global compression within a grammatical category, semantic specialization of syntactic arguments, and the co-evolution of lexical and compositional meaning.

</details>


### [61] [CARVE: Content-Aware Recurrent with Value Efficiency for Chunk-Parallel Linear Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27229)
*Sayak Dutta*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CARVE introduces content-aware gating for recurrent models by restricting erasures to the key axis, enabling a valid WY-form triangular chunk solver. This yields better perplexity, reasoning, and retrieval benchmarks than GDN-2 with fewer parameters and lower memory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current state-of-the-art recurrent architectures (specifically GDN-2) suffer from three coupled defects: (1) memory-blind gating where the erase decision ignores stored content, (2) value-axis erase masks that waste parameters, and (3) a mathematical incompatibility with the WY-form triangular chunk solver that makes recurrent training competitive with Transformers.

Method: CARVE resolves all three issues with one principle: erase only on the key axis, which is proven necessary and sufficient for WY-form solver validity. It reuses the recurrent output tensor as a free content signal for the erase gate and replaces the per-value write-gate projection with a single scalar per head. At initialization, CARVE is bit-identical to GDN-2.

Result: At 1.3B parameters trained on 100B tokens, CARVE achieves WikiText perplexity of 15.72 (−0.18 vs. GDN-2, a 4.5-sigma effect), leads all recurrent baselines on nine common-sense reasoning benchmarks, and sets SOTA on every RULER retrieval probe, with only 0.4% throughput overhead, 13% lower peak memory, and 19% fewer parameters.

Conclusion: The work provides six formal theorems covering memory capacity, Lyapunov stability, gradient flow, expressivity separation, Pareto-optimal chunk size, and hybrid optimality, establishing CARVE as a theoretically grounded and empirically superior recurrent architecture.

Abstract: Recurrent models must forget in order to remember, yet the state of the art decides what to erase without consulting what is stored -- the gate sees only the arriving token, not the memory it is about to modify. This memory-blind gating is one of three coupled defects in the leading delta-rule architecture (GDN-2): the value-axis erase mask wastes parameters at the scale of the value projection, and -- as we prove -- mathematically prevents the WY-form triangular chunk solver that makes recurrent training competitive with Transformers.
  We introduce CARVE (Content-Aware Recurrent with Value Efficiency), which resolves all three problems through one principle: erase only on the key axis. This is provably necessary and sufficient for the WY-form solver to remain valid. Within it, CARVE reuses the recurrent output tensor -- already written to GPU memory -- as a free content signal for the erase gate, and replaces the per-value write-gate projection with a single scalar per head. At initialisation CARVE is bit-identical to GDN-2; any quality difference emerges from what the content gate learns.
  At 1.3B parameters trained on 100B tokens, CARVE achieves WikiText perplexity 15.72 (minus 0.18 vs. GDN-2, a 4.5-sigma effect), leads every recurrent baseline on nine common-sense reasoning benchmarks, and sets state of the art on every RULER retrieval probe -- at 0.4% throughput overhead, 13% lower peak memory, and 19% fewer parameters. Six formal theorems cover memory capacity, Lyapunov stability, gradient flow, expressivity separation, Pareto-optimal chunk size, and hybrid optimality.

</details>


### [62] [Bridging Talk and Thought: Understanding Dialogue Dynamics Across Collaborative Problem-Solving Contexts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27233)
*Zhengyuan Liu,Stella Xin Yin,Min-Yen Kan,Nancy F. Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A hierarchical two-layer coding framework is proposed to analyze dialogue in collaborative problem-solving, integrating cognitive, non-cognitive, and metacognitive dimensions. Validated across nine datasets, it reveals metacognitive regulation as a key discriminator of deeper collaboration in human-AI and multi-agent settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current analytical approaches lack the nuance to capture the emerging dynamics of human-AI and multi-agent collaborative dialogue, particularly as intelligent systems evolve into autonomous reasoning and strategic cooperation partners. A more comprehensive framework is needed to optimize and evaluate such partnerships.

Method: The authors propose a conceptual framework employing a hierarchical two-layer coding scheme: one layer captures cognitive and non-cognitive problem-solving aspects, while the second layer addresses metacognitive regulatory mechanisms. The framework is applied and validated across nine diverse datasets from multiple domains.

Result: The framework effectively generalizes across nine datasets spanning multiple domains, demonstrating robust applicability. Analysis reveals how humans and agents coordinate knowledge, skills, and efforts. Notably, metacognitive regulation emerges as an essential discriminator distinguishing deeper, more sophisticated forms of collaboration.

Conclusion: The proposed framework successfully addresses limitations in existing dialogue analysis methods for collaborative problem-solving. Metacognitive regulation is highlighted as a critical indicator of collaboration depth, offering valuable insights for designing and evaluating future human-AI and multi-agent collaborative systems.

Abstract: We present a conceptual framework for analyzing dialogue in collaborative problem-solving contexts, with an emphasis on the emerging dynamics of human-AI and multi-agent collaboration. As intelligent systems become active agents capable of autonomous reasoning and strategic cooperation, understanding the dialogic interaction during collaborative problem solving is increasingly important for optimizing and evaluating such partnerships. Our framework addresses key limitations in current analytical approaches through a hierarchical two-layer coding scheme that integrates cognitive and non-cognitive problem solving with metacognitive regulatory mechanisms. We demonstrate its effectiveness and generalizability across nine datasets spanning multiple domains, and provide insights into how humans and agents coordinate their knowledge, skills, and efforts to solve complex problems, showing in particular that metacognitive regulation can be an essential discriminator of deeper collaboration.

</details>


### [63] [LMs as Task-Specific Knowledge Bases: An Interpretability Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27237)
*Amit Elhelo,Amir Globerson,Mor Geva*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LMs encode factual knowledge in a task-specific rather than task-agnostic manner, meaning the same fact may not be consistently accessible across different query formats, and distinct parameter subsets underlie different tasks for the same fact.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Knowledge bases return consistent answers for the same fact regardless of how they are queried. The authors investigate whether LMs satisfy this consistency property or instead encode knowledge in a task-dependent way, challenging the prevalent "LM-as-knowledge-base" analogy.

Method: The authors conduct both behavioral analyses (tracking whether facts learned on one task co-emerge on other tasks during training) and mechanistic analyses (parameter localization experiments to identify which parameter subsets are responsible for different tasks targeting the same fact). They also analyze chain-of-thought reasoning to study task-specific parameter engagement.

Result: Behaviorally, facts acquired on one task frequently fail to transfer to other tasks during training. Mechanistically, distinct parameter subsets underlie different query formats for the same fact. Chain-of-thought reasoning partially works by recruiting task-specific parameters beyond those used for the evaluation task.

Conclusion: What an LM "knows" and how it is asked are intertwined in parameter space, undermining the knowledge base analogy and raising concerns about the reliability and controllability of factual knowledge in LMs.

Abstract: Language models (LMs) capture large amounts of factual knowledge applicable to a wide range of tasks, motivating the view of their parameters as a knowledge base. An important property of knowledge bases is that different queries for the same fact return consistent results, drawing on a single source of truth. We investigate whether LMs satisfy this property through behavioral and mechanistic analyses. Our results suggest that they encode knowledge in a task-specific manner. Behaviorally, facts acquired on one task frequently fail to co-emerge on others during training. Parameter localization experiments suggest a mechanistic explanation, revealing distinct parameter subsets underlying different tasks for the same fact. Finally, we show that chain-of-thought reasoning draws part of its effectiveness from engaging task-specific parameters beyond those tied to the evaluation task. Our findings suggest that what the model knows and how it is asked are intertwined in parameter space, undermining the "knowledge base" analogy and carrying implications for the reliability and controllability of factual knowledge in LMs.

</details>


### [64] [How Surprising Is Historical Italian to Language Models? Tokenization Tax, Comprehension Tax, and a Simple Mitigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27275)
*Maria Levchenko*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces a diagnostic framework that decomposes historical language difficulty for LLMs into four dimensions: tokenization cost, surprisal, semantic robustness, and context sensitivity. Evaluated on 17th-century Italian, 19th-century Italian, and 18th-century Russian corpora, results show that while historical texts impose consistent encoding penalties, semantic representation remains robust. A minimal temporal context prompt reduces surprisal by ~60%, suggesting LLMs can safely support semantic retrieval in digital libraries with appropriate adaptation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in digital library workflows, yet their capacity to process historical language is poorly characterized. Existing approaches treat historical difficulty as monolithic, conflating orthographic variation, linguistic drift, and uneven pretraining exposure. The authors aim to disentangle these factors into measurable, actionable dimensions.

Method: The authors propose a four-dimensional diagnostic framework: (1) tokenization cost (subword fragmentation rate), (2) predictive uncertainty measured via surprisal, (3) semantic robustness assessed through embedding similarity between historical and modern paraphrases, and (4) context sensitivity. The framework is evaluated on three datasets: a newly curated 17th-century Italian corpus (1610–1689), 19th-century Italian ("I Promessi Sposi") as a high-exposure control, and 18th-century Russian civil print books as a contrastive orthographic stress test. A temporal context prompting intervention is also tested for mitigation.

Result: Key findings include: (1) 17th-century Italian and 18th-century Russian both incur 25–30% tokenization inflation; (2) 17th-century Italian surprisal is 2.4× higher than modern Italian (3.2× for academic prose), while Russian shows only a modest increase—revealing a dissociation between encoding cost and predictive difficulty; (3) embedding similarity remains >0.85 across all datasets, indicating robust semantic representation despite generation instability; (4) a minimal temporal context prompt reduces historical surprisal by approximately 60%.

Conclusion: Historical text imposes a consistent encoding tax on LLMs, but semantic representations remain robust, meaning digital libraries can safely deploy LLMs for retrieval tasks. Generative applications, however, require careful adaptation. The 60% surprisal reduction from temporal context prompting offers a simple, model-agnostic mitigation strategy.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly critical to digital library workflows, yet their ability to process historical language remains poorly understood. Historical difficulty is typically treated as a monolithic barrier, conflating orthographic variation, linguistic distance, and pretraining exposure. In this paper, we propose a diagnostic framework that decomposes this difficulty into four distinct dimensions: tokenization cost, predictive uncertainty (surprisal), semantic robustness, and context sensitivity.
  We evaluate this framework on three datasets spanning three centuries: (1) a newly curated corpus of 17th-century Italian texts (1610-1689) digitized from original page images; (2) canonical 19th-century Italian "I Promessi Sposi" serving as a high-exposure control; and (3) 18th-century Russian civil print books as a contrastive orthographic stress test.
  Our results reveal a distinct dissociation between encoding cost and comprehension. While Russian and early modern Italian incur comparable tokenization penalties (25-30% inflation), their predictive difficulty diverges sharply. 17th-century Italian is on average 2.4 times more surprising than its modern equivalent - with academic prose reaching 3.2 times - whereas Russian shows only a modest increase. But predictive uncertainty does not imply representational degradation: embedding similarity remains robust (> 0.85) across all datasets, confirming that models can represent historical meaning even when generation is unstable.
  Finally, we demonstrate that a minimal temporal context prompt reduces historical surprisal by approximately 60%, offering a simple, model-agnostic mitigation. These findings suggest that while historical text imposes a consistent encoding tax, digital libraries can safely deploy LLMs for semantic retrieval tasks, provided that generative applications are carefully adapted.

</details>


### [65] [Multilingual Reasoning Cascades Need More Context](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27306)
*Arnav Mazumder,Dengjia Zhang,Shuyue Stella Li,Yulia Tsvetkov,Niyati Bafna*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A context-aware translation cascade that preserves the original query, English translation, and reasoning trace through to the final translation stage yields strong gains across multilingual reasoning benchmarks, with the original-language question carrying most of the benefit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard translation cascades for multilingual reasoning are structurally lossy: each stage (translate→reason→translate back) discards information that later stages may need — cultural grounding, register, disambiguation cues. The authors investigate whether simply providing upstream context to the final translation module can mitigate this error propagation.

Method: A training-free, context-aware translation cascade: the final translation module receives not only the English reasoning trace but also the original-language question and the English translated question as additional context. Evaluated across 9 multilingual benchmarks, 3 backbone models, and 285 languages spanning high-, mid-, and low-resource regimes.

Result: Strong gains for open-ended generation across all models and resource regimes. The original-language question carries most of the beneficial context. The intervention is simple, training-free, and actionable.

Conclusion: Better information flow design in machine translation cascades is critical for mitigating error propagation. A simple default strategy — preserving the original user question until the end of the pipeline — yields reliable improvements.

Abstract: Translation cascades for reasoning translate the query from another language to English, reason in English, and translate the answer back to the original language. This is a competitive approach to multilingual reasoning, but structurally lossy, since each stage discards information later stages may need, including cues for cultural grounding, register, and disambiguation. We examine the benefits of a simple and training-free intervention: a context-aware translation cascade, which additionally provides the original question, the English translated question, and the reasoning trace to the context of the final translation module. We evaluate gains across nine multilingual benchmarks including various task types, three backbone models, and 285 high-, mid-, and low-resource languages, and demonstrate strong gains for open-ended generation across models and resource regimes. We show that the original language question carries most of the beneficial context. Our study emphasizes the need to better design information flow in machine translation cascades for mitigating error propagation, and provides a simple and actionable default strategy: preserve the original user question until the end of the pipeline.

</details>


### [66] [Beyond Surface Forms: A Comprehensive, Mechanism-Oriented Taxonomy of Indirect Linguistic Encoding for LLM-Based Coded Language Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27314)
*Hamid Reza Firoozfar,Mohammadsadegh Abolhasani,Reza Mousavi,Paul Jen-Hwa Hu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper proposes a mechanism-oriented taxonomy for indirect linguistic expressions (ILE) used to evade social media moderation, categorizing encoding operations rather than communicative intent. Tested across 2,000 TikTok and Bluesky posts with three LLMs, the taxonomy outperforms four existing taxonomies and a no-taxonomy baseline by 4.7% accuracy and 5.4% F1, demonstrating its utility as a stable scaffold for detecting emerging coded language.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Social media users increasingly employ indirect linguistic expressions (algospeak, euphemisms, adversarial obfuscation) to evade moderation and surveillance. Existing taxonomies are fragmented by communicative intent, limiting their generalizability for automated detection. A unified, mechanism-focused taxonomy is needed to serve as a robust scaffold for identifying emerging coded language across diverse contexts.

Method: The authors developed a comprehensive, mechanism-oriented taxonomy of ILE that abstracts away from communicative goals, instead categorizing underlying encoding/recovery operations. They evaluated it by incorporating the taxonomy into LLM prompts, benchmarking against four existing taxonomies and a no-taxonomy baseline. Evaluation used 2,000 manually annotated posts from TikTok and Bluesky, measuring document- and span-level detection performance across three LLMs.

Result: The proposed taxonomy achieved the strongest performance across all three LLMs at both document and span levels, with a 4.7% improvement in accuracy and 5.4% in F1 over the best-performing existing taxonomy. Results demonstrate that a comprehensive, mechanism-oriented taxonomy provides a stable scaffold for detecting emerging coded language and serves as a useful input for content moderation systems.

Conclusion: A mechanism-oriented taxonomy of indirect linguistic expressions, decoupled from specific communicative intent, offers superior generalizability and detection performance compared to intent-based alternatives. The approach provides a practical, stable framework for content moderation systems tasked with identifying evolving forms of obfuscated language on social media platforms.

Abstract: To avoid moderation and surveillance on social media, some users routinely invent indirect linguistic expressions (ILE) that camouflage sensitive meanings. Such expressions surface as algospeak, euphemisms, and adversarial obfuscation, depending on intent and context, and they involve recurring encoding mechanisms. We propose a comprehensive, mechanism-oriented taxonomy of ILE that abstracts away from communicative goals and instead categorizes the underlying operations through which meaning is encoded and recovered. We evaluate the taxonomy by incorporating it into LLM prompts and comparing it with four existing taxonomies and a no-taxonomy baseline, using 2,000 manually annotated TikTok and Bluesky posts. The proposed taxonomy attains the strongest document- and span-level performance across the three LLMs, achieving an improvement of 4.7% in accuracy and 5.4% in F1 over the best-performing benchmark. The empirical results reveal the importance of a comprehensive, mechanism-oriented taxonomy as a stable scaffold for detecting emerging coded language and a useful input to content moderation. Disclaimer: This paper contains content that may be profane, vulgar, or offensive.

</details>


### [67] [LLM-Based Examination of Eligibility Criteria from Securities Prospectuses at the German Central Bank](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27316)
*Serhii Hamotskyi,Akash Kumar Gautam,Christian Hänig*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A case study on applying LLMs to automate the German Central Bank's collateral eligibility verification from noisy, bilingual prospectuses, shifting from traditional NER to a generative IE pipeline with decomposition into extraction, normalization, and interpretation, achieving 91% precision with a conservative profile.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual verification of securities collateral eligibility is resource-intensive due to lengthy, semi-structured, bilingual (German-English) prospectuses. Traditional NER approaches struggle with OCR noise, linguistic variance, rigid span constraints, and require costly manual annotation for each entity type. A more flexible, robust solution is needed.

Method: The authors propose a generative Information Extraction pipeline using LLMs, decomposing the task into three stages: extraction (identifying relevant information), normalization (standardizing extracted values), and interpretation (determining eligibility). They also introduce a value-based evaluation methodology using LLM-as-a-judge for semantic assessment, replacing traditional location-based (span overlap) metrics.

Result: The LLM-based system achieves up to 91% precision at the document level for collateral eligibility decisions, demonstrating a conservative operating profile that minimizes false acceptance (i.e., erroneously approving ineligible securities).

Conclusion: LLM-based generative IE pipelines offer a viable, flexible alternative to traditional NER for regulatory document processing, particularly where noisy OCR and multilingual content are present. The conservative error profile is operationally desirable in high-stakes financial compliance settings.

Abstract: Verifying the eligibility of securities as collateral is a key responsibility of the German Central Bank. However, manually verifying these assets against legal and financial criteria within lengthy, semi-structured, and often bilingual prospectuses is a resource-intensive task. While previous efforts utilized traditional Named Entity Recognition (NER) for information extraction, these methods can struggle with OCR noise, linguistic variance, and rigid span-based constraints, and the need for manually annotated training data for each relevant annotation type. In this paper, we present the first case study applying Large Language Models (LLMs) to the eligibility examination process, shifting the paradigm toward a generative Information Extraction pipeline. Our approach decomposes the task into extraction, normalization, and interpretation, allowing for greater flexibility in handling noisy text and interleaved German-English content. We further introduce a value-based evaluation methodology using LLM-as-a-judge, which offers a more semantic assessment than location-based metrics. Our results demonstrate that LLM-based systems achieve high precision (up to 91%) in document-level eligibility, exhibiting a conservative operating profile that minimizes false acceptance.

</details>


### [68] [Empowering GUI Agents via Autonomous Experience Exploration and Hindsight Experience Utilization for Task Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27330)
*Tianyi Men,Zhuoran Jin,Pengfei Cao,Yubo Chen,Kang Liu,Jun Zhao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PEEU introduces autonomous experience exploration and hindsight-based high-level training data synthesis to improve small MLLMs' web agent planning, achieving superior OOD generalization. A 7B model trained this way outperforms Qwen2.5-VL-32B (30.6% accuracy). The TDHAF framework reveals that high-level task training, not atomic skill mastery, drives compositional generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Small open-source MLLMs for web agents are cost-efficient and privacy-preserving but suffer from weak task planning and poor cross-website generalization. Existing approaches fail to provide the high-level planning data needed for compositional generalization, motivating a method that autonomously discovers and synthesizes such training data.

Method: (1) **PEEU (Planning Experience Exploration and Utilization)**: The agent autonomously explores GUI environments to discover planning experiences, then uses hindsight experience replay to synthesize strictly aligned high-level training data from those explorations. (2) **TDHAF (Task Decomposition Hierarchical Analysis Framework)**: A systematic evaluation framework that studies compositional generalization across three granularity levels — low (atomic skills), middle, and high (complex planning).

Result: A 7B MLLM trained with PEEU achieves 30.6% accuracy on real-world benchmarks, surpassing the much larger Qwen2.5-VL-32B model. TDHAF analysis reveals that low-level atomic skill mastery does not guarantee high-level planning ability, whereas training on high-level tasks yields stronger OOD generalization.

Conclusion: Constructing hindsight-based high-level tasks and leveraging planning experiences are crucial for improving out-of-distribution planning capabilities in small MLLMs. The findings suggest that data composition (high-level vs. atomic tasks) matters more than model scale for cross-website generalization.

Abstract: Multimodal web agents can assist humans in operating repetitive GUI tasks, where effective task planning is essential for decomposing complex tasks into executable actions. While small open source MLLMs are cost efficient and privacy preserving compared with commercial large models, they suffer from weak planning and limited cross website generalization. To address these limitations, we introduce the planning experience exploration and utilization (PEEU) method, which autonomously explores environments to discover experiences and utilizes hindsight experience to synthesize strictly aligned, high level training data. To quantitatively analyze the generalization behaviors driving this performance, we propose the task decomposition hierarchical analysis framework (TDHAF) to systematically study compositional generalization across three task granularities: low, middle and high levels. Our analysis reveals that mastering low level atomic skills does not guarantee high level planning competence, while high level task training yields stronger OOD generalization. Experiments on real world benchmarks demonstrate PEEU's superior effectiveness: our 7B model achieves 30.6% accuracy, outperforming the much larger Qwen2.5-VL-32B model. These demonstrate constructing hindsight high level tasks and leveraging experiences is crucial for OOD planning abilities of small MLLMs.

</details>


### [69] [Mapping Political-Elite Networks in Europe with a Multilingual Joint Entity-Relation Extraction Pipeline](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27347)
*Kirill Solovev,Jana Lasser*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A fully open-weight, multilingual pipeline extracts signed, temporal knowledge graphs from news corpora using span-based NER, Wikidata entity linking, and ontology-constrained mixture-of-experts relation extraction. Validated against a 3,491-relation gold standard (68.2% strict, 93.7% lenient accuracy), it reconstructs Austrian party lifecycles and Polish state-enterprise patronage plus polarized PO-PiS conflict networks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods for observing elite political networks—either rent-seeking coalitions or civic governance ties—suffer from three limitations: manual coding is too labor-intensive for scale, traditional automated text-as-data approaches are limited to simple co-occurrence, and recent LLM methods rely on proprietary APIs, lack cross-lingual support, and struggle with scalable entity resolution. There is a need for an open, replicable, multilingual pipeline that can extract structured relational data from unstructured news text at scale.

Method: The authors propose a modular, fully open-weight pipeline: (1) span-based multilingual NER identifies mentions; (2) a three-stage linking cascade maps mentions to language-independent Wikidata identifiers for entity resolution; (3) a high-throughput, ontology-constrained mixture-of-experts model with guided decoding extracts directed, signed relationships grounded in a domain ontology, producing temporal knowledge graphs.

Result: A spot-check against a 3,491-relation gold standard yields 68.2% strict and 93.7% lenient textual correctness. In Austria, the pipeline reconstructs a political party's full lifecycle, including internal fractures, successor factions, and court convictions. In Poland, it reveals overlapping economic-governance patronage networks and the structurally balanced, signed conflict network of the PO-PiS duopoly.

Conclusion: The framework bridges raw multilingual text and structured relational data, providing a robust, replicable foundation for cross-national empirical computational social science, overcoming the limitations of proprietary, monolingual, and coarse-grained prior approaches.

Abstract: Whether political elites organise into rent-seeking coalitions that capture public resources or civic networks that sustain governance is a central question in comparative politics. Yet observing these complex, informal, and adversarial ties at scale has historically required intensive manual coding, while automated text-as-data methods have largely been limited to simple co-occurrence. Recent large language model (LLM) approaches offer a path forward but often rely on proprietary APIs, lack cross-lingual capability, and struggle with scalable entity resolution. We present a modular, fully open-weight pipeline for multilingual joint entity-relation extraction that builds signed, temporal knowledge graphs from massive unstructured news corpora. It combines span-based named-entity recognition (NER) with a three-stage linking cascade mapping mentions to language-independent Wikidata identifiers; a high-throughput, ontology-constrained mixture-of-experts model then uses guided decoding to extract directed, signed relationships grounded in a domain ontology. A full-coverage spot-check against a 3491-relation gold standard shows high textual correctness (68.2% strict to 93.7% lenient). Two large-scale case studies validate the pipeline against the public record. In Austria, it reconstructs a political party's complete lifecycle, dating internal fractures and tracking personnel into successor factions and court convictions. In a Polish corpus, it uncovers the overlapping economic and governance networks of state-enterprise patronage, alongside the structurally balanced, signed conflict network of the polarized Civic Platform (Platforma Obywatelska, PO)--Law and Justice (Prawo i Sprawiedliwość, PiS) duopoly. By bridging raw multilingual text and structured relational data, our framework provides a robust, replicable foundation for cross-national empirical computational social science.

</details>
