### [70] [Reducing Redundancy in Whole-Slide Image Patching for Scalable Indexing and Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26157)
*Jialiang Geng,Ghazal Alabtah,Saghir Alfasly,Wataru Uegami,H. R. Tizhoosh*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: ARReST is a framework that compresses whole slide image indices by pruning "antithetical" patches — those that contribute little to cross-class discrimination — achieving 3–60% storage savings without compromising retrieval accuracy for most organs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The proliferation of digital pathology and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in clinical AI has created an urgent need for scalable WSI indexing. However, high-performance storage costs limit the accessibility of WSI search for many healthcare institutions, making storage-efficient indexing a critical research priority.

Method: ARReST (Antithetical Redundancy Reduction Strategy) is a principled oppositional framework that, unlike traditional within-class deduplication, identifies and prunes "antithetical patches" — patches whose feature representations contribute minimally to cross-class discrimination. This selectively compresses the searchable index while preserving morphological diversity and retrieval fidelity.

Result: Experiments on the TCGA repository covering 21 organs show storage savings ranging from 3% to 60% (mean 14% ± 13%), achieved reliably without degrading retrieval performance for many organs.

Conclusion: ARReST enables scalable, cost-efficient WSI indexing suitable for next-generation retrieval-driven clinical AI systems, addressing the storage bottleneck that currently limits widespread adoption of content-based WSI retrieval.

Abstract: The rapid growth of digital pathology has created an urgent need for efficient indexing and retrieval of whole slide images (WSIs). This need is intensified by emerging generative AI workflows, particularly retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which require dependable similarity search to support high-stakes clinical decision-making. Yet the substantial cost of high-performance storage limits the scalability and accessibility of WSI indexing for many healthcare institutions. Consequently, methods that can reduce storage demands while preserving retrieval accuracy have become a critical research priority. We propose ARReST (Antithetical Redundancy Reduction Strategy), a principled oppositional framework that leverages redundancy across dissimilar tissue classes to markedly decrease the number of patches that must be indexed from each WSI. Instead of eliminating only within-class duplicates, ARReST identifies antithetical patches-those whose representations contribute minimally to cross-class discrimination-and prunes them from the searchable archive. This targeted reduction substantially compresses the index without sacrificing morphological diversity or retrieval fidelity. By minimizing superfluous patch representations, ARReST reduces storage footprint, lowers computational overhead, and accelerates similarity search across large pathology repositories. Extensive experiments on TCGA repository (The Cancer Genome Atlas with 21 organs) demonstrate that ARReST achieves significant index compression while maintaining competitive retrieval performance. The observed storage savings of 3% to 60% (14%$\pm$13%) can be reliably achieved without compromising retrieval performance for many organs. The proposed strategy enables scalable, cost-efficient WSI indexing and is well-suited for next-generation retrieval-driven clinical AI systems.

</details>


### [71] [From Clicks to Intent: Cross-Platform Session Embeddings with LLM-Distilled Taxonomy for Financial Services Recommendations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26277)
*Dianjing Fan,Yao Li,Kyaw Hpone Myint,Dwipam Katariya,Alexandre G. R. Day,Pranab Mohanty,Giri Iyengar*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Proposes a dual-purpose intent prediction framework that uses a self-supervised Transformer for session embeddings and an LLM-based taxonomy distillation pipeline for interpretable intent labels. The session embedding improves mobile homepage tile ranking (Recall@1 +1.88%, Log Loss −13.38%) and user conversion prediction (micro F1 +4.3% over LLM labels), while the distilled labels provide interpretability with only a 7% performance drop at ultra-low latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Financial services exhibit a cross-channel gap: pre-login web users explore new products while logged-in app users focus on account servicing. Web-based intent signals remain underutilized for post-authentication personalization due to the difficulty of cross-channel entity resolution (matching anonymous web sessions to authenticated mobile accounts). Existing web-intent capture methods are ad-hoc, narrow, and cannot simultaneously support quantitative downstream recommendations and qualitative understanding at scale.

Method: A scalable intent prediction framework that processes raw web clickstreams into two complementary outputs: (1) a self-supervised Transformer that encodes multi-modal clickstreams into compact session embeddings for downstream quantitative tasks; (2) an LLM-based taxonomy generation and distillation pipeline that produces interpretable intent labels with low latency for qualitative understanding.

Result: On mobile homepage tile ranking, the session embedding improves macro Recall@1 by 1.88% and reduces Log Loss by 13.38% over production baselines. On user conversion prediction, the embedding outperforms LLM labels by 4.3% on micro F1. The distillation layer delivers interpretable labels at ultra-low latency with only a 7% performance drop compared to the embedding.

Conclusion: Self-supervised clickstream representations paired with LLM-distilled taxonomies can jointly serve quantitative and qualitative needs in production financial recommender systems, effectively bridging the pre-login web and post-login app personalization gap.

Abstract: Sequential user behavior modeling is widely adopted in industrial recommender systems; however, significant gaps remain in financial services, where pre-login web interactions and authenticated in-app experiences differ drastically. Specifically, pre-login web users typically explore new products, whereas logged-in app users focus on account servicing. Due to the challenge of cross-channel entity resolution (e.g., matching anonymous web sessions to authenticated mobile accounts), web-based intent signals remain underutilized for post-authentication personalization. Existing methods for capturing web-based intent are often ad-hoc and narrow, lacking the flexibility to support both quantitative downstream recommendations and qualitative understanding at scale. In this work, we propose a scalable and dual-purpose intent prediction framework for web-based interactions and demonstrate its applicability for personalization. Our approach transforms raw web clickstreams into two outputs: a self-supervised Transformer encodes multi-modal clickstreams into a compact session embedding, while an LLM-based taxonomy generation and distillation pipeline produces interpretable intent labels. Our system demonstrates that self-supervised clickstream representations combined with LLM-distilled taxonomies can jointly serve quantitative tasks and qualitative understanding in production: on the mobile homepage tile ranking task, the session embedding improves macro Recall@1 by 1.88% and reduces Log Loss by 13.38% over production baselines. On the user conversion prediction task, the embedding outperforms the LLM labels by 4.3% on micro F1, while the distillation layer delivers interpretable labels at ultra-low latency with only a 7% performance drop.

</details>


### [72] [Scoring Is Not Enough: Addressing Gaps in Utility-fairness Trade-offs for Ranking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26369)
*Shubham Singh,Ian A. Kash,Mesrob I. Ohannessian*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Scoring functions are inherently sub-optimal for achieving utility-fairness trade-offs in ranking — a limitation that holds across deterministic/randomized scoring and single/multi-query fairness scopes. Semi-greedy post-processing is proposed as a tractable alternative that approaches exhaustive post-processing performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: With growing interest in algorithmic fairness for ranking and recommendation, existing approaches that learn fairness-aware scoring functions implicitly assume scoring is sufficient to achieve any desired utility-fairness trade-off. This work challenges that assumption and investigates whether scoring is fundamentally adequate for fairness-aware ranking.

Method: The authors provide a theoretical analysis using a generic fairness formulation, constructing a series of counter-examples that demonstrate scoring functions cannot achieve certain points on the utility-fairness Pareto frontier. The analysis covers deterministic scoring, randomized scoring, single-query fairness, and cross-query fairness. Empirically, they evaluate semi-greedy post-processing as an alternative and compare it against exhaustive post-processing baselines.

Result: The counter-examples prove that scoring functions — whether deterministic or randomized, and regardless of fairness scope — fail to achieve the full range of utility-fairness trade-offs attainable via post-processing. Semi-greedy post-processing empirically achieves trade-offs close to the exhaustive (optimal) post-processing ideal while remaining computationally tractable.

Conclusion: Scoring is fundamentally sub-optimal for fairness-aware ranking. Post-processing, particularly semi-greedy approaches, offers a more expressive and effective framework for navigating the utility-fairness trade-off frontier. This suggests a need to rethink prevailing fairness-aware learning-to-rank paradigms.

Abstract: Scoring functions are used to represent the relevance of individual documents. In modern information retrieval or recommendation systems, they are often learned from data and play a pivotal role in ranking sets of documents or items in a way that maximizes utility to a query or user. With the recent interest in algorithmic fairness, the success of scoring has naturally led to methods that learn scores that simultaneously trade off fairness and utility. In this work, we show that in stark contrast with utility-centric objectives, scoring is sub-optimal in achieving all utility-fairness trade-offs. We establish this with a series of counter-examples with a generic fairness formulation. We show that the issue persists whether we have a deterministic scoring function or a randomized one, or whether we measure fairness at the scope of a single query or across multiple queries. On the positive side, we empirically demonstrate that semi-greedy post-processing has the potential to achieve much better trade-offs, often approaching the ideal of exhaustive post-processing in a tractable way.

</details>


### [73] [TileMaxSim: IO-Aware GPU MaxSim Scoring with Dimension Tiling and Fused Product Quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26439)
*Ashutosh Sharma*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: TileMaxSim introduces IO-aware Triton kernels for efficient MaxSim scoring in multi-vector retrieval, achieving 80.2% peak HBM bandwidth on H100 GPUs and up to 220× speedup over naive implementations while preserving exact retrieval quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing GPU implementations of ColBERT-style MaxSim scoring are severely bandwidth-bound, reaching only 5–18% of peak HBM bandwidth because they materialize the full Nq × Nd similarity matrix, wasting memory traffic on intermediate data consumed only once.

Method: TileMaxSim employs three key techniques: (1) multi-query SRAM tiling that streams document embeddings through shared memory, accumulating per-query-token maxima in registers with a single HBM read per embedding; (2) dimension tiling into 128-wide chunks to support d > 128 embeddings that overflow shared memory; and (3) fused product-quantization (PQ) scoring via shared-memory lookup tables, reducing HBM I/O by up to ~31×. Implemented as Triton kernels and evaluated on NVIDIA H100 GPUs.

Result: On H100 GPUs, TileMaxSim achieves 80.2% of peak HBM bandwidth, scores 82M documents/second (71.6M/s on MS MARCO), yielding a 220× speedup over loop-based scoring, 6.5× over fused PyTorch, 6.6–8.5× over torch.compile, and 469× over WARP's CPU engine. As a drop-in replacement in ColBERTv2/PLAID, end-to-end scoring latency at 100K candidates drops from 268 ms to 1.2 ms (98% reduction). Throughput remains constant from 100K to 500K documents, with multi-GPU sharding, robust performance across dimensions 64–768, and FP16/BF16/FP32 support.

Conclusion: TileMaxSim demonstrates that IO-aware kernel design can close the bandwidth gap in MaxSim scoring, delivering orders-of-magnitude speedups without sacrificing retrieval quality. The approach is practical as a drop-in replacement and scales effectively across GPU configurations and embedding dimensions.

Abstract: Multi-vector retrieval models such as ColBERT achieve state-of-the-art accuracy through fine-grained token-level MaxSim scoring, yet existing GPU implementations leave most hardware performance unused. We give a roofline analysis of MaxSim on modern GPUs and identify a severe bandwidth gap: naive implementations reach only 5-18% of peak HBM bandwidth because they materialize the Nq x Nd similarity matrix, wasting memory traffic on data that is consumed once and discarded. We present TileMaxSim, a family of IO-aware Triton kernels that close this gap via (1) multi-query SRAM tiling that streams document embeddings through shared memory while accumulating per-query-token maxima in registers, reading each embedding from HBM exactly once; (2) dimension tiling that partitions the embedding dimension into 128-wide chunks, enabling scoring for d > 128 embeddings that overflow shared memory; and (3) fused product-quantization scoring via shared-memory lookup tables, cutting HBM I/O by up to ~31x. On NVIDIA H100 GPUs, TileMaxSim reaches 80.2% of peak HBM bandwidth and scores 82M documents/second (71.6M/s on real MS MARCO passages), a 220x speedup over loop-based scoring, 6.5x over fused PyTorch, 6.6-8.5x over torch.compile, and 469x the scoring throughput of WARP's CPU engine on the same node. TileMaxSim preserves exact retrieval quality: on MS MARCO and three BEIR benchmarks, rankings match reference MaxSim. As a drop-in replacement in ColBERTv2/PLAID, it cuts scoring latency at 100K candidates from 268 ms to 1.2 ms (98% lower end-to-end latency). We further show constant throughput from 100K to 500K documents, data-parallel multi-GPU sharding, robustness across dimensions 64-768, and FP16/BF16/FP32 support. Concurrent work independently develops an IO-aware fused MaxSim kernel; we differ in dimension tiling for d > 128 and fused product-quantization scoring.

</details>


### [74] [GPUSparse: GPU-Accelerated Learned Sparse Retrieval with Parallel Inverted Indices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26441)
*Ashutosh Sharma*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: GPUSparse accelerates exact learned sparse retrieval (SPLADE) on GPUs via a fused-kernel, scatter-add approach over a GPU-parallel inverted index, achieving 235x speedup over CPU baselines while maintaining exact scoring parity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Learned sparse retrieval models like SPLADE offer competitive quality and interpretability, but inference is bottlenecked by CPU-bound inverted index traversal (WAND/Block-Max WAND), limiting real-time serving at scale.

Method: GPUSparse introduces three components: (1) a GPU-parallel inverted index with block-aligned, warp-coalesced posting lists; (2) a batched scatter-add scoring algorithm processing hundreds of queries simultaneously; and (3) fused Triton kernels analyzing the tradeoff between work-efficiency and hardware utilization. Scoring is reformulated as scatter-add over an inverted index, realized via fused kernels.

Result: On MS MARCO passage ranking (8.8M passages) with SPLADE embeddings, GPUSparse matches CPU exact scoring to three decimals (MRR@10=0.383; Recall@1000≥0.999 vs. dense matmul). It achieves 235x speedup over Pyserini CPU (1.27ms vs. 298ms/query), and 787 QPS throughput at batch 500 with 1.3ms/query. The document-parallel kernel reaches 62.6% of H100 peak HBM bandwidth. Compared to a faithful SPARe iterative reimplementation, GPUSparse is 23–270x faster.

Conclusion: GPUSparse demonstrates that exact learned sparse retrieval can be efficiently performed on GPUs by reformulating scoring as fused-kernel scatter-add, overcoming the CPU bottleneck of inverted index traversal and revealing a fundamental work-efficiency vs. bandwidth-efficiency tradeoff in GPU sparse retrieval.

Abstract: Learned sparse retrieval models such as SPLADE achieve retrieval quality competitive with dense models while preserving the interpretability and exact-match advantages of sparse representations. However, inference-time scoring still relies on CPU-bound inverted index traversal algorithms (WAND, Block-Max WAND), creating a fundamental bottleneck for real-time serving at scale. We present GPUSparse, a system for GPU-accelerated exact learned sparse retrieval that introduces: (1) a GPU-parallel inverted index with block-aligned, warp-coalesced posting lists; (2) a batched scatter-add scoring algorithm that processes hundreds of queries simultaneously; and (3) fused Triton kernels with an analysis of the tradeoff between work-efficiency and hardware utilization. On MS MARCO passage ranking (8.8M passages) with real SPLADE embeddings, GPUSparse matches CPU exact scoring to three decimals (MRR@10=0.383, equal to Pyserini SPLADE at this precision; Recall@1000>=0.999 vs. dense matmul, the residual from floating-point tie-breaking) while providing a 235x speedup over Pyserini CPU at 8.8M documents (1.27ms vs. 298ms per query). Compared to Seismic (the fastest CPU sparse retrieval system), which trades 25% recall for speed (R@1000=0.738 vs. 0.983 exact), GPUSparse achieves exact scoring at 787 QPS throughput (batch 500) on the full 8.8M collection, with 1.3ms per query. Our document-parallel kernel reaches 62.6% of H100 peak HBM bandwidth, revealing a fundamental work-efficiency vs. bandwidth-efficiency tradeoff in GPU sparse retrieval. The reformulation of sparse scoring as scatter-add over an inverted index is shared with SPARe's iterative mode; our contribution is its fused-kernel realization, which we measure to be 23-270x faster than a faithful SPARe iterative reimplementation.

</details>


### [75] [Attributed, But Not Incremental: Cannibalization-Corrected Attribution for Large-Scale Advertising](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26690)
*Donghui Li,Bowen Yuan,Zili Yang,Qinxin Chen,Lijing Song*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Paid attribution outputs often overstate incremental growth due to cannibalization of organic/brand traffic. This paper proposes an experiment-calibrated correction framework that uses incrementality experiments as causal anchors to produce daily corrected estimates, with hierarchical allocation under consistency constraints. Deployed at TikTok, it reduced cannibalization rate by ~15pp.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In large-scale paid advertising systems, production attribution outputs (e.g., daily new users) are used for budget allocation and channel diagnosis, but they systematically overstate true incremental growth when paid channels overlap with organic demand, brand traffic, or other acquisition channels. This attribution-cannibalization mismatch distorts incremental ROI measurement and budget decisions at scale.

Method: An experiment-calibrated attribution correction framework that: (1) uses incrementality experiments as causal anchors to convert sparse lift measurements into daily correction estimates; and (2) allocates the calibrated cannibalization volume across business hierarchies under structural consistency constraints, making the corrected signal actionable at production granularity.

Result: Offline forward-in-time validation against channel-level incrementality experiment readouts showed the framework substantially reduces calibration error compared to raw attribution and fine-grained ML baselines. Deployed across multiple global TikTok markets, the system supported budget and traffic strategy adjustments that led to an approximately 15-percentage-point reduction in measured cannibalization rate.

Conclusion: The proposed framework effectively bridges the gap between sparse incrementality experiments and daily production attribution needs, enabling more accurate incremental ROI measurement and cannibalization-aware budget allocation at scale in real-world advertising systems.

Abstract: In large-scale paid acquisition and growth advertising systems, production attribution outputs are widely used for daily budget allocation and channel diagnosis. However, paid-attributed conversions such as daily new users (DNU) may systematically overstate true incremental growth when paid channels overlap with organic demand, brand-driven traffic, or other acquisition channels. This attribution-cannibalization mismatch can distort incremental ROI measurement and budget decisions at scale.
  We propose an experiment-calibrated attribution correction framework that uses incrementality experiments as causal anchors to convert sparse lift measurements into daily correction estimates. To make the corrected signal actionable at production granularity, we further allocate calibrated cannibalization volume across business hierarchies under structural consistency constraints. Offline forward-in-time validation against channel-level incrementality experiment readouts shows that the proposed framework substantially reduces calibration error relative to raw attribution and fine-grained ML baselines. Deployed across multiple global TikTok markets, the system supported budget and traffic strategy adjustments that were followed by an approximately 15-percentage-point reduction in the measured cannibalization rate.

</details>


### [76] [A Shared IPTC Topic Space for Cross-Source Topic Modelling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26845)
*Din Iskakov,Sebastian Gonçalves,Marco Idiat,Mendeli Vainstein,Aline Villavicencio,Ronaldo Menezes,Rodrigo Wilkens*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: This paper proposes a reproducible framework that uses the IPTC Media Topics taxonomy to project topics from different corpora into a single shared topic space via guided BERTopic, enabling valid cross-source topic comparison.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Comparing topic attention across different media is fundamentally hindered because topic models fitted independently to each corpus produce corpus-specific latent spaces that cannot be directly aligned, preventing meaningful cross-source analysis.

Method: The framework uses guided BERTopic to discover topics, scores them against the 94 IPTC Media Topics (level-1) taxonomy using weighted keyword and target centroids, then collapses topics upward to 17 IPTC parent topics via a maximum-similarity rule. Development followed a narrowing sequence on a controlled NYT 2011 corpus: broad model screen, focused mapping refinement, strict finalist comparison, target-construction ablation, and threshold calibration.

Result: The guided family retained substantially stronger mapped coverage than a zero-shot benchmark under stricter assignment thresholds. A parent-enriched target construction improved both coverage and parent consistency. Coverage declined gradually rather than collapsing as the assignment threshold was tightened.

Conclusion: The framework provides an externally anchored method for constructing a shared topic space grounded in a standardized taxonomy, enabling reproducible cross-source topic comparison that overcomes the corpus-specific alignment problem.

Abstract: Comparing topic attention across different media is hindered by a fundamental modelling problem: topic models fitted separately to each corpus produce corpus-specific topic spaces that cannot be aligned directly. This paper presents a reproducible framework that places corpora in a single shared topic space defined by a taxonomy. Discovered topics are obtained with guided BERTopic, scored against the ninety-four IPTC Media Topics' taxonomy topics (level-1) through weighted keyword and target centroids, and then collapsed upward to seventeen IPTC parent topics by a maximum-similarity rule. The framework was developed and selected on a controlled New York Times 2011 corpus through a narrowing sequence: a broad model screen, a focused mapping refinement, a strict finalist comparison, a target-construction ablation, and a threshold calibration. In this corpus, the guided family retained substantially stronger mapped coverage than a zero-shot benchmark under stricter assignment thresholds, a parent-enriched target construction improved both coverage and parent consistency, and coverage declined gradually rather than collapsing as the assignment threshold was tightened. The contribution is an externally anchored method for constructing a shared topic space that enables reproducible cross-source topic comparison.

</details>


### [77] [TriPAH: Imbalance-Aware Tri-Prompt Affinity Hashing for Cross-Modal Medical Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27010)
*Jiaming Bian,Songming Li,Yurui Song,Yunfei Chen,Yichao Cao,Jun Long*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: TriPAH is a cross-modal medical hashing framework that uses ontology-grounded prompts, hierarchical multi-granularity alignment, and patient-level consistency to overcome semantic fragmentation in medical image-text retrieval, achieving SOTA results on three public datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current cross-modal medical hashing methods suffer from semantic fragmentation caused by noisy clinical language, long-tailed label distributions, and brittle quantization, which collectively weaken image-text alignment and degrade retrieval performance in big medical data applications.

Method: TriPAH employs three components: (1) ontology-grounded, patient-level prompts conditioned on normalized clinical cues for low-noise textual representations; (2) a lightweight prompt-token mixer performing hierarchical multi-granularity alignment with an asymmetric multi-task objective combining multi-positive contrastive alignment, imbalance-aware classification, and progressive quantization regularization; and (3) a patient-level consistency module that stabilizes binary codes across complementary views.

Result: Extensive experiments on three public datasets show TriPAH significantly outperforms all state-of-the-art cross-modal hashing methods.

Conclusion: TriPAH effectively addresses semantic fragmentation in medical cross-modal hashing through prompt-based denoising, hierarchical alignment, and consistency regularization, establishing a new state-of-the-art for efficient medical image-text retrieval.

Abstract: In the era of big medical data, efficient cross-modal retrieval is pivotal for evidence-based diagnosis and large-scale case management. Cross-modal medical hashing retrieval aims to enable efficient image-text search and support downstream tasks such as case-based reasoning and decision support by learning compact, semantically aligned binary codes. However, current methods suffer from semantic fragmentation due to noisy clinical language, long-tailed labels, and brittle quantization that weakens alignment. We propose TriPAH, a Tri-Prompt Affinity Hashing framework. TriPAH synthesizes ontology-grounded, patient-level prompts conditioned on normalized clinical cues to yield low-noise textual representations for initial alignment. A lightweight prompt-token mixer performs hierarchical, multi-granularity alignment and produces quantization-ready features under an asymmetric multi-task objective coupling multi-positive contrastive alignment, imbalance-aware classification, and progressive quantization regularization. A patient-level consistency module further stabilizes codes across complementary views. Extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that TriPAH significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

</details>


### [78] [UniFormer: Efficient and Unified Model-Centric Scaling for Industrial Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27058)
*Bo Chen,Jinlong Jiao,Tijian Hu,Ruihao Zhang,Yanzhi Liu,Chenghou Jin,Qinglin Jia,Baixuan He,Hechang Pan,Yiwu Liu,Jian Liang,Chaoyi Ma,Ruiming Tang,Han Li,Kun Gai*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: UniFormer is a unified model-centric scaling framework for industrial recommender systems that decomposes modeling into feature and task spaces, employs semantic tokenization for user-item decoupling, uses multi-sequence cross-attention to prevent preference collapse, and introduces multi-view FFNs for flexible parameter scaling. It achieved significant gains in A/B tests on Kuaishou platforms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing industrial recommendation methods scale individual components (behavior modeling, feature interaction, task modeling) independently, and even cross-module approaches like HyFormer and OneTrans remain confined to feature space, lacking a unified model-centric scaling framework over the entire modeling space.

Method: (1) Decomposes the overall modeling space into Feature-space Interaction Modules and Task-space Interaction Modules, stacked separately. (2) Introduces a semantic-based tokenization scheme enabling user-item decoupling for request-level inference acceleration. (3) Employs multi-sequence cross-attention to separately capture heterogeneous behavior patterns, followed by self-attention for enhanced interaction modeling. (4) Introduces dedicated multi-view FFNs for flexible and scalable parameter scaling across different modeling components.

Result: Extensive online A/B testing on Kuaishou and Kuaishou Lite: App Stay Time improved by +0.101% and +0.260%, Watch Time improved by +0.729% and +1.113%, respectively. User engagement and interaction metrics consistently improved.

Conclusion: UniFormer provides an effective unified model-centric scaling paradigm that outperforms component-centric and cross-module co-scaling approaches, with both efficiency gains (via user-item decoupling and tokenization) and effectiveness gains (via multi-sequence cross-attention and multi-view FFNs) validated in large-scale production environments.

Abstract: Recently, substantial progress has been made in industrial recommendation through component-centric model scaling, where individual components such as behavior modeling, feature interaction, or task modeling are independently scaled to improve model capacity. Although recent methods such as HyFormer and OneTrans further explore cross-module co-scaling by jointly modeling behavior and interaction, their designs are still confined to the feature space and lack a unified model-centric scaling framework over the overall modeling space. In this paper, we propose UniFormer, an efficient and unified model-centric scaling framework for industrial recommender systems. To improve efficiency, UniFormer decomposes the overall modeling space into feature and task spaces, which are modeled by stacked Feature-space Interaction Modules and Task-space Interaction Modules, respectively. Moreover, UniFormer introduces semantic-based tokenization scheme to enable user-item decoupling, thereby achieving request-level inference acceleration. To prevent preference collapse, UniFormer employs multi-sequence cross-attention to separately capture heterogeneous behavior patterns, followed by the self-attention to enhance interaction modeling. Besides, dedicated multi-view FFNs are introduced to support flexible and scalable parameter scaling across different modeling components. Extensive online A/B testing in two production scenarios, Kuaishou and Kuaishou Lite, shows that UniFormer consistently improves user engagement and interaction metrics, achieving gains of +0.101%/+0.260% in App Stay Time and +0.729%/+1.113% in Watch Time, respectively.

</details>


### [79] [TRUST: Item-Calibrated Interval Evidence for Temporal Session-Based Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27214)
*Linjiang Guo,Nitin Bisht,Shiqing Wu,Yifan Yin,Guandong Xu*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: TRUST proposes interpreting temporal intervals relative to each item's own empirical interval distribution, rather than using absolute interval values. A unified scoring function guides neighbor sampling, graph encoding, and interest aggregation, yielding consistent improvements over both temporal and non-temporal session-based recommenders.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing temporal session-based recommenders use absolute interval values under the implicit assumption that identical intervals carry similar interest signals across all items. The authors empirically demonstrate this assumption is flawed: each item exhibits its own interval distribution, so an interval's significance should be calibrated relative to the item it belongs to.

Method: The TRUST framework introduces a score function that evaluates each observed interval against the empirical interval distribution of the corresponding item. This scoring mechanism is applied to three key components: (1) global neighbor sampling, (2) session graph encoding, and (3) final interest aggregation, providing a unified relative temporal calibration across the entire recommendation pipeline.

Result: TRUST consistently outperforms representative temporal and non-temporal baselines on public datasets. Plug-in experiments demonstrate the scoring function can improve existing temporal session recommenders as a model-agnostic method. Component-wise ablation confirms that calibrating temporal signals within each module yields consistent gains, rather than simply removing modules.

Conclusion: Relative temporal interpretation, where intervals are calibrated per-item rather than used as absolute values, is a principled and effective approach for session-based recommendation. The unified scoring function provides a model-agnostic mechanism that can enhance existing temporal recommenders.

Abstract: Temporal signals have been widely used in session-based recommendation to infer user interest. Existing temporal session-based recommenders primarily rely on absolute interval values, implicitly assuming that the same interval carries similar interest signals across items. However, we empirically find that this assumption does not hold: each item has its own interval distribution, so an interval should be interpreted relative to the item it belongs to. Based on this observation, we propose TRUST, a framework that evaluates each observed interval relative to the empirical interval distribution of the corresponding item. Specifically, we propose a score function to guide global neighbor sampling, session graph encoding, and final interest aggregation. Experiments on public datasets show that TRUST consistently improves over representative temporal and non-temporal baselines, and plug-in experiments further show that the proposed scoring function can improve existing temporal session recommenders as a model-agnostic method. Component-wise ablations further show that calibrating the temporal signals within each module, rather than removing the module itself, consistently improves neighbor sampling, session graph encoding, and interest aggregation.

</details>


### [80] [NOVA: A Verification-Aware Agent Harness for Architecture Evolution in Industrial Recommender Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27243)
*Shaohua Liu,Liang Fang,Yilong Sun,Shudong Huang,Qingsong Luo,Xiaoyang Chen,Dongqiang Liu,Chuangang Ma,Zhenzhen Chai,Henghuan Wang,Shijie Quan,Changyuan Cui,Zhangbin Zhu,Peng Chen,Wei Xu,Lei Xiao,Haijie Gu,Jie Jiang*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: NOVA is a verification-aware agent harness that automates recommender architecture evolution using an SGD-inspired "architecture gradient" signal and a multi-level verification cascade. It achieves high pass rates on architecture improvement tasks, reduces silent failures, and delivers significant online GMV gains in an industrial advertising system.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Industrial advertising recommender systems benefit from architecture evolution (e.g., RankMixer, TokenMixer), but developing such upgrades requires expert-intensive cross-module changes that are difficult to scale. Existing solutions fail: AutoML only tunes hyperparameters, and LLM coding agents produce runnable but architecturally invalid code that causes silent failures undetected by local tests.

Method: NOVA introduces: (1) Architecture Gradient — an SGD-inspired non-differentiable update signal aggregating prior modifications, verification diagnostics, metric feedback, and trajectory memory to guide modifications; (2) Verification Cascade — a multi-stage check (structure semantics, local executability, offline effectiveness, online impact) that blocks invalid candidates early and records failure patterns as forbidden directions; (3) L1–L4 task-level control that routes high-risk tasks to human Copilot oversight. The system is evaluated on L2 (ScaleUp) and L3 (Literature-to-Production) tasks.

Result: NOVA achieves 54.5% and 60.0% effective pass rates on L2 and L3 tasks respectively, reduces silent failures compared to coding-agent baselines, and shortens one literature-to-production cycle by over 13x in human-attended time. In online A/B testing, the L3 candidate improves GMV on three pCVR objectives by +1.25%, +1.70%, and +2.02%, while reducing pCVR bias by 58.8%, 66.7%, and 37.3%.

Conclusion: NOVA demonstrates that verification-aware architecture evolution with structured gradient signals and cascaded validation can effectively automate complex recommender model upgrades, delivering measurable business impact while minimizing silent failures and expert involvement.

Abstract: Industrial advertising recommender models are continuously improved through architecture evolution. Upgrades such as RankMixer, TokenMixer-Large, and MixFormer show that better structures remain a key source of quality and business gains. Yet developing such upgrades in production is expert-intensive and difficult to scale. Existing automation is insufficient: AutoML mainly tunes hyper-parameters, while effective gains often require cross-module changes under strict constraints; generic LLM coding agents optimize for runnable code, but runnable code does not imply a valid recommender architecture. Candidates may pass local tests while causing silent failures that degrade performance.
  We present NOVA, a level-aware agent harness for verification-aware architecture evolution. NOVA uses an architecture gradient, an SGD-inspired, non-differentiable update signal that aggregates prior modifications, verification diagnostics, metric feedback, and trajectory memory to guide the next modification. A verification cascade checks structure semantics, local executability, offline effectiveness, and online impact; invalid candidates are blocked early, with failure patterns recorded as forbidden directions. L1--L4 task-level control matches automation to task complexity and risk, routing high-risk tasks to Copilot for human oversight. Deployed in an industrial advertising system, NOVA achieves the highest effective pass rate on L2 ScaleUp and L3 Literature-to-Production tasks (54.5% and 60.0%), reduces silent failures compared with coding-agent baselines, and shortens one literature-to-production cycle by over 13x in human-attended time. In online A/B testing, the selected L3 candidate improves GMV on three pCVR objectives by +1.25%, +1.70%, and +2.02%, while reducing pCVR bias by 58.8%, 66.7%, and 37.3%.

</details>

### [81] [Kiko: Programming Agents to Enact Interaction Protocols](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26156)
*Samuel H. Christie,Munindar P. Singh,Amit K. Chopra*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: Kiko is a protocol-based programming model for multiagent systems that simplifies agent implementation by abstracting communication details and letting developers focus on decision-making logic through composable "decision makers," with formal guarantees of protocol compliance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current programming models for multiagent systems offer poor abstractions for decision making. They fail to properly bridge an agent's internal decision logic with its external, protocol-governed interactions. This gap makes it difficult for developers to implement decentralized decision-making agents that interact according to a protocol.

Method: Kiko introduces a protocol-based programming model where agents are implemented via one or more decision makers. Each decision maker selects from a set of valid decisions and produces mutually compatible decisions about message sending. The model completely abstracts away the underlying communication service and supports practical decision-making patterns. The authors provide an operational semantics for Kiko and formally establish two key properties.

Result: The paper establishes two formal results: (1) Kiko agents are protocol compliant — they never deviate from the specified interaction protocol, and (2) Kiko is capable of realizing any protocol enactment, demonstrating the model's completeness and expressiveness.

Conclusion: Kiko successfully bridges the gap between an agent's internal decision logic and its public protocol-governed behavior by providing a clean programming abstraction. The formal semantics and proven properties of protocol compliance and enactment completeness validate Kiko as a principled and practical contribution to multiagent system development.

Abstract: Realizing a multiagent system involves implementing member agents who interact based on a protocol while making decisions in a decentralized manner. Current programming models for agents offer poor abstractions for decision making and fail to adequately bridge an agent's internal decision logic with its public decisions.
  We present Kiko, a protocol-based programming model for agents. To implement an agent, a programmer writes one or more decision makers, each of which chooses from among a set of valid decisions and makes mutually compatible decisions on what messages to send. By completely abstracting away the underlying communication service and by supporting practical decision-making patterns, Kiko enables agent developers to focus on business logic. We provide an operational semantics for Kiko and establish that Kiko agents are protocol compliant and able to realize any protocol enactment.

</details>

### [82] [Physics-guided Convolutional Neural Network for Domain Growth Prediction in Systems with Conserved Kinetics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26128)
*Vijay Yadav,Madhu Priya,Manish Dev Shrimali,Prabhat K. Jaiswal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a physics-guided, attention-based convolutional neural network as a surrogate model for efficiently predicting the spatiotemporal evolution of phase separation governed by the Cahn-Hilliard equation, demonstrating long-term stability, mass conservation, and consistency with Lifshitz-Slyozov domain-growth scaling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional numerical solvers for nonlinear PDEs describing spatiotemporal system evolution are computationally expensive. Deep learning surrogates offer faster alternatives, but existing models may struggle with long-time stability and preservation of physical invariants (e.g., conserved quantities).

Method: An attention-based, physics-guided convolutional neural network (CNN) is designed as a surrogate model. The model is trained to predict the full time-evolution of phase separation in binary mixtures governed by the Cahn-Hilliard equation (a conservative, fourth-order nonlinear PDE). Physics guidance ensures preservation of mixture composition (conserved order parameter) throughout the rollout.

Result: The trained surrogate yields stable and accurate long-time predictions for both critical and off-critical mixtures. It preserves mixture composition over time and correctly captures domain size growth consistent with the Lifshitz-Slyozov domain-growth law.

Conclusion: The proposed attention-based, physics-guided CNN framework is effective for modeling systems with conserved kinetics and can be extended to other complex dynamical systems governed by PDEs.

Abstract: The spatiotemporal evolution of many physical, chemical, and biological systems is described by nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs). Recently, deep neural network-based surrogate models have gained increasing interest as efficient alternatives to computationally expensive traditional numerical solvers. In this work, we propose an attention-based, physics-guided convolutional neural network as a surrogate model to learn the microstructural evolution of such systems. We train the model to accurately predict the full time-evolution of phase separation in binary mixtures governed by the Cahn-Hilliard equation. We show that predictions from our trained surrogate model remain stable and accurate over long-time rollouts for both critical and off-critical mixtures and preserve the mixture composition throughout evolution. We also show that our model accurately captures the growth of domain size and is consistent with the Lifshitz-Slyozov domain-growth law. The prediction results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework for modeling systems with conserved kinetics and can be extended to other complex dynamical systems.

</details>


### [83] [The Red Queen Gödel Machine: Co-Evolving Agents and Their Evaluators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26294)
*Alex Iacob,Andrej Jovanović,William F. Shen,Daniel Burkhardt,Meghdad Kurmanji,Nurbek Tastan,Lorenzo Sani,Niccolò Alberto Elia Venanzi,Ambroise Odonnat,Zeyu Cao,Bill Marino,Xinchi Qiu,Nicholas D. Lane*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces the Red Queen Godel Machine (RQGM), an evolutionary framework enabling recursive self-improvement under non-stationary utilities. The RQGM organizes search into epochs with fixed within-epoch evaluation criteria while allowing utility evolution at boundaries, demonstrating gains on coding tasks, scientific writing/reviewing, and Olympiad-level proof grading, including correcting reviewer bias toward AI-generated papers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current self-improving agents assume stationary evaluation criteria (fixed verifiers, benchmarks, or labeled datasets), ignoring the evolutionary principle that environments co-evolve with the adapting species. The authors aim to bring dynamic, evolving evaluators into the recursive self-improvement loop, enabling adversarial objectives and utilities that may surpass static benchmarks.

Method: The RQGM framework structures recursive self-improvement into epochs. Within each epoch, the evaluation criterion is fixed, preserving self-improvement guarantees. At epoch boundaries, the utility function can be updated — enabling controlled utility evolution. This is applied across three domains: (1) verifiable coding tasks with an agent-as-a-judge code-review signal, (2) scientific paper writing and reviewing with co-evolved writers and diverse judge panels, and (3) Olympiad-level proof writing and grading. An adversarial objective is introduced for paper reviewing to correct over-acceptance of AI-generated papers.

Result: On coding tasks: improved test pass rate over prior SOTA with 1.35x–1.72x fewer tokens. On scientific writing: co-evolved writers achieved 1.78x–1.86x higher acceptance rates under diverse agent-as-a-judge panels. On proof grading: co-evolved graders reached 9% higher ground-truth accuracy. In paper reviewing: the RQGM's adversarial objective discovered reviewers equally stringent on AI and human work, correcting baseline reviewer bias that over-accepted AI papers at up to 1.91x the human rate.

Conclusion: Embedding evaluation inside the recursive self-improvement loop via controlled utility evolution yields consistent gains over static-evaluator baselines across multiple domains. The RQGM demonstrates that evolving evaluators alongside agents — in line with co-evolutionary principles — improves both performance and fairness, suggesting a promising direction for general-purpose self-improving systems.

Abstract: Self-improving agents are state-of-the-art (SOTA) on agentic coding benchmarks and have recently been extended to general domains. However, their search methods generally assume a stationary evaluation criterion: a fixed verifier, benchmark, or labeled dataset that remains valid as the agent improves. This ignores a central feature of evolution: species adapt as their environments change with them. We aim to bring the same principle to recursive self-improvement, making evaluation part of the improvement loop and opening search to evolving evaluators, adversarial objectives, and dynamic utilities that may surpass static benchmarks. We introduce the Red Queen Godel Machine (RQGM), an evolutionary framework for recursive self-improvement under non-stationary utilities. The RQGM makes this possible through controlled utility evolution: search is organized into epochs with a fixed within-epoch evaluation criterion, while the utility can be updated at epoch boundaries, so self-improvement guarantees hold per epoch as the objective evolves across them. We begin by showing that even on verifiable coding tasks, the RQGM improves test pass rate over the prior SOTA by adding a complementary agent-as-a-judge code-review signal. This signal is cheaper and the RQGM uses 1.35x-1.72x fewer tokens. We then turn to scientific paper writing and reviewing, and Olympiad-level proof writing and grading, where the RQGM improves performance over prior self-improving agents: co-evolved writers reach 1.78x-1.86x higher acceptance rates under a diverse agent-as-a-judge panel, while co-evolved graders reach 9% higher ground-truth accuracy. In paper reviewing, the strongest baseline reviewer over-accepts AI-generated papers at up to 1.91x the human rate. The RQGM corrects this by introducing an adversarial objective that discovers reviewers equally stringent on AI and human work.

</details>


### [84] [\chisao{}: A GPU-Native Parallel Optimizer for Multimodal Black-Box Functions via Convergence-Anticonvergence Oscillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26164)
*Ira Wolfson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CHISOA is a GPU-native population optimizer that uses a convergence-anticonvergence oscillation cycle to find all modes of multimodal black-box functions, achieving 100% mode recovery on the SFU benchmark suite with up to 34× speedup over basin-hopping, and maintaining 100% reliability under substantial likelihood noise.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal optimization methods (basin-hopping, CMA-ES, multistart gradient descent) are inherently sequential and cannot leverage GPU parallelism. There is a need for a massively parallel, derivative-free optimizer that can locate all modes of a black-box function simultaneously without getting trapped in local optima.

Method: CHISAO (Convergence-Halt-Invert-Stick-And-Oscillate) runs an entire sample batch on GPU simultaneously. Its core mechanism is an asymmetric convergence-anticonvergence cycle: samples reaching true peaks are frozen/preserved ("stuck"), while remaining samples continue exploring via momentum-based anti-convergence and stochastically smoothed gradients. Adaptive reseeding employs two strategies—Repulse Monkey and Golden Rooster—to maintain population diversity. Gradients are obtained via finite differences (derivative-free).

Result: On all 42 functions of the SFU benchmark suite (d ∈ {2,4,8,16,32,64}), CHISAO achieves 100% mode recovery, whereas all CPU baselines fail at d ≥ 8 on the hardest multimodal functions. Speedups reach 34× over basin-hopping on Michalewicz (d=64) where all methods succeed, and 39× on unimodal Rotated Hyper-Ellipsoid (d=64). Mode detection remains 100% reliable under likelihood noise up to σ_noise = 1.0.

Conclusion: CHISAO demonstrates that a GPU-native, population-based oscillation strategy can robustly and efficiently solve multimodal black-box optimization at scale, offering dramatic speedups and superior mode recovery compared to sequential CPU methods, even under substantial noise and without requiring analytic gradients.

Abstract: Finding all modes of a multimodal black-box function is a fundamental challenge in optimization, Bayesian inference, and scientific computing. Existing approaches -- basin-hopping, CMA-ES, multistart gradient descent -- operate sequentially and cannot exploit the massive parallelism of modern GPU hardware. We introduce \chisao{} (\textbf{C}onvergence-\textbf{H}alt-\textbf{I}nvert-\textbf{S}tick-\textbf{A}nd-\textbf{O}scillate), a GPU-native population optimizer that runs an entire sample batch simultaneously and exploits a deliberate convergence-anticonvergence oscillation cycle to escape local traps while freezing confirmed modes. The structural move is asymmetric: samples that reach true peaks are frozen (``stuck'') and preserved, while the rest keep exploring via momentum-based anti-convergence and stochastically smoothed gradients. Adaptive reseeding via two complementary strategies (Repulse Monkey and Golden Rooster) maintains population diversity throughout. On all 42 functions of the Simon Fraser University optimization benchmark suite across dimensions $d \in \{2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64\}$, \chisao{} achieves \textbf{100\%} mode recovery where all CPU baselines collapse at $d \geq 8$ on the hardest multimodal functions, at up to \textbf{$34\times$} speedup over basin-hopping on functions where all methods succeed (Michalewicz $d=64$) and up to \textbf{$39\times$} on unimodal functions (Rotated Hyper-Ellipsoid $d=64$, pure GPU dividend). All benchmarks evaluate the objective by value alone -- gradients come from finite differences -- so the reported speedups are a derivative-free worst case. Under substantial likelihood noise ($σ_{\mathrm{noise}}$ up to 1.0), mode detection remains 100\% reliable. The algorithm is available as a standalone open-source Python package on PyPI.

</details>


### [85] [Implementation of reinforcement learning in chemical reaction networks: application to phototaxis as curiosity-driven exploration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26168)
*Ruyi Tang,Grégoire Sergeant-Perthuis,David Colliaux*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper reframes unicellular algal phototaxis as an information-driven sensorimotor process using a POMDP framework coupled with biochemical reaction dynamics (CRN-ODEs). The model treats environmental variables as hidden states, employs memoryless Bayesian updates, and demonstrates through inverse reinforcement learning on Chlamydomonas trajectories that run-tumble behavior emerges as an optimal information-acquisition strategy to resolve sensory ambiguity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional mechanistic run-tumble models of phototaxis in unicellular algae overlook how organisms actively sample their environment to reduce sensory ambiguity. The authors aim to bridge this gap by adopting a minimal cognition perspective, treating navigation as a subjective information-acquisition process rather than purely stimulus-response behavior.

Method: The authors propose a framework linking a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) with Chemical-Reaction-Network Ordinary Differential Equations (CRN-ODEs). Environmental variables are hidden, and the cell performs memoryless Bayesian updates on a minimal internal state from each photoreceptor observation. The framework includes a biophysical observation process and a chemically computable polynomial bound on information gain. Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) is applied to 30 experimentally recorded Chlamydomonas trajectories to infer the behavioral objective, and results are benchmarked against standard Stochastic Simulation Algorithm (SSA) baselines.

Result: The IRL-inferred model reproduces the empirical alignment-to-light distribution comparably to objective SSA baselines. Run-tumble alternation emerges as an information-acquisition strategy: tumbling reorients the cell to sample new sensory configurations, resolving sensor ambiguity. This demonstrates that intracellular biochemical networks can support adaptive information-seeking behavior.

Conclusion: Phototactic run-tumble behavior can be understood as an adaptive information-seeking strategy rather than a fixed stimulus-response mechanism. The POMDP-CRN-ODE framework shows how minimal biochemical machinery can implement subjective, uncertainty-reducing sensorimotor loops, supporting the minimal cognition perspective on cellular navigation.

Abstract: Living systems navigate environments using noisy and incomplete sensory signals. In unicellular algae, phototaxis is often modeled as a mechanistic run--tumble process driven by stimulus--response rules. However, such descriptions overlook how organisms actively sample their environment to reduce sensory ambiguity. From a minimal cognition perspective, we reframe this navigation as a subjective, information-driven sensorimotor process. To this end, we propose a framework linking a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) with biochemical reaction dynamics. Environmental variables are hidden, while the cell updates a minimal internal state from each observation through a memoryless Bayesian step. These internal dynamics balance orienting toward light with exploratory reorientation and can be implemented through Chemical-Reaction-Network Ordinary Differential Equations (CRN--ODEs). Our model includes a biophysical observation process for photoreception and a chemically computable polynomial bound on information gain. Using Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) on 30 experimentally recorded Chlamydomonas trajectories, we infer the behavioral objective consistent with observed phototactic motion and benchmark the resulting dynamics with standard Stochastic Simulation Algorithm (SSA) baselines. Our model reproduces the empirical alignment-to-light distribution, comparable to objective SSA baselines on this dataset. Within this framework, run--tumble alternation emerges as an information-acquisition strategy: tumbling reorients the cell to sample new sensory configurations and resolve sensor ambiguity, demonstrating how intracellular biochemical networks can support adaptive information-seeking behavior in cellular navigation.

</details>


### [86] [SOLAR: AI-Powered Speed-of-Light Performance Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26383)
*Qijing Huang,Sana Damani,Zhifan Ye,Athinagoras Skiadopoulos,Siva Kumar Sastry Hari,Jason Clemons,Sahil Modi,Jingquan Wang,Aditya Kane,Edward C Lin,Humphrey Shi,Christos Kozyrakis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SOLAR is a framework that automatically computes Speed-of-Light (SOL) bounds—theoretical minimum execution times—directly from PyTorch and JAX source code, using an LLM frontend for IR translation and an analytical backend for multi-fidelity bound computation, enabling headroom analysis, optimization identification, and hardware provisioning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deriving SOL bounds for deep learning workloads is currently manual, error-prone, and not integrated into rapid model development workflows. There is no automated tool that can take arbitrary PyTorch/JAX source code and produce validated, multi-fidelity SOL bounds.

Method: SOLAR combines (1) an LLM-based frontend that translates source programs into an executable Affine Loop IR with output-comparison validation, (2) a deterministic flow that lifts the IR into an einsum graph, and (3) an analytical backend that computes SOL bounds at three fidelity levels: unfused, fused, and cache-aware. The system ensures zero observed SOL violations through validation.

Result: Evaluated across KernelBench, JAX/Flax models, and robotics workloads, SOLAR demonstrates zero SOL violations, provides multi-fidelity headroom analysis, identifies optimization opportunities, enables cross-platform exploration, and supports inverse-roofline hardware provisioning.

Conclusion: SOLAR bridges the gap between rapid model development and performance analysis by automating SOL bound derivation with validated correctness, offering actionable insights for software, hardware, and algorithm co-optimization.

Abstract: How fast could a deep-learning model run on target hardware, and how far is today's implementation from that limit? These questions are central to software, hardware, and algorithm optimizations. Speed-of-Light (SOL) analysis answers them by computing a workload's theoretical minimum execution time on a given architecture. Yet deriving SOL bounds remains manual, error-prone, and disconnected from rapid model development. To close this gap, we introduce SOLAR, a framework that automatically derives validated SOL bounds from PyTorch and JAX source code. SOLAR leverages both generative and deterministic components in its flow: an LLM frontend translates any source programs into an executable Affine Loop IR, validated by output comparison; a deterministic flow lifts the IR into an einsum graph; and an analytical backend computes unfused, fused, and cache-aware SOL bounds. SOLAR provides comprehensive operator and language coverage, produces validated bounds with zero observed SOL violations, and offers multi-fidelity analysis that tightens bounds and surfaces optimization insights. We evaluate SOLAR across KernelBench, JAX/Flax models, and robotics workloads. These experiments demonstrate four use cases: headroom analysis at multiple fidelity levels, identifying optimization opportunities, cross-platform exploration, and inverse-roofline hardware provisioning.

</details>


### [87] [Neural Architecture Search for Generative Adversarial Networks: A Comprehensive Review and Critical Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26169)
*Abrar Alotaibi,Moataz Ahmed*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A comprehensive review of Neural Architecture Search (NAS) methods applied to GANs, categorizing approaches by search strategies and evaluation metrics. The paper finds evolutionary algorithms and gradient-based methods excel in specific contexts, emphasizes the need for robust metrics beyond IS and FID, and calls for more diverse datasets in GAN evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual design of GAN architectures is challenging and suboptimal. NAS offers automation for discovering effective GAN architectures, but the landscape of NAS-GAN methods is fragmented. A structured review and comparison is needed to guide future research.

Method: This is a survey/review paper that systematically categorizes and compares existing NAS approaches for GANs based on search strategies, evaluation metrics, and performance outcomes. No novel algorithm is proposed; instead, it provides a structured taxonomy and comparative analysis of the literature.

Result: Key findings: (1) evolutionary algorithms and gradient-based NAS methods demonstrate superiority in particular settings; (2) standard metrics like IS and FID are insufficient for robust GAN evaluation; (3) existing benchmarks lack dataset diversity, limiting the generalizability of performance assessments.

Conclusion: NAS significantly benefits GAN performance, stability, and efficiency. Future work should develop more robust evaluation metrics, employ diverse datasets, and build on the strengths of evolutionary and gradient-based search strategies to advance NAS-GAN research.

Abstract: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has emerged as a pivotal technique in optimizing the design of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), automating the search for effective architectures while addressing the challenges inherent in manual design. This paper provides a comprehensive review of NAS methods applied to GANs, categorizing and comparing various approaches based on criteria such as search strategies, evaluation metrics, and performance outcomes. The review highlights the benefits of NAS in improving GAN performance, stability, and efficiency, while also identifying limitations and areas for future research. Key findings include the superiority of evolutionary algorithms and gradient-based methods in certain contexts, the importance of robust evaluation metrics beyond traditional scores like Inception Score (IS) and Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), and the need for diverse datasets in assessing GAN performance. By presenting a structured comparison of existing NAS-GAN techniques, this paper aims to guide researchers in developing more effective NAS methods and advancing the field of GANs.

</details>


### [88] [KG-TRACE: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Mechanistic Grounding in Antimicrobial Resistance Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26179)
*Naman Garg,Sarika Jain,Sourav Yadav,Bharat K. Bhargava,Ghanapriya Singh,Abhishek Srivastava,Parimal Kar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KG-TRACE is a neuro-symbolic framework that integrates the WHO mutation knowledge graph with a neural genomic model for AMR prediction in M. tuberculosis. It uses RotatE-based KG embeddings and a learned epistemic trust gate to dynamically balance neural and symbolic evidence. Beyond achieving competitive predictive accuracy (AUROC 0.9760 for isoniazid), its core contribution is symbolic grounding, measured by the novel Biological Grounding Ratio (BGR), achieving 92.5% symbolic coverage and providing a verifiable audit trail for clinical trust.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing WGS-based AMR prediction models achieve high accuracy but operate as black boxes, lacking mechanisms to ground neural attributions in established biological pathways. This gap undermines clinical trust because predictions cannot be traced back to known resistance mechanisms recognized by clinicians.

Method: KG-TRACE is a neuro-symbolic framework that fuses (1) genomic features with (2) RotatE-based embeddings derived from the WHO mutation knowledge graph. A learned epistemic trust gate dynamically weights neural evidence against symbolic biological knowledge. The framework introduces the Biological Grounding Ratio (BGR) as a dataset-level metric quantifying alignment between neural attributions and established biology. It also flags 'UNCERTAIN' cases to identify potential MDR co-occurrence artifacts.

Result: Evaluated on the CRyPTIC M. tuberculosis cohort, KG-TRACE achieves an AUROC of 0.9760 for isoniazid resistance prediction. It attains 92.5% symbolic coverage of isoniazid-resistant predictions. The framework successfully identifies MDR co-occurrence artifacts via uncertainty flags.

Conclusion: Neuro-symbolic grounding bridges the gap between predictive accuracy and clinical trust by providing a verifiable audit trail. KG-TRACE demonstrates that integrating structured biological knowledge as a constraint yields not only competitive accuracy but, more critically, clinically interpretable and trustworthy predictions.

Abstract: While WGS-based AMR prediction has reached high accuracy, existing models lack a mechanism to ground neural attributions in established biological pathways. We present KG-TRACE, a novel neuro-symbolic framework that integrates the WHO mutation knowledge graph (KG) as a structured biological constraint on a neural genomic model. Unlike existing methods that learn statistical patterns in isolation, KG-TRACE fuses genomic features and RotatE-based KG embeddings through a learned epistemic trust gate, dynamically weighting neural evidence against symbolic biological knowledge.
  Evaluated on the CRyPTIC M. tuberculosis cohort, KG-TRACE achieves an AUROC of 0.9760 for isoniazid, achieving competitive accuracy while its primary value lies in symbolic grounding, not predictive uplift. More importantly, we introduce the Biological Grounding Ratio (BGR), a dataset-level metric that quantifies alignment between neural attributions and established biology. Our framework achieves a 92.5% symbolic coverage of isoniazid-resistant predictions and effectively identifies MDR co-occurrence artifacts by issuing laboratory follow-up flags for 'UNCERTAIN' cases. We demonstrate that neuro-symbolic grounding provides a verifiable audit trail for clinicians, bridging the gap between predictive accuracy and clinical trust.

</details>


### [89] [Necessary but Not Sufficient: Temperature Control and Reproducibility in LLM-as-Judge Safety Evaluations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26185)
*Hiroki Tamba*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Authors demonstrate that LLM-as-judge safety graders produce non-deterministic verdicts even at temperature=0, with non-trivial pass/fail flipping across identical runs. Two root causes identified: (1) harnesses failing to set temperature/seed, allowing provider defaults (T=1.0) to cause ~50% disagreement; (2) residual non-determinism persisting even under greedy decoding, affecting 1-2 of 7 borderline items. Claude's deprecation of temperature control further compounds the issue.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety evaluations using LLM graders gate downstream deployment decisions, yet the widespread assumption that temperature=0 guarantees deterministic grading has not been systematically tested. A single-run pass/fail verdict that is actually noisy could present instability as a safety property, warranting empirical investigation.

Method: The authors stress-tested Japan AISI's open-source aisev safety-evaluation harness against the determinism assumption at two levels: (1) default harness behavior where temperature/seed are unspecified, allowing provider-side defaults; (2) explicitly pinned temperature=0 with top_k=1 (greedy decoding). They ran 690 API calls across two providers, three model tiers, and five sampling configurations, measuring per-item pass/fail agreement across 20 identical runs on 7 borderline items.

Result: Without temperature/seed specification, per-item disagreement reached up to ~50% over 20 runs. Pinning temperature=0 substantially reduced but did not eliminate flips — 1-2 of 7 borderline items remained non-reproducible under greedy decoding. Claude Opus 4.7/4.8 has deprecated temperature entirely, making the primary mitigation (T=0) unavailable for newer models.

Conclusion: A structural gap exists in evaluation harnesses that report single-run verdicts without variance or grader-disagreement metrics. The authors recommend treating grader disagreement as a first-class health metric and release a reproduction harness (690 calls, 7 conditions) for community validation.

Abstract: LLM-as-judge ("grader") components are now standard in evaluation harnesses, including safety evaluations where a pass/fail verdict may gate downstream deployment decisions. A widespread assumption is that setting the grader's sampling temperature to 0 makes grading deterministic. We test this assumption against a real safety-evaluation codebase (Japan AISI's open-source aisev) and show it fails on two levels. First, the harness invokes its grader without setting temperature or seed; the underlying provider silently applies its default of 1.0, so items near the decision boundary flip pass/fail across identical runs (per-item disagreement up to ~50% over 20 runs). Second, pinning temperature=0 reduces but does not eliminate flips: across 690 API calls spanning two providers, three model tiers, and five sampling configurations, 1-2 of 7 borderline items remain non-reproducible even under forced greedy decoding (top_k=1). Claude Opus 4.7/4.8 has since deprecated temperature entirely, rendering the primary mitigation inapplicable to newer model generations. These findings expose a structural gap: evaluation harnesses that report single-run verdicts without variance or grader-disagreement metrics can present noise as a safety property. We release a reproduction harness (690 calls, 7 conditions) and recommend that harnesses treat grader disagreement as a first-class health metric alongside the scores themselves.

</details>


### [90] [Clue-Guided Money Laundering Group Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26189)
*Boyang Wang,Jianing Cao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes Clue-Guided Group Discovery (CGGD), a new AML paradigm where investigators start from an initial clue and iteratively recover the full laundering group. Introduces Clue2Group, a framework using local context construction, multi-semantic local-temporal GNN-based risk field estimation, and multi-evidence integration to progressively uncover criminal groups, bridging graph AML research with real investigation workflows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing node-level anomaly detection and global group discovery methods are mismatched with real AML investigations, where analysts start from a concrete clue (e.g., a suspicious account) and gradually expand outward to recover the entire responsible criminal group. No existing method addresses this clue-driven, interactive investigation paradigm.

Method: Proposes CGGD, a task formulation where a laundering group is progressively recovered from an initial clue set through analyst interaction. The Clue2Group framework has three components: (1) compact local investigation context construction to reduce noise while preserving chain-like and cycle-like laundering structures; (2) a multi-semantic local-temporal GNN that estimates a clue-conditioned local risk field; (3) integration of risk, structural, and prior-pattern evidence to recover a coherent laundering group.

Result: Experiments on two large-scale AML benchmarks demonstrate that Clue2Group provides a practical clue-driven analysis framework, effectively supporting real-world AML investigation paradigms.

Conclusion: Clue2Group offers a feasible step toward bridging the gap between graph-based AML research and real investigation workflows by introducing clue-guided, interactive group discovery that aligns with how analysts actually conduct money laundering investigations.

Abstract: Money Laundering Group Discovery (MLGD) aims to identify hidden criminal groups and recover their complete structures in large-scale financial networks. Existing graph anomaly detection methods mainly produce node-level risk alerts, while global group discovery methods passively search for suspicious groups over the whole network. Both are mismatched with real Anti-money-laundering (AML) investigations, where analysts usually start from a concrete clue and gradually expand the investigation to recover the responsible group. To address this gap, we propose Clue-Guided Group Discovery (CGGD), where a laundering group is progressively recovered from an initial clue set through analyst interaction. We further propose Clue2Group, a framework that first constructs a compact local investigation context to reduce noise and preserve chain-like and cycle-like laundering structures. It then estimates a clue-conditioned local risk field with a multi-semantic local-temporal GNN, and finally integrates risk, structural, and prior-pattern evidence to recover a coherent laundering group. Experiments on two large-scale AML benchmarks show that Clue2Group provides a practical clue-driven analysis framework for AML investigations, offering a feasible step toward bridging the gap between graph-based AML research and real investigation workflows.

</details>


### [91] [Federated Hash Projected Latent Factor Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26192)
*Jialan He*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FHPLF integrates Hash Learning into Federated Learning by replacing real-valued gradients with binary gradient-like matrices, using Projected Hamming Distance for similarity modeling, and employing a secure binary gradient reassembly strategy — achieving strong accuracy, efficiency, and privacy trade-offs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional Hash Learning requires centralized data upload, violating data privacy regulations. Federated Learning avoids centralization but incurs high communication overhead and privacy risks from transmitting real-valued gradients. Existing HL+FL integration suffers from limited binary code representational capacity, degrading accuracy. A method is needed that simultaneously achieves low communication cost, strong privacy, and high accuracy.

Method: FHPLF proposes three innovations: (a) binary gradient-like matrices replace real-valued gradient matrices to reduce computation, storage, and communication while enhancing privacy; (b) Projected Hamming Distance captures per-bit importance for improved similarity modeling and representational capacity; (c) a Secure Binary Gradient Reassembly and Privacy-Enhanced Upload (SBG-PEU) strategy mitigates leakage of user interaction patterns during transmission.

Result: Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets show FHPLF consistently outperforms state-of-the-art Hash Learning and Federated Learning methods, achieving a favorable trade-off among accuracy, efficiency, and privacy preservation.

Conclusion: FHPLF effectively addresses the integration of Hash Learning and Federated Learning, overcoming representational capacity limitations of binary codes while significantly reducing communication costs and privacy risks. The model demonstrates superior performance across multiple real-world datasets.

Abstract: Hash Learning (HL) is an efficient representation learning approach that maps real-valued data into compact binary representations. Traditional HL methods typically require users to upload personal data to a central server, which is incompatible with increasingly stringent data security regulations. Federated Learning (FL) provides a decentralized paradigm for learning globally optimal models without centralizing private data. However, most FL methods rely on transmitting large-scale real-valued gradient information, leading to high communication overhead and potential privacy risks. Integrating HL into FL is a promising solution. Nevertheless, existing HL methods suffer from limited representational capacity of binary codes, which may degrade model accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose a Federated Hash Projected Latent Factor (FHPLF) model. FHPLF introduces three key innovations: (a) replacing real-valued gradient matrices with binary gradient-like matrices, significantly reducing computation, storage, and communication costs while enhancing privacy protection; (b) leveraging Projected Hamming Distance for similarity modeling, which captures the importance of individual binary bits to improve representation capability; and (c) proposing a Secure Binary Gradient Reassembly and Privacy-Enhanced Upload (SBG-PEU) strategy to further reduce the risk of user interaction leakage during transmission. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate that FHPLF consistently outperforms state-of-the-art HL and FL methods, achieving a favorable trade-off among accuracy, efficiency, and privacy preservation.

</details>


### [92] [Statistical and Structural Approaches to Algorithmic Fairness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26200)
*Antonio Ferrara*

Main category: cs.LG
