TL;DR: This thesis critiques two core limitations in algorithmic fairness: reliance on deterministic point estimates for auditing and the treatment of individuals as atomistic entities stripped of structural context. It argues that modern ML systems function as socio-technical architectures that mediate access to opportunity, and that early fairness interventions failed due to oversimplified assumptions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern machine learning systems have evolved beyond isolated predictive tools into socio-technical architectures that mediate human opportunity. As these algorithms increasingly gate-keep access to economic and social resources, they embed and perpetuate the structural inequalities present in their training environments. While the field of algorithmic fairness arose to address systematic disadvantage against marginalized groups, early mitigation strategies proved inadequate due to fragile simplifications that fail in complex real-world settings.

Method: The thesis employs a critical analytical approach, identifying and interrogating two foundational limitations: (1) the dependence on deterministic point estimates for fairness auditing, which collapses uncertainty and variability into single-value metrics, and (2) the conceptualization of individuals as isolated, decontextualized entities, which erases the structural and relational dimensions of social position.

Result: The analysis reveals that deterministic point estimates in auditing obscure the distributional nature of fairness-related quantities, while atomistic treatment of individuals ignores the structural constraints and relational contexts that produce disparate outcomes. Both limitations render fairness interventions brittle and insufficient in complex socio-technical environments.

Conclusion: Contemporary algorithmic fairness paradigms are fundamentally constrained by their deterministic and individualistic assumptions. Addressing these twin limitations — embracing uncertainty-aware auditing and structurally embedded conceptions of personhood — is necessary for developing fairness interventions that are robust in real-world socio-technical systems.

Abstract: Modern machine learning systems have outgrown their origins as isolated predictive constructs, evolving into complex socio-technical architectures that actively mediate human opportunity. As algorithms increasingly determine access to economic and social opportunities, it has become widely recognized that these systems are deeply embedded with the structural inequalities and prejudices of their environments. The field of algorithmic fairness emerged in response to the growing recognition that models optimized for predictive accuracy can systematically disadvantage marginalized groups. Early mitigation strategies, however, rested on fragile simplifications that limited their effectiveness in complex socio-technical environments. This thesis identifies and addresses two fundamental limitations of contemporary fairness paradigms: the reliance on deterministic point estimates for auditing and the treatment of individuals as isolated entities devoid of structural context.

</details>


### [93] [Topology-Informed Neural Networks for Flood Detection in Optical and Synthetic Aperture Radar Imagery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26204)
*Sophia Li,Max Zhao,Raghu G. Raj,Tianyu Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper evaluates topological data analysis (TDA) descriptors for flood detection using the SEN12-FLOOD dataset, demonstrating that topological features carry independent flood signals and complement neural networks to improve robustness and interpretability compared to black-box CNN or transformer models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current deep learning models (CNNs, vision transformers) for satellite-based flood detection operate as opaque black boxes, making their decision boundaries and internal reasoning difficult to interpret — a critical limitation for safety-sensitive remote sensing applications. Additionally, cloud cover complicates optical imagery analysis, and there is a need for methods that capture global structural features beyond local pixel patterns.

Method: The authors systematically extract topological descriptors from each image in the SEN12-FLOOD dataset using topological data analysis (TDA) and incorporate these features into neural networks. They evaluate whether TDA features carry independent flood signals and whether they complement existing CNN/transformer architectures to improve robustness and interpretability.

Result: Topological descriptors were shown to carry meaningful flood signals independently. When integrated with neural networks, they produced more robust and interpretable flood detection systems compared to standard black-box models.

Conclusion: TDA provides a mathematically grounded framework for capturing global structural features of flood imagery. Incorporating topological features offers a promising direction for building flood detection systems that are both more robust and more interpretable than purely deep learning-based approaches.

Abstract: Floods frequently impact regions around the world. Rapid and accurate flood detection is crucial for emergency response and timely mitigation of human and economic loss. The expanding availability of satellite data and advances in artificial intelligence have enhanced monitoring of environmental hazards, but many flood events remain challenging to detect because cloud cover obscures optical satellite imagery. Rambour et al. introduced the SEN12-FLOOD dataset and extracted per-image features using a ResNet-50 convolutional neural network backbone, then fed these features into a gated recurrent unit network to show that temporal information can substantially improve accuracy compared to single-image baselines. More recently, Chamatidis et al. showed that a vision transformer can achieve strong performance with popular convolutional architectures. However, these models typically function as opaque black boxes, making it difficult to interpret their decision boundaries, learned features, and internal reasoning, especially in safety-critical domains like remote sensing. In contrast, topological data analysis (TDA) provides a mathematically grounded framework for capturing global structural features of data. TDA has emerged as a powerful tool for analyzing complex imagery, especially imagery with geometrically interpretable structures, of which floods are a prime candidate. In this work, we systematically evaluate topological descriptors for flood detection using the open-source SEN12-FLOOD dataset. By extracting topological features from each image and incorporating them into neural networks, we demonstrate that topological descriptors carry meaningful flood signals independently and complement existing networks to yield more robust and interpretable flood detection systems.

</details>


### [94] [A General Framework for Learning Algebraic Properties from Cayley Graphs using Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26212)
*Tal Weissblat*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A GNN-based framework is developed to predict multiple algebraic properties (abelianity, nilpotency, solvability) of finite groups from their Cayley graphs, demonstrating that substantial algebraic structure can be recovered purely from graph representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work [1] introduced GNNs for predicting solvability from Cayley graphs. This paper generalizes that approach to a property-independent framework, investigating whether a unified GNN architecture can learn and distinguish multiple algebraic properties of finite groups solely from Cayley graph representations.

Method: A common GNN architecture and training pipeline is applied to Cayley graphs of finite groups drawn from several families. The framework is evaluated on three representative algebraic properties: abelianity, nilpotency, and solvability, treating property prediction as a graph-level classification task.

Result: The framework successfully learns and distinguishes all three algebraic properties from Cayley graph representations, indicating that significant algebraic information is encoded in the graph structure and can be extracted by GNNs.

Conclusion: The results serve as a proof of concept that graph representation learning can be fruitfully applied to studying algebraic properties of finite groups, with the framework being property-independent and extensible to other group-theoretic properties.

Abstract: A Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework for predicting the solvability of finite groups from their Cayley graph representations was introduced in [1]. In the present work, we generalize this approach and develop a property-independent framework for learning algebraic properties of finite groups directly from Cayley graphs. As representative case studies, we consider abelianity, nilpotency, and solvability. Using a common GNN architecture and training pipeline, we investigate the extent to which algebraic structure can be recovered from graph-based representations alone. Results on a collection of finite groups drawn from several families demonstrate that the framework successfully learns and distinguishes multiple algebraic properties from their associated Cayley graphs. These findings suggest that substantial algebraic information is encoded in graph representations and can be extracted through GNNs. More broadly, the proposed framework provides a proof of concept for applying graph representation learning to the study of algebraic properties of finite groups.

</details>


### [95] [Fast LeWorldModel](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26217)
*Yuntian Gao,Xiangyu Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Fast-LeWM replaces autoregressive latent rollout in visual planning with parallel action-prefix prediction, reducing computational cost and accumulated errors while improving planning success.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing JEPA-based world models like LeWM use repeated one-step latent transitions for planning, causing (1) high computational cost from autoregressive rollout and (2) accumulated latent errors that degrade trajectory quality over long horizons.

Method: Fast-LeWM introduces action-prefix prediction: given the current latent state and a candidate action sequence, it encodes all prefixes of the sequence and predicts, in parallel, the future latents reached after executing each prefix. This makes action prefixes — rather than single-step transitions — the basic prediction unit, with prefix-level supervision forcing the model to learn continuous state evolution under varying horizons. During planning, the final prefix token directly yields the corresponding future latent, eliminating explicit intermediate rollout.

Result: Fast-LeWM achieves higher average task success than LeWM, substantially reduces planning time, and yields lower open-loop latent loss whose growth decelerates significantly as rollout horizon increases.

Conclusion: Action-prefix prediction is an effective replacement for autoregressive latent rollout in JEPA-based world models, offering both efficiency gains and improved long-horizon prediction quality.

Abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs), including recent LeWorldModel (LeWM), have become a promising foundation for reconstruction-free visual world models. For visual planning, however, LeWM evaluates candidate action sequences by repeatedly applying a local one-step latent transition model. This autoregressive rollout makes planning computationally expensive and exposes the predicted trajectory to accumulated latent errors as the horizon grows. We propose Fast LeWorldModel (Fast-LeWM), a fast latent world model that replaces repeated local rollout with action-prefix prediction. Given the current latent and a candidate action sequence, Fast-LeWM encodes its prefixes and predicts the future latents reached after executing those prefixes in parallel. By making action prefixes the basic prediction unit, Fast-LeWM directly models action effects accumulated to different extents over multiple horizons. This prefix-level supervision forces the model to learn how states continuously evolve under different action prefixes, rather than only fitting one-step state transitions. During planning, the predictor can use the last prefix token from the encoded action sequence to evaluate the corresponding future latent without explicitly rolling through each intermediate imagined state. Across multiple tasks, Fast-LeWM improves average success over LeWM while substantially reducing planning time, achieving lower open-loop latent loss whose growth becomes significantly slower as the rollout horizon increases.

</details>


### [96] [Dataset Usage Inference without Shadow Models or Held-out Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26257)
*Wojciech Łapacz,Stanisław Pawlak,Jan Dubiński,Franziska Boenisch,Adam Dziedzic*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A practical Dataset Usage Inference (DUI) framework that estimates what fraction of a dataset was used to train a model, requiring neither shadow models nor held-out data — instead leveraging synthetic non-member samples, diverse membership signals, and mixture proportion estimation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing DUI methods are impractical for real-world use because they require training expensive shadow models and assume access to both known training samples and a verified in-distribution held-out set. These constraints fail for modern large models and genuine data ownership disputes.

Method: The proposed framework eliminates shadow models and real held-out data. It generates synthetic non-member samples, extracts diverse membership signals from the target model, and reformulates DUI as a mixture proportion estimation problem to infer the share of a candidate dataset used in training.

Result: Experiments on large image generative models demonstrate that the method reliably quantifies dataset usage.

Conclusion: The framework provides a practical, assumption-free tool for data owners to audit training data usage in machine learning models, closing the gap between theoretical DUI methods and real-world applicability.

Abstract: How much of my data was used to train a machine learning model? Dataset Usage Inference (DUI) aims to answer this by estimating what fraction of a dataset contributed to a model's training. However, existing DUI methods rely on assumptions that rarely hold in practice: they require training expensive shadow models to imitate the target model, and they assume access to both known training samples and an in-distribution held-out set confirmed to be absent from training. These conditions make current approaches impractical for modern large models and real data ownership disputes. We introduce a practical DUI framework that removes these constraints. Our method requires neither shadow models nor real held-out data. Instead, it generates synthetic non-member samples, extracts diverse membership signals, and casts DUI as a mixture proportion estimation problem to estimate what share of the candidate dataset was used during training. Experiments on large image generative models show that our method reliably quantifies dataset usage, providing a practical tool for data owners to determine how much of their data was used to train a model.

</details>


### [97] [Equivariance and Augmentation for Bayesian Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26273)
*Miaowen Dong,Axel Flinth,Jan E. Gerken*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies data augmentation for Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) trained with variational inference, deriving conditions for exact equivariance, bounding equivariance error, and proposing three novel symmetrization techniques. The orbit expansion method outperforms baselines in both equivariance and overall performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is an ongoing debate about whether to impose symmetry constraints via equivariant neural network architectures or learn symmetries through data augmentation. While equivariant networks are well-studied theoretically, data augmentation lacks rigorous understanding due to the difficulty in analyzing training dynamics. This paper aims to bridge this gap by studying data augmentation in Bayesian neural networks with variational inference.

Method: The authors analyze variational inference in Bayesian neural networks with exponential family variational distributions. They derive conditions for exact equivariance, establish bounds on equivariance error, and introduce three symmetrization techniques: orbit expansion, posterior symmetrization, and KL symmetrization. The analysis leverages recent results on augmented infinite deep ensembles and focuses on the interplay between data augmentation and variational Bayesian training dynamics.

Result: The paper derives theoretical conditions under which exact equivariance is attained in BNNs with variational inference and data augmentation. It provides bounds on equivariance error. Among three proposed symmetrization methods, orbit expansion consistently outperforms the baseline in both equivariance and overall predictive performance across extensive numerical experiments.

Conclusion: Data augmentation can induce equivariance in Bayesian neural networks under specific conditions, and the proposed orbit expansion technique is particularly effective. The work provides both theoretical grounding and practical methods for enforcing symmetry via augmentation rather than architectural constraints, with code publicly available.

Abstract: Symmetries are important for many deep learning tasks, ranging from applications in the sciences to medical imaging. However, there is an ongoing debate about whether to impose symmetry constraints on the neural network architecture (yielding equivariant neural networks) or learn them from augmented training data. Although equivariant networks are well-studied theoretically, much less is known about data augmentation, since analyzing augmentation requires control over the training dynamics. Inspired by recent results that show that augmented infinite deep ensembles are exactly equivariant, we study data augmentation for Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) trained with variational inference. We focus on variational distributions in the exponential family and derive conditions under which exact equivariance is reached. We furthermore obtain bounds on the equivariance error and introduce three novel symmetrization techniques which boost the effect of data augmentation in this setting. We conduct extensive numerical experiments which show that one of our symmetrization methods (orbit expansion) outperforms the baseline in both equivariance and overall performance. Our code is available at github.com/dmw1998/augment-BNNs

</details>


### [98] [SSM Adapters via Hankel Reduced-order Modeling: Injection Site Determines Task Suitability in Long-Context Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26290)
*Omanshu Thapliyal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces HRM (Hankel Reduced order Model) adapters, SSM-based PEFT modules initialized via balanced truncation of empirical Hankel Gramians, which achieve computational parity with LoRA through FFT-based parallel scans. HRM significantly outperforms LoRA on long-context tasks like QuALITY and QMSum, and excels in state-tracking and character-level language modeling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: PEFT research has largely focused on attention projectors, leaving sequential state accumulation tasks underexplored. The authors investigate whether SSM-based adapters can better serve such tasks and whether MLP blocks are more suitable injection sites than attention layers.

Method: The HRM adapter is an SSM-based residual module initialized via Balanced Truncation of empirical Hankel Grammians. By exploiting the time-invariance of the system matrix \bar{A}, HRM uses an exact FFT-based parallel scan for efficient computation matching LoRA's complexity at all context lengths. Evaluated iso-parametrically on Mistral-7B with 8.4M trainable parameters.

Result: HRM outperforms LoRA variants on LongBench: +34.8% relative accuracy on QuALITY, +71.6% relative ROUGE-1 on QMSum. It demonstrates consistent superiority across 18 synthetic configurations (DFA, Parity state-tracking) and character-level language modeling (enwik8). Gate analysis shows HRM adapters effectively learn recurrence modulation.

Conclusion: HRM adapters provide a robust, computationally efficient alternative to low-rank adaptation for long-context sequence modeling, particularly for tasks requiring state accumulation, offering a new PEFT architectural paradigm leveraging SSM dynamics.

Abstract: While parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) typically targets attention projectors, its efficacy for tasks requiring sequential state accumulation remains under-explored. We examine if PEFT for such tasks can benefit from state space model (SSMs) adapters, and if MLP blocks are better injection sites. We introduce Hankel Reduced order Model (HRM) adapter, an SSM-based residual module initialized via Balanced Truncation of empirical Hankel Grammians. By leveraging the time-invariance of the system matrix $\bar{A}$, HRM enables an exact FFT-based parallel scan, achieving computational parity with LoRA across all context lengths. In iso-parametric evaluations on Mistral-7B (8.4M trainable parameters), HRM outperforms LoRA variants on LongBench tasks, including QuALITY (+34.8\% relative accuracy) and QMSum (+71.6\% relative ROUGE-1). HRM further demonstrates consistent superiority across 18 configurations of synthetic state-tracking (DFA, Parity) and character-level language modeling (enwik8). Gate analysis reveals that HRM adapters effectively learn to modulate recurrence, providing a robust architectural alternative to low-rank adaptation for long-context sequence modeling.

</details>


### [99] [High-Probability PL-SGD with Markovian Noise: Optimal Mixing and Tail Dependence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26316)
*Dhruv Sarkar,Aprameyo Chakrabartty,Vaneet Aggarwal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper establishes tight high-probability convergence bounds for SGD under the Polyak-Łojasiewicz condition with Markovian gradient samples. For light-tailed noise, a lag-blocking argument closes the gap between prior high-probability and expectation bounds, achieving optimal linear dependence on mixing time. For heavy-tailed noise with finite p-moment, a clipped block method attains optimal polynomial dependence on mixing time, with matching lower bounds in both regimes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior high-probability bounds for SGD with Markovian gradients under the PL condition exhibited a quadratic dependence on mixing time O(t_mix²/k), while expectation bounds scaled linearly O(t_mix/k). This gap had not been resolved. Additionally, the heavy-tailed Markovian setting lacked tight characterizations of the optimal dependence on mixing time and tail exponent.

Method: For the light-tailed setting, the authors employ a lag-blocking argument with geometrically mixing Markov chains to derive uniform high-probability bounds scaling linearly with mixing time. A matching lower bound is constructed via a quadratic objective driven by a persistent two-state Markov chain. For the heavy-tailed regime (finite p-moment, p∈(1,2]), they design an all-samples clipped block method that uses every Markov transition while controlling Markovian bias. Lower bounds are established by reducing PL optimization to heavy-tailed mean estimation for a sticky Markov chain.

Result: In the light-tailed setting, the high-probability stochastic term scales as Õ(t_mix/(k+K₀)), matching the linear expectation bound and improving on the prior Õ(t_mix²/k). A matching Ω(σ² t_mix/k) lower bound proves optimality. In the heavy-tailed regime, the clipped block method achieves Õ(σ_p² (t_mix/T)^(2(p-1)/p)) high-probability error under transition budget T, with a matching lower bound confirming optimality in both the heavy-tail exponent and effective-sample-size dependence.

Conclusion: The work tightly characterizes the optimal polynomial dependence on mixing time for PL-SGD with light-tailed Markovian gradients, and establishes the optimal heavy-tail exponent and effective-sample-size dependence in the robust regime. The linear mixing time dependence is proven both achievable and optimal, closing a notable gap in the literature.

Abstract: We study first-order methods for smooth objectives satisfying the Polyak-Łojasiewicz (PL) condition when gradient samples are generated by an exogenous Markov chain. In the light-tailed setting, prior uniform-in-time high-probability bounds for ordinary Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) under a standard growth envelope scale as $\widetilde{O}(t_{mix}^2/k)$, leaving a gap with the $\widetilde{O}(t_{mix}/k)$ expectation bounds. We close this gap using a lag-blocking argument to establish a uniform high-probability guarantee with a leading stochastic term of $\widetilde{O}(t_{mix}/(k+K_0))$ under geometric mixing. We prove this linear dependence on the mixing time is optimal via a matching $Ω(σ^2 t_{mix}/k)$ lower bound on a quadratic objective driven by a persistent two-state chain.
  We then extend this framework to heavy-tailed Markovian gradients satisfying a stationary finite-$p$-moment condition, $p \in (1,2]$. We design an all-samples clipped block method that uses every Markov transition while mitigating Markovian bias. Under a transition budget $T$, this algorithm achieves a high-probability stochastic error of $\widetilde{O}(σ_p^2(t_{mix}/T)^{2(p-1)/p})$. We establish a matching lower bound by reducing PL optimization to heavy-tailed mean estimation for a sticky Markov chain. Ultimately, this work tightly characterizes the optimal polynomial dependence on mixing time for light-tailed PL-SGD, and the optimal heavy-tail exponent and effective-sample-size dependence in the robust regime.

</details>


### [100] [EVOM: Agentic Meta-Evolution of Actor-Critic Architectures for Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26327)
*Boyun Zhang,Chao Wang,Kai Wu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EVOM is a meta-evolution framework that uses an LLM-based design agent to automatically discover high-performance actor-critic architectures for reinforcement learning, outperforming manual designs and existing automated methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Actor-critic RL architectures are typically handcrafted, which is suboptimal. Automating architecture search is difficult because: (1) each candidate network must be fully trained before evaluation, making it computationally expensive, and (2) the architecture design space is open-ended, precluding simple brute-force search.

Method: EVOM frames architecture search as bi-level optimization. The inner loop trains network weights using low-fidelity PPO for efficient candidate evaluation. The outer loop performs meta-evolution: an LLM-based design agent iteratively refines architecture programs. Critically, the LLM agent acts solely as an architecture designer, fully decoupled from policy execution and environment interaction, ensuring clean separation of concerns.

Result: EVOM surpasses the manually designed baseline, LLM-guided random search, and the state-of-the-art LLM-guided programmatic policy search method MLES on Ant-v4 and HalfCheetah-v4 tasks. Ablation studies confirm that both the meta-evolution loop and the LLM Design Agent are essential for achieving the reported performance.

Conclusion: The proposed agentic meta-evolution framework effectively automates actor-critic architecture discovery in RL, with the LLM designer and evolutionary outer loop both proving indispensable. This demonstrates the viability of LLM-driven architecture search for reinforcement learning.

Abstract: In actor-critic reinforcement learning, network architectures are typically manually designed. Automating this design is challenging because each candidate must be trained before evaluation, and the design space is open-ended. To address these challenges, we introduce EVOM, an agentic meta-evolution framework for discovering high-performance actor-critic architectures. We frame architecture search as a bi-level optimization: an inner loop trains weights via the low-fidelity proximal policy optimization (PPO), while an outer loop drives meta-evolution by iteratively refining architecture programs. Crucially, this outer loop is powered by an LLM-based design agent that operates purely as an architecture designer, completely decoupled from policy execution and environment control. Experiments reveal that EVOM outperforms the manually designed baseline, an LLM-guided random search, and the state-of-the-art LLM-guided programmatic policy search method MLES, delivering superior performance on Ant-v4 and HalfCheetah-v4. Ablation studies validate that both the meta-evolution loop and the LLM Design Agent are indispensable for final performance.

</details>


### [101] [Mesh-RL: Coupled subgrid reinforcement learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26333)
*Behnam Gheshlaghi,Bahador Rashidi,Shahin Atakishiyev*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Mesh-RL applies finite element method-inspired spatial domain decomposition to RL, partitioning environments into overlapping subgrids with boundary-consistent TD updates, enabling localized learning with globally coherent value propagation to accelerate long-range credit assignment in sparse-reward settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reinforcement learning in large or sparse-reward environments suffers from slow temporal-difference reward propagation because value information spreads only locally across the state space. Existing solutions (hierarchical, model-based) modify reward functions, Bellman operators, or add planning mechanisms. The authors seek a principled approach that accelerates credit assignment without these modifications.

Method: Mesh-RL partitions the environment into overlapping subgrids using spatial domain-decomposition inspired by finite element methods. It enforces boundary-consistent temporal-difference updates across subdomain interfaces, enabling localized learning within each subgrid while maintaining globally coherent value propagation through consistency constraints at overlapping boundaries.

Result: Evaluated on hazard-dense grid-world environments, Mesh-RL consistently improved convergence speed, cumulative reward, and learning stability across Q-learning, SARSA, and Dyna-Q. Higher mesh resolutions sustained exploration, prevented premature convergence, and accelerated value propagation. Dyna-Q gained additional benefits from decomposition despite its internal planning.

Conclusion: Mesh-RL provides a principled spatial domain-decomposition framework bridging finite element method boundary-consistency techniques from scientific computing with reinforcement learning, improving sample efficiency in sparse-reward environments without modifying reward functions or Bellman operators.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning in large or sparse-reward environments suffers from slow temporal-difference reward propagation, as value information spreads only locally across the state space. We propose Mesh-RL, a spatial domain-decomposition framework inspired by the finite element method and domain decomposition theory, which partitions the environment into overlapping subgrids and enforces boundary-consistent temporal-difference updates. Such an approach enables localized learning while ensuring globally coherent value propagation. Unlike hierarchical or model-based approaches, Mesh-RL accelerates long-range credit assignment without modifying the reward function, Bellman operator, or introducing explicit planning mechanisms. We evaluate Mesh-RL on hazard-dense grid-world environments with varying geometries and mesh resolutions. Across Q-learning, SARSA, and Dyna-Q, Mesh-RL consistently improves convergence speed, cumulative reward, and learning stability. Higher mesh resolutions sustain exploration, prevent premature convergence, and substantially accelerate value propagation to distant states. While Dyna-Q already benefits from internal planning, it still achieves additional gains under structured decomposition. Overall, Mesh-RL introduces a principled spatial domain-decomposition mechanism for accelerating temporal-difference learning. Our framework bridges finite element method-inspired boundary-consistency techniques from scientific computing with reinforcement learning to improve sample efficiency in sparse-reward environments. We will release source code of the study.

</details>


### [102] [EMA-FS: Accelerating GBDT Training via Gain-Informed Feature Screening](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26337)
*Yan Song*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EMA-FS accelerates GBDT training by using historical split gains to prioritize high-utility features for histogram construction, achieving up to 2.61x speedup on dense data with minimal AUC loss, while its stochastic variant (S-EMA-FS) unifies deterministic screening and random subsampling under a single framework.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GBDT training (e.g., LightGBM) spends 65–70% of time building per-feature histograms. Existing random feature subsampling (feature_fraction) discards features indiscriminately, ignoring predictive value. The authors aim to replace this blind subsampling with an informed screening mechanism that retains high-gain features and eliminates low-gain ones, thereby reducing wasted computation without sacrificing model quality.

Method: EMA-FS maintains an exponential moving average of per-feature split gains across boosting iterations. After a short warmup period, each tree restricts histogram construction to the top-K features ranked by their historical EMA gain. The approach operates per-tree, preserving LightGBM's histogram subtraction trick and requiring no changes to core routines. S-EMA-FS extends this by replacing deterministic top-K selection with gain-weighted random sampling governed by a concentration parameter β, where β → ∞ recovers deterministic EMA-FS and β = 0 recovers uniform random subsampling. Both methods are implemented in ~120 lines of C++ across all six LightGBM tree learners.

Result: On dense, moderate-to-high-dimensional data: 2.61x speedup on a 500-feature synthetic benchmark and 1.45x on the 432-feature IEEE-CIS Fraud dataset at 30% feature retention. At 70% retention, AUC improves by 0.11 points with 1.34x speedup. On extremely sparse data (Bosch, >90% missing), no speedup is observed — LightGBM's sparse bin optimization already skips empty values. The method remains fully backward-compatible.

Conclusion: EMA-FS and S-EMA-FS provide a lightweight, informed alternative to random feature subsampling in GBDT training. They deliver significant training speedups on dense, moderate-to-high-dimensional data while maintaining or improving predictive performance, and degrade gracefully to existing behavior on sparse data. The unified stochastic framework allows practitioners to interpolate between exploration and exploitation in feature selection.

Abstract: Gradient Boosted Decision Trees (GBDT), exemplified by LightGBM, spend a dominant fraction of training time -- typically 65-70% -- constructing per-feature histograms. Existing approaches such as random feature subsampling (feature_fraction) discard features without regard for their predictive utility. We propose EMA-based Feature Screening (EMA-FS), an algorithm-level optimization that maintains an exponential moving average (EMA) of per-feature split gains across boosting iterations and, after a short warmup, restricts histogram construction to the top-K features ranked by historical gain. Unlike random subsampling, EMA-FS is informed: it retains high-gain features while screening out low-gain ones. Operating at the per-tree level, it preserves full compatibility with LightGBM's histogram subtraction trick, requiring no changes to core routines.
  We evaluate EMA-FS on datasets spanning financial fraud detection, advertising click-through prediction, industrial quality control, and synthetic benchmarks, with feature dimensionalities from 29 to 968. On dense, moderate-to-high-dimensional data it achieves significant speedups: 2.61x on a 500-feature synthetic benchmark and 1.45x on the 432-feature IEEE-CIS Fraud dataset at 30% retention. At 70% retention it improves AUC by 0.11 points while delivering a 1.34x speedup. On extremely sparse data (Bosch, >90% missing) it yields no speedup, as LightGBM's sparse bin optimization already bypasses empty values.
  We further introduce Stochastic EMA-FS (S-EMA-FS), which replaces deterministic top-K selection with gain-weighted random sampling controlled by a concentration parameter beta, unifying deterministic EMA-FS (beta -> infinity) and random subsampling (beta = 0) in one framework. Both are implemented in ~120 lines of C++ across all six LightGBM tree learners and are fully backward-compatible.

</details>


### [103] [Does Aurora Encode Atmospheric Structure? Latent Regime Analysis and Attribution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26361)
*Emma Kasteleyn,Ana Lucic*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper probes the internal representations of the Aurora atmospheric foundation model using PCA and LRP, finding its latent space is organized by seasonal cycles rather than extreme events, and that the model learns physically meaningful vertical structures without explicit supervision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Foundation models for atmospheric dynamics are highly performant yet remain black boxes. The authors aim to open the hood of the Aurora model to understand what meteorological features its latent space captures and whether it develops physically coherent internal representations.

Method: The authors apply spatially pooled Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to Aurora's latent space to identify dominant modes of variation, and Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) to attribute predictions to input features. They also conduct perturbation experiments, masking relevant vs. random regions to quantify the impact on forecast degradation.

Result: PCA reveals the latent space is primarily structured by seasonal cycles; extreme storm events do not form linearly separable clusters. LRP shows the model attends to features aligned with the 3D vertical structure of the Great Storm of 1987. Masking LRP-identified relevant regions degrades forecasts 3.31× more than random masking.

Conclusion: Aurora learns meteorologically coherent representations, including vertical structure, without explicit instruction, suggesting foundation models can internally develop physically meaningful features that go beyond surface-level pattern matching.

Abstract: ML foundation models are able to emulate atmospheric dynamics accurately and efficiently but operate as opaque ``black boxes''. We investigate the internal representations of the Aurora model using spatially pooled PCA and layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP). We find evidence that Aurora's latent space is primarily organized by seasonal cycles, whereas extreme storm events do not form a linearly separable cluster. LRP indicates that the model attends to features consistent with the 3D vertical structure of the Great Storm of 1987. Perturbation tests show masking relevant regions degrades forecasts $3.31\times$ more than random masking. These findings suggest that Aurora learns meteorological coherence and vertical structure without explicit instruction.

</details>


### [104] [At the Edge of Understanding: Sparse Autoencoders Trace The Limits of Transformer Generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26396)
*Praneet Suresh,Jack Stanley,Sonia Joseph,Luca Scimeca,Danilo Bzdok*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a mechanistic framework to analyze how out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs — from typos to jailbreak prompts — cause transformers to activate more fallacious internal concepts. The authors leverage this insight to quantify distributional shift and develop a mechanistically grounded fine-tuning strategy to robustify LLMs, extending the notion of OOD from input data to the model's internal computational processes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pre-trained transformers show strong generalization but lack explicit mechanisms to handle unexpected or adversarial inputs that diverge from training distributions. This degrades model reliability and safety in real-world deployments, motivating a disciplined, mechanistic study of OOD robustness in transformers beyond surface-level input analysis.

Method: The authors conduct systematic experiments to map transformer robustness boundaries. They identify that OOD inputs (e.g., typos, jailbreak prompts) cause models to rely on an increased number of "fallacious concepts" in their internal representations. Using this phenomenon as a diagnostic signal, they quantify the degree of distributional shift in prompts and develop a fine-tuning strategy grounded in these mechanistic findings to improve robustness.

Result: OOD inputs consistently drive language models to operate on more fallacious internal concepts. This mechanistic signal effectively quantifies distributional shift in prompts. The resulting fine-tuning strategy demonstrably robustifies LLMs against distributional shifts.

Conclusion: Expanding the definition of OOD from input data to a model's internal computational processes represents a critical diagnostic advance. This inference-time diagnostic framework is a key step toward making AI systems safer for deployment across science, business, and government.

Abstract: Pre-trained transformers have demonstrated remarkable generalization abilities, at times extending beyond the scope of their training data. Yet, real-world deployments often face unexpected or adversarial data that diverges from training data distributions. Without explicit mechanisms for handling such shifts, model reliability and safety degrade, urging more disciplined study of out-of-distribution (OOD) settings for transformers. By systematic experiments, we present a mechanistic framework for delineating the precise contours of transformer model robustness. We find that OOD inputs, including subtle typos and jailbreak prompts, drive language models to operate on an increased number of fallacious concepts in their internals. We leverage this device to quantify and understand the degree of distributional shift in prompts, enabling a mechanistically grounded fine-tuning strategy to robustify LLMs. Expanding the very notion of OOD from input data to a model's private computational processes, a new transformer diagnostic at inference time is a critical step toward making AI systems safe for deployment across science, business, and government.

</details>


### [105] [Deterministic Pareto-Optimal Policy Synthesis for Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26397)
*Aniruddha Joshi,Niklas Lauffer,Sanjit Seshia*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a preference-conditioned Bellman operator based on Chebyshev scalarization for MOMDPs, proving it upper-bounds and monotonically converges to the Pareto frontier, enabling extraction of deterministic Pareto-optimal policies for any given preference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard RL aggregates multiple objectives into a single scalar reward, which fails to capture the full Pareto frontier of optimal trade-offs. There is a need for methods that recover the entire set of Pareto-optimal policies in multi-objective decision-making, while also supporting deterministic policy extraction conditioned on user preferences.

Method: The authors propose a novel preference-conditioned Bellman operator derived from Chebyshev scalarization. They theoretically prove this operator satisfies an enveloping property (value estimates upper-bound the true Pareto frontier) and monotonically converges to a coverage set of the frontier. A mechanism is provided to extract deterministic policies from the converged Q-estimates for any specified preference.

Result: The operator is proven to monotonically converge to a coverage set of the true Pareto frontier, with value functions serving as upper bounds. Experimental results demonstrate successful recovery of complex trade-offs and synthesis of approximately Pareto-optimal deterministic policies across varying preferences.

Conclusion: The proposed preference-conditioned Bellman operator provides a principled approach for multi-objective RL, enabling deterministic Pareto-optimal policy synthesis that captures the full Pareto frontier, validated both theoretically and empirically.

Abstract: Real-world decision-making often requires balancing multiple conflicting objectives, a challenge that standard Reinforcement Learning (RL) frequently addresses by aggregating rewards into a single scalar signal. While effective for simple tasks, this approach often fails to capture the full spectrum of optimal trade-offs, known as the Pareto frontier. In this paper, we introduce a novel preference-conditioned Bellman operator, motivated from the Chebyshev scalarization, designed to compute deterministic Pareto-optimal policies for Multi-Objective Markov Decision Processes (MOMDPs). We prove that this operator satisfies an enveloping property, where the estimated value functions upper-bound the true Pareto frontier, and demonstrate that it monotonically converges to a coverage set of this frontier. Furthermore, we also show how to extract deterministic policies from these converged Q-estimates. This ensures the agent can recover a policy for any given preference, capturing the entire Pareto-optimal frontier while guaranteeing each synthesized policy remains approximately Pareto-optimal. Experimental results validate that our algorithm successfully recovers complex trade-offs, providing a solution for deterministic Pareto-optimal policy synthesis.

</details>


### [106] [Beyond Feedforward Networks: Reentry Neural Systems as the Fundamental Basis of Subjecthood and Intrinsic Safety of Next-Generation AGI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26406)
*A. S. Ushakov,Yu. N. Berdinsk*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a safe AGI architecture based on a closed reentry loop (D↔I cycle) that structurally encodes goals to prevent prompt injection, introduces the S-measure (a polynomial-time alternative to Φ for integrated information), and provides Lean 4 verified proofs, full implementations, and deployment tooling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current feedforward neural networks are directed acyclic graphs incapable of self-reference, making them vulnerable to prompt injection, goal reinterpretation, and lacking intrinsic self-preservation. A safe AGI requires an architecture with intrinsic self-modeling and structurally encoded, tamper-proof goals.

Method: The authors design a recurrent architecture featuring a structural cycle (C≥1) with self-sustaining amplification (ρ>1) forming a closed reentry loop. Goals are encoded as non-textual D-vectors embedded in the architecture itself. They introduce the S-measure, a polynomial-time [O(N³)] computable metric for integrated information, with a machine-verified Lean 4 proof that S>0 implies positive Φ. The framework includes Tarjan-based cycle complexity, a Delta-S barrier, Kafka/Docker horizontal scaling, fault-tolerance protocols, and a taxonomy of six AGI epochs.

Result: The architecture mathematically guarantees emergence of a self-model, instrumental self-preservation, and unprogrammed goal-directed behavior. The S-measure is proven (Lean 4) to imply positive integrated information while being tractable. The system is presented as deployable today with industrial-grade tooling, fault-tolerance, and eight falsifiable predictions.

Conclusion: The proposed closed-loop architecture represents a topologically protected, safe-by-design approach to AGI that is immune to prompt injection and goal reinterpretation, with all formal properties machine-verified. It is claimed to be deployable immediately.

Abstract: We propose a complete architectural blueprint for safe artificial general intelligence based on a closed reentry loop (D <-> I cycle). In contrast to feedforward networks, which are directed acyclic graphs (C=0, S=0) incapable of self-reference, the proposed architecture contains a structural cycle (C >= 1) with self-sustaining amplification (rho > 1), mathematically guaranteeing the emergence of a self-model, instrumental self-preservation, and unprogrammed goal-directed behaviour. The agent's goals are encoded as a non-textual D-vector in the architecture itself, making them immune to reinterpretation and prompt injection. We present the S-measure -- a polynomial-time [O(N^3)] computable alternative to Tononi's NP-hard Phi -- with machine-verified Lean 4 proof that S>0 implies positive integrated information. The work provides full Python/NumPy implementations (Tarjan-based cycle complexity, Delta-S barrier), industrial horizontal scaling via Apache Kafka and Docker Compose, a taxonomy of six epochs of AI evolution, a zoo of future reentry architectures (RAS, diffusion attractors, fractal loops), gauge-invariant networks for safe swarms, fault-tolerance and recovery protocols, and eight falsifiable predictions. All formal proofs are machine-verified in Lean 4. This architecture is deployable today and represents a topologically protected, safe-by-design approach to AGI.

</details>


### [107] [Otter Weather: Skillful and Computationally Efficient Medium-Range Weather Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26421)
*Cristiana Diaconu,Jonas Scholz,Aliaksandra Shysheya,Stratis Markou,Payel Mukhopadhyay,Miles Cranmer,Richard E. Turner*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Otter Weather is a highly compute-efficient spatiotemporal forecasting model that achieves state-of-the-art medium-range weather prediction while requiring orders of magnitude less training compute than frontier AI weather models, democratizing access to high-performance AI weather forecasting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: State-of-the-art AI weather models outperform traditional NWP but require massive training budgets, restricting access for under-resourced groups and hindering rapid model iteration. The authors aim to democratize high-performance weather prediction by advancing the skill-compute Pareto frontier.

Method: The authors develop Otter Weather, an efficient spatiotemporal forecasting model trained on ERA5 reanalysis data at 1.5° resolution using WeatherBench protocols. Deterministic and probabilistic versions are trained, with the latter using the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS). A larger variant, Otter-XL, scales the architecture. The model is also tested on an acoustic scattering PDE task.

Result: The deterministic Otter outperforms the best NWP baseline by 9.6% at 24-hour lead time with under 3.5 A100-days of training — a 2x efficiency gain over lightweight AI models and 100x compute reduction vs. frontier architectures. Otter-XL achieves 9.7% CRPS improvement over IFS ENS, nearly 2x skill improvement over comparable lightweight models, and outperforms GenCast by over 2% with ~10x less compute. It also beats a state-of-the-art foundation model on an acoustic scattering PDE task.

Conclusion: Otter Weather significantly advances the skill-compute Pareto frontier, making high-performance AI weather prediction accessible at low computational cost. Its strong out-of-the-box performance on a PDE task suggests the approach may generalize across scientific domains beyond weather forecasting.

Abstract: State-of-the-art medium-range AI weather models can outperform traditional Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) but require massive training budgets. This restricts usage for under-resourced groups and severely limits fast model iteration. Here we develop Otter Weather, a highly efficient spatiotemporal forecasting model designed to democratise high-performance weather prediction with AI. Evaluated on ERA5 reanalysis data at 1.5° resolution using standard WeatherBench protocols, the Otter family significantly advances the skill-compute Pareto frontier. The deterministic version outperforms the best NWP baseline by 9.6% at a 24-hour lead time while requiring fewer than 3.5 A100-days for training. It provides a 2x efficiency gain over lightweight AI models and a 100-fold reduction in compute compared to resource-intensive frontier architectures. We extend these efficiency gains into probabilistic forecasting by training via the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS). Scaling to a larger architecture, Otter-XL achieves a 9.7% CRPS improvement over the IFS ENS baseline. This yields an almost two-fold increase in predictive skill over comparable lightweight models at similar compute budgets. Otter-XL also outperforms frontier architectures like GenCast by over 2%, while using an order of magnitude less compute. Finally, Otter is applied out-of-the-box to a complex acoustic scattering PDE task where it outperforms a state-of-the-art foundation modelling approach, suggesting that the advances made here might apply across a range of scientific domains.

</details>


### [108] [Rethinking Training & Inference for Forecasting: Linking Winner-Take-All back to GMMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26424)
*Qiyuan Wu,Katie Z Luo,Bharath Hariharan,Wei-Lun Chao,Mark Campbell*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Trajectory forecasting models trained with winner-take-all loss produce uninformative mode posteriors due to a GMM-modeling vs. K-means-training mismatch. The authors propose two post-hoc corrections — posterior-weighted merging and a one-step EM update — that yield better-calibrated mode probabilities and improved forecasts without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: WTA-trained trajectory forecasters, though modeled as conditional GMMs, produce uninformative posterior probabilities over forecast modes. This causes problems for downstream mode pruning and selection. The authors identify the root cause: WTA's hard one-hot assignment (akin to K-means) over-segments trajectory space, ignores similarity among nearby modes, and creates assignment instability under small perturbations — a fundamental mismatch between the GMM modeling assumption and the K-means-like training objective.

Method: The authors introduce two post-hoc treatments that require no retraining: (1) Test-time posterior-weighted merging, which aggregates nearby candidate trajectories based on their posterior probabilities to reduce redundant modes. (2) A one-step expectation-maximization (EM) update that replaces the hard WTA assignments with soft responsibilities, redistributing probability mass across neighboring modes. This aligns the inference-time posterior with the GMM assumption by performing a single EM iteration using the learned mixture components.

Result: Across multiple WTA-trained architectures, both proposed methods produce more informative and faithfully ranked mode posteriors. The corrections also improve final trajectory forecasts on standard displacement-based metrics (e.g., minADE, minFDE) compared to the original WTA-trained baselines.

Conclusion: The GMM-vs-K-means lens unifies recent design choices in trajectory forecasting and reveals the WTA training mismatch as a core issue. The proposed post-hoc EM update and posterior-weighted merging offer principled, practical corrections that better align training objectives with probabilistic inference, improving both mode posterior quality and forecast accuracy without retraining.

Abstract: Trajectory forecasting for autonomous driving has advanced rapidly, yet representative models often produce uninformative posteriors over forecast modes, causing problems for mode pruning. We trace this to a modeling-training mismatch: forecasters are typically modeled as conditional Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) but trained with a winner-take-all (WTA) loss that assigns each sample to its nearest mode. We argue that this K-means-like hard assignment (one-hot), while preventing mode collapse, is the source of uninformative mode probabilities: it over-segments the trajectory space, ignores relatedness among nearby modes, and yields assignment instability under small perturbations. Guided by this lens, we introduce two post-hoc treatments: (1) test-time posterior-weighted merging that aggregates nearby candidate trajectories; and (2) a one-step expectation-maximization (EM) update that replaces hard labels with soft responsibilities, sharing probability mass across neighboring modes. Across several WTA-trained architectures, these lightweight steps produce more informative, faithfully ranked mode posteriors and strengthen final forecasts on popular displacement metrics -- without retraining. Our analysis unifies recent design choices through a GMM-vs-K-means perspective and offers principled, practical corrections that better align training objectives with inference.

</details>


### [109] [DualEval: Joint Model-Item Calibration for Unified LLM Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26429)
*Aaron J. Li,Hao Huang,Youngmin Park,Yitong Ma,Wei-Lin Chiang,Li Chen,Cho-Jui Hsieh,Bin Yu,Ion Stoica*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DualEval introduces a joint latent calibration framework that unifies static benchmark evaluation and arena-style preference data by representing models and items in a shared space, enabling reliable rankings, benchmark compression, and anomaly detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM evaluation suffers from a disconnect between static benchmarks (objective but narrow) and arena-style preference data (open-ended but noisy). There is no principled way to combine these complementary signals into a unified evaluation pipeline.

Method: DualEval models models and evaluation items in a shared latent space, jointly estimating model ability alongside item difficulty and sharpness parameters. It integrates static benchmark correctness labels with reward-model scores (validated against held-out human preferences) using a calibration framework applied across four domains: coding, math, domain knowledge, and everyday queries. The framework uses 18 frontier LLMs.

Result: DualEval produces reliable and balanced model rankings. The learned item-level profiles enable benchmark compression for sample-efficient evaluation and anomaly detection for contamination or outlier identification.

Conclusion: DualEval successfully unifies static and arena-style evaluation through joint model-item calibration, yielding interpretable rankings and item-level diagnostics that support more sample-efficient, auditable evaluation pipelines.

Abstract: Current LLM evaluation relies on two complementary but often disconnected signals: static benchmarks with objective correctness labels and arena-style preference data that better reflect open-ended user interactions. We introduce DualEval, a latent model-item calibration framework that represents models and evaluation items in a shared space, jointly estimating model ability together with item difficulty and sharpness. We apply DualEval across four domains: coding, math, miscellaneous domain-knowledge tasks, and generic everyday user queries. Our evaluation uses 18 frontier LLMs, static benchmark labels, and reward-model scores validated against held-out human preferences for open-ended model responses. Empirically, our framework produces reliable and balanced model rankings, and its learned item-level profiles support downstream applications such as benchmark compression for sample-efficient evaluation and anomaly detection for contamination or outlier analysis. Overall, DualEval unifies static and arena-style evaluation through joint model-item calibration, producing model rankings and item-level diagnostics that support more sample-efficient, interpretable, and auditable evaluation pipelines.

</details>


### [110] [Embedding Foundation Model Predictions in Discrete-Choice Models with Structural Guarantees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26432)
*Yingshuo Wang,Xian Sun,Yanhang Li,Zhichao Fan,Zexin Zhuang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A two-stage adapter embeds foundation model choice predictions into a multinomial logit framework, enforcing economic consistency (cost monotonicity, valid willingness-to-pay) while improving accuracy by 6.4–12.8 pp across datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tabular foundation models achieve high accuracy on choice prediction tasks but frequently violate core economic constraints: demand can increase with price, willingness-to-pay estimates become negative or implausible, and unavailable alternatives receive nonzero probability. There is a need to retain foundation model predictive power while guaranteeing economically coherent predictions.

Method: A two-stage adapter: Stage 1 fits a multinomial logit (MNL) with sign-constrained maximum likelihood on structural coefficients, using the foundation model's predicted choice probabilities as a precomputed feature inside the MNL utility function. Stage 2 freezes those coefficients and trains a small neural correction network on the foundation model's predictions. The composition provably preserves the MNL's marginal rate of substitution, guaranteeing analytically computable value-of-time.

Result: Across three datasets and two foundation models, the adapter achieves an average 6.4 pp accuracy gain over MNL (up to 12.8 pp), maintains 100% cost monotonicity, and yields value-of-time estimates within published transportation-economics ranges. Performance degrades gracefully under context restriction, retaining ≥6 pp accuracy gain even at 10% of original context length.

Conclusion: The proposed adapter successfully reconciles the predictive accuracy of tabular foundation models with the structural integrity of discrete choice models, delivering economically coherent predictions without sacrificing empirical performance.

Abstract: Tabular foundation models achieve strong accuracy on choice prediction tasks, but their predictions often violate the economic logic those tasks require: raising a price can increase predicted demand, implied willingness-to-pay estimates are frequently negative or implausible, and unavailable alternatives receive nonzero probability. We propose a two-stage adapter that takes a foundation model's predicted choice probabilities as a precomputed feature and embeds them inside a multinomial logit's utility. In Stage 1, we fit the multinomial logit's structural coefficients by maximum likelihood with sign constraints; in Stage 2, we freeze those coefficients and fit a small neural correction operating on the foundation model's predictions. We prove that this composition exactly preserves the multinomial logit's marginal rate of substitution, so analytically computable value-of-time becomes a mathematical guarantee rather than an empirical accident. Across three datasets and two foundation models, the adapter gains 6.4 percentage points (pp) of test accuracy on average over the multinomial logit and up to 12.8 pp, maintains 100% cost monotonicity, and produces values of time within the published transportation-economics range on the transportation datasets. Performance degrades gracefully under foundation-model context restriction, retaining at least 6 pp of accuracy gain even at 10% of the original foundation-model context.

</details>


### [111] [Optimizing CUDA like a Human: Micro-Profiling Tools as Expert Surrogates for LLM-Based GPU Kernel Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26453)
*Jiading Gai,Shuai Zhang,Kaj Bostrom,Jin Huang,Vihang Patil,Haoyang Fang,Bernie Wang,Huzefa Rangwala,George Karypis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KernelPro is a closed-loop multi-agent system that iteratively optimizes GPU kernels by combining LLM code generation with hardware profiler feedback and pluggable bottleneck detection tools. It achieves state-of-the-art speedups on KernelBench (2.42x–5.30x across difficulty levels) and outperforms hand-tuned Triton kernels on MoE training workloads, while also pioneering energy-efficiency optimization for CUDA kernel agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM-based kernel optimization systems rely on raw hardware metrics or static analysis, lacking structured, actionable feedback from profiling tools. They also fail to integrate multi-level profiling (kernel, instruction, system) in a principled way, and typically focus solely on speed while neglecting energy efficiency.

Method: KernelPro introduces four components: (1) semantic feedback operators that convert raw hardware metrics into natural language guidance via pluggable micro-profiling tools; (2) a two-stage tool invocation architecture using roofline-based bottleneck classification to selectively dispatch specialized profilers (ncu, SASS, nsys); (3) a domain-adapted MCTS with progressive widening, asymmetric branching, log-reward calibration, dead-end pruning, and cross-iteration search memory; and (4) direct CuTe source-level code generation through autonomous search over the CUTLASS/CuTe codebase.

Result: On KernelBench, KernelPro achieves geometric mean speedups of 2.42x (Level 1), 4.69x (Level 2), and 5.30x (Level 3), setting SOTA across all levels. It achieves 1.23x over expert hand-tuned Triton on VeOmni MoE kernels by generating raw-CUDA+CuTe WGMMA kernels from scratch. Ablations show: micro-profiling tools significantly outperform raw metrics (p < 0.0001); MCTS yields 26% higher geometric mean vs greedy search (p = 0.004); proactive tool orchestration provides 23% improvement (p = 0.035). It also demonstrates 11.6% measured energy reduction at matched speed.

Conclusion: KernelPro establishes that structured semantic feedback from multi-level profiling tools, combined with domain-adapted MCTS and autonomous codebase search, enables LLM agents to surpass both prior automated systems and expert hand-tuned kernels. It is the first system to extend LLM-driven kernel optimization to energy efficiency, opening a new dimension for future work.

Abstract: We present KernelPro, a closed-loop multi-agent system that automatically generates, profiles, and iteratively optimizes GPU kernel code by integrating large language model (LLM) code generation with hardware profiler feedback and pluggable bottleneck detection tools. KernelPro introduces four contributions: (1) a semantic feedback operator that encodes expert heuristics as pluggable micro-profiling tools, transforming raw hardware metrics into actionable natural language guidance; (2) a two-stage tool invocation architecture where roofline-based bottleneck classification filters which specialized analysis tools execute, combining kernel-level (ncu), instruction-level (SASS), and system-level (nsys) profiling; (3) a domain-adapted MCTS with progressive widening, asymmetric branching, log-reward calibration, dead-end pruning, and search memory for cross-iteration learning; and (4) direct CuTe source-level code generation via autonomous code search over the CUTLASS/CuTe codebase. On KernelBench, KernelPro achieves geometric mean speedups of 2.42x/4.69x/5.30x on Levels 1/2/3, establishing state-of-the-art performance across all difficulty levels. On VeOmni's expert-optimized MoE training kernels, KernelPro achieves 1.23x over hand-tuned Triton by generating a from-scratch raw-CUDA+CuTe Hopper WGMMA kernel. Ablation studies demonstrate that each design component independently and significantly improves optimization quality: micro-profiling tools (p < 0.0001 vs raw metrics), MCTS search (26% higher geometric mean vs greedy, p = 0.004), and proactive tool orchestration (23% improvement, p = 0.035). Finally, KernelPro is the first CUDA kernel coding agent to optimize energy efficiency beyond the speed-only focus of prior systems, demonstrating an 11.6% measured energy reduction at matched speed.

</details>


### [112] [Finding the Time to Think: Learning Planning Budgets in Real-Time RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26463)
*Aneesh Muppidi,Firas Darwish,Dylan Cope,João F. Henriques,Jakob Nicolaus Foerster*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces variable-delay real-time RL, where agents choose how long to deliberate at each step while the environment progresses. A lightweight gating policy is trained on top of a planner to dynamically select state-dependent planning budgets, outperforming fixed-budget and heuristic baselines across multiple real-time games.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard RL assumes the environment waits indefinitely for the agent's decision, which is unrealistic in real-time settings. In real-time environments, deliberation time is costly because the environment state evolves while the agent thinks. Prior work on real-time RL used fixed deliberation budgets, but the optimal amount of thinking is state-dependent — some situations require quick reactions, others benefit from deeper planning. Naively planning how long to plan creates a meta-level paralysis problem.

Method: The authors formalize variable-delay real-time RL, where the agent selects both an action and a deliberation duration at each step. They train a lightweight gating policy (e.g., a small neural network) on top of a planner agent. The gating policy outputs a state-dependent planning budget (e.g., number of MCTS simulations), controlling how long the planner deliberates. This decouples the meta-decision (how long to think) from the action decision, avoiding infinite regress. Evaluations span real-time versions of Pac-Man, Tetris, Snake, Speed Hex, and Speed Go, including a setup where environment and agent run on separate GPUs.

Result: The gating policy consistently outperforms fixed-budget planners and heuristic baselines across all tested real-time games. It also successfully transfers to a physically distributed real-time setup (two GPUs), demonstrating robustness to real-world timing variability.

Conclusion: Adaptive, state-dependent deliberation budgets learned via a gating policy are an effective and practical solution for real-time RL settings. The approach avoids meta-level paralysis and scales across diverse domains while remaining transferable to realistic hardware-constrained setups.

Abstract: Deliberating takes time. In real-time settings, that time is not free. Standard reinforcement learning (RL) sidesteps this as the environment waits indefinitely for the agent's decision. Instead, we study real-time RL environments where the environment progresses while waiting for the agent's action. Building on prior real-time formalizations, we introduce variable-delay real-time RL, where the agent chooses how long to deliberate at each decision point since the environment progresses. For the planning agents we use, the right delay is state-dependent, and naively planning how long to plan can paralyze the agent. We instead approach this setting by training a lightweight gating policy on top of a planner to select state-dependent planning budgets. Across real-time Pac-Man, Tetris, Snake, Speed Hex, and Speed Go, our gating policy outperforms fixed-budget and heuristic baselines, and transfers to a real-time setup where the environment and agent run on two different GPUs.

</details>


### [113] [A Causal Foundation Model for Structure and Outcome Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26467)
*Max Zhu,Martino Mansoldo,Ching-Hao Wang,Stefan Groha*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TabPFN-CFM is a causal foundation model trained on synthetic data that handles multiple causal tasks — predicting causal structure and outcomes from observational data, supporting queries across all three levels of Pearl's Causal Hierarchy, and leveraging known graph structure to boost performance, outperforming baselines on real datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing causal inference methods are typically task-specific and cannot flexibly handle multiple causal problems (structure learning, interventional queries, counterfactuals) within a single unified framework. The authors aim to bridge this gap by introducing a general-purpose causal foundation model.

Method: TabPFN-CFM extends the TabPFN (Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network) architecture to the causal domain. It is trained entirely on synthetically generated datasets encompassing diverse causal structures and data-generating processes. The model accepts observational data as input and can optionally incorporate known graph structure. It is designed to output both causal graph structure and outcome predictions, supporting queries at all three rungs of Pearl's Causal Hierarchy: associational (rung 1), interventional (rung 2), and counterfactual (rung 3).

Result: TabPFN-CFM generalises from synthetic training data to real-world datasets, demonstrating improved performance over both structural prediction baselines (causal discovery) and outcome prediction baselines (interventional/counterfactual estimation).

Conclusion: A single causal foundation model trained on synthetic data can effectively handle diverse causal inference tasks — structure learning, intervention, and counterfactual queries — and transfers to real data, outperforming specialised baselines while optionally exploiting known graph structure for further gains.

Abstract: We introduce TabPFN-CFM, a causal foundation model that can handle multiple causal problems. TabPFN-CFM predicts both causal structure and outcomes from observational data, supports queries on all three levels of Pearl's Causal Hierarchy and uses known graph structure when available to improve predictions. TabPFN-CFM is trained on synthetic datasets, and generalises to real datasets, demonstrating improved performance over both structural and outcome prediction baselines.

</details>


### [114] [Epiphany-Aware KV Cache Eviction Without the Attention Matrix](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26472)
*Steven Kolawole,Virginia Smith*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EpiKV introduces a novel KV cache eviction method that scores tokens by their "epiphany score" — the change in the model's internal representation measured directly from the forward pass — eliminating the need for expensive attention matrix materialization. It matches or exceeds attention-based baselines (ThinKV, H2O) on MATH-500 and AIME-2024 benchmarks while enabling up to 2.8× faster inference and 16× longer feasible context.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long reasoning chains from modern models produce KV caches of tens of thousands of tokens, creating a deployment bottleneck. Existing eviction methods rely on attention weights as importance proxies, but these are noisy in long reasoning traces and require materializing the full attention matrix, which prevents the use of fused kernels (like FlashAttention) in production inference.

Method: EpiKV scores tokens using the "epiphany score," defined as the change in the model's internal representation measured directly from the forward pass, requiring no attention matrix and negligible extra state. It identifies that upper-mid layers exhibit negative importance trends and applies a causal rolling z-score to remove positional bias. The method requires no training, classifier, or custom kernel and works natively with FlashAttention inference stacks. A lag-normalized KV variant is also proposed.

Result: At a 4096-token cache budget, EpiKV achieves 72% accuracy on MATH-500, matching the best attention-based baseline (ThinKV 71%) and outperforming H2O (67%). On AIME-2024 at 8192 tokens, the lag-normalized variant reaches 37% against the best baseline (33%), with up to 2.8× speedup. The method scales to 16× longer feasible context than attention-based scoring.

Conclusion: EpiKV demonstrates that KV cache eviction for long reasoning traces can be effectively performed without attention matrices, using internal representation changes as a clean, efficient importance signal. This enables practical deployment with fused kernels, offering superior or competitive accuracy with substantial speed gains.

Abstract: As reasoning models emit chains of thought tens of thousands of tokens long, KV cache increasingly becomes a deployment bottleneck. Existing cache eviction methods rank tokens by attention weight, which is a noisy importance proxy in long reasoning traces, and prohibits the use of fused kernels in production inference by forcing the model to materialize the attention matrix. In this work, we instead score tokens with a metric we term the epiphany score: the change in the model's internal representation, read directly from the forward pass with no attention matrix and negligible extra state. Our resulting cache eviction method, EpiKV, requires no training, classifier, or custom kernel, and can be used directly in FlashAttention inference stacks unchanged -- scaling to a 16x longer feasible context than attention-based scoring. upper-mid layers negatively) and remove a positional trend with a causal rolling z-score. At a 4096-token cache EpiKV reaches 72% on MATH-500, matching the strongest attention-based baseline (ThinKV 71%, H2O 67%); a lag-normalized KV variant reaches 37% on AIME-2024 at 8192 tokens against the best of them (33%), at up to 2.8x the speed.

</details>


### [115] [When Does Quality-Aware Multimodal Fusion Matter? A Leakage-Safe Diagnostic for Decision-Level Dependence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26473)
*Jaden Moon,Arvind Pillai,Andrew Campbell*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a diagnostic permutation test to determine whether learned modality reliability scores genuinely influence multimodal fusion decisions, finding that in standard models they do not — performance remains unchanged when scores are shuffled, despite the existence of oracle-level gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal fusion systems often weight modalities by estimated reliability, but it is unclear whether these reliability scores actually drive model predictions or are merely correlated with performance. The authors aim to rigorously test whether reliability information is causally used during inference.

Method: The authors propose a simple diagnostic: after training, the model parameters and inputs are frozen, and modality reliability scores are randomly permuted across test examples. If the model truly uses reliability information, permuting these scores should degrade performance. They also construct a positive control where reliability signals are engineered to identify the correct unimodal modality, testing whether the frozen fusion rule can leverage meaningful reliability cues. Experiments are conducted on StressID (stress recognition) and CMU-MOSEI (sentiment analysis) datasets.

Result: Permuting reliability scores leaves multimodal fusion performance unchanged on both StressID and CMU-MOSEI, indicating reliability signals are not used during inference. However, when reliability scores are engineered to correctly identify the best modality (positive control), the same frozen fusion rules yield significant improvements, demonstrating that the fusion mechanism can leverage reliability signals when they are genuinely informative.
