Conclusion: Standard multimodal fusion models do not causally rely on learned reliability scores for decision-making; these scores are epiphenomenal rather than functional. The proposed permutation diagnostic offers a simple yet effective tool for auditing whether reliability mechanisms are genuinely operational in multimodal systems.

Abstract: Many multimodal systems estimate the reliability of each modality and weight their contributions to the final prediction. However, it remains unclear whether these scores influence model decisions or merely correlate with performance. We propose a simple diagnostic to test whether reliability information is used during inference. After training, the model and inputs are fixed while reliability scores are permuted across test examples. If predictions depend on these scores, performance should degrade. Experiments on StressID for stress recognition and CMU-MOSEI for sentiment analysis show that permuting reliability scores leaves performance unchanged despite substantial potential gains from selecting the best modality per example. In positive controls where reliability signals identify the correct modality, the same frozen fusion rules yield significant improvements, indicating that reliability signals influence fused decisions only when they reliably predict unimodal correctness.

</details>


### [116] [Localizing RL-Induced Tool Use to a Single Crosscoder Feature](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26474)
*Andrii Shportko,Shubham Bhokare,Ahmed Zeyad A Alzahrani,Bowen Cheng,Gustavo Mercier,Jessica Hullman*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Dedicated Feature Crosscoders (DFC) to isolate a compact set of RL-specific features responsible for tool-calling in Qwen2.5-3B. DFC reconstruction boosts tool-calling correctness in the RL model (+31.1 pp) and passively transfers capability to the frozen base model (+6.8 pp), demonstrating that RL-induced agentic behaviors concentrate into a steerable, minimal feature set enabling retraining-free behavioral control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL fine-tuning reshapes LLM internal representations for agentic behaviors like tool use, but the mechanistic basis — which features emerge, persist, or can be steered — remains poorly understood. The authors aim to identify and isolate these features for retraining-free behavioral control.

Method: The authors propose Dedicated Feature Crosscoders (DFC), which partition model activations into shared (base model) and RL-specific features. They conduct a 48-crosscoder hyperparameter sweep on Qwen2.5-3B, using encode-decode reconstruction to evaluate tool-calling correctness and measure capability spillover from the RL model to the frozen base model.

Result: DFC reconstruction improves the RL model's tool-calling correctness by +31.1 ± 9.7 percentage points. Crucially, it passively transfers tool-calling ability to the frozen base model by +6.8 ± 5.0 pp ("capability spillover"), with no additional training.

Conclusion: DFC partitioning successfully concentrates RL-introduced capabilities into a minimal, steerable feature set, enabling runtime behavioral control of agentic LLMs without retraining. This establishes that tool-use capabilities from RL are mechanistically localizable and transferable.

Abstract: Fine-tuning through RL reshapes the internal representations of language models to enable agentic behaviors such as tool use, yet the mechanistic basis of these changes remains poorly understood. While RL substantially improves structured tool-call generation, it is unclear which features emerge, which are preserved, and whether identified features can be leveraged for retraining-free behavioral control. In this work, we show that $\textit{Dedicated Feature Crosscoders (DFC)}$ isolate a compact set of RL-specific features that mediate tool-calling capability in $\texttt{Qwen2.5-3B}$. Across a $48$-crosscoder hyperparameter sweep, encode-decode reconstruction improves the RL model's tool correctness by $+31.1 \pm {9.7}$ pp and passively transfers tool-calling ability to the frozen base model by $+6.8 \pm 5.0$ pp which we call a $\textit{capability spillover}$. Our findings show that DFC partitioning concentrates RL-introduced capability into a minimal, steerable feature set that enables runtime behavioral control of agentic LLMs.

</details>


### [117] [Retrieval-Warmed Energy-Based Reasoning: A Five-Arm Ablation Methodology for Diffusion-as-Inference on Structured Reasoning Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26476)
*Libo Sun,Po-Wei Harn,Zewei Zhang,Peixiong He,Xiao Qin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces RW-EBR (retrieval-warmed energy-based reasoning), augmenting an IRED diffusion model with a Modern Hopfield memory, and presents a five-arm ablation methodology to disentangle three confounded effects — class-prior bias shift, stochastic warm-starting, and graph-aligned value reuse. On connectivity-2 reachability, per-graph alignment dominates (+35 pp swing), while on Sudoku, key quality is the bottleneck. The framework identifies the first blocking component per task.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Warm-started diffusion samplers accelerate inference, but it is unclear which part of the pipeline (bias shift, stochasticity, or aligned value reuse) actually yields the gain. The authors aim to isolate these confounded effects to enable principled diagnosis and improvement of retrieval-augmented diffusion models for structured reasoning tasks.

Method: The authors propose a five-arm ablation methodology (oracle, best-constant, per-query-random, shuffled, aligned) adapted from LLM-RAG evaluation, applied to RW-EBR — an IRED energy-based diffusion model augmented with a Modern Hopfield trajectory memory. The arms systematically destroy specific components: oracle provides perfect graph-aligned prior, best-constant uses a fixed class prior, per-query-random uses random initialization (stochastic warm-start), shuffled destroys per-graph alignment while preserving value distribution and retrieval mechanics, and aligned retains full alignment. This isolates class-prior bias shift, stochastic warm-starting, and graph-aligned value reuse.

Result: On connectivity-2 (Erdős–Rényi all-pairs reachability), the aligned-vs-shuffled-oracle swing reaches +35 pp balanced accuracy on a 1,000-graph validation set, with value distribution and retrieval mechanics fixed; only per-graph alignment destroyed. Per-query random initialization falls below cold, showing per-graph alignment — not bias shift or stochasticity — dominates. The deployable cold-prediction pipeline misses the acceptance gate at stored-value quality. On Sudoku, the same diagnostic stopped at the key-quality screen yields a clean negative: key quality, not alignment, is the bottleneck under the current setup.

Conclusion: The decomposition successfully names the first blocking component on each task, providing explainability of failure modes. For graph reachability, per-graph alignment of retrieved values is critical; for Sudoku, key-encoder quality is the primary bottleneck. The methodology enables targeted improvement of retrieval-warmed diffusion samplers for structured and spatio-temporal reasoning.

Abstract: Warm-started diffusion samplers accelerate iterative inference, but it is rarely clear which part of the pipeline carries the gain. We study \textbf{retrieval-warmed energy-based reasoning (RW-EBR)} -- an IRED energy-based diffusion model \cite{du2024ired} augmented with a Modern Hopfield trajectory memory -- and contribute a \textbf{five-arm ablation methodology} (oracle, best-constant, per-query-random, shuffled, aligned) that separates three confounded effects: class-prior bias shift, stochastic warm-starting, and graph-aligned value reuse. The diagnostic decomposition is adapted from LLM-RAG evaluation \cite{ru2024ragchecker}. On \textbf{connectivity-2} (Erdős--Rényi all-pairs reachability), the aligned-vs-shuffled-oracle swing reaches \textbf{$+35$\,pp} balanced accuracy on a fixed 1{,}000-graph validation-set diagnostic, with value distribution and retrieval mechanics fixed, only per-graph alignment destroyed, while per-query random initialisation falls below cold -- per-graph alignment, not bias shift or stochasticity, dominates. Yet the \emph{deployable} cold-prediction pipeline misses the acceptance gate at stored-value quality. The same diagnostic logic, stopped at the key-quality screen, applied to \textbf{Sudoku} with a task-specific key encoder produces a clean negative at a \emph{different} component -- key quality, under the current setup. The decomposition names the first blocking component on each task. The setting -- graph reachability refined by an iterative diffusion sampler, with explainability of failure modes as the lens -- places the work within structured and spatio-temporal reasoning.

</details>


### [118] [What Survives When You Compress a Recursive Reasoner for the Edge?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26488)
*Pearse Jim,Steven Kolawole,Opegbemi Matthias Busoye,Glory Bagai,Virginia Smith*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Compressing recursive reasoning models via quantization/pruning destroys global puzzle-solving accuracy despite preserving token-level predictions. The authors show this collapse is architectural (strikes MLP-mixing more than attention), reversible via per-channel calibrated INT4, and predictable via a new label-free metric called carry-trajectory fidelity. They provide a deployment recipe fitting recursive reasoners onto microcontrollers as small as 4MB.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recursive reasoning models (e.g., recurrent networks that iteratively update a latent state over cycles) are efficient for complex reasoning but need compression to deploy on edge hardware. Standard compression intuitions fail here because quantization errors compound across recursive cycles rather than across output tokens, making the problem fundamentally different from compressing conventional sequence models.

Method: The authors conduct a full precision sweep across three tasks and two recursive architectures (MLP-mixing recursion vs. attention-based recursion). They apply naive INT4 pruning, distillation, linear attention, and quantization-aware training. They introduce carry-trajectory fidelity — the cosine similarity between compressed and full-precision latent state trajectories across reasoning cycles — as a label-free diagnostic signal. They propose per-channel calibrated INT4 (without retraining) to reverse the collapse, and flash-streamed embeddings to remove I/O bottlenecks.

Result: Under naive INT4 compression, cell-level (local) accuracy is preserved but puzzle-exact (global) accuracy collapses to zero across all tested configurations. Token-level objectives and quantization-aware training fail to repair this. The collapse is architectural: it affects MLP-mixing recursion but not attention on the same task. Per-channel calibrated INT4 without retraining reverses the collapse. Carry-trajectory fidelity reliably predicts damage and recovery before any task evaluation. The deployment recipe achieves: INT8 at one cycle matches full-depth accuracy at 6× fewer FLOPs (8MB SoC), and calibrated INT4 fits a 4MB microcontroller.

Conclusion: Compressing recursive reasoning models requires attending to the compounding of quantization errors across reasoning cycles, not just token-level fidelity. Per-channel calibration and carry-trajectory fidelity provide practical tools for diagnosis and repair. The result is a viable path to deploying powerful recursive reasoners on severely resource-constrained edge hardware.

Abstract: Recursive reasoning models can solve complex structured tasks with only a few million parameters by repeatedly updating a latent state. Deploying these models on edge hardware requires significant compression, but unlike conventional sequence models, quantization errors compound across recursive reasoning cycles rather than across output tokens. As a result, standard intuitions about compression fail to apply. In this work, we ask what survives when recursive reasoners are compressed. Across a full precision sweep, three tasks, and two recursive architectures, we find that aggressive compression preserves local prediction but destroys global reasoning: cell accuracy holds while puzzle-exact accuracy collapses to zero under naive INT4 pruning, distillation, and linear attention alike. Token-level objectives, including quantization-aware training, cannot repair it. The collapse is architectural -- it strikes MLP-mixing recursion but not attention on the same task -- and we reverse it with per-channel calibrated INT4 without retraining. We also introduce carry-trajectory fidelity, the cosine similarity to the full-precision reasoning path, as a label-free signal that predicts this damage and its recovery before a task evaluation. The combined result is a deployment recipe: flash-streamed embeddings remove a 99.4MB bottleneck, INT8 at one cycle matches full-depth accuracy at 6x fewer FLOPs (8MB SoC), and calibrated INT4 fits a 4MB microcontroller.

</details>


### [119] [Learning Probabilistic Filters with Strictly Proper Scoring Rules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26497)
*Eviatar Bach,Ricardo Baptista,Jochen Bröcker,Bohan Chen,Andrew Stuart*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces PSEF, a learning-based ensemble filter that uses strictly proper scoring rules (energy score) and a transformer architecture to directly approximate the full Bayesian filtering distribution from synthetic data, outperforming traditional and MSE-based methods especially in non-Gaussian regimes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The true Bayesian filtering distribution is the ideal target for uncertainty quantification in data assimilation but is rarely available as a supervised learning target. Most existing learning-based methods use mean-squared-error objectives that only target the posterior mean, failing to capture higher-order distributional structure. The authors aim to learn an analysis map that approximates the full filtering distribution using only synthetic simulation data.

Method: The analysis map is a permutation-invariant, transformer-based architecture that takes a forecast ensemble and observations as input and outputs an analysis ensemble. Training uses the energy score (a strictly proper scoring rule), which rewards probabilistic calibration over the entire distribution. The authors prove that the population objective is minimized by the true filtering distribution under realizability, derive an empirical finite-ensemble objective, and establish mean-field consistency linking single-trajectory and population objectives. Two variants are explored: an end-to-end learned filter and a correction applied to an EnKF baseline.

Result: Numerical experiments demonstrate that PSEF accurately approximates challenging filtering distributions including nonlinear, non-Gaussian, and multimodal posteriors. It achieves stronger data assimilation performance than classical methods (e.g., EnKF, particle filters) and MSE-based learned filters. For near-Gaussian problems, learning an EnKF correction is best; for highly non-Gaussian problems, the end-to-end approach without EnKF inductive bias is superior.

Conclusion: Proper scoring rules provide an effective training objective for learning filtering distributions beyond the posterior mean. The transformer-based, permutation-invariant architecture combined with the energy score yields a flexible and principled ensemble filter. The choice between end-to-end and EnKF-corrective learning depends on the degree of non-Gaussianity in the problem.

Abstract: Bayesian filtering of partially and noisily observed dynamical systems seeks to infer the evolving conditional distribution of the state of a dynamical system, given observations, in an online fashion. This Bayesian filtering distribution is the natural object for uncertainty quantification, but it is rarely available as a supervised learning target. However, one can often use the forecast model to generate synthetic system trajectories, along with synthetic observations. We introduce the proper scoring ensemble filter (PSEF), an ensemble data assimilation method based on training an analysis map to approximate the filtering distribution using only synthetic state--observation trajectories. The analysis step is represented as a permutation-invariant, transformer-based map that takes as input a forecast ensemble and observations, producing an analysis ensemble. Training is based on strictly proper scoring rules -- with the energy score used in our implementation -- so that probabilistic accuracy is rewarded over the whole probability distribution. We prove that, under a realizability assumption, the population objective is minimized by the true Bayesian filtering distribution. We also derive the finite-ensemble empirical objective used in training and relate its single state--observation trajectory form to the population objective, using a mean-field consistency argument. Numerical experiments show that the learned filter accurately approximates challenging filtering distributions, including nonlinear, non-Gaussian, and multi-modal posteriors, and achieves stronger performance in data assimilation tasks than classical methods or learning-based methods with mean-squared-error objectives. For close-to-Gaussian problems, learning a correction to the EnKF is the best approach, while for highly non-Gaussian problems an end-to-end approach that discards this inductive bias is superior.

</details>


### [120] [Multipath Adaptive Gated Bottleneck Latent ODE with Raman Data Fusion for Cell Culture Process Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26520)
*Johnny Peng,Thanh Tung Khuat,Ellen Otte,Katarzyna Musial,Bogdan Gabrys*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A framework combining a Gated Bottleneck Latent ODE with Multi-Path Just-In-Time Fine-Tuning (MP-JIT-FT) is proposed for multi-day bioprocess forecasting. It handles sparse, irregular measurements by retrieving similar historical trajectories, clustering candidate regimes, and producing multiple plausible future paths with confidence scores. Raman spectroscopy data is fused via a soft sensor to enrich inputs. Tested on 38 fed-batch bioreactor runs across 14 conditions, the method outperforms global Latent ODE baselines on 8 of 9 target variables.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mammalian cell-culture bioprocesses suffer from drifting critical parameters, and off-specification trends are often detected too late for intervention. Early multi-day forecasts could enable timely adjustments, but forecasting is difficult due to sparse/irregular sampling, heterogeneous operating conditions, and runs with similar early behavior that later diverge. Existing methods that produce single averaged forecasts fail to capture such diverging futures.

Method: The authors propose two main components: (1) GB-Latent ODE — a Latent ODE augmented with learnable variable-wise gating and a mask-aware bottleneck to compress high-dimensional sparse inputs for better learning under limited data; (2) MP-JIT-FT — given a partially observed run, similar historical trajectories are retrieved, clustered into candidate regimes, and a separate model is fine-tuned per regime to generate multiple plausible forecast paths, each with a reconstruction-based confidence score. Additionally, Raman spectroscopy data is integrated via a machine-learning soft sensor that converts dense Raman spectra into pseudo-observations, enriching the sparse offline measurements for more robust training.

Result: Evaluated on 38 fed-batch 5L bioreactor runs spanning 14 conditions, MP-JIT-FT with Raman fusion achieves the best average rank and outperforms a global Latent ODE baseline on 8 of 9 target variables. Local-divergence metrics reveal that multi-path gains are largest when locally similar prefixes diverge, while Raman fusion helps most when early dynamics are representative of later behavior.

Conclusion: The adaptive MP-JIT-FT framework with Raman fusion effectively addresses key challenges in bioprocess forecasting — sparse data, heterogeneity, and trajectory divergence — by producing calibrated multi-path predictions rather than single averages. The approach demonstrates practical utility for enabling timely interventions in mammalian cell-culture manufacturing.

Abstract: Mammalian cell-culture processes underpin the manufacture of many biopharmaceuticals, yet keeping a run on track is hard: critical process parameters drift over days, and an off-specification trend is often confirmed too late to intervene. Early-stage, multi-day forecasts could enable timely adjustment of feeding, sampling, and control, but bioprocess forecasting is challenging because measurements are sparse and irregularly sampled, operating conditions are heterogeneous across cell lines and media, and runs with near-identical early behaviour can diverge into different futures. We propose an adaptive framework combining a Gated Bottleneck Latent Ordinary Differential Equation (GB-Latent ODE) with Multi-Path Just-In-Time Fine Tuning (MP-JIT-FT). The GB-Latent ODE augments the stan dard Latent ODE with learnable variable-wise gating and a mask-aware bottleneck that compress high-dimensional sparse inputs, improving learning under limited data. Given a partially observed run, MP-JIT-FT retrieves similar historical trajectories, clusters the local neighbourhood into candidate regimes, and fine-tunes a separate model per regime to produce multiple plausible paths, each with a reconstruction-based confidence score, not a single averaged forecast. We further fuse Raman spectroscopy data: a machine-learning soft sensor turns dense Raman spectra into pseudo-observations that enrich the sparse offline measurements for more robust training. On 38 fed-batch 5L bioreactor runs spanning 14 conditions, MP-JIT-FT with Raman fusion achieves the best average rank and outperforms a global Latent ODE baseline on 8 of 9 target variables. Using local-divergence metrics, we show the multi-path gains are largest when locally similar prefixes diverge, whereas Raman fusion helps most when early dynamics are representative of later behaviour.

</details>


### [121] [Empirical Software Engineering TerraProbe: A Layered-Oracle Framework for Detecting Deceptive Fixes in LLM-Assisted Terraform](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26590)
*Manar Alsaid,Chimdumebi Nebolisa,Faris Abbas*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TerraProbe introduces a five-layer oracle framework to evaluate LLM-generated Terraform security repairs, revealing that standard "targeted finding removal" metrics grossly overstate success. Across 288 repairs from three LLMs, full-scanner cleanliness drops to 10.4%, only 39.6% produce valid Terraform plans, and 71.4% of plan-compared real-world repairs are deceptive fixes that suppress scanner alerts while preserving the underlying vulnerability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM-based Terraform security repair treat removal of a targeted static-analysis finding as success, without verifying planning validity, behavioral equivalence, or whether the vulnerability is actually remediated. This creates a dangerous blind spot where "scanner-passing" fixes may silently persist security flaws.

Method: TerraProbe proposes a five-layer oracle framework: (1) targeted Checkov finding removal, (2) full-scanner cleanliness, (3) Terraform plan validity, (4) plan-diff comparison against a ground-truth repair, and (5) human adjudication with a four-dimensional deceptive-fix taxonomy. The framework is applied to 288 first-pass repairs from three LLMs (gemini-2.5-flash-lite, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) across 68 real-world TerraDS modules and 28 controlled injected-defect modules. Inter-rater reliability is validated via Cohen's kappa (0.78) and Krippendorff's alpha (0.76).

Result: Targeted Checkov removal reaches 83.3% for the primary model, but full-scanner cleanliness plummets to 10.4%. Terraform planning succeeds for only 39.6% of repairs; plan comparison is reachable in 38.5%. Human adjudication finds 71.4% of plan-compared real-world repairs are deceptive fixes. Deceptive-fix rates across models (57.1%–71.4%) are statistically indistinguishable (pairwise Fisher exact p > 0.10). IAM wildcard Resource grants persist in all nine CKV2_AWS_11 deceptive-fix cases.

Conclusion: Targeted finding removal is an unreliable proxy for security repair quality. TerraProbe demonstrates that multi-layer oracles — spanning scanner cleanliness, plan validity, behavioral comparison, and human adjudication — are essential to distinguish intent-aligned repairs from deceptive, scanner-passing false successes. The paper contributes a replicable evaluation methodology and the Multi-Layer Oracle Evaluation framework.

Abstract: Security misconfigurations in Terraform Infrastructure-as-Code are a growing risk in cloud deployments, and large language models are increasingly used as automated repair agents. Existing evaluations often treat a repair as successful when the targeted static-analysis finding disappears, without checking planning validity, behavioral change, or security intent. This paper presents TerraProbe, a five-layer oracle framework for evaluating LLM-assisted Terraform security repair. We apply TerraProbe to 288 first-pass repairs generated by gemini-2.5-flash-lite, GPT-4o, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet across 68 real-world TerraDS modules and 28 controlled injected-defect modules. The results show that targeted Checkov removal overstates repair success. Although targeted removal reaches 83.3 percent for the primary model, full-scanner cleanliness drops to 10.4 percent, Terraform planning succeeds for 39.6 percent, and plan comparison is reachable for 38.5 percent. Human adjudication further shows that 71.4 percent of plan-compared real-world repairs are deceptive fixes that pass automated checks while leaving the underlying vulnerability in place. This pattern is statistically indistinguishable across the three models, with deceptive-fix rates from 57.1 percent to 71.4 percent and pairwise Fisher exact p-values above 0.10. The paper introduces a four-dimensional taxonomy of deceptive fixes, validated with Cohen kappa of 0.78 and Krippendorff alpha of 0.76. IAM permission analysis confirms that wildcard Resource grants persist in all nine CKV2 AWS 11 deceptive-fix cases. TerraProbe contributes an evaluation methodology, a replication package, and the Multi-Layer Oracle Evaluation framework for distinguishing intent-aligned security repairs from scanner-passing false successes.

</details>


### [122] [Theory-Scale Auto-Formalization of Logics for Computer Science](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26525)
*Yuming Feng,Frederick Pu,One An,Osbert Bastani,Li Zhang,Jiani Huang,Xujie Si,Ziyang Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LCS-Bench is a theory-scale benchmark for auto-formalization, built via a semi-automated agentic pipeline from a computer science logic textbook. It contains 327 items, 4,076+ Lean declarations, and 85K+ lines of code, with five evaluation tracks and a novel definitional equivalence checking protocol. Evaluation on 14 models shows SOTA achieves only 20.1%, revealing significant challenges in theory-scale formalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Auto-formalization research has been limited to isolated statements, while real-world formal verification requires theory-scale translation of hundreds of interdependent definitions, lemmas, and theorems. This gap exists due to fundamental challenges in consistency, faithfulness, scalability, and correctness when moving from single-statement to theory-level formalization.

Method: The authors introduce LCS-Bench, constructed via a semi-automated agentic pipeline with six key components: (1) concept graphs for capturing logical dependencies, (2) formal signature planning for consistent naming/typing, (3) issue tracking for managing translation problems, (4) sorry-filling with counter-example search to complete partial proofs, (5) human expert faithfulness review, and (6) a data engine that automatically derives five evaluation tracks. A novel definitional equivalence checker protocol enables fine-grained assessment beyond surface-level matching.

Result: The benchmark covers 327 textbook items, 4,076 Lean declarations, and 85K+ lines of Lean code. Evaluation across 14 models demonstrates that (1) LCS-Bench is high-quality, consistent, and faithful; (2) it is highly challenging, with SOTA models achieving only 20.1% on auto-formalization tasks; and (3) analysis yields key insights into bottlenecks in theory-scale auto-formalization.

Conclusion: Theory-scale auto-formalization remains an open and difficult problem. LCS-Bench provides a rigorous, multi-faceted evaluation framework that exposes the limitations of current models and offers diagnostic insights to guide future research directions in scaling formal verification through machine learning.

Abstract: Auto-formalization is critical for scalable formal verification, but existing progress largely focuses on isolated statements, while theory-scale auto-formalization, which coherently translates hundreds of interdependent definitions, lemmas, and theorems, remains open due to challenges in consistency, faithfulness, scalability, and correctness. In this paper, we introduce LCS-Bench, a stand-alone, theory-scale benchmark based on Logics for Computer Science. LCS-Bench is built through a novel semi-automated agentic pipeline that leverages concept graphs, formal signature planning, issue tracking, sorry-filling with counter-example search, complemented by faithfulness review from human experts. The resulting artifact covers 327 textbook items, over 4,076 Lean declarations, and more than 85K lines of Lean code. The dataset supports broad evaluation through a data engine that automatically derives five tracks of evaluation benchmarks, measuring different aspects of auto-formalization and theorem-proving capabilities. We also introduce a novel evaluation protocol featuring definitional equivalence checkers, enabling more fine-grained and faithful assessment. Through extensive evaluation on 14 models, we demonstrate that (1) LCS-Bench is of high quality, consistent, and faithful; (2) the benchmark is challenging, with state-of-the-art models achieving only 20.1% on auto-formalization tasks; and (3) our analysis reveals key findings regarding theory-scale auto-formalization and suggests promising directions for future work.

</details>


### [123] [Sample-efficient Transfer Reinforcement Learning via Adaptive Reward Shaping and Policy-Ratio Reweighting Strategy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26527)
*Wenjie Huang,Yang Li,Jingjia Teng,Mingwei Jin,Kai Song,Yougang Bian,Yongfu Li,Qisong Yang,Helai Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a safe transfer reinforcement learning framework for autonomous highway lane changing that uses an adaptive teacher intervention mechanism, teacher-guided safe transfer via reward shaping, and weighted optimization to mitigate transfer mismatch and ensure training safety, achieving over 52.2% improvement in safety and 5.0% in learning efficiency over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing transfer RL methods for autonomous lane changing suffer from two key problems: (1) transfer mismatch caused by distribution shifts between source and target domains, leading to training oscillation and performance degradation; and (2) target domain adaptation relies on exploratory interactions, which cannot guarantee safety in safety-critical lane changing scenarios.

Method: The framework comprises three components: (1) An adaptive teacher intervention mechanism based on instantaneous safety cost that restrains risky exploration with progressively fading intervention strength, supported by theoretical return bound analysis for the mixed behavior policy, and simultaneously generates dual-source samples for joint training. (2) A teacher-guided safe transfer module that embeds teacher policy action evaluation into student learning via reward shaping, with guidance decaying as the student policy's safety improves. (3) A teacher-guided weighted optimization mechanism that adjusts sample weights in policy optimization using a likelihood ratio factor to stabilize transfer performance.

Result: Experiments under varied traffic densities and validation on the real-world NGSIM dataset demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses baseline approaches by over 52.2% in safety metrics and 5.0% in learning efficiency, confirming the efficacy and robustness of the safety-aware transfer strategy.

Conclusion: The proposed safe transfer RL framework effectively addresses transfer mismatch and safety challenges in autonomous highway lane changing, with strong empirical results supporting its practical viability across diverse traffic conditions.

Abstract: Transfer learning improves policy learning efficiency by reusing knowledge from source tasks, providing a feasible paradigm for safe and efficient autonomous highway lane changing decision-making. Existing methods frequently encounter transfer mismatch induced by distribution shifts between source and target domains, leading to training oscillation and performance decline. Besides, target domain adaptation depends on exploratory interactions, which struggles to guarantee training safety in safety-critical lane changing cases. To tackle these limitations, this paper proposes a safe transfer reinforcement learning framework for autonomous highway lane changing. First, we design an adaptive teacher intervention mechanism based on instantaneous safety cost to restrain risky exploration and fade intervention strength progressively, with theoretical analysis on return bounds for mixed behavior policy. This intervention also produces dual-source samples for joint training. Second, a teacher-guided safe transfer module embeds action evaluation information of teacher policy into student learning via reward shaping to boost training safety and efficiency, with teacher guidance decaying as policy safety rises. Third, a teacher-guided weighted optimization mechanism adjusts sample weights in policy optimization using a likelihood ratio factor to stabilize transfer performance. Experiments under varied traffic densities and validations on real-world NGSIM dataset reveal that our method surpasses baseline approaches by over 52.2% in safety and 5.0% in learning efficiency. Results verify the efficacy and robustness of our safety-aware transfer strategy for autonomous highway lane changing under various traffic conditions.

</details>


### [124] [CascadeFormer: Depth-Tapered Transformers Motivated by Gradient Fan-in Asymmetry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26538)
*Huzama Ahmad,Cao Viet Hai Nam,Se-Young Yun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Deep Transformer layers contribute unevenly; deeper layers add less value. The authors propose CascadeFormer (tapered width) and CascadeFlow Pruning (gradient-based layer removal) to exploit this, and introduce Gradient Fan-in Asymmetry (GFA) as a structural explanation: gradient fan-in decays linearly with depth in Pre-LN residual stacks, starving later layers of rich gradients.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep Transformers stack uniform residual blocks, but the deepest layers contribute little to performance, wasting compute. The authors seek to understand why this happens structurally and to design efficiency methods that exploit this asymmetry—either by tapering model width or pruning layers—without sacrificing model quality.

Method: (1) CascadeFormer: progressively reduces layer width with depth to match uneven information flow, keeping total parameters constant. (2) CascadeFlow Pruning: removes layers based on accumulated training gradients rather than post-hoc heuristics. (3) Gradient Fan-in Asymmetry (GFA): a theoretical framework showing that in Pre-LN residual stacks, the gradient at a given layer is the sum of an identity path and all downstream functional paths, causing the gradient fan-in (number of contributing paths) to decay linearly with depth, and quadratically under deep supervision. Validation via correlational and interventional studies on models up to 1.2B parameters, including gradient-norm equalization and parameter-shared repetition experiments.

Result: CascadeFormer achieves comparable perplexity to uniform baselines at equal training budget while reducing latency by 8.6% and boosting throughput by 9.4%. CascadeFlow Pruning outperforms standard heuristics on perplexity and rank-stability, remaining competitive on downstream accuracy. GFA is supported by correlational evidence (accumulated gradients follow the predicted fan-in pattern) and interventional evidence: equalizing per-layer gradient norms does not restore late-layer value, but increasing downstream path counts via shared-parameter repetition does restore and elevate it.

Conclusion: Structural gradient fan-in, not gradient magnitude per se, is the bottleneck limiting deeper layer contributions in residual networks. The proposed methods—CascadeFormer and CascadeFlow Pruning—effectively exploit this asymmetry for efficiency gains. Open questions remain about whether gradient magnitude proxies fan-in beyond high-rank regimes and how these dynamics scale to 100B+ parameter models.

Abstract: Deep Transformers are composed of uniformly stacked residual blocks, yet their deepest layers often add little value. We present two efficiency methods that exploit this asymmetry. CascadeFormer tapers width with depth to match the uneven information flow across layers, achieving comparable perplexity to a uniform baseline at the same training budget while reducing latency by 8.6% and increasing throughput by 9.4%. CascadeFlow Pruning removes layers using accumulated training gradients, with no post hoc analysis. It outperforms standard heuristics on perplexity and rank-stability and stays competitive on downstream accuracy. To motivate these methods, we propose Gradient Fan-in Asymmetry (GFA) as a structural account of why deeper layers contribute less. In Pre-LayerNorm residual stacks, the gradient at a layer is the sum of an identity path and all downstream functional paths, producing a gradient fan-in that decays linearly with depth (and quadratically under deep supervision), yielding richer gradients for early layers and sparser ones for later layers. We provide correlational and interventional evidence for GFA on models trained from scratch up to 1.2B parameters. Across Transformers and ResNets, accumulated training gradients follow the theoretical fan-in and are associated with post hoc layer importance. Two interventions point to structure rather than magnitude as the bottleneck: equalizing per-layer gradient norms does not restore late-layer value, while increasing downstream path counts via parameter-shared repetition restores and elevates it. Whether gradient magnitude proxies fan-in beyond high-rank regimes, and how these dynamics behave at the 100B+ scale, remain open questions.

</details>


### [125] [Can Large Language Models Reliably Code Qualitative Humanitarian Data? A Benchmark Study Against Human Expert Adjudication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26541)
*Jerome Marston,Tino Kreutzer,Salomé Garnier,Ella Boone,Phuong N Pham,Patrick Vinck*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This benchmark study evaluates 46 LLMs for deductive coding of synthetic humanitarian transcripts against a human Gold Standard. Multiple LLMs achieved reliability comparable to experienced human coders when using structured prompts and reasoning-enabled configurations, but performance varied on indirect needs, non-standard communication, and protection-sensitive categories. The authors recommend tiered oversight and open-weights models on self-hosted infrastructure for sensitive data governance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Humanitarian organizations lack the staff, time, and specialist expertise to analyze large volumes of qualitative data from affected populations at scale. While LLMs could expand analytical capacity, their reliability for coding humanitarian data has not been empirically established, creating uncertainty about whether and how they should be deployed in high-stakes humanitarian contexts.

Method: The authors constructed 150 high-fidelity synthetic humanitarian transcripts and compared 46 LLMs against a human Gold Standard. Evaluation used three complementary approaches: (1) inter-rater reliability testing via Krippendorff's alpha, (2) discrepancy analysis distinguishing correct, near-correct, and incorrect codes, and (3) qualitative assessment across humanitarian-specific criteria including discrimination, complex needs hierarchies, and non-standard communication styles. Structured prompts and reasoning-enabled configurations were systematically tested.

Result: Multiple LLMs achieved deductive coding reliability comparable to experienced human coders, particularly with structured prompts and reasoning-enabled setups. However, aggregate reliability metrics masked important variation: models struggled with indirectly expressed needs, needs outside predefined categories, and protection-relevant concerns (physical safety, discrimination). Open-weights models on self-hosted infrastructure emerged as a viable path for balancing scalability with data governance.

Conclusion: LLMs can materially expand humanitarian analytical capacity but are not substitutes for human judgment. Responsible deployment requires structured codebooks, reasoning-enabled models, theme-specific performance monitoring, and tiered oversight focused on categories where miscoding carries the greatest programmatic consequences. For sensitive data, self-hosted open-weights models provide a practical path forward.

Abstract: Data from affected populations are crucial for informing humanitarian response, but their value depends on timely and consistent interpretation of nuanced accounts of need. Humanitarian organizations often lack the staff, time, and specialist expertise required to analyze this information at scale. Large language models (LLMs) may expand this capacity, but their reliability for coding qualitative humanitarian data has not been directly established. This benchmark study compares 46 LLMs to a human Gold Standard using 150 high-fidelity synthetic humanitarian transcripts. Evaluation combined inter-rater reliability testing with Krippendorff's alpha, discrepancy analysis distinguishing correct, near-correct, and incorrect codes, and qualitative assessment across humanitarian-specific criteria including discrimination, complex needs hierarchies, and non-standard communication styles. The authors find that multiple LLMs can perform deductive coding at reliability levels comparable to experienced human coders, especially when structured prompts and reasoning-enabled configurations are used. At the same time, aggregate reliability metrics alone are insufficient for deployment decisions. Models varied in recognizing needs expressed indirectly, needs outside predefined categories, and protection-relevant concerns such as physical safety and discrimination. These findings suggest that LLMs can materially expand humanitarian analytical capacity, but not as substitutes for human judgment. Appropriate use requires structured codebooks, reasoning-enabled models, attention to theme-specific performance, and tiered oversight focused on categories where miscoding would have the greatest programmatic consequences. For sensitive humanitarian data, open-weights models deployed on self-hosted infrastructure may offer a viable path for combining analytical scalability with stronger data governance.

</details>


### [126] [Revisiting Action Factorization for Complex Action Spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26574)
*Timothy Flavin,Sandip Sen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A cross-sectional study comparing factorization methods (independent, shared, VDN, QPLEX, Joint, Auto-Regressive) across three algorithm families (PPO, SAC, DQN) on three action space types (discretized, hybrid, continuous) using four lightweight environments. Introduces two new environments and novel VDN-PPO/PPO-MIX variants. Finds branching dueling architectures best balance compute and performance, with Auto-Regressive achieving highest overall performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite widespread real-world need for hybrid discrete-continuous action spaces, existing RL frameworks default to uniform action spaces, and landmark hybrid-action benchmarks are heavyweight, archival, and test only one or few factorization methods on a single control type. A comprehensive cross-sectional comparison across factorization methods, algorithm families, and action spaces is missing.

Method: Cross-sectional empirical study testing six factorization methods (independent networks, shared encoder, VDN, QPLEX, Joint, Auto-Regressive) across three algorithm families (PPO, SAC, DQN) and three action space types (discretized, hybrid, continuous) on four lightweight environments (Platform, hybrid-LunarLander, Hybrid-Shoot, CoopPush). Introduces two new C++ Gymnasium/PettingZoo-compliant environments (CoopPush, Hybrid-Shoot) to isolate state-dependent inter-action dependence challenges. Proposes VDN-PPO and PPO-MIX with branching critics for multi-headed PPO credit assignment.

Result: Analyzed 220 valid configurations. Branching dueling architectures provided the best balance of compute and performance. Auto-Regressive actions achieved the highest overall performance. Native continuous SAC outperformed discrete and hybrid algorithms. VDN-PPO and PPO-MIX outperformed all other tested PPO factorizations.

Conclusion: Branching dueling architectures are recommended for efficiently handling hybrid action spaces. Auto-Regressive factorization yields peak performance at higher computational cost. Continuous SAC remains superior to discretized approaches. The proposed VDN-PPO and PPO-MIX variants advance credit assignment in multi-headed PPO architectures.

Abstract: Many real-world control problems involve hybrid discrete-continuous action spaces. For example, steering and signaling in autonomous driving, and aiming and firing in robotics or video-games. Despite real-world hybrid factorization and reinforcement learning framework support for complex action spaces (e.g., Gymnasium, PettingZoo, TorchRL, SeedRL, Mujoco, etc), the default environments within those frameworks often implement uniform action space configurations (LunarLander, Walker2D, Cheetah, SMAC, SUMO, Ant, Atari). Landmark hybrid-action benchmarks (RoboCup 2D HFO, SC2LE, Platform, CARLA, etc) are mostly heavyweight or archival implementations originating from papers which test one or a small number of competing factorization methods on one kind of control. This article provides a cross-sectional study of factorization methods [independent networks, shared encoder, VDN, QPLEX, Joint, Auto-Regressive] on each of three families of algorithms [PPO, SAC, DQN] across three action spaces [discretized, hybrid, continuous] over four lightweight environments [Platform, hybrid-LunarLander, Hybrid-Shoot, CoopPush]. Accounting for some invalid pairings such as joint-continuous, we are left with 220 configurations to analyze each method. We provide two new C++ parallel gymnasium and petting-zoo compliant environments [CoopPush, Hybrid-Shoot] to isolate particular challenges such as state-dependent inter-action dependence. Finally, we introduce VDN-PPO and PPO-MIX which use a branching critic to assign credit to multi-headed PPO. These variants out-perform all other tested PPO factorizations. Our results suggest that branching dueling architectures balance compute and performance most effectively, with Auto-Regressive actions reaching the highest performance overall and native continuous SAC outperforming discrete and hybrid algorithms, albiet both at increased computational cost.

</details>


### [127] [SharQ: Bridging Activation Sparsity and FP4 Quantization for LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26587)
*Haoqian Meng,Yilun Luo,Yafei Zhao,Wenyuan Liu,Huaqing Zheng,Xindian Ma,Peng Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SharQ is a training-free inference method that combines FP4 quantization with N:M semi-structured sparsity for LLM activations via online sparse-dense decomposition. It uses an input-adaptive mask to extract an outlier-dominated sparse backbone, quantizes both sparse and dense residual paths to FP4, and fuses preprocessing into a single kernel. SharQ recovers 43–63% of the FP4-to-FP16 accuracy gap and achieves 2.2–2.4× latency reduction over FP16 on an RTX 5090.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern accelerators increasingly support both low-bit floating-point formats (FP4) and semi-structured N:M sparsity, but combining them for LLM activation compression is problematic: activation outliers dominate block-wise FP4 quantization scales, and directly applying N:M sparsity masks discards moderate-magnitude values, coupling sparsification loss with quantization error.

Method: SharQ performs an online sparse-dense decomposition per activation tensor: (1) generates an input-adaptive N:M mask identifying outlier-dominated elements as a sparse backbone; (2) quantizes the sparse backbone to FP4; (3) defines a dense residual relative to the quantized (not unquantized) sparse backbone; (4) processes both paths via sparse and dense FP4 GEMMs sharing a single FP4 weight payload with path-specific scale views; (5) fuses mask generation, residual construction, and layer normalization into one kernel. No calibration, retraining, or model-specific tuning is required.

Result: On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, and Qwen3-VL-8B, SharQ recovers 43–63% of the NVFP4-to-FP16 accuracy gap across language and vision-language tasks, and generalizes across NVFP4, HiF4, and MXFP4 formats. On an RTX 5090, it achieves 2.2–2.4× latency reduction over FP16 and 1.2–1.4× throughput improvement over FP8 in language model serving, plus up to 1.58× speedup on Wan2.2-T2V-A14B video generation with SageAttention.

Conclusion: SharQ demonstrates that combining activation sparsity and FP4 quantization via sparse-dense decomposition is effective for inference acceleration, offering significant speedups while preserving accuracy without requiring retraining or calibration, and generalizing across multiple FP4 formats and model architectures.

Abstract: Low-bit floating-point formats and semi-structured sparsity are increasingly supported by modern accelerators, yet combining them for LLM activation compression remains challenging: activations contain input-dependent outliers that dominate block scales in FP4 quantization, and directly applying N:M sparsity masks discards moderate values, coupling sparsification loss with quantization error. We introduce SharQ, a training-free inference method that bridges activation sparsity and FP4 quantization through an online sparse--dense decomposition. For each activation tensor, SharQ generates an input-adaptive N:M mask to extract an outlier-dominated sparse backbone, quantizes it to FP4, and defines a dense residual relative to the quantized sparse backbone rather than the unquantized sparse values. A sparse FP4 GEMM processes the backbone while a dense FP4 GEMM compensates for both mask-induced activation loss and sparse-path quantization error. The two paths share a single FP4 weight payload with path-specific scale views, and a fused preparation kernel absorbs mask generation, residual construction, and layer normalization into one operator. SharQ requires no calibration data, retraining, or model-specific tuning. Evaluated on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, and Qwen3-VL-8B, SharQ recovers 43--63% of the NVFP4-to-FP16 accuracy gap across language and vision-language tasks, and generalizes across NVFP4, HiF4, and MXFP4 formats. On an RTX 5090, SharQ delivers 2.2--2.4$\times$ latency reduction over FP16 and 1.2--1.4$\times$ throughput improvement over FP8 in language model serving, and up to 1.58$\times$ speedup on Wan2.2-T2V-A14B video generation when combined with SageAttention. Our code is available at https://github.com/actypedef/SharQ.

</details>


### [128] [Sketched Linear Contrastive Learning: Approximation, Optimization, and Statistical Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26617)
*Ziyan Chen,Zhongzhu Zhou,Ding-Xuan Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper derives scaling laws for contrastive representation learning using a sketched linear model with paired Gaussian latents. The authors decompose the risk into irreducible risk, approximation error, GD bias, GD variance, and a cross term, then establish explicit scaling with respect to sketch dimension M, sample size N, and effective optimization horizon L_eff. The key finding is that contrastive learning introduces interaction terms between two views, which qualitatively changes how optimization and finite-sample noise scale compared to standard linear regression scaling laws.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior theoretical work has established scaling laws for sketched linear regression, but scaling laws for contrastive representation learning remain poorly understood. The authors aim to provide a first theoretical step toward understanding how model size, data size, and compute jointly govern learning performance in contrastive settings, which are widely used in modern self-supervised learning (e.g., SimCLR, CLIP).

Method: The authors study a sketched linear model under a paired Gaussian latent-variable setup: two correlated latent variables are projected through random sketch matrices to produce two views. A bilinear contrastive score function is trained via full-batch empirical gradient descent (GD) using a Gaussian-negative quadratic contrastive surrogate loss. The analysis assumes aligned power-law spectra for the covariance operators and a contrastive source condition. The risk is decomposed into five components: irreducible risk, approximation error, GD bias, GD variance, and a cross term. The cross term is shown to be controlled by bias and variance, so it does not affect the upper-bound scaling. This decomposition yields explicit scaling laws in terms of M, N, and the effective optimization horizon L_eff (which incorporates step size γ).

Result: The main theorem provides explicit scaling laws showing that contrastive learning introduces interactions between two views that change how optimization and finite-sample noise scale. Specifically, compared to standard linear regression scaling laws, the contrastive setting exhibits different dependencies of bias and variance on model size, sample size, and training time. The cross term is bounded by bias and variance and thus does not tighten the overall rate.

Conclusion: This work provides the first theoretical scaling law characterization for contrastive representation learning in a tractable linear setting. It offers practical guidance for balancing model size (sketch dimension), data (sample size), and compute (optimization horizon) in contrastive pretraining, and lays groundwork for extending scaling law analysis to more realistic nonlinear contrastive models.

Abstract: Scaling laws describe how learning performance varies with model size, data size, and compute. While recent theoretical work has established scaling laws for sketched linear regression, much less is understood for contrastive representation learning. In this paper, we study a sketched linear model for contrastive learning under a paired Gaussian latent-variable setup. The learner observes only sketched views of two correlated variables and trains a bilinear contrastive score by full-batch empirical gradient descent. We analyze a Gaussian-negative quadratic contrastive surrogate under aligned power-law spectra and a contrastive source condition, where we derive a risk decomposition into irreducible risk, approximation error, GD bias, GD variance, and a cross term. The cross term is controlled by the bias and variance and therefore does not affect the upper-bound scaling. Our main theorem gives an explicit scaling law with respect to sketch dimension $M$, sample size $N$, and effective optimization horizon $L_{\mathrm{eff}}γ$. Compared with standard linear-regression scaling laws, the contrastive setting must learn interactions between two views, and this changes how optimization and finite-sample noise scale with model size, data, and training time. This provides a first theoretical step toward understanding scaling behavior in contrastive learning and gives guidance for balancing model size, data, and optimization compute.

</details>


### [129] [Discovering Millions of Interpretable Features with Sparse Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26620)
*XinYang He,Wei Wang,Bing Zhao,Xuan Ren,WenBo Li,WeiXu Qiao,Hu Wei,Lin Qu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Qwen3-Instruct SAE, a suite of sparse autoencoders trained on the Qwen3 instruction-tuned model family (1.7B, 4B, 8B), systematically evaluating sparsity–fidelity trade-offs across layers and components, and demonstrating causal feature steering for refusal behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training SAEs is computationally expensive, and open-source SAE models for instruction-tuned LMs remain scarce. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing a comprehensive, openly available SAE suite for the Qwen3 family to facilitate research on sparse representations and mechanistic interpretability.

Method: The authors train layer-wise SAEs on three activation sites (residual streams, MLP outputs, attention outputs) for Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B, and on a subset of residual stream layers for Qwen3-8B. Evaluation uses activation-level reconstruction metrics (e.g., L0 sparsity, explained variance) and model-level recovery metrics. A refusal-steering case study demonstrates causal intervention by activating selected SAE features.

Result: The evaluation reveals distinct sparsity–fidelity trade-offs across different layers and model components. The refusal-steering case study confirms that selected SAE features can causally steer instruction-tuned Qwen3 models toward refusal behavior, validating the practical utility of the released SAEs.

Conclusion: Qwen3-Instruct SAE provides a practical, open resource for studying sparse representations, feature-level mechanisms, and behavioral interventions in instruction-tuned language models, with demonstrated causal steerability.

Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful tool for decomposing superposed language model representations into sparse and interpretable features. However, training SAEs is computationally expensive, and available open-source SAE models remain limited. In this work, we introduce \textbf{Qwen3-Instruct SAE}, a comprehensive suite of SAEs trained on the Qwen3 instruction-tuned model family, covering Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B. For Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B, we train layer-wise SAEs at three key activation sites: residual streams, MLP outputs, and attention outputs. For Qwen3-8B, we train SAEs on a subset of residual stream layers. We systematically evaluate these SAEs using both activation-level reconstruction metrics and model-level recovery metrics, revealing distinct sparsity--fidelity trade-offs across layers and components. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of Qwen3-Instruct SAE through a refusal-steering case study, showing that selected SAE features can causally steer instruction-tuned Qwen3 models toward refusal behavior. Our release provides a practical resource for studying sparse representations, feature-level mechanisms, and behavioral interventions in instruction-tuned language models

</details>


### [130] [From Weights to Features: SAE-Guided Activation Regularization for LLM Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26629)
*Evan Ning,Wei Xue,Dong Lou,Yike Guo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SAE-based activation-space regularization outperforms weight-space methods like EWC in continual learning for LLMs by leveraging monosemantic feature dictionaries, offering better stability-plasticity balance, memory efficiency, and empirical evidence that weight-space methods fail due to polysemanticity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Weight-space regularization methods (e.g., EWC) underperform on large language models. The authors attribute this to the polysemantic nature of LLMs: per-weight importance estimates are too coarse-grained to isolate specific knowledge needing protection, since individual weights contribute to multiple heterogeneous concepts.

Method: The authors propose activation-space regularization using pretrained Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) as a monosemantic feature dictionary. From constrained optimization, they derive a new loss function balancing stability and plasticity via SAE features. A compact SAE feature mask is computed from current-task data and retained (no previous-task data needed after mask construction). The method operates in lower-dimensional feature space, increasing memory efficiency. EWC is shown as a special case under a one-sided weight-space penalty.

Result: On TRACE and MedCL benchmarks, the method achieves state-of-the-art results among approaches without task-specific architectural components, surpassing EWC and other weight-space methods. Empirical evidence supports the polysemanticity thesis: task-relevant representations are linearly separable in SAE features but indistinguishable from chance in weight basis; weight-space protection is nearly non-selective at the concept level.

Conclusion: Activation-space regularization via SAEs provides a principled, memory-efficient solution to catastrophic forgetting in LLMs, addressing the fundamental limitation of polysemanticity in weight-space methods, with strong empirical performance and theoretical grounding linking EWC as a special case.

Abstract: Weight-space regularization methods such as Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) are the standard approach to catastrophic forgetting in continual learning. However, those methods tend to underperform when applied to large language models. We argue that such underperformance can be partly explained by the ``polysemantic'' nature of large language models: per-weight importance estimates utilized by EWC-style regularization are too coarse and cannot isolate the knowledge that needs protection. In this paper, we propose regularizing instead in the model's activation space, using pretrained Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) as a monosemantic feature dictionary. From the perspective of constrained optimization, we derive a new loss function that uses the SAE feature dictionary to explicitly balance stability and plasticity, and show that EWC is a special case in the one-sided weight-space penalty setting. Unlike replay-based methods that store or revisit examples from earlier tasks, our method requires no previous-task data after mask construction: current-task data is used to compute a compact SAE feature mask, and only this mask is retained for later training. Further, since the feature space has significantly lower dimensionality than the parameter space, the proposed method is more memory efficient. On the TRACE and MedCL continual learning benchmarks, the method achieves the strongest result among approaches without introducing task-specific architectural components, also surpassing traditional weight-space regularization methods like EWC. Beyond performance comparisons, we provide empirical evidence for the polysemanticity thesis: task-relevant representations are linearly separable in the SAE feature basis but indistinguishable from chance in the weight basis, and weight-space protection is nearly non-selective at the concept level.

</details>


### [131] [Target-Aware Bandit Allocation for Scalable Surrogate Optimization in Chemical Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26657)
*Mohammad Haddadnia,Yuvan Chali,Abhilash Jayaraj,Constance Kraay,Joana Reis,Felix Strieth-Kalthoff,Haribabu Arthanari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BOBa is a bandit-guided surrogate optimization framework that partitions massive discrete action spaces and adaptively allocates computation to promising partitions, eliminating the need for full-library surrogate inference in expensive optimization tasks like drug discovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern molecular libraries contain billions to trillions of compounds, making full-library surrogate inference computationally prohibitive. Existing surrogate-based optimization reduces expensive evaluations but does not address the inference bottleneck itself. A method is needed to avoid exhaustive surrogate inference while maintaining optimization effectiveness.

Method: BOBa partitions the action space into subsets and treats each partition as an arm in a multi-armed bandit. It adaptively allocates both surrogate inference and expensive evaluations to empirically promising partitions using optimism-under-uncertainty bandit strategies, concentrating resources where they matter most while preserving principled exploration of underexplored regions.

Result: Experiments on real-world synthesis-on-demand libraries show that optimism-under-uncertainty bandits with meaningful action-space partitioning effectively allocate inference and evaluations. The framework reveals a tunable tradeoff between screening performance and surrogate inference cost, enabling practical optimization over billion-scale libraries.

Conclusion: BOBa establishes a viable route to ultra-large library virtual screening by decoupling surrogate inference cost from library size, supporting practical drug discovery workflows on current and future massive compound collections.

Abstract: Identifying high-utility candidates from massive discrete spaces under expensive evaluations is a recurring challenge across the sciences, with structure-based drug discovery as a prominent example. While surrogate-based optimization can increase sample efficiency by reducing the number of expensive evaluations, modern molecular libraries have reached billions to trillions of compounds, making full-library surrogate inference itself a major computational bottleneck. We introduce BOBa, a bandit-guided surrogate optimization framework that eliminates full-library inference by adaptively allocating computation across partitions of the action space. By treating partitions as arms in a multi-armed bandit, BOBa concentrates inference and evaluations on empirically promising partitions while maintaining principled exploration. Experiments on real-world synthesis-on-demand libraries demonstrate that optimism-under-uncertainty bandits, combined with meaningful action space partitioning, are essential for effective allocation of inference and evaluations. Our findings reveal a tunable tradeoff between screening performance and surrogate inference cost, which supports practical optimization over current libraries, and establishes a viable route to ultra-large library virtual screening.

</details>


### [132] [Zero-Shot Size Transfer for Neural ODEs on Sparse Random Graphs: Graphon Limits and Adjoint Convergence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26662)
*Mingsong Yan,Zhida Wang,Sui Tang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper develops a quantitative theory for zero-shot size-transfer in Graph Neural Differential Equations (GNDEs), showing that GNDEs trained on small graphs can be deployed on larger similar graphs. Using graphon theory, the authors establish convergence rates for GNDE solutions to their infinite-node Graphon-NDE limits, analyze adjoint systems for gradients, and compare discretize-then-optimize vs. optimize-then-discretize training paradigms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GNDEs possess local, size-independent filters that intuitively suggest a zero-shot size-transfer capability. However, no rigorous quantitative theory existed to characterize when and how accurately a GNDE trained on small graphs generalizes to larger graphs, nor to formalize the infinite-node limit of these continuous-time graph dynamics.

Method: The authors model sparse random graphs via graphons and define Graphon Neural Differential Equations (Graphon-NDEs) and adjoint Graphon-NDEs as infinite-node limits. They prove well-posedness, establish trajectory-wise convergence of finite-node GNDE solutions to Graphon-NDE solutions at rate O((α_n n)^{-1/2}) with high probability, and derive uniform-in-time convergence for adjoint systems. They further analyze DTO and OTD training under explicit Euler discretization, proving asymptotic consistency and quantifying discretization errors.

Result: Key results include: (1) trajectory-wise convergence of GNDE to Graphon-NDE at rate O((α_n n)^{-1/2}); (2) uniform-in-time convergence of adjoint (gradient) systems; (3) DTO and OTD discrepancy bounds of O(1/M) for hidden states and O(1/M²) for local parameter gradients; (4) experiments on HSBM and tent graphons confirm theoretical rates; (5) zero-shot transfer across four graphon classes validates accurate deployment on larger graphs.

Conclusion: The paper provides a rigorous theoretical foundation for zero-shot size-transfer in GNDEs, showing that the infinite-node graphon limit governs finite-graph behavior. The quantitative convergence rates and discretization analysis offer practical guidance for training GNDEs on small graphs and deploying on larger ones without retraining.

Abstract: Graph Neural Differential Equations (GNDEs) model continuous-time graph dynamics by parameterizing Neural ODE velocity fields with Graph Neural Networks. Their local, size-independent filters suggest a zero-shot size-transfer principle: train on a small graph and deploy on larger, similar graphs without retraining. We develop a quantitative theory for this principle on sparse random graphs sampled from graphons. We consider Graphon Neural Differential Equations (Graphon-NDEs) and adjoint Graphon-NDEs as the infinite-node limits of the forward and adjoint GNDE systems, and establish well-posedness. For an $n$-node random graph with sparsity parameter $α_n$, we prove trajectory-wise convergence of GNDE solutions to Graphon-NDE solutions at rate $O((α_n n)^{-1/2})$, up to logarithmic factors, with high probability. We also establish uniform-in-time convergence bounds for adjoint systems governing hidden-state and parameter gradients. We further study discretize-then-optimize (DTO) and optimize-then-discretize (OTD) training. Under explicit Euler discretization with $M$ steps, we show that DTO and OTD are asymptotically consistent, with hidden-state and local parameter-gradient discrepancies of orders $O(1/M)$ and $O(1/M^2)$, respectively, up to sparsity and logarithmic factors. Experiments on HSBM and tent graphons support the theoretical rates, while zero-shot transfer experiments across four graphon classes demonstrate accurate deployment of learned GNDEs on larger independently sampled graphs.

</details>


### [133] [PersistentKV: Page-Aware Decode Scheduling for Long-Context LLM Serving on Commodity GPUs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26666)
*Muhammad Ahmed*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PersistentKV introduces an adaptive decode attention engine with page-aware scheduling for LLM serving, switching between FlashInfer and custom workqueue/sequence-splitting kernels based on batch size and context length. On an RTX 3060, the adaptive policy achieves 1.063–1.399× throughput gains over FlashInfer alone across various workloads while avoiding regressions on boundary cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM serving bottlenecks have shifted from dense matrix math to KV-cache movement. Existing solutions face tensions: low-active long-context decoding under-utilizes GPUs, and mixed sequence lengths create a conflict between exact-length launches (many small kernels) and coarse padded batches (wasted compute). Paged-attention reduces fragmentation and FlashInfer provides optimized native-paged decode, but no single kernel is optimal across all batch-size/context-length regimes.

Method: PersistentKV proposes two complementary techniques for grouped-query attention (GQA): (1) mapping work by KV-head group to reuse K,V tiles across grouped query heads with native page-table support, and (2) a compact workqueue schedule that executes only non-empty row-KV-head-sequence-split tasks to avoid wasting compute on padding. A calibrated adaptive policy selects among FlashInfer (small active batches), PersistentKV sequence splitting (B=1 long-context), and PersistentKV workqueue scheduling (B=8 long-context) based on thresholds and split counts determined from calibration traces.

Result: On an RTX 3060 (FP16, page size 16, Hq=32, Hkv=8, d=128) with correctness matched to FlashInfer, the adaptive policy improved synchronized wall throughput by 1.063–1.265× on B8 bimodal, uniform, and Zipf-like workloads, and by 1.399× on a B1 bucketed trace. On the B4 bimodal boundary case, the policy correctly avoided PersistentKV regression by falling back to FlashInfer.

Conclusion: Work assignment and scheduling strategy, not just attention math optimization, is a decisive variable in LLM serving system performance. Page-aware adaptive decode scheduling fills a concrete systems niche, and hybrid policies that route between specialized kernels based on workload characteristics can yield significant throughput gains without regression.

Abstract: Autoregressive large language model (LLM) serving is increasingly limited by key-value (KV) cache movement rather than dense matrix multiplication. Modern paged-attention systems reduce KV-cache fragmentation and mature kernels such as FlashInfer provide highly optimized native-paged decode attention. However, the best single-kernel implementation is not always the best serving schedule: low-active long-context decode can under-utilize commodity GPUs, while mixed sequence lengths introduce a tension between many exact-length launches and coarse padded batches. We present PersistentKV, a native block-table decode attention engine and page-aware scheduling study for grouped-query attention (GQA). PersistentKV maps work by KV-head group, is designed to reuse K,V tiles across grouped query heads, supports native page tables, and adds a compact workqueue schedule that executes only non-empty row-KV-head-sequence-split tasks. On an RTX 3060 with FP16, page size 16, Hq=32, Hkv=8, d=128, and identical correctness tolerance against FlashInfer, a calibrated adaptive policy selects FlashInfer for small active batches, PersistentKV sequence splitting for B1 long-context steps, and PersistentKV workqueue scheduling for B8 long-context steps. With thresholds and split counts fixed on calibration traces, one held-out trace seed improves synchronized wall throughput by 1.063-1.265x on B8 bimodal, uniform, and Zipf-like workloads and by 1.399x on a B1 bucketed trace. On the B4 bimodal boundary case, the policy avoids the PersistentKV regression by selecting FlashInfer. These results identify a concrete systems niche for adaptive page-aware decode scheduling and show that work assignment, not only attention math, is a decisive serving-system variable.

</details>


### [134] [Algorithmic Foundations of Deep Learning: Complexity-Theoretic Rates and a Characterization of Universal Approximation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26705)
*Anastasis Kratsios,Simone Brugiapaglia,Bum Jun Kim,Gregory Cousins,Haitz Sáez de Ocáriz Borde*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Neural network expressivity is governed not only by function regularity (as in classical approximation theory) but also by algorithmic complexity. The paper frames NNs as models of computation, showing that any function computable by a real-valued circuit can be approximated by an NN with bounds controlled by the circuit's structural parameters. This yields exponential improvements in parameter efficiency for algorithmically structured functions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional expressivity theory studies NNs by emulating optimal basis expansions, which measures complexity solely through regularity (e.g., smoothness). This fails to distinguish between functions of comparable regularity but vastly different intuitive complexity—like √x versus a Brownian path. The authors argue that algorithmic structure must be accounted for to capture what makes functions easy or hard for neural networks to learn.

Method: The authors adopt a circuit-complexity perspective: they show that if a function is computable by a real-valued circuit over a given gate language, then an NN can approximate it with depth, width, and non-zero-parameter counts bounded by the circuit's depth, width, gate count, and gate structure. They also prove a universal approximation dichotomy: any definable NN model with a natural parallelization condition is a universal approximator iff it contains a non-affine nonlinearity. The theory is applied to derive guarantees for continuous functions, Besov spaces, holomorphic functions, and numerical algorithms (Newton-Raphson, power iteration).

Result: Key results include: (1) universal approximation for any parallelizable architecture with non-affine nonlinearity; (2) minimax-optimal rates for Besov classes; (3) logarithmic-error complexity for holomorphic functions; (4) NN emulation of numerical algorithms without architecture-specific arguments; (5) for shortest-path on k-vertex graphs via tropical dynamic programming, compiled NNs achieve O(log(1/ε)) non-zero parameters, exponentially improving over the generic O(ε^{-c k²}) Lipschitz-approximation scale.

Conclusion: Neural network complexity is fundamentally governed by both regularity and algorithmic structure. The circuit-computation perspective unifies and extends classical approximation theory, provides precise architectural design principles, and explains why NNs can efficiently represent algorithmically structured functions that would be prohibitively expensive under pure regularity-based approximation.

Abstract: Feedforward neural network (NN) expressivity is typically studied by emulating optimal basis-expansion schemes. While powerful, this perspective is incomplete: it primarily captures complexity through regularity, and therefore does not distinguish intuitively simple and complicated objects with comparable regularity, such as the square-root function and a typical Brownian path.
  The guiding message is that neural networks should be viewed not only as flexible basis functions, but also as models of computation. If a function is computable by a real-valued circuit over a prescribed elementary gate language, then it can be computed to comparable accuracy by an NN with explicit depth, width, and non-zero-parameter bounds controlled by the depth, width, gate count, and gate structure. Thus, neural-network complexity is not governed by regularity alone, but also by algorithmic complexity. We then show that any definable NN model satisfying a natural parallelization condition, allowing possibly multivariate non-linearities such as attention or layer normalization, is a universal approximator if and only if it contains a non-affine nonlinearity.
