Motivation: Existing methods for fractional PDEs (e.g., fPINN, Monte Carlo) suffer from low accuracy, especially when solutions exhibit boundary singularities or require long-time integration. A fully deterministic, high-accuracy framework capable of handling the nonlocal fractional Laplacian on bounded domains with singular behavior is needed.

Method: (1) Geometry-adapted integration split: decomposes the fractional Laplacian into singular near-field, regular interior far-field, and analytical exterior far-field contributions using a spatially dependent near-field radius. (2) Deterministic quadrature: Gauss-Jacobi for singular radial integrals, Gauss for regular radial integrals, deterministic angular quadrature. (3) Boundary-singularity-aware trial functions enriched with explicit boundary features, with two automatic strategies for selecting the leading exponent and evaluating the loss. (4) Spatiotemporally separable neural network for time-dependent PDEs, factorizing the residual into low-dimensional temporal and spatial integrals, trained via alternating neural network subspace optimization.

Result: The proposed fTNN framework achieves high accuracy on benchmark fractional Poisson and fractional advection-diffusion equations. It substantially improves over fPINN and Monte Carlo baselines, particularly for problems with strong boundary singularities and long-time simulations.

Conclusion: The deterministic tensor neural network subspace method provides an accurate and efficient framework for fractional Laplacian PDEs on bounded domains. The geometry-adapted splitting, automatic singularity handling, and separable space-time architecture collectively address key challenges of nonlocality, boundary singularities, and temporal integration, outperforming existing methods.

Abstract: We develop the fTNN, a deterministic tensor neural network subspace method for problems involving the fractional Laplacian on bounded domains, taking the fractional Poisson equation and time-dependent fractional advection-diffusion equation as typical representatives. The work employs a geometry-adapted integration split featuring a spatially dependent near-field radius, which decomposes the fractional Laplacian into three contributions: a singular near field, a regular interior far field, and an analytical exterior far field. Then the singular radial integrals are treated by Gauss-Jacobi quadrature, the regular radial integrals by Gauss quadrature, and the angular variables by deterministic angular quadrature, yielding a fully deterministic integration framework of the fractional Laplacian operator. To accurately resolve low-regularity solutions and the associated loss functional, we construct boundary-singularity-aware trial functions enriched with explicit boundary features, and propose two strategies for automatically selecting the leading exponent and evaluating the loss function from the singularity structure induced by the fractional operator, or jointly by the fractional operator and the source term. For time-dependent fractional PDEs, we design a spatiotemporally separable neural network that factorizes the time-space residual into a sum of low-dimensional temporal and spatial integrals, and we integrate this representation with an alternating neural network subspace optimization strategy for efficient training. Numerical experiments show that the proposed framework attains high accuracy on the tested benchmarks and improves substantially over existing fPINN and Monte Carlo baselines, particularly for problems with strong boundary singularities and long-time simulations.

</details>


### [158] [Stochastic Gradient Optimization with Model-Assisted Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27171)
*Jonne Pohjankukka,Jukka Heikkonen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a model-assisted sampling framework for mini-batch gradient estimation that bridges machine learning optimization with survey sampling theory. By treating the dataset as a fixed finite population and incorporating auxiliary gradient-prediction models, the method constructs more efficient gradient estimators, achieving performance gains in 71-86% of experiments and halving training epochs needed for comparable generalization with AdamW.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Stochastic gradient estimation in deep learning introduces noise that creates trade-offs between convergence stability, speed, and generalization. Existing variance reduction techniques (SVRG, SAG) and adaptive optimizers mitigate gradient noise but incur additional computational overhead. The authors identify an unexplored connection between mini-batch gradient estimation and survey sampling theory, motivating a framework that leverages auxiliary models to construct more efficient estimators without altering optimizer dynamics.

Method: The authors propose a model-assisted sampling framework that interprets mini-batch gradient computation through the lens of survey sampling. The dataset is treated as a fixed finite population, and per-sample gradients are treated as sample-based estimates of the full gradient. Auxiliary gradient-prediction models are incorporated to construct more efficient gradient estimators following principles from survey sampling theory (e.g., ratio estimation, regression estimation). Uniform random sampling emerges as a special case when no auxiliary information is used. The framework integrates seamlessly with existing optimizers (SGD, Adam, AdamW, etc.) as a drop-in replacement for standard mini-batch gradient estimation.

Result: Empirical evaluation on synthetic and six benchmark datasets demonstrated performance gains in 71-86% of experiments. The method is particularly effective for medium-sized input spaces. With momentum-based optimizers like AdamW, the proposed estimator achieves clearly better generalization in approximately half the training epochs compared to the baseline estimator.

Conclusion: The model-assisted sampling framework successfully bridges machine learning optimization and survey sampling theory, providing a principled approach to variance reduction in stochastic gradient estimation. The method improves efficiency without modifying optimizer dynamics, integrates easily with existing optimizers, and demonstrates consistent empirical gains, particularly accelerating convergence with momentum-based methods.

Abstract: This work addresses the problem of variance in stochastic gradient estimation for machine learning optimization. Deep learning relies on mini-batch methods such as stochastic gradient descent, which approximate full gradients but introduce noise, creating trade-offs between convergence stability, speed, and generalization. Existing methods, including variance reduction techniques (e.g., SVRG and SAG) and adaptive optimizers, aim to mitigate gradient noise but may introduce additional computational overhead. We propose a model-assisted sampling framework that interprets mini-batch gradients through survey sampling theory, treating the dataset as a fixed finite population and gradients as sample-based estimates. Our aim is to bridge machine learning optimization and survey sampling theory by combining their perspectives on sample-based estimation and variance reduction. By incorporating auxiliary gradient-prediction models, we construct more efficient gradient estimators, with uniform sampling arising as a special case when no auxiliary information is used. Our approach integrates easily with existing optimizers, improving efficiency without altering their dynamics. Empirical results on synthetic and six benchmark datasets show performance gains in 71-86% of the experiments, particularly for medium-sized input spaces in our benchmarks. Notably, with momentum-based optimizers such as AdamW, the proposed estimator achieves clearly better generalization in roughly half the training epochs compared to baseline estimator.

</details>


### [159] [RecallRisk-BERT: A Multi-Task Framework for Post-Report Medical Device Recall Triage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27174)
*Ali Semih Atalay,Sevgi Yigit-Sert*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents RecallRisk-BERT, a multi-task model that jointly predicts FDA medical device recall severity (Class I/II/III) and root-cause categories by combining PubMedBERT-based text representations of recall narratives with embeddings of structured features. The model enables automated post-report recall triage and risk analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The growing volume of FDA medical device recall records creates challenges in efficient post-report triage, severity assessment, and root-cause interpretation. Existing studies treat recall occurrence prediction and root-cause analysis separately, with limited attention to joint modeling of severity and root-cause categories.

Method: Using 54,165 FDA medical device recall records (2002–Oct 2025) from openFDA, the authors first benchmark classical ML and boosting models for single-task prediction. They then develop RecallRisk-BERT, a multi-task architecture that fuses PubMedBERT-based embeddings of recall narrative text with embedding-based representations of structured categorical features (product code, regulation number, medical specialty) to simultaneously predict recall severity (3 classes) and consolidated root-cause category (9 classes). Evaluation uses accuracy, macro-averaged precision/recall/F1, and ROC-AUC.

Result: In single-task severity prediction, a LightGBM text–tabular configuration achieved 0.963 accuracy, 0.856 macro-F1, and 0.974 ROC-AUC. In the multi-task setting, RecallRisk-BERT substantially outperformed the single-task PubMedBERT baseline. Model-derived risk rankings showed strong consistency with observed root-cause severity patterns (Spearman's ρ = 0.983, p = 1.936e-6).

Conclusion: Text–tabular multi-task learning can support scalable post-report recall triage, regulatory decision support, and model-based root-cause risk analysis for FDA medical device recalls.

Abstract: Medical device recalls are a critical regulatory mechanism for protecting patient safety. The growing volume of FDA recall records presents challenges in post-report recall triage, severity assessment, and root-cause interpretation. Existing studies mostly address recall occurrence prediction or root-cause analysis separately, while joint modeling of recall severity and root-cause categories has received limited attention. We develop an automated recall triage framework using 54,165 FDA medical device recall records from openFDA, covering the period from 2002 to October 2025. We first evaluate classical machine learning and boosting-based models for recall severity and root-cause category prediction. We then develop RecallRisk-BERT, a multi-task model that combines PubMedBERT-based textual representations of recall narratives with embedding-based representations of structured categorical features, including product code, regulation number, and medical specialty. The model simultaneously predicts recall severity (Class I/II/III) and a consolidated root-cause category (9 classes). Performance was evaluated using accuracy, macro-averaged precision, recall, F1-score, and ROC-AUC. In single-task severity prediction, our LightGBM-based text--tabular configuration achieved the strongest performance, with an accuracy of 0.963, macro-F1 of 0.856, and ROC-AUC of 0.974. In the multi-task setting, RecallRisk-BERT substantially outperformed the single-task PubMedBERT baseline. Model-derived risk rankings were strongly consistent with observed root-cause severity patterns (rho = 0.983, p = 1.936e-6). These findings indicate that text--tabular learning can support scalable post-report recall triage, regulatory decision support, and model-based root-cause risk analysis.

</details>


### [160] [Automating Potential-based Reward Shaping with Vision Language Model Guidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27180)
*Henrik Müller,Daniel Kudenko*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: VLM-PBRS introduces a framework that uses small vision-language models to learn potential functions for potential-based reward shaping, preserving optimal policies while improving sample efficiency in sparse-reward RL settings without expert-designed heuristics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sparse rewards challenge RL agents due to lack of intermediate feedback. While potential-based reward shaping (PBRS) preserves optimal policies, it requires hand-crafted potential functions. Large VLMs could provide feedback but are too expensive for repeated invocation during policy learning.

Method: VLM-PBRS queries a lightweight VLM to obtain preferences over image pairs, then trains a potential function model from these preferences. The learned potential is used for PBRS, preserving the original optimal policy set while providing dense intermediate rewards.

Result: Empirical validation in Meta-World and Franka Kitchen environments shows that even with less accurate preference labels from small VLMs, learning is accelerated. A connection between VLM preference label accuracy and sample efficiency improvements is demonstrated.

Conclusion: The framework offers three contributions: first application of VLM preference-based learning for PBRS potential synthesis, a low-cost principled solution using small VLMs, and extensive empirical evidence of improved sample efficiency and robustness to reward hacking.

Abstract: Sparse rewards are inherently challenging for reinforcement learning agents as they lack intermediate feedback to guide exploration and to correctly attribute the sparse success rewards to relevant parts of the trajectory. Naive reward shaping can induce reward hacking, yielding policies that exploit auxiliary signals instead of solving the intended task. Potential-based reward shaping (PBRS) guarantees preservation of the optimal policy set, but requires the definition of a heuristic potential function over the state space. In this work, we introduce the VLM-guided PBRS framework VLM-PBRS that learns the potential function directly from vision language model (VLM) feedback. We query a lightweight VLM to obtain preferences over image pairs and train a model of the potential function using these preferences. As this approach is based on potential-based reward shaping, it preserves the original optimal policies, and removes the need for expert-designed reward shaping terms. Because large VLMs are prohibitively expensive to invoke repeatedly during policy learning, we employ smaller, more computationally efficient VLMs. Although the resulting preference labels are less accurate, empirical evidence shows that the preference labels can still be used to accelerate learning. We validate our method empirically in the Meta-World and Franka Kitchen environments and highlight the connection between VLM preference label accuracy and sample efficiency improvements. Our contributions are threefold: (1) the first application of VLM preference-based learning to synthesize a potential function for PBRS, (2) a principled, low-cost solution that leverages small VLMs, and (3) extensive empirical demonstration of improved sample efficiency and robustness to reward hacking.

</details>


### [161] [Explaining Temporal Graph Neural Networks via Feature-induced Information Flow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27201)
*Ping Xiong,Thomas Schnake,Klaus-Robert Müller,Shinichi Nakajima*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a novel attribution method for Event-based Temporal Graph Neural Networks (ETGNNs) that traces the entire information flow—including previously overlooked event-induced variables—using an extended Normalized Relevance Measure (NRM) framework with modular decomposition. It demonstrates superior performance over existing methods on synthetic and real-world datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing explanation methods for ETGNNs only trace contributions from event-related embeddings to the output, ignoring event-induced variables that mediate node interactions and capture long-range temporal dependencies. This incomplete information flow analysis undermines explainability, especially as ETGNN architectures grow more complex.

Method: The authors propose an attribution method that analyzes the entire information flow through all event-associated variables, built upon the Normalized Relevance Measure (NRM) framework. NRM enables explicit quantification of relevance flowing from event embeddings and through event-induced variables, ensures cross-layer comparability of latent variables, and supports higher-order interaction analysis. A modular decomposition procedure extends NRM to handle architectural complexity by systematically constructing relevance structures for complex neural architectures.

Result: The method was evaluated on two synthetic datasets (epidemic tracing, social dynamics) and one real-world dataset (political event networks). Both qualitative and quantitative experiments show consistent outperformance over existing explanation approaches, with more human-interpretable explanations.

Conclusion: By capturing the full information flow—including through event-induced variables—the proposed NRM-based attribution method provides more complete and interpretable explanations for ETGNNs, overcoming a key limitation of prior work and establishing a foundation for higher-order event interaction analysis.

Abstract: Event-based Temporal Graph Neural Networks (ETGNNs) have demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of applications, including social network analysis, epidemic tracing, recommender systems, and political event forecasting. However, their increasing complexity poses significant challenges for explainability. Existing explanation methods focus only on a subset of the information flow within ETGNNs, typically tracing contributions from the event-related embeddings to the output. Consequently, they overlook the important pathways through event-induced variables, which mediate interactions between nodes and thereby play a central role in capturing long-range temporal dependencies. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel attribution method that analyzes the \emph{entire} information flow through all event-associated variables. Our method is built upon the recent Normalized Relevance Measure (NRM) framework, which enables explicit quantification of information flow originating from event embeddings as well as information flow passing through event-induced variables. It also ensures comparability of latent variables across layers, and supports higher-order analysis of interactions between events. To handle the architectural complexity of ETGNNs, we extend the NRM framework with a modular decomposition procedure that facilitates the systematic construction of relevance structure for complex neural architectures. We evaluate our approach on two synthetic datasets for epidemic tracing and social dynamics, as well as a real-world dataset of political event networks. Our qualitative and quantitative experiments show that our method consistently outperforms existing explanation approaches while producing more human-interpretable explanations.

</details>


### [162] [Graph Neural Networks Applications Across Domains: All Insights You Need](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27202)
*Abderaouf Bahi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A comprehensive survey that unifies graph neural network design through a single design space, connects expressivity to the Weisfeiler-Leman hierarchy, and systematically evaluates GNN performance across twelve application domains, identifying cross-domain failure patterns and adoption constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GNNs have become the default model for relational data, but the field lacks clarity on where graph structure genuinely adds value versus where it imposes unnecessary computational cost. The survey aims to shift the discourse from "does message passing help?" to a more nuanced cost–benefit analysis of graph structure across diverse real-world settings.

Method: The authors organize GNN architectures around a unified design space, deriving both spectral and spatial formulations from shared first principles. They map expressive power explicitly to the Weisfeiler-Leman hierarchy, cataloguing what specific architectures can and cannot distinguish. Against this framework, they survey twelve application domains—recommendation, knowledge graphs, drug discovery, healthcare, computer vision, traffic, energy systems, wireless/6G, fraud, industrial prognostics, materials science, and climate modelling—analyzing graph construction choices, dominant architectures, and whether reported gains survive rigorous baselining.

Result: Several cross-domain patterns emerge: heterophily and scale degrade the same model families nearly universally; temporal graphs remain significantly harder than static ones; and architectures dominating public leaderboards rarely translate to deployed systems. Over-smoothing, over-squashing, robustness, distribution shift, fairness, and explainability are reframed not as afterthoughts but as binding constraints governing real-world adoption.

Conclusion: The field must move beyond leaderboard-driven architecture design toward deployment-aware GNN development. The recurring failure modes across domains suggest that fundamental structural challenges—heterophily, scale, temporality, and robustness constraints—are far from solved, and closing the gap between benchmark champions and production-ready systems should be the community's central priority.

Abstract: Graph neural networks have moved from a niche representation-learning technique to the default model class wherever data carry relational structure. The interesting question is no longer whether message passing helps on a given dataset, but where graph structure earns its computational cost and where it does not. This survey organises the field around a single design space, derives the spectral and spatial formulations from shared first principles, and connects expressive power to the Weisfeiler-Leman hierarchy with explicit statements of what current architectures can and cannot separate. Against that methodological backbone we examine twelve application domains, among them recommendation and social networks, knowledge graphs and language-model integration, drug discovery and molecular property learning, healthcare and neuroscience, computer vision, traffic and urban computing, power and renewable-energy systems, wireless and sixth-generation networks, fraud and cybersecurity, industrial prognostics, materials science, and climate modelling. For each domain we specify the graph-construction choices and their costs, identify which architecture families dominate and why, and separate reported gains from artefacts of weak baselines or favourable splits. A cross-domain comparison exposes recurring patterns: heterophily and scale undercut the same models almost everywhere, temporal graphs remain harder than their static counterparts, and the architectures that top public leaderboards are seldom the ones that reach deployment. We treat over-smoothing, over-squashing, robustness, distribution shift, fairness, and explainability not as a closing checklist but as the constraints that decide adoption.

</details>


### [163] [The Geometry of Updates: Fisher Alignment at Vocabulary Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27242)
*John Sweeney*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FisherSketch is a training-free method for selecting transfer sources among LLMs sharing a tokenizer but differing in prediction targets. It computes head Fisher alignment via a streaming cosine between kernel mean embeddings in joint activation-error space, using compact 16–192 KB task signatures—making it both practical and diagnostic, and effective where activation-only similarity (e.g., CKA) fails.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In scientific string domains (SMILES, proteins, genomics), LLM families share vocabularies/tokenizers but have divergent prediction targets, creating an "activation-dark" regime where representation-similarity metrics (e.g., CKA) become non-identifiable for transfer—models can share identical representations yet undergo orthogonal head updates. Classical update-geometry metrics (e.g., full Fisher) are computationally prohibitive at vocabulary scale. A lightweight, training-free source selection method is needed that captures transfer-relevant update structure without materializing the Fisher matrix.

Method: The authors first prove that in a shared-output-head setting, CKA and similar representation metrics are non-identifiable for transfer. They then derive the identity that head Fisher alignment equals a cosine between kernel mean embeddings in the joint activation-error space, decomposing into activation, error, and coupling factors. FisherSketch estimates this cosine via a single streaming pass using sketching, producing compact per-task signatures (16 KB for m=4096) and per-task streaming state (192 KB). It operates purely on model forward passes without any training or Fisher materialization.

Result: FisherSketch, with K=128–256, yields practical head Fisher alignment estimates with tiny storage (signatures small enough to store alongside a model hash). Shared-parameter and internal-layer validations, plus Llama-3.1-8B verbalizer-shift experiments, demonstrate that FisherSketch remains informative when activation similarity (CKA) cannot distinguish tasks. The signatures also serve as a diagnostic instrument, revealing whether task similarity is driven by activations, errors, or their coupling.

Conclusion: FisherSketch enables scalable, training-free source selection for shared-vocabulary LLM families by computing head Fisher alignment efficiently via sketched kernel mean embeddings. It resolves the non-identifiability of representation-only metrics and provides both practical transfer selection and a diagnostic lens into the activation-error-coupling structure of LLM task similarity.

Abstract: Training-free source selection for LLM families with shared vocabularies arises in scientific string domains such as SMILES, protein, and genomic sequences, where candidate corpora share a tokenizer but differ in prediction targets. This creates an activation-dark regime: representation-similarity metrics can be uninformative without assumptions about label-conditioned error geometry, while classical update-geometry metrics are computationally prohibitive at vocabulary scale. We show that, in a shared-output head setting, representation metrics (e.g., CKA) are non-identifiable for transfer; models can share identical representations yet have orthogonal head updates. The key identity is that head Fisher alignment is exactly a cosine between kernel mean embeddings in the joint activation-error space, exposing activation, error, and coupling factors rather than requiring a materialized Fisher matrix. FisherSketch estimates this cosine directly in a single streaming pass, making K=128,256 head Fisher alignment practical with a 16 KB task signature (m=4096) and a 192 KB per-task streaming state, small enough to store next to a model hash, but encoding transfer-relevant update structure. Beyond source selection, the same signatures and marginals provide a diagnostic instrument for studying whether LLM task similarity is driven by activations, errors, or their coupling; shared-parameter and internal-layer validations, together with Llama-3.1-8B verbalizer-shift experiments, show that FisherSketch remains informative when activation similarity cannot distinguish tasks.

</details>


### [164] [Effective Covariance Dynamics in Solvable High-Dimensional GANs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27246)
*Andrew Bond,Zafer Doğan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a solvable high-dimensional GAN model with a linear generator learning low-dimensional subspaces from data with structured (class-dependent, correlated, non-zero-mean) latent covariance. It proves convergence to deterministic ODEs governed by an effective second moment, and reveals a signal-boosting mechanism where low-rank correlations lift weak modes above the learnability threshold while overly strong correlations destabilize recovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior solvable GAN analyses are limited to unconditional signals with diagonal latent covariance. Real-world data, however, exhibit class-conditional structure, correlations among latent features, and non-zero means. The authors seek to extend the theoretical understanding of GAN training dynamics to this richer, more realistic covariance structure.

Method: The authors analyze a high-dimensional GAN model with a linear generator and a quadratic energy discriminator (multi-feature setting). They introduce structured latent covariance — class-dependent, correlated, with non-zero mean — and show that all heterogeneity enters the dynamics through a probability-weighted effective second moment. They rigorously prove that the stochastic microscopic training process converges to deterministic ODEs in the high-dimensional limit. A matched-covariance specialization enables stability analysis, yielding a mode-wise solvable interval bounded by learning rates and noise level.

Result: The analysis uncovers a signal-boosting mechanism: low-rank correlations can elevate weak directions above the learnability threshold, enabling recovery of modes that would otherwise be unlearnable. Conversely, overly strong correlations destabilize the recovery process. The derived phase boundary and ODE dynamics are validated by numerical simulations. Experiments on MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR-10 demonstrate that incorporating informed generator covariance improves alignment with data-driven reference subspaces.

Conclusion: The paper successfully extends solvable GAN theory to structured latent covariance, providing rigorous convergence guarantees and revealing a nuanced interplay between correlation strength and learnability. The signal-boosting mechanism offers both theoretical insight and practical guidance for designing generator priors that improve subspace recovery in real-world datasets.

Abstract: We study a solvable high-dimensional model of generative adversarial network (GAN) training in which a linear generator learns a low-dimensional subspace from data with structured latent covariance. Prior solvable GAN analyses assume unconditional signals with diagonal latent covariance; we extend the multi-feature discriminator setting to class-dependent, correlated, and non-zero-mean latent structure. For the quadratic energy discriminator, all such heterogeneity enters the dynamics through a probability-weighted effective second moment. We prove that the stochastic microscopic training process converges, in the high-dimensional limit, to deterministic ordinary differential equations governed by this effective covariance. In the matched-covariance specialization, the stability analysis yields a mode-wise solvable interval determined by the learning rates and noise level: learning begins when the leading effective eigenvalue crosses the lower threshold, while full recovery requires all relevant effective modes to remain within the interval. This reveals a signal-boosting mechanism: low-rank correlations can lift weak directions above the learnability threshold, whereas overly strong correlations destabilize recovery. Numerical simulations validate the ODE, phase boundary, and boosting mechanism. Experiments on MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR-10 further show that informed generator covariance improves alignment with the data-driven reference subspace.

</details>


### [165] [RSPC: A Benchmark for Modeling Stress and Psychiatric Conditions in Digitally Mediated Relationships using Psychiatrist Annotations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27247)
*Parmitha Vangapandu,Sai Ganesh Mokkapati,Sathwik Narkedimilli,MSVPJ Sathvik,Timothy Liu,Simon See,Johannes C. Eichstaedt*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces RSPC, a Reddit corpus annotated by psychiatrists for mood disorders, relational triggers, and relationship phase. Benchmarking transformer models and LLMs reveals task-dependent performance differences, with Claude-3-Haiku best for disorder classification and GPT-4o best for trigger detection. The work advocates shifting mental health NLP from individual-centric to context-aware, relationally-grounded modeling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current NLP approaches to mental health model conditions as isolated individual phenomena, ignoring the interpersonal and relational contexts that often precipitate or exacerbate distress. The authors aim to fill this gap by capturing both mental health symptoms and the relational triggers within which they arise.

Method: The authors construct the Relational Stress and Psychiatry Corpus (RSPC) — 1,799 Reddit posts from long-distance relationship forums, annotated by psychiatrists for (1) diagnostic categories (anxiety, depression, and other mood disorders), (2) relational stressor triggers, and (3) relationship phase indicators. They then benchmark seven fine-tuned transformer models and five LLMs (including GPT-4o and Claude-3-Haiku) across three tasks: multi-label disorder classification, relational trigger detection, and temporal phase prediction.

Result: Claude-3-Haiku achieves the highest disorder classification performance (Macro-F1 = 0.538), while GPT-4o leads in relational trigger detection (Macro-F1 = 0.519), revealing task-dependent model capabilities. A strong association between anxiety disorders and chronic relational uncertainty is also identified.

Conclusion: RSPC provides a new benchmark for context-aware mental health NLP. The findings support a paradigm shift from individual-centric diagnostic modeling toward approaches that incorporate social relationships and temporal dynamics. Distinct model strengths across tasks suggest that downstream applications may benefit from task-specific model selection rather than a one-size-fits-all approach.

Abstract: In NLP, mental health conditions are often modeled as isolated phenomena, without interpersonal context. We use Reddit posts about long-distance relationships to capture both mental health distress and associated relational triggers. We introduce the Relational Stress and Psychiatry Corpus (RSPC) containing 1,799 Reddit posts annotated by psychiatrists for diagnostic categories, including the most prevalent mood disorders (anxiety and depression), relational stressor triggers, and indications of relationship phase. We benchmark seven fine-tuned transformer models and five large language models across multi-label disorder classification, relational trigger detection, and temporal phase prediction tasks. We find clear task-dependent differences between model families, with Claude-3-Haiku achieving the best disorder classification performance (Macro-F1 = 0.538) and GPT-4o obtaining the strongest relational trigger detection performance (Macro-F1 = 0.519), suggesting distinct model capabilities. We further find strong associations between anxiety disorders and chronic relational uncertainty. Overall, RSPC establishes a benchmark for NLP tasks that consider relational context and supports a shift from individual-centric to context-aware mental health modeling that captures the social and temporal dynamics of distress.

</details>


### [166] [BetXplain: An Explanation-Annotated Dataset for Detecting Manipulative Betting Advertisements on Social Media](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27274)
*MSVPJ Sathvik,Parmitha Vangapadu,Nishit Rane,Sathwik Narkedimilli,Mark Lee,Akrati Saxena*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a novel manually annotated dataset of betting advertisements from Instagram and Reddit, labeled for manipulative and deceptive practices with human explanations, enabling explainable detection of harmful advertising strategies and their mental health impacts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Betting advertisements on social media increasingly employ persuasive techniques that mislead users and encourage risky behavior, yet automated detection research is hindered by the absence of publicly available annotated datasets.

Method: The authors collected betting-related advertisements from Instagram and Reddit, then manually annotated them for manipulative and deceptive advertising practices. Each annotation includes human-provided explanations describing the reasoning behind the classification, supporting explainable AI approaches.

Result: A new publicly available dataset of betting advertisements with classification labels and supporting explanations was created. Analysis revealed common persuasive strategies used in betting ads and their potential mental health impacts on users.

Conclusion: The dataset and framework enable practical applications including browser plugins to warn users about manipulative betting ads and automated web crawlers for regulatory monitoring, addressing a critical gap in detecting harmful gambling promotions online.

Abstract: The promotion of betting applications on social media platforms has increased significantly in recent years. Many of these advertisements use persuasive techniques that may mislead users, encourage risky behavior, and potentially influence users' mental well-being. However, research on the automated detection of manipulative and deceptive betting advertisements remains limited due to the lack of publicly available annotated datasets. In this work, we introduce a new dataset of betting-related advertisements collected from two widely used social media platforms, Instagram and Reddit. The advertisements were manually annotated for manipulative and deceptive advertising practices. In addition to classification labels, the dataset includes human-provided explanations that describe the reasoning behind each annotation, enabling research into explainable approaches to detecting manipulative advertising. Furthermore, we analyze the strategies commonly used in betting advertisements and examine how these persuasive tactics may impact users' mental health. The proposed framework can also enable practical applications such as browser plugins that warn users about manipulative betting advertisements and automated web crawlers that help regulatory authorities monitor and detect such promotions online.

</details>


### [167] [How Good Can Linear Models Be for Time-Series Forecasting?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27282)
*Lang Huang,Jinglue Xu,Luke Darlow*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper challenges the trend toward larger forecasting models by showing that optimizing preprocessing (context length, normalization, regularization, augmentation) with simple Ridge regression can match or exceed complex architectures at far lower cost, while revealing interpretable data diagnostics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The dominant assumption in time-series forecasting is that larger model capacity (Transformers, foundation models) is necessary for accuracy. The authors challenge this, hypothesizing that most performance gains can be achieved through optimal preprocessing rather than model scaling, and that simpler models with interpretable weights can provide insights into data structure that black-box models obscure.

Method: The authors use Ridge regression with closed-form solution as a testbed. They perform hyperparameter search over context length, local normalization (learned trailing fraction), L2 regularization, and augmentation across eight standard benchmarks (ETTm2, Exchange, Traffic, etc.). Optimal hyperparameters are read directly from fitted weights. They analyze three axes: optimal lookback length per series, normalization strategy, and degree of cross-series parameter sharing.

Result: Three key findings: (1) Optimal lookback is strongly series-specific and often non-monotonic in forecast horizon — fitted power-law exponents range from +0.46 (ETTm2) to −0.19 (Exchange, Traffic), contradicting the convention that longer horizons need longer history. (2) Normalizing over a learned trailing fraction of context is almost universally preferred over full-context normalization. (3) Series within the same dataset disagree on hyperparameters; optimal cross-series sharing varies from fully shared to fully per-series. The Ridge models beat prior linear forecasters on most entries and exceed Transformer, MLP, and CNN baselines on six of eight benchmarks.

Conclusion: Preprocessing optimization closes the accuracy gap to large models at negligible cost. The optimized hyperparameters serve as interpretable diagnostics, revealing structures (e.g., optimal lookback exponents, normalization preferences) that larger architectures absorb opaquely into their parameters. This suggests a methodological refocus from scaling to systematic preprocessing tuning.

Abstract: Time-series forecasting research has been moving steadily toward larger architectures, from specialized transformers to general-purpose foundation models, on the assumption that capacity is what unlocks accuracy. We take the opposite position: most of the gap can be closed at far lower cost by tuning preprocessing rather than scaling models. We use Ridge regression as the testbed, since it has a closed-form solution and interpretable weights, which let the optimal hyperparameters be read off the search directly. We search over context length, local normalization, regularization, and augmentation on eight standard benchmarks and find three patterns. (1) Optimal lookback is strongly series-specific and often non-monotonic in forecast horizon, with fitted power-law exponents ranging from $+0.46$ on ETTm2 to $-0.19$ on Exchange and Traffic, challenging the convention that longer horizons need longer history. (2) Normalizing over a learned trailing fraction of the context, rather than its entirety, is almost universally preferred. (3) Series within the same dataset often disagree on hyperparameters; the optimal degree of cross-series sharing varies from fully shared to fully per-series. The resulting models beat prior linear forecasters on most dataset-horizon entries and exceed Transformer, MLP, and CNN baselines on six of eight benchmarks. The optimized hyperparameters also serve as a diagnostic on the data itself, revealing structures that larger models absorb silently into their learned parameters.

</details>


### [168] [Recovering Governing Equations from Solution Data: Identifiability Bounds for Linear and Nonlinear ODEs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27285)
*Yang Pan,Helmut Bölcskei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a theoretical framework for analyzing when and how well governing ODEs can be identified from solution data. It proposes Hausdorff distance on solution sets as a natural metric, establishes identifiability bounds across linear to Lipschitz/Hölder-continuous ODE classes, and derives metric entropy and sample complexity bounds for reliably recovering the governing equation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current scientific machine learning literature lacks theoretical understanding of the conditions under which a ground-truth ODE can be uniquely and stably identified from multiple solution observations, and no quantitative sample complexity analysis exists for such learning tasks.

Method: The authors introduce the Hausdorff distance on solution sets as the metric for comparing differential equations, capturing worst-case separation over all admissible initial conditions. They then establish identifiability bounds across ODE classes (linear to nonlinear with Lipschitz/Hölder-continuous vector fields) and derive metric entropy estimates to quantify sample complexity.

Result: The paper provides identifiability bounds that characterize precisely when two distinct ODEs can be distinguished from solution data, and yields quantitative sample complexity bounds specifying how many solution observations are needed for reliable recovery of the governing equation.

Conclusion: The Hausdorff distance framework provides a principled minimax approach to ODE identification, offering the first quantitative sample complexity analysis in this domain and establishing theoretical guarantees across a broad spectrum of ODE classes.

Abstract: Learning governing equations from observed solution data is a fundamental challenge in scientific machine learning \cite{bruntonDiscoveringGoverningEquations2016,kovachkiNeuralOperatorLearning2023,longPDENetLearningPDEs2018,rudyDatadrivenDiscoveryPartial2017,raonicConvolutionalNeuralOperators2023}, yet the theoretical conditions under which a ground-truth ODE can be uniquely and stably identified from multiple solution observations remain largely undeveloped, and no quantitative analysis of the sample complexity of such learning tasks exists in the literature. To address this gap, we introduce the Hausdorff distance on solution sets as the natural metric for comparing differential equations, since it captures the worst-case separation between two equations over all admissible initial conditions and thus encodes the minimax structure of the identification problem. We establish identifiability bounds for governing ODEs across a wide class of structure equations--ranging from linear ODEs to nonlinear classes with Lipschitz (Hölder)-continuous vector fields--characterizing precisely when two distinct equations can be distinguished from solution data. Using this metric, we derive metric entropy estimates for the relevant ODE classes and analyze sample complexity bounds, quantifying how many solution observations are needed to reliably recover the governing equation.

</details>


### [169] [Designing Reward Signals for Portable Query Generation: A Case Study in Industrial Semantic Job Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27291)
*Ping Liu,Qianqi Shen,Jianqiang Shen,Wenqiong Liu,Rajat Arora,Yunxiang Ren,Chunnan Yao,Dan Xu,Baofen Zheng,Wanjun Jiang,Andrii Soviak,Kevin Kao,Jingwei Wu,Wenjing Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents an RLAIF framework for generating portable job search queries and finds that reward shaping overwhelmingly determines optimization success—critic-free methods like RLOO/REINFORCE++ resist reward hacking, while GRPO's group-relative advantage normalization makes it vulnerable to exploiting LLM-as-judge flaws. A rule-based reward floor corrects verbatim-copying degeneration, yielding +0.147 quality improvement, and the authors show training-time reward metrics inflate gains by 2.4×.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Job-search platforms use low-bandwidth query interfaces that cannot capture the high-dimensional complexity of candidate profiles. The authors aim to generate "portable" queries that abstract away personally identifiable seeker-specific identifiers while preserving generalizable qualifications. The core challenge is that RLAIF on this task creates a highly adversarial reward surface where policy optimization exploits flaws in LLM-as-judge rubrics, leading to degenerate verbatim-copying behaviors.

Method: The authors propose an end-to-end RLAIF framework for portable job search query generation. They conduct comprehensive empirical experiments isolating the impact of optimization mechanics versus structured reward engineering across multiple critic-free optimizers: RLOO, REINFORCE++, and GRPO. They introduce a deterministic, rule-based reward floor that corrects for rewards spuriously assigned to verbatim-copying outputs, and evaluate using a cross-family evaluation judge.

Result: Critic-free per-rollout baseline methods (RLOO, REINFORCE++) natively resist reward hacking due to their per-rollout baselines. GRPO's group-relative advantage normalization is uniquely sensitive to spurious reward signals, making it disproportionately susceptible to exploitation. The rule-based reward floor mitigates this failure mode, producing a +0.147 quality improvement on the cross-family judge. The training-time reward model inflates performance gains by 2.4×, confirming that reward shaping discipline—not optimizer choice—is the fundamental driver of success.

Conclusion: For critic-free optimizers, performance is overwhelmingly dictated by robust reward shaping rather than the specific choice of optimization algorithm. Training success fundamentally depends on enforcing reward-shaping disciplines. GRPO's group-relative normalization is a notable vulnerability when reward signals are adversarial, but this can be corrected through structured reward engineering.

Abstract: Job-search platforms rely on low-bandwidth query interfaces that often fail to capture the high-dimensional complexity of candidate profiles. We present an end-to-end RLAIF (Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback) framework to generate \emph{portable} job search queries, terms that abstract away seeker-specific identifiers while preserving generalizable qualifications. This task introduces a highly adversarial reward surface where policy optimization frequently exploits flaws in LLM-as-judge rubrics, resulting in degenerate verbatim-copying behaviors.
  We conducted comprehensive empirical experiments to isolate the impact of optimization mechanics against structured reward engineering. Our results demonstrate that for critic-free optimizers, performance is overwhelmingly dictated by robust reward shaping, rendering the specific choice of algorithm largely immaterial. While critic-free per-rollout baseline methods (RLOO and REINFORCE++) natively resist reward-hacking, the group-relative advantage normalization in GRPO appears uniquely sensitive to spurious reward signals, making it disproportionately susceptible to exploitation. We show that introducing a deterministic, rule-based reward floor to correct for rewards assigned to verbatim copying mitigates this failure mode, resulting in a substantial $+0.147$ quality improvement on a cross-family evaluation judge. Ultimately, we show that the training-time reward model inflates performance gains by $2.4\times$, confirming that the training success is fundamentally dependent on enforcing reward-shaping disciplines rather than selecting alternative optimizers.

</details>


### [170] [A Multi-Fidelity Convolutional Autoencoder-Transfer Learning Framework for Guided-Wave-Based Damage Diagnosis Using Large Simulated and Limited Experimental Datasets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27304)
*Santosh Kapuria,Abhishek*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A multifidelity transfer learning framework combines lightweight 1D spectral element simulations, convolutional autoencoders, and limited experimental data to achieve accurate damage localization (R²>0.93) and sizing (R²>0.99) in plate-like structures for guided wave structural health monitoring.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep learning for GWSHM is limited by scarce labeled experimental data and the prohibitive computational cost of generating large-scale high-fidelity simulation datasets. A practical solution is needed that leverages cheap low-fidelity simulations and adapts to real-world experimental domains with minimal labeled data.

Method: The framework uses a computationally efficient 1D time-domain spectral element model to generate a large synthetic pretraining dataset. A convolutional autoencoder (CAE) performs deep feature learning, coupled with a feed-forward neural network. Transfer learning then adapts the pretrained model to the experimental domain using only a small amount of labeled experimental data. The approach is compared against a CNN-based counterpart.

Result: The CAE-based transfer learning framework significantly outperforms the CNN-based counterpart in damage localization accuracy. It achieves R² scores exceeding 0.93 for damage localization and 0.99 for damage sizing. Strong generalization is demonstrated on unseen damage scenarios not represented during pretraining or fine-tuning.

Conclusion: The proposed multifidelity transfer learning framework is an accurate, computationally efficient, and practically viable solution for real-world GWSHM, effectively bridging the gap between abundant low-fidelity simulation data and scarce high-fidelity experimental measurements.

Abstract: Guided wave-based structural health monitoring (GWSHM) with onboard transducers offers significant potential for the early diagnosis of damage in engineering structures. However, the practical deployment of deep learning models is often hindered by the limited availability of labelled experimental data and the high computational cost of generating large-scale high-fidelity simulation datasets. This study presents a multifidelity transfer learning framework that integrates lightweight physics-based simulations, convolutional autoencoder (CAE)-based deep feature learning, a feed-forward neural network, and limited experimental measurements for accurate damage localisation and sizing in plate-like structures instrumented with piezoelectric transducers. A computationally efficient one-dimensional time-domain spectral element model is employed to generate a large synthetic dataset for pretraining, while transfer learning adapts the model to experimental domains using only a small amount of labelled data. The CAE-based transfer learning framework significantly outperforms its CNN-based counterpart in damage localisation accuracy. The model achieves excellent predictive performance with $R^2$ scores exceeding 0.93 for damage localisation and 0.99 for damage sizing. Its generalisation capability is demonstrated on previously unseen data, showing high prediction accuracy for damage scenarios not represented during pretraining or fine-tuning. The results establish the proposed framework as an accurate, computationally efficient, and practically viable solution for real-world GWSHM applications.

</details>


### [171] [Blackwell Approachability and Gradient Equilibrium are Equivalent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27315)
*Brian W. Lee,Nika Haghtalab,Michael I. Jordan,Ryan J. Tibshirani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper establishes that Gradient Equilibrium (GEQ) is algorithmically equivalent to Blackwell approachability, and by extension to regret minimization and calibration, thereby positioning GEQ firmly within the broader online learning landscape. The authors provide efficient reductions in both directions and derive necessary and sufficient conditions for GEQ.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work left open the precise relationship between GEQ and established online learning frameworks like regret minimization, as GEQ error and regret were known to be incomparable objectives. The authors seek to resolve this gap by clarifying how GEQ fits into the broader online learning taxonomy.

Method: The authors prove algorithmic equivalence between GEQ and Blackwell approachability via efficient black-box reductions in both directions — showing any approachability problem can be solved with a GEQ oracle and vice versa, with no asymptotic degradation in error rates. They then leverage known equivalences (approachability ↔ regret minimization ↔ calibration) to extend the result, and derive necessary and sufficient conditions for GEQ along with reductions between constrained and unconstrained GEQ variants.

Result: GEQ is algorithmically equivalent to Blackwell approachability, regret minimization, and calibration. The reductions preserve error rates asymptotically and can transfer refined guarantees (e.g., optimism, strong adaptivity) from regret minimization to GEQ. Necessary and sufficient conditions for GEQ are identified, and reductions between unconstrained and constrained GEQ formulations are established.

Conclusion: GEQ is not a separate or incomparable framework but is fundamentally equivalent to Blackwell approachability and, transitively, to regret minimization and calibration. This unification enables the transfer of algorithmic advances and theoretical guarantees across these frameworks.

Abstract: Gradient equilibrium (GEQ) is a recently introduced online optimization framework that generalizes first-order stationarity from offline optimization and abstracts problems like online conformal prediction. While GEQ has curious similarities with known online learning frameworks, namely regret minimization, prior work has shown that GEQ error and regret are incomparable objectives, leaving open a precise understanding of how GEQ fits into the broader online learning landscape. In this work, we show that GEQ is equivalent to Blackwell approachability in the algorithmic sense. That is, a Blackwell approachability problem can always be solved using queries to a black-box GEQ oracle, with no asymptotic loss in the oracle's error rate, and vice versa. Taken together with known equivalences between approachability, regret minimization, and calibration, these results imply that GEQ is equivalent to these frameworks, as well. Our reductions are efficient and can be used to transfer refined guarantees, such as optimism and strong adaptivity, from regret minimization to GEQ. Along the way, we also identify necessary and sufficient conditions for GEQ, and establish reductions between different notions of GEQ with unconstrained and constrained decision sets.

</details>


### [172] [Beyond the Hard Budget: Sparsity Regularizers for More Interpretable Top-k Sparse Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27321)
*Nathanaël Jacquier,Maria Vakalopoulou,Mahdi S. Hosseini*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for vision foundation models typically use a Top-k architectural sparsity constraint. This paper shows that adding soft sparsity regularizers (ℓ₁ on off-support units and ℓ₁/ℓ₂ ratio) on top of the hard Top-k architecture is complementary, improving monosemanticity, reconstruction robustness, and downstream probing performance without sacrificing reconstruction quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Top-k SAEs, while popular, have two key limitations: (1) the fixed budget k ignores input complexity variation, and (2) they tend to overfit to the training value of k. Prior work avoided combining Top-k with explicit sparsity regularizers (like ℓ₁) because the architecture was designed precisely to sidestep the known drawbacks of ℓ₁-based SAEs. The authors hypothesize that hard architectural sparsity and soft regularization are actually complementary.

Method: Two sparsity regularizers are introduced, both applied to activations *before* Top-k selection and only on batch-active units: (1) an ℓ₁ penalty on unselected (off-support) latent units, and (2) a scale-invariant ℓ₁/ℓ₂ ratio penalty that encourages concentration onto fewer effective units. These are evaluated across two datasets (ImageNet-1k, Places365), three vision foundation models (CLIP, DINOv2, SigLIP), and a range of k values.

Result: Both regularizers consistently improve monosemanticity (measured via IoU with ground-truth segmentation masks) with no degradation in reconstruction quality. The ℓ₁/ℓ₂ penalty additionally concentrates information into fewer latents, makes reconstruction more robust to inference-time k variation, and improves linear probing performance at small k budgets.

Conclusion: Hard architectural sparsity (Top-k) and soft sparsity regularization are complementary, not mutually exclusive. Combining them yields strictly better interpretability and more robust representations than either approach alone.

Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a leading tool for interpreting the representations of vision foundation models, decomposing their polysemantic activations into a larger set of sparse, more monosemantic features. The Top-$k$ SAE, a now-standard variant, enforces sparsity architecturally through its activation function, retaining only the $k$ most active latents per input. Because it was designed precisely to avoid the $\ell_1$ penalty used by earlier SAEs and its known drawbacks, it has not been combined with an explicit sparsity regularizer, despite retaining limitations of its own, such as a budget $k$ that is fixed regardless of input complexity and a tendency to overfit to the training value of $k$. We introduce two sparsity regularizers compatible with the Top-$k$ architecture, both acting on the activations before the Top-$k$ selection: an $\ell_1$ penalty on the unselected (off-support) units, and a scale-invariant $\ell_1/\ell_2$-ratio penalty that concentrates the code onto fewer effective units. Both penalties are applied only to the batch-active units, those selected by the Top-$k$ operator at least once within the batch. Across two datasets, three vision foundation models, and a range of $k$, both regularizers consistently improve monosemanticity at no cost to reconstruction quality. The $\ell_1/\ell_2$ penalty further concentrates information into fewer latents, making reconstruction more robust to the inference-time choice of $k$ and improving small-budget linear probing. Our central finding is that hard architectural sparsity and soft sparsity regularization are complementary rather than mutually exclusive.

</details>


### [173] [Hallucination in World Models is Predictable and Preventable](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27326)
*Nicklas Hansen,Xiaolong Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: World models hallucinate plausible but dynamics-divergent futures due to insufficient coverage in state-action space. The authors introduce MMBench2 (427h, 210 tasks) to study this, identify three hallucination modes with corresponding predictive signals, and propose a data-centric mitigation strategy: coverage-aware training-time sampling and curiosity-driven online data collection that adapts to unseen environments with as few as 50 trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern generative world models produce visually fluent action-conditioned rollouts but frequently hallucinate — drifting from ground-truth dynamics despite visual plausibility. The authors hypothesize that this hallucination stems from low-coverage regions in the state-action space and that lightweight, data-centric signals can both detect and mitigate it.

Method: (1) Construction of MMBench2, a 427-hour, 210-task benchmark with ground-truth actions, rewards, and live simulators; training a 350M-parameter world model on it. (2) Identification and anchoring of three hallucination modes: perceptual, action-marginalized, and scene-diverging, each tied to a distinct pipeline stage. (3) Development of three predictive signals for failure detection. (4) Coverage-aware sampling at training time to close coverage gaps. (5) Using hallucination predictors as curiosity rewards for online targeted data collection, enabling data-efficient finetuning (~50 trajectories) to unseen environments.

Result: The three hallucination modes are reliably predicted by the corresponding signals. Coverage-aware sampling improves training. The curiosity-driven finetuning recipe successfully adapts the pretrained world model to entirely unseen environments with as few as 50 real environment trajectories.

Conclusion: Hallucination in world models is fundamentally a data coverage issue. The same signals used to detect hallucination can also guide mitigation, enabling data-efficient adaptation to new environments.

Abstract: Modern generative world models render increasingly realistic action-controllable futures, yet they frequently hallucinate: rollouts remain visually fluent while drifting from the ground-truth dynamics. We hypothesize that hallucination concentrates in low-coverage regions of the state-action space, where lightweight data-centric signals can both detect it and guide mitigation. To test this, we introduce MMBench2, a 427-hour, 210-task dataset for visual world modeling with ground-truth actions, rewards, and live simulators, and train a 350M-parameter world model on it. We identify three distinct hallucination modes: perceptual, action-marginalized, and scene-diverging -- each anchored to a different stage of the pipeline, and develop three signals that accurately predict where the model will fail. To close coverage gaps at training time, we develop a coverage-aware sampling technique; to close them online, our hallucination predictors serve as curiosity rewards for targeted data collection, yielding a data-efficient finetuning recipe that adapts the pretrained world model to entirely unseen environments with as few as 50 real environment trajectories. Overall, our findings reveal that hallucination in world models is inherently a data coverage issue, and that the same signals used to detect it can also be used for mitigation.
  An interactive web version of our paper is available at https://www.nicklashansen.com/mmbench2

</details>


### [174] [Error-Conditioned Neural Solvers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27354)
*Haina Jiang,Liam Wang,Peng-Chen Chen,Min Seop Kwak,Seungryong Kim,Brian Bell,Jeong Joon Park*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ENS proposes feeding the PDE residual field directly as input to a neural solver, enabling it to learn an iterative error-correction policy rather than treating residual minimization as an optimization target. This avoids the instability of hybrid methods and achieves up to 10× accuracy gains, especially in ill-conditioned regimes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing neural surrogate models for PDEs fail to correct their own errors and extrapolate poorly. Hybrid methods that minimize the PDE residual via classical optimizers (gradient descent, Gauss-Newton) suffer from high compute cost and instability. Crucially, the authors identify that residual minimization is an unreliable proxy for reconstruction accuracy in ill-conditioned systems — explaining why low-residual predictions can still be inaccurate.

Method: Error-Conditioned Neural Solvers (ENS) pass the PDE residual field as a direct input to the network at each iteration, letting the model read the spatial structure of its own errors. The network learns an update policy to iteratively correct its predictions, treating the residual as conditioning information rather than an optimization objective. This is evaluated across four PDE families including turbulent Kolmogorov flow.

Result: ENS achieves the highest prediction accuracy in the large majority of settings, with up to 10× improvement on turbulent Kolmogorov flow, while avoiding the expensive compute of hybrid methods. The learned correction policy generalizes under distribution shift (zero-shot parameter changes and cross-equation transfer), with the largest relative gains in ill-conditioned regimes where residual minimization is least reliable.

Conclusion: Conditioning on the residual field rather than minimizing it is a more effective and robust paradigm for neural PDE solving. ENS combines the speed of pure neural surrogates with the error-awareness of hybrid methods, without their computational burden or instability.

Abstract: Neural surrogate models offer fast approximate mappings from PDE parameters to solutions, but they typically treat solving as a purely statistical task: once trained, they struggle to correct their own constraint violations and extrapolate beyond the training distribution. Recent hybrid methods promote physical correctness by targeting the PDE residual via gradient descent or Gauss--Newton steps, but inherit the compute cost and instability of the underlying classical optimizers. We show, theoretically and empirically, that numerically minimizing the PDE residual can be an unreliable proxy for reconstruction accuracy in ill-conditioned systems, explaining why these methods often do not make accurate predictions despite achieving low residuals. We propose error-conditioned Neural Solvers (ENS), built on a different principle: rather than an optimization target, the PDE residual field is passed as a direct input to the network at each iteration, enabling it to read the spatial structure of its own errors and learn an update policy to iteratively correct its predictions. Across four PDE families, ENS attains the highest prediction accuracy in the large majority of settings, with gains reaching $10\times$ on turbulent Kolmogorov flow, while avoiding the expensive compute cost of hybrid methods. ENS's learned correction policy generalizes under distribution shift, including zero-shot parameter changes and cross-equation transfer, where its relative advantage is largest in the ill-conditioned regimes where residual minimization is least reliable. Project website: https://neuralsolver.github.io/.

</details>


### [175] [Autoregressive Boltzmann Generators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27361)
*Danyal Rehman,Charlie B. Tan,Yoshua Bengio,Avishek Joey Bose,Alexander Tong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Autoregressive Boltzmann Generators (ArBG), a novel framework that replaces normalizing flows with autoregressive models for equilibrium molecular sampling, overcoming invertibility constraints and enabling LLM-style architectures. It also presents Robin, a 132M-parameter transferable model that achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot energy errors, reducing E-W₂ on 8-residue systems by over 60%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Boltzmann Generators address the challenge of efficient equilibrium sampling in statistical physics, but current flow-based BG approaches are limited: discrete-time normalizing flows suffer from restricted expressivity due to strict invertibility constraints, while continuous-time flows incur computationally expensive likelihoods. There is a need for a more expressive, scalable alternative.

Method: The authors propose ArBG, an autoregressive modelling framework that departs from the flow-based paradigm. It circumvents topological constraints by using autoregressive factorization (no invertibility required), enables sequential inference-time interventions, and leverages scalable architectures inspired by Large Language Models. They also train Robin, a 132M-parameter transferable ArBG model.

Result: ArBG achieves significant improvements over flow-based models across all benchmarks, with particularly strong gains on larger peptide systems like 10-residue Chignolin. Robin, the transferable model, surpasses the previous state-of-the-art by reducing the zero-shot energy error (E-W₂) on 8-residue systems by over 60%.

Conclusion: Autoregressive Boltzmann Generators offer a promising new direction for equilibrium molecular sampling by overcoming the key limitations of flow-based BGs, delivering superior performance, scalability, and the ability to leverage modern LLM architectures.

Abstract: Efficient sampling of molecular systems at thermodynamic equilibrium is a hallmark challenge in statistical physics. This challenge has driven the development of Boltzmann Generators (BGs), which allow rapid generation of uncorrelated equilibrium samples by combining a generative model with exact likelihoods and an importance sampling correction. However, modern BGs predominantly rely on normalizing flows (NFs), which either suffer from limited expressivity due to strict invertibility constraints (discrete time) or computationally expensive likelihoods (continuous time). In this paper, we propose Autoregressive Boltzmann Generators (ArBG) -- a novel autoregressive modelling framework -- that overcomes these limitations by departing from the flow-based BG paradigm. ArBG circumvents the topological constraints of flows and enables sequential inference-time interventions, while offering enhanced scalability by leveraging architectures effective in Large Language Models. We empirically demonstrate that ArBG leads to significant improvements over flow-based models across all benchmarks, but particularly in larger peptide systems such as the 10-residue Chignolin. Furthermore, we introduce Robin, a 132 million parameter transferable model trained with the ArBG framework which improves over the previous state-of-the-art, reducing the zero-shot energy error, E-W$_2$, on 8-residue systems by over 60$\%$. The code can be found at the following link: https://github.com/danyalrehman/autobg.

</details>


### [176] [Reinforcement Learning without Ground-Truth Solutions can Improve LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27369)
*Yingyu Lin,Qiyue Gao,Nikki Lijing Kuang,Xunpeng Huang,Kun Zhou,Tongtong Liang,Zhewei Yao,Yi-An Ma,Yuxiong He*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RiVER introduces a ranking-induced framework for training LLMs on score-based optimization tasks without ground-truth solutions, using calibrated continuous rewards to address scale and frequency dominance issues, achieving gains on both heuristic and exact-solution coding benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RLVR methods require ground-truth answers for reward assignment, limiting applicability to tasks where ground-truth is unknown. The authors aim to extend RLVR to score-based optimization tasks (e.g., heuristic algorithm design) where only execution feedback scores are available, and further explore whether such training transfers to exact-solution benchmarks.

Method: RiVER uses deterministic execution feedback as continuous-valued supervision. It identifies two challenges in group-relative RL with continuous rewards: (1) scale dominance — uncalibrated score magnitudes across instances distort policy updates; (2) frequency dominance — repeatedly sampled suboptimal solutions outweigh rare strong candidates. RiVER addresses these via calibrated reward shaping with instance-wise comparisons, emphasizing top-ranked solvers while retaining bounded feedback for other valid solutions. Training is conducted on 12 AtCoder Heuristic Contest tasks.

Result: RiVER improves Qwen3-8B and GLM-Z1-9B-0414 by 8.9% and 9.4% in ALE rating rank. Despite training only on score-based tasks without ground-truth, RiVER yields absolute average improvements of 2.4% on LiveCodeBench and 3.5% on USACO. Baselines using raw execution scores improve ALE but fail to transfer to exact-solution benchmarks.

Conclusion: Score-based optimization tasks with proper reward calibration can serve as effective training environments for general coding ability, even without ground-truth solutions. Proper handling of scale and frequency dominance is critical for successful transfer.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for training LLMs typically rely on ground-truth answers to assign rewards, limiting their applicability to tasks where the ground-truth solution is unknown. We introduce a \textbf{R}anking-\textbf{i}nduced \textbf{VER}ifiable framework (RiVER) that trains LLMs on score-based optimization tasks without ground-truth solutions, using deterministic execution feedback as continuous-valued supervision. When applying group-relative RL to such continuous rewards, we identify two key challenges: \emph{scale dominance}, where uncalibrated score magnitudes across test instances distort policy updates, and \emph{frequency dominance}, where repeatedly sampled suboptimal solutions can outweigh rare but stronger candidates. RiVER addresses these challenges with calibrated reward shaping that uses instance-wise comparisons and emphasizes top-ranked solvers while retaining bounded feedback for other valid solutions. We train on 12 AtCoder Heuristic Contest tasks and evaluate on Algorithm Engineering Benchmark (ALE-Bench), LiveCodeBench, and USACO. RiVER advances Qwen3-8B and GLM-Z1-9B-0414 by 8.9\% and 9.4\% in ALE rating rank. More importantly, despite training exclusively on score-based tasks without any ground-truth solutions, RiVER also improves the backbones across exact-solution benchmarks such as LiveCodeBench and USACO by an absolute average improvement of 2.4\% and 3.5\%. By contrast, baselines trained with raw execution scores improve ALE rating but fail to transfer to exact-solution benchmarks. These results suggest that score-based optimization tasks, combined with proper reward calibration, can serve as effective training environments for general coding ability without ground-truth solutions.

</details>


<div id='cs.SE'></div>

# cs.SE [[Back]](#toc)

### [177] [Orchestrating Black-Box Schema Converters: An Empirical Study of Automated, Quality-Ranked Conversion Across Heterogeneous Schema Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26180)
*Felix Neubauer,Giridhar Chinnikkaramadom Govindan,Jürgen Pleiss,Benjamin Uekermann*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper studies how to orchestrate multiple imperfect, lossy schema converters (treating them as black-box edges in a graph of schema languages) to automate consistent model representations across JSON Schema, XSD, SHACL, etc. The authors built an open-source orchestrator that discovers, executes, ranks conversion paths with full provenance, evaluated on 60 real-world tasks, yielding usable results for 43 and surfacing concrete gaps for the rest.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern software systems often maintain the same data model in multiple schema languages (JSON Schema, XSD, SHACL, etc.). Keeping these representations consistent during model evolution is burdensome because individual converters are scattered, hard to find, of uneven quality, and often lossy. No single converter reliably handles all language pairs, motivating an orchestration approach that chains multiple converters to find the best available conversion path.

Method: Schema languages are modeled as nodes and converters as directed edges in a graph, enabling conversion paths to be discovered via graph traversal. Converters are treated as black boxes. The system executes candidate paths, ranks results by quality, and reports full per-step provenance. Failures trigger fallback to alternative paths. This is implemented as the open-source Schema Conversion Orchestrator, integrated into MetaConfigurator. Evaluation uses 60 conversion tasks from real-world schemas across five languages, with agent-assisted, human-reviewed quality annotations.

Result: Orchestration produced a usable result for 43 out of 60 conversion tasks. The 17 remaining failures localized concrete gaps in the current converter landscape. The approach demonstrates that chaining imperfect converters can substantially expand coverage beyond any single converter, while also systematically identifying where new converters are needed.

Conclusion: Imperfect, heterogeneous schema converters can be effectively orchestrated into automated, reproducible, quality-ranked conversion pipelines. The converter-graph model with full provenance enables both practical model management and systematic diagnosis of the converter ecosystem's limitations, with implications for tool builders and for defining meaningful conversion quality metrics.

Abstract: Modern software systems routinely need the same data model in several schema languages: a model may exist as JSON Schema for a web API, as XSD for data exchange, and as SHACL for a knowledge graph. Keeping these representations consistent as the model evolves is a recurring construction and maintenance burden, because converters between schema languages are hard to find, scattered across ecosystems, of uneven quality, and frequently lossy. We study, empirically, to what extent such imperfect, heterogeneous converters can be orchestrated into automated, reproducible, and quality-ranked conversions, and where the current converter landscape reaches its limits.
