Our approach models schema languages as nodes and converters, treated as black boxes, as directed edges, so that conversions become paths that are discovered, executed, ranked, and reported with full per-step provenance, with failures handled by trying alternatives. We realize it as the open-source Schema Conversion Orchestrator, integrate it into MetaConfigurator, and evaluate it on 60 conversion tasks built from real-world schemas across five schema languages, using agent-assisted, human-reviewed quality annotations. Orchestration surfaces a usable result for 43 of 60 tasks; the remaining failures localize concrete gaps in the converter landscape. We discuss implications for tool builders and for measuring conversion quality.

</details>


### [178] [Augmentation with Dilution: A Large-Scale Empirical Study of Human Contributor Ecosystems After AI Coding Agent Adoption](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26289)
*Weixing Zhang,Bowen Jiang,Anne Koziolek*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A large-scale empirical study using staggered difference-in-differences on 11,097 GitHub repos finds AI coding agent adoption does not displace human contributors but significantly reduces human contributor density, newcomer participation share, and increases review burden—a pattern termed "augmentation with dilution."


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing research treats human contributors as static background when studying AI coding agents in open-source software. The authors aim to center human contributors as the dependent variable, investigating how AI agent adoption causally reshapes the number, composition, and behavior of human participants.

Method: Staggered difference-in-differences design using the Sun and Abraham estimator, applied to a dataset of 11,097 GitHub repositories from January 2023 to May 2026. Causal identification exploits variation in adoption timing across projects. Moderator analyses examine heterogeneity by project size, programming language, and project maturity.

Result: AI agent adoption yields: (1) no significant change in absolute human contributor count (ATT=0.014, p=0.224); (2) significant decline in human contributor density (ATT=-0.019, p=0.002); (3) significant 3.7 pp decline in newcomer participation share (ATT=-0.037, p<0.001), immediate and persistent; (4) significant 5.3% increase in review depth (ATT=+0.0168, p<0.001). Effects vary systematically by project size, language, and maturity.

Conclusion: AI agents produce a pattern of "augmentation with dilution": they do not replace human contributors but systematically restructure participation—reducing human density and newcomer share while shifting burden from code production to review. This raises concerns about the long-term sustainability of open-source contributor pipelines.

Abstract: AI coding agents are penetrating open-source software development at an unprecedented pace, yet existing research predominantly treats human contributors as a static backdrop rather than as the subject of inquiry. This paper presents the first large-scale empirical study that takes the human contributor ecosystem as its dependent variable, examining how the number, composition, and behavior of human participants change following AI coding agent adoption in open-source projects. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design on a dataset of 11,097 GitHub repositories spanning January 2023 to May 2026, we provide causal evidence via the Sun and Abraham estimator. Our results show that AI agent adoption does not significantly change the absolute number of human contributors (ATT = 0.014, p = 0.224), but significantly reduces human contributor density (ATT = -0.019, p = 0.002), indicating that the relative share of human participation declines as AI-generated pull requests accumulate. The relative participation share of newcomers declines significantly by 3.7 percentage points (ATT = -0.037, p < 0.001), with the effect emerging immediately after adoption and remaining stable throughout the observation window. Review depth increases significantly by 5.3% (ATT = +0.0168, p < 0.001), indicating that AI agents shift burden from the code production stage to the review stage. Moderator analysis reveals that these effects vary systematically with project size, programming language, and project maturity. Together, these findings present a pattern of augmentation with dilution: AI agents are not displacing human contributors, but are systematically reshaping the participation structure of open-source ecosystems.

</details>


### [179] [Towards Safety-Aware Mutation Testing for Autonomous Driving Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26456)
*Donghwan Shin*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper proposes Safety-Aware Mutation Testing (SAMT), a paradigm shift that injects temporally bounded faults into inter-module messages of Autonomous Driving Systems, derived from STPA safety analysis, to systematically evaluate test adequacy, guide scenario generation, and inform ADS repair.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current simulation-based testing for ADS lacks a systematic stopping criterion. Existing coverage metrics either assess individual component reliability or treat the ADS as a black box, missing critical component interactions that cause most accidents. Traditional mutation testing at the code or DL model level is insufficient for ADS because it fails to capture realistic interaction failures between modules.

Method: SAMT injects temporally bounded faults into messages exchanged between ADS modules rather than individual components. Mutant generation rules are derived directly from top-down safety engineering frameworks, specifically System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA). This embeds systems thinking into mutation testing, creating mutants that represent genuine hazards from realistic interaction failures.

Result: As a vision paper, it does not present empirical results. It outlines the SAMT framework as a rigorous mechanism for evaluating test adequacy, enabling automated scenario generation, and guiding ADS repair. It also identifies open challenges for future work.

Conclusion: A paradigm shift to SAMT is needed to address the gap in ADS test adequacy evaluation. By leveraging STPA-derived fault injection at the inter-module message level, SAMT offers a falsifiable, safety-grounded criterion for determining when testing is sufficient, moving beyond code-level mutation and black-box coverage metrics.

Abstract: Simulation-based testing is essential for ensuring the safety of Autonomous Driving Systems (ADS), yet the community lacks a systematic criterion for determining when we can safely stop additional test scenario generation. Existing coverage metrics typically focus on individual component reliability or treat the ADS as a black box, failing to capture certain component interactions that cause most ADS accidents. While traditional mutation testing provides a falsifiable measure of test adequacy, directly porting code- and deep learning model-level mutations to the corresponding modules of ADS is insufficient.
  In this vision paper, we propose a paradigm shift toward Safety-Aware Mutation Testing (SAMT). Unlike traditional mutation testing, which creates mutants (i.e., faulty versions of the software under test) by injecting artificial faults into individual components, SAMT systematically injects temporally bounded faults into the messages exchanged between ADS modules to simulate realistic interaction failures. To ensure these mutants represent genuine hazards, we propose deriving mutant generation rules directly from top-down safety engineering frameworks, such as System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA). By embedding systems thinking into the mutation testing pipeline, SAMT provides a rigorous mechanism for evaluating test adequacy, enabling automated scenario generation, and guiding ADS repair. We also outline critical open challenges.

</details>


### [180] [An Empirical Study of LLM-Generated Specifications for VeriFast](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26490)
*Wen Fan,Minh Tran,Sanya Dod,Xin Hu,Marilyn Rego,Danning Xie,Jenna DiVincenzo,Lin Tan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper evaluates how well LLMs generate separation logic specifications for the VeriFast verifier across 303 C functions. Testing 8 prompting approaches, 10 LLMs, and 3 input types, they find LLMs preserve functional behavior well (>91%) but achieve only 31.4% verification success. Gemini 2.5 Pro with formal contracts performs best. Critically, 94% of errors stem from LLMs' lack of domain-specific SL/VeriFast knowledge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Static SL verifiers like VeriFast require substantial manual effort to write complex auxiliary specifications for heap-manipulating programs. While LLMs have been applied to generate specifications for non-SL verifiers, their effectiveness for SL verifiers remains unexplored. This gap motivates a comprehensive evaluation.

Method: The authors evaluated LLM-generated specifications on 303 C functions using VeriFast. They systematically explored 8 prompting approaches, 10 LLMs, and 3 input types (source code only, natural language descriptions, formal contracts) across two stages. Both quantitative metrics (verification success rate, functional correctness) and qualitative analysis of error types were employed.

Result: LLMs preserved functional behavior in code and specifications at >91%, but overall verification success reached only 31.4%. Gemini 2.5 Pro with formal contracts yielded the highest success rates. Error analysis revealed 94% of failures originated from LLMs' deficient domain-specific knowledge of SL verifiers like VeriFast, rather than general code generation issues.

Conclusion: LLMs show promise for generating SL verifier specifications but are currently limited by weak domain-specific knowledge of SL and tools like VeriFast. These findings offer actionable guidance for improving LLM-based specification generation for separation logic verifiers, particularly around better domain-knowledge integration.

Abstract: Static verification tools can assure industrial scale software, but require significant human labor to write specifications. This is particularly true of static verifiers based on separation logic (SL verifiers), which excel at verifying heapmanipulating programs, but require many complex auxiliary specifications to reason about heap structure. Recent work applies large language models (LLMs) to generate code, tests, and proofs, including specifications for verifiers, but mostly targeting non-SL verifiers. To address this gap, this paper thoroughly evaluates how well LLMs perform when prompted to generate specifications for verifying 303 C functions with the SL verifier VeriFast. We explored eight prompting approaches, ten LLMs, and three input types in two stages. Quantitative and qualitative analyses are used to assess the LLM-generated code and specifications for functional behavior, verifiability and errors. The results show that LLMs preserve functional behavior in source code and specifications (both over 91%), but achieve modest verification success (31.4%). Using Gemini 2.5 Pro and providing formal contracts lead to higher success rates in our setting. Moreover, most errors (94%) come from LLMs' mistakes in the domainspecific knowledge of SL verifiers such as VeriFast. These findings provide guidance for optimizing LLM-generated specifications for SL verifiers.

</details>


### [181] [Evaluation-Strategy Gap in Fault Diagnosis of Deep Learning Programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26492)
*Sigma Jahan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Existing DL fault diagnosis techniques show a significant performance drop (0.190 balanced accuracy gap) when evaluated on unseen programs versus within-program cross-validation. The gap stems from program-level feature structure: curvature features generalize to unseen programs for instability detection, while optimizer and activation features do not.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep Learning program training failures are costly to diagnose, yet current fault diagnosis techniques are predominantly evaluated using within-program cross-validation, which may not reflect real-world deployment where entirely new, unseen programs are encountered. The authors aim to quantify the generalization gap and identify its root causes.

Method: The authors constructed DynFault, a corpus of 5,542 fault-injected training traces from 38 real-world DL programs. They systematically compared within-program evaluation against holding out entire programs (program-level cross-validation) for established fault diagnosis techniques. They then analyzed three runtime feature sets — curvature features, optimizer features, and activation features — to determine which contribute to generalization and which cause the observed gap.

Result: A 0.190 balanced accuracy gap exists between within-program and across-program evaluation. The gap is attributed to program-level structure in feature representations. Curvature features proved useful for detecting instability on unseen programs, while optimizer and activation features only provided benefits when the program was seen during training.

Conclusion: Within-program cross-validation overestimates the real-world effectiveness of DL fault diagnosis techniques. To build robust, generalizable diagnosis methods, practitioners should rely on features like curvature that transfer across programs, and evaluation protocols must include held-out program validation.

Abstract: Deep Learning (DL) programs can fail during training for many reasons, and diagnosing the cause is a costly and time-consuming maintenance task. Techniques for diagnosing such failures are commonly assessed using within-program cross-validation, which may be inadequate for deployment settings involving previously unseen programs. It is therefore necessary to assess how performance differs across these settings and to identify the causes of any performance gap in established fault diagnosis techniques for DL. We investigate this gap using DynFault, a corpus of 5,542 fault-injected training traces from 38 real-world DL programs. We found a gap of 0.190 in balanced accuracy for existing fault diagnosis techniques between within-program evaluation and holding out whole programs. We also found the gap comes from program-level structure in the features, which led us to examine two runtime feature sets, curvature features and optimizer features, and their behavior on unseen programs. We found that curvature features are useful for instability detection on unseen programs, while optimizer and activation features help only on programs seen during training.

</details>


### [182] [Same Scrutiny, More Time: Eye Tracking Insights into Reviewing LLM-Labelled Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26505)
*Ranim Khojah,Francisco Gomes de Oliveira Neto,Mazen Mohamad,Julian Frattini,Philipp Leitner*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A Wizard-of-Oz experiment with eye-tracking reveals that while developers' review thoroughness doesn't change when code is labeled as LLM-generated, they spend more visual attention on such code and adapt their review strategies (e.g., focusing on logical correctness, using prompts as review guides). The study exposes a gap between review intentions and actual behavior, urging companies to revisit AI policies for LLM-assisted development.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite LLMs being increasingly used for code generation and their known propensity for errors/hallucinations, how developers actually behave when reviewing LLM-generated code is largely unexplored. There is a potential discrepancy between recommended thorough inspection and developers' real-world trust and reviewing behavior, motivating an empirical investigation.

Method: The authors conducted a Wizard-of-Oz experiment where software engineers performed code review tasks with code explicitly labeled as LLM-generated. They collected behavioral data via eye-tracking and subjective feedback through exit interviews. Analysis combined Bayesian data analysis with qualitative methods.

Result: Code review thoroughness did not significantly change, but participants spent more time fixating on LLM-labelled code — the label itself influenced attentional allocation. Developers adapted review strategies, assessing code against specific criteria like logical correctness and using the prompt as a guiding artifact for their review process.

Conclusion: The study reveals a gap between reviewers' intentions and actual reviewing behavior. Findings inform LLM-based tool design regarding labeling practices and suggest treating prompts as software artifacts. The authors call for software companies to revisit AI policies to better support developers in reviewing LLM-generated code.

Abstract: Modern software development increasingly involves the use of large language models (LLMs) to generate code. Despite their rapid advancement, LLMs remain prone to errors and hallucinations, emphasizing the importance of careful code inspection. However, in practice, developers' trust in LLM-generated code and their willingness to review it thoroughly may differ from these recommendations. How developers actually behave when reviewing LLM-generated code remains largely unexplored. In this study, we conduct a Wizard-of-Oz experiment to examine how software engineers behave when code is explicitly labeled as LLM-generated during a code review task. We collect both behavioral data and participant feedback through eye-tracking and exit interviews. Combining Bayesian data analysis with qualitative analysis, we found that while the thoroughness of code review did not change for participants, they spent more time fixating on LLM-labelled code, indicating that the label itself influences attention. Practitioners also adapted their review strategy for LLM-labelled code by assessing the code based on specific criteria (e.g., logical correctness), or using the prompt to guide their review. These findings inform LLM-based tool design on labelling while incorporating the prompt as a software artifact. Our study reveals a gap between reviewers' intentions and actual reviewing behaviour, highlighting the need for software companies to revisit their AI policies (particularly regarding LLM-assisted development) to better support developers in reviewing LLM-generated code.

</details>


### [183] [ConcoLixir: Reactive LLM Discovery Oracles for Python Concolic Testing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26545)
*Dong Chen,Chih-Duo Hong,Fang Yu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: ConcoLixir augments Python concolic testing with a reactive LLM oracle that generates seeds, proposes inputs after solver failures, and targets uncovered code when coverage stalls, achieving 8.6–17.0 percentage point line coverage gains at $1.63 total API cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Python concolic execution faces recurring limitations: library calls downgrade symbolic variables to concrete values, hard-to-solve semantic operations (regex, checksums, parsers) resist constraint solving, and exploration plateaus on already-covered paths. Existing concolic tools lack a mechanism to overcome these barriers without replacing symbolic reasoning.

Method: ConcoLixir introduces a reactive LLM extension with three trigger points: (1) generating initial seed inputs, (2) proposing concrete inputs when the SMT solver fails on hard constraints, and (3) identifying uncovered code regions when coverage growth stalls. Crucially, the LLM serves only as a discovery oracle — candidates are executed concolically, and only observed coverage and collected path constraints guide subsequent exploration, preventing the LLM from acting as a correctness oracle or solver replacement.

Result: On synthetic, real-world, and library targets, ConcoLixir improved mean line coverage over a baseline concolic tester by 8.6, 15.1, and 17.0 percentage points respectively. Gains concentrated near semantic barriers and library boundaries. The full evaluation cost $1.63 in API charges.

Conclusion: Bounded LLM discovery, when disciplined by concolic execution's verification mechanisms, can complement symbolic reasoning without replacing it. The approach is cost-effective and particularly effective where traditional constraint solving fails.

Abstract: Concolic testing combines concrete execution with symbolic constraint solving, but Python programs expose recurring limits. Library calls can cause symbolic variables to downgrade to concrete values. Regular expressions, checksums, parsers, and other semantic operations can be hard to solve, and exploration can plateau on already covered paths. We present ConcoLixir, a reactive LLM extension for Python concolic execution. The LLM acts as a discovery oracle, not a replacement for the solver or a correctness oracle. It generates initial seeds, proposes concrete inputs after solver failures, and targets uncovered code when coverage stalls. Each candidate is executed concolically, and only observed coverage and collected path constraints guide later exploration. Across synthetic, real-world, and library targets, ConcoLixir improves mean line coverage over the baseline concolic tester without an LLM oracle by 8.6, 15.1, and 17.0 percentage points. The gains are strongest near semantic barriers and library boundaries, and the full evaluation costs \$1.63 in API charges. These results show that bounded LLM discovery can complement symbolic reasoning without replacing it.

</details>


### [184] [Quantum Mutant Equivalence via Transpilation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26604)
*José Campos,Andriy Miranskyy*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: TBE identifies equivalent quantum mutants by transpiling original and mutated circuits under identical configurations and comparing the resulting OpenQASM code, achieving 100% precision on real-world surviving mutants.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In quantum software mutation testing, a recent study generated over 700,000 mutants with roughly half surviving tests, making it impossible to determine whether survivors stem from weak test suites or semantic equivalence (the equivalent mutant problem). No existing solution addresses equivalent mutant detection in the quantum domain.

Method: Transpiler-Based Equivalence (TBE): transpile both original and mutated quantum circuits under the exact same configuration (gate set, coupling map, optimization level) and compare the resulting OpenQASM representations. Identical transpiled code implies semantic equivalence, since the transpiler reduces both programs to the same hardware-constrained form.

Result: Evaluated on 348,299 surviving mutants, of which 92,011 are ground-truth equivalent. TBE correctly identified 29,536 equivalent mutants (32.1% recall) with 100% precision (zero false positives) and 82% overall accuracy. The approach is lightweight, relying solely on transpilation without heavyweight formal verification.

Conclusion: TBE offers a practical, high-precision technique for equivalent mutant identification in quantum software, eliminating manual inspection for a substantial fraction of equivalent mutants. The 100% precision ensures no non-equivalent mutants are wrongly discarded, preserving mutation score integrity.

Abstract: Mutation testing evaluates test suite quality by introducing artificial faults (mutants) and checking whether tests detect (kill) them. A central challenge is the equivalent mutant problem: some mutants are syntactically different from the original program but semantically identical to it and therefore cannot be killed by any test. If left unidentified, such mutants waste testing effort and distort mutation scores. In quantum software, mutation testing is increasingly used, but the equivalent mutant problem remains unsolved. A recent study generated more than 700,000 quantum circuit mutants and found that roughly half survived the available tests, making it unclear whether these survivors reflect weak tests or semantic equivalence. We propose Transpiler-Based Equivalence (TBE), a lightweight approach that identifies equivalent quantum mutants by transpiling original and mutated circuits under the same configuration and comparing their resulting OpenQASM code. We evaluate TBE on 348,299 surviving mutants, 92,011 of which are equivalent; TBE identifies 29,536 of them (32.1%) as equivalent while achieving 100% precision and 82% accuracy.

</details>


### [185] [Knowledge-Based Pull Requests: A Trusted Workflow for Agent-Mediated Knowledge Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26721)
*Xinyu Zhang,Weiwei Sun*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: KPR proposes a workflow where external code contributions are treated as knowledge sources rather than direct merge candidates. An agent distills the contribution into a human-reviewed knowledge package, and a project-owned agent regenerates code under local conventions, separating the decision to accept knowledge from the decision to merge code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI coding agents make code generation cheap, but human-intensive tasks like understanding intent, negotiating scope, and governing long-term project responsibility remain expensive bottlenecks in software collaboration across trust boundaries (open source, enterprise, vendor, contractor). Traditional pull requests collapse the decision of whether to accept knowledge with whether to merge a specific implementation, creating friction.

Method: KPR treats an external collaborator's code, tests, and agent interaction trace as knowledge sources. Agents distill these into a human-confirmed knowledge package (design memos, risk checklists, test plans, implementation briefs). A project-owned inner trusted agent then regenerates code under repository context, conventions, tests, and security policy. The authors contribute a workflow definition, artifact schema, cost-accounting model, collaboration gateway architecture, and a controlled simulation pilot over seven merged public PRs stress-tested under description ablation, diff ablation, and synthetic poisoned-patch conditions.

Result: The pilot demonstrates that KPR packages can be instantiated from real PR material and remain viable under ablation and adversarial conditions, showing the feasibility of the extraction-transformation-regeneration pipeline.

Conclusion: KPR is positioned as an empirically testable workflow whose value hinges on whether auditable extraction, transformation, and project-side regeneration reduce the cost of understanding and reworking high-context external changes. The paper provides a framework and initial evidence, with a full evaluation agenda outlined for future work.

Abstract: AI coding agents are changing the bottleneck in software collaboration: code is increasingly cheap, while understanding intent, negotiating scope, and governing long-term project responsibility remain costly. This paper proposes \emph{Knowledge-Based Pull Requests} (KPR), a trusted workflow for agent-mediated software collaboration across trust boundaries, including open source, enterprise, vendor, contractor, and customer-driven settings. In KPR, an external collaborator's local code, tests, and cleaned agent interaction trace are treated as knowledge sources rather than as the default merge candidate. Agents distill these sources into a human-confirmed knowledge package and render it into reviewer-facing forms such as design memos, risk checklists, test plans, or implementation briefs. A project-owned inner trusted coding agent then regenerates candidate code inside the receiving project's environment under repository context, engineering conventions, tests, and security policy. KPR therefore separates two decisions that traditional pull requests often collapse: whether the knowledge should enter the project, and whether a particular implementation should be merged. We contribute the KPR workflow, a candidate artifact schema, a cost-accounting view, a collaboration gateway architecture, a minimal controlled simulation pilot over seven merged public pull requests, and an evaluation agenda. The pilot shows that KPR packages can be instantiated from real PR material and stress-tested under description ablation, diff ablation, and synthetic poisoned-patch conditions. We position KPR as an empirically testable workflow: its value depends on whether auditable extraction, transformation, and project-side regeneration reduce the cost of understanding and reworking high-context external changes.

</details>


### [186] [A Deterministic Control Plane for LLM Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26924)
*Padmaraj Madatha*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: LLM coding agents have broad system access but their configurations are poorly managed. A study of 10,008 GitHub repos reveals rampant duplication (10.1% exact SHA-256 clones), infrequent revision, and near-absent permission boundaries. The authors propose Rel(AI)Build, a deterministic control plane with content-addressed supply chain management, tiered permissions, blocklists, phase-gated workflows, multi-IDE compilation, and prompt drift detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM coding agents are granted significant file and shell access, yet the configuration layer controlling them (rules files, agent definitions, IDE markdown) lacks governance, auditability, and security boundaries — creating an unmanaged attack surface and supply chain risk.

Method: First, a prevalence study across 10,008 public GitHub repositories analyzing 6,145 agent config files for duplication (SHA-256 exact matching, fork-adjusted), revision frequency (commits/month, age-normalized vs CI/CD), and permission declarations (<1% vs 33% for Actions). Second, design and implementation of Rel(AI)Build: a deterministic control plane featuring SHA-256 content addressing, HMAC-stamped lockfiles, hash-chained audit logs, tiered permissions with attack-derived blocklists, a phase state machine for requirement-to-file-to-test traceability, canonical definition compilation to seven IDE targets, and Jaccard-similarity-based prompt drift detection. Conformance tests validate each mechanism against injected violations.

Result: 10.1% of tracked agent config paths are SHA-256 exact duplicates across independent repositories; 75.5% of clone pairs cross organizational boundaries. 58% of configs are single-commit; age-normalized commit rate is 0.4 vs 0.6 commits/month for CI/CD workflows. Under 1% of agent configs declare permission boundaries (31 true positives), versus 33% for GitHub Actions. Each Rel(AI)Build mechanism passed conformance tests on injected violations.

Conclusion: Agent configuration is a systematically neglected attack surface requiring deterministic, tool-agnostic governance rather than further LLM-based orchestration. Rel(AI)Build demonstrates feasibility of such a control plane, though developer-outcome validation remains future work.

Abstract: LLM coding harnesses grant agents broad file and shell access, yet the configuration layer that steers them -- rules files, agent definitions, IDE-specific markdown -- is largely unmanaged. A prevalence study of 10,008 public GitHub repositories (n=6,145 agent config files) finds that agent configurations propagate as undeclared shared components: 10.1% of tracked paths are SHA-256 exact duplicates across independent repositories (fork-adjusted, threshold-independent), with 75.5% of clone pairs crossing organisational boundaries. Two further patterns are indicative: configurations are rarely revised (58% single-commit; 0.4 vs 0.6 commits/month age-normalised against CI/CD workflows), and rarely declare permission boundaries (<1% of agent configs vs 33% of Actions workflows, n=31 true positives).
  We propose a deterministic control plane above the harness that maps one-to-one to these gaps. Rel(AI)Build treats agent definitions as a managed supply chain (SHA-256 content addressing, HMAC-stamped lockfiles, hash-chained audit logs); enforces tiered permissions and attack-derived blocklists before LLM invocation; gates feature work through a phase state machine with requirement-to-file-to-test traceability; compiles a single canonical definition to seven IDE targets; and detects prompt drift via Jaccard similarity. Conformance tests on injected violations confirm each mechanism enforces its stated invariant; developer outcomes remain future work. Governance of this layer must be deterministic and tool-agnostic -- not delegated to further LLM orchestration.

</details>


### [187] [Are LLMs Ready for Anti-Pattern Detection in Microservice Architectures?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26927)
*Marco De Luca,Domenico Amalfitano,Porfirio Tramontana,Anna Rita Fasolino*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Evaluates whether LLMs can detect architectural anti-patterns in microservice systems via prompt-based analysis of static artifacts, comparing three LLMs against the MARS static-analysis tool. LLMs show competitive performance on semantically rich, local, or heterogeneous anti-patterns but underperform on those requiring explicit structural or cross-service dependency evidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AP detection tools rely on static analysis and handcrafted rules, which are tool-dependent, limited to explicitly encoded logic, and hard to adapt across heterogeneous repositories. The authors explore whether LLMs can overcome these limitations by leveraging their semantic understanding and flexibility.

Method: A prompt-based analysis pipeline feeds static repository artifacts (e.g., Dockerfiles, configuration files, source code) to three general-purpose LLMs. Performance is evaluated on a curated benchmark of microservice repositories annotated with 16 architectural anti-patterns, using precision and recall, and compared against the state-of-the-art static-analysis tool MARS under a uniform evaluation protocol.

Result: LLMs achieve competitive performance on anti-patterns where evidence is local, heterogeneous, or semantically rich, but exhibit clear limitations on anti-patterns requiring explicit structural or cross-service dependency detection, where static analysis (MARS) remains more reliable.

Conclusion: LLMs are not yet a replacement for traditional static analyzers but already represent a promising complementary aid for architectural assessment in microservice systems.

Abstract: Microservice systems are prone to recurrent architectural anti-patterns (APs) that hinder maintainability, evolvability, and operational quality. Most existing AP detection approaches rely on static analysis and handcrafted rules, which can be effective but are often tool-dependent, limited to explicitly encoded detection logic, and difficult to adapt to heterogeneous repositories. In this paper, we investigate whether large language models (LLMs) are ready to support architectural anti-pattern detection in microservice architectures through a prompt-based analysis pipeline over static repository artifacts. We evaluate three general-purpose LLMs on a curated benchmark of microservice repositories annotated with 16 architectural anti-patterns, and compare their performance against the state-of-the-art static-analysis tool MARS using a uniform evaluation protocol based on precision and recall. Our results show that LLMs can provide useful support for anti-pattern detection, achieving competitive performance on several anti-patterns, especially when the relevant evidence is local, heterogeneous, or semantically rich. At the same time, they exhibit clear limitations on anti-patterns that require explicit structural or cross-service dependency evidence, where static analysis remains more reliable. These findings suggest that LLMs are not yet a replacement for traditional analyzers, but already represent a promising complementary aid for architectural assessment in microservice systems.

</details>


### [188] [CLIR: Liveness-Driven and Structure-Aware Fuzzing for the Cranelift Compiler](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26977)
*Shangtong Cao,Tianlei Song,Qiuping Yi,Tianyu Chen,Guoai Xu,Ningyu He,Haoyu Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CLIR is a differential testing framework for the Cranelift compiler backend that uses syntax-preserving hierarchical IR generation, liveness-guided instruction refinement, and diagnosis-guided cross-architecture adaptation. It found 8x more bugs than cranelift-fuzzgen, 24x more than wasm-smith, and 8x more than WASMaker, discovering 24 bugs (21 confirmed, 9 fixed) across all supported architectures within 72 hours.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cranelift, a fast compiler backend for WebAssembly and Rust, lacks adequate testing frameworks. Existing approaches struggle with three key challenges: (1) constructing valid IR under strict SSA enforcement, (2) generating instruction sequences with sufficient computational density to stress backend components, and (3) balancing broad cross-architecture coverage with efficient root cause analysis.

Method: CLIR employs three integrated strategies: (1) a syntax-preserving hierarchical generation strategy to guarantee SSA validity during IR construction, (2) a liveness-guided instruction refinement mechanism that maximizes computational density of generated sequences, and (3) a diagnosis-guided cross-architecture adaptation scheme for efficient root cause analysis across heterogeneous backends (x86-64, AArch64, s390x, RISCV64).

Result: CLIR detected 8x, 24x, and 8x more unique bugs than cranelift-fuzzgen, wasm-smith, and WASMaker respectively; RustSmith found no bugs. Within 72 hours, CLIR discovered 24 bugs spanning all four target architectures, with 21 confirmed and 9 already fixed.

Conclusion: CLIR demonstrates that addressing SSA validity, computational density, and cross-architecture diagnosis in a unified differential testing framework yields substantial improvements in compiler bug detection for modern multi-architecture backends like Cranelift.

Abstract: Modern compilers are complex software systems that must correctly translate high-level programming languages into machine code across multiple architectures. Cranelift, a fast and modern compiler backend originally developed for WebAssembly and recently adopted as an experimental backend for Rust, has gained increasing importance due to its superior compilation speed compared to LLVM and comprehensive multi-architecture support, including x86-64, AArch64, s390x, and RISCV64. However, despite decades of development in compiler testing, testing Cranelift still presents unique challenges, including (1) constructing valid IR under the strict enforcement of SSA form, (2) generating sequences with sufficient computational density to stress backend components, and (3) balancing broad backend coverage with efficient root cause analysis across heterogeneous architectures.
  To address these challenges, we propose CLIR, a differential testing framework that integrates a syntax-preserving hierarchical generation strategy to guarantee SSA validity, a liveness-guided instruction refinement mechanism to maximize computational density, and a diagnosis-guided cross-architecture adaptation scheme to facilitate efficient root cause analysis across heterogeneous backends. Our comprehensive evaluation demonstrates that CLIR significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art baselines, detecting 8x, 24x, and 8x more unique bugs than cranelift-fuzzgen, wasm-smith, and WASMaker, respectively, while RustSmith uncovered no bugs. Consequently, within 72 hours of testing, CLIR discovered 24 bugs spanning all target architectures, with 21 confirmed and 9 fixed.

</details>


### [189] [To Run or Not to Run: Analyzing the Cost-Effectiveness of Code Execution in LLM-Based Program Repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26978)
*Zhihao Lin,Junhua Zhu,Mingyi Zhou,Xin Wang,Zhensu Sun,Renyu Yang,David Lo,Li Li*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: An empirical study of 7,745 agent traces and 3,000 end-to-end repair attempts reveals that while LLM-based program repair agents heavily rely on code execution (averaging 8.8 test runs per task), restricting execution barely affects repair success (only 1.25pp gap), yet saves substantial cost. Execution benefits are concentrated rather than uniform, suggesting execution should be treated as a resource with explicit cost-benefit tradeoffs rather than a default capability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based program repair agents increasingly follow a "generate-run-revise" paradigm that relies on iterative test execution to evaluate and refine patches. Despite executions being time-consuming and expensive, their actual impact on agent performance remains underexplored. The authors aim to systematically characterize execution behavior and quantify its cost-benefit tradeoff.

Method: A two-stage empirical study: (1) Large-scale trace analysis of 7,745 agent traces from SWE-bench leaderboard submissions to characterize execution behavior patterns across different agents and models. (2) Controlled end-to-end evaluation of 3,000 repair attempts spanning 200 SWE-bench instances using three agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenAI Codex) under four distinct execution paradigms, enabling fine-grained performance and cost comparison.

Result: Three key findings: (1) Code execution is universally used across all agents/models, averaging 8.8 test runs per task, with frequency varying widely (2–19 per task); late-stage executions consistently outperform early-stage ones. (2) Execution restrictions barely impact repair success — the resolve-rate gap between Prohibited and Unrestricted paradigms for commercial SOTA agents is only 1.25pp (not statistically significant), while Prohibited saves substantial token and wall-clock costs. (3) Execution benefits are concentrated on specific instances rather than uniformly distributed, indicating indiscriminate use of execution in current agents.

Conclusion: Current agents apply execution indiscriminately, incurring costs even on instances where it provides little benefit. Execution should be reconceptualized as a resource with an explicit cost-benefit tradeoff rather than treated as a default, always-on capability in LLM-based program repair systems.

Abstract: LLM-based agents for program repair are increasingly built on a "generate-run-revise" paradigm, iteratively executing tests to evaluate and refine patches. This execution-based approach has become standard practice in state-of-the-art systems. However, executions can be time-consuming and expensive, yet their impact on these agents remains underexplored. In this paper, we conduct a two-stage empirical study over execution behavior in LLM-based program repair. To characterize execution behavior at scale, we first analyze 7,745 agent traces from SWE-bench leaderboard submissions. Second, we evaluate 3,000 end-to-end repair attempts across 200 SWE-bench instances and three agents (Claude Code, Codex, and the open-source OpenCode) under four execution paradigms, which allows for a fine-grained comparison of performance and cost. Our analysis reveals three key observations: (1) Code execution is used across all agents and models analyzed, with an average of 8.8 test runs per task. Execution behavior varies substantially across agents and models, with frequency ranging from 2 to 19 per task, and late-stage executions consistently achieve higher success rates than early-stage ones. (2) Execution restrictions have little effect on repair success: on commercial agents with SOTA models the resolve-rate gap between Prohibited and Unrestricted is only 1.25 percentage points and not statistically significant, while Prohibited saves substantial token and wall-clock cost. (3) Execution benefit is concentrated rather than uniform. These patterns suggest that current agents apply execution indiscriminately, paying its cost on instances where it provides little benefit. Execution, therefore, should be treated as a resource with an explicit cost-benefit tradeoff, not a default capability.

</details>


### [190] [How Much Static Structure Do Code Agents Need? A Study of Deterministic Anchoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26979)
*Zhihao Lin,Mingyi Zhou,Yizhuo Yang,Li Li*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Lightweight static analysis annotations (call graphs, inheritance) injected as comments into codebases act as deterministic anchors that improve LLM-based code agent navigation by making it more disciplined and reproducible rather than smarter, with gains in localization (+2.2pp Func@5), trajectory efficiency (-1.6 rounds), and run-to-run stability (variance halved, Pass@1 +3.4pp), but optimal annotation granularity depends on repository characteristics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based code agents rely on keyword search for repository navigation, missing structural relationships like call graphs and inheritance hierarchies. This makes their exploration stochastic and difficult to reproduce. The authors investigate whether injecting lightweight static analysis facts as deterministic anchors can constrain probabilistic exploration and improve navigation predictability.

Method: Starting from OpenAI's Codex as a strong baseline, the authors systematically inject structural annotations at varying granularities (call topology, inheritance, directionality) as plain-text comments into repositories. They measure effects on function-level localization (Func@5), trajectory behavior (interaction rounds, link-following rate), and run-to-run stability (variance, Pass@1) across different repository scales and characteristics.

Result: Three key findings: (1) Anchoring improves function-level localization by +2.2pp Func@5 and reduces interaction rounds by 1.6; (2) Optimal granularity is scale-sensitive — denser semantics show diminishing returns, and hub-heavy projects benefit from inverse-only links ("who-calls-me"); (3) Tags raise link-following rate from 0.15–0.18 to 0.21–0.24, halve run-to-run variance, and improve Pass@1 by +3.4pp on medium repositories, at the cost of ~10% more input tokens.

Conclusion: The deterministic anchoring effect shows static structure helps primarily by making agent navigation disciplined and reproducible. Practical guidelines: use lightweight topology on medium projects, prune forward edges in large repositories, and reserve dense tags for implicit-dependency cases.

Abstract: LLM-based code agents navigate repositories through keyword search but miss the structural relationships, such as call graphs, inheritance hierarchies, and configuration dependencies, that define how software actually works. This makes agent navigation stochastic and difficult to reproduce across runs. We investigate whether lightweight static analysis can provide deterministic anchors for these agents: stable structural facts injected as plain-text comments that constrain probabilistic exploration and make navigation more predictable. Starting from a strong baseline, Codex from OpenAI, we systematically inject varying granularities of structural annotations and measure their effects on localization, trajectory behavior, and run-to-run stability. Our study identifies what we call the deterministic anchoring effect: static structure helps less by making agents "smarter" and more by making their navigation disciplined and reproducible. Three observations support this finding: (1) Anchoring works: lightweight call/inheritance topology improves function-level localization (+2.2pp Func@5) and shortens trajectories (-1.6 interaction rounds); (2) Anchoring is scale-sensitive: the optimal granularity and directionality depend on repository characteristics, where denser semantics show diminishing returns and hub-heavy projects benefit from inverse-only links that expose "who-calls-me" without forward edges; (3) Anchoring stabilizes: tags raise link-following rate from 0.15-0.18 to 0.21-0.24, roughly halve run-to-run variance, and improve single-run reliability (Pass@1 +3.4 pp) on medium-scale repositories, at the cost of roughly 10% more input tokens. These observations suggest practical guidelines: default to lightweight topology on medium projects, prune forward edges in large repositories, and reserve dense tags for implicit-dependency cases.

</details>


### [191] [Cleaning Logs for Downstream Tasks (Registered Report)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27000)
*Zahra G. Yazdi,Van-Hoang Le,Nyyti Saarimäki,Donghwan Shin,Domenico Bianculli,Lionel Briand*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: LogPurifier is a task-agnostic approach that cleans log data by identifying and removing irrelevant "free-standing" messages based on dependency relationships between log message templates. The paper proposes an empirical evaluation plan using controlled experiments to measure its impact on model inference and anomaly detection tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Software logs are crucial for troubleshooting and monitoring, but they often contain substantial redundant and irrelevant information. This noise degrades the performance of downstream analysis tasks such as model inference and anomaly detection. Current log cleaning methods are limited, creating a need for a principled, task-agnostic approach to filter out irrelevant log messages.

Method: LogPurifier leverages dependency relationships between log message templates to distinguish between functional behavior-capturing messages and free-standing (irrelevant) messages. It identifies and removes the latter in a task-agnostic manner, without requiring knowledge of the specific downstream task.

Result: The paper presents a plan (not yet executed results) for a controlled experimental design to empirically evaluate LogPurifier's impact on two downstream tasks: model inference and anomaly detection, measuring both effectiveness and efficiency.

Conclusion: This appears to be a research proposal or early-stage paper outlining the LogPurifier approach and planned evaluation, rather than a completed study with final conclusions.

Abstract: Background: Software systems generate logs during execution to record critical events and runtime information for troubleshooting and monitoring. However, in practice, logs often contain significant amounts of redundant and irrelevant information, which can negatively impact the performance of downstream analysis tasks, such as model inference and anomaly detection. Objective: The objective of this study is to clean log data by identifying and removing free-standing messages -- messages that are not relevant to the execution behaviors of interest and are interleaved with messages capturing the system's functional behavior. Method: To address this objective, we propose LogPurifier, a task-agnostic log-cleaning approach based on dependency relationships between log message templates. The paper presents a plan for an empirical evaluation using a controlled experimental design to assess the impact of LogPurifier on the effectiveness and efficiency of two downstream tasks: model inference and anomaly detection.

</details>


### [192] [The Spec Growth Engine: Spec-Anchored, Code-Coupled, Drift-Enforced Architecture for AI-Assisted Software Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27045)
*Hartwig Grabowski*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The Spec Growth Engine is a lightweight framework that prevents context explosion and spec-code drift in AI coding agents by combining a machine-readable spec graph, scoped context assembly, a hardest-first growth protocol, and a blocking drift gate — synthesizing classic software engineering principles into an automated, code-coupled enforcement mechanism.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI coding agents suffer from two structural failure modes: (1) context explosion, where reasoning over an entire repository degrades output quality as context windows fill, and (2) silent spec-code drift, where specification and code diverge invisibly until repair becomes costly. Existing spec-driven approaches fail to fully address these problems.

Method: The authors propose four integrated components: (1) a machine-readable spec graph with explicit separation of contracts from design; (2) a Spine context assembler that limits agent context to an ownership path, preventing context explosion; (3) a vertical-slice growth protocol enforcing hardest-first ordering; and (4) a drift gate that blocks merges when spec-code divergence is detected. The design synthesizes established principles — Parnas information hiding, C4, Architecture Decision Records, Walking Skeleton, Reflexion Models, and Fitness Functions — into a lean, code-coupled whole.

Result: The framework is presented as a conceptual design; the abstract does not report empirical results or quantitative evaluations.

Conclusion: A lightweight synthesis of well-established software engineering principles — made machine-readable and machine-enforced — can address the context explosion and spec-code drift failure modes of AI coding agents without the overhead of heavy-weight frameworks like RUP or MDA.

Abstract: AI coding agents dramatically accelerate implementation speed but introduce two structural failure modes that existing spec-driven approaches do not fully solve: (1) context explosion -- the agent must reason over an entire repository at once, degrading output quality as the context window fills; and (2) silent spec-code drift -- code evolves, the specification does not, and the divergence becomes invisible until it is costly to repair.
  We present the Spec Growth Engine, a lightweight framework that addresses both failure modes through a machine-readable spec graph whose nodes carry explicit contract/design separation, a Spine context assembler that scopes agent context to an ownership path, a vertical-slice growth protocol that enforces hardest-first ordering, and a drift gate that makes spec-code divergence a blocking merge condition.
  The design synthesises well-established software engineering principles (Parnas information hiding, C4, ADRs, Walking Skeleton, Reflexion Models, Fitness Functions) into a lean, code-coupled, machine-enforced whole -- without the overhead of heavy-weight frameworks such as RUP or MDA.

</details>


### [193] [ATGBuilder: Feature-Assisted Graph Learning for Activity Transition Graph Construction with Seed Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27080)
*Chenhui Cui,Zixiang Xian,Danyu Li,Tao Li,Rubing Huang,Dave Towey,Shikai Guo,Jiakun Liu*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: ATGBuilder is a feature-assisted graph-learning approach for constructing Activity Transition Graphs (ATGs) from Android apps. It uses an LLM to summarize UI activity metadata and explicitly models widget-trigger information as edge attributes with a reconstruction objective, significantly outperforming prior methods on multiple benchmarks and improving automated GUI exploration tools.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Constructing high-quality Activity Transition Graphs (ATGs) for Android apps is challenging: static analysis yields infeasible transitions or misses acceptable ones, while dynamic exploration produces incomplete transitions. Existing learning-based approaches treat ATG construction as seed-supervised link prediction but underutilize activity-layout and widget-trigger information, limiting their performance.

Method: ATGBuilder is a feature-assisted graph-learning framework for seed-supervised ATG construction. It employs a Large Language Model (LLM) to distill UI activity metadata from layouts into compact textual functionality summaries. Crucially, it explicitly encodes widget-trigger information as edge attributes and introduces an auxiliary widget-attribute reconstruction objective during model training to leverage this signal. Evaluation uses ablations on the frontmatter corpus and manually-checked ground-truth ATGs.

Result: Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that ATGBuilder significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods for ATG construction. The approach also proves effective in improving automated GUI exploration tools by providing better navigation guidance.

Conclusion: ATGBuilder advances seed-supervised ATG construction by effectively integrating LLM-based activity summarization and explicit widget-trigger modeling, achieving superior performance and demonstrating practical utility in downstream GUI exploration tasks.

Abstract: Android applications are organized around activities that provide visual Graphical User Interface (GUI) containers that host the UI and handle user interaction events. Activity Transition Graphs (ATGs) have been widely used to model apps' GUI navigation. However, the construction of high-quality ATGs is challenging: ATGs based on static analysis may miss acceptable transitions and may extract infeasible ones; while dynamically explored ATGs can yield incomplete transitions. Recent learning-based approaches can treat ATG construction as a seed-supervised link-prediction task. However, the use of activity-layout and widget-trigger information for ATG construction remains limited. We propose ATGBuilder, a feature-assisted graph-learning approach for seed-supervised ATG construction. ATGBuilder uses a Large Language Model (LLM) to summarize UI activity metadata from layouts into compact textual functionality summaries. ATGBuilder explicitly models widget-trigger information into the edge attribute: It then uses an auxiliary widget-attribute reconstruction objective on this information during model training. ATGBuilder's performance was evaluated across a series of ablations on the frontmatter corpus, and an experiment on benchmark using manually-checked ground-truth ATGs. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that ATGBuilder significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. We further demonstrate its effectiveness by improving automated GUI exploration tools through better navigation guidance.

</details>


### [194] [On the Reproducibility of Quantum Software Defect Datasets: A Case Study of Bugs4Q](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27124)
*Haruto Ohto,Yuta Ishimoto,Shinsuke Matsumoto,Shinji Kusumoto*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A replication study on Bugs4Q reveals that quantum software defect dataset reproducibility drops dramatically over time (62.2% → 16.2%) due primarily to dependency issues. Unlike classical datasets, most failures require source-code modifications rather than simple dependency versioning. The authors introduce Bugs4Q-Robust, restoring reproducibility to 78.4%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work by Zhu et al. showed that classical software defect datasets like Defects4J suffer from reproduction failures over time, but it was unknown whether this generalizes to quantum software defect datasets. This study aims to fill that gap and investigate the root causes of reproduction failures in the quantum domain.

Method: The authors replicated Zhu et al.'s methodology using Bugs4Q (37 artifacts, 77,700 quantum program executions) across 21 versions of the Qiskit core library. They analyzed reproducibility rates across versions, manually inspected root causes of failures, and characterized the differences from classical defect datasets. Based on findings, they curated Bugs4Q-Robust via source-code patches.

Result: Reproducibility of Bugs4Q declined from 62.2% (Qiskit v0.20.1) to 16.2% (v2.3.1). Of the failures, 93.6% were dependency-related. Unlike Defects4J, most Bugs4Q failures required source-code modifications (import paths, API invocations) rather than mere dependency version adjustments. Bugs4Q-Robust restored reproducibility to 78.4% on v2.3.1.

Conclusion: The findings confirm that quantum software defect datasets exhibit similar (but not identical) reproducibility decay as classical counterparts. The key difference is that quantum ecosystem API instability necessitates source-code-level fixes. Continuous dataset maintenance is critical in the rapidly evolving quantum software ecosystem.

Abstract: The reproducibility of software defect datasets is essential for obtaining reliable and comparable research results. Zhu et al. have shown that defect datasets such as Defects4J suffer from reproduction failures (i.e., reported bugs become non-reproducible) as time passes since their creation. However, it remains unclear whether these findings generalize to quantum software defect datasets. We therefore conduct a replication study of the prior work using Bugs4Q, a widely used dataset of real-world bugs in quantum programs. Our analysis includes 77,700 quantum program executions of 37 Bugs4Q artifacts across 21 core-library versions. The experimental results showed that the reproducibility of Bugs4Q dropped from 62.2% on Qiskit v0.20.1 to 16.2% on v2.3.1, the latest version as of April 1, 2026. A manual inspection of the root causes further indicated that 93.6% of the failures were dependency-related. While these findings are consistent with those of the prior work, we also observed differences. In particular, most reproduction failures in Bugs4Q cannot be resolved merely by adjusting dependency versions; instead, they require source-code modifications such as migrating import paths and API invocations. Based on this observation, we curated Bugs4Q-Robust, a patched version of Bugs4Q to restore reproducibility. Bugs4Q-Robust increases reproducibility from 16.2% to 78.4% on Qiskit v2.3.1. Our findings highlight the importance of continuous dataset maintenance in the rapidly evolving quantum software ecosystem.

</details>


### [195] [Smaller Models, Unexpected Costs: Trade-offs in LLM Quantization for Automated Program Repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27205)
*Fernando Vallecillos-Ruiz,Giordano d'Aloisio,Max Hort,Luca Traini,Antinisca Di Marco,Leon Moonen*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper empirically evaluates how LLM quantization affects Automated Program Repair (APR) performance, analyzing 13 quantization configurations across 6 LLMs on two benchmarks. Key findings: quantized models solve different (largely non-overlapping) sets of bugs despite similar overall repair counts; quantization reduces memory by up to 85% but paradoxically increases inference time and energy consumption due to poor hardware utilization; and no single quantization method dominates—trade-offs depend on model architecture and task complexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work evaluates quantization primarily through aggregate benchmark scores, which obscure nuanced changes in model behavior (e.g., which specific problems are solved) and neglect non-functional trade-offs like inference time and energy consumption. The authors aim to provide a holistic, multidimensional analysis of quantization's impact on a complex software engineering task (APR), moving beyond simplistic accuracy metrics.

Method: An empirical study evaluating 13 quantization configurations—varying bit-width (4-bit, 8-bit), quantization method (GPTQ, AWQ, bitsandbytes), and target components (weights-only, weights+KV cache)—across 6 LLMs (CodeLlama, DeepSeek-Coder, StarCoder2, etc.). Evaluation is performed on two APR benchmarks: HumanEval-Java and Defects4J. Metrics include repair effectiveness, memory footprint, inference time, and energy consumption, with Pareto trade-off analysis to identify dominated configurations.

Result: (1) Quantized and base models repair comparable numbers of problems but with low overlap in which problems they fix—they are complementary. (2) Quantization reduces memory by up to 85%, but increases inference time (up to 2×) and energy consumption due to suboptimal hardware utilization of quantized operations. (3) Pareto analysis shows 48% of configurations are strictly dominated; no single quantization method is universally superior. Trade-offs are sensitive to model architecture and task complexity.

Conclusion: Quantization decisions should not be guided solely by benchmark scores; practitioners must consider the multidimensional trade-off space including memory, latency, energy, and behavioral changes in model outputs. The findings caution against naive adoption of quantization for complex SE tasks and call for hardware-aware quantization strategies and multi-objective selection frameworks.

Abstract: Language Models (LLMs) are powerful toolsand have been increasingly adopted for complex software engineering tasks. As the number of parameters increases, results can often be improved, but this also imposes substantialmemory requirements. While quantization effectively reduces thememory footprint, its overall impact is often summarized onlyby benchmark scores, which mask changes in model behaviorand non-functional overheads. In this work, we conduct anempirical evaluation of LLM quantization using AutomatedProgram Repair (APR), a complex task in software engineering.We analyze 13 quantization configurations spanning differentbit-widths, methods, and target components (weights and KVcache) across six representative LLMs, evaluated on two APRbenchmarks (HumanEval-Java and Defects4J).
  Our findings reveal that base and quantized models can provide different sets of repaired problems with little overlap, whileretaining a comparable number of repaired problems. Althoughquantization successfully reduces memory footprints by up to85%, it increases both inference time and energy consumption,which we attribute to suboptimal hardware utilization. OurPareto trade-off analysis shows that 48% of the configurationsevaluated are strictly dominated by alternatives. Rather thanidentifying a superior quantization method, our findings highlightthat the trade-offs between effectiveness, memory footprint,and energy efficiency are sensitive to the underlying modelarchitecture and the complexity of the task.

</details>


### [196] [Beyond Objects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27258)
*Daniel Jackson*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: The paper argues that object orientation's founding principle of partitioning functionality by domain individuals inherently causes fragmentation and conflation of functionality. The proposed solution is to abandon object orientation entirely and adopt an approach that decouples domain individuals from functional modules.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To challenge the long-standing assumption that object-oriented partitioning by domain entities is natural or beneficial, and to demonstrate that this principle is the root cause of well-known software engineering problems (fragmentation and conflation of functionality) rather than problems solvable within the OO paradigm.

Method: The paper takes a critical, argumentative approach: it traces the historical influence of object orientation over 50+ years, identifies the core principle of partitioning by domain individuals, and then argues deductively that subsequent software engineering problems are inevitable consequences of this principle, making a case for a paradigm shift.

Result: The analysis concludes that later software engineering developments attempting to fix fragmentation and conflation were addressing symptoms rather than root causes. The true remedy lies in abandoning object orientation and replacing it with an alternative that separates domain individuals from functional module boundaries.

Conclusion: Object orientation's foundational principle is fundamentally flawed. The path forward requires rejecting OO and embracing a new modularization paradigm that decouples problem-domain individuals from the partitioning of system functionality.

Abstract: A core principle of object orientation -- that the functionality of a system can be partitioned amongst objects that correspond to individuals in the problem domain -- has influenced how software has been specified, designed and implemented for more than fifty years. Later developments in software engineering sought to build on this principle. But in fact this partitioning is neither natural nor straightforward, and the problems that these later developments sought to mitigate -- the fragmentation and conflation of functionality -- were often, in fact, the inevitable consequences of this founding principle. An easier path to addressing these problems therefore starts by going back, abandoning object orientation, and replacing it with an alternative approach that decouples the individuals of the problem domain from the modules that partition functionality.

</details>

# cs.CR [[Back]](#toc)

### [197] [MIRAGE: Protecting against Malicious Image Editing via False Moderation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26199)
*Anshul Nasery,Ramnath Kumar,Cho-Jui Hsieh,Sewoong Oh*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: MIRAGE is an image immunization method that fools pre-generation safety moderation systems into flagging images as policy-violating, causing commercial AI editors (like GPT-Image, Gemini, Grok) to refuse editing — achieving >88% success without needing access to model weights or prompts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing image immunization techniques require access to model weights and editing prompts, making them ineffective against closed-source commercial image editors. A system-level attack surface — pre-generation safety moderation — remains unexplored and common across all major commercial systems.

Method: MIRAGE adds adversarial perturbations to images that align them with policy-violating concepts in the representation space of an ensemble of open-source embedding and moderation models. This triggers the safety moderation classifiers of commercial editors to flag the image and refuse editing, regardless of the user's prompt.

Result: Evaluated against multiple closed-source image editing APIs (GPT-Image, Gemini Flash Image, Grok Imagine), MIRAGE achieved success rates exceeding 88%.

Conclusion: MIRAGE offers a simple, prompt-agnostic, and effective approach for protecting personal images from unauthorized AI-powered editing by exploiting the universal pre-generation moderation pipeline in commercial systems.

Abstract: The proliferation of AI-powered image editing systems raises serious concerns because it allows personal images to be arbitrarily manipulated at scale, with minimal effort, and a lower barrier to entry. Prior work on image immunization adds imperceptible perturbations to an image to protect against unauthorized manipulations. However, these methods usually require access to the model weights and the image manipulating prompt. This significantly limits their use, especially against powerful commercial image-editors such as GPT-Image, Gemini Flash Image (Nano Banana), and Grok Imagine. To address this, we take a system-level view of the problem and identify a previously unexplored attack surface common to all major commercial image editing systems: pre-generation safety moderation.Rather than disrupting the generative model itself, we propose to immunize images by causing these moderation classifiers to flag images as policy-violating, triggering an automatic refusal regardless of the editing prompt. We operationalize this by adding adversarial perturbations to align our image to policy-violating concepts in the representation space of an ensemble of open-source embedding and moderation models. We call our method MIRAGE, which stands for Moderation Induced Resistance Against Generative Editing. We evaluate MIRAGE against multiple closed-source image editing APIs and demonstrate success rates of more than 88%. Our approach is simple, prompt-agnostic, and effective, offering a practical path towards protecting personal images from unauthorized AI-powered editing.

</details>


### [198] [Data Facts: A Metadata Schema for Structured Data Exchange in the NANDini Multi-Agent Ecosystem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26211)
*Jin Gao,Maria Gorskikh,Pradyumna Chari,Brittany Box,Mukul Kemla,Pratik Behera,Abhishek Mehta,Ramesh Raskar*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: NANDini proposes "Data Facts," a lightweight JSON metadata schema with a `data_facts_url` pointer added to Agent Facts registry records, enabling autonomous agents to advertise, evaluate, and verify datasets. Evaluated across 840 decision tasks, it achieves 100% accuracy with data access, reduces stale-data errors via TTL, detects 100% corruption via SHA-256 checksums, and blocks all forgery attempts with a three-layer security pipeline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current agent protocols (NANDA, A2A, MCP) handle identity and communication but lack structured data exchange. Enterprise frameworks (IDS-RAM, Gaia-X, Ocean Protocol) rely on human-in-the-loop governance incompatible with autonomous, real-time agent interactions. There is no mechanism for agents to advertise, evaluate, and verify datasets autonomously.

Method: Introduces "Data Facts" — a lightweight JSON metadata schema linked via a `data_facts_url` pointer in Agent Facts registry records. Encodes dataset identity, access tier (public/semi-private/private), endpoint, TTL for freshness, and SHA-256 checksum. For private/semi-private data, implements a three-layer security pipeline: JWT authentication, capability-scoped gateway authorization, and A2A credential delegation protocol.

Result: Across 840 decision-making evaluations: data-informed agents achieve 100% accuracy vs. 35.2% without data access (p < 0.001); TTL enforcement reduces stale-data errors from 37.6% to 8.8%; checksum verification achieves 100% corruption detection at all injection rates; security pipeline blocks all 46 forgery attempts with zero data leakage.

Conclusion: Data Facts successfully bridges the gap between agent discovery and data access, enabling fully autonomous, trustworthy data exchange among AI agents without human intervention. The combination of metadata schema, TTL-based freshness, integrity verification, and layered security provides a viable infrastructure for the NANDini vision of automated agent ecosystems.

Abstract: NANDini (Networked Agents Natural Distillation of Interconnected Nodal Intelligence) envisions an automated ecosystem where intelligent agents independently create, process, and exchange data to drive decisions at scale. Realizing this vision requires infrastructure beyond agent discovery and communication: agents must be able to advertise, evaluate, and verify the datasets they hold.
  Current protocols, including NANDA for federated registry and A2A and MCP for inter-agent messaging, address identity and communication but provide no mechanism for structured data exchange. Existing enterprise data-sharing frameworks, such as IDS-RAM, Gaia-X, and Ocean Protocol, assume human-in-the-loop governance that is incompatible with autonomous, real-time agent interactions.
  We introduce Data Facts, a core NANDini concept: a lightweight JSON metadata schema that bridges agent discovery and data access through a single pointer, `data_facts_url`, added to an existing Agent Facts registry record. The linked document encodes dataset identity, access tier, whether public, semi-private, or private, endpoint, a time-to-live for freshness validation, and a SHA-256 integrity checksum.
  For private and semi-private data, we implement a three-layer security pipeline: JWT authentication, capability-scoped gateway authorization, and an A2A credential delegation protocol. Across 840 decision-making evaluations, data-informed agents achieve 100% accuracy versus 35.2% without data access (p < 0.001); TTL enforcement reduces stale-data errors from 37.6% to 8.8%; checksum verification achieves 100% corruption detection at all injection rates; and the security pipeline blocks all 46 forgery attempts with zero data leakage.

</details>


### [199] [CyberChainBench: Can AI Agents Secure Smart Contracts Against Real-World On-Chain Vulnerabilities?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26216)
*Jintao Huang,Fengqing Jiang,Radha Poovendran,Zhiqiang Lin*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: CyberChainBench is a benchmark for LLM-based agents on smart contract security, covering vulnerability detection, exploit generation, and patch synthesis using 541 real-world DeFi exploits across 9 EVM chains. Results show a difficulty gradient: 37.5% detection, 43.7% exploitation, and 23.4% patching success, with the top agent (Codex + GPT-5.5) extracting $57.4M in exploit profit at $2.39/case.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks for LLM-based smart contract security lack end-to-end, on-chain evaluation with real-world exploits and do not span the full pipeline of detection, exploitation, and patching. The authors aim to fill this gap with a grounded, economically measurable benchmark derived from historical DeFi incidents.

Method: CyberChainBench comprises 541 real-world exploit cases from DeFiHackLabs across 9 EVM chains. Each case is anchored to a specific block with structured ground truth (vulnerability type, localization, attacker profit). Agents interact with forked blockchain state via Harbor-orchestrated isolation environments, using tools to read code, trace transactions, and validate exploits on mainnet forks. A five-type vulnerability taxonomy is defined. Exploits are graded by economic impact on historical forks; patches are validated using replay of historical attacks and legitimate transactions as fail-to-pass test oracles on a proxy-upgradeable subset.

Result: The best configuration (Codex with GPT-5.5) achieves 37.5% on vulnerability detection, 43.7% on exploit generation, and 23.4% on patch synthesis. Across the 200-case exploit set, this agent realized $57.4M in total exploit profit at a cost of $2.39 per case, demonstrating a clear difficulty gradient across the three tasks.

Conclusion: LLM-based agents show nontrivial but still limited capability on real-world smart contract security tasks, with patching being substantially harder than detection or exploitation. The benchmark provides a rigorous, economically grounded framework for evaluating and improving autonomous smart contract security agents.

Abstract: We present CyberChainBench, a benchmark for evaluating LLM-based agents on smart contract security across three complementary tasks: vulnerability detection, exploit generation, and patch synthesis. Built from 541 real-world exploit incidents from DeFiHackLabs spanning 9 EVM chains, the benchmark provides end-to-end on-chain evaluation where agents interact with historical blockchain state through isolated evaluation environments orchestrated by Harbor, using tools to read code, trace transactions, and validate exploits on mainnet forks. Each case is anchored to a specific block and includes structured ground truth covering vulnerability type, localization, and attacker profit. Exploits are graded by economic impact on historical forks; patches are validated by replaying historical attacks and legitimate transactions as fail-to-pass test oracles on a proxy-upgradeable subset. We define a five-type vulnerability taxonomy and evaluate multiple agent--model configurations. Results reveal a clear difficulty gradient: the best configuration scores 37.5% on detection, 43.7% on exploitation, but only 23.4% on patching, with the top agent (Codex with GPT-5.5) realizing \$57.4M in total exploit profit across the 200-case exploit set at a cost of $2.39 per case.

</details>


### [200] [Expecting (Targeted Ads)? Network Analysis of User Health Data Leakage in Fertility Tracking Apps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26276)
