*Yeeun Jo,Shahanaasree Sivakumar,Mahnoor Jameel,Camille Cobb,Adam Bates,Brad Reaves*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A network measurement study of 20 Android fertility tracking apps reveals that a subset (n=5) leak user health data to third-party advertisers, both explicitly and implicitly through contextual advertising URLs, while other apps use ad-based monetization without apparent leakage, highlighting both privacy risks and the role of consumer choice.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior research on fertility tracking app privacy has focused extensively on human factors but has largely neglected the technical data handling practices of these apps, creating a gap in understanding how user health data is actually transmitted to third parties.

Method: The authors conducted a network-based measurement study of 20 Android fertility tracking apps from Google Play. They systematized app features, performed standardized user interactions across all apps in a controlled environment, and captured TLS-stripped network traffic to analyze data flows to third-party advertising services.

Result: Five apps exhibited explicit leakage of user health data and implicit leakage via highly targeted contextual advertising URLs. Other apps employing ad-based monetization showed no apparent leakage, and several apps had minimal interaction with ad services altogether.

Conclusion: The findings provide technical evidence substantiating widespread user privacy concerns, while also demonstrating that consumer choice matters — not all ad-supported fertility trackers leak data, indicating viable privacy-preserving monetization models exist.

Abstract: While human factors in the privacy of fertility tracking apps -- health trackers that record user's menstrual or pregnancy data -- has been the subject of extensive study, little attention has been paid to the technical aspects of apps' data handling practices. We conduct a network-based measurement study of a corpus of 20 Android fertility tracking apps from the Google Play Store, focusing on how user data is shared with third party advertising services. After systematizing app features, we conduct a series of standardized user interactions across all apps in an environment that records TLS-stripped network traffic. In a subset of apps (n=5) we identify explicit leakage of user health data as well implicit leakage through highly targeted contextual advertising URL's. Equally importantly, we observe additional apps that use an ad-based monetization model without apparent leakage of user data, as well as several apps the interact only minimally with ad services. These findings provide technical grounding for widespread user concerns, but also underscore the importance of consumer choice in the privacy implications of app-based fertility tracking.

</details>


### [201] [TEMPO-Diffusion: Temporally Exposed Malicious Poisoning of Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26285)
*William Aiken,Paula Branco,Guy-Vincent Jourdan,Iosif-Viorel Onut*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: TEMPO-Diffusion introduces a targeted backdoor attack on diffusion models that uses temporal, in-distribution triggers instead of input-time injection, enabling class-specific targeting, multi-location sub-image backdoors, and time-conditioned in-painting. The authors also release CALISA, a traffic-sign dataset for evaluating synthetic data poisoning. Experiments show high attack success rates in downstream classifiers trained on poisoned synthetic data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing noise-based backdoor attacks on diffusion models suffer from three key limitations: they inject triggers at input time (reducing stealthiness), use untargeted activation, and generate out-of-distribution targets. These assumptions diminish both the stealthiness and practical relevance of such attacks. This work aims to address these gaps with a more realistic, targeted backdoor framework.

Method: TEMPO-Diffusion localizes the malicious distribution shift to a temporal, in-distribution exposure within the diffusion process. The framework supports: (i) targeted attacks on and to specific classes, (ii) multiple sub-image backdoors that reconstruct specific features across multiple output images at multiple locations, and (iii) in-painting with time-conditioned triggers. The authors also introduce CALISA, a balanced, region-aware traffic-sign dataset covering Canadian and U.S. road signs, to study practical security concerns in synthetic data pipelines.

Result: Experiments on CIFAR10, GTSRB, and CALISA demonstrate that TEMPO-Diffusion reliably poisons class-specific synthetic data generation and induces high attack success rates in downstream classifiers trained on the poisoned synthetic data.

Conclusion: TEMPO-Diffusion demonstrates that temporal, in-distribution backdoor triggers in diffusion models pose a significant practical threat, particularly in synthetic-data training pipelines. The introduction of CALISA further highlights the need for region-aware, balanced benchmarks when evaluating such security vulnerabilities in real-world contexts like traffic-sign recognition.

Abstract: Noise-based backdoor attacks on diffusion models typically rely on input-time trigger injection, untargeted activation, and out-of-distribution target generation. Such assumptions reduce both the stealthiness and the practical relevance of these attacks. In this work, we present TEMPO-Diffusion, a targeted backdoor framework that localizes the malicious distribution shift to a temporal, in-distribution exposure. TEMPO-Diffusion supports: (i) targeted attacks on and to specific classes, (ii) multiple sub-image backdoors that reconstruct specific features within multiple, different output images and at multiple locations, and (iii) in-painting with time-conditioned triggers. To study relevant, practical security concerns in leveraging backdoored diffusion models for synthetic training data, we also introduce CALISA: a balanced, region-aware traffic-sign dataset emphasizing Canadian and U.S. road signs. Across CIFAR10, GTSRB, and CALISA, our experiments show that TEMPO-Diffusion can reliably poison class-specific synthetic data generation and induce high attack success rates in downstream classifiers trained on that data.

</details>


### [202] [Beyond Takedown: Measuring Malicious Go Module Persistence in the Wild](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26291)
*Minjae Bae,Carter Yagemann*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A study measuring a supply chain campaign in the Go ecosystem where attackers repackaged legitimate modules with obfuscated downloaders. Using manual GitHub searches and a custom AST scanner (GOAST) across 12.3M entries, researchers identified 2,289 malicious module versions and revealed that GitHub-only detection fails significantly — over 99.4% of removed artifacts remained accessible via Go proxy, exposing a critical takedown-remediation gap.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To quantify the scale and sophistication of an automation-based supply chain attack in the Go ecosystem, and to evaluate the effectiveness of GitHub-centric detection versus broader proxy-based scanning in identifying and remediating malicious modules.

Method: A dual-approach analysis: (a) manual search across 2,113 GitHub repositories for repackaged malicious Go modules, and (b) a large-scale automated scan of 12.3M index entries using GOAST, a custom deobfuscating AST scanner that detects obfuscated import-triggered downloader code. Proxy-based measurements were also conducted to assess the takedown-remediation gap.

Result: 2,289 malicious versions of legitimate Go modules were identified. GitHub-only searches missed the full scope of compromise and were effective only while malicious code remained on the platform. At least 99.4% of GitHub-unobservable (removed/suspended) artifacts remained retrievable via Go proxy. Post-disclosure, GitHub removed 684 repositories and Google Go team remediated 1,377 module versions.

Conclusion: GitHub-centric detection is insufficient for Go ecosystem supply chain security due to the persistence of malicious artifacts on Go proxy infrastructure. Comprehensive scanning via proxy endpoints is essential for effective detection and remediation of module-based supply chain attacks.

Abstract: We measure an automation-based supply chain campaign in the Go ecosystem. The attackers repackage legitimate Go modules under attacker-controlled owners, and embed them with obfuscated code for an import-triggered downloader. Our results come from two complementary analyses: a) a manual search on GitHub across 2,113 repositories and b) a large-scale scan of 12.3M index entries using a deobfuscating AST scanner (GOAST) that we implemented. As a result, we identified 2,289 malicious versions of legitimate Go modules. We demonstrate that purely GitHub-centric searches fail to identify the full extent of the compromise and are only effective for as long as the affected code is present on the platform. Moreover, our proxy-based measurements of the takedown-remediation gap reveal that among artifacts later found to be GitHub-unobservable (i.e., removed or suspended), at least 99.4% remained retrievable via Go proxy. Following our disclosure, GitHub has removed 684 malicious repositories and the Google Go team has remediated 1,377 module versions.

</details>


### [203] [Hybrid privacy-aware semantic search: SVD-truncated document geometry and CKKS-encrypted query reranking under a restricted threat model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26373)
*Sergey Kurilenko*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper proposes a hybrid privacy-preserving semantic search scheme: document vectors are protected geometrically via SVD truncation and secret orthogonal rotation, while queries are protected cryptographically via CKKS homomorphic encryption for reranking. This balances efficiency and privacy, avoiding the extremes of fully homomorphic encryption or noise-based obfuscation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vector database leaks expose embedded documents to embedding-inversion attacks. Existing defenses are impractical — fully homomorphic encryption is too slow at scale, and differential-privacy noise destroys ranking quality. The authors exploit the asymmetry between a static document collection and dynamic queries to design a practical middle-ground defense.

Method: Document vectors are truncated to a lower-dimensional SVD subspace and rotated by a secret orthogonal matrix (geometric protection). Query vectors are kept encrypted under CKKS fully homomorphic encryption during reranking, so the server never sees them (cryptographic protection). CKKS parameters are tuned via a small offline benchmark. The scheme is evaluated on one million documents across five encoders. Security is analyzed via theoretical lower bounds on reconstruction error in the protected subspace, and empirically against inversion attacks, known-plaintext Procrustes attacks, and product-quantization leakage.

Result: The scheme preserves (and sometimes slightly improves) ranking quality at sub-second latency. Off-the-shelf inversion attacks on the protected space collapse to the noise floor. However, a known-plaintext adversary can recover the secret rotation via orthogonal Procrustes using approximately as many leaked (query, document) pairs as the retained dimension. Product-quantization codes largely preserve nearest-neighbor structure. Ablation studies show SVD truncation incurs an encoder-dependent accuracy cost, not a free denoising gain.

Conclusion: Query confidentiality is cryptographically guaranteed via CKKS, but document protection (SVD truncation + secret rotation) is an empirical obfuscation layer, not a cryptographic primitive. The authors clearly delimit the threat model, acknowledging that document vectors remain vulnerable to certain attacks (e.g., known-plaintext Procrustes) and that truncation benefits are encoder-dependent.

Abstract: Dense embeddings power semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation, but embedding-inversion attacks can reconstruct source text from a vector: when a vector database leaks, the documents behind it leak too. The textbook defences are extremes - encrypting the whole search homomorphically is sound but too slow at million-document scale, while privacy noise degrades ranking long before it protects. We study a middle path exploiting the asymmetry between the static collection and the dynamic query. The collection is protected geometrically: each vector is truncated onto a lower-dimensional SVD subspace and rotated by a secret orthogonal transform known only to the owner. The query is protected cryptographically: it is reranked under CKKS homomorphic encryption, so an honest-but-curious server never sees the query or the scores. CKKS parameters come from a small offline benchmark.
  We prove a tight lower bound on the reconstruction error of any attacker confined to the protected subspace. On one million documents and five encoders the scheme preserves ranking quality (slightly improving it on strong encoders, as a linear denoiser) at sub-second latency, and an off-the-shelf inversion attack on the protected space collapses to the noise floor. We then test stronger adversaries: a known-plaintext attacker recovers the rotation by orthogonal Procrustes from about as many leaked pairs as the retained dimension; the public product-quantization codes preserve most nearest-neighbour structure; and random-projection, calibrated-noise and BEIR baselines show the truncation is an encoder-dependent accuracy cost, not a free denoiser. We state the limits: query confidentiality is cryptographic, but document protection is an empirical obfuscation layer (SVD truncation plus a secret rotation), not a cryptographic primitive, and we delimit the threat model for each claim.

</details>


### [204] [Verifying Intent and Harm: A Unified Defense Against LLM-Generated Threats](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26377)
*Poojitha Thota,Yun Lei,Santhosh Thangaraj,Siddhartha Reddy Jonnalagadda,Shirin Nilizadeh*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper proposes a verification-centric defense framework that jointly evaluates both prompt intent and response harm before delivering LLM outputs. Using specialized intent/harm analysts and a Judge for conflict resolution, the approach outperforms single-sided and single-agent baselines across five threat categories, improving F1 from 0.90 to 0.95 and reducing attack success rate to 4.1%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world adversarial attacks exploit a separation between benign-looking prompts that conceal malicious intent and harmful responses that appear actionable only in retrospect. Prompt-only and response-only defenses fail because neither side alone captures the full threat. There is a need for joint verification that bridges this gap.

Method: A verification-centric defense framework with three components: (1) a specialized Intent Analyst that assesses adversarial intent in user prompts, (2) a specialized Harm Analyst that evaluates harm in generated responses, and (3) a Judge that resolves conflicts when the two analysts disagree. The framework operates before the response is delivered to the user. A formal threat model for prompt-response attacks is defined. Evaluation covers five threat categories: jailbreaks, prompt injection, phishing, cyber abuse, and harmful content. Also tested against architecture-aware adaptive attacks where the attacker knows the verifier structure.

Result: The framework improves average F1 from 0.90 (strongest baselines) to 0.95, reduces average attack success rate to 4.1%, and lowers false positive rate on benign-sensitive requests from 0.12 to 0.06 compared to Single-Agent+CoT. It also demonstrates robustness against adaptive attacks targeting individual verification components.

Conclusion: Joint prompt-response verification provides a practical and effective foundation for securing LLM applications against evolving adversarial threats, consistently outperforming single-sided and single-agent alternatives.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in interactive applications, yet they remain vulnerable to adversarial interactions that induce harmful, deceptive, or policy-violating outputs. Existing defenses typically analyze either user prompts or generated outputs, but not both. However, many real-world attacks exploit a separation between adversarial intent expressed in the prompt and actionable harm manifested only in the response. As a result, prompt-only and response-only defenses frequently miss unsafe interactions that appear benign when viewed from either side in isolation. We present a verification-centric defense framework that jointly evaluates prompt intent and response harm before an LLM response is delivered to a user. The framework employs specialized analysts for intent and harm assessment together with a Judge for conflict resolution. We formalize a threat model for prompt-response attacks and evaluate the framework across five threat categories: jailbreaks, prompt injection, phishing, cyber abuse, and harmful content. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets show that jointly verifying prompt intent and response harm consistently outperforms single-sided defenses and single-agent reasoning baselines. Across threat categories, the framework improves average F1 from 0.90 for the strongest applicable baselines to 0.95 while reducing the average attack success rate to 4.1 percent. Compared with a Single-Agent+CoT baseline, it improves average F1 from 0.87 to 0.95 and reduces the false positive rate on benign-sensitive requests from 0.12 to 0.06. We further evaluate architecture-aware adaptive attacks in which the attacker knows the verifier structure and attempts to bypass individual verification components. Our results suggest that prompt-response verification provides a practical foundation for securing LLM applications against evolving adversarial threats.

</details>


### [205] [Lessons from the Adoption and Deprecation of the Privacy Sandbox Web APIs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26390)
*Yohan Beugin,Paul Barford,Patrick McDaniel*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A seven-year longitudinal study of Google's Privacy Sandbox APIs reveals limited, uneven adoption across web actors, with Chrome's tracking protections remaining largely opt-in unlike competitors. The analysis offers insights into why the initiative failed and provides recommendations for future web privacy proposals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite years of effort to reduce web tracking, balancing utility (especially advertising) with privacy remains unresolved. Google's Privacy Sandbox (2019–2025) was a major industry attempt to address this, but its eventual cancellation provides a rare opportunity to study how the web ecosystem responds to privacy-preserving API proposals and to understand the structural reasons behind its failure.

Method: The authors conducted a longitudinal measurement study using historical HTTP Archive crawls and public Chrome telemetry data. They tracked the prevalence of each Privacy Sandbox feature over its entire lifetime (5+ years for some APIs) across the CrUX top 100k popular websites, characterizing adoption and deprecation patterns by different web actors and analyzing how Chrome users experienced these features during real browsing journeys.

Result: Adoption of Privacy Sandbox APIs remained limited and uneven throughout the initiative's lifespan. Only a small subset of web actors adopted specific APIs, and implementations varied significantly. The analysis attributes this to misaligned incentives (interest, resources, timelines) and perceived risks (privacy violations, legal exposure, potential trade-offs). Chrome's third-party cookie and tracking limitations remain largely opt-in, in stark contrast to Brave, Firefox, and Safari, where such protections are enabled by default.

Conclusion: The Privacy Sandbox's failure illustrates fundamental limitations of "fix it in the browser" approaches when they lack default enforcement and broad ecosystem alignment. The paper distills actionable recommendations for next-generation web privacy proposals and highlights the persistent disparity in tracking protection defaults across major browsers.

Abstract: While several web actors have been trying to reduce web tracking for years, it remains unclear how to achieve both desirable levels of utility and privacy. In 2019, Google launched the Privacy Sandbox initiative to balance that trade-off and find privacy alternatives to common use cases such as advertising. Yet, in late 2025, Google canceled the project and deprecated most of the newly introduced APIs. Despite its end, the Privacy Sandbox represents a unique opportunity to learn about how the ecosystem reacted to the proposed changes and make observations about why and how it failed. In this paper, we present a longitudinal measurement and analysis study of the Privacy Sandbox APIs to characterize their adoption and deprecation over the past seven years by different web actors. Leveraging historical HTTP Archive crawls and public Chrome telemetry data, we offer the largest study of its kind into the prevalence of each Privacy Sandbox feature, during their entire respective lifetime (5+ years for some), on popular websites (CrUX top 100k), and as experienced by Chrome users during their browsing journey. Our results showcase an adoption that remained limited and uneven across the years; only few web actors implemented very specific APIs, and in disparate manners. We motivate our interpretation of these results by considering the incentives (interest, resources, timeline, etc.) and risks (potential trade-offs, privacy violations, and legal exposure, etc.) for these actors. Finally, our analysis also yields actionable recommendations for the next generation of web privacy proposals. More broadly, the Privacy Sandbox illustrates the limitations and disparities across browsers of ``fix it in the browser'' remedies: today, tracking and third-party cookies limitations in Chrome still remain largely opt-in, while they have been enabled by default on other browsers like Brave, Firefox, or Safari.

</details>


### [206] [What Browsers Do in the Shaders: A Measurement Study of WebGPU Privacy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26412)
*Igor Santos-Grueiro*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: WGPULens presents a measurement framework for analyzing privacy-relevant signals exposed through WebGPU's GPU programming model. Through controlled experiments, a participant field study, and a web crawl, the authors identify persistent pipeline compilation state as the primary privacy surface, demonstrate browser-native GPU activity inference, and show that real-world WebGPU usage remains largely limited to adapter probing rather than shader-intensive workloads.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: WebGPU provides validated, memory-safe GPU access to web pages, but shared browser, driver, OS, and GPU state may still leak privacy-relevant signals (e.g., cross-origin state, hardware fingerprinting, side-channel inference). No systematic framework existed to measure, categorize, and evaluate these privacy surfaces under realistic deployment conditions.

Method: The authors build WGPULens, a multi-tier measurement framework: (1) controlled lab scenarios isolating specific leakage surfaces (pipeline compilation, resource allocation, GPU timing), with cold/warm probes across origin, profile, and browser boundaries; (2) a participant field study (N unspecified) measuring fingerprintability via active WebGPU behavior stability within/between visits; (3) a Tranco top-list crawl assessing real-world WebGPU deployment; and (4) mitigation pilots evaluating source-level key separation as a proxy for pipeline-cache partitioning.

Result: Pipeline compilation state emerges as the clearest privacy surface — cold/warm probes reliably reveal prior compilation state across origins, browser profiles, and browser instances. Browser-visible observables can infer native GPU activity under labeled workloads. Other resource probes yield weaker positive results. The field study finds highly distinctive active WebGPU behavior with strong within-run stability but lower cross-visit stability. The crawl shows WebGPU usage is predominantly adapter probing and static support code, with zero observed page-load shader, pipeline, queue, query, or map operations. Mitigation pilots demonstrate pipeline-cache key separation as a viable evaluation proxy.

Conclusion: WebGPU privacy analysis must be surface-specific. Browsers should systematically measure which GPU state crosses which boundary, which browser-visible signals reveal that state, and what mitigation costs are incurred. The pipeline cache represents the most pressing target for partitioning or key-separation mitigations.

Abstract: WebGPU lets ordinary web pages run GPU workloads through a validated programming model. Validation protects memory safety, but shared browser, driver, OS, and GPU state can still expose privacy-relevant signals. We present WGPULens, a framework for measuring those signals across controlled scenarios, browser-native co-residency, a participant field study, public page loads, and mitigation policies. Our framework separates measurements: controlled scenarios support leakage, boundary, and mitigation claims; participant runs support deployment, compatibility, and fingerprintability; and a Tranco crawl measures WebGPU exposure in real-world pages.
  Our controlled results identify persistent pipeline compilation state as the clearest surface. Cold/warm pipeline probes reveal prior compilation state across selected origin, profile, and browser placements. Controlled browser/native experiments also show native GPU activity can be inferred from browser-visible observables under labeled workloads. Other resource probes provide weaker positive results and negative controls.
  The participant field study shows active WebGPU behavior is highly distinctive within the sample, with deterministic components stable within runs and lower exact stability across repeated visits. A page-load crawl finds WebGPU use mainly as adapter probing and static support code, with no observed page-load shader, pipeline, queue, query, or map activity. Mitigation pilots identify source-level key separation as a proxy for evaluating pipeline-cache partitioning. Overall, WGPULens shows that WebGPU privacy analysis must be surface-specific: browsers need to measure which GPU state crosses which boundary, which browser-visible signals reveal it, and what the corresponding mitigations cost.

</details>


### [207] [Adaptive Evaluation of Out-of-Band Defenses Against Prompt Injection in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26479)
*Praneeth Narisetty,Shiva Nagendra Babu Kore,Uday Kumar Reddy Kattamanchi,Jayaram Kumarapu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper surveys recent out-of-band defenses against indirect prompt injection in LLM agents (CaMeL, FIDES, Progent, etc.), framing them through classical security principles (Biba integrity, reference monitoring, least privilege). It critiques their reliance on static benchmarks and demonstrates through an independent reproduction that Progent's deterministic enforcement withstands adaptive black-box attacks, reducing success rates ~6×, though white-box attacks remain untested.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recent tool-using LLM agent defenses have shifted toward out-of-band (deterministic, external) enforcement rather than in-band training. However, all such systems are validated only on static benchmarks — the same flawed methodology that previously made in-band defenses appear robust until adaptive attacks broke them. The paper aims to (1) systematically compare these defenses under classical security frameworks and (2) subject one (Progent) to adaptive evaluation to test whether deterministic enforcement is genuinely harder to circumvent.

Method: First, a conceptual analysis organizing CaMeL, FIDES, Progent, RTBAS, and FORGE as instances of Biba integrity, reference monitoring, and least privilege. Second, an empirical adaptive-attack evaluation: the authors independently reproduce and extend Progent on the AgentDojo benchmark using a self-hosted Qwen2.5-7B model on a single H200 GPU. They run three trials with a hand-crafted black-box adaptive attack template, measuring attack success rate against Progent's out-of-band enforcement.

Result: The conceptual analysis yields a structured comparison table of what each defense covers. Empirically, Progent reduced mean attack success rate from 25.8% (no defense) to 4.2% (defended), roughly a sixfold reduction. The hand-crafted adaptive attack achieved only 2.6% success — not statistically higher than the standard attack against the defense. This is a single data point on a weak open-weight model; stronger white-box (GCG) attacks remain an open question.

Conclusion: The result is consistent with the hypothesis that deterministic out-of-band enforcement is a harder target for adaptive attackers than in-band detection, but does not establish it definitively. The paper calls for the community to adopt adaptive, defense-aware evaluation protocols as standard practice when validating LLM agent security defenses.

Abstract: Recent work (2024 to 2026) has converged on a strategy for defending tool-using LLM agents against indirect prompt injection: rather than training the model to refuse malicious instructions, enforce security outside the model with a deterministic policy that mediates the agent's actions. Systems such as CaMeL, FIDES, Progent, RTBAS, and FORGE realize this with capabilities, information-flow labels, and reference monitors, and several report near-elimination of attacks on the AgentDojo benchmark. We make two contributions. First, we organize these out-of-band defenses as instances of classical integrity protection (Biba), reference monitoring, and least privilege, yielding a structured comparison of what they do and do not cover. Second, we warn that every one of them is validated only on static benchmarks (a fixed set of injection attempts), the same methodology that made in-band defenses look strong until adaptive, defense-aware attacks broke twelve of them at over 90% success; we specify the threat model and protocol an adaptive evaluation requires. We then run that protocol as an independent reproduction and extension of Progent's own adaptive-attack analysis, on AgentDojo, with an open-weight agent (Qwen2.5-7B) self-hosted on a single H200, a setting its authors did not test. Averaged over three runs, the defense held: Progent cut mean attack success roughly sixfold (25.8% to 4.2%), and a hand-crafted adaptive attack did not raise it (2.6%). This is one small-scale data point on a weak model with a single black-box attack template; a stronger optimized (white-box GCG) attack remains open. The result is consistent with, but does not establish, the hypothesis that deterministic out-of-band enforcement is a harder target for an adaptive attacker than in-band detection.

</details>


### [208] [DKVE: Decentralized Key Validation for End-to-End Encrypted Messaging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26486)
*Subin Song,Taekyoung Kwon*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: DKVE is a privacy-preserving protocol that validates public keys by cross-checking them across mutual contacts in users' social graphs, using OPRF/OKVS cryptography and SPRT-based aggregation to detect MitM attacks with >97% accuracy on moderate-to-strong-tie networks, offering a complementary mechanism to reduce reliance on costly key transparency systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: End-to-end encrypted messengers face a trade-off: out-of-band verification is secure but unscalable, while key transparency (KT) systems are automated but incur high storage costs and operational complexity — neither scales well to billion-user systems.

Method: DKVE introduces social graph-based cross-validation: when a client fetches a contact's public key from a server, it queries mutual contacts to verify key consistency. Privacy is preserved via Oblivious Pseudorandom Functions (OPRF) and Oblivious Key-Value Stores (OKVS). A Sequential Probability Ratio Test (SPRT) aggregates responses with configurable error bounds to detect server misbehavior.

Result: Simulations on real social network datasets show >97% MitM detection rates for strong-to-moderate-tie networks. The remaining 3% of cases require fallback methods (KT/OOB). Proof-of-concept implementation confirms feasibility on commodity hardware. DKVE can reduce KT query frequency by two orders of magnitude, enabling a shift to space-efficient KT data structures like RSA accumulators.

Conclusion: DKVE is not a full replacement for existing methods — it has bootstrapping challenges and weak performance on weak-tie networks — but serves as a practical complementary validation layer that makes secure messaging more deployable at billion-user scale.

Abstract: End-to-end encrypted messaging systems depend on authentic public key distribution to prevent man-in-the-middle (MitM) attacks. Current solutions present a stark trade-off: out-of-band (OOB) verification provides strong security but lacks scalability for large contact lists, while key transparency (KT) systems enable automated verification at high storage costs and operational complexity.
  We propose DKVE, a protocol that validates public keys through privacy-preserving cross-validation within users' social graphs. When obtaining a contact's public key from a key server, clients query mutual contacts to verify they hold the same key, combining Oblivious Pseudorandom Functions (OPRF) and Oblivious Key-Value Stores (OKVS) to preserve privacy of both queries and contact lists. DKVE employs a Sequential Probability Ratio Test (SPRT) to aggregate responses and detect server misbehavior with user-configurable error bounds.
  We evaluate DKVE through simulations on real social network datasets, demonstrating DKVE can detect MitM attacks with exceeding 97% for strong-to-moderate-tie networks. The remaining 3% of cases require validation through alternative methods such as KT and OOB verification. Our proof-of-concept implementation confirms feasibility for background operation on commodity hardware, in terms of the latency and bandwidth.
  As DKVE can reduce the frequency of KT queries by two orders of magnitude, it enables fundamental architectural shifts: KT directories can migrate from fast but space-inefficient Merkle trees to space-efficient data structures like RSA accumulators. While DKVE cannot replace existing methods entirely -- suffering from bootstrapping problems and degraded performance on weak-tie networks -- it provides a practical complementary key validation mechanism, making secure messaging more deployable for billion-user systems.

</details>


### [209] [VIGIL: Runtime Enforcement of Behavioral Specifications in AI Agent Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26524)
*Ying Li,Yanju Chen,Hongbo Wen,Bosi Zhang,Hanzhi Liu,Peiran Wang,Yu Feng,Yuan Tian*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: VIGIL is a runtime enforcement framework for agentic systems that translates behavioral policies (from skill specs, operator constraints, and global rules) into SMT constraints over finite execution traces, enabling detection of violations that depend on event order, argument relationships, or cross-call value flow. It achieves >95% recall and <10% false-positive rate on real LLM-agent runs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic systems increasingly use third-party skills with natural-language specifications defining access, disclosure, execution, and precondition boundaries. However, these specifications lack executable runtime enforcement. The core challenge is contextual granularity: a monitor must decide what events to observe, what state to retain, how far across execution to reason, and where to intervene. Wrong granularity risks blocking benign actions or missing multi-action violations. Existing enforcement mechanisms assume fixed event models or enforcement points, which are insufficient for the dynamic, cross-call nature of agentic system violations.

Method: VIGIL provides three components: (1) a policy language capturing context-specific enforcement requirements over agent-tool events, including temporal dependencies, argument constraints, and value-flow conditions; (2) symbolic evaluation rules that translate these policies into SMT constraints over finite execution traces, enabling detection beyond single-call filters; (3) an end-to-end runtime framework that checks actual agent execution traces against policies derived from skill specifications, operator-defined constraints, and global cross-skill rules.

Result: On real LLM-agent runs covering office-document, operational, and engineering tasks, VIGIL detected policy violations with over 95% recall and a false-positive rate below 10%.

Conclusion: VIGIL demonstrates that expressive, context-aware runtime policy enforcement for agentic systems is feasible by combining a dedicated policy language with SMT-based symbolic evaluation over finite traces, addressing the granularity challenge that fixed event-model approaches cannot handle.

Abstract: Agentic systems increasingly act through third-party skills, allowing model-generated decisions to affect files, communication channels, and cyber-physical devices. These skills often include natural-language specifications that define access permissions, disclosure limits, execution privileges, and required preconditions. Although such specifications describe the intended boundaries of skill behavior, they do not by themselves provide executable runtime enforcement. Enforcing them raises a contextual granularity challenge: even when a policy is written for a particular task context, a monitor must still decide which events to observe, what state to retain, how far across the execution to reason, and where to intervene. Choosing the wrong granularity can either block benign executions or miss violations that emerge only across multiple actions. Most existing enforcement mechanisms, however, assume a fixed event model or enforcement point.
  In this work, we present VIGIL, an end-to-end runtime enforcement framework for agentic systems. VIGIL checks an agent's actual execution trace against behavioral policies from skill specifications, operator-defined constraints, and global rules spanning multiple skills. To make such policies executable, VIGIL introduces a policy language that captures context-specific enforcement requirements over agent-tool events, including temporal dependencies, argument constraints, and value-flow conditions. The language is paired with symbolic evaluation rules that translate policies into SMT constraints over finite traces, allowing VIGIL to detect violations that depend on event order, argument relationships, or cross-call value flow rather than relying on fixed single-call filters. On real LLM-agent runs spanning office-document, operational, and engineering tasks, VIGIL detects policy violations with over 95% recall and a false-positive rate below 10%.

</details>


### [210] [TESLA-for-5G: Broadcast Authentication for 5G Networks Using TESLA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26528)
*Subin Song,Michael K. Reiter,Taekyoung Kwon*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: TF5 is a broadcast authentication protocol for 5G SIB1 that combines TESLA (symmetric MAC with delayed key disclosure) for steady-state efficiency with GG09 identity-based signatures for lightweight bootstrapping, eliminating per-message digital signature overhead on UEs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 5G base stations broadcast unauthenticated system information (SI), enabling attackers to deploy fake base stations (FBS) that deceive UEs into camping on them. Prior solutions require UEs to verify digital signatures on every SIB1 reception, which is computationally prohibitive for resource-constrained devices. A lightweight, efficient broadcast authentication mechanism is needed.

Method: TF5 is a two-phase protocol: (1) Bootstrapping phase — during cell entry, a lightweight GG09 Schnorr-like identity-based signature (IBS) authenticates TESLA parameters without certificate distribution overhead; (2) Steady-state phase — each subsequent SIB1 is authenticated via symmetric MAC with TESLA delayed key disclosure, avoiding per-message asymmetric crypto. Formal verification is performed in Tamarin under a Dolev-Yao adversary model. The protocol is implemented on the OpenAirInterface 5G stack and evaluated via trace-driven analysis.

Result: Tamarin formal verification confirms TF5's security under the Dolev-Yao model. Implementation on OpenAirInterface and trace-driven analysis demonstrate favorable computation, communication, and storage costs compared to prior digital-signature-based approaches.

Conclusion: TF5 provides a practical and formally verified broadcast authentication solution for 5G SIB1, significantly reducing UE computational burden by replacing per-message digital signatures with symmetric MAC in the steady state, while using lightweight IBS for initial trust establishment.

Abstract: 5G base stations broadcast unauthenticated system information (SI) that every user equipment (UE) reads during cell selection. This enables attackers to broadcast forged SI from a fake base station (FBS), deceiving UEs into camping on it. Prior approaches require UEs to authenticate System Information Block 1 (SIB1) using digital signatures. This necessitates computation-heavy verification for every SIB1 reception, imposing a significant burden on resource-constrained UEs. We propose TESLA-for-5G (TF5), a broadcast authentication protocol for 5G SIB1 that combines TESLA with GG09 Schnorr-like identity-based signatures (IBS). In the steady state, TF5 enables UEs to authenticate each SIB1 message using a symmetric MAC and delayed key disclosure, eliminating the need for per-message digital signatures. Initial trust is bootstrapped during cell entry using a lightweight GG09 IBS over the TESLA parameters, avoiding certificate distribution overhead. We formally verify TF5 in Tamarin under a Dolev-Yao adversary and demonstrate its favorable computation, communication, and storage costs through both an implementation on the OpenAirInterface 5G stack and trace-driven analysis.

</details>


### [211] [Adversarial Diffusion Across Modalities: A Fusion Survey of Attacks, Defenses, and Evaluation for Text, Vision, and Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26566)
*Abrar Alotaibi,Moataz Ahmed*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This survey unifies four disconnected tracks of adversarial AI research—text/LLM attacks, image classifier attacks, VLN jailbreaks, and diffusion-based defenses—into a single conceptual framework with a unified taxonomy, six-class diffusion role classification, five-dimension evaluation criteria, and a research agenda, cataloging 50+ papers and identifying five recurring weaknesses in LLM-side adversarial literature.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Adversarial evaluation of AI systems has matured along four largely disconnected tracks, each with its own vocabulary, threat models, and benchmarks. Denoising diffusion models have emerged as a shared generative mechanism with recipes actively ported between communities, creating a need for information-fusion at the meta-research level to integrate these siloed efforts into a coherent framework.

Method: The authors conduct a narrative review (not PRISMA-compliant systematic review) cataloging 50 published papers across four scope areas plus additional baseline entries. They propose: (1) a six-class taxonomy of diffusion roles in adversarial pipelines, (2) a threat-model axis capturing attacker knowledge, query budget, and target accessibility, and (3) a five-dimension evaluation framework (attack success rate, transferability, query budget, perplexity, defense-evasion) applied uniformly across modalities. The review adopts a dual attacker-defender perspective.

Result: The survey catalogs 50 papers across text/LLM, image classifier, vision-language model, and defense areas, plus 4 diffusion-LLM-as-victim entries and 10 non-diffusion baselines. Critical analysis identifies five recurring weaknesses in current LLM-side literature. The companion catalog and spreadsheet are released with the paper.

Conclusion: The field would benefit from unified evaluation protocols across modalities. The authors provide a research agenda with open questions and concrete experimental designs, advocating for cross-community standardization of threat models and evaluation criteria, and discuss implications for replication given the narrative review methodology.

Abstract: Adversarial evaluation of AI systems has matured along four largely disconnected tracks: diffusion-based attacks on text and large language models (LLMs), diffusion-based attacks on image classifiers, jailbreak pipelines against vision-language models, and diffusion-based input purification defenses. Each has developed its own vocabulary, threat models, and benchmarks, with denoising diffusion models emerging as a shared generative mechanism whose recipes are now actively ported between communities. This survey performs an information-fusion exercise at the meta-research level: we integrate these four tracks into a single conceptual framework with a unified taxonomy, evaluation criteria, and research agenda, focusing on the LLM-side slice. We catalog fifty published papers across four scope areas (text/LLM, image classifier, vision-language model, defense), plus four diffusion-LLM-as-victim entries and ten non-diffusion baselines against which any new attack must be compared. We propose a six-class taxonomy of diffusion roles in adversarial pipelines, augmented by a threat-model axis recording attacker knowledge, query budget, and target accessibility, and apply a five-dimension framework (attack success rate, transferability, query budget, perplexity, defense-evasion) uniformly across modalities. The review adopts a dual attacker-defender perspective: alongside the attack catalog we cover four diffusion-based defenses that form the natural evaluation backdrop for new attacks. Our critical analysis identifies five recurring weaknesses of the current LLM-side literature, and we close with a research agenda of open questions and concrete experimental designs. The companion catalog and spreadsheet are released with the paper. We are explicit that this is a narrative review with quality assessment, not a PRISMA-compliant systematic review, and discuss the implications for replication.

</details>


### [212] [Agents That Know Too Much: A Data-Centric Survey of Privacy in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26627)
*Nada Lahjouji,Ashwin Gerard Colaco*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This survey paper examines privacy risks in LLM agents from a data-centric perspective, organizing findings around the data sources agents touch (queries, intermediate results, memory, APIs) rather than attack types. It taxonomizes data sources, privacy risks, and governance mechanisms, maps existing benchmarks, and identifies gaps—notably that information-flow control is the only mechanism addressing compositional and cross-session inference leakage, and that no benchmark tests an agent across all its data surfaces under a unified privacy policy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM agents transition from simple question-answering to operating over sensitive data across multiple sources, multi-step workflows, persistent memory, and delegated permissions, existing privacy mechanisms become inadequate. The research landscape is fragmented across disparate subfields (RAG, text-to-SQL, prompt injection, access control, etc.), necessitating a unified survey that organizes knowledge around the data an agent touches.

Method: The authors conduct a data-centric survey, introducing the concept of "data agent" as shorthand for an LLM agent working with data. They taxonomize: (1) data sources an agent touches, (2) privacy risks per source, (3) governance mechanisms addressing those risks, and (4) existing benchmarks. They then identify gaps in both mechanisms and evaluation tools.

Result: Two key findings emerge: (1) only information-flow control among all governance mechanisms can address compositional and cross-session inference leakage—the two least-protected risks; (2) no existing benchmark drives an agent across all its data surfaces under a single coherent privacy policy, representing the field's most critical missing instrument.

Conclusion: The survey provides a common reference and framing for scattered privacy literature on LLM agents. It identifies open problems, with particular urgency around developing both information-flow control mechanisms and comprehensive cross-surface privacy benchmarks under unified policies.

Abstract: Large language model agents increasingly query databases, search document collections, call external APIs, remember past interactions, and act on a user's behalf. As they move from answering questions to operating over sensitive data, privacy becomes harder to enforce. An agent touches many data sources, runs multi-step workflows, keeps state across sessions, and acts with delegated permissions. Sensitive information can therefore leak not only through its final answer but through the queries it issues, the intermediate results it handles, the memory it writes, and the messages it exchanges with other agents. We survey the privacy of LLM agents from a data-centric view, organizing the field around the data an agent touches rather than by attack type, and we use data agent as shorthand for an LLM agent that works with data. Research on these risks is active but scattered across retrieval-augmented generation, text-to-SQL interfaces, agent memory, prompt injection, access control, and contextual privacy. This survey brings that work together: we taxonomize the data sources an agent touches, the privacy risks each source creates, and the governance mechanisms that address them; we map the benchmarks used to measure these risks and identify what is missing; and we set out the open problems. Two findings recur: among governance mechanisms only information-flow control covers both compositional and cross-session inference leakage, the two least-protected risks; and no benchmark drives an agent across its data surfaces under one privacy policy, the instrument the field most lacks. Our goal is a reference that situates the scattered literature and gives future work a common framing.

</details>


### [213] [TGHE: Template-based Graph Homomorphic Encryption for Privacy-Preserving GNN Inference in Edge-Cloud Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26664)
*Ngoc Bao Anh Le,Thai T. Vu,John Le,Heath Cooper,Jun Shen*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: TGHE proposes an ego-centric framework for encrypted GNN inference that groups structurally identical ego-graphs ("templates") into shared CKKS ciphertexts, achieving 66.9x speedup over sequential baselines on a 3.7M-node financial graph with negligible accuracy loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing HE-based GNN systems use a graph-centric paradigm where per-query cost scales with global graph size, limiting scalability to ~20k nodes and preventing application to dynamic, large-scale financial transaction graphs (3.7M+ nodes).

Method: TGHE introduces an ego-centric paradigm exploiting the "template phenomenon": local computation trees in transaction graphs converge to a small set of structural shapes. It canonicalizes ego-graphs at the edge, packs structurally identical trees into shared CKKS ciphertexts for SIMD-parallel encrypted inference, and employs two optimizers — Approximate Template Fitting and Topology Collapse — to ensure full SIMD coverage across long-tail distributions.

Result: On the DGraphFin dataset (3.7M nodes, 4.3M edges), TGHE-Collapse achieves a 66.9x speedup over the sequential encrypted baseline with less than 0.002 AUC loss.

Conclusion: The template-based ego-centric approach decouples inference cost from global graph size, enabling practical encrypted GNN inference on large-scale financial graphs that were previously infeasible for HE-based methods.

Abstract: Existing homomorphic encryption (HE)-based GNN systems adopt a graph-centric paradigm that couples per-query cost to global graph size, limiting evaluations to at most ~20k nodes and making them incompatible with dynamic, large-scale financial graphs. We propose TGHE (Template-based Graph Homomorphic Encryption), an ego-centric framework that resolves this by exploiting a template phenomenon: local computation trees in transaction graphs converge into a small set of structural shapes. TGHE canonicalizes ego-graphs at the edge and packs structurally identical trees into shared CKKS ciphertexts for SIMD-parallel encrypted inference, with two long-tail optimizers (Approximate Template Fitting and Topology Collapse) ensuring full SIMD coverage. On DGraphFin (3.7M nodes, 4.3M edges), TGHE-Collapse achieves a 66.9x speedup over the sequential encrypted baseline with less than 0.002 AUC loss.

</details>


### [214] [The Fungible Reserve Standard: A Deterministic Framework for Encoding Carrying Costs in Asset-Backed Tokens](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26704)
*JJ Jia Jing Tan,Eva Meng,Josh Ng,Zack Zhang,September Liu,Teelet Wang,Ludwig Zhang,Seth Yan*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper proposes the Fungible Reserve Standard (FRS), an on-chain framework that transparently encodes the carrying costs (custody, insurance, audit) of real-world assets into a deterministic token design, using a declining asset-per-token variable q(t) with supply reconciliation to preserve ERC-20 composability without rebasing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RWA tokenization models handle structural negative carry (custody, insurance, audit costs) off-chain at the issuer level or via mechanisms like token rebasing, which break fungibility and DeFi composability. A transparent, on-chain method for encoding these costs is needed.

Method: The FRS framework defines an asset-per-token variable q(t) that decays deterministically at a predefined annualized carrying cost rate. A supply reconciliation mechanism preserves holder balances and ERC-20 composability, avoiding rebasing while transparently encoding operational costs on-chain.

Result: The paper presents a formal, asset-agnostic framework applicable to any real-world asset with positive, predictable holding costs, providing institutional-grade accounting clarity without compromising DeFi compatibility.

Conclusion: The FRS offers a deterministic, on-chain solution for transparently managing RWA carrying costs, bridging institutional accounting requirements with DeFi's fungibility and composability needs.

Abstract: The tokenization of real-world assets (RWAs) has emerged as a transformative application of blockchain technology, with market projections estimating trillions of dollars in tokenized assets within the coming decade. However, a fundamental challenge remains unaddressed: physical assets such as precious metals, stored commodities, and warehoused goods incur structural negative carry -- custody, insurance, and audit costs that accumulate over time. While existing tokenization models have successfully established the market for digital gold and treasuries, they typically manage operational costs at the issuer level. The FRS introduces a framework to bring these economics directly on-chain, avoiding mechanisms such as token rebasing that compromise fungibility and composability with decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols. This paper proposes the Fungible Reserve Standard (FRS), a deterministic token design framework that encodes carrying costs transparently into on-chain logic. The FRS introduces an asset-per-token variable q(t) that decreases according to a predefined annualized carrying cost rate, coupled with a supply reconciliation mechanism that preserves holder balances and ERC-20 composability. While mathematically inspired by the daily expense ratio accrual in traditional asset management -- which often embed centralized profit margins -- the FRS design specifically encodes actual operational carrying costs to provide pure institutional-grade accounting clarity without compromising DeFi compatibility. The framework is asset-agnostic and applicable to any real-world asset with positive, predictable holding costs.

</details>


### [215] [DroidBreaker: Practical and Functional Problem-Space Attacks on Machine-Learning Android Malware Detectors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26707)
*Christian Scano,Diego Soi,Angelo Sotgiu,Luca Demetrio,Davide Maiorca,Giorgio Giacinto,Fabio Roli,Battista Biggio*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: DROIDBREAKER is a practical, build-safe, semantics-preserving adversarial attack framework for Android malware detection that achieves high evasion rates with minimal side effects by manipulating only the most influential APK components and enforcing runtime equivalence through execution log comparison.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing problem-space adversarial attacks on Android malware detectors are impractical — they either introduce excessive side-effect features causing build failures, or are too narrow to be effective. Prior work also overestimates success by only testing installation and basic execution rather than verifying semantic preservation of intended app behavior.

Method: DROIDBREAKER introduces three key components: (i) query-efficient white- and black-box attacks targeting only the most influential APK components; (ii) fine-grained, build-safe manipulations (API call injection/obfuscation, module injection, permission/URL manipulation) with minimal side effects; and (iii) a semantics-preserving functionality test comparing execution logs and API-level traces between original and modified APKs.

Result: Evaluated on a recent Android application corpus, DROIDBREAKER achieved high evasion rates with few queries and minimal side effects in both white-box and black-box settings, and significantly reduced detection by commercial malware scanners on VirusTotal.

Conclusion: DROIDBREAKER represents the first practical, build-safe, and semantics-preserving problem-space attack framework for Android malware detection, overcoming the fundamental limitations of prior approaches and demonstrating real-world effectiveness against both ML-based detectors and commercial antivirus scanners.

Abstract: Adversarial APKs are Android applications modified in the problem space to evade machine-learning malware detectors. In this work, we first show that, despite claims, existing problem-space attacks remain largely impractical. Most techniques leverage software transplantation to inject entire benign modules, introducing many side-effect features and often causing build-time failures. Fine-grained methods that inject only a narrow subset of components exhibit limited effectiveness, while those that also use obfuscation rely on brittle bytecode rewriting, producing APKs that are syntactically valid but semantically unusable. Prior work further overestimates attack success rates by running smoke tests that only validate installation and basic execution, without assessing whether the modified APK still preserves its intended behavior. To overcome these limitations, we present DROIDBREAKER, a practical (build-safe) and functional (semantics-preserving) problem-space attack framework that provides: (i) query-efficient white- and black-box attacks by manipulating only the APK components most influential to the target model; (ii) a set of fine-grained, build-safe manipulations (including injection and obfuscation of API calls, app modules, permissions, and URLs) with minimal side effects; and (iii) a semantics-preserving functionality test that enforces runtime equivalence by comparing execution logs and API-level traces between the initial and the modified APK. Evaluated on a recent corpus of Android applications, DROIDBREAKER achieves high evasion rates with few queries and minimal side effects in both white-box and black-box settings, and drastically reduces detections by commercial malware scanners hosted on VirusTotal.

</details>


### [216] [MergeLLL: A Hierarchical Divide-and-Conquer Framework for LLL-Based Lattice Reduction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26784)
*Niharika Gauraha*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: MergeLLL is a divide-and-conquer lattice reduction algorithm that splits a lattice basis into sub-bases, reduces them independently, and merges them hierarchically with PotLLL-style deep insertions, achieving better Gram-Schmidt orthogonality, numerical stability, parallelism, and reduced computational cost compared to classical LLL.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Lattice basis reduction algorithms like LLL suffer from rapidly increasing complexity with dimension. The authors are motivated by the divide-and-conquer strategy of merge sort to design a parallelizable framework that reduces overall computational cost while improving basis quality.

Method: The basis is split into sub-bases, each reduced locally and independently. These are then recombined through hierarchical merging using PotLLL-style deep insertions. The process prioritizes local lattice structure improvement before global refinement, and all transformations are unimodular, preserving lattice structure. The method achieves logarithmic parallel depth.

Result: Experiments on subset-sum and NTRU-derived lattices show improvements over classical LLL: better Gram-Schmidt orthogonality, fewer expensive swap operations, and an improved Hermite factor, indicating higher-quality reduced bases.

Conclusion: MergeLLL effectively combines divide-and-conquer parallelism with deep insertion techniques to produce higher-quality reduced bases at lower computational cost, with natural scalability to multicore and distributed systems.

Abstract: Lattice basis reduction algorithms have various applications in computational number theory and lattice-based cryptography, but their complexity increases rapidly with the dimension. Motivated by the divide-and-conquer strategy of merge sort and incorporating PotLLL-style deep insertions during recombination, MergeLLL is proposed. In this framework, a lattice basis is split into sub-bases, local reductions are performed independently, and the full basis is reconstructed through hierarchical merging.
  The approach is focused on improving local lattice structure first before global basis properties are refined, resulting in enhanced Gram-Schmidt orthogonality and numerical stability, while overall computational cost is reduced. The method is naturally parallelizable, allowing efficient multicore and distributed execution. It is shown that the reduction and merging steps preserve the lattice structure through unimodular transformations and achieve logarithmic parallel depth. In experiments on subset-sum and NTRU-derived lattices, improvements over classical lattice reduction algorithms are demonstrated, including better orthogonality, a reduced number of expensive swap operations, and an improved Hermite factor, indicating higher-quality reduced bases.

</details>


### [217] [MIRROR: Novelty-Constrained Memory-Guided MCTS Red-Teaming for Agentic RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26793)
*Inderjeet Singh,Andrés Murillo,Motoyoshi Sekiya,Yuki Unno,Junichi Suga*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: MIRROR is a unified red-teaming framework for multimodal agentic RAG systems that uses memory-guided Monte Carlo tree search with a Novelty Gate to generate diverse attacks across text, image, direct-query, and orchestrator surfaces. It achieves high attack success rates with low variance, outperforming specialized baselines that fail on unfamiliar surfaces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing red-teaming approaches for multimodal agentic RAG are surface-specific and suffer from severe template recycling (73-84% exact duplication on text-poisoning benchmarks). This limits their effectiveness against the expanded attack surface of agentic RAG systems, which include text poisoning, image injection, direct-query attacks, and orchestrator manipulation. A unified cross-surface framework is needed.

Method: MIRROR employs memory-guided Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) conditioned on retrieved context with an explicit novelty constraint. A deterministic Novelty Gate rejects candidate attacks that match the retrieval set under normalized comparison, enabling retrieval to inform search priors without allowing prompt copying. This unified framework operates across four attack surfaces.

Result: MIRROR achieves 76% ASR on image poisoning (vs. 52% for baselines), 97% ASR on orchestrator attacks at half the query cost, and the lowest cross-surface variance (coefficient of variation 0.47). Specialized baselines collapse: suffix optimization reaches 79% ASR on text poisoning but only 1% on direct queries. ART-SafeBench is released with 41,815 in-package records and runtime adapters yielding 41,991+ total records.

Conclusion: A unified cross-surface red-teaming approach with novelty-constrained retrieval significantly outperforms surface-specific methods in both ASR and consistency. The framework and ART-SafeBench benchmark enable more robust evaluation of multimodal agentic RAG security.

Abstract: Multimodal agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems expand the attack surface beyond prompt injection to include text poisoning, image injection, direct-query attacks, and orchestrator-level tool manipulation. Existing red-teaming approaches are typically surface-specific and often recycle known attack templates; on text-poisoning benchmarks we measure 73-84% exact duplication. We present MIRROR, a unified cross-surface framework that performs memory-guided Monte Carlo tree search while conditioning candidate generation on retrieved context under an explicit novelty constraint. A deterministic Novelty Gate rejects any candidate matching the retrieval set under normalized comparison, allowing retrieval to inform search priors without enabling prompt copying. Across four attack surfaces on a multimodal agentic RAG target, MIRROR attains 76% ASR on image poisoning compared with 52% for baselines, 97% ASR on orchestrator attacks at half the query cost, and the lowest cross-surface variance (coefficient of variation 0.47). In contrast, specialized baselines collapse across surfaces: suffix optimization reaches 79% ASR on text poisoning but 1% on direct queries. We release ART-SafeBench with 41,815 in-package records and runtime adapters yielding 41,991+ total records across four surfaces.

</details>


### [218] [SpikeTimer: Exploring Active Copyright Protection in Spiking Neural Networks via Temporal Backdoor Regularization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26841)
*Xiao Yang,Gaolei Li,Jun Wu,Jianhua Li,Zhiquan Liu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: SpikeTimer is an active copyright protection framework for Spiking Neural Networks that uses temporal backdoor learning—embedding authorized tokens in specific timeslices so that the network responds correctly only to authorized data with correct temporal token placement, while producing erroneous outputs on unauthorized data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While DNN copyright protection has been extensively studied, SNN copyright protection remains underexplored due to the unique challenges of temporal coding and spike-driven computation in neuromorphic systems. With SNNs increasingly deployed in energy-efficient edge AI and robotics, protecting intellectual property becomes critical.

Method: SpikeTimer partitions neuromorphic data into designated timeslices and embeds authorized tokens exclusively within authorized slices. It establishes a time-dependent authorization mechanism where token validity is temporally bound. The framework natively supports multi-user authorization and tokens of arbitrary morphology. During inference, only inputs containing valid tokens in the correct timeslice trigger correct predictions; unauthorized inputs yield erroneous (≈10% accuracy) results.

Result: Evaluations on multiple neuromorphic datasets show: ~10% accuracy on unauthorized data (effectively dysfunctional), with only ~1.5% degradation on authorized inputs. SpikeTimer also demonstrates robust resistance against model finetuning and pruning attacks.

Conclusion: SpikeTimer provides the first effective active copyright protection framework tailored for SNNs, leveraging inherent temporal segmentation properties to enable a novel temporal backdoor-based authorization mechanism that is both precise and robust against adversarial removal attempts.

Abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNN) have emerged as a revolutionary paradigm compared to traditional Deep Neural Networks (DNN) in energy-efficient computing, showcasing exceptional capabilities in processing event-driven sensory data for real-time applications like robotics and edge AI systems. However, unlike extensive studies on DNN copyright solutions, SNN copyright protection remains largely underexplored due to their inherent temporal coding complexities and spike-driven computation. In this study, we propose a novel active copyright protection framework named SpikeTimer for SNNs via temporal backdoor learning. SpikeTimer partitions neuromorphic data into designated timeslices and exclusively embeds authorized tokens within authorized slices. Furthermore, the inherent temporal segmentation characteristic intrinsically enables SpikeTimer to support multi-user authorization mechanisms and accommodates token embedding of arbitrary morphology. Based on this, SpikeTimer precisely responds to authorized data containing a token within the correct timeslice, while producing erroneous responses to unauthorized data. Our key innovation lies in establishing a time-dependent authorization mechanism that protects the SNN copyright by temporal token validity. Additionally, SpikeTimer retains its defensive efficacy even under adversarial attempts. Evaluations on multiple neuromorphic datasets manifest that SpikeTimer achieves around 10% accuracy on unauthorized data with merely around 1.5% degradation on authorized inputs. Moreover, SpikeTimer demonstrates robust resistance against model finetuning and pruning threats.

</details>


### [219] [Fortress and Gatekeeper: Theorizing Transitive Trust in Third-Party Cybersecurity Risk Governance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26866)
*Yijun Chen,Misita Anwar*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper analyzes the OpenAI-Mixpanel security incident to theorize how third-party vendor relationships create cybersecurity governance challenges. It introduces the concepts of "transitive trust" and the "Fortress and Gatekeeper" framework, arguing that customer trust in a service provider is contingent on the security practices of its vendors. Four propositions are developed regarding vendor integration, metadata exposure, vendor assurance, and data proliferation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Digital service delivery increasingly depends on third-party vendors (analytics, cloud, identity, software supply chains), yet customers rarely have visibility into or control over these vendors' security practices. When a security incident occurs in a vendor environment, it becomes a governance and accountability problem for the focal organization. Existing cybersecurity governance literature lacks adequate frameworks for understanding how delegated data processing creates customer-facing accountability across organizational boundaries.

Method: The paper employs a document analysis of the November 2025 OpenAI-Mixpanel security incident as an illustrative case study. It draws on organizational trust research and agency theory as theoretical lenses to interpret the incident and develop conceptual frameworks.

Result: Two core conceptual contributions: (1) the concept of "transitive trust," where customer trust in a digital service depends on the security practices of vendors authorized by that service provider; and (2) the "Fortress and Gatekeeper" framework, which defines cybersecurity governance boundaries through trust and data flows rather than formal organizational ownership. Four propositions are derived: concerning vendor integration depth, metadata exposure risks, vendor assurance mechanisms, and data proliferation challenges.

Conclusion: Delegated data processing creates customer-facing accountability that existing governance models inadequately address. The paper offers implications for practice including vendor tiering, data classification, contractual design, continuous assurance, and data minimization strategies to manage transitive trust and fortify governance boundaries.

Abstract: Third-party vendors, such as analytics platforms, cloud services, identity providers, and software suppliers, are increasingly embedded in digital service delivery. While these arrangements enable scale and specialization, they also move customer data and security-relevant practices into environments that customers rarely see, select, or evaluate. This paper examines this problem through a document analysis of the November 2025 OpenAI-Mixpanel security incident. The incident serves as an illustrative case for showing how a security event in a vendor environment can become a governance and accountability problem for the focal organization that maintains the customer relationship. Drawing on organizational trust research and agency theory, the paper argues that third-party cybersecurity risk is both a trust relationship and a delegation problem. Customers trust the visible service provider, while the provider relies on vendors whose security practices are only partially visible and controllable. The paper develops the concept of transitive trust, where customer trust in a digital service depends on the security practices of vendors authorized by that service provider. It then presents the Fortress and Gatekeeper framework, which explains cybersecurity governance boundaries through trust and data flows rather than formal organizational ownership alone. The analysis develops four propositions concerning vendor integration, metadata exposure, vendor assurance, and data proliferation. The paper contributes to cybersecurity governance scholarship by explaining how delegated data processing creates customer-facing accountability and by identifying implications for vendor tiering, data classification, contractual design, continuous assurance, and data minimization.

</details>


### [220] [Chai: Agentic Discovery of Cryptographic Misuse Vulnerabilities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26933)
*Corban Villa,Sohee Kim,Austin Chu,Alon Shakevsky,Raluca Ada Popa*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Chai is an AI-driven system that discovers cryptographic misuse vulnerabilities by inverting the traditional approach: instead of auditing one codebase for many flaws, it catalogs vulnerabilities at the library level and propagates them across a cryptographic dependency graph using differential testing enhanced by AI. It identified over 100 vulnerabilities, including a critical flaw in an SSL library powering billions of devices.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI-assisted vulnerability discovery relies heavily on instrumentation (e.g., for memory safety bugs) to filter false positives, but many dangerous vulnerability classes like cryptographic misuse lack comparable instrumentation. The authors aim to fill this gap by finding a reliable signal for detecting and validating cryptographic misuse at scale without requiring runtime instrumentation.

Method: Chai combines AI with differential testing in two novel ways: (1) using AI to improve precision in detecting real security issues in cryptographic libraries, and (2) repurposing commonly overlooked discrepancies as leads for tangible vulnerabilities in downstream applications. The system catalogs flaws at the library level and propagates findings across a cryptographic dependency graph, achieving compounding efficiency gains. It targets X.509, JWT, and SAML libraries.

Result: Chai discovered a previously unknown critical vulnerability in an SSL library powering billions of devices, security bugs in a library used by a major web browser, and flaws in a library shipped in major Linux distributions. In total, over 100 vulnerabilities were surfaced.

Conclusion: Chai demonstrates that AI-enhanced differential testing, combined with dependency graph propagation, is a highly effective paradigm for discovering cryptographic misuse vulnerabilities at scale, achieving results that rival or exceed traditional instrumentation-dependent approaches without needing runtime instrumentation.

Abstract: AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has proven effective for bug classes like memory safety, where instrumentation confirms memory violations and efficiently filters false positives. Many dangerous vulnerability classes, such as cryptographic misuse, however, lack any comparable instrumentation. In this work, we present Chai, an AI-based system that discovers and validates cryptographic misuse vulnerabilities through naturally occurring signals. To achieve this, Chai rethinks the classical technique of differential testing by leveraging AI to 1) improve precision for detecting real security issues in libraries, and 2) repurpose commonly overlooked discrepancies as leads for tangible vulnerabilities in downstream applications. In doing so, Chai inverts the prevailing paradigm of AI vulnerability discovery: instead of auditing one codebase for many flaws, it catalogs flaws at the library level and propagates them across a cryptographic dependency graph, delivering compounding efficiency gains. We evaluate Chai across X.509, JWT, and SAML libraries. Chai discovered a previously unknown critical vulnerability in an SSL library that powers billions of devices, along with security bugs in one library behind a major web browser and another in major Linux distributions. In total, these techniques surfaced over 100 vulnerabilities.

</details>


### [221] [Jailbreaking for the Average Jane: Choosing Optimal Jailbreaks via Bandit Algorithms for Automatically Enhanced Queries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26936)
*Prarabdh Shukla,Ritik,Suhas Rao,Arpit Agarwal,Arjun Bhagoji*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A bandit-based jailbreak attack achieves up to 97% success rate on 15 open-weight LLMs, and adding complexity to malicious queries further boosts success by up to 26%, confirming that non-expert actors can elicit actionable harmful responses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The proliferation of LLM jailbreaks raises concern that non-expert malicious actors ("the average Jane") could successfully elicit harmful responses. The authors investigate whether this concern is justified by examining the two ingredients needed: an effective jailbreak and an effective malicious query.
