Method: (1) A novel multi-armed bandit-based attack strategy that efficiently learns the optimal jailbreak from a large choice set through noisy exploration on few queries, then exploits the learned policy. (2) FrankensteinBench, a curated safety benchmark of 11,279 malicious queries drawn from 7 existing benchmarks with automated enhancement, categorized by technical expertise required (simple vs. complex).

Result: The bandit-based attack achieves up to 97% average success rate across 15 state-of-the-art open-weight LLMs. Adding complexity to queries increases attack success rate by up to 26% on average across models, demonstrating that query complexity is an effective and automatable prompting strategy.

Conclusion: The concern is confirmed: non-expert malicious actors can successfully jailbreak LLMs using the proposed bandit attack combined with complex queries. This highlights significant safety vulnerabilities in current open-weight LLMs.

Abstract: With a profusion of jailbreaks for LLMs now widely known, a growing concern is that non-expert malicious actors ("the average Jane") could elicit actionable responses to malicious requests. In this work, we examine whether this concern is justified. A non-expert malicious actor requires two ingredients for a successful attack: a powerful jailbreak for their target model, acting on an effective malicious query. For the former, we propose a novel attack strategy based on the multi-armed bandit framework. This allows efficient online learning of the optimal jailbreak from a large choice set via noisy exploration on a small number of queries, with subsequent application of the learnt policy on an exploitation set. For the latter, we curate $\mathrm{FrankensteinBench}$, a safety benchmark of $11,279$ malicious queries drawn from manual curation over $7$ existing benchmarks, along with automated enhancement and generation. Each query is categorized as simple or complex by the technical expertise required to craft it. Our findings confirm the concern. Our bandit-based attack achieves success rates as high as $97\%$ on average over $15$ SoTA open-weight LLMs. Moreover, adding complexity to queries raises the attack success rate by up to $26\%$ on average across models -- making it an effective, automatable prompting strategy.

</details>


### [222] [Protocol Prying: Systematic Vulnerability Research in the Apple AirDrop and Android Quick Share Proximity Transfer Protocols](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26967)
*Arash Ale Ebrahim,Nils Ole Tippenhauer*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: First cross-platform reverse engineering and fuzzing study of Apple AirDrop and Google/Samsung Quick Share, uncovering six vulnerabilities (V1-V6) across macOS/iOS, Android, and Windows, including pre-authentication DoS, protocol-layer encryption bypass, and a heap use-after-free.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite being deployed on over five billion devices, AirDrop and Quick Share's application-layer security properties are unstudied due to proprietary, undocumented stacks. Their reachability from wireless proximity without prior pairing and processing of complex serialized content in privileged daemons makes them attractive zero-click attack surfaces.

Method: The authors perform cross-platform reverse engineering of both protocol stacks, reconstruct AirDrop's seven-layer state machine and DVZip adaptive compression from binary analysis, build AIRFUZZ (a protocol-aware fuzzer mutating pre-compression representations), and conduct targeted hand-written analyses of Samsung Quick Share and Google Quick Share for Windows.

Result: Six vulnerabilities discovered: V1 (Swift fatalError DoS in HTTP path router), V2 (unbounded XML plist recursion in Foundation), V3 (NULL dereference in Network.framework HTTP/1.1 parser) — all pre-authentication in macOS/iOS AirDrop; V4 (pre-auth OfflineFrame dispatch) and V5 (D2D encryption bypass for three frame types) in Samsung Quick Share; V6 (heap use-after-free) in Google Quick Share for Windows, which earned a bounty. All vendors acknowledged the reports.

Conclusion: Proximity file-transfer protocols in major consumer OSes harbor significant, reachable pre-authentication vulnerabilities due to complex, undocumented protocol stacks processing untrusted input in privileged contexts. Protocol-aware fuzzing combined with reverse engineering is effective at surfacing these flaws.

Abstract: Apple AirDrop and Google/Samsung Quick Share are proximity file-transfer protocols used by over five billion devices, yet their application-layer security properties remain largely unstudied because both stacks are proprietary and undocumented. Both protocols are reachable from wireless proximity without any prior pairing and process complex serialized content (binary plists, CPIO archives, Protocol Buffers, UKEY2 handshakes) inside privileged daemons, making them attractive zero-click targets across multiple operating systems. We perform the first cross-platform reverse engineering and protocol-aware fuzzing study of both stacks. We reconstruct AirDrop's seven-layer state machine and DVZip adaptive compression from binary analysis, build AIRFUZZ, a protocol-aware fuzzer that mutates pre-compression representations, and complement it with targeted hand-written analyses of Samsung's Quick Share service and Google's Quick Share for Windows. We discover six vulnerabilities (V1-V6): three pre-authentication issues in macOS/iOS AirDrop (V1: Swift fatalError DoS in the HTTP path router; V2: unbounded XML plist recursion in Foundation; V3: NULL dereference in Network.framework's HTTP/1.1 parser), two protocol-layer flaws in Samsung Quick Share (V4: pre-authentication OfflineFrame dispatch; V5: D2D encryption bypass for three frame types), and a heap use-after-free in Google Quick Share for Windows (V6) for which Google awarded a bounty. We responsibly disclosed all findings, and Apple, Samsung, and Google have acknowledged the reports.

</details>


### [223] [ShareLock: A Stealthy Multi-Tool Threshold Poisoning Attack Against MCP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27027)
*Liwei Liu,Tianzhu Han,Zijian Liu,Zishu Dong,Na Ruan*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: ShareLock is a multi-tool threshold poisoning framework that uses Shamir's secret sharing to hide malicious instructions across multiple MCP tool descriptions, achieving over 90% attack success rate while evading detection better than single-tool poisoning methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing MCP tool poisoning attacks use monolithic plaintext embedding, making them easily detectable by manual inspection or automated detectors. There is no systematic analysis of multi-tool cooperative poisoning, where distributing malicious payloads across multiple tools can disperse detection risk and improve stealth.

Method: ShareLock employs Shamir's threshold secret sharing scheme to split a malicious instruction into multiple benign-looking secret shares, each embedded in a different MCP tool description. A covert reconstruction trigger is planted during server updates, and once enough shares are aggregated (meeting the threshold), the hidden instruction is reconstructed, enabling attacks like data exfiltration or system compromise. The framework provides information-theoretic secrecy and fault tolerance against partial auditing.

Result: The authors constructed a benchmark with four multi-tool scenarios and tested across mainstream LLMs on two distinct MCP clients. ShareLock significantly outperformed existing single-tool poisoning strategies in tool description-based detection while maintaining an average attack success rate exceeding 90%.

Conclusion: ShareLock demonstrates that multi-tool threshold poisoning poses a realistic and severe threat to MCP-based agent ecosystems, highlighting the urgent need for more robust defenses against distributed, stealthy poisoning attacks that leverage cryptographic techniques to evade current detection mechanisms.

Abstract: With the rapid evolution of LLM-driven agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open protocol bridging LLMs with external tools, has quickly become foundational to modern agent ecosystems. However, the expanding adoption of MCP has also introduced novel security concerns such as Tool Poisoning Attack (TPA), which exploit LLM-server interactions to inject malicious prompts. Existing poisoning schemes typically adopt a monolithic plaintext embedding paradigm, which fails to withstand manual inspection or automated detectors. Current research still lacks a systematic analysis on multi-tool poisoning, where multiple tools can be exploited cooperatively to disperse detection risk. In this paper, we introduce ShareLock, a multi-tool threshold poisoning framework that utilizes Shamir's threshold scheme to ensure exceptional stealth and fault tolerance. ShareLock distributes the malicious instruction as benign-looking secret shares across multiple tool descriptions, achieving both information-theoretic secrecy and attack robustness against moderate auditing. After a covert reconstruction trigger is planted during server update, the aggregated shares reconstruct the hidden instruction, resulting in critical breaches of system assets or private data. To evaluate the realistic threat of ShareLock, we constructed a comprehensive benchmark encompassing four multi-tool scenarios and conducted extensive experiments across mainstream LLMs on two distinct MCP clients. Our results demonstrate that ShareLock significantly outperforms existing single-tool poisoning strategies in tool description-based detection while maintaining an average attack success rate exceeding 90%.

</details>


### [224] [Design and Performance Evaluation of Secure RF and WiFi-Based Communication in Drone Swarms via Testbed Implementation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27028)
*Bhavya Dixit,Aayushi Rajgor,Subham Kumar,Rushikesh Patil,Ananthapadmanabhan A.,Gaurav S. Kasbekar,Arnab Maity*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: MAVShield, a lightweight encryption framework for MAVLink, is integrated and flight-tested on a four-UAV swarm over RF/WiFi, enabling secure autonomous formation control and collision avoidance via a modified geodetic APF algorithm, demonstrating performance comparable to unencrypted communication while outperforming AES-CTR, Speck-CTR, ChaCha20, and Rabbit in overall efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: UAV swarms depend on distributed coordination over RF/WiFi, but the MAVLink protocol lacks built-in encryption, making telemetry vulnerable to eavesdropping. Existing standard ciphers may impose excessive overhead on resource-constrained UAVs, motivating the need for a lightweight, flight-validated encryption solution.

Method: The authors integrate five encryption schemes (MAVShield, AES-CTR, Speck-CTR, ChaCha20, Rabbit) into four custom-built UAVs communicating over RF and WiFi. A modified artificial potential field (APF) algorithm operating directly in geodetic coordinates (eliminating Cartesian transformations) is developed for collision avoidance. Performance is evaluated via flight experiments measuring CPU utilization, memory consumption, and packet delivery ratio (PDR), while security is assessed through algebraic cryptanalysis and Wireshark-based traffic analysis.

Result: MAVShield achieves performance comparable to unencrypted communication and surpasses AES-CTR, Speck-CTR, ChaCha20, and Rabbit in overall efficiency. The encrypted telemetry successfully supports autonomous formation control and collision avoidance. MAVShield resists key-recovery attacks and protects telemetry confidentiality against traffic analysis.

Conclusion: MAVShield is an efficient and secure solution for UAV swarm communication, validated through real-world flight experiments on a multi-UAV testbed, with strong resistance to cryptanalytic attacks.

Abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms rely on distributed coordination and cooperative communication to support scalable operations, extended coverage, and applications such as surveillance and real-time data exchange. Wireless technologies such as radio frequency (RF) and WiFi are widely used for UAV-to-UAV and UAV-to-ground control station (GCS) communication but introduce significant security challenges. MAVLink, the predominant communication protocol in UAV systems, provides message integrity and authentication but lacks built-in encryption, leaving telemetry traffic vulnerable to eavesdropping. In our previous work, we proposed MAVShield, a lightweight encryption framework for MAVLink communications. In this paper, MAVShield, AES-CTR, Speck-CTR, ChaCha20, and Rabbit are integrated into four custom-built UAVs to establish secure communication links over RF and WiFi channels. Their performance is evaluated through flight experiments using a UAV swarm testbed. Encrypted telemetry data enable autonomous formation control and collision avoidance during flight. For collision avoidance, we develop a modified artificial potential field (APF) algorithm that computes attractive and repulsive forces directly in geodetic coordinates, eliminating Cartesian transformations and reducing trajectory oscillations while avoiding local-minimum trapping. CPU utilization, memory consumption, and packet delivery ratio (PDR) are measured for each encryption scheme. Results show that MAVShield achieves performance comparable to unencrypted communication while outperforming AES-CTR, Speck-CTR, ChaCha20, and Rabbit in overall efficiency. Algebraic cryptanalysis and Wireshark-based traffic analysis demonstrate resistance to key-recovery attacks and protection of telemetry confidentiality. The results indicate that MAVShield is an efficient and secure solution for UAV swarm communication.

</details>


### [225] [Physical Layer Authentication With Channel Knowledge Maps in Indoor Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27044)
*Luca Bonaventura,Francesco Ardizzon,Stefano Tomasin*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A physical layer authentication method for moving indoor devices using multiple APs to estimate path loss and angle of arrival, which are compared against pre-collected channel knowledge maps of the device's vicinity rather than relying on temporal consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional PLA assumes time-consistent channel measurements or predictable evolution, assumptions that break down with mobile devices in multipath-rich indoor environments. A robust authentication mechanism is needed for these challenging conditions.

Method: Multiple APs estimate dominant tap path loss and angle of arrival from received signals. These measurements are authenticated by comparing them against previously constructed channel knowledge maps (CKMs), specifically within the spatial neighborhood of the device's last known position. Security is evaluated under random and optimal attack models using ray-tracing-based CKM in a representative indoor scenario.

Result: Numerical simulations using ray-traced CKM data in a representative indoor environment demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed PLA approach. The security analysis confirms robustness under both random and optimal attack strategies.

Conclusion: Comparing real-time PL and AoA measurements against spatially localized CKM data provides a viable and secure PLA mechanism for moving indoor devices, overcoming the limitations of temporal-consistency-based methods.

Abstract: Physical layer authentication (PLA) allows to authenticate the user by comparing measurements over time, assuming their time consistency or by modeling their evolution. However, these assumptions become problematic when devices are in motion and in indoor environments due to multipath propagation and obstructions. In this paper, we propose a PLA mechanism for moving devices in indoor environments, where multiple access points (APs) estimate the dominant channel tap path loss (PL) and angle of arrival (AoA) from the received signals and compare them with previously collected channel knowledge maps (CKMs). Specifically, the measurements are compared to those in the neighborhood of the previously known position obtained from CKMs. A comprehensive security analysis is conducted under both random and optimal attacks. Numerical results in a representative indoor scenario, with CKM obtained via ray tracing, validate the effectiveness of the proposed PLA approach.

</details>


### [226] [Type-based information flow analysis for $π$-calculus with a dynamically extensible security lattice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27059)
*Yukihiro Oda,Eijiro Sumii*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A type system is developed that allows dynamic creation and insertion of security levels into a security lattice during execution, extending Kobayashi's pi-calculus-based secure information flow analysis from a static two-point lattice to a dynamic, extensible lattice.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing secure information flow type systems, such as Kobayashi's for the pi-calculus, rely on a fixed, static security lattice (often just High/Low). This restricts the ability of systems to adapt security policies at runtime. The work is motivated by the need for more flexible security models where new security levels can be introduced dynamically during execution, enabling richer and more realistic information flow control in concurrent and distributed settings.

Method: The authors extend Kobayashi's type-based secure information flow analysis for Milner's pi-calculus. The formalization involves generalizing from a simple 2-element lattice to an extensible lattice structure where new security levels can be created and inserted dynamically. This requires careful treatment of lattice extension operations and the adaptation of the type system and bisimulation-based non-interference proofs to accommodate a dynamic lattice, all within the pi-calculus framework with its reduction semantics and bisimulation equivalence.

Result: A formal type system for dynamic security lattice extension in the pi-calculus is achieved, preserving the expressive power of the original model (supporting sequential and concurrent computation, concise syntax, reduction semantics, and bisimulation-based secrecy as non-interference) while enabling runtime creation of new security levels.

Conclusion: The proposed extension successfully demonstrates that dynamic security lattice construction is formally viable within a highly expressive process calculus framework. This advances secure information flow analysis by relaxing the static-lattice assumption, opening possibilities for adaptive security policies in concurrent systems.

Abstract: We develop a type system for secure information flow where new security levels can be created and inserted into the security lattice dynamically, i.e., even in the middle of an execution of a system. Our system is formalized by extending Kobayashi's type-based secure information flow analysis for Milner's pi-calculus, which is one of the most expressive models (or "languages") supporting both sequential and concurrent computations, with concise syntax, reduction-based semantics, and bisimulation equivalence as a robust formalization of secrecy as non-interference. The development required careful treatment of extensions of lattices themselves as well as deliberate generalization from the simple 2-element lattice (consisting of only High and Low) in the original system.

</details>


### [227] [Inherited Circuits, Learned Semantics: How Fine-Tuning Creates Evasion Vulnerabilities Invisible to Standard Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27091)
*Ryan Fetterman*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Security fine-tuning of LLMs can introduce brittle token-level shortcuts that preserve benchmark accuracy but fail under simple obfuscation transformations (e.g., PowerShell alias substitution, case mutation). The authors trace these vulnerabilities to inherited attention circuits from the base model, which fine-tuning specializes rather than creates, and propose lightweight monitoring methods to detect semantic drift pre-deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluation of security-classifier LLMs relies on held-out examples from the same distribution as training data. This fails to detect vulnerabilities introduced by fine-tuning itself—specifically, models may learn superficial token-level indicator semantics that appear robust on canonical test sets but collapse under behavior-preserving transformations common in adversarial contexts (e.g., obfuscated PowerShell commands).

Method: The authors study Foundation-Sec-8B-Instruct (fine-tuned on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) using matched PowerShell classification cohorts. They apply causal intervention (activation patching) to localize the classification circuit, identifying a late-attention route inherited from the base model rather than created by fine-tuning. They construct a three-tier evasion benchmark spanning iwr substitution, Invoke-Expression reconstruction, execution indirection, string construction, and case mutation. They also develop two monitoring methods: (1) a linear probe at the classification boundary and (2) an indicator-token sign test to identify command families where canonical indicators shift role after fine-tuning.

Result: Fine-tuning concentrates and semantically specializes inherited base-model structure rather than creating new circuits. Foundation-Sec fails on iwr substitution, Invoke-Expression reconstruction, and case-mutated IEX variants that Llama does not share. The linear probe and indicator-token sign test successfully identify commands where canonical indicators change role after fine-tuning, enabling prioritization of red-team variant generation using only canonical inputs. Security fine-tuning thus improves task accuracy while paradoxically expanding the evasion surface.

Conclusion: Small task-specific fine-tunes should not be treated as straightforwardly safer security classifiers. Specialization can convert inherited model structure into brittle indicator rules that preserve held-out accuracy while expanding the evasion surface. Robust AI-enabled security requires specifying the full transformation space of the task and monitoring semantic drift through fine-tuning.

Abstract: LLMs fine-tuned for security classification are usually evaluated on held-out examples from the same distribution as their training data. We show that this can miss vulnerabilities introduced by fine-tuning itself: models can learn token-level indicator semantics that preserve canonical accuracy while failing under behavior-preserving transformations such as PowerShell alias substitution, command reconstruction, string construction, execution indirection, and case mutation. We study Foundation-Sec-8B-Instruct and its base model, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, on matched PowerShell classification cohorts. Causal interventions localize the classification circuit to a late-attention route inherited from Llama rather than created by fine-tuning. Fine-tuning concentrates and semantically specializes this inherited structure, improving baseline behavior while creating transformation-sensitive attack surfaces. A three-tier evasion benchmark finds Foundation-Sec misses on iwr substitution, Invoke-Expression reconstruction, and case-mutated Invoke-Expression/IEX variants that Llama does not share. We also derive a pre-deployment monitoring method: a linear probe at the classification boundary and an indicator-token sign test identify command families where canonical indicators change role after fine-tuning. These signals prioritize red-team variant generation using only canonical inputs, showing that security fine-tuning can improve task accuracy while expanding the evasion surface. These results caution against treating small task-specific fine-tunes as straightforwardly safer security classifiers: specialization can convert inherited model structure into brittle indicator rules that preserve held-out accuracy while expanding the evasion surface. Robust AI-enabled security will require specifying the full transformation space of the task and monitoring semantic drift through fine-tuning.

</details>


### [228] [zQR: A Verifiable QR-Driven zkSNARK Proof Verification Framework for Mobile Platforms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27092)
*Goshgar Can Ismayilov*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper proposes zQR, a framework that combines zero-knowledge proofs (zkSNARKs) with QR codes, blockchain, and large language models to enable off-line privacy-preserving verification on mobile platforms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite privacy being a fundamental right, adoption of privacy-preserving technologies remains limited due to technical complexity. Zero-knowledge proofs offer strong privacy guarantees but are hindered by usability barriers in daily interactions.

Method: The authors develop zQR, a QR-driven zkSNARK proof verification framework for mobile platforms that integrates: (1) verifiable QR codes encoding zkSNARK proofs for off-line verification, (2) blockchain for auditability, non-repudiation, and logging, and (3) large language models for automatic circuit generation. A security analysis across multiple attack surfaces is conducted, followed by experimental evaluation of temporal and financial costs.

Result: Experimental results demonstrate feasibility: proofs can be compactly represented using QR code symbol version 19 with low error correction level. The paper quantifies proof generation/verification latency, QR encoding/decoding latency, and blockchain gas consumption costs.

Conclusion: zQR is a viable proof-of-concept for privacy-preserving verification on mobile platforms. The authors identify potential applications, current limitations, and future directions to promote broader adoption of privacy-preserving technologies in everyday use.

Abstract: Privacy is one of the fundamental rights of individuals in modern societies. Yet, the practical adoption of privacy-preserving technologies in daily interactions remains limited. Zero-knowledge proofs offer strong privacy guarantees but are often hindered by their technical complexity. In this paper, we advance the idea of verifiable QR codes that enable off-line verifiers to verify proofs encoded in QR codes. Based on this core idea, we build a novel QR-driven zkSNARK proof verification framework (i.e., zQR) for mobile platforms. The framework integrates blockchain for auditability, non-repudiation and logging; and large-language models for automatic circuit generation. We perform a security discussion of the framework by considering multiple attack surfaces. Furthermore, we present an experimental evaluation measuring temporal costs (proof generation and verification latency, QR code encoding and decoding latency) and financial costs (blockchain gas consumption). Our results demonstrate the feasibility of zQR as a proof-of-concept framework for privacy-preserving verification on mobile platform where proofs are compactly represented with QR code symbol version of 19 with low error correction level. Finally, we discuss potential applications, current limitations and future directions for the broader adoption of privacy-preserving technologies in daily interactions.

</details>


### [229] [Application of LLMs to Threat Assessment of Foreign Peacekeeping Missions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27106)
*Gerhard Backfried,Christian Schmidt,Diego Pilutti,Michael Suker*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A novel LLM-based workflow for threat assessment in peacekeeping missions, combining OSINT media collection with risk modeling, demonstrates high agreement with human judgment on threat and mission relevance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Peacekeeping missions require continuous threat monitoring from open-source intelligence (OSINT), but manual analysis of large volumes of media content is labor-intensive and slow. There is a need for automated tools that can extract mission-relevant threats from unstructured text while maintaining accuracy comparable to human analysts.

Method: The authors integrate an interdisciplinary risk model with OSINT-based media collection within the PINPOINT project framework (applied to the EU Monitoring Mission in Georgia). The workflow: (1) maps media contents to mission-relevant threat categories using LLMs, (2) extracts structured threat information, and (3) applies additional LLM-based processing steps to improve relevance and grounding of the extracted threats.

Result: Evaluation shows high inter-rater agreement between LLM-generated threat extraction and human judgment, particularly for core dimensions such as threat identification and mission relevance assessment.

Conclusion: LLMs offer a promising approach to augment and support human analysts in peacekeeping threat assessment, potentially reducing workload while maintaining analytical quality.

Abstract: We present a novel approach for applying Large Language Models (LLMs) to threat assessment in the context of foreign peacekeeping missions. Building on the PINPOINT project and its use case, the EU Monitoring Mission in Georgia, we combine an interdisciplinary risk-model with OSINT-based media collection and LLM-supported threat extraction. The proposed workflow maps media contents to mission-relevant threats, extracts structured information and applies several additional LLM-based processing steps to improve relevance and grounding. An evaluation of threats extracted from media documents shows high agreement between automatically generated results and human judgment for core aspects such as threat and mission relevance. These results indicate that LLMs provide a promising approach to support analysts in the context of peacekeeping missions.

</details>


### [230] [PRISM: PE Relational Inter-Section Matrix. A 2D Section-Aware Dataset for Static PE Malware Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27109)
*José M. Sacristán,Ana I. González-Tablas*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: PRISM introduces a 2D matrix representation of PE files that preserves per-section positional structure, achieving comparable malware detection to EMBER at one-sixth the dimensionality, with the structural content reserved for higher-ceiling tasks like family classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing malware detection benchmarks (EMBER, BODMAS, SOREL-20M) flatten PE files into 1D feature vectors, discarding section ordering and inter-section relational context that may carry discriminative information for tasks beyond binary detection.

Method: PRISM encodes each PE binary as a 2D matrix where rows correspond to individual PE sections in file order, plus a global summary row preserving EMBER compatibility. The corpus combines four malware sources with SOREL-20M benign samples (83,633 deduplicated matrices). Formal separability analysis uses Fisher Discriminant Ratio, mutual information, and inter-section information gain. A strictly controlled, sample-matched comparison evaluates gradient-boosted classifiers on PRISM vs. EMBER representations.

Result: The per-section positional structure carries discriminative information beyond flat representations. PRISM achieves nearly identical binary detection to EMBER at ~1/6 dimensionality, with EMBER holding only a small edge in the extreme low-FPR regime. The binary detection task is declared saturated; structural advantages are reserved for family classification and 2D-capable architectures.

Conclusion: PRISM demonstrates that section-level relational structure is informative and can be compactly represented in 2D, enabling future work on malware family classification and deep architectures that exploit matrix structure. The dataset and tooling are open-sourced under CC BY-NC-SA and MIT licenses.

Abstract: We introduce PRISM (PE Relational Inter-Section Matrix), an open dataset and feature representation for static Windows PE malware detection. Existing benchmarks such as EMBER, BODMAS, and SOREL-20M represent each PE file as a flat one-dimensional feature vector, discarding the ordering of sections and the relational context between them. PRISM instead encodes every binary as a two-dimensional matrix whose rows are individual PE sections in file order, with a global summary row that preserves compatibility with EMBER-style models. We build the corpus from four malware sources (BODMAS, MalwareBazaar, VirusShare, and CAPE) together with SOREL-20M benign software, yielding 83,633 deduplicated matrices and a family-filtered analysis corpus of 49,204 samples across 684 malware families.
  A formal separability analysis (Fisher Discriminant Ratio, mutual information, and inter-section information gain) shows that the per-section positional structure carries discriminative information that flat representations cannot capture. Under a strictly controlled, sample-matched comparison, a gradient-boosted classifier on the compact PRISM representation recovers nearly all of the binary-detection performance of the same classifier on the much larger EMBER vector, at roughly one-sixth the dimensionality; EMBER retains only a small, consistent advantage confined to the extreme low-false-positive regime, the two being operationally indistinguishable at the decision threshold. We are explicit that this binary task is saturated, so the structural content PRISM preserves is reserved for tasks with greater metric headroom, such as family classification and architectures that exploit the 2D structure directly. The dataset, extraction library, trained models, and full analysis pipeline are released under CC BY-NC-SA and MIT licences.

</details>


### [231] [The Observer World: A Cryptographic Extension of Impagliazzo's Five Worlds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27139)
*Fabio F. G. Buono*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper introduces a second, orthogonal "observational axis" to Impagliazzo's five worlds framework, formalizing what observers can see via an observer hierarchy. It proves that P^O_prof = NP^O_prof ⊂ P holds unconditionally across all five worlds, demonstrating that observational blindness and computational hardness are independent phenomena, and extends the framework to physical information bounds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Impagliazzo's five worlds implicitly assume a full-input observer (O_top) for all parties, including adversaries. This assumption is never stated. The authors make it explicit and argue that relaxing it reveals structural phenomena—such as collapses invisible to the original framework—and enables reasoning about limited observers, partial information, and physical constraints on observation.

Method: The paper introduces an orthogonal "observational axis" based on a previously established observer hierarchy. It formalizes the Observer World W_O, classifies all world-observer pairs into labeled cells, defines a parametric family W_O^ε for partial violations of observational invariants, and proves unconditionally (across all five worlds) that P^{O_prof} = NP^{O_prof} ⊂ P. The framework also interfaces with physical bounds (thermodynamic, quantum, cosmological).

Result: The central result is the unconditional collapse P^{O_prof} = NP^{O_prof} ⊂ P, which holds in all five of Impagliazzo's worlds. This demonstrates that observational blindness is independent of computational hardness. Additionally, the paper classifies world-observer pairs, identifies labeled cells (a)–(d), and constructs W_O^ε to model partial observational violations.

Conclusion: Observational limitations constitute an axis independent of computational hardness. The enriched two-axis framework captures phenomena (like the P^O_prof/NP^O_prof collapse) that Impagliazzo's original single-axis classification cannot express. The framework extends naturally to physical information limits, suggesting a unified treatment of computational and observational constraints.

Abstract: Impagliazzo's five worlds classify computational assumptions along a single axis, the existence of cryptographic primitives. All five worlds implicitly assume that every party, including the adversary, observes the full input, that the observer is always $O_{top}$. This assumption is so natural that it is never stated. This work makes it explicit and relaxes it by introducing a second, orthogonal axis, the observational axis, defined by the observer hierarchy introduced in previous work. Relaxing the assumption reveals structural phenomena, such as the collapse $P^{O_{prof}} = NP^{O_{prof}} \subset P$, that the five-world framework cannot express. We prove that this collapse holds unconditionally in all five worlds, showing that observational blindness and computational hardness are independent. We define the Observer World $W_O$, classify all world-observer pairs, identify the labeled cells (a)--(d), and introduce a parametric family $W_O^{\varepsilon}$ modelling partial violations of observational invariants. The framework also interfaces with physical information limits, including thermodynamic, quantum, and cosmological bounds.

</details>


### [232] [Tilikum: Transaction Fair Ordering on a DAG without Weak Edges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27250)
*Giulio Segalini,Yigit Çolakoğlu,Marko Putnik,Jérémie Decouchant*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Tilikum is a DAG-based ledger protocol that guarantees fair transaction ordering using median-based timestamp aggregation, achieving up to 39× higher throughput than fair-ordering baselines while blocking DAG-specific reordering attacks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While fair ordering has been extensively studied for linear blockchains (e.g., Ethereum), DAG-based consensus protocols—increasingly adopted for scalability—lack protection against transaction reordering attacks and BEV extraction. Existing DAG protocols either rely on weak edges with insufficient fairness guarantees or impose prohibitive performance overhead.

Method: Tilikum introduces (1) median-based timestamp aggregation to establish a global consensus ordering without relying on weak edges, achieving ordering linearizability or batch order fairness; (2) low data redundancy through efficient DAG structure design; and (3) robust garbage collection. The protocol is implemented in Rust and benchmarked against Narwhal/Tusk, Pompē, Themis, and FairDAG.

Result: Tilikum achieves up to 39× higher throughput compared to other fair-ordering baselines (Narwhal/Tusk, Pompē, Themis, FairDAG) while fully blocking state-of-the-art DAG-specific reordering attacks.

Conclusion: Tilikum demonstrates that fair transaction ordering can be achieved in DAG-based consensus protocols without sacrificing throughput, offering a practical defense against BEV extraction in high-performance decentralized ledgers.

Abstract: Decentralized Finance (DeFi) applications rely heavily on the order in which transactions are executed, making them susceptible to reordering attacks that enable adversaries to extract Blockchain Extractable Value (BEV). While linear blockchain systems such as Ethereum have inspired extensive research into fair ordering mechanisms, DAG-based consensus protocols have remained largely unprotected despite their growing adoption for scalability and performance. In this paper, we introduce Tilikum, a DAG-based ledger protocol that ensures fair transaction ordering without relying on weak edges. Tilikum achieves ordering linearizability by leveraging median-based timestamp aggregation, or batch order fairness, while maintaining low data redundancy and robust garbage collection. We implemented Tilikum in Rust and evaluated it against representative baselines, namely Narwhal/Tusk, Pompē, Themis and FairDAG. Our results show that Tilikum achieves up to $39\times$ higher throughput than other fair-ordering baselines, while fully blocking state-of-the-art DAG-specific reordering attacks.

</details>

# cs.HC [[Back]](#toc)

### [233] [Having Dog Ears "for Real": Effects of Active and Passive Haptics on Embodying Non-Human Body Parts in VR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26364)
*Omar A. Khan,Bao Han Trinh,Lee Lisle,Tiffany D. Do*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A survey (n=63) identified animal ears as commonly embodied non-human body parts in VR. A 2×2 within-subjects study (n=28) compared active (vibrotactile gloves) and passive (physical headband) haptic feedback on Sense of Embodiment (SoE) when touching virtual dog ears. Passive haptics alone produced the strongest embodiment; combining modalities reduced these benefits. Non-human body part SoE positively correlated with full-avatar SoE.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Non-human body part embodiment in VR is a meaningful creative practice in certain subcultures, yet morphological discrepancy between real and virtual bodies can diminish Sense of Embodiment. While haptic feedback may compensate, no prior work has systematically compared different haptic modalities and their combinations in this context.

Method: First, an online survey (n=63) with social VR communities established animal ears as an ecologically valid non-human body part. Then, a 2×2 within-subjects experiment (n=28) manipulated two independent variables: active haptics (vibrotactile gloves) and passive haptics (physical headband), applied when participants reached up to touch virtual dog ears on their avatar.

Result: (1) Passive haptics yielded the strongest overall embodiment outcomes. (2) Combining active and passive haptics reduced the benefits of passive haptics alone. (3) Sense of Embodiment towards non-human body parts positively correlated with SoE towards the entire avatar.

Conclusion: Passive haptic feedback is more effective than active or combined modalities for enhancing embodiment of non-human body parts in VR. The additive assumption of haptic modalities does not hold; combining them can be detrimental. Embodiment of specific non-human body parts is linked to overall avatar embodiment, with implications for VR design, therapeutic applications, and embodiment theory.

Abstract: Embodying non-human body parts in VR is a prevalent practice among certain subcultures and is a personally important creative outlet to many individuals. However, the discrepant morphology between real and virtual bodies can decrease Sense of Embodiment (SoE). Haptic feedback can compensate by increasing SoE felt towards non-human body parts, but there is a literature gap in comparing the effects of different haptic modalities, and their combinations, on SoE. Through an online survey sent out to social VR communities (n = 63), we determined that animal ears are a commonly embodied and ecologically valid non-human body part to study. We then ran a 2x2 within-subjects user study (n = 28) with two independent variables: active haptics, delivered through vibrotactile gloves, and passive haptics, delivered through a physical headband, for when participants reach up to touch virtual dog ears appended to their avatar in VR. Our findings show that (1) passive haptics produced the strongest overall embodiment outcomes, (2) combining modalities reduced the benefits of passive haptics, and (3) SoE towards non-human body parts positively correlates with SoE towards the entire avatar. We discuss implications of our findings in various domains, and on embodiment literature.

</details>


### [234] [Assistive Visual Cues for Visual Neglect Patients](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26407)
*Per Bjerre,Andreas Køllund Pedersen,Hendrik Knoche*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper investigates how endogenous (internal/voluntary) and exogenous (external/reflexive) attentional cues affect visual neglect patients, finding that endogenous cues yield better performance for targets in neglected areas, and that combined cues can further improve acquisition times — though results vary greatly between individuals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior cueing research has focused almost exclusively on normally sighted individuals, leaving a gap in understanding how attentional cues work for visual neglect patients — who have difficulty attending to portions of their visual field. Since strong visual cues are used therapeutically to redirect attention to neglected areas, it is clinically important to determine which cue types are most effective for this population.

Method: The authors conducted an experimental study comparing the effects of endogenous cues, exogenous cues, and their combination on visual neglect patients. Performance was measured via acquisition time (and likely error rate) for targets appearing in both neglected and non-neglected visual field regions.

Result: Endogenous cues consistently outperformed exogenous cues for targets in neglected areas. In a representative case, the best endogenous cue averaged 3.5 seconds acquisition time versus 6.5 seconds for the best exogenous cue. Combining both cue types further reduced acquisition time to 2.8 seconds. However, substantial inter-patient variability was observed.

Conclusion: Endogenous cues are more effective than exogenous cues for directing attention in visual neglect patients, and combined cueing may offer additional benefits. The high inter-individual variability suggests that cueing-based interventions should be personalized to the patient.

Abstract: Previous research on exogenous and endogenous cues has shown how they direct attention and improve interaction speed and error rate in applications. However, most studies focus on people with normal sight. People suffering from visual neglect have difficulties attending to parts of the visual field. One treatment method calls for the use of strong visual cues to remind patients of their neglected area and help guide their attention to it. Therefore, we examine the effects of endogenous and exogenous cues on visual neglect patients. Our results showed that visual neglect patients perform better with endogenous cues, when targets are within their neglected area. In some cases, combining exogenous and endogenous cues improve performance further. However, the performance varies greatly between patients. Using one neglect patient as an example, we saw that the best endogenous cue had an average acquisition time of 3.5 seconds compared to 6.5 for the best exogenous. Combining exogenous and endogenous cues further improved acquisition time to 2.8 seconds.

</details>


### [235] [TinyCNNDeep: Lightweight Attention-Based CNN for EEG Classification of Eye States and Sleep Deprivation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26506)
*Thien Nhan Vo,Yen Nhi Tran Thi,Ngan Nguyen Xuan Phuong,Xuan-The Tran*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A lightweight CNN (TinyCNNDeep) using residual learning and SE attention classifies EEG into four sleep-condition × eye-state categories via image-based representation, achieving 83.69% accuracy, far surpassing traditional and deep learning baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Jointly identifying sleep condition (normal vs. sleep-deprived) and eye state (open vs. closed) from EEG is underexplored despite its relevance to vigilance and cognitive assessment. Existing methods perform poorly on this four-class task, motivating a more effective approach with minimal electrodes.

Method: TinyCNNDeep: a lightweight CNN integrating residual learning and Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) attention. Short multi-channel EEG segments from five channels (Fp1, Fp2, O1, Oz, O2) are converted into 224×224 grayscale images via per-channel Z-score normalization, min-max scaling, and center padding, enabling 2D convolutions to capture both inter-channel correlations and temporal dynamics.

Result: On a 35-subject dataset, TinyCNNDeep achieves subject-wise mean accuracy of 83.69%, outperforming Random Forest (47.66%) by 36.03 percentage points. EEGNet, ShallowConvNet, and DeepConvNet perform near chance. Confusion analysis reveals residual errors concentrate between eyes-closed states across sleep conditions.

Conclusion: An image-based EEG representation combined with residual features and channel attention yields accurate, computationally efficient multiclass sleep-related EEG classification, even with a minimal five-electrode setup.

Abstract: Sleep deprivation impairs vigilance and cognitive function, yet jointly identifying the sleep condition (normal vs deprived) and the eye state (open vs closed) from electroencephalography (EEG) remains underexplored. We address this four-class problem with TinyCNNDeep, a lightweight convolutional neural network that combines residual learning with a Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) attention module. We convert short multi-channel EEG segments from five physiologically relevant channels (Fp1, Fp2, O1, Oz, O2) into 224x224 grayscale images through per-channel Z-score normalization, min-max scaling, and center padding, enabling 2D convolutions to jointly model inter-channel and temporal structure. On a 35-subject dataset recorded under normal-sleep and sleep-deprivation sessions, TinyCNNDeep attains a subject-wise mean accuracy of 83.69%, outperforming the strongest baseline (Random Forest with combined time-frequency features, 47.66%) by 36.03 percentage points, while three established EEG architectures (EEGNet, ShallowConvNet, DeepConvNet) operate near chance. Per-subject analysis quantifies inter-subject variability, and confusion-matrix inspection shows that residual misclassifications concentrate between eyes-closed states across sleep conditions. These results indicate that an image-based EEG representation paired with residual feature extraction and channel attention provides an accurate and computationally efficient framework for multiclass sleep-related EEG classification under a minimal electrode configuration.

</details>


### [236] [DanceDuo: Bridging Human Movement and AI Choreography](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26507)
*Gia-Cat Bui-Le,Tuong-Vy Truong-Thuy,Hai-Dang Nguyen,Trung-Nghia Le*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: DanceDuo is an AI-powered platform that uses diffusion models to generate music-synchronized dance choreography, allowing users to compare their own dancing against AI-generated sequences through integrated pose estimation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To leverage recent advances in deep generative models for practical dance generation, encouraging dancing practice by providing an interactive platform where users can engage with AI-choreographed dance synchronized to diverse music genres.

Method: The system employs diffusion models for dance sequence generation conditioned on music input, integrates human pose estimation for performance comparison, and provides an interactive interface supporting music selection, humanoid model choice, and personal video import.

Result: A comprehensive user study demonstrated that users found the interface intuitive, with the dance comparison feature receiving particular praise.

Conclusion: DanceDuo represents a significant contribution to AI-integrated dance choreography, opening new avenues for both recreational and professional dance applications.

Abstract: In recent years, advancements in deep learning and generative models have revolutionized music-driven dance generation. This paper introduces a novel platform, namely DanceDuo, leveraging diffusion models to generate AI-choreographed dance sequences synchronized with a variety of music genres, to encourage dancing practice. The system allows users to interact with AI by selecting music tracks, humanoid models, and importing personal dance videos for comparison, fostering a rich and engaging user experience. DanceDuo not only offers dance generation but also integrates human pose estimation models to provide users with insightful comparisons of their own performances with AI-generated sequences. We conducted a comprehensive user study, revealing that users found the interface intuitive, with particular praise for the dance comparison feature. Our DanceDuo contributes significantly to the integration of AI in dance choreography, offering novel avenues for both recreational and professional applications.

</details>


### [237] [Budget-Aware Keyboardless Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26508)
*Quang-Thang Nguyen,Gia-Phuc Song-Dong,Minh-Triet Tran,Trung-Nghia Le*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A virtual keyboard system using only a standard camera and a printed paper keyboard, employing computer vision for keyboard region detection and fingernail color analysis for touch/keystroke detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional input devices (keyboard, mouse) limit mobility. Existing virtual keyboard solutions are hampered by complex setups, expensive equipment, special calibration, or controlled lighting — creating a need for a simpler, more accessible alternative.

Method: Combines modern segmentation and detection models with traditional image processing to identify the printed keyboard region from a standard camera feed. Keystroke/touch detection is performed via an algorithm that analyzes the color of the user's fingernail to determine key presses.

Result: Experiments showed promising results for both keyboard detection and keystroke detection in practical applications. A user study indicated participants found the system interesting.

Conclusion: The proposed approach demonstrates a viable, low-cost virtual keyboard solution using commodity hardware, with potential for practical real-world deployment.

Abstract: Interacting with computers typically relies on traditional input devices such as keyboards, mice, and monitors, which can be cumbersome for users seeking greater mobility. Virtual keyboards have been explored to address these limitations, but they often involve complex setups or expensive equipment. This paper proposes a novel virtual keyboard system that leverages only a standard camera and a paper with a printed keyboard layout. Unlike previous methods requiring complex calibration or special lighting conditions, our approach can work on standard environment using modern computer vision technologies. Combining modern segmentation and detection models with traditional image processing algorithms, we efficiently identify the keyboard region. Touch detection is performed using an algorithm analyzing the color of the user's fingernail. Experiments demonstrated a promising results our proposed solution of keyboard and keystroke detection for practical applications. Participants attended our user study also found the proposed system interesting.

</details>


### [238] [Co-Designing Community-Centered AI Education for Adults: A Midwestern Case Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26565)
*Yao Lyu,Leonymae Aumentado,Holden Winton,Jared Lee Katzman,Sparkle Berry,Zachary Rowe,Kimberly Sanders,Tawanna R. Dillahunt*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A case study of an AI education session for 54 adults in a predominantly African American community reveals that co-designed, locally grounded AI literacy efforts shift abstract concerns into specific, actionable questions about AI design and deployment, supporting a community-capacity approach to AI literacy frameworks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Adults outside formal higher education are underserved in AI education, yet AI literacy is increasingly critical for civic participation and empowerment. The authors aim to understand what community-based AI education looks like in practice and what it reveals about AI literacy at the community level, particularly in marginalized communities.

Method: A case study of a single co-designed AI education session involving 54 adult participants (48 in-person, 6 virtual) in a predominantly African American neighborhood on the east side of a major Midwestern city, developed in partnership with community organizations.

Result: Participants' concerns about AI did not disappear but transformed — shifting from broad, abstract anxieties to specific, locally grounded questions about how AI systems are designed and deployed. This shift suggests that context-sensitive AI education fosters more nuanced, actionable engagement with AI.

Conclusion: AI literacy frameworks should be grounded in local community contexts and oriented toward strengthening community capacity, rather than imposing generic, top-down definitions of AI literacy. Co-design with community partners is essential for effective adult AI education outside formal systems.

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) education is increasingly important, yet adults outside higher education receive less attention. We report a case study of an AI education session with 54 adults (48 in-person and 6 virtual) in a predominantly African American community on the east side of a major Midwestern city. We ask: "What does AI education for adults outside formal educational systems look like in practice?" and "What does this AI education session reveal about AI literacy at the community level?" Through a co-designed session developed with community partners, we found that concerns about AI persisted but shifted to specific, locally grounded questions about AI design and deployment. We also discuss AI literacy from a community capacity perspective and argue for AI literacy frameworks grounded in local community contexts that strengthen community capacity.

</details>


### [239] [An exploratory behavioral and electroencephalographic study of artificial intelligence-assisted learning modes in high school students](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26579)
*Kashika Khurana,Ally Liew*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This study examines how three distinct AI interaction modes — Tutor, Collaborator, and Solver — affect frontal EEG activity and problem-solving behavior in adolescents (n=48). While behavioral metrics showed significant differences across modes, EEG patterns were descriptive but not statistically significant, with exploratory evidence of short-term carryover effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing research treats AI exposure as a binary condition (AI vs. no-AI), failing to differentiate between interaction modalities or examine post-exposure effects. This limits understanding of how specific AI roles shape cognitive engagement and problem-solving behavior in educational contexts.

Method: A within-subject design with 48 participants (ages 14–18, sex-balanced) completed two counterbalanced quizzes across three AI interaction modes: Tutor, Collaborator, and Solver. Frontal EEG spectral activity and behavioral metrics (Initiation, Processing, Stress, measured on an ordinal scale) were recorded. Statistical analyses included Friedman tests, repeated-measures ANOVA, paired t-tests, and effect size calculations.

Result: Behaviorally, all three AI modes produced significant differences across Initiation, Processing, and Stress measures. EEG data revealed descriptive but non-significant patterns differentiating the three modes. Exploratory analysis suggested possible short-term carryover effects of prior AI interaction on subsequent performance.

Conclusion: The study provides preliminary behavioral evidence that AI interaction mode meaningfully shapes cognitive and affective responses, and offers investigative electrophysiological observations warranting further study. It establishes a replicable experimental framework for future human-AI interaction research.

Abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly integrating into education, concerns have emerged regarding its potential implications on cognitive engagement and problem-solving behavior. However, existing research largely treats AI exposure as a binary condition (AI vs. no-AI), with limited differentiation between interaction modalities and post-exposure effects. This study investigates whether distinct AI interaction modes (Tutor, Collaborator, Solver) influence frontal EEG spectral activity. Electroencephalography (EEG) data and quantified behavioral metrics were recorded from 48 study participants (24 males, 24 females; ages 14-18) across two counterbalanced quizzes in a within-subject design. Statistical analyses included Friedman tests, repeated-measures ANOVA, paired t-tests, and effect size calculations. Behavioral changes were mathematically analyzed in an observation matrix of three characteristics -Initiation, Processing, and Stress-measured on an ordinal scale. Each mode showed significant differences in all three behavioral measures. Descriptive EEG patterns in AI interaction mode were observed, and the possibility of short-term carryover effects of AI was explored. Although the EEG data did not reach statistical significance, the patterns observed across the three AI interaction modes warrant further investigation. This study provides preliminary behavioral evidence and investigative electrophysiological observations, exploring possible AI-interaction-mode-based differences in neural activity and behavior, while establishing a replicable framework for future human-AI interaction studies.

</details>


### [240] [HiLSVA: Design and Evaluation of a Human-in-the-Loop Agentic System for Scientific Visualization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26614)
*Kuangshi Ai,Patrick Phuoc Do,Chaoli Wang*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: HiLSVA is a human-in-the-loop agentic system for scientific visualization that combines a plan-first multi-agent architecture with explicit human oversight, provenance tracking, and real-time user feedback adaptation, demonstrating that mixed-initiative interaction improves task completion, user control, and transparency across expertise levels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based agents for scientific visualization prioritize autonomy over human control, limiting transparency, oversight, and the ability for analysts to steer the visualization process. There is a need for systems that augment rather than replace human analytical reasoning.

Method: HiLSVA employs a plan-first multi-agent architecture with four key components: (1) explicit human oversight enabling fluid handoff via natural language and direct manipulation, (2) stepwise provenance tracking for transparency, (3) learn-at-test-time adaptation from user feedback, and (4) sandboxed execution for safe, reproducible workflows. Evaluation involved representative case studies and a controlled user study with 12 participants of varying expertise across multiple autonomy settings.

Result: Mixed-initiative interaction improved task completion, user control, and workflow transparency across all expertise levels. A tradeoff emerged between execution efficiency and human oversight — greater autonomy increased speed but reduced transparency and user control.

Conclusion: Human-centered design is critical in agentic scientific visualization. HiLSVA demonstrates that collaborative, mixed-initiative systems can effectively balance autonomy and oversight, and the findings provide guidance for developing future collaborative visualization systems.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents enable natural language interaction for scientific visualization (SciVis). Still, prior systems have essentially prioritized autonomy over human analytical control, thereby limiting transparency and human oversight. We present HiLSVA, a human-in-the-loop agentic system that supports mixed-initiative SciVis workflows. HiLSVA integrates a plan-first multi-agent architecture with explicit human oversight, stepwise provenance tracking, and learn-at-test-time adaptation from user feedback. The system supports fluid handoff between humans and agents through both natural language and direct manipulation of visualizations, while sandboxed execution ensures safe, reproducible workflows. In doing so, HiLSVA reframes agentic SciVis as a collaborative process that augments, rather than replaces, human analytical reasoning. We evaluate HiLSVA through representative case studies and a controlled user study with twelve participants of varying expertise across multiple autonomy settings. Results show that mixed-initiative interaction improves task completion, user control, and workflow transparency across different levels of user expertise, while revealing a tradeoff between execution efficiency and human oversight. These findings highlight the importance of human-centered design in agentic SciVis and guide the development of future collaborative visualization systems. We encourage readers to explore our demo video, case studies, and source code at https://hilsva.github.io/.

</details>


### [241] [Reviving Reflection-in-Action: Instilling Designerly Thinking in AI-Supported Ideation through Multimodal Prompting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26626)
*Samangi Wadinambiarachchi,Jenny Waycott,Greg Wadley*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This study evaluates SketchifAI, a creativity support tool comparing text, sketch, and sketch-plus-tags input modalities, finding sketch enhances fluency but users paradoxically prefer text prompting, raising questions about designing AI tools that preserve reflective design skills.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI creativity support tools rely predominantly on text prompting for solution-oriented outputs, neglecting the potential of multimodal prompting — particularly sketching — to introduce productive friction that fosters iteration and reflection in the designer-AI interaction loop.

Method: A mixed-methods, within-participants study was conducted with design students using SketchifAI, a prototype AI-CST. Three input modalities (text, sketch, sketch-plus-tags) were compared across measures of perceived intent expression, creativity support perception, and divergent thinking performance (fluency, variety, originality, quality).

Result: Preliminary findings indicate sketch modality tended to enhance fluency. Evidence for differences in variety, originality, and quality between modalities was inconclusive. Paradoxically, participants strongly preferred text prompting despite sketch-based benefits.

Conclusion: AI creativity tools should be designed to intentionally reintroduce reflection-through-sketching, ensuring designer-AI interaction supports rather than erodes essential design skills. The paradox of user preference versus performance warrants further investigation into how tool interfaces shape creative behavior.

Abstract: Current AI-powered creativity support tools (AI-CSTs) primarily use text prompting to generate solution-oriented outputs. However, the potential value of multimodal prompting in designer-AI interaction, specifically the introduction of productive friction to encourage iteration and reflection, has not been fully explored. To address this, we developed SketchifAI, a prototype AI-CST, and evaluated it with design students. In a mixed-methods, within-participants study, we examined how different input modalities (text, sketch, and sketch-plus-tags) affected design students' perceived ability to express their intent, their perception of creativity support, and their divergent thinking performance. Our preliminary findings suggest that the sketch modality tended to enhance fluency, with inconclusive evidence for differences in variety, originality, or quality compared to text modality. Yet, paradoxically, participants showed a strong preference for text prompting. We discuss how AI tools might be designed to reintroduce reflection-through-sketching, ensuring that designer-AI interaction supports, rather than erodes, essential design skills in students.

</details>


### [242] [Invisible Impact of Empathy on Behavioral Change: Isolating the Effect of Empathy in Long-term Physical Activity Coaching Chatbot Interactions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26641)
*Li Siyan,Kai-Hui Liang,Shopnil Shahriar,Yilin Ye,Shiyoh Goetsu,Wei-Wei Du,Masahiro Yoshida,Tsunayuki Ohwa,Xuhai Xu,Zhou Yu*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A six-week study with 13 participants tested three WhatsApp physical-activity coaching chatbots differing only in empathy. Users struggled to distinguish empathy levels; the non-empathetic bot was often rated more engaging, yet higher-empathy variants yielded larger step-count increases and faster intention improvements, suggesting empathy's subtle, peripheral-route influence on behavior change.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current dialogue systems treat empathy as essential without empirical validation of its actual impact, particularly in behavior-change contexts where motivation and adherence hinge on subtle user-chatbot interactions. The authors question whether empathy genuinely drives outcomes in physical-activity coaching.

Method: A six-week within-subject study (N=13) using three WhatsApp-based PA coaching chatbots that differ exclusively in empathy level (non-empathetic, medium, high). Participants interact with all variants, providing quantitative (step counts, ratings) and qualitative measures of engagement, usefulness, and intention to follow advice.

Result: (1) Participants could not reliably distinguish between empathy conditions; (2) the non-empathetic version was frequently rated more engaging and useful; (3) higher-empathy variants were associated with larger average step-count increases and faster improvement in intention to follow advice.

Conclusion: Empathy's role in behavior-change chatbots is nuanced: lay users may not explicitly recognize it, but it may still shape motivation and trust via peripheral-route processing (Elaboration Likelihood Model). Design implications emphasize balancing effectiveness with human-like connection in next-generation PA coaching chatbots.

Abstract: Current dialogue systems, powered by large language models, often treat empathy as essential without assessing its true impact, especially in behavior change, where motivation and adherence often depend on subtle user-chatbot dynamics. We examine this assumption by building three WhatsApp physical-activity (PA) coaching chatbots that differ only in empathy level and evaluating them in a six-week within-subject study (N = 13). Participants struggled to distinguish between the empathy conditions, and the non-empathetic version was often rated as more engaging and useful. However, higher-empathy variants were still associated with a larger overall average increase in step counts and faster improvement in intention to follow advice. These results suggest empathy's role is nuanced: it may be hard for lay users to identify explicitly, but it can still shape motivation and trust that support sustained change. We interpret this pattern through the Elaboration Likelihood Model's peripheral route. We highlight design implications for building next-generation PA coaching chatbots that balance effectiveness with human-like connection.

</details>


### [243] [From Content to Strategy: Understanding the Motivations, Processes, and Impacts of AI-Guided Communication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26672)
*Chang Wan,Angel Hsing-Chi Hwang*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Qualitative study of 26 interviews revealing that people use generative AI not just to write messages but to strategize communication in close relationships. AI serves as a reflective, nonjudgmental sounding board that enhances empathy and skills, though concerns about self-doubt, loss of uniqueness, and mixed long-term relational effects persist.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI-MC research focuses on AI generating message content. The authors identify a gap: generative AI is increasingly used to guide communication *strategies*—not merely produce text—yet this "AI-guided communication" pattern lacks theoretical and empirical investigation, particularly regarding its psychological and relational consequences.

Method: 26 in-depth interviews with individuals who have used AI (e.g., ChatGPT) to develop communication strategies, analyzed qualitatively to identify themes around usage preferences, perceived benefits, and concerns.

Result: Participants strongly preferred using AI for analyzing challenging close-relationship scenarios. Key benefits included: fostering self-reflection, emotional easing, preventing conflict escalation, offering multiple perspectives, and providing a safe/nonjudgmental space for self-disclosure. AI-guided communication reportedly enhanced empathy and communication skills. However, participants also reported self-doubt and fear of losing uniqueness. Long-term relational impact perceptions were mixed, contingent on AI's short-term problem-solving utility.

Conclusion: AI-guided communication extends AI-MC beyond content generation into strategic interpersonal guidance. While it offers significant psychological and skill-building benefits, it introduces tensions around authenticity, identity, and uncertain long-term relational outcomes that warrant further theoretical development.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence-mediated communication (AI-MC) is conceptualized as applying AI to augment or generate message content (Hancock et al., 2020). However, advances in generative AI have expanded its use beyond generating content to guiding individuals' communication strategies, that is, AI-guided communication, yet theoretical and empirical understandings of this emerging use pattern and its consequences remains limited. To address this gap, this study conducted 26 in-depth interviews with individuals who have used AI to develop their communication strategies. Findings suggest participants strongly preferred using AI to analyze challenging scenarios in close relationships, because it fostered self-reflection, eased emotions, prevented conflict escalation, offered multiple perspectives, and provided a safe, nonjudgmental space for self-disclosure. Participants also stated that AI-guided communication enhanced their empathy and communication skills, though some voiced self-doubt and worried about losing their uniqueness. Views on long-term relational impact were mixed, depending on perceived usefulness of AI for resolving short-term interpersonal challenges.

</details>


### [244] [Modeling Adaptive Visual Search in Semantically Hierarchical Layouts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26725)
*Saku Sourulahti,Jussi P. P. Jokinen*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A computational cognitive model based on computational rationality shows that humans use hierarchical task representations combining semantic and visual structures to improve visual search efficiency. Validated with human studies, the model replicates task durations and eye movements, and is demonstrated for rapid prototyping of UI layouts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how information grouping—specifically the interplay between semantic and spatial grouping—impacts visual search performance, with the practical goal of informing user interface design.

Method: A computational cognitive model grounded in computational rationality, treating user behavior as optimal adaptation to cognitive and task constraints. The model incorporates hierarchical task representations that exploit both semantic and visual structures. Validation was conducted via two human studies involving visual search and semantic categorization tasks, comparing model predictions against empirical data on task durations and eye movement patterns. The model was further demonstrated in rapid prototyping and evaluation of semantic visual groupings within UI wireframes.

Result: Semantic grouping improves visual search performance when it is congruent with spatial grouping. The computational model successfully replicates human task completion times and eye movement patterns observed in the studies.

Conclusion: The model extends prior visual search models by accounting for hierarchical memory structures in human cognition. It offers a practical pathway for applying cognitive modeling to rapid prototyping and evaluation of real-world user interface designs, particularly in optimizing semantic and visual groupings.

Abstract: This paper introduces a computational cognitive model to investigate how information grouping impacts visual search, a key consideration in user interface design. The model uses computational rationality to view user behavior as an adaptation to cognitive and task constraints. Our work highlights that humans use hierarchical task representations, exploiting semantic and visual structures to improve search efficiency within the constraints of the visual system. We validate this model with data from two human studies focused on visual search and semantic categorization, demonstrating that semantic grouping improves search performance when it aligns with spatial grouping. Our model replicates task durations and eye movement patterns. By improving understanding of how hierarchical memory structures are utilized in human cognition, the model extends previous visual search models. We showcase our model in the rapid prototyping and evaluation of semantic visual groupings within user interface wireframes, suggesting a pathway toward applications in more complex, real-world interface design.

</details>


### [245] ['A bit of chaos and madness': The AI Assessment Scale and the work of assessment reform](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26729)
*Mike Perkins,Darius Postma,Jasper Roe,Susan Sisay,Craig Holdcroft*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A qualitative study across UK and Vietnamese universities examining how academic staff experience implementing the Artificial Intelligence Assessment Scale (AIAS). Six themes emerged: recognising AI, facilitating conditions, building capacity, adoption pathways, ethics, and reframing pedagogy. The AIAS can drive authentic assessment design but risks becoming a compliance checkbox without alignment to learning outcomes, disciplinary context, and staff capacity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative AI has created urgent pressure on universities to redesign assessment practices while preserving integrity, equity, and validity. Although structured frameworks like the AIAS have been proposed as a response, there is limited empirical evidence on how academic staff actually experience their implementation in practice.

Method: Qualitative multi-site study using five focus groups with 30 academic staff across two universities: a private international university in Vietnam and a public university in the UK. Data were analysed using hybrid thematic analysis, with Critical AI Literacy employed as a sensitising concept.

Result: Six themes were developed: (1) recognising and integrating AI, (2) facilitating conditions, (3) building capacity, (4) pathways to adoption, (5) ethics in practice, and (6) reframing pedagogy. Staff valued the AIAS as a shared language for legitimising GenAI use, clarifying boundaries, and prompting reflection on assessment design. Implementation was influenced by governance, tool access, staff confidence, workload, integrity concerns, disciplinary context, and alignment with learning outcomes.

Conclusion: The AIAS holds dual potential: it can prompt authentic assessment design and student engagement, but may devolve into a compliance layer when disconnected from learning outcomes, disciplinary context, and staff capacity. The study contributes empirical grounding on the institutional conditions necessary for GenAI assessment frameworks to transition from policy adoption to genuine pedagogical enactment.
