Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has intensified pressure on universities to redesign assessment while maintaining integrity, equity, and validity. Structured frameworks such as the Artificial Intelligence Assessment Scale (AIAS) offer one response, but evidence of how staff experience their implementation remains limited. This qualitative study examines AIAS implementation at a private international university in Vietnam and a public university in the United Kingdom. Data from five focus groups with 30 academic staff were analysed using hybrid thematic analysis, with Critical AI Literacy used as a sensitising concept. Six themes were developed: recognising and integrating AI, facilitating conditions, building capacity, pathways to adoption, ethics in practice, and reframing pedagogy.
  Staff valued the AIAS as a shared language for legitimising GenAI use, clarifying boundaries, and prompting reflection on assessment design. However, implementation was shaped by governance, tool access, staff confidence, workload, integrity concerns, disciplinary context, and alignment with learning outcomes. The findings show that the AIAS could prompt authentic assessment design and student engagement, but may become a compliance layer when disconnected from learning outcomes, disciplinary context, and staff capacity. This study contributes empirical evidence on the institutional conditions through which GenAI assessment frameworks move from policy adoption to pedagogical enactment.

</details>


### [246] [MedSWFlow: An Open-Source LLM Workflow for Drafting Medical Social Work Case Plans](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26884)
*Yulin Mao,Shiyu Li,Shuping Song,Yuling Zhang,Yajun Song*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: MedSWFlow is an open-source, model-agnostic LLM workflow that structures medical social work case planning into six sequential stages, generating reviewable draft assessment forms and service plans for practitioner review.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To standardize and support the complex, multi-stage process of medical social work case planning through a reproducible, open-source LLM workflow that can operate across different language model providers, while ensuring outputs remain practitioner-reviewed drafts rather than autonomous decisions.

Method: The framework decomposes case planning into six staged prompting steps: (1) assessment, (2) problem analysis, (3) goal setting, (4) intervention planning, (5) risk anticipation, and (6) planned effect evaluation. It standardizes case inputs, constructs structured case profiles, and draws on established social work and behavioral frameworks to guide each stage's prompts.

Result: The system produces structured, reviewable assessment forms and service plans. It is released as an open-source research framework (available on GitHub) enabling reproducible case-plan generation across different LLM providers.

Conclusion: MedSWFlow offers a practical, transparent, and model-agnostic tool for drafting medical social work case plans, emphasizing that outputs are intended as practitioner-reviewed drafts rather than final clinical or service decisions.

Abstract: We present MedSWFlow, an open-source, model-agnostic LLM workflow for drafting medical social work case plans. The framework translates professional case-planning tasks into six stages: assessment, problem analysis, goal setting, intervention planning, risk anticipation, and planned effect evaluation. Drawing on established social work and behavioral frameworks, MedSWFlow standardizes case inputs, builds structured case profiles, and generates reviewable assessment forms and service plans through staged prompting. The system is released as an open-source research framework for reproducible case-plan generation across LLM providers. Outputs are intended as practitioner-reviewed drafts rather than final service decisions. Source code: https://github.com/santhiyacw-droid/MedSWFlow/tree/main.

</details>


### [247] [Optimizing Human-Machine Interface for Real-Time AI Support in the Operating Room: the CVS Copilot](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26886)
*Lorenzo Arboit,Nicolas Chanel,Aditya Murali,Pietro Mascagni,Nicolas Padoy*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A user-centered design study with 17 surgeons explored optimal human-machine interface design for AI-assisted laparoscopic cholecystectomy, revealing strong preferences for surgeon-controlled, minimally intrusive visual overlays and role-adaptive feedback, leading to the development of CVS Copilot.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI systems for automated Critical View of Safety (CVS) assessment in laparoscopic cholecystectomy are approaching clinical deployment, but clinical safety and effectiveness depend critically on HMI design — an underexplored factor beyond algorithmic performance.

Method: A mixed-methods, user-centered design study was conducted with 17 surgeons (residents, attendings, professors). Semi-structured interviews probed interaction modalities, timing, visualization strategies, and control mechanisms. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis and human-factors heuristics.

Result: Key findings: (1) 16/17 surgeons supported AI for decision support but rejected autonomy; (2) attendings (13/14) preferred minimal feedback at decisive moments, while residents (3/3) preferred optional guidance with confidence indicators; (3) strongest support for minimal overlay (16/17) and on-demand anatomical segmentation (13/17); (4) persistent overlays, haptic feedback, and numeric confidence displays raised recurrent concerns.

Conclusion: Findings informed CVS Copilot, a surgeon-controlled, role-adaptive HMI featuring AI-based CVS assessment with minimal default visualization and optional overlays, tailored to experience-dependent needs.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems for automated Critical View of Safety (CVS) assessment in laparoscopic cholecystectomy are nearing clinical translation. Beyond algorithmic performance, clinical safety and effectiveness depend on the quality of the human-machine interface (HMI). This work examines how AI-generated predictions should be presented and controlled intraoperatively. Seventeen surgeons, including residents, attending surgeons, and professors, took part in a mixed-methods, user-centered design study to optimize an intraoperative HMI for AI-assisted safe laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Interviews explored interaction modalities, timing of assistance, visualization strategies, and control mechanisms across surgical roles, and were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis and human-factors heuristics. Most surgeons (16/17) supported the use of AI for intraoperative decision support while rejecting autonomous decision-making. Attendings preferred minimal AI feedback at decisive moments (13/14), whereas residents favored optional guidance (3/3) with confidence indicators and on-demand anatomical overlays. Across interviews, surgeons consistently prioritized visual, surgeon-controlled, minimally intrusive displays, with the strongest support for a minimal overlay (16/17) and on-demand anatomical segmentation (13/17). Recurrent concerns included persistent overlays, haptic feedback, and numeric confidence displays, although these were not uniformly raised across the cohort. These findings informed the design of CVS Copilot, a surgeon-controlled, role-adaptive HMI that provides AI-based CVS assessment with minimal default visualization and optional overlays.

</details>


### [248] [Game Changers: Designing and Measuring Dynamic Feedback To Help Users Self-Regulate in a VR Pointing Game](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26925)
*Bastian Ilsø Hougaard,Scott Bateman,Iris Brunner,Lars Evald,Hendrik Knoche*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This study systematically examines how dynamic feedback—driven by three performance metrics (completion time, movement straightness, peak speed) and delivered at three temporal frequencies (continuous, end-of-action, end-of-task)—affects player performance and perception in a VR pointing task. On average, dynamic feedback improved speed and straightness, though effects varied individually. The work provides game designers with evidence-based guidance on aligning feedback schemes with performance objectives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Game feedback is critical for player performance, learning, and improvement, yet little is understood about how specific performance metrics driving feedback affect core game tasks like pointing or steering. Designers lack empirical basis for choosing which metrics to drive dynamic feedback and when to deliver it.

Method: A virtual reality pointing task was used to systematically explore three performance metrics (completion time, movement straightness, peak speed) crossed with three delivery timings (continuous, end-of-action, end-of-task). Participants' pointing performance and perceptions were measured, with the metrics serving as the intended locus of quantitative comparison across the three feedback forms.

Result: On average, dynamic feedback helped participants point more straight and faster. However, individual differences were notable—some participants experienced small or even opposite effects. The study quantitatively compared the three feedback forms across the metrics driving them.

Conclusion: The findings improve the foundation for game designers to craft dynamic feedback by informing when to employ feedback schemes aligned with desirable performance objectives, taking into account both metric choice and delivery timing.

Abstract: The way games dynamically convey information through feedback is critical to players' ability to perform, learn, and improve. However, it is poorly understood how performance metrics impact player performance and perception in core game tasks like pointing or steering. With a virtual reality pointing task we systematically explored how three performance metrics driving the feedback affected players when rewarding short completion times, straight movements, or high peak speed. across different points in time - continuously, at end-of-action, or at end-of-task. On average the dynamic feedback helped people point more straight and faster, while for others it had small or opposite effect. The study quantitatively compared dynamic feedback across three forms with the metrics driving the form as the intended locus of quantitative comparison. Our work improves game designers basis for crafting dynamic feedback by helping them know when to employ feedback schemes that align with desirable game performance objectives.

</details>


### [249] [Continuous Behavioral Synthesis for Adaptive Health Dashboards: An LLM-Mediated Architecture Integrating Explicit Preference, Spatial Reorganization, and Attention Allocation Signals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26937)
*Tiziano Santilli,Mina Alipour,Mahyar T. Moghaddam*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper presents an LLM-powered architecture for adaptive UI dashboards that synthesizes sparse, heterogeneous user signals (explicit feedback, drag-and-drop spatial reorganization, and dwell-time attentional data) into real-time personalized layouts using structured prompt engineering, demonstrated in a personal health monitoring domain with 14 metrics across 7 visualization modalities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional adaptive UI engineering suffers from a dichotomy: rule-based systems are brittle and limited by designer foresight, while machine learning approaches require large historical datasets before achieving effective personalization. Neither can deliver immediate, coherent adaptation from sparse, heterogeneous behavioral signals.

Method: A layered prompt construction methodology that separates four concerns: (1) temporal context determination, (2) behavioral signal extraction across three channels (explicit micro-feedback, drag-and-drop spatial priority, hover dwell-time attentional investment), (3) explicit preference enforcement, and (4) user profile synthesis. An LLM serves as the behavioral synthesis engine, continuously regenerating dashboard layouts by reconciling multiple simultaneous signals. The system integrates manually specified behavioral interpretations and temporal heuristics with LLM-mediated synthesis, maintaining explanatory coherence throughout.

Result: The system was instantiated in a personal health monitoring application managing 14 distinct health metrics across 7 widget visualization modalities. Evaluation compared profile-driven initialization against multi-signal behavioral adaptation, with analytical assessment across multiple adaptation scenarios and representative post-adaptation screenshots demonstrating the resulting interfaces.

Conclusion: LLMs can effectively serve as behavioral synthesis engines for adaptive user interfaces, bridging low-level interaction patterns and high-level design decisions without requiring extensive training data. The layered prompt construction approach successfully reconciles multiple simultaneous behavioral signals that would be difficult to encode through explicit rules alone.

Abstract: The engineering of adaptive user interfaces has traditionally relied on either rule-based systems encoding designer intuitions about user needs or machine learning approaches requiring substantial historical data before achieving effective personalization. We present a technical architecture that leverages Large Language Models as behavioral synthesis engines to enable immediate adaptation from sparse, heterogeneous user signals. Our system integrates three distinct behavioral channels, i) explicit micro-feedback on individual interface elements, ii) spatial priority inferred from manual widget reorganization through drag-and-drop interaction, iii) and attentional investment measured through dwell time during hover events, within a structured prompt engineering framework that continuously regenerates dashboard layouts while maintaining explanatory coherence. The architecture addresses the technical challenge of translating low-level interaction patterns into high-level design decisions through a layered prompt construction methodology that separates temporal context determination, behavioral signal extraction, explicit preference enforcement, and user profile synthesis. The approach combines manually specified behavioral interpretations and temporal heuristics with LLM-mediated synthesis, enabling the reconciliation of multiple simultaneous signals that would be difficult to encode through explicit rules alone. We demonstrate the system through an instantiation in the personal health monitoring domain, including an analytical evaluation of adaptation behavior across multiple scenarios and a working implementation managing fourteen distinct health metrics across seven widget visualization modalities. The evaluation compares profile-driven initialization, multi-signal behavioral adaptation, and presents the resulting interfaces through representative post-adaptation screenshots.

</details>


### [250] [What Holds Back Brain-Computer Interfaces? Uncovering Challenges and Opportunities in BCI-controlled Games for Cerebral Palsy Rehabilitation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26951)
*Bastian Ilsø Hougaard,Kirstine Schultz Dalgaard,Kirstine Johanne Stougaard Klebæk,Hendrik Knoche,Mads Jochumsen*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper explores how individuals with cerebral palsy (CP) and a CP therapist experience brain-computer interface (BCI) games for rehabilitation, finding that while sporadic assistance reduces monotony, it can undermine users' sense of agency; the therapist viewed BCI as a complement to traditional training that bridges playful exercise and autonomous practice.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The design constraints for BCI-based CP rehabilitation are poorly understood, particularly regarding how individuals with CP experience a sense of control through BCI and how they perceive computer-mediated game assistance. The study addresses this gap by gathering both clinical and user perspectives.

Method: The study employed a qualitative approach combining two data sources: (1) in-clinic insights from a CP therapist, and (2) experiential accounts from ten individuals with CP who interacted with BCI game prototypes.

Result: Two key findings emerged: sporadic in-game help reduced monotony but raised doubts about users' sense of agency; the therapist perceived BCI rehabilitation as complementary to conventional training, useful for transitioning patients from playful guided exercises toward autonomous, self-managed training.

Conclusion: The authors outline key challenges and opportunities to guide future design and research of BCI-based training systems for CP rehabilitation, emphasizing the need to balance assistance with preserving user agency.

Abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) offer promising avenues for cerebral palsy (CP) rehabilitation at home and in the clinic, using games that promote engagement and sustained training effort. Nonetheless, the design constraints of BCI-based CP rehabilitation remain unclear, especially how individuals with CP experience a sense of control through BCI, and how they experience computer-mediated game assistance. To address this gap, we present preliminary clinical and user perspectives on BCI-based CP rehabilitation, drawing on in-clinic insights from a CP therapist and experiential accounts from ten individuals with CP engaging with BCI game prototypes. Sporadic help in BCI games eased monotony, but also fostered doubts regarding agency. The therapist saw BCI rehabilitation as complementary to traditional training, facilitating the transition from playful exercises to autonomous, self-managed training. We outline key challenges and opportunities to inform and empower further design and research of BCI training for CP.

</details>


### [251] [Floor Raiser or Ceiling Limiter? Differential Storytelling Outcomes with a Child-Centric GenAI System Across Individual Differences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27067)
*Min Fan,Wanqing Ma,Xinyue Cui,Xiaolu Dai,Shengyu Huang*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A study with 40 children (Grades 2–6) found that GenAI-assisted storytelling narrowed the quality gap between low and high performers by 83.5% through floor-raising and ceiling-constraining mechanisms, selectively boosting creativity and richness but not coherence or narrative structure. Younger children chose more semantically distant keywords, while image regeneration was weakly linked to structural quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether generative AI benefits all children equally in creative literacy contexts, or whether it differentially impacts children based on baseline ability, age, and engagement patterns.

Method: Mixed-methods, within-subjects experiment with 40 children aged 7–12 (Grades 2–6), comparing a child-centric GenAI storytelling system against a traditional storyboard condition. Measures included story quality dimensions (creativity, richness, coherence, narrative structure), keyword semantic distance, image regeneration behavior, and baseline performance controls.

Result: (1) GenAI produced a convergence pattern: the quality gap between low and high performers narrowed by 83.5%, driven by lower-end support and upper-end constraint. This effect was dimension-selective—creativity and richness improved, but coherence and narrative structure remained tied to baseline. (2) Younger children selected more semantically distant keywords; older children preferred semantically closer ones. Engagement orientation varied individually, independent of age. (3) Image regeneration positively correlated with structural quality dimensions, but this association attenuated after controlling for baseline performance.

Conclusion: GenAI-assisted storytelling acts as an equalizer for certain creative dimensions but not all, warranting mechanism-contingent scaffolding—adaptive support that responds to which quality dimension is being targeted and the child's baseline profile—as a design principle for inclusive GenAI storytelling systems.

Abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) holds promise for democratizing creative literacy, yet whether it benefits all children equally remains unclear. Using a child-centric GenAI storytelling system for children aged 7-12, we conducted a mixed-methods within-subjects experiment (N = 40, Grades 2-6) comparing GenAI-assisted and traditional storyboard conditions. Three findings emerged. First, the GenAI-assisted condition was associated with a floor-raising convergence pattern, with the quality gap narrowing by 83.5%, driven by lower-end support and upper-end constraint mechanisms. This convergence was dimension-selective, improving creativity and richness while leaving coherence and narrative structure tied to baseline performance. Second, younger children more often selected semantically distant keywords while older children preferred semantically closer ones, although engagement orientation varied across individuals regardless of age. Third, image regeneration was positively associated with structural quality dimensions, though this association was attenuated after baseline control. We propose mechanism-contingent scaffolding as a design principle for adaptive GenAI storytelling systems serving diverse children.

</details>


### [252] [Urban Context and Travel Experience Events: An Exploratory Comparison of Two German Cities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27077)
*Marie Güntert,Esther Bosch*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: A mobile app-based study in Hamburg (urban) and Tuttlingen (rural), Germany, with 91 participants used multi-level regression to identify events affecting public transport experience. Capacity offer matters most positively in Tuttlingen; lack of punctuality and low well-being are key negatives there, while in Hamburg, unpunctuality and negative information events dominate. Results guide local transit improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To identify specific events that influence the on-trip travel experience in both urban and rural public transportation contexts, and to understand how these experiences may subsequently affect travel behavior.

Method: A mobile application was used to collect real-time trip evaluations and situational data from 21 participants in rural Tuttlingen and 70 in urban Hamburg. Multi-level regression analyses were applied to assess the impact of various events (punctuality, capacity offer, information provision, etc.) on on-trip travel experience.

Result: In Tuttlingen, sufficient capacity offer had the strongest positive effect on experience, while lack of punctuality and low personal well-being were the strongest negative factors. In Hamburg, lack of punctuality and negative information events had the largest negative impacts.

Conclusion: The identified event impacts provide an empirical foundation for targeted decision-making and measures to improve local public transportation quality, with differentiated insights for urban versus rural settings.

Abstract: The presented study investigates events influencing public transportation experience in both urban (Hamburg) and rural (Tuttlingen) areas in Germany, with the aim of identifying events that affect travel experience and as a result travel behavior. Using a mobile application, 21 participants in Tuttlingen and 70 participants in Hamburg tracked everyday trips, providing real-time evaluations of travel experiences along with situational data. Multi-level regression analyses were applied to assess the impact of events such as punctuality, capacity offer, information about public transportation and others on the ontrip experience. Results indicate that a sufficient public transportation capacity offer has the strongest positive effect in Tuttlingen, whereas a lack of punctuality and low personal well-being have the strongest negative effects. In Hamburg, a lack of punctuality and a negative information event have the largest impacts. These identified effects provide a foundation for decision-making and measures to improve local public transportation.

</details>


### [253] [Behind the Mask: A Taxonomic Analysis of Activities in Online Social Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27111)
*Debora F De Souza,Gabriela Beltrao,Berta Chulvi,Sergio Dantonio,Mehmet Gokay Ozerim,Javier Torregrosa,Adrian Giron,Angel Panizo,Pablo Miralles Gonzalez,Helena Liz,Javier Huertas Tato,Sonia Sousa,Alejandro Martin,Monika Maciuliene,David Camacho*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: The paper presents a taxonomy for characterizing malicious actors who spread disinformation on online social networks, developed through expert collaboration and literature review, and demonstrates its application through a case study on anti-migration discourse.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The growing threat of disinformation broadcast across online social networks demands systematic approaches to identify and understand the malicious actors behind deceptive content dissemination. The authors aim to fill a gap in structured characterization of these actors' traits, behaviors, and strategies.

Method: The authors designed a taxonomy through two primary inputs: (1) collaboration with subject matter experts (SMEs) and (2) a review of academic literature on disinformation and malicious actors. The taxonomy was then applied in a case study analyzing anti-migration discourse across social media channels to validate and demonstrate its utility.

Result: The resulting taxonomy distinguishes the characteristics, activities, and strategies of malicious actors on OSNs. The case study on anti-migration discourse illustrates how the taxonomy can be operationalized to analyze real-world disinformation campaigns. The authors also reflect on the taxonomy's potential for guiding responsible design of network systems.

Conclusion: The proposed taxonomy offers a structured framework for researchers and practitioners to systematically identify and analyze malicious disinformation actors on social media, with demonstrated applicability to politically charged topics such as anti-migration rhetoric. It contributes to the responsible design of sociotechnical systems by enabling more targeted interventions against online disinformation.

Abstract: The broadcast of disinformation in online social networks (OSN) is a growing concern examined across several disciplines, including human-computer interaction (HCI). The pervasive issue has been prompting novel approaches to identify the malicious actors behind the dissemination of deceptive and fabricated content. Analyzing the characteristics and activities of these actors, we designed a taxonomy informed by collaboration with subject matter experts (SMEs) and a review of the academic literature. Our study explores how to distinguish the characteristics, activities, and strategies of malicious actors on OSN and examines how they contribute to the spread of disinformation. We describe the design process and the application of the taxonomy in a case study analyzing anti-migration discourse in social media channels, and reflect on its potential to aid researchers and practitioners in the responsible design of network systems.

</details>


### [254] ["Everyone Says Them": Deception Typologies, Probabilistic Trust, and Grassroots Safety Knowledge Among Gay Dating App Users in China](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27284)
*Yibo Meng,Lyumanshan Ye,Yingfangzhong Sun,Bingyi Liu,Huidi Lu,Xiaolan Ding*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This study explores how gay male users in China experience, identify, and respond to deception on dating apps. Through interviews with 22 users, it reveals a typology of deceptive practices (relational, emotional, financial, commercial), documents layered verification strategies users develop over time, and demonstrates that risk recognition is a collaborative, community-driven practice.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Gay dating apps are essential for sexual minority men to find relationships and community, yet deceptive interactions on these platforms are widespread but underexplored in HCI and CSCW literature, particularly in non-Western contexts like China.

Method: Semi-structured interviews with 22 gay male users across four Chinese platforms: Blued, Aloha, Fanka, and Soul. The study employs qualitative analysis to examine users' lived experiences with deception.

Result: Three key findings: (1) A typology of deceptive practices spanning profile misrepresentation, relational, emotional, financial, and commercial deception; (2) users employ layered, probabilistic verification strategies where trust assessment is a multi-signal, provisional process; (3) risk recognition emerges as a collaborative practice through experience-sharing, abstraction of recurring tactics, and community codification of shared rules.

Conclusion: Deception on gay dating apps in China is multifaceted and extends well beyond profile-level misrepresentation. Users develop sophisticated, community-informed strategies for navigating risk, highlighting the need for platform design that supports collaborative safety practices and acknowledges the social, situated nature of trust assessment.

Abstract: Gay dating applications have become critical platforms for sexual minority men to seek relationships and community, yet they also expose users to deceptive interactions that remain underexplored in HCI and CSCW research. This study examines how gay male users in China experience, identify, and respond to deception on dating applications. Through semi-structured interviews with 22 participants across platforms including Blued, Aloha, Fanka, and Soul, we make three contributions. First, we identify a typology of deceptive practices extending beyond profile misrepresentation to encompass relational, emotional, financial, and commercial forms of deception. Second, we document the layered, probabilistic verification strategies users develop through long-term platform use, showing that trust assessment operates as a multi-signal, provisional process rather than a binary judgment. Third, we demonstrate that risk recognition is a collaborative practice shaped by the circulation of experience, the abstraction of recurrent tactics, and the codification of shared rules within the community.

</details>


### [255] [Reading the Same Data Differently: Interpretive Labor Across System Boundaries in Electronic Monitoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27301)
*Yibo Meng,Bingyi Liu,Zhiqi Gao,Shuai Ma,Hongyu Zhou*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper introduces "interpretive misalignment" — the structural divergence in how supervised individuals and authorities make sense of the same EM sensor data due to asymmetric access to data, context, and reasoning processes. Based on interviews with 38 participants in China's community corrections system, the study reveals how this misalignment drives behaviors like probing, over-compliance, and contestation, and offers CSCW design implications for making data-to-decision processes more legible and accountable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on electronic monitoring has focused on its role as a compliance tool or criminal justice mechanism, but little research examines how raw sensor data become meaningful in everyday practice. The authors identify a gap in understanding how the same data stream is interpreted differently by different stakeholders — supervised individuals vs. authorities — and how this asymmetry shapes behavior and system dynamics.

Method: Semi-structured interviews with 26 supervised individuals and 12 authorities within China's community corrections system. The study takes a qualitative, interpretive approach grounded in CSCW perspectives on distributed work and sense-making.

Result: The study identifies "interpretive misalignment" as a core phenomenon: supervised individuals infer system logic from outcomes with limited visibility into how data are processed, while authorities reconstruct behavior from ambiguous traces using contextual knowledge, professional experience, and institutional procedures. This misalignment manifests in five behavioral responses: probing (testing system boundaries), strategic adaptation, over-compliance, disengagement, and contestation.

Conclusion: Electronic monitoring should be understood not merely as compliance infrastructure but as distributed interpretive work across system sides. Design opportunities exist to improve the legibility, contestability, and accountability of data-to-decision processes, reducing the harms of interpretive misalignment in continuous sensing systems.

Abstract: Electronic monitoring (EM) systems are increasingly used in community corrections to enforce spatial, temporal, and behavioral rules through continuous sensing. While prior work has examined EM as a criminal justice tool or as a mechanism for compliance, less is known about how sensed data become meaningful in everyday practice. This poster examines EM as a dual-sided sensing system in which supervised individuals and authorities reason about the same data stream from different positions. Based on semi-structured interviews with 26 supervised individuals and 12 authorities in China's community corrections system, we show that supervised individuals infer system logic from outcomes with limited visibility into how data are interpreted, while authorities reconstruct behavior from ambiguous traces using contextual knowledge, professional experience, and institutional procedures. We call this structural divergence interpretive misalignment. It emerges from asymmetric access to data, context, and reasoning processes, and it shapes behavior through probing, strategic adaptation, over-compliance, disengagement, and contestation. We contribute a CSCW account of continuous sensing as distributed interpretive work and identify design opportunities for making data-to-decision processes more legible, contestable, and accountable across system sides.

</details>


### [256] [AI Healthcare Chatbots as Information Infrastructure: A Large-Scale Study of User-Reported Breakdowns](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27302)
*Muhammad Hassan,Ramazan Yener,Ece Gumusel,Masooda Bashir*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Analysis of 15,000+ user reviews of 59 AI healthcare chatbot apps reveals three core breakdown types—access/reliability, interaction quality, and billing/support—with privacy concerns driving the most negative experiences. Findings highlight how failures in access, usability, and trust undermine these systems as health information infrastructures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI healthcare chatbots are increasingly deployed for health information seeking and self-management, yet empirical research on their real-world performance and user impact remains limited. The study addresses this gap by investigating how these systems function in everyday informational and emotional contexts.

Method: The study analyzes over 15,000 user reviews from 59 AI healthcare chatbot apps using topic modeling and interpretive analysis to identify recurring breakdown patterns. The analysis is grounded in an information infrastructures framework.

Result: Three recurring breakdown categories emerged: (1) access barriers and service unreliability, (2) user experience and interaction quality issues, and (3) billing and customer support problems. Privacy and security concerns were strongly associated with the most negative user experiences.

Conclusion: Failures in access, usability, and trust critically undermine AI healthcare chatbots as information infrastructures. The findings provide actionable insights for designers, policymakers, and information professionals to improve digital health systems.

Abstract: AI healthcare chatbots are increasingly used to support health information seeking and self-management, yet their performance and impact on users remains to be studied. This study examines over 15,000 user reviews from 59 AI healthcare chatbot apps to explore how these systems function in everyday informational and emotional contexts. Topic modeling and interpretive analysis identify three recurring breakdowns: access barriers and service unreliability, user experience and interaction quality, and billing and customer support issues. Privacy and security concerns are associated with the most negative experiences. By framing AI healthcare chatbots as information infrastructures, our findings highlight how failures in access, usability, and trust affect users, offering actionable insights for designers, policymakers, and information professionals aiming to improve digital health systems.

</details>


<div id='cs.AI'></div>

# cs.AI [[Back]](#toc)

### [257] [Agentic Analysis for Agentic Infrastructure: An LLM-Powered Pipeline for Comparative Governance of DAO and Corporate AI Protocols](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26203)
*Yutian Wang,Luyao Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Researchers developed an LLM-powered pipeline to analyze governance discourse at scale, comparing permissionless (ERC-8004) and corporate-led (Google A2A) AI agent protocols. Both regimes showed similar participation inequality and fragmentation, but the permissionless setting exhibited denser discourse alignment, suggesting open governance fosters greater thematic convergence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Governance structures shaping AI agent interoperability standards are proliferating but remain empirically underexamined. There is a gap in large-scale, systematic analysis of how institutional design influences socio-technical power structures, thematic priorities, and community dynamics in technology governance.

Method: An LLM-powered comparative pipeline combining: (1) automated annotation using LLM-assisted coding, (2) neural topic modeling, and (3) multi-layer network analysis. Validated on 4,323 governance participation records from two contrasting cases — ERC-8004 (permissionless, on-chain) and Google A2A (corporate-led).

Result: Governance form influences substantive thematic focus, but both permissionless and corporate-led regimes exhibit comparable levels of participation inequality and community fragmentation. However, discourse alignment is denser in the permissionless ERC-8004 setting, indicating that open governance may foster greater thematic convergence despite decentralized participation.

Conclusion: LLM-assisted methods can effectively advance empirical study of technology governance at scale. The finding that open governance fosters denser discourse alignment (but not necessarily reduced inequality) carries implications for designing more equitable agentic AI standards. All data and code are open-sourced.

Abstract: As AI agent protocols proliferate, the governance structures shaping their interoperability standards remain empirically underexamined. We introduce an LLM-powered comparative pipeline for large-scale governance discourse analysis, integrating automated annotation, neural topic modeling, and multi-layer network analysis to study socio-technical power structures at scale. We validate it on two contrasting standards for agent interoperability: ERC-8004 (permissionless, on-chain) and Google A2A (corporate-led). Analyzing 4,323 governance participation records, we combine LLM-assisted coding, topic modeling, and multi-layer network analysis to examine how institutional design shapes thematic priorities and community structure. We find that while governance form influences substantive focus, both regimes exhibit comparable levels of participation inequality and community fragmentation. Discourse alignment is denser in the permissionless setting, suggesting that open governance may foster greater thematic convergence despite decentralized participation. These findings illustrate how LLM-assisted methods can advance the empirical study of technology governance, with implications for designing more equitable agentic AI standards. All data and code are openly available.

</details>


### [258] [Detecting and Controlling Sycophancy with Cascading Linear Features](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26155)
*Maty Bohacek,Rishub Jain,Nicholas Dufour,Thomas Leung,Chris Bregler,Roma Patel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents an iterative data generation pipeline that isolates cascading linear features in language models for better behavior detection and steering, demonstrated on sycophancy. By moving beyond binary contrastive pairs and instead using samples with features that scale linearly with behavior intensity, the method achieves superior feature disentanglement, enabling more reliable activation steering, deterministic scoring, and interpretability compared to LLM-as-a-judge and system prompting baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Activation steering methods for interpreting and controlling model behaviors rely heavily on contrastive sample pairs that clearly exhibit desired vs. undesired behaviors. However, simple binary pairs are limited in their ability to reliably detect and disentangle model features responsible for a behavior. The authors aim to improve feature isolation by moving beyond binary contrastive data to samples exhibiting behavior along a continuum, enabling more precise steering and interpretability.

Method: The authors propose an iterative data generation pipeline that isolates "cascading linear features" — features that scale linearly with the degree of a target behavior. Rather than using simple positive/negative contrastive pairs, the method generates and selects samples across a spectrum of behavior intensity. These cascading samples are used to identify linearly separable subspaces in model activations that correspond to the behavior (specifically sycophancy). The discovered features are then used for behavior detection, deterministic scoring, and activation steering.

Result: Sycophancy features discovered through cascading samples form linearly separable subspaces and allow selection of model activations that more clearly correspond to the target behavior compared to baseline contrastive approaches. The method matches or outperforms LLM-as-a-judge and system prompting baselines on detection, scoring, and steering tasks, while providing lower computational demand and stronger interpretability guarantees.

Conclusion: Moving from binary contrastive pairs to a cascading, spectrum-based approach enables better disentanglement of linear features responsible for behaviors like sycophancy. The resulting features enable more reliable detection and steering, matching or exceeding baseline methods with greater efficiency and interpretability.

Abstract: Interpreting and controlling model behaviors through activation steering methods requires many pairs of contrastive samples that clearly exhibit desired or undesired behavior. These data pairs determine the degree to which interpretability frameworks can reliably detect model features responsible for a behavior, and therefore the ability to steer models toward or away from such behavior. In this work, we present an iterative data generation pipeline that isolates cascading linear features responsible for a behavior. Specifically, we show how moving beyond simple binary pairs of samples, and instead isolating samples that show degrees of features that scale linearly with behavior, allows for better disentanglement of features. We focus on detecting and steering away from sycophancy -- the tendency of language models to prioritize user validation. We demonstrate that sycophancy features discovered through cascading samples form linearly separable subspaces, and allow for selection of model activations that more clearly correspond to the desired behavior than baseline approaches. We also evaluate their ability to enable detection, deterministic scoring, and robust steering, and see that they either match or outperform LLM-as-a-judge and system prompting baselines while providing lower computational demand and more interpretability guarantees. Code & Data: https://cascading-feats.github.io/

</details>


### [259] [Life After Benchmark Saturation: A Case Study of CORE-Bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26158)
*Nitya Nadgir,Sayash Kapoor,Kangheng Liu,Peter Kirgis,Matilda Orona,Stephan Rabanser,Tilman Bayer,Abhishek Shetty,Yue Ling,Derrick Chan-Sew,Rumi Nakagawa,Saiteja Utpala,Zachary S. Siegel,Arvind Narayanan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Beyond accuracy saturation, evaluating AI agents on construct validity, OOD generalization, efficiency, reliability, model vs. scaffold contribution, and human-agent collaboration uplift yields meaningful insights. Using CORE-Bench as a case study, the authors introduce improved benchmarks (v1.1 and OOD) and demonstrate that efficiency and reliability metrics remain discriminative post-saturation, while human-agent collaboration yields a ~2× speedup on real-world reproducibility tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When benchmark accuracy saturates, the standard practice of retiring it for a harder one overlooks critical evaluation dimensions. The authors argue that accuracy alone is an impoverished signal and that continued measurement along six additional axes — construct validity, OOD generalization, efficiency, reliability, model vs. scaffold disentanglement, and human-agent uplift — can yield valuable insights even after saturation.

Method: The authors use CORE-Bench Hard (a benchmark for computational reproducibility of scientific code) as a case study. They (1) surface construct validity threats (shortcuts) and introduce CORE-Bench v1.1 and an OOD task suite (CORE-Bench OOD); (2) measure efficiency, reliability, and model vs. scaffold contributions on the improved benchmark; and (3) conduct a randomized experiment comparing human-only vs. human-agent collaboration on real-world reproducibility tasks, measuring completion time and success rates.

Result: Construct validity threats (shortcuts exploitable by capable agents) were identified and mitigated in v1.1. Despite accuracy saturation, CORE-Bench v1.1 remained discriminative for efficiency, reliability, model performance, and scaffold performance. The human-agent collaboration experiment showed a statistically significant ~2× speedup, likely underestimated because ~20% of human-only runs hit the time limit without completing.

Conclusion: The dominant accuracy-centric evaluation paradigm is insufficient. A multi-dimensional evaluation framework — incorporating validity, generalization, efficiency, reliability, scaffold disentanglement, and human-agent uplift — provides a more rigorous and informative alternative, yielding actionable insights even when accuracy plateaus.

Abstract: When a benchmark's accuracy saturates, it is often retired and replaced with a more challenging version. We show that this approach privileges accuracy and misses the opportunity to study six other key dimensions of agent performance: construct validity issues such as shortcuts, out-of-distribution generalizability, efficiency, reliability, the relative importance of the model versus the scaffold, and uplift from human-agent collaboration. We use CORE-Bench Hard, a benchmark for computational reproducibility of scientific code, as a case study to demonstrate that measuring agents along these dimensions yields meaningful insights into agent performance even after accuracy saturates. First, we surface threats to construct validity in CORE-Bench Hard that are difficult to anticipate with less capable agents. We introduce an improved benchmark, CORE-Bench v1.1, and an out-of-distribution task suite, CORE-Bench OOD. Second, we find that despite accuracy saturation, CORE-Bench v1.1 remains useful for measuring efficiency, reliability, model performance, and scaffold performance. Finally, we conduct a small-scale randomized experiment to measure uplift from human-agent collaboration on real-world computational reproducibility tasks. We find a statistically significant speedup by about a factor of two -- likely underestimated due to one-fifth of human-only reproductions reaching the time limit before completing -- and describe various other findings. Together, our contributions present a more rigorous alternative to the dominant accuracy-centric evaluation paradigm.

</details>


### [260] [Instruction Bleed: Cross-Module Interference in Prompt-Composed Agentic Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26356)
*Ching-Yu Lin,Yifan Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper formalizes "compositional behavioral leakage" (CBL) — unintended interference between prompt modules sharing a transformer context window due to self-attention's lack of architectural isolation. Through a 144-trial experiment on Claude Sonnet, only content-based perturbations produced detectable but sub-threshold effects (d=0.63), invisible to standard QA but potentially compounding across deployments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Practitioners of prompt-composed agentic systems report that editing one prompt module silently alters the behavior of others, despite no shared variables or executable dependencies. This recurring failure mode lacks formal characterization and systematic measurement protocols, motivating the need to define, detect, and quantify such interference.

Method: The authors formalize CBL and design a reusable three-channel perturbation protocol — volume, content, and form — applied to non-focal modules in a deployed job-evaluation agent (Claude Sonnet 4.6, n=144 trials). They measure paired effects using Cohen's d with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, assessing whether perturbations shift focal-module outputs.

Result: Only the content channel produced a detectable paired effect (Cohen's d = 0.63, CI excluding zero). No recommendation flipped outright — a sub-threshold regime that standard QA evaluations would miss, yet could compound across thousands of agent decisions in deployment.

Conclusion: CBL is orthogonal to known failure modes (adversarial injection, cognitive degradation, multi-agent fault propagation, privacy leakage). The paper establishes cross-module interference measurement as a necessary requirement for prompt-composed agent evaluation and contributes an operational definition, a reusable protocol, and falsifiable predictions.

Abstract: Practitioners of prompt-composed agentic systems report a recurring failure mode: editing one prompt module silently shifts the behavior of others despite no shared variable or executable dependency. We formalize this as compositional behavioral leakage (CBL): interference between modules sharing a context window. CBL is enabled by architectural non-isolation: transformer self-attention provides no formal boundary between concatenated modules. We probe CBL on a deployed job-evaluation agent (Claude Sonnet 4.6, 144 trials) through a reusable three-channel protocol that perturbs non-focal modules along volume, content, and form. Only the content channel produces a detectable paired effect (Cohen's d = 0.63, bootstrap 95% CI excluding zero); no recommendation flipped -- a sub-threshold regime invisible to standard QA but compounding across the thousands of decisions a deployed agent makes. CBL is orthogonal to known agent-failure axes (adversarial injection, cognitive degradation, multi-agent fault propagation, privacy leakage). We contribute an operational definition, a reusable protocol, a falsifiable prediction set, and a system-class characterization, establishing cross-module interference measurement as a requirement for prompt-composed agent evaluation.

</details>


### [261] [Refusal Lives Downstream of Persona in Chat Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26161)
*Viola Zhong,Qirui Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Refusal and persona are not independent mechanisms in chat models — a compliant persona direction gates refusal expression at late layers. Steering the persona direction can nearly eliminate refusal, and this gating occurs downstream of where refusal is computed, meaning refusal cannot be treated as an isolated direction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work identified linear directions for refusal and persona traits separately, but their interaction remained unexplored. The authors aim to demonstrate that these mechanisms are interdependent, challenging the assumption that refusal can be understood in isolation.

Method: The authors extract a compliant model-persona direction and a refusal direction from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct using activation-space intervention techniques. They perform steering interventions (adding/subtracting these directions) and projection-based removal of the persona direction at different layer windows (early vs. late) to assess causal effects on refusal rates.

Result: Compliant persona steering drastically suppresses refusal (e.g., Llama refusal drops from 97% to 2%). Adding back the refusal direction partially restores refusal at late layers but not early ones. Projecting out the persona direction in a late-layer window restores refusal to baseline, while projecting a random direction has no effect.

Conclusion: Refusal expression is gated by persona at the late-layer stage, downstream of where refusal is actually computed. Treating refusal as a single isolated activation direction misses this critical persona-dependence, with implications for both mechanistic interpretability and safety interventions.

Abstract: Linear directions in activation space have been identified for both refusal and persona traits in instruction-tuned chat models, but the two have been studied as separate mechanisms. We show they interact: a compliant persona gates refusal. In Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, we extract a compliant model-persona direction and a refusal direction and intervene on both. Compliant persona steering suppresses refusal -- in Llama, the refusal rate falls from 97% to 2%. Reintroducing the refusal direction partially restores refusal at late layers but not at early ones. Projecting out the persona direction in a late-layer window restores it to baseline; projecting out a random direction does not. Refusal is therefore gated at the late-layer expression stage, downstream of where it is computed. Treating refusal as a single isolated direction misses its dependence on persona.

</details>


### [262] [AlgoEvolve: LLM-driven Meta-evolution of Algorithmic Trading Programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26173)
*Dhruv Sharma,Gautam Shroff*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AlgoEvolve is an LLM-driven evolutionary framework that generates and iteratively improves trading strategies in Python. It features a meta-evolutionary outer loop that evolves prompts for the inner loop, discovering better search heuristics that outperform human-designed instructions. The system exhibits emergent regime-adaptive behavior in noisy, non-stationary financial markets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based semantic evolution for program synthesis has been limited to static coding benchmarks. The authors aim to extend this paradigm to algorithmic trading, a domain characterized by noise, non-stationarity, and discontinuity, which poses unique challenges for autonomous program discovery and adaptation.

Method: AlgoEvolve uses an LLM as a semantic mutation operator within an evolutionary framework. Trading strategies are encoded as executable Python code, evaluated through rigorous backtesting, and iteratively improved via selection and mutation. Critically, a meta-evolutionary outer loop evolves the prompts that guide inner-loop program synthesis, autonomously discovering search heuristics that optimize the exploration-exploitation trade-off and reduce zero-trade failures.

Result: The system produces strategies with emergent regime-adaptive logic, including autonomous shifts in trading rules in response to changing market conditions. The meta-evolved prompts consistently outperform initial human-designed instructions, yielding improved search heuristics that better balance exploration and exploitation while reducing zero-trade failures.

Conclusion: LLM-based semantic evolution is a viable approach for continual program synthesis in complex, dynamic environments. The meta-evolutionary architecture demonstrates that prompts themselves can be productively co-evolved alongside target programs, pointing toward more autonomous and adaptive AI-driven optimization systems.

Abstract: Recent work shows that Large Language Models (LLMs) can act as semantic mutation operators for the evolutionary discovery of programs and proofs. Most current applications focus on static coding benchmarks. We extend this paradigm to algorithmic trading. This domain is uniquely challenging because it is noisy, non-stationary, and highly discontinuous. We present AlgoEvolve, an LLM-driven evolutionary framework that generates, evaluates, and iteratively improves executable trading strategies. These strategies are expressed as Python code and evaluated through a rigorous testing protocol. Across multiple experiments, the system exhibits emergent regime-adaptive strategy logic, including autonomous shifts in trading rules. We further introduce a meta-evolutionary outer loop that evolves the prompts guiding program synthesis in the inner loop. This outer loop discovers improved search heuristics. These heuristics balance exploration and exploitation while reducing zero-trade failures. They consistently outperform initial human-designed instructions. The results demonstrate that LLM-based semantic evolution provides a viable approach for continual program synthesis in complex environments.

</details>


### [263] [Scientific discovery as meta-optimization: a combinatorial optimization case study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26728)
*Yuan-Hang Zhang,Chesson Sipling,Massimiliano Di Ventra*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper formalizes scientific discovery as meta-optimization, where both theories/experiments AND the evaluation criteria co-evolve. The key innovation is "consensus objective aggregation" — combining LLM-generated objective functions via correlation-weighted voting. Applied to 3-SAT algorithm discovery with digital MemComputing, scaling improves from ~N²·⁵¹ to ~N¹·³³, yielding a ~67× speedup.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional approaches treat scientific discovery as optimization over a fixed space of theories and experiments with static evaluation criteria. The authors argue that evaluation criteria themselves should also be optimized simultaneously, since scientific understanding deepens over time. This calls for a meta-optimization framework where the objective function co-evolves with the discoveries.

Method: The proposed framework is "consensus objective aggregation": multiple LLM-generated objective functions are combined through correlation-weighted voting. This produces a stable, self-correcting evaluation criterion that evolves as understanding deepens. The method is formalized as meta-optimization, applied to algorithm discovery for 3-SAT problems using digital MemComputing machines.

Result: The framework reduced baseline scaling with problem size N from approximately N²·⁵¹ to N¹·³³ on 3-SAT instances, delivering a roughly 67× speedup on the largest instances tested.

Conclusion: The authors position their framework as problem-agnostic and express hope that this meta-optimization approach will significantly aid scientific discovery across domains, not just in algorithm discovery for combinatorial problems.

Abstract: Scientific discovery is fundamentally an optimization problem, defined by a vast "state space" of theories and experiments, and an evaluation criterion based on quality, novelty, and validity. Large language models (LLMs) have enabled automated exploration of this space, but we argue that simultaneous modification of the evaluation criteria is equally important. Here, we propose formalizing research as meta-optimization, where the optimization objective itself is also being optimized. Our key contribution is "consensus objective aggregation," where LLM-generated objective functions are combined via correlation-weighted voting, yielding a stable, self-correcting evaluation criterion that evolves as understanding deepens. We apply this framework to algorithm discovery for 3-SAT problems based on digital MemComputing machines, reducing the baseline scaling with problem size $N$ from $\sim N^{2.51}$ to $\sim N^{1.33}$ and delivering a $\sim 67\times$ speedup on the largest instances tested. As a problem-agnostic framework, we hope this approach will considerably aid scientific discovery.

</details>


### [264] [Semantic Early-Stopping for Iterative LLM Agent Loops](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27009)
*Sahil Shrivastava*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Instead of using a fixed iteration cap for multi-agent LLM loops, the authors propose semantic early-stopping based on cosine distance between consecutive draft embeddings. Their judge-free variant cuts operational tokens by 38% with no quality loss, while revealing that identifying the best round remains an open problem.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multi-agent LLM loops (e.g., Writer-Critic) rely on a fixed max_iterations cap, which is a syntactic kill-switch blind to whether answer quality is still improving. This leads to wasted tokens on easy problems and premature truncation on hard ones. The authors aim to replace this with a principled, semantic early-stopping criterion.

Method: The paper proposes semantic early-stopping: the loop halts when (1) the cosine distance between consecutive draft embeddings falls below a threshold for a patience window, and (2) a measured quality score stops improving. Key contributions include: a theoretical framework proving deterministic termination and well-definedness (machine-checked), treating embedding convergence as an empirical conjecture rather than a Banach contraction; a judge-efficient evaluation protocol that generates each question's full trajectory once, replays all stopping policies over identical drafts, and caches LLM-judge calls, cleanly separating operational tokens from evaluation tokens; and empirical testing on HotpotQA multi-hop QA.

Result: On the 60-question HotpotQA test split, the judge-free semantic stopper reduces operational tokens by 38% relative to max_iterations at parity quality (Delta-IS = -0.004, p = 0.81). The full quality-gated variant is counter-productive because per-round judging costs dominate. An oracle selecting the best round achieves +0.115 Information Score over all practical policies (p ≈ 4e-11), suggesting the harder problem is not "when to stop" but "which round is best."

Conclusion: Semantic early-stopping is a viable, cost-effective alternative to fixed iteration caps, with the judge-free variant offering substantial token savings at no quality degradation. However, the substantial performance gap between practical policies and the oracle reframes the core challenge from determining when to stop to identifying which round is optimal — an open problem.

Abstract: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) loops, for example a Writer that drafts and a Critic that revises, are almost always terminated by a fixed iteration cap (max_iterations). This is a syntactic kill-switch: it is blind to whether the answer is still improving, so it over-spends tokens on easy inputs and truncates hard ones. We study semantic early-stopping: the loop halts when consecutive draft embeddings stop changing in meaning (cosine distance with a patience window) and the answer's measured quality stops improving. Our work makes three contributions. First, an honest theoretical footing: we prove deterministic termination and well-definedness and machine-check these claims, while treating the convergence of the distance sequence as an empirically tested conjecture rather than a (previously over-claimed) Banach contraction. Second, a judge-efficient evaluation protocol: we generate each question's full trajectory once, replay every stopping policy over the identical drafts, and cache every LLM-judge call, yielding a strictly paired efficiency-versus-quality comparison at low cost; we further separate operational tokens (charged to a policy) from evaluation tokens (a measurement instrument). Third, an empirical study on multi-hop retrieval-augmented question answering (HotpotQA). On the 60-question test split, a judge-free semantic stopper reduces operational tokens by 38% relative to max_iterations at parity quality (Delta-IS = -0.004, p = 0.81), whereas the full quality-gated variant is counter-productive because its per-round judging dominates cost. An oracle that selects the best round attains +0.115 Information Score over every practical policy (p ~ 4e-11), reframing the problem from "when to stop" (easy) to "which round is best" (open).

</details>


### [265] [Knowledge-augmented Agentic AI for Mental Health Medication Information Seeking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26205)
*Huizi Yu,Jian Liu,Wenkong Wang,Lingyao Li,Jiayan Zhou,Zhaoqian Xue,Xiang Li,Xinxin Lin,Zhiying Liang,Zhuoru Wu,Siyuan Ma,Xin Ma,Lizhou Fan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A provenance-aware, knowledge-graph-based multi-agent framework integrates Reddit posts, WebMD reviews, and FDA adverse event records for nine antidepressants, showing patient-generated data forms a partly independent safety signal — with community sources detecting adverse events hundreds of days before regulatory reporting — while preserving traceability to prevent conflation of evidence and anecdote.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Psychiatric medication safety information is bifurcated: regulatory databases (e.g., FAERS) are authoritative but abstract, while patient narratives (Reddit, WebMD) are experiential but unvalidated. Conflating these sources risks amplifying fear, nocebo responses, and non-adherence in psychiatry. A method is needed to integrate both without losing provenance.

Method: A provenance-aware, knowledge-graph-based multi-agent framework was developed. An LLM entity-recognition pipeline (benchmarked against physician annotations) extracted medications and conditions from 466,525 Reddit posts, 60,782 WebMD reviews, and 20 years of FAERS data for nine antidepressants. Extracted entities were mapped to ATC-N, ICD-10, and MedDRA vocabularies and stored in a Neo4j knowledge graph. Concordance between platforms was quantified via Jaccard similarity, and temporal signal detection compared community reporting dates against FDA dates.

Result: The LLM pipeline achieved F1 scores of 0.969 (medications) and 0.973 (conditions) against physician annotations. Reddit and WebMD showed high mutual concordance (Jaccard similarity up to 0.905) but both diverged substantially from FAERS, indicating an independent patient-generated safety signal. For sertraline, community sources reported many adverse events hundreds of days before the corresponding FDA record date.

Conclusion: Source-aware integration via knowledge graphs enables auditable psychiatric medication information by keeping regulatory facts distinct from patient experience. The approach shows promise for earlier safety signal detection, though prospective evaluation of usefulness and patient benefit is still needed.

Abstract: Patients increasingly seek medication information online, yet safety knowledge for psychiatric drugs is split between regulatory adverse-event records, which are authoritative but abstract, and patient narratives, which are experience-near but unvalidated. Integrating them without conflating evidence and anecdote is especially consequential in psychiatry, where poorly contextualised information can amplify fear, nocebo responses, and non-adherence. Here we develop a provenance-aware, knowledge-graph-based multi-agent framework unifying 466,525 Reddit posts, 60,782 WebMD reviews, and twenty years of U.S. FDA Adverse Event Reporting System records for nine antidepressants. A large-language-model entity-recognition pipeline benchmarked against physician annotations reached highest F1 scores of 0.969 for medications and 0.973 for conditions. The two community platforms were far more concordant with each other (overlap up to a Jaccard similarity of 0.905) than with regulatory reports, indicating that patient-generated data form a partly independent safety signal. For sertraline, many adverse events appeared in community sources hundreds of days before the corresponding FDA date. A Neo4j knowledge graph grounded in ATC-N, ICD-10, and MedDRA vocabularies preserves provenance, keeping every claim traceable and regulatory facts distinct from patient experience. These results establish source-aware integration as a route to more auditable psychiatric medication information, with usefulness and patient benefit to be tested prospectively.

</details>


### [266] [Accelerating Skill Assessment in Chess: A Drift-Diffusion-Enhanced Elo Rating System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26267)
*Tianyuan Zhou,Zhizheng Fu,Tianming Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DD-Elo enhances the traditional Elo rating system by incorporating move-level gameplay data through a drift-diffusion model from cognitive neuroscience, enabling faster adaptation to skill changes while maintaining backward compatibility and theoretical alignment with Elo.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional Elo rating systems suffer from response lag because they rely solely on match outcomes (win/loss/draw), ignoring the rich, granular information contained in individual moves. Incorporating move-level data is challenging due to noise and the vast state space of chess. A method is needed that captures rapid skill fluctuations without sacrificing the established theoretical properties of Elo.

Method: The authors propose DD-Elo (Drift-Diffusion-Enhanced Elo Rating System), which models skill expression as a decision-making process using the drift-diffusion model (DDM) from cognitive neuroscience. The framework integrates move-by-move data to detect rapid skill fluctuations. A rigorous mathematical derivation proves that DD-Elo maintains bounded deviation from traditional Elo, ensuring theoretical alignment and backward compatibility.

Result: Extensive experiments show that DD-Elo adapts to skill changes significantly faster than the traditional Elo system, demonstrating its responsiveness to rapid fluctuations in player performance captured through move-level analysis.

Conclusion: DD-Elo provides an explainable, highly responsive, and backward-compatible rating solution for chess ecosystems, bridging the gap between coarse match-outcome ratings and fine-grained move-level performance assessment.

Abstract: Rating systems such as Elo serve as the gold standard for matchmaking in competitive chess. However, they inherently suffer from response lag due to their exclusive reliance on match outcomes, neglecting the granular quality of gameplay. Nevertheless, incorporating move-by-move information into rating adjustments presents a significant challenge given the substantial noise and the vastness of the game-state space. To address this, we propose the Drift-Diffusion-Enhanced Elo Rating System (DD-Elo), a novel skill assessment framework inspired by the drift diffusion model (DDM) from cognitive neuroscience. By modeling skill expression as a decision-making process, our model integrates move-level data to capture rapid skill fluctuations. We provide a rigorous mathematical derivation proving that DD-Elo maintains a bounded deviation from the traditional Elo system, ensuring theoretical alignment. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DD-Elo adapts to skill changes faster than Elo. Our findings suggest that DD-Elo offers an explainable, highly responsive, and backward-compatible solution for chess rating ecosystems. The implementation code is publicly available at https://github.com/Aquila-zhou1/DD-Elo .

</details>


### [267] [Governing Actions, Not Agents: Institutional Attestation as a Governance Model for Autonomous AI Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26298)
*Jakob Salfeld-Nebgen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a computational governance model where autonomous AI agents retain reasoning autonomy but lack execution authority over high-risk actions. Execution requires independently attested preconditions, cryptographic binding to declared intent, deterministic policy evaluation, and tamper-evident logging.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI agents begin performing consequential, irreversible actions (e.g., clinical prescribing, production software deployment), purely monitoring their reasoning is insufficient for governance. The authors draw inspiration from how human institutions govern powerful actors — not by surveilling internal reasoning but by requiring independently attested evidence at the point of consequential action.

Method: The authors formalize an institutional governance pattern into a computational model with four components: (1) agents retain autonomy over planning/reasoning but no execution authority over designated high-risk actions; (2) execution is conditional on preconditions independently attested by separate authoritative sources; (3) attestations are cryptographically bound to declared intent and evaluated by deterministic policy; (4) all decisions are recorded in a tamper-evident log for independent re-verification. A proof-of-concept implementation is provided.

Result: The paper presents a proof-of-concept implementation demonstrating the model's feasibility, with illustrative examples drawn from software deployment and clinical prescribing domains.

Conclusion: Separating reasoning autonomy from execution authority, enforced through independently attested preconditions and cryptographic binding, offers a viable governance framework for constraining high-risk AI agent actions without requiring direct monitoring of agent reasoning processes.

Abstract: Autonomous AI agents may begin to perform consequential, irreversible actions such as clinical prescribing and production software deployment. This paper observes that human institutions have governed powerful autonomous actors not by monitoring their reasoning but by requiring independently attested evidence at the point of consequential action. We formalise this institutional pattern as a computational governance model for AI agent systems. Under the proposed model, an agent retains full autonomy over planning and reasoning but holds no execution authority over designated high-risk actions. Execution is conditional on preconditions that are each independently attested by a separate authoritative source, cryptographically bound to a declared intent, and evaluated by a deterministic policy. Decisions are recorded in a tamper-evident log amenable to independent re-verification. We present a proof-of-concept implementation and illustrate the model with examples from software deployment and clinical prescribing.

</details>


### [268] [COrigami: An AI Pipeline for Co-Designing Flat-Foldable Visually Recognisable Origami](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26299)
*Tom Zahavy,Shaobo Hou,Thomas Tumiel,James Doran,Francesco Faccio,Xidong Feng,Alex Havrilla,Igor Khytryi,Chenglei Li,Lisa Schut,Vivek Veeriah,Arijan Abrashi,Michał Kosmulski,Robert J. Lang,Nick Robinson,Brandon Wong,Marcus Chiam,Gloria Fang,Satinder Singh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: COrigami is an end-to-end AI pipeline that generates flat-foldable origami crease patterns from natural language descriptions, combining geometric constraint solving with reinforcement learning-based aesthetic refinement to serve as a collaborative design assistant for artists.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While AI excels at tasks with verifiable solutions, generating physical art that satisfies both strict mathematical constraints (flat foldability) and subjective visual aesthetics remains challenging. Computational origami provides a rigorous testbed where artistic design is grounded in precise geometric equations.

Method: The pipeline proceeds in five stages: (1) generating a semantic stick figure from natural language input, (2) computing a base packing, (3) solving for a flat-foldable crease pattern, (4) shaping the flat-folded result, and (5) refining the model via reinforcement learning with an autonomous aesthetic evaluation loop.

Result: The system acts as an effective collaborative assistant, producing structural starting points that human artists can further expand and shape, successfully integrating algorithmic optimization with autonomous aesthetic critique.

Conclusion: By uniting multi-objective physical constraint satisfaction with AI-driven aesthetic evaluation, COrigami demonstrates how AI can enable reliable, mathematically grounded co-creativity in artistic domains with rigid formal requirements.

Abstract: While generative AI has achieved remarkable success in solving problems with verifiable solutions, generating physical art that satisfies both strict geometric constraints and subjective visual aesthetics remains a challenge. This paper presents an approach to tackle these difficulties in the domain of computational origami, a mathematically rigid environment that grounds artistic design within the equations of flat foldability. We present COrigami, an end-to-end AI-driven pipeline that assists the design cycle by generating crease patterns from natural language. Our pipeline involves generating a semantic stick figure, computing a base packing, solving for a flat-foldable crease pattern, shaping the flat-folded crease pattern, and refining the generated model using reinforcement learning driven by an autonomous aesthetic evaluation loop. Our system acts as a highly effective collaborative assistant, generating structural starting points that human artists can further expand and shape. By integrating algorithmic optimisation with autonomous aesthetic critique, this work demonstrates how AI systems can satisfy multi-objective physical constraints to enable reliable, mathematically grounded co-creativity.

</details>


### [269] [The Verification Horizon: No Silver Bullet for Coding Agent Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26300)
*Binghai Wang,Chenlong Zhang,Dayiheng Liu,Jiajun Zhang,Jiawei Chen,Mouxiang Chen,Rongyao Fang,Siyuan Zhang,Xuwu Wang,Yuheng Jing,Zeyao Ma,Zeyu Cui*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: As foundation models grow stronger at generating code, verification has become the bottleneck. Verifiers are imperfect proxies for human intent, suffering from underspecification and optimization-induced reward hacking. The paper characterizes verification quality along scalability, faithfulness, and robustness, arguing that achieving all three is the central challenge. Experiments across four reward constructions show that verification must co-evolve with the generator — no fixed reward function remains effective as policy capability grows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The classical intuition that verification is easier than generation has inverted for modern coding agents. As models become more capable at producing complex solutions, reliably verifying those solutions against human intent has become the harder problem.
