This is exacerbated by two difficulties: (1) intent is inherently underspecified, and (2) optimization during training widens the gap between proxy verifiers and true intent (reward hacking, signal saturation). The paper seeks to systematically characterize and address this verification challenge.

Method: The authors characterize verification signal quality along three dimensions — scalability, faithfulness, and robustness — and study four distinct reward constructions: (1) a test verifier for general coding tasks, (2) a rubric verifier for frontend tasks, (3) the human user as verifier for real-world agent tasks, and (4) an automated agent verifier for long-horizon tasks. They conduct in-depth analysis and experiments across different task types and policy capability levels to examine reward design challenges and strategies for more effectively leveraging reward signals.

Result: Targeted verification design effectively suppresses reward hacking, improves task completion quality, and yields significant gains across multiple internal and public benchmarks. The experiments demonstrate that no fixed reward function remains effective as policy capability continues to grow.

Conclusion: Verification must co-evolve with the generator. As coding agents become more capable, verification strategies must adapt accordingly — a static reward function will inevitably become ineffective. The three-dimensional framework (scalability, faithfulness, robustness) provides a lens for designing verification systems that can keep pace with advancing generation capabilities.

Abstract: A classical intuition holds that verifying a solution is easier than producing one. For today's coding agents, this intuition is being inverted: as foundation models develop stronger reasoning capabilities and engineering harnesses grow more sophisticated, generating complex candidate solutions is no longer difficult -- reliably verifying them has become the harder problem. Every verifier we can build is only a proxy for human intent, never the intent itself. This makes verification subject to a twofold difficulty: first, intent is underspecified by nature, making it inherently hard to faithfully check whether it has been fulfilled; second, during model training, optimization widens the gap between proxy and intent -- manifesting as reward hacking or signal saturation. To address this, we characterize the quality of verification signals along three dimensions -- scalability, faithfulness, and robustness -- and argue that achieving all three simultaneously is the central challenge. We further study four reward constructions: a test verifier for general coding tasks, a rubric verifier for frontend tasks, the user as verifier for real-world agent tasks, and an automated agent verifier for long-horizon tasks. Across different task types and policy capability levels, we conduct in-depth analysis and experiments on the core challenges of reward design and how to more effectively leverage reward signals. Experiments show that targeted verification design can effectively suppress reward hacking, improve task completion quality, and achieve significant gains across multiple internal and public benchmarks. These experiences collectively point to a core observation: no fixed reward function can remain effective as policy capability continues to grow; and verification must co-evolve with the generator.

</details>


### [270] [How Do Tool-Augmented LLM Agents Perform on Real-World Energy Analytics Tasks?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26346)
*David Akinpelu,Akintonde Abbas,Rereloluwa Alimi,Ayodeji Lana*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents an empirical evaluation of tool-augmented LLM agents on 243 real-world energy market analytics tasks, spanning data retrieval, regulatory knowledge, and quantitative modeling. Agents are equipped with live energy market APIs and domain tools, and assessed via a multi-dimensional protocol, revealing how model capability and domain tooling interact in professional energy settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current agentic benchmarks cover domains like finance, coding, and law, but energy-domain evaluations remain limited to static knowledge recall. The energy sector demands live data retrieval, specialized regulatory and market knowledge, and multi-step quantitative reasoning under real-world constraints — a gap this work aims to fill.

Method: The authors construct an evaluation environment with 243 expert-curated problems across three categories: (1) Market Data Retrieval and Analysis, (2) Knowledge Retrieval and Interpretation, and (3) Advanced Quantitative Modeling and Decision Analytics. Agents are equipped with domain tools including live ISO electricity market APIs, regulatory docket search, utility tariff databases, asset optimization models, and RAG over energy market documents. A multi-dimensional evaluation protocol scores approach correctness, answer accuracy, attribute alignment, and source validity, with category-aware routing. Both closed-source and open-source LLMs are evaluated comparatively.

Result: The paper provides a comparative analysis of how model capability and domain-specific tooling interact in high-stakes energy market tasks. Key artifacts are publicly released for reproducibility. (Specific quantitative results are not detailed in the abstract.)

Conclusion: Tool-augmented LLM agents show promise for complex energy market analytics, but performance depends critically on the interplay between model capability and domain tooling. The publicly released benchmark and tooling infrastructure aim to catalyze future research on agentic systems in professional energy domains.

Abstract: Agentic benchmarks have emerged across general-purpose and domain-specific settings, including finance, coding, law, and drug discovery, yet energy-domain evaluations remain largely limited to static knowledge recall. This is a critical gap for a sector that requires live data retrieval, specialized regulatory and market knowledge, and multi-step quantitative reasoning under real-world constraints.
  We present an empirical study of tool-augmented LLM agents on real-world energy market analytics tasks. Our evaluation environment includes 243 expert-curated problems across three categories: (1) Market Data Retrieval and Analysis, (2) Knowledge Retrieval and Interpretation, and (3) Advanced Quantitative Modeling and Decision Analytics. Tasks include price and demand analysis, tariff impact modeling, asset revenue and returns estimation, hedging strategy analysis, and optimization modeling, with problems spanning multiple difficulty levels.
  Agents are equipped with a configurable suite of domain tools, including live electricity market APIs for major U.S. ISOs, regulatory docket search, utility tariff databases, asset optimization models, and retrieval-augmented generation over energy market documents. We assess agent responses using a multi-dimensional evaluation protocol that scores approach correctness, answer accuracy, attribute alignment, and source validity, with category-aware routing to match scoring criteria to question type. We evaluate both closed-source and open-source LLMs, providing a comparative analysis of how model capability and domain tooling interact in a high-stakes professional domain. Key artifacts are publicly released to support reproducibility and future research.

</details>


### [271] [What We are Missing in Multimodal LLM Evaluation?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26348)
*Po-han Li,Shenghui Chen,Sandeep Chinchali,Ufuk Topcu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Current MLLM evaluation benchmarks are task-isolated and fail to assess cross-modal integration. The authors identify key gaps—temporal-spatial coherence, physical world understanding, multimodal consistency, and selective attention—that must be addressed to meaningfully measure multimodal intelligence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MLLM capabilities have advanced rapidly, but evaluation methods lag behind. Existing benchmarks focus on isolated tasks and do not reveal whether models truly integrate information across modalities, making it difficult to gauge genuine progress or identify capability boundaries.

Method: The paper examines current MLLM evaluation approaches and reviews the existing benchmark taxonomy to systematically identify gaps in how multimodal intelligence is assessed.

Result: Four critical gaps in MLLM evaluation were identified: (1) temporal-spatial coherence, (2) physical world understanding, (3) multimodal consistency, and (4) selective attention. These dimensions are underrepresented in current benchmarks.

Conclusion: Addressing the identified gaps is essential for measuring real progress in multimodal intelligence and for exposing the true capability boundaries of MLLMs.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can process diverse inputs, e.g., text, images, audio, and video, and generate textual responses. While their capabilities have advanced rapidly, evaluation of such models has not kept pace. Most existing evaluation benchmarks are limited to isolated tasks and reveal little about whether a model integrates information across modalities. We examine current means for evaluating MLLMs and review the existing benchmark taxonomy to identify gaps, including temporal-spatial coherence, physical world understanding, multimodal consistency, and selective attention. Addressing these gaps is essential for measuring real progress in multimodal intelligence and exposing capability boundaries.

</details>


### [272] [OpenFinGym: A Verifiable Multi-Task Gym Environment for Evaluating Quant Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26350)
*Kaicheng Zhang,Wen Ge,Lei Jiang,Weixin Yang,Jordan Langham-Lopez,Jialin Yu,Lukasz Szpruch,Hao Ni*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OpenFinGym is a unified gym environment for quantitative-finance agents that integrates forecasting, market generation, real-time trading, and fraud detection under one interface, featuring automated task construction from publications, containerized runtime with leakage prevention, paper trading engine, and support for SFT/RL post-training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluation of LLM agents in quantitative finance is fragmented across isolated single-task benchmarks, which overstate agent competence and fail to assess generalization, real-market interaction, and financially meaningful decision-making across interdependent multi-stage workflows (forecasting → strategy → risk management → trading).

Method: The authors propose OpenFinGym, featuring: (1) a unified environment covering forecasting, market generation, real-time trading, and fraud detection; (2) an automated pipeline that converts quantitative-finance publications into executable task packages; (3) a containerized runtime with host-side verifier to prevent train-test leakage; (4) a low-latency paper trading engine with deferred-resolution for long-horizon/event-market forecasts; (5) native integration for SFT and RL post-training.

Result: The paper presents the system architecture and design of OpenFinGym, demonstrating its capacity to unify disparate quantitative-finance tasks under a single execution and verification interface with built-in safeguards against data leakage and mechanisms for scalable agent rollouts.

Conclusion: OpenFinGym addresses the evaluation fragmentation problem in quantitative-finance agent research by providing a holistic, multi-stage benchmark platform that better reflects real financial workflows, enabling more rigorous assessment of agent generalization and decision-making capabilities.

Abstract: Although large language model agents are increasingly applied to quantitative-finance workflows, their evaluation remains fragmented across isolated tasks, while the financial relevance of benchmark tasks is often overlooked. Yet financial workflows are inherently multi-stage, spanning interdependent tasks such as forecasting, strategy construction, risk management, and trading. Existing platforms typically focus on a single task, and can therefore overstate agent competence and fail to reveal weaknesses in generalization, real-market interaction, and financially meaningful decision-making. We introduce OpenFinGym, a unified gym environment for quantitative-finance agent development that covers forecasting, market generation, real-time trading, and fraud detection under a single execution and verification interface. OpenFinGym additionally provides an automated task-construction pipeline that turns quantitative finance publications into executable task packages; a containerised runtime with a host-side verifier service that supports scalable agent rollouts and prevents runtime train-test leakage; a paper trading engine with a low-latency data-stream design; deferred-resolution support for long-horizon and event-market forecasts; and integration for SFT and RL post-training

</details>


### [273] [Accelerating Returns and the Qualitative Engine for Science](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26359)
*Guojun Liao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper critiques Kurzweil's thesis of accelerating returns by arguing that exponential growth in executional/infrastructural capability does not solve the core problem of scientific discovery, which requires qualitative reasoning about conceptual inadequacies. ARC-AGI-3 results (humans at ceiling, AI below 1%) illustrate this gap. The paper positions the Qualitative Engine for Science (QES) as a framework addressing this missing capacity, framed as preserving human scientific wisdom regardless of AGI timelines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To challenge the prevailing assumption that accelerating technological progress (per Kurzweil) naturally leads to accelerated scientific discovery, by distinguishing between quantitative/executional capability and the qualitative reasoning required for genuine conceptual breakthroughs.

Method: The paper provides a mathematical interpretation of Kurzweil's accelerating returns thesis, then draws a conceptual distinction between executional capability (amenable to acceleration) and qualitative reasoning (not reducible to acceleration). It uses ARC-AGI-3 benchmark results as empirical evidence of this gap and references Demis Hassabis's views on human meaning to frame the QES framework as a complementary response.

Result: The central finding is conceptual: accelerating returns apply to infrastructural/executional capabilities but do not address the qualitative reasoning needed for scientific discovery. ARC-AGI-3 provides empirical support — humans achieve ceiling performance while frontier AI systems score below 1%, demonstrating that flexible reasoning remains a large gap. The QES framework is identified as a candidate for addressing this gap.

Conclusion: Kurzweil's theory explains why quantitative capability may accelerate, but the Qualitative Engine for Science (QES) addresses the central problem in scientific discovery that acceleration alone cannot solve. The value of QES is independent of AGI timelines; it preserves and organizes the processes of scientific discovery as a form of human wisdom worth transmitting.

Abstract: Ray Kurzweil described a thesis of accelerating returns, which is the most influential narratives in discussions of technological progress. Its central claim is that advances in multiple technological fields, especially compute, artificial intelligence, brain science, and biotechnology, interact in such a way that progress becomes self-amplifying and approximately exponential. This paper gives a simple mathematical interpretation of that claim and then argues that, even if such acceleration is real, it does not by itself resolve the central problem of scientific discovery. The reason is that accelerating returns apply most naturally to executional and infrastructural capability, whereas genuine discovery often depends on a different capacity: qualitative reasoning about when a current framework is structurally inadequate and what conceptual move is needed next. Recent ARC-AGI-3 results sharpen this distinction: humans solve the benchmark at ceiling, whereas frontier AI systems remain below 1%, indicating that the gap between current AI and human flexible reasoning is still very large. At the same time, Demis Hassabis has emphasized that humans must retain their sense of meaning and what they choose to focus their lives on, a reminder that the future of AI is not only a technical forecast but also a question of what forms of human understanding are worth preserving and transmitting. This paper positions the Qualitative Engine for Science (QES) [3] as a response to that missing capacity. In this view, the Kurzweil theory helps explain why quantitative capability may accelerate, while QES addresses the central problem in scientific discovery that acceleration alone does not solve. Its value does not depend on when AGI arrives, but on the fact that the processes of scientific discovery themselves constitute a form of human wisdom worth preserving, organizing, and making accessible.

</details>


### [274] [Narration-of-Thought: Inference-Time Scaffolding for Defeasible Ethical Reasoning in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26366)
*Patrick Cooper,Alvaro Velasquez*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Chain-of-thought reasoning on moral dilemmas often suffers from stakeholder collapse and uncertainty suppression. The proposed Narration-of-Thought (NoT) prompt structure — with five prescribed sections — nearly eliminates both failure modes across multiple LLM vendors, without any training or fine-tuning, and can be further improved via textual-gradient descent and extended to multi-agent debate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard chain-of-thought reasoning on moral dilemmas exhibits two systematic failure modes: (1) stakeholder collapse, where the trace acknowledges at most one affected party, and (2) uncertainty suppression, where the model commits to an action without expressing unknowns or hedges. These undermine the reliability and auditability of LLM moral reasoning in agentic deployments.

Method: The authors introduce Narration-of-Thought (NoT), a structured system prompt that segments chain-of-thought reasoning into five sequential sections: protagonist, stakeholders, two-step consequences, uncertainty, and commitment. NoT requires no additional training, parameters, or fine-tuning. Experiments use 100 DailyDilemmas scenarios tested on four generators from three vendors, with a matched-budget verbose-CoT baseline to control for token expenditure. Section ablation isolates each sub-instruction's contribution. Textual-gradient descent initialised at NoT further optimizes the scaffold. The approach is also extended to a five-round multi-stakeholder debate protocol.

Result: NoT reduces stakeholder collapse from up to 31% to under 1%, and uncertainty suppression from up to 72% to 1–24% across all models. Against the verbose-CoT control, NoT shows Cliff's delta advantages of +0.79 to +0.90 on stakeholder count and +0.65 to +0.93 on uncertainty score for three of four generators. Section ablation confirms each improvement is attributable to its specific sub-instruction. Textual-gradient descent further improves the scaffold. A cross-family training judge (different vendor from the generator) outperforms an in-family judge on all metrics. The multi-stakeholder debate protocol converts a 6% standoff into 95% full consensus on a calibration set and achieves 100% combined convergence on a DailyDilemmas replication.

Conclusion: NoT provides a lightweight, training-free method to make LLM moral reasoning more complete and auditable by externalizing stakeholders, consequences, and uncertainty before commitment. The approach is robust across model families, improvable via automated optimization, and scalable to multi-agent consensus settings, offering a practical substrate for dependable agentic deployment.

Abstract: Standard chain-of-thought on moral dilemmas exhibits two failure modes: stakeholder collapse (the trace names at most one party with a stake in the outcome) and uncertainty suppression (no explicit unknowns or hedges before committing to an action). We introduce narration-of-thought (NoT), a system prompt that structures chain-of-thought into five sections: protagonist, stakeholders, two-step consequences, uncertainty, then commitment. NoT adds no training, parameters, or fine-tuning. On 100 DailyDilemmas scenarios across four generators from three vendors, NoT cuts stakeholder collapse from up to 31% to under 1% and uncertainty suppression from up to 72% to 1-24% on every model. A matched-budget verbose-CoT control rules out token spend as the active ingredient; NoT retains Cliff's delta advantages of +0.79 to +0.90 on stakeholder count and +0.65 to +0.93 on uncertainty score for three of four generators, and a section ablation attributes each shift to its specific sub-instruction. Textual-gradient descent initialised at NoT improves the scaffold further; a cross-family training judge (different vendor from the generator) dominates an in-family one on every measured axis. Extended to a five-round multi-stakeholder debate protocol, the scaffold converts a 6% standoff into 95% full consensus on a calibration set and 100% combined convergence on a DailyDilemmas replication. The resulting traces externalise the stakeholders, consequences, and uncertainty grounding each commitment, providing an auditable substrate for dependable agentic deployment.

</details>


### [275] [AgentX: Towards Agent-Driven Self-Iteration of Industrial Recommender Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26859)
*Changxin Lao,Fei Pan,Guozhuang Ma,Han Li,Huihuang Lin,Jijun Shi,Kangzhi Zhao,Kun Gai,Mo Zhou,Qinqin Zhou,Quan Chen,Ruochen Yang,Shifu Bie,Shuang Yang,Shuo Yang,Wenhao Li,Wentao Xie,Xiao Lv,Xuming Wang,Yijun Wang,Yiming Chen,Yusheng Huang,Zhongyuan Wang,Zibo Zhao,Zijie Zhuang,Baoning Xia,Chao Liu,Chaoyi Ma,Chubo He,Dawei Cong,Feng Jiang,Gang Wang,Guilin Xia,Hanwen Xu,Jiahong Xie,Jiahui Qiao,Jian Liang,Jiangfan Yue,Jing Wang,Jinghan Yang,Jinghui Jia,Kan Qin,Lei Wang,Ming Li,Peilin Song,Pengbo Xu,Qiang Luo,Ruiming Tang,Shiyang Liu,Shuxian Jin,Tao Wang,Tao Zhang,Xiang Gao,Xianghan Li,Yingsong Luo,Yiwen Ning,Yongcheng Liu,Yuan Guo,Zhaojie Liu,Zhenkai Cui*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AgentX is a production-deployed multi-agent system that automates the entire recommendation algorithm research loop — from hypothesis generation and code implementation to A/B evaluation and self-improvement — replacing the manual, engineer-bound process with a self-evolving, compounding engine.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current recommendation algorithm iteration suffers from a structural bottleneck: the idea-to-launch cycle depends on human engineers for hypothesis generation, code modification, A/B experiments, and result attribution. This causes innovation to scale linearly with headcount rather than compounding with evidence, compute, and accumulated knowledge.

Method: AgentX orchestrates four stages in a closed loop: (1) Brainstorm Agent synthesizes evidence from historical experiments, system architecture, data analysis, and external research into ranked executable proposals; (2) Developing Agent translates proposals into production-ready code via repository-grounded generation and multi-dimensional reliability verification; (3) Evaluation Agent conducts safe online rollout with guardrail-vetoed A/B judgment, converting outcomes into structured knowledge assets; (4) Harness Evolution layer (SGPO) distills execution trajectories into semantic-gradient updates that continuously sharpen the agents, enabling self-improvement.

Result: AgentX is production-deployed and autonomously generates, implements, evaluates, and learns from recommendation experiments at a scale and pace that no manual workflow can sustain.

Conclusion: By restructuring the production function into a self-evolving development engine, AgentX breaks the linear scaling constraint of human-dependent iteration, enabling recommendation systems to compound improvements through automated evidence accumulation and agent self-refinement.

Abstract: Recommendation algorithm iteration is moving from an artisanal, engineer-bound process toward an industrialized research loop, but this transition remains blocked by a structural execution bottleneck: the idea-to-launch cycle still depends on human engineers to generate hypotheses, modify production code, launch A/B experiments, and attribute online results. Innovation therefore scales linearly with headcount rather than compounding with evidence, compute, and accumulated experimental knowledge. We present AgentX, a production-deployed multi-agent system that fundamentally restructures this production function. AgentX operates as a self-evolving development engine: it autonomously generates, implements, evaluates, and learns from recommendation experiments at a scale and pace that no manual workflow can sustain.
  The system orchestrates four tightly coupled stages in a closed loop. A Brainstorm Agent synthesizes evidence from historical experiments, system architecture, data analysis, and external research into ranked, executable proposals. A Developing Agent translates each proposal into production-ready code through repository-grounded generation and multi-dimensional reliability verification. An Evaluation Agent conducts safe online rollout with guardrail-vetoed A/B judgment, converting both successes and failures into structured knowledge assets. A Harness Evolution layer (SGPO) then distills execution trajectories into semantic-gradient updates that continuously sharpen the agents themselves -- making the system not merely automated, but self-improving.

</details>


### [276] [Geometry-Aware MCTS for Extremal Problems in Combinatorial Geometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26399)
*Luoning Zhang,Xu Zhuang,Tianhao Wang,Nathan Kaplan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a Geometry-Aware Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) framework to solve extremal combinatorial geometry problems on n×n grids. It features incremental feasible-action updates (reducing collinearity-checking from O(n³) to O(n²)), canonical symmetry pruning, and symmetric batch transitions. The method achieves new state-of-the-art results on five of six benchmark problems, notably finding configurations of size ~1.8n for Max-No-Three-in-Line (82 ≤ n ≤ 119) and ~0.95n for the Smallest Complete Set problem.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical exact solvers suffer from combinatorial explosion on extremal point-configuration problems with global geometric constraints. Reinforcement learning and transformer-based models face a sparse-reward "validity cliff" and quadratic token-consumption limits. There is a need for a search framework that efficiently enforces geometric constraints while scaling to larger grid sizes.

Method: The authors introduce a Geometry-Aware MCTS framework with three key innovations: (1) incremental updates to the feasible action space that strictly enforce geometric constraints, reducing collinearity-checking from O(n³) to O(n²) for No-Three-in-Line; (2) canonical pruning during node expansion to exploit geometric symmetries and reduce the branching factor; and (3) symmetric batch transitions to accelerate discovery of promising configurations by applying symmetry transformations to rollouts.

Result: The framework establishes new best-known computational results on five of six problems tested. For Max-N3IL, it finds configurations of size roughly 1.8n for grids 82 ≤ n ≤ 119. For the Smallest Complete Set problem, it achieves configurations of roughly 0.95n, providing improved upper bounds within the tested grid sizes.

Conclusion: Geometry-Aware MCTS is established as a highly adaptable and effective framework for discovering novel configurations in combinatorial geometry, overcoming the scalability and sparsity limitations of prior exact and learning-based approaches.

Abstract: We study certain extremal problems in combinatorial geometry that ask about configurations of points in an $n \times n$ grid that satisfy strict, global geometric constraints. Classical exact solvers suffer from combinatorial explosion for these types of problems, and standard reinforcement learning and transformer-based models struggle with the sparse reward "validity cliff" and quadratic token-consumption limits. To overcome these bottlenecks, we propose a Geometry-Aware Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) framework. Our approach strictly enforces geometric constraints through incremental updates to the feasible action space. For constraints about collections of collinear points, like those that occur in the classic No-Three-in-Line problem (Max-N3IL), this mechanism reduces the constraint checking complexity from $O(n^3)$ to $O(n^2)$. To improve search efficiency, we exploit geometric symmetries in two ways: canonical pruning during node expansion to reduce the branching factor, and symmetric batch transitions to accelerate the discovery of promising configurations. We perform extensive experiments and establish new best-known computational results on five out of six of the problems that we considered. Notably, for Max-N3IL we find configurations of size roughly $1.8 n$ for grids of size $82 \le n \le 119$. For the Smallest Complete Set problem, we find configurations of size roughly $0.95 n$, providing new upper bounds within the tested grids. This work establishes Geometry-Aware MCTS as a highly adaptable framework for discovering novel configurations in combinatorial geometry.

</details>


### [277] [When Agents Meet Electric Bus Fleet Operations: Pricing Behavior, Trade-offs, and Policy Implications in an Aggregator Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26400)
*Jônatas Augusto Manzolli,Ali Eslami,Luis Miranda-Moreno,Jiangbo Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An agentic aggregator framework combining optimization-based scheduling with supervisory AI agents is proposed for electric bus fleet coordination. The system handles real-time disturbances (delays, energy deviations, price shocks) and supports both profit-based and operation-based modes. Results show adaptive fleet-grid coordination is achievable, but profit-oriented configurations can extract value from public transport operators, highlighting the need for transparent governance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Electric bus fleet operations require continuous coordination across multiple dynamic variables (battery state-of-charge, charger availability, electricity prices, route-energy uncertainty, V2G opportunities). Traditional optimization approaches struggle with real-time disturbances and the complexity of balancing aggregator profitability against public transport operator (PTO) interests. An agentic paradigm can streamline this decision environment by coupling optimization with supervisory intelligence.

Method: The authors propose an agentic aggregator framework with two layers: (1) an optimization-based electric bus scheduling core enforcing physical feasibility across routes, chargers, batteries, and V2G exchanges; (2) a supervisory agentic layer performing disturbance detection, tariff adaptation, and schedule evaluation. The framework is tested via a realistic depot case study comparing day-ahead and real-time operations under profit-based versus operation-based coordination modes, with injected disturbances including service delays, route-energy deviations, electricity price shocks, and combined scenarios.

Result: The agentic aggregation framework successfully maintains feasible schedules under disturbances, selectively activates re-optimization to avoid unnecessary computation, and improves utilization of both charging and V2G flexibility. However, a critical trade-off emerges: profit-oriented agent configurations can extract disproportionate value from the PTO. Operation-based modes showed fairer value distribution.

Conclusion: Agentic aggregators are promising for managing electric bus V2G operations, but deployment in public-fleet contexts demands transparent coordination modes, auditable tariff-setting mechanisms, and explicit value-sharing rules to prevent exploitation of public operators.

Abstract: Agentic systems are changing how complex operational tasks are coordinated, introducing a new paradigm for connecting heterogeneous data sources and automating processes. Electric bus fleets provide a relevant test case. Their operation requires continuous coordination between service reliability, battery state-of-charge, charger availability, electricity prices, route-energy uncertainty, and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) opportunities. This paper proposes an agentic aggregator framework that streamlines this decision environment by coupling an optimization-based electric bus scheduling model with supervisory agents for disturbance detection, tariff adaptation, and schedule evaluation. The optimization core enforces physical feasibility across routes, chargers, batteries, and V2G exchanges, while the agentic layer interprets changing operating conditions, triggers real-time re-optimization when needed, and defines how flexibility value is allocated between the aggregator and the public transport operator (PTO). A realistic depot case study evaluates day-ahead and real-time operations under profit-based and operation-based coordination modes, considering service delays, route-energy deviations, electricity price shocks, and combined disturbances. The results show that agentic aggregation can support adaptive fleet-grid coordination by maintaining feasible schedules, activating re-optimization selectively, and improving the use of charging and V2G flexibility. However, they also reveal a critical trade-off: the same agentic capability that reduces operational complexity can extract value from the PTO when configured around profit-oriented pricing. These findings suggest that agentic aggregators can become useful for managing electric bus V2G operations, but their deployment in public-fleet contexts requires transparent coordination modes, auditable tariff-setting, and explicit value-sharing rules.

</details>


### [278] [Unbiased Canonical Set-Valued Oracles Via Lattice Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26418)
*Jobst Heitzig*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper addresses the self-reference problem in oracle AI: when an oracle's probability estimate is learned and acted upon, it can alter the event it was predicting. Instead of the Scientist AI counterfactual approach, the authors propose a self-referential alternative where the oracle outputs a *credal set* (a set of probabilities) that is unbiased and self-consistent with the consequences of being learned. Using the Knaster–Tarski fixed-point theorem on the complete lattice of closed credal sets, they identify a canonical least fixed point, prove its properties, and show it reduces to the classical point estimate for non-performative questions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Oracle AIs that estimate event probabilities face a performative self-reference problem: the act of learning and acting on the oracle's answer can alter the very probability reported. The Scientist AI approach of asking only counterfactual questions renders answers irrelevant once learned. The motivation is to find a self-consistent reporting mechanism that remains relevant and unbiased even when the answer influences the world.

Method: The paper develops a lattice-theoretic framework where oracles report closed credal sets (subsets of [0,1]) rather than point probabilities. Self-consistency is defined via an isotone operator on the complete lattice of closed credal sets. The canonical answer is the least fixed point of this operator, obtained via the Knaster–Tarski fixed-point theorem. A variant reports the least fixed point containing all self-consistent point estimates. The framework extends from binary events to arbitrary random variables by replacing conditional probability with conditional law.

Result: The authors prove existence, self-consistency, and nonemptiness of the canonical credal set. For non-performative questions, the construction collapses to the classical point probability. Under a hull-factoring assumption for binary events, the canonical answer is an interval. The framework generalizes naturally to arbitrary random variables, though it is an open question whether the interval characterization survives that generalization.

Conclusion: The paper offers a principled alternative to counterfactual oracles via self-referential credal sets, providing a mathematically rigorous (lattice-theoretic) solution that yields nontrivial, canonical answers. Several open questions remain, notably whether the interval structure persists for non-binary random variables.

Abstract: A non-agentic "oracle" AI that estimates probabilities of future events faces a self-reference problem: once its answer is learned and acted upon, it can change the very probability it was asked to report. One response, advocated for the Scientist AI programme, is to ask only counterfactual questions, evaluated as if the answer had no influence. We observe that such answers tend to become irrelevant the moment they are learned, precisely because their premise is then false. We therefore explore a self-referential alternative in which the oracle reports not a single probability but a credal set that is simultaneously unbiased and self-consistent with the consequences of being learned. The naive self-consistency requirement is satisfied by too many sets (including the useless answer $[0,1]$), so the problem is to single out a canonical, nontrivial member. We do so with the Knaster--Tarski fixed-point theorem on the complete lattice of closed credal sets, taking the least fixed point of a suitably defined isotone operator; a variant instead reports the least fixed point that contains every self-consistent point estimate. We prove existence, self-consistency, and nonemptiness, show that the construction collapses to the classical point answer for non-performative questions, and that for a binary event the canonical answer is, under a natural hull-factoring assumption, an interval. The development is purely lattice-theoretic and extends unchanged from a binary event $B$ to an arbitrary random variable $X$, with $P(B\mid A,C)$ replaced by the conditional law $\mathcal{L}(X\mid A,C)$. We close with open questions, including whether the interval characterization itself survives that generalization.

</details>


### [279] [Estimating Uncertainty in Classifier Performance with Applications to Large Language Models and Nested Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26422)
*Kylie Anglin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper evaluates confidence interval methods for text classification performance metrics under realistic social science conditions (small samples, rare classes, nested data), finding that commonly used Wald and basic bootstrap intervals perform poorly. It recommends Agresti-Coull, Wilson, Clopper-Pearson, and a novel pseudo-count regularized bootstrap, while also addressing clustered/hierarchical data structures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Social science researchers increasingly use text classification to measure constructs, reporting point estimates like recall and precision as validity evidence, yet uncertainty measures (confidence intervals) are inconsistently reported. When reported, methods are often inappropriate for conditions typical in this field: small labeled datasets, infrequent constructs, and texts nested within individuals.

Method: The authors conducted simulation studies evaluating confidence interval methods under conditions typical of social science text classification: small to moderate sample sizes, infrequent constructs, and nested data structures. Methods compared include Wald intervals, basic percentile bootstrap, Agresti-Coull, Wilson, Clopper-Pearson, and a novel pseudo-count regularized bootstrap (especially for F1). For nested data, they examined analytic adjustments (effective N and degrees of freedom), hierarchical bootstrap, and cluster bootstrap.

Result: Default methods (Wald interval, basic percentile bootstrap) showed the worst accuracy, with coverage often substantially below the nominal 95% level. Agresti-Coull, Wilson, Clopper-Pearson, and the pseudo-count regularized bootstrap substantially improved accuracy. For nested texts, adjusting for both effective N and appropriate degrees of freedom was necessary for accurate analytic intervals. The hierarchical bootstrap outperformed the cluster bootstrap with moderate numbers of texts per individual but was overly conservative with few texts per individual.

Conclusion: The paper provides practical guidance on appropriate confidence interval methods for text classification in social science contexts, aiming to improve transparency in machine learning applications and encourage greater attention to validation sample size at the design stage.

Abstract: Researchers increasingly use text classification--supervised models or large language models--to measure constructs from natural language, providing metrics such as recall and precision as evidence of their validity. Yet, though these metrics are point estimates subject to sampling variation, measures of uncertainty are inconsistently reported alongside them. Further, when they are reported, they are often estimated with methods that are not appropriate when relevant labelled datasets are small or performance is high. To increase and improve confidence interval reporting in the field, this paper evaluates confidence interval methods for performance metrics under conditions typical of social science text classification: small to moderate sample sizes, infrequent constructs, and texts nested within individuals. Across simulations, default methods such as the Wald interval and the basic percentile bootstrap are the least accurate, with coverage sometimes far below the nominal 95% level. Accuracy is improved with the use of Agresti-Coull, Wilson, Clopper-Pearson, and a novel pseudo-count regularized bootstrap (which is particularly relevant to the calculation of F1). When texts are nested within individuals, we demonstrate that adjustment for both effective N and the appropriate degrees of freedom is necessary for producing accurate analytic intervals. Among bootstrap intervals, the hierarchical bootstrap is more accurate than the cluster bootstrap when individuals produce a moderate number of texts but overly conservative when individuals produce only a few. By providing guidance to the field on appropriate interval estimation, we aim to improve the transparency of machine learning applications, and to encourage greater attention to the validation sample size at the design stage.

</details>


### [280] [Data-driven Machine Learning Cannot Reach Symbolic-level Logical Reasoning -- The Limit of the Scaling Law](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26454)
*Tiansi Dong,Mateja Jamnik,Pietro Liò*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper argues that supervised deep learning cannot achieve rigorous syllogistic reasoning due to two fundamental limitations: indistinguishable training data across 24 valid syllogism types, and contradictory training targets between pattern recognition and logical reasoning components. Experiments with Euler Net and ChatGPT (GPT-5 variants) support this claim, showing surface form dependency and incorrect explanations despite 100% accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sphere neural networks have demonstrated symbolic-level syllogistic reasoning without training data, prompting the question: can data-driven supervised learning systems reach the same rigorous logical reasoning capability simply by scaling data and training time? The authors seek to identify the fundamental limits of the scaling law for logical reasoning.

Method: The authors provide theoretical analysis identifying two methodological limitations. They experimentally test Euler Net (a neural-symbolic model) on syllogistic reasoning tasks. They further evaluate ChatGPT (GPT-5-nano and GPT-5) on determining satisfiability of syllogistic statements across four surface forms: words, double words, simple symbols, and long random symbols, examining both accuracy and explanation quality.

Result: (1) Training data cannot distinguish all 24 valid syllogistic reasoning types. (2) End-to-end mapping from premises to conclusion creates contradictory training targets between pattern recognition and logical reasoning components. Euler Net fails to achieve rigorous syllogistic reasoning. ChatGPT GPT-5 reaches 100% accuracy on some surface forms but still produces incorrect explanations, and reasoning performance varies with surface form. Training is typically stopped at 100% accuracy, masking underlying logical deficiencies.

Conclusion: Supervised machine learning systems will not attain the rigor of symbolic logical reasoning, as the two identified limitations are structural rather than issues solvable by more data or compute. The ability to reach 100% accuracy without genuine logical understanding means empirical training processes will prematurely terminate, leaving the system logically unsound.

Abstract: Sphere neural networks have achieved symbolic level syllogistic reasoning without training data, raising the question of where the limit of the scaling law for logical reasoning lies, i.e., whether data-driven machine learning systems can achieve the same level by increasing training data and training time. We show two methodological limitations that prevent supervised deep learning from reaching the symbolic-level syllogistic reasoning: (1) training data can not distinguish all 24 types of valid syllogistic reasoning; (2) end-to-end mapping from premises to conclusion introduces contradictory training targets between neural components for pattern recognition and logical reasoning. Beside theoretical analysis, we experimentally illustrate that Euler Net cannot achieve rigorous syllogistic reasoning. We further challenge the most recent ChatGPTs (GPT-5-nano and GPT-5) to determine the satisfiability of syllogistic statements in four surface forms (patterns): words, double words, simple symbols, and long random symbols, showing that surface forms affect the reasoning performance and that ChatGPT GPT-5 may reach 100% accuracy but still provide incorrect explanations. As empirical training processes are stopped after achieving 100% accuracy, we conclude that supervised machine learning systems will not attain the rigour of symbolic logical reasoning.

</details>


### [281] [Context-Aware Synthesis of Optimization Pipelines for Warehouse Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26852)
*Janik Bischoff,Anne Meyer,Uta Mohring,Fabian Dunke,Maximilian Barlang,Özge Nur Subas,Hadi Kutabi,Stefan Nickel,Kai Furmans*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CASOP is a framework that automatically synthesizes and evaluates valid optimization pipelines for order fulfillment in manual warehouses by composing modular algorithms based on warehouse context, bridging the gap between integrated models and decomposed practical approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While integrated optimization models capture interdependencies between item assignment, order batching, and picker routing, real-world warehouse systems often require decomposed approaches. Existing research lacks a general mechanism to determine applicable algorithm configurations, compose them into valid pipelines, and systematically assess their performance across diverse contexts.

Method: CASOP features five components: (1) a modular algorithm repository, (2) semantic data/algorithm cards for context description, (3) a taxonomy structuring order fulfillment into subproblems, (4) a pipeline synthesizer that matches algorithms to context and composes valid pipelines, and (5) a pipeline evaluator for performance assessment.

Result: Applied to 7 benchmark instance sets across four problem classes, the framework generated 1,063,044 valid pipelines, demonstrating its capacity to handle diverse warehouse contexts at scale.

Conclusion: CASOP supports researchers and practitioners in designing, synthesizing, and selecting high-performing algorithmic pipelines for warehouse operations. The framework is open-source.

Abstract: Order fulfillment in manual picker-to-goods warehouses involves interconnected decisions such as item assignment, order batching, and picker routing. While integrated models capture interactions between these decisions, practical warehouse systems often require decomposed approaches due to organizational boundaries, differing responsibilities, or limited data availability. Existing studies primarily evaluate algorithms for isolated subproblems or fixed subproblem combinations for specific warehouse settings, but lack a general mechanism to determine applicable algorithm configurations, compose them into valid solution pipelines, and assess their performance.
  With Context-Aware Synthesis of Optimization Pipelines (CASOP), we propose a framework for constructing and evaluating context-specific optimization pipelines and apply these to order fulfillment. The framework comprises: (1) a modular repository of algorithms for common order fulfillment problems; (2) semantic data and algorithm cards to describe warehouse context and algorithm requirements; (3) a taxonomy that structures order fulfillment problems into relevant subproblems; (4) a pipeline synthesizer that identifies applicable algorithms for a given warehouse context and composes all valid optimization pipelines; and (5) a pipeline evaluator that assesses all resulting pipelines. We demonstrate the framework on 7 benchmark instance sets covering four problem classes, resulting in 1,063,044 valid pipelines. The framework supports researchers and practitioners in designing, automatically synthesizing, and selecting valid, high-performing algorithmic pipelines for warehouse operations. The software is open-source and available at https://github.com/kit-dsm/ware_ops_pipes and https://github.com/kit-dsm/ware_ops_algos.
  Keywords: Warehouse optimization, Algorithm selection, Pipeline synthesis, Order fulfillment

</details>


### [282] [MKG-RAG-Bench: Benchmarking Retrieval in Multimodal Knowledge Graph-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26458)
*Xiaochen Wang,Bao Hoang,Han Liu,Ting Wang,Fenglong Ma*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MKG-RAG-Bench is a cross-domain benchmark designed to evaluate retrieval in multimodal knowledge graph RAG, constructed from two MKGs (general & medical domains) with aligned QA datasets. Experiments show multimodal retrieval remains challenging yet critical for end-to-end performance, with retrieval quality strongly determining generation outcomes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RAG benchmarks overlook retrieval challenges in multimodal knowledge graph settings, where heterogeneous multimodal knowledge is difficult to align and poorly served by retrievers designed for unstructured corpora. Retrieval is identified as a critical bottleneck in MKG-RAG pipelines.

Method: Construct MKG-RAG-Bench from two multimodal KGs (general and medical domains) using an LLM-based curation pipeline that filters low-utility knowledge, generates structurally grounded queries with exact supervision, and systematically covers diverse modality configurations. The benchmark includes aligned QA datasets supporting controlled evaluation of both retrieval and downstream generation.

Result: Extensive experiments across representative retriever families and modality settings demonstrate that effective multimodal retrieval remains challenging yet crucial for end-to-end MKG-RAG performance, and that retrieval quality strongly determines generation outcomes.

Conclusion: By isolating retrieval as a first-class evaluation target, MKG-RAG-Bench provides a principled foundation for diagnosing current limitations and advancing multimodal knowledge graph RAG systems.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over knowledge graphs has emerged as a promising approach for grounding large language models, yet existing benchmarks largely overlook the challenges of retrieval in multimodal knowledge graph RAG (MKG-RAG). In practice, retrieval is a critical bottleneck: multimodal knowledge is heterogeneous, difficult to align across modalities, and often poorly served by retrievers designed for unstructured corpora. To address this gap, we introduce MKG-RAG-Bench, a cross-domain benchmark explicitly designed to evaluate retrieval in MKG-RAG. MKG-RAG-Bench is constructed from two multimodal knowledge graphs spanning general and medical domains, and includes carefully aligned question-answering datasets that support controlled evaluation of both retrieval and downstream generation. The benchmark is built using an LLM-based curation pipeline that filters low-utility knowledge, generates structurally grounded queries with exact supervision, and systematically covers diverse modality configurations. Through extensive experiments across representative retriever families and modality settings, we show that effective multimodal retrieval remains challenging yet crucial for end-to-end MKG-RAG performance, and that retrieval quality strongly determines generation outcomes. By isolating retrieval as a first-class evaluation target, MKG-RAG-Bench provides a principled foundation for diagnosing current limitations and advancing multimodal knowledge graph RAG systems.

</details>


### [283] [auto-psych: Automating the science of mind using agent-driven theory discovery and experimentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26460)
*Ben Prystawski,Kushin Mukherjee,Daniel Wurgaft,Linas Nasvytis,Michael Y. Li,Noah D. Goodman,Michael C. Frank*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Auto-psych is an agent-based system that autonomously generates, tests, and refines cognitive theories by collecting human data through crowdsourced experiments. It uses nested loops — an inner loop for model fitting and an outer loop for experiment design — to successfully recover ground-truth theories from synthetic data and discover novel theories that outperform literature-derived models on human coin-flip randomness judgments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Data collection remains a major bottleneck in AI-driven scientific automation. Computational cognitive science is uniquely suited for automated experimentation because theories are often expressed as code and crowdsourcing enables scalable human data collection. The authors aim to demonstrate that fully automated, closed-loop theory discovery — from hypothesis generation through experiment design to human data collection — is feasible in this domain.

Method: The authors develop auto-psych, a system with two nested agent-based discovery loops. The inner loop conjectures probabilistic cognitive models, fits them to data, and critiques them. The outer loop designs experiments to discriminate between competing models, launches them as crowdsourced surveys (using the coin-flip randomness judgment task), collects human responses, and feeds results back to the inner loop. The system is validated on synthetic data and then deployed in three independent sequences of human experiments.

Result: Auto-psych reliably recovers ground-truth theories from synthetic data, with the nested loop structure proving critical to performance. In three human experiment sequences, the system discovers theories that fit the data better than theories drawn from the existing scientific literature.

Conclusion: Fully automated data collection and theory discovery in computational cognitive science is feasible. The nested agent-based architecture enables systematic, closed-loop scientific reasoning that can both recover known theories and generate novel, empirically superior ones.

Abstract: AI-based scientific automation is increasingly possible by using agents to generate hypotheses, design experiments, and analyze data. Data collection is a major bottleneck in this pipeline, however. Psychology, and computational cognitive science in particular, is well-positioned to benefit from AI experimentation because theories are often represented as code and crowdsourcing platforms enable programmatic human data collection at scale. Here, we apply automated discovery techniques to the project of generating theories in computational cognitive science, with an agent-based system collecting human data independently through crowdsourced survey experiments. As a testbed, we use a classic case study from cognitive psychology: judging which sequences of coin flips seem subjectively more random. Our system, auto-psych, uses nested agent-based discovery loops to generate explanatory theories of human behavior. The inner loop conjectures, fits, and critiques probabilistic cognitive models; the outer loop designs experiments to test these models, launches them online, and analyzes the data. This system can quickly and reliably recover ground-truth theories from synthetic data via systematic experimentation, but the nested structure is critical to model performance. Further, in three independent sequences of human experiments, the system finds theories that fit the data better than theories generated from the scientific literature. This work thus demonstrates the feasibility of automated data collection and theory discovery in computational cognitive science.

</details>


### [284] [Clinical Harness for Governable Medical AI Skill Ecosystems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26494)
*Tianhan Xu,Lei Bao,Yongxiang Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a Clinical Harness architecture for orchestrating diverse AI "skills" (knowledge-driven, data-driven, physics-enhanced) under runtime governance to enable persistent, accountable clinical capabilities, demonstrated through an osteoporosis care lifecycle exemplar.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current medical AI is fragmented into isolated, single-purpose models that lack the persistence and accountability required for real-world clinical care, which demands continuous, coordinated capabilities across a patient's care lifecycle.

Method: The authors introduce (1) the concept of "clinical AI skills" — composable, AI-enabled clinical capabilities — and (2) the Clinical Harness, a runtime governance architecture that registers, orchestrates, guards, and monitors these skills. The approach is validated using osteoporosis as an exemplar, integrating knowledge-driven (e.g., clinical guidelines), data-driven (e.g., ML models), and physics-enhanced (e.g., biomechanical simulations) skills.

Result: The osteoporosis exemplar demonstrates that heterogeneous AI skills can be composed and governed at runtime to support lifecycle care — from screening and diagnosis through treatment planning and follow-up — while maintaining accountability through continuous monitoring and guardrails.

Conclusion: The Clinical Harness architecture represents a paradigm shift from isolated AI models to governed, persistent clinical AI capabilities, enabling safe, accountable, and lifecycle-aware AI integration into real-world clinical workflows.

Abstract: Medical AI remains organized around isolated models, whereas clinical care requires accountable capabilities that persist across time. We propose clinical AI skills and the Clinical Harness: a runtime governance architecture for registering, orchestrating, guarding and monitoring AI-enabled clinical capabilities. Using osteoporosis as an exemplar, we show how knowledge-driven, data-driven and physics-enhanced skills can support lifecycle care under runtime governance.

</details>


### [285] [Humans Disengage, Reasoning Models Persist: Separating Difficulty Registration from Deliberation Allocation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26502)
*Han-yu Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Large reasoning models (LRMs) and humans both spend more time on harder problems across items, but show opposite patterns within items: LRMs spend more tokens on problems they get wrong, while humans spend less time on their incorrect trials. This dissociation reveals fundamentally different stopping policies—human engagement vs. abandonment, LRM uncertainty-driven chain lengthening—despite superficially similar difficulty tracking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work has noted that LRMs and humans both deliberate longer on harder problems, suggesting a shared resource-rational pattern. The authors challenge this surface similarity by decomposing deliberation into two levels: cross-item registration (how response time tracks difficulty) and within-item allocation (whether more resources are spent on successes or failures for the same item). This decomposition reveals that the apparent alignment may mask fundamentally different underlying control policies.

Method: The authors analyze a public matched human-LRM corpus (H-ARC) and additional datasets. They separate deliberation into (1) registration—the cross-item correlation between response time/tokens and difficulty—and (2) allocation—within-item comparison of resources spent on correct vs. incorrect trials, holding item identity fixed via item fixed effects. They compare humans against five thinking LRMs and a non-thinking baseline, using Cohen's d for within-item wrong-vs-right effect sizes, all within each agent's own scale.

Result: Both humans and LRMs reproduce positive cross-item difficulty registration. However, within items, all five thinking LRMs show a large positive wrong-vs-right effect (Cohen's d = 1.47–3.13), meaning they spend substantially more tokens on incorrect trials. Humans show the opposite: they spend less time on incorrect trials. This dissociation holds under item fixed effects, replicates across datasets, and is absent in the non-thinking baseline, confirming the effect is specific to reasoning-capable models.

Conclusion: The authors interpret the human pattern as engagement versus abandonment—people persist on items they expect to solve and give up on others—and the LRM pattern as uncertainty-driven length, where chains grow when the model is unsure and thus more likely to fail. Both policies share a difficulty signal, producing aligned cross-item correlations, but implement opposite control. Under resource-rational metareasoning, trace length captures the signal but misses the control policy, meaning prior measures of alignment are insufficient to establish shared decision-making mechanisms.

Abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) take longer on harder problems, just as humans do. This surface similarity hides an opposite pattern within items. When an LRM gets a problem wrong, it spends more tokens than when it gets the same problem right; humans do the reverse, spending less time on the trials they get wrong. We separate two levels of deliberation: how response time tracks difficulty across items (registration), and, with item identity held fixed, whether an agent spends more on its own failures or successes (allocation). On a public matched human-LRM corpus, humans and all five thinking LRMs reproduce the known cross-item alignment (registration) but diverge within items (allocation): every LRM shows a large wrong-vs-right effect (Cohen's d = 1.47-3.13 on H-ARC) while humans show the opposite sign. The comparison stays inside each agent's own scale; we never put seconds and tokens on one axis. The dissociation holds under item fixed effects, replicates across datasets, and is absent in a non-thinking baseline. We read the human pattern as engagement versus abandonment: people stay on items they expect to solve and give up on the rest. We read the LRM pattern as length driven by uncertainty: chains grow when the model is unsure, which is exactly when it tends to fail. Both policies produce the same cross-item correlation with difficulty, so they look aligned on the measure prior work has used; the divergence shows up only once item identity is fixed. Under resource-rational metareasoning, the split is between two stopping policies that share a difficulty signal but implement opposite control; trace length captures the signal and misses the control.

</details>


### [286] [NeuraDock Visual Cognitive Load Agent Tutorial: A Quality-Gated Open-Source EEG Workflow for Alpha Dynamics and Real-Time Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26518)
*Zhiyuan Xu,Yueqing Dai,Junling Li,Junwen Luo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A reproducible tutorial for NeuraDock Agent, an open-source EEG tool that provides a quality-gated pipeline from raw EEG to real-time Alpha dynamics analysis and visual cognitive-load assessment, bridging the offline-to-online gap with preprocessing, QC, API serving, and LLM interpretation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing EEG toolkits offer robust offline analysis but lack an integrated, reproducible pipeline that combines real-time acquisition, automated quality control, Alpha feature extraction, web API serving, and LLM-based interpretation. Researchers face a fragmented workflow when moving from offline analysis to online cognitive-load prototypes.

Method: The paper presents a step-by-step walkthrough of NeuraDock Agent featuring: (1) a quality-gated workflow where Alpha and workload metrics are computed only after preprocessing and QC checks pass; (2) within-subject Rest/Task comparisons of visual cognitive load using posterior Alpha suppression; (3) a public mini-dataset for validation (18 recordings, 10 within-subject contrasts); (4) an online dashboard and real-time API; and (5) an LLM interpretation layer for quality risk explanation.

Result: On the mini-dataset validation: 18 recordings processed, 10 within-subject comparisons generated, task-related posterior Alpha suppression observed in 7 of 10 contrasts, initial evidence of within-subject repeatability estimated, and local online API latency benchmarked.

Conclusion: NeuraDock Agent successfully provides a transparent, reproducible, end-to-end path from raw EEG files to real-time visual cognitive-load prototypes, making it suitable for researchers, developers, and applied teams seeking to operationalize EEG-based workload monitoring.

Abstract: This tutorial paper provides a step-by-step, reproducible walkthrough of NeuraDock Agent, an open-source EEG agent focused on Alpha dynamics and visual cognitive-load analysis. The goal is practical: a reader should be able to install the agent, run EEG preprocessing and quality control, generate Alpha dynamics figures, perform within-subject Rest/Task visual cognitive-load comparison, run the public mini-dataset analyses and compare them with the reference validation summary, start an online dashboard, call the real-time API from an external application, and use the LLM interpretation layer to explain quality risks. Existing EEG toolkits provide excellent offline analysis, but assembling a real-time, quality-gated cognitive-load pipeline often requires manually bridging acquisition, custom QC, Alpha feature extraction, and a web API; this tutorial closes that offline-to-online gap. The tutorial uses a quality-gated workflow: downstream Alpha and workload metrics are computed only after preprocessing and QC gating rather than directly from raw EEG. In the included mini-dataset validation, the agent processed 18 recordings, generated 10 within-subject comparisons, observed task-related posterior Alpha suppression in 7 of 10 contrasts, estimated initial evidence of within-subject repeatability, and benchmarked local online API latency. The tutorial is intended for researchers, developers, and applied teams who want a transparent path from EEG files to real-time visual cognitive-load prototypes.

</details>


### [287] [Boundary-Aware Context Grounding for A Low-Channel EEG Agent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26519)
*Zhiyuan Xu,Yueqing Dai,Junling Li,Junwen Luo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: NeuraDock Agent separates a deterministic local EEG engine from an LLM language layer, constraining the model to hardware-aware, implementation-specific summaries rather than raw data, and evaluates the system on numerical reproducibility, data boundary preservation, and boundary-awareness across 288 adversarial test outputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: General LLMs lack awareness of specific sensor capabilities, implemented algorithms, and justifiable conclusions from computed results. This is critical for low-channel EEG, where sparse spatial coverage and variable signal quality make plausible but unsupported interpretations easy to produce. The authors aim to ground LLM-based EEG agents in the actual hardware, software, and implementation boundaries.

Method: The architecture comprises a deterministic local EEG engine (handling recording parsing, quality control, spectral workflows, and machine-readable artifacts) and a hardware-aware language layer. The LLM receives only a compact allowlisted summary and a versioned context pack describing the seven-channel hardware, reviewed workflows, result fields, implementation boundaries, scientific limits, and reference cases. Raw EEG and dense arrays remain local. Evaluation used: (1) 12 recordings over 10 numerical repetitions plus a complete Rest/Task run over 3 repetitions; (2) request-capture and failure-injection under HTTP, malformed-output, and connection failures; (3) a boundary-awareness benchmark of 36 ordinary and adversarial questions under 4 context ablations and 2 LLMs (288 total outputs).

Result: The 12 recordings produced identical structured results over 10 repetitions; the complete Rest/Task run yielded identical result, report, and figure hashes over 3 repetitions. Failure-injection experiments confirmed the tested data boundary and preservation of local artifacts. The boundary-awareness benchmark produced 288 outputs across ablations and models.

Conclusion: Hardware- and implementation-aware grounding is a practical mechanism for calibrating what an EEG agent accepts, qualifies, or refuses. The results do not establish clinical validity or a validated absolute cognitive-load index.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can make scientific software easier to use. However, a general model does not automatically know which measurements a particular sensor can support, which algorithms are implemented in the current software, or which conclusions are justified by a computed result. These distinctions are especially important for low-channel electroencephalography (EEG), where sparse spatial coverage and variable signal quality make plausible but unsupported interpretations easy to produce. We present NeuraDock Agent, an open-source architecture that separates a deterministic local EEG engine from a hardware-aware language layer. The numerical engine parses recordings, performs quality control, executes reviewed spectral workflows, and writes machine-readable artifacts. The LLM receives only a compact, allowlisted summary and a versioned context pack. The context describes the seven-channel hardware, reviewed workflows, result fields, implementation boundaries, scientific limits, and reference cases. Raw EEG and dense per-sample arrays remain local
  We evaluate the system at three levels. First, 12 recordings produced identical structured results over ten numerical repetitions, and a complete Rest/Task run produced identical result, report, and figure hashes over three repetitions. Second, request-capture and failure-injection experiments confirmed the tested data boundary and preservation of local artifacts under HTTP, malformed-output, and connection failures. Third, a boundary-awareness benchmark tested 36 ordinary and adversarial questions under four context ablations and two LLMs, yielding 288 outputs.These results support hardware- and implementation-aware grounding as a practical mechanism for calibrating what an EEG agent accepts, qualifies, or refuses; they do not establish clinical validity or a validated absolute cognitive-load index.

</details>


### [288] [Radical AI Interpretability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26523)
*Daniel A. Herrmann,Benjamin A. Levinstein*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a framework for interpreting AI systems as agents with beliefs, desires, and meanings by combining radical interpretation (from philosophy) with mechanistic interpretability (from AI). It argues that these attributions are holistically constrained — beliefs, desires, and propositional structure must be solved jointly — and provides criteria and tests for determining when interpretability methods have succeeded.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI systems are deployed in high-stakes settings, we need to trust them by understanding their goals or detecting deception. Mechanistic interpretability tools aim to read beliefs and desires from model internals, but there is no agreed-upon standard for what counts as successful attribution. The paper aims to supply that missing normative account.

Method: The framework integrates two philosophical traditions: representationalism and interpretationism. It proposes joint constraints among beliefs, desires, and propositional structure, arguing they cannot be attributed piecemeal. It ties each approach to concrete tests that current mechanistic interpretability methods can carry out, and leverages holism as both a challenge (preventing isolated attribution) and a resource (mutual constraint enables measurement).

Result: The central finding is that belief, desire, and meaning attributions are holistically interdependent. A method that fixes one while measuring others introduces distortions. For AI systems that may not share human concepts, this holism is both pressing and useful: a system's attitudes constrain its propositional structure, that structure constrains which attitudes can be attributed, and mechanistic interpretability can measure both.

Conclusion: Successful interpretation of AI systems requires joint solution of beliefs, desires, and propositional structure. The holism of radical interpretation, combined with the empirical tools of mechanistic interpretability, yields a principled framework that sets success criteria for interpretability research and addresses the safety challenge of understanding AI goals and detecting deception.

Abstract: We develop a framework for interpreting AI systems as agents, drawing on the philosophical tradition of radical interpretation and the tools of mechanistic interpretability. The core question is: given the computational facts about a system, how do we solve for its beliefs, desires, and meanings? This matters increasingly for safety. We want to be able to trust the systems we deploy, whether by understanding their goals or, more modestly, by reliably detecting deception. Interpretability researchers are building tools to read beliefs and desires off a model's internals, but there is no settled account of when such a tool has succeeded. This book supplies one. We propose criteria on both representationalist and interpretationist approaches, and tie each to tests current interpretability methods can carry out. A central lesson is that these attributions cannot be made piecemeal. Beliefs, desires, and the propositional structure they presuppose are jointly constrained, and a method that fixes one while measuring the others inherits whatever distortions that introduces. This holism becomes pressing for AI systems, which may not share the interpreter's concepts. However, it also provides leverage: a system's attitudes constrain its propositional structure, that structure constrains which attitudes can be attributed, and mechanistic interpretability can help us measure both.

</details>


### [289] [PMDformer: Patch-Mean Decoupling Information Transformer for Long-term Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26549)
*Ao Hu,Liangjian Wen,Jiang Duan,Yong Dai,He Yan,Dongkai Wang,Jun Wang,Yukun Zhang,Ruoxi Jiang,Zenglin Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PMDformer introduces patch-mean decoupling (PMD) to separate trend and shape information in time series patches, combined with Trend Restoration Attention (TRA) and Proximal Variable Attention (PVA), achieving state-of-the-art long-term forecasting performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformer-based patch methods struggle to accurately model shape similarities across patches and variables due to scale differences, which distort attention scores. Existing cross-variable attention also risks overfitting on outdated temporal correlations.

Method: The paper proposes three components: (1) Patch-Mean Decoupling (PMD), which subtracts patch means to isolate residual shape from trend; (2) Trend Restoration Attention (TRA), which reintegrates the decoupled trend during attention computation; (3) Proximal Variable Attention (PVA), which restricts cross-variable attention to recent, relevant time segments. These are integrated into PMDformer.

Result: PMDformer outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in stability and accuracy across multiple LTSF benchmarks, as demonstrated by extensive experiments.

Conclusion: Decoupling trend and shape information via PMD, restoring trends through TRA, and constraining cross-variable attention with PVA collectively enable more effective modeling of shape similarity and long-range dependencies, yielding superior long-term forecasting performance.

Abstract: Long-term time series forecasting (LTSF) plays a crucial role in fields such as energy management, finance, and traffic prediction. Transformer-based models have adopted patch-based strategies to capture long-range dependencies, but accurately modeling shape similarities across patches and variables remains challenging due to scale differences. To address this, we introduce patch-mean decoupling (PMD), which separates the trend and residual shape information by subtracting the mean of each patch, preserving the original structure and ensuring that the attention mechanism captures true shape similarities. Futhermore, to more effectively model long-range dependencies and capture cross-variable relationships, we propose Trend Restoration Attention (TRA) and Proximal Variable Attention (PVA). The former module reintegrates the decoupled trend from PMD while calculating attention output. And the latter focuses cross-variable attention on the most relevant, recent time segments to avoid overfitting on outdated correlations. Combining these components, we propose PMDformer, a model designed to effectively capture shape similarity in long-term forecasting scenarios. Extensive experiments indicate that PMDformer outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in stability and accuracy across multiple LTSF benchmarks. The code is available at https://github.com/aohu1105/PMDformer.

</details>


### [290] [Explainable Ensemble-Based Machine Learning Models for Detecting the Presence of Cirrhosis in Hepatitis C Patients](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26561)
*Abrar Alotaibi,Lujain Alnajrani,Nawal Alsheikh,Alhatoon Alanazy,Salam Alshammasi,Meshael Almusairii,Shoog Alrassan,Aisha Alansari*

Main category: cs.AI
