TL;DR: This study applies four machine learning algorithms (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, Extra Trees) to detect cirrhosis in hepatitis C patients using a 28-attribute dataset of 2038 Egyptian patients. The Extra Trees model achieved the best performance (96.92% accuracy, 99.81% precision, 94% recall, 0.96 AUC) using only 16 features.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cirrhosis is a severe, often asymptomatic complication of hepatitis C that can progress to liver failure, neurological damage, and gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Early detection is critical to prevent complications, yet no prior studies have applied machine learning to detect cirrhosis specifically in hepatitis C patients. This gap motivates the use of ML for accurate, early diagnosis.

Method: The authors used a publicly available dataset (UCI ML Repository) containing 28 attributes from 2038 Egyptian patients with hepatitis C. Four tree-based ensemble algorithms were trained and compared: Random Forest, Gradient Boosting Machine, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Extra Trees. Feature selection reduced the input from 28 to 16 attributes. Model evaluation employed accuracy, recall, precision, and AUC-ROC metrics.

Result: The Extra Trees model outperformed all others, achieving 96.92% accuracy, 94.00% recall, 99.81% precision, and an AUC of 96% using only 16 of the 28 available features.

Conclusion: Machine learning, particularly the Extra Trees algorithm, is highly effective for early cirrhosis detection in hepatitis C patients, offering a precise and accurate diagnostic tool that can aid in preventing disease progression and associated complications.

Abstract: Hepatitis C is a liver infection caused by a virus, which results in mild to severe inflammation of the liver. Over many years, hepatitis C gradually damages the liver, often leading to permanent scarring, known as cirrhosis. Patients sometimes have moderate or no symptoms of liver illness for decades before developing cirrhosis. Cirrhosis typically worsens to the point of liver failure. Patients with cirrhosis may also experience brain and nerve system damage, as well as gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Treatment for cirrhosis focuses on preventing further progression of the disease. Detecting cirrhosis earlier is therefore crucial for avoiding complications. Machine learning (ML) has been shown to be effective at providing precise and accurate information for use in diagnosing several diseases. Despite this, no studies have so far used ML to detect cirrhosis in patients with hepatitis C. This study obtained a dataset consisting of 28 attributes of 2038 Egyptian patients from the ML Repository of the University of California at Irvine. Four ML algorithms were trained on the dataset to diagnose cirrhosis in hepatitis C patients: a Random Forest, a Gradient Boosting Machine, an Extreme Gradient Boosting, and an Extra Trees model. The Extra Trees model outperformed the other models achieving an accuracy of 96.92%, a recall of 94.00%, a precision of 99.81%, and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 96% using only 16 of the 28 features.

</details>


### [291] [EvoOptiGraph: Weakness-Driven Coevolution via Graph-Based Structural Generation for Optimization Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26578)
*Qingcan Kang,Mingyang Liu,Xiaojin Fu,Shixiong Kai,Tao Zhong,Mingxuan Yuan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EvoOptiGraph is a framework where MILP instances (represented as attributed bipartite graphs) and LLMs co-evolve: evolutionary operators generate structurally diverse graphs, which are compiled into code/text for two-stage training (SFT + RLVR), where model weaknesses guide further data generation in a closed loop, significantly outperforming baselines on optimization modeling tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM-based approaches for automating optimization modeling suffer from (1) lack of structural diversity in training corpora and (2) static, decoupled data generation pipelines that do not adapt to model weaknesses. This limits model generalization and accuracy.

Method: EvoOptiGraph represents each MILP as an attributed bipartite graph and applies validity-preserving evolutionary operators to generate structurally diverse instances. Graphs are deterministically compiled into solver code and back-translated into natural language. Training uses two stages: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on an initial dataset, then reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), where graph-derived weakness signals identify failure modes and guide targeted generation of new training instances, forming a closed co-evolution loop.

Result: On six public datasets, EvoOptiGraph significantly outperforms larger generalist models, agentic methods, and specialized baselines in accuracy, executability, and generalization.

Conclusion: Targeted data-model coevolution is an effective strategy for improving LLM performance on optimization modeling tasks, demonstrating that dynamically adapting the training distribution to model weaknesses yields superior results compared to static training paradigms.

Abstract: Automating optimization modeling from natural language with large language models (LLMs) faces two key challenges. First, training corpora lack structural diversity. Second, data generation pipelines remain static and decoupled from model learning. To address these challenges, we propose EvoOptiGraph, a novel framework where data and model co-evolve, driven by model weaknesses. EvoOptiGraph represents each mixed-integer linear program (MILP) as an attributed bipartite graph and applies validity-preserving evolutionary operators to generate structurally diverse instances. The evolved graphs are converted into solver code and natural language via deterministic compilation and verified back-translation. Training proceeds in two stages: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on an initial dataset, followed by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), where graph-derived weakness signals guide the generation of new instances targeting the model's failures. This forms a closed loop that continuously updates the training distribution. Empirical results on six public datasets show that EvoOptiGraph significantly outperforms larger generalist models, agentic methods, and specialized baselines in accuracy, executability, and generalization. These results demonstrate that targeted data-model coevolution is an effective strategy for improving LLMs on optimization modeling tasks.

</details>


### [292] [A Multi-Level Validation and Traceability Framework for AI-Generated Telescope Scheduling Decisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26585)
*Hengchu Xiao,Chuanjun Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a multi-level validation and traceable reasoning framework that verifies AI-generated telescope scheduling decisions before execution, using data reference validation, logical consistency checks, and constraint verification, plus atomic reasoning units with dependency tracking for error localization and correction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI-based telescope scheduling suffers from inconsistent data references, reasoning errors, and non-executable decisions, limiting its use in high-reliability observational tasks. A systematic approach is needed to verify decisions and make reasoning traceable.

Method: A framework with three components: (1) multi-level validation covering data reference validation, logical consistency checks, and observational/instrumental constraint verification to filter and correct invalid decisions; (2) atomic reasoning units with explicit dependency relationships to represent scheduling decisions as interconnected reasoning steps; (3) feedback correction and structured validation enabling error localization, post hoc analysis, and repair/blocking of erroneous decisions.

Result: The framework improves executability and reliability of AI scheduling, reduces loss of transient observational opportunities, and enhances error repair and blocking—particularly in complex scenarios. It maintains AI flexibility while substantially improving reliability and executability over pure AI methods.

Conclusion: The framework demonstrates a feasible and verifiable pathway for deploying AI in high-reliability astronomical observation scheduling, combining flexibility with the rigor needed for mission-critical tasks.

Abstract: With the gradual introduction of AI into telescope scheduling, AI-based decision-making has shown advantages in handling complex multi-constraint problems. However, its outputs often suffer from inconsistent data references, reasoning errors, and non-executable decisions, limiting applicability in high-reliability observational tasks. In this work, we propose a multi-level validation and traceable reasoning framework that performs systematic reliability verification of AI-generated decisions prior to execution, and enables explicit representation of the reasoning process to support traceable decision-making. The framework integrates data reference validation, logical consistency checks, and observational and instrumental constraint verification to filter and correct invalid decisions. It also introduces atomic reasoning units and their dependency relationships, representing scheduling decisions as a sequence of interconnected reasoning steps that support error localization and post hoc analysis. Experiments show that the framework improves executability and reliability of AI scheduling and reduces loss of transient opportunities. In particular, feedback correction and structured validation of reasoning steps enhance the ability to repair and block erroneous decisions, especially in complex scenarios. Compared with pure AI methods, the framework-enhanced approach maintains flexibility while substantially improving reliability and executability. These results demonstrate a feasible and verifiable pathway for applying AI to high-reliability astronomical observation scheduling.

</details>


### [293] [Content-Based Smart E-Mail Dispatcher Using Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26593)
*K. Paramesha,K R Sriram,Sujan Shetty,Shamanth Kishore,R. Tejaswini*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents an LLM-powered agent system that automatically analyzes incoming emails and forwards them to the appropriate WhatsApp groups of engineering students, eliminating manual email triage and reducing cognitive load.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual handling of large volumes of organizational emails is error-prone, time-consuming, and causes productivity loss and undue stress. The need is for an automated mechanism to route email contents to relevant recipients on instant messaging platforms.

Method: A dispatcher system built on agents that query large language models (LLMs). The system uses a structured agent framework prompt containing the email content, instructions, and context. The LLM analyzes textual content and determines the relevant WhatsApp groups (e.g., specific semester/program student groups) for routing, without relying on any labeled datasets.

Result: The system successfully figures out the relevant groups for email dispatch, provides timely information delivery, enhances productivity, and reduces cognitive load associated with manual email reading and forwarding.

Conclusion: LLM-based agent systems offer a viable, label-free alternative for automating organizational email dispatch to messaging platforms, improving information flow and workplace efficiency.

Abstract: Email communication has become an integral part of personal and professional life, but handling its vast volume is still a significant issue for large organisations. Manual perusal of emails and forwarding their contents and attachments to intended recipients using other instant messaging platforms has proved to be error-prone and time-consuming leading to losses in terms of productivity and creating undue stress. The main objective of this paper is to explore an alternative mechanism that is to automate the task of dispatching emails based on their contents to the respective WhatsApp groups of students of various semesters of programs in an engineering college, facilitating a smooth flow of information from one end to another end in an organisation. The dispatcher system is built using agents querying large language models (LLMs) to enable it to analyze the contents of emails and route them to the relevant groups of students for their information and consumption. The system harnesses the capabilities of LLMs in analysing the textual contents for decision-making. With a well-structured agent framework prompt that includes email content as input with instructions and context, the system figures out the relevant groups to which the email message is dispatched, thus providing the required information on time. The proposed system does not rely on labelled datasets and provides several benefits, including enhanced productivity and a reduction in the cognitive load associated with reading emails.

</details>


### [294] [LLM-based Models for Detecting Emerging Topics in Service Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26595)
*Mahsa Tavakoli,Ruth Bankey,Cristián Bravo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A novel methodology combining fine-tuned quantized LLMs, statistical techniques, and human-in-the-loop oversight for multilingual customer feedback analysis in tax administrations, demonstrating improved detection of emerging service quality issues and potential inequities compared to baseline models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Public sector tax administrations face growing volumes of multilingual customer feedback that are difficult to analyze at scale. Traditional manual review and static expert-defined indicators cannot effectively capture complex patterns or detect emerging service quality issues and disparities across diverse populations, threatening trust and compliance.

Method: A framework integrating fine-tuned, quantized large language models (LLMs) with statistical techniques and human-AI collaboration. The approach employs a human-in-the-loop framework where expert tax officers provide oversight to reduce LLM fabrication and improve contextual relevance. Similarity analysis and expert assessments are used for evaluation.

Result: The proposed methodology demonstrated stronger alignment with expert judgments than baseline models. The human-in-the-loop framework effectively reduced LLM fabrication while improving the reliability and relevance of generated insights for detecting emerging service quality topics and potential service delivery inequities.

Conclusion: Combining LLMs with human expertise provides a practical, scalable approach for evidence-based decision-making in public sector organizations. This contributes to responsible AI systems that enhance service quality, responsiveness, fairness, and public trust through effective multilingual feedback analysis.

Abstract: Enhancing the analysis of service feedback is essential for public sector organizations, particularly tax administrations, where trust and compliance depend on fair and effective service delivery. As feedback volumes grow, identifying emerging service quality issues and potential disparities across diverse populations becomes increasingly challenging. Traditional approaches often rely on manual review or static expert-defined indicators, limiting scalability and the ability to capture complex patterns in textual feedback.
  This paper presents a novel methodology that integrates large language models (LLMs), statistical techniques, and human-AI collaboration to improve multilingual customer feedback analysis. The primary objective is to detect emerging service quality topics that may also reveal potential inequities in service delivery. Our framework combines fine-tuned, quantized LLMs with expert oversight to produce accurate, computationally efficient, and context-aware analyses.
  The proposed approach was evaluated using similarity analysis and assessments from experienced tax officers, demonstrating stronger alignment with expert judgments than baseline models. By incorporating a human-in-the-loop framework, the methodology reduces LLM fabrication while improving the reliability and relevance of generated insights.
  The results demonstrate the practicality of combining LLMs with human expertise to support scalable, evidence-based decision-making in public sector organizations. This work contributes to the development of responsible AI systems that enhance service quality, responsiveness, fairness, and public trust through more effective analysis of multilingual customer feedback.

</details>


### [295] [Autoformalization of Agent Instructions into Policy-as-Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26649)
*Adam Mondl,Matthew Maisel,John H. Brock*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents an autoformalization pipeline that uses an LLM-based generator-critic loop to translate natural-language prompts, tool descriptions, and policy documents into formally verified policies in the Cedar Policy Language, achieving broader specification coverage on MedAgentBench than prior hand-coded symbolic enforcement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches to agent safety policy enforcement fall into two unsatisfactory categories: probabilistic guardrails (fine-tuned classifiers, prompt-based steering) that lack formal guarantees, and hand-coded symbolic enforcement that cannot scale to the breadth and complexity of real-world policy specifications. A scalable method for producing formally verified policies is needed.

Method: An autoformalization pipeline employing an LLM-based generator-critic loop: the generator translates natural-language inputs (agent prompts, MCP tool descriptions, policy documents) into Cedar Policy Language specifications, and the critic verifies correctness, feeding back corrections iteratively until the formal policy is verified.

Result: On the MedAgentBench benchmark, the autoformalized policies achieved substantially greater coverage of the source natural-language specification compared to the hand-coded symbolic enforcement from prior work.

Conclusion: Autoformalization via an LLM-based generator-critic loop is a viable and scalable approach for producing formally verified agent safety policies, outperforming manual symbolic encoding in specification coverage while retaining formal guarantees.

Abstract: Agent safety in high-stakes domains requires formal policy enforcement, but most existing approaches either rely on probabilistic guardrails (fine-tuned classifiers, prompt-based steering) that offer no formal guarantees, or on hand-coded symbolic enforcement that does not scale to the breadth of real policy specifications. We present an autoformalization pipeline that translates agent prompts, MCP tool descriptions, and natural language policy documents into formally verified policies using an LLM-based generator-critic loop. The resulting policies are written in the Cedar Policy Language. On the MedAgentBench benchmark, our autoformalized policies cover substantially more of the source natural-language specification than the hand-coded symbolic enforcement in prior work.

</details>


### [296] [SKILL-DISCO: Distilling and Compiling Agent Traces into Reusable Procedural Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26669)
*Zhongxin Guo,Danrui Qi,Hanwen Gu,Peng Cheng,Yongqiang Xiong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillDisCo proposes a framework that distills reusable procedural skills from successful agent execution traces by representing shared procedural structure as parameterized control-flow subgraphs (PFSMs). It compiles these subgraphs into callable, executable, and verifiable skills, improving success rates and reducing agent turns on ALFWorld and WebArena.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agents waste computation by repeatedly solving similar tasks from scratch, producing long reasoning traces. Prior work on workflow reuse and skill induction lacks clarity on (1) which task scenarios admit procedural skills and (2) how shared procedural structure should be represented across successful traces.

Method: The authors focus on FSM-defined task scenarios, modeling successful traces as paths in a transition graph and procedural skills as reusable parameterized control-flow subgraphs (PFSMs). They introduce SkillDisCo, a distillation-and-compilation framework: distillation extracts reusable PFSM subgraphs from successful traces, and compilation transforms them into callable, executable, and verifiable procedural skills.

Result: Experiments on ALFWorld and WebArena benchmarks demonstrate that SkillDisCo improves task success rates and reduces the number of agent turns across multiple model scales, showing the effectiveness of reusing shared execution structures.

Conclusion: Representing shared experience as reusable, parameterized procedural structures (PFSMs) yields tangible benefits in agent efficiency and effectiveness. The distillation-and-compilation paradigm offers a principled approach to skill reuse in sequential decision-making tasks.

Abstract: Agents often repeatedly solve similar task instances from scratch, leading to unnecessary reasoning cost and long execution traces. Prior work has explored workflow reuse and executable skill induction, but it remains unclear which task scenarios admit procedural skills and how the shared procedural structure should be represented across successful traces. We study this problem in FSM-defined scenarios, where successful traces can be viewed as paths in an unknown transition graph, and formulate procedural skills as reusable parameterized control-flow subgraphs. Based on this view, we introduce SkillDisCo, a distillation-and-compilation framework that distills reusable PFSM subgraphs from successful traces and compiles them into callable, executable, and verifiable procedural skills. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebArena show that SkillDisCo improves success rates and reduces agent turns across benchmarks and model scales, demonstrating the benefits of representing shared experience as reusable execution structures.

</details>


### [297] [NebulaExp-8B: An Empirical Post-Training Pipeline via Full-Scale Ablation Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26671)
*Qiaobo Hao,Yangqian Wu,Shunyi Wang,Zhongjian Zhang,Ziqun Li,Yayin He,Muqing Li,Chen Zhong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: NebulaExp presents a fully transparent, reproducible post-training pipeline for Qwen3-8B, covering instruct and reasoning branches with detailed data processing, multi-stage SFT, GRPO-based RL, and OPD distillation. The instruct model achieves 61.85 average score (up from 55.01), while the reasoning model reaches 75.17, with OPD methods outperforming RL baselines on instruction-following tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most existing post-training alignment works withhold critical details on data construction, filtering rules, and training recipes, hindering reproducibility and optimization for smaller models. The authors aim to provide a fully transparent, ablation-driven pipeline to enable community reproduction and systematic understanding of capability trade-offs.

Method: A comprehensive post-training pipeline built on Qwen3-8B-base, comprising: (1) Curation of 3.84M multi-source SFT samples and 200K verifiable RL candidates; (2) An end-to-end data processing stack with response distillation, multi-dimensional cross-verification filtering, fine-grained difficulty grading, task classification, and diversity-aware sampling; (3) For the Instruct branch: three-stage optimized SFT (NebulaExp-Ins-SFT) followed by GRPO reinforcement learning; (4) For the Reasoning branch: medium-difficulty GRPO RL; (5) Single-teacher and multi-teacher Off-Policy Distillation (OPD/MOPD) using only 4K-10K instruction-following samples to address RL's dependency on task-specific verifiers.

Result: Instruct branch: SFT raises average benchmark from 55.01 (Qwen3-8B-nothink) to 60.99; GRPO further lifts it to 61.85. Reasoning branch: GRPO improves average reasoning score from 73.88 to 75.17. OPD with 4K samples outperforms RL baseline by 3.26 points on IFEval and +4.43 overall; MOPD with 10K samples and four domain-specialist teachers yields +4.18 average improvement over the base model.

Conclusion: The work delivers a fully reproducible post-training recipe for 8B-scale LLMs, with comprehensive dissection of capability trade-offs across instruction adherence, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and general knowledge. OPD methods emerge as a data-efficient alternative to RL, particularly for tasks lacking robust verifiers.

Abstract: Post-training alignment determines the reasoning and human preference following capabilities of large language models, yet most existing works withhold detailed data construction, filtering rules and training recipes, which hinders community reproducibility and lightweight model optimization. This work presents NebulaExp, a fully transparent, ablation-driven post-training pipeline built on Qwen3-8B-base, covering two orthogonal model branches: general instruct model and complex reasoning-specialized model. We curate a raw corpus of 3.84M multi-source SFT samples and a 200K verifiable RL candidate pool, and design an end-to-end data processing stack including response distillation, multi-dimensional cross-verification filtering, fine-grained difficulty grading, task classification and diversity-aware sampling. For the Instruct branch, our three-stage optimized supervised fine-tuning approach NebulaExp-Ins-SFT improves the average benchmark score from the 55.01 baseline of Qwen3-8B-nothink to 60.99. GRPO reinforcement learning then further elevates the average score to 61.85. For the Reasoning branch, medium-difficulty GRPO RL improves average reasoning score from 73.88 to 75.17. To address RL's dependency on task verifiers, we systematically investigate single-teacher and multi-teacher OPD (MOPD): utilizing merely 4K instruction-following samples and outperforms RL baseline by 3.26 points on IFEval with +4.43 average overall gain; MOPD fuses four domain-specialist teachers with merely 10K samples, lifting average performance by 4.18 over the base model. This report provides a fully reproducible empirical post-training recipe for 8B-scale LLMs, and comprehensively dissects the capability trade-offs among instruction adherence, mathematical reasoning, code generation and general knowledge.

</details>


### [298] [Do Safety Guardrails Need to Reason? LeanGuard: A Fast and Light Approach for Robust Moderation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26686)
*Dongbin Na*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper challenges the necessity of chain-of-thought reasoning for safety guardrails, showing that a lightweight bidirectional encoder (LeanGuard, 395M parameters) without reasoning matches or exceeds the accuracy of heavier reasoning-based guards while using ~100x less inference compute.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current guardrail methods rely on chain-of-thought reasoning before issuing verdicts, making them heavy and slow — unsuitable for on-device deployment (e.g., embodied robots). The authors question whether CoT reasoning is truly necessary for moderation tasks.

Method: The authors train both a lightweight bidirectional encoder (label-only) and a reasoning guard on the same corpus. They then remove only the reasoning component while keeping everything else fixed, enabling a controlled same-base comparison. The resulting model, LeanGuard (395M parameters), uses a single forward pass over at most 512 tokens.

Result: LeanGuard achieves an average F1 of 82.90 ± 0.26 on public benchmarks, matching much larger decoder-based reasoning guards. It provides ~100x reduction in inference compute, remains robust under training-label noise, and retains far more recall at strict false-positive rates than reasoning guards.

Conclusion: CoT reasoning does not improve moderation accuracy, suggesting current guardrail benchmarks may not be hard enough to reward reasoning. The necessity of chain-of-thought for safety moderation remains unproven.

Abstract: In order to screen a prompt or a response, the recent guardrail methods generate a chain-of-thought (CoT) before they issue a verdict. This design follows a common belief that step-by-step reasoning improves a decision. However, CoT also makes the guard heavy and slow, because the model must generate many tokens before it decides. This may not match how guardrails are actually deployed. A guardrail sometimes should not be heavy and slow, and it often runs on-device, for example on an embodied robot. In this paper, we pose a question whether a safety guardrail really needs to reason. To answer this question, we train a lightweight bidirectional encoder and a reasoning guard on the same corpus, and we then remove only the reasoning while we keep everything else fixed. With this controlled same-base comparison, we show that the chain does not improve moderation accuracy. We name the resulting guard LeanGuard. A 395M label-only encoder reaches an average F1 of 82.90 $\pm$ 0.26 over public benchmarks. It matches a reasoning guard that is built on a much larger decoder, while it uses only a single forward pass over an input of at most 512 tokens. This is about a ~100x reduction in inference compute. We further show that this label-only encoder stays robust under training-label noise and retains far more recall at a strict false-positive rate than the reasoning guard, so a heavier reasoning guard is not the more robust choice either. Our finding suggests that the current guardrail benchmarks may not be hard enough to reward reasoning, and that the necessity of CoT for moderation is still not proven. We release all source codes and models including LeanGuard at https://github.com/ndb796/LeanGuard.

</details>


### [299] [Kalman Prototypical Networks for Few-shot Fault Detection in Combined Cycle Gas Turbines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26710)
*Mohammed Ayalew Belay,Lucas Ferreira Bernardino,Adil Rasheed,Rubén M. Montañés,Pierluigi Salvo Rossi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes the Kalman Prototypical Network (KPN), a few-shot learning framework for combined-cycle gas turbine fault diagnosis that models class prototypes as latent stochastic states via Kalman filtering to reduce episodic variance and improve robustness, outperforming Matching Networks, Relation Networks, and MAML on simulated leak fault detection tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CCGT fault detection is challenging due to complex thermo-fluid and mechanical interactions, and labeled fault data are scarce in real-world settings. Existing few-shot learning methods suffer from high episodic variance and unstable class representations, motivating a more robust prototype estimation approach.

Method: The KPN framework treats class prototypes as latent stochastic states evolving in a dynamic system. A Kalman filter is used to recursively estimate these prototypes across episodes, reducing variance and stabilizing embedding representations. The method is evaluated on synthetic datasets generated from a high-fidelity Modelica-based dynamic simulation of an offshore CCGT system under normal and progressive leak fault transient conditions.

Result: KPN outperforms conventional few-shot learning methods (Matching Networks, Relation Networks, MAML) in both accuracy and stability across varying support set sizes and query configurations. It also demonstrates improved training convergence and generalization capability.

Conclusion: By stabilizing class representations through Kalman filtering of prototypes, KPN is well-suited for real-world CCGT fault detection where labeled fault data are limited, offering significant improvements in convergence and generalization over existing few-shot learning approaches.

Abstract: Combined-cycle gas turbines (CCGTs) play a key role in modern power generation, offering both high efficiency and reduced environmental impact. However, their complex thermo-fluid and mechanical interactions complicate fault detection, particularly when labeled fault data are scarce. In this paper, we introduce the Kalman Prototypical Network (KPN), a metric-based few-shot learning (FSL) framework specifically tailored for CCGT fault diagnosis. We model the evolution of class prototypes as latent stochastic states in a dynamic system to reduce episodic variance and improve robustness in embedding representation. Synthetic data sets generated with a high-fidelity Modelica-based dynamic simulation of an offshore CCGT system were used, simulating both normal operation and progressive leak faults under transient conditions. Application of the proposed framework on simulated leak fault detection tasks demonstrate that KPN outperforms conventional FSL methods such as Matching Networks, Relation Networks, and MAML in both accuracy and stability under varying support and query configurations. The proposed framework significantly improves training convergence and generalization by stabilizing class representations, making it well-suited for real-world CCGT fault detection where labeled data is limited.

</details>


### [300] [LithoDreamer: A Physics-Informed World Model for Multi-Stage Computational Lithography](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26713)
*Yuqi Jiang,Yumeng Liu,Zimu Li,Jinyuan Deng,Qian Jin,Yucheng Cui,Yu Li,Xunzhao Yin,Qi Sun,Cheng Zhuo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LithoDreamer is a physics-informed World Model that formulates computational lithography as a decision-driven multi-step evolution system, using contrastive variational optimization to achieve SOTA forward and inverse performance without continuous supervision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing models fail to capture the continuous physical process of computational lithography (mask optimization, optical imaging, resist exposure, development) as semiconductor nodes scale. A unified framework that models the entire pipeline with physical fidelity is needed.

Method: LithoDreamer formalizes the Layout→Mask→Resist Image→ADI pipeline as a decision-driven multi-step evolution system. It captures feature changes between adjacent states to build stage-specific physics-informed latent spaces, enabling process intervention exploration and state transitions. A contrastive variational optimization paradigm contrasts latent differences between intervention paths with variational evolution constraints, guiding physically consistent evolution generation without continuous supervision.

Result: LithoDreamer achieves state-of-the-art performance on both forward evolution (simulating the lithography process) and inverse planning (optimizing from desired output back to mask/layout) tasks.

Conclusion: LithoDreamer demonstrates that physics-informed world models with contrastive variational optimization can effectively unify the computational lithography pipeline, outperforming existing methods. The associated dataset is publicly released.

Abstract: As semiconductor technology nodes scale, computational lithography is essential for ensuring yield and performance. However, lithography is a continuous physical process involving mask optimization, optical imaging, resist exposure, and development, which existing models fail to capture. To overcome this limitation, we present LithoDreamer, the first physics-informed World Model (WM) framework for computational lithography, which formulates the ``Layout-Mask-Resist Image-After Development Image (ADI)'' pipeline as a decision-driven multi-step evolution system. LithoDreamer captures feature changes between adjacent states to model stage-specific physics-informed latent spaces, in which it controls process intervention exploration and drives subsequent state transitions. To achieve interpretable intervention optimization without continuous supervision, we propose a contrastive variational optimization paradigm that contrasts the latent differences between intervention paths with variational evolution constraints, guiding the model to generate evolutions consistent with real lithography physics. Experiments show LithoDreamer achieves state-of-the-art performance in forward evolution and inverse planning. Our lithography dataset is publicly available at GitHub (https://github.com/7jiangyq/lithodreamer.git).

</details>


### [301] [A Latent ODE Approach to Spatiotemporal Modeling of Cine Cardiac MRI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26718)
*David Brüggemann,Ekaterina Krymova,Firat Özdemir,Jochen von Spiczak,Sebastian Kozerke,Samia Mora,Robert Manka,Mathieu Salzmann,Olga V. Demler*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A latent dynamical model using neural ODEs and graph-based mesh autoencoders encodes full-cycle bi-ventricular motion from CMR. Applied to 72,386 UK Biobank participants, the model's latent score improved heart failure risk prediction (C-index from 0.704 to 0.785) over conventional markers, demonstrating that continuous full-cycle motion modeling yields superior prognostic phenotypes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional cardiac risk models reduce rich CMR spatiotemporal data to a few static indices from selected cardiac phases, discarding potentially valuable information about ventricular structure and motion dynamics across the full cardiac cycle.

Method: A latent dynamical model combining: (1) a graph-based mesh autoencoder to reconstruct 3D+t bi-ventricular anatomy, (2) heart-rate-aware neural ODE dynamics encoding continuous latent trajectories, (3) a covariate-conditioned prior defining expected end-diastolic latent state, and (4) a Cox proportional hazards model testing whether deviations from this prior predict incident heart failure.

Result: In 72,386 UK Biobank participants (367 incident HF events), adding the latent score to refitted pooled cohort equations raised the stratified C-index from 0.704 to 0.785, outperforming seven established cardiac markers (C-index 0.764). The proposed model also gave the best trade-off between reconstruction fidelity, generative realism, and prognostic performance versus non-graph and non-ODE baselines.

Conclusion: Continuous full-cycle ventricular motion modeling yields informative cardiac phenotypes beyond conventional CMR summaries, though external validation in more representative cohorts is needed before clinical deployment.

Abstract: Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) captures rich spatiotemporal information about ventricular structure and motion, but conventional risk models use only a few image-derived indices from selected cardiac phases. We present a latent dynamical model that encodes bi-ventricular anatomy and full-cycle cine motion as a continuous latent trajectory, using heart-rate-aware neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) dynamics and a graph-based mesh autoencoder to reconstruct anatomically consistent 3D+t ventricular motion. A covariate-conditioned prior defines the expected end-diastolic latent state, and a Cox proportional hazards model tests whether deviations from this prior predict incident heart failure. We studied 72,386 UK Biobank participants without baseline cardiovascular disease, including 367 incident heart failure events. In a held-out evaluation subset, adding the latent score to refitted pooled cohort equations improved the stratified C-index from 0.704 to 0.785, compared with 0.764 for seven established cardiac markers. Compared with non-graph and non-ODE approaches, the proposed model gave the best trade-off between reconstruction fidelity, generative realism, and downstream prognostic performance. These results suggest that continuous full-cycle modeling of ventricular motion provides informative cardiac phenotypes beyond conventional CMR summaries, while external validation in more representative patient cohorts is required before clinical risk-prediction use.

</details>


### [302] [Socratic agents for autonomous scientific discovery in high-dimensional physical systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26722)
*Xianrui Zeng,Pengfei Liu,Yirui Zang,Yang Shen,Fei Yu,Chunlei Yu,Minghao Liu,Yang Du*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AHOIS is a multi-agent AI scientist that integrates Socratic midwifery into closed-loop experimentation, enabling a physics-critic agent to interrogate hypotheses through causal questioning, constraint checking, and falsification. Tested on a multimode-fibre optical platform, it autonomously discovered a random-interference encoding hypothesis, adaptive sparse-measurement strategies, and diagnosed failure modes—achieving strong classification performance (76.97% MNIST, 83.17% Fashion-MNIST) from 16×16 measurements, with ablations confirming Socratic interrogation improves physical consistency and experimental validity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI-driven scientific automation systems are largely procedural, executing fixed workflows designed by humans. True autonomous science requires epistemic autonomy—the ability to construct, challenge, and revise physical explanations based on evidence. AHOIS addresses this gap by embedding Socratic questioning into the discovery loop, moving beyond parameter optimization toward genuine hypothesis formation and self-correction.

Method: AHOIS employs a multi-agent architecture centered on Socratic midwifery: a physics-critic agent interrogates candidate hypotheses using four mechanisms—causal questioning, constraint checking, counterexample generation, and falsification-criteria formulation—within a closed-loop experimentation framework. The system was deployed on a real multimode-fibre optical platform featuring high-dimensional wave transformations, indirect detection, environmental drift, and multi-modal acquisition, without any prior encoding schemes or speckle models.

Result: AHOIS autonomously proposed and validated a random-interference encoding hypothesis, discovered task-adaptive sparse-measurement strategies, and diagnosed three distinct failure modes: encoding instability, fluorescence contamination, and detector noise. It also translated a published imaging protocol into an executable workflow on a non-original configuration. The discovered encoding achieved 16×16 measurements (effective rank 56.9) with 76.97% accuracy on MNIST and 83.17% on Fashion-MNIST. Ablation studies demonstrated that Socratic interrogation improves physical consistency, hypothesis completeness, uncertainty calibration, and experimental-plan validity.

Conclusion: The results demonstrate a viable path from workflow automation toward evidence-grounded, self-correcting autonomous discovery. By embedding Socratic midwifery into the scientific process, AHOIS shows that AI systems can achieve meaningful epistemic autonomy in complex physical environments, generating and refining physical explanations rather than merely optimizing predefined procedures.

Abstract: The automation of scientific discovery has reached an inflection point. While AI systems now operate instruments, optimize parameters and generate hypotheses, most remain procedural: they execute workflows fixed by human designers. True autonomous science demands epistemic autonomy--the capacity to construct, challenge and revise physical explanations in response to evidence. Here we introduce AHOIS, a multi-agent AI scientist that embeds Socratic midwifery into closed-loop experimentation. A physics-critic agent interrogates hypotheses through causal questioning, constraint checking, counterexample generation and falsification-criteria formulation. We evaluate AHOIS on a real multimode-fibre optical platform, a high-dimensional system with complex wave transformations, indirect detection, environmental drift and multi-modal acquisition. Without prior encoding schemes, classifiers or speckle models, the system autonomously proposed and validated a random-interference encoding hypothesis, discovered task-adaptive sparse-measurement strategies, diagnosed distinct failure modes (encoding instability, fluorescence contamination and detector noise) and translated a published imaging protocol into an executable workflow on a non-original configuration. The discovered encoding yielded 16x16 measurements with effective rank 56.9 and classification accuracies of 76.97% on MNIST and 83.17% on Fashion-MNIST. Ablations show that Socratic interrogation improves physical consistency, hypothesis completeness, uncertainty calibration and experimental-plan validity. These results establish a route from workflow automation towards evidence-grounded, self-correcting autonomous discovery in complex physical environments.

</details>


### [303] [EGG: An Expert-Guided Agent Framework for Kernel Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26758)
*Yaochen Han,Ke Fan,Hongxu Jiang,Wanqi Xu,Weiyu Xie,Runhua Zhang,Chenhui Zhu,Yixiang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EGG is a two-stage expert-guided agent framework for GPU kernel generation that decomposes the task into algorithmic structure design and hardware-specific tuning, using a multi-agent collaboration mechanism to achieve 2.13× speedup over PyTorch on KernelBench.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automating high-performance GPU kernel generation for LLMs is challenging because existing LLM-based approaches lack domain-specific optimization guidance, leading to poor correctness and suboptimal performance. Expert workflows are needed to structure the optimization space effectively.

Method: EGG employs a hierarchical two-stage pipeline: Stage 1 designs algorithmic structure (foundational computation patterns); Stage 2 performs hardware-specific tuning (parallel mapping, tensor tiling, memory optimization). A stage-aware multi-agent collaboration mechanism manages inter- and intra-stage context to maintain stable optimization trajectories.

Result: On KernelBench and real-world workloads, EGG achieves a 2.13× average speedup over PyTorch and outperforms both existing agent-based and RL-based kernel generation approaches.

Conclusion: Decomposing kernel generation into expert-inspired hierarchical stages with explicit optimization objectives, combined with multi-agent collaboration, effectively guides LLMs to produce both correct and high-performance GPU kernels.

Abstract: High-performance GPU kernels are critical for reducing the exponentially growing computational costs of large language models (LLMs), but their development heavily relies on manual tuning by domain experts. While recent advances in LLM-based approaches show promise for automating kernel generation, they still struggle to achieve both correctness and high performance. This limitation primarily arises from the lack of domain-specific optimization guidance, hindering effective exploration of the optimization space. We propose EGG, an Expert-Guided Agent Framework for Kernel Generation, which incorporates expert optimization principles to guide LLMs' decisions. Inspired by expert workflows, we decompose kernel generation into two hierarchical stages: 1) algorithmic structure design, which establishes a high-quality computational structure foundation; 2) hardware-specific tuning, which performs targeted adjustments through parallel mapping, tensor tiling, and memory optimization. This staged decomposition defines explicit optimization objectives, structuring the design space to achieve progressive refinement. To this end, a stage-aware multi-agent collaboration mechanism is designed for inter and intra-stage context management, ensuring stable optimization trajectories. Experiments on KernelBench and real-world workloads show that EGG achieves a 2.13x average speedup over PyTorch, outperforming existing agent-based and RL-based approaches.

</details>


### [304] [ResilPhase: Plug-and-Play Phase Mapping and Noise-Resilient Macro-Trajectory Extrapolation for Diffusion Acceleration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26769)
*Qicheng Zhao,Yu Li,Qi Sun,Zheyu Yan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper identifies that existing cache-based acceleration methods for diffusion models suffer from quality degradation due to misaligned discrete extrapolation on continuous ODE trajectories, numerical instability, and noisy derivatives. It proposes ResilPhase, which reformulates acceleration as stable macro-trajectory extrapolation using Global Drift alignment, a derivative-free barycentric Lagrange extrapolator, and bounded Phase Mapping to suppress errors, achieving SOTA fidelity on FLUX.1-dev and HunyuanVideo under aggressive acceleration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion models suffer from high inference latency. Existing "cache-then-forecast" acceleration schemes using derivative-based polynomials degrade severely at high acceleration ratios. The root cause is identified as: discrete extrapolation on representations misaligned with the continuous diffusion trajectory, leading to accumulated spatial errors, noisy derivative amplification, and high-order numerical instability.

Method: The authors reformulate accelerated inference as stable macro-trajectory extrapolation in ODE space with three key components: (1) Global Drift (GD) — aligning forecasting with the model's end-to-end state evolution instead of intermediate features, eliminating feature inconsistency and memory overhead; (2) a derivative-free barycentric Lagrange extrapolator to bypass noisy higher-order temporal derivatives (the "derivative fallacy"); and (3) a bounded Phase Mapping that regularizes the extrapolation domain to suppress oscillatory error growth. These collectively form the ResilPhase framework.

Result: Experiments on FLUX.1-dev and HunyuanVideo demonstrate state-of-the-art fidelity under aggressive acceleration ratios, significantly outperforming prior cache-then-forecast methods that suffer from quality collapse at high speedups.

Conclusion: By shifting from discrete intermediate feature prediction to continuous macro-trajectory extrapolation with derivative-free and domain-bounded techniques, ResilPhase achieves noise-resilient, high-fidelity acceleration of diffusion transformers, overcoming the fundamental instability limitations of prior polynomial-based forecasting approaches.

Abstract: The adoption of powerful diffusion models is hindered by their significant inference latency. Recent ``cache-then-forecast'' schemes alleviate this issue by accelerating DiTs using derivative-based polynomials, but they suffer from severe quality degradation at high acceleration ratios. Our analysis reveals its root cause: the discrete extrapolation performed on representations that are misaligned with the continuous diffusion trajectory and are numerically unstable. Thus, accelerated DiTs suffer from accumulated spatial errors, noisy derivative amplification, and high-order instability. We therefore reformulate accelerated inference as stable macro-trajectory extrapolation in ordinary differential equation (ODE) space. Instead of predicting intermediate features, we align forecasting with the model's Global Drift (GD), i.e., the end-to-end state evolution, thereby eliminating feature inconsistency and memory overhead. However, even this smooth macro-trajectory remains vulnerable to the derivative fallacy: its higher-order temporal derivatives are intrinsically noisy. Thus, we introduce a derivative-free barycentric Lagrange extrapolator to effectively bypass derivative instability and approximation error. We further propose a bounded Phase Mapping that regularizes the extrapolation domain, suppressing oscillatory error growth. These elements collectively constitute ResilPhase, a noise-resilient acceleration framework. Experiments on FLUX.1-dev and HunyuanVideo demonstrate state-of-the-art fidelity under aggressive acceleration ratios.

</details>


### [305] [Memory Depth, Not Memory Access: Selective Parametric Consolidation for Long-Running Language Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26806)
*Haoliang Han*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper distinguishes between retrieval access (fetching past facts on demand) and memory depth (durable, goal-conditioned behavioral tendencies stored parametrically). The authors introduce the loop-drift protocol to test memory depth and propose EVAF, a surprise- and valence-gated LoRA consolidation mechanism. EVAF outperforms retrieval on goal persistence after context unloading, using only 2–3 parametric writes per 200 events. Key findings include factorizable selection/actuation dimensions, model-dependent inner-loop write strength, and asymmetric coupling under miscalibrated actuation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current retrieval-augmented language agents can access past facts at query time but lack a mechanism for determining which experiences should persistently influence behavior after the working context is unloaded. This gap—termed "memory depth"—motivates the study of selective, goal-conditioned parametric consolidation as a complementary capability to retrieval.

Method: The authors propose: (1) the loop-drift protocol, a stress test where the retrieval index is preserved but working context is unloaded, requiring goal-conditioned behavior to survive long-loop interference; (2) EVAF, a consolidation mechanism gated by surprise and valence signals that writes into a low-rank (LoRA) parametric store; and (3) a suite of mechanism controls including matched random gates, fixed-inner controls across multiple model scales (GPT-2, TinyLlama, Mistral-7B), and a matched-gate inversion to probe selection-actuation coupling.

Result: Retrieval excels at shallow factual recall (0.956–0.973 accuracy), while EVAF excels at goal persistence and post-unload recovery (0.812–0.904) with only 2–3 parametric writes per 200 events. Selective consolidation factorizes into two controllable dimensions: selection and actuation. Inner-loop write strength is model-dependent. The Mistral-7B matched-gate inversion reveals asymmetric selection-actuation coupling under miscalibrated actuation. Stale-memory invalidation is identified as an unresolved boundary via the Memora diagnostic.

Conclusion: Selective parametric consolidation provides memory depth that is distinct from and complementary to retrieval access. The factorization into selection and actuation offers controllable knobs for building long-running agents, while the loop-drift protocol and Memora streams provide reusable evaluation diagnostics. Stale-memory invalidation remains an open challenge.

Abstract: Long-running language agents need more than memory access. Retrieval systems can fetch past facts at query time, but they do not decide which experiences should continue to shape behavior after the working context is unloaded. We study this separate problem as memory depth: durable goal-conditioned tendencies written into a small parametric store. We introduce the loop-drift protocol, a controlled stress test in which the retrieval index remains intact while working context is unloaded and goal-conditioned behavior must persist under long-loop interference. We evaluate EVAF, a surprise- and valence-gated LoRA consolidation mechanism. Across GPT-2 and TinyLlama, retrieval is strongest on shallow factual recall (short-fact accuracy 0.956--0.973), while EVAF is strongest on goal persistence and post-unload recovery (0.812--0.904) with only 2--3 parametric writes per 200 events. Mechanism controls show that selective consolidation factorizes into two controllable dimensions: selection and actuation. Matched random gates isolate selection beyond sparse writing; fixed-inner controls across GPT-2, TinyLlama, and Mistral-7B show that inner-loop write strength is model-dependent; and a Mistral-7B matched-gate inversion reveals asymmetric selection-actuation coupling under miscalibrated actuation. Public Memora event streams serve as an external diagnostic, exposing stale-memory invalidation as an unresolved boundary. Within this probe, selective parametric consolidation supplies memory depth distinct from and complementary to retrieval access.

</details>


### [306] [KARLA: Knowledge-base Augmented Retrieval for Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26807)
*Francois Crespin,Fabian M. Suchanek,Nils Holzenberger*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A method enabling LLMs to query a knowledge base during token generation via special trigger tokens, improving factual accuracy, enabling knowledge updates without retraining, and providing traceability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs suffer from outdated or hallucinated factual knowledge, lack transparency in sourcing facts, and require larger models for factual accuracy. The authors aim to address these issues by decoupling factual knowledge from model parameters.

Method: Train the LLM to emit special trigger tokens at positions where factual knowledge is needed. These tokens invoke a query to an external knowledge base (KB), whose retrieved facts are then incorporated into the ongoing generation. The model learns when and how to perform these KB lookups during token-by-token decoding.

Result: The method improved factual grounding in both short-form and long-form generation tasks. Factual revisions could be achieved by editing the knowledge base directly, without any model retraining or parameter updates.

Conclusion: Integrating KB queries into the token generation process via learned trigger tokens offers a promising path toward updatable, transparent, and size-efficient factual generation in LLMs.

Abstract: We propose a new method that allows an LLM to automatically pull in factual knowledge from a knowledge base during token generation. This means that (1)~factual knowledge in the LLM output can be updated without retraining the LLM, (2)~facts in the LLM output can be traced to the knowledge base for transparency and explainability, and (3)~smaller models can achieve the same factual accuracy as larger models. Our core idea is to train the model to produce special tokens that trigger a query to the knowledge base. Our experiments show that our method improves factual grounding in both short and long-form generation, and allows factual revisions to take effect through KB edits rather than parameter updates.

</details>


### [307] [Computational Analysis of Heart Rate Variability in Healthy Adults](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26816)
*María J. Lado,Arturo J. Méndez,Leandro Rodriguez-Liñares,Baltasar García Pérez-Schofield,Pedro Cuesta-Morales,Brais Iglesias-Otero,Xose A. Vila*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This study evaluates HRV indices in 40 healthy adults across time, frequency, and nonlinear domains to assess normality, stability, correlation, reproducibility, and consistency, ultimately recommending a reduced set of indices (ApEn, IRRR, HRVi, SD2, MADRR/rMSSD) for optimal clinical and research utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: HRV analysis is a key cardiac health indicator, yet research on HRV parameters in healthy individuals is limited and no gold standard exists for which indices to use, limiting clinical applicability.

Method: Computational signal processing and data analysis of HRV indices (time-domain, frequency-domain, nonlinear) in 40 healthy adults (20 men, 20 women, aged 30–50), addressing five evaluation questions: normality testing, stability assessment, correlation analysis, reproducibility comparison against the Fantasia database, and inter-study consistency evaluation.

Result: (1) Time-domain and nonlinear indices, plus global and LF components, follow normal distributions with gender differences. (2) Most indices are stable except HF-related ones. (3) HF-related indices are highly intercorrelated (redundant). (4) Most indices show <10% error vs. Fantasia database, except SD2 and SDNN in women (>15%). (5) Time-domain and nonlinear indices have low inter-study variability; frequency-domain indices show high variability. The recommended index set: ApEn + IRRR (global), HRVi + SD2 (LF), MADRR/rMSSD (HF).

Conclusion: A parsimonious set of HRV indices—ApEn, IRRR, HRVi, SD2, and MADRR or rMSSD—can accurately represent global, LF, and HF HRV components, improving standardization and cross-study comparability for both clinical and research applications.

Abstract: Heart Rate Variability (HRV) analysis is a key indicator of cardiac physiological state and aids in disease diagnosis. However, research on HRV parameters in healthy individuals remains limited, and no gold standard exists. This study evaluates HRV indices in 40 healthy adults (20 men, 20 women, aged 30-50) to improve HRV's clinical utility. Using computational methods for signal processing and data analysis, time, frequency, and nonlinear indices were analyzed to address five questions: (1) normality, (2) stability, (3) correlation, (4) reproducibility, and (5) consistency. Key findings: (1) Time-domain and nonlinear indices, particularly global and LF (low frequency), follow normal distributions, with gender differences noted. (2) Most indices are stable except HF (high frequency)-related ones. (3) High correlations in HF-related indices suggest redundancy, indicating only one is necessary in studies. (4) Comparisons with the Fantasia database revealed less than 10% error for most indices, except SD2 and SDNN in women (greater than 15%). (5) Time-domain and nonlinear indices show low inter-study variability, while frequency-domain indices exhibit high variability, limiting cross-study comparisons. The selected indices-ApEn and IRRR (global variability), HRVi and SD2 (LF), and MADRR or rMSSD (HF)-are best suited for accurately representing HRV components and enhancing its clinical and research relevance.

</details>


### [308] [The Capability Frontier: Benchmarks Miss 82% of Model Performance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26836)
*Bradley Fowler,Ryan Smith,Daniel Thi Graviet,William Myers,Joshua Greaves,Narmeen Fatimah Oozeer,Antía García,Philip Quirke,Amirali Abdullah,Fazl Barez,Shriyash Kaustubh Upadhyay*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Current benchmarks underestimate LLM capabilities by evaluating single models on single runs. This paper introduces the Capability Frontier—a Pareto frontier capturing optimal performance across multiple models and multiple generations at each cost level—and shows that correcting for these biases yields up to 82% error rate reduction, with SOTA accuracy matched at 85% lower cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard LLM benchmarks suffer from two systematic biases: (1) single-model single-run evaluation underestimates real-world capabilities because different models excel on different queries, and (2) simple maximization over noisy samples overestimates performance. The authors aim to rigorously quantify the gap between reported and achievable performance under optimal model selection and multi-sampling with a budget constraint.

Method: The authors construct a Capability Frontier—a Pareto frontier over a set of 21 LLMs across 16 benchmarks (coding, reasoning, medicine, factuality, instruction following, agentic tasks). Under an oracle selector that optimally routes each query to the best model-generation pair at a given cost, they measure the best achievable accuracy at each budget level. They compare frontier performance against each benchmark's top single model, quantifying error rate reductions from correcting for single-model bias (54%) and single-run bias (82% combined). Controlled probabilistic simulations further analyze how query topic entropy affects the oracle-to-best-model performance gap.

Result: Correcting for single-model evaluation reduces error rates by 54%; additionally correcting for single-run (single-generation) bias yields an 82% total improvement. SOTA accuracy is matched at 85% lower cost on the Capability Frontier. Simulations show that higher query topic entropy produces a near-monotonic increase in the performance gap between oracle routing and the best single model, indicating greater underestimation in heterogeneous, multi-domain settings.

Conclusion: Collective LLM capabilities are substantially underestimated by standard evaluation practices. The Capability Frontier framework reveals that optimal model selection and multi-generation strategies can dramatically reduce cost or improve accuracy, with implications for both benchmarking methodology and real-world deployment in data-heterogeneous environments.

Abstract: Existing benchmarks typically report accuracy for a single model on a single run. This systematically understates real-world LLM capabilities, particularly under heterogeneous data distributions: (i) different models get different questions correct according to their specializations, and (ii) given a budget, multiple generations can be sampled and selectively retained. To quantify this gap, we introduce the Capability Frontier: a Pareto frontier over a set of models that characterizes the best achievable performance at each cost level under optimal selection across models and generations (i.e., via an oracle). Our construction corrects for two opposing biases: underestimation from single-model evaluation and overestimation from taking maxima over noisy samples. We study 21 LLMs across 16 widely used benchmarks spanning coding, reasoning, medicine, factuality, instruction following, and agentic tasks, comparing Capability Frontier performance at matched cost to each benchmark's top-performing model. Correcting for single-model evaluation yields a 54% error rate reduction; additionally correcting for single runs yields an 82% improvement, with SOTA accuracy matched at 85% cost reduction. Complementing these empirical results, we use controlled probabilistic simulations to show that higher query topic entropy produces a near-monotonic increase in the performance gap between oracle routing and the best single model. Our findings suggest collective LLM capabilities are substantially underestimated, with implications for evaluation and deployment in data-heterogeneous, multi-domain settings.

</details>


### [309] [LCAi: Life Cycle Assessment with big data fusion and retrieval-augmented generation-assisted interpretation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26857)
*Georgios Tsironis,Juan D. Medrano-Garcia,Gonzalo Guillen-Gosalbez*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a perspective-conditioned retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework for LCA interpretation, integrating multi-source retrieval (academic, industry, public discourse, EU funding) with controlled synthesis to translate environmental hotspots into actionable strategies under uncertainty, demonstrated via a hydrogen-enabled diesel reduction case study in Italian apple production.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LCA interpretation phase lacks structured mechanisms for translating quantified environmental improvement opportunities into actionable strategic pathways, especially under technological, social, and policy uncertainty. Conventional interpretation falls short in bridging impact results with implementation-oriented decision-making.

Method: A perspective fusion RAG architecture combining: (1) scenario anchor defining system boundaries and decarbonization targets; (2) perspective-specific micro-queries with constrained retrieval from academic, industry, public discourse, and EU funding datasets; (3) neutral synthesis integrating only ledger-stored outputs without further retrieval. GPT-5 nano serves as the reasoning model, applied to a hydrogen-enabled diesel reduction use case in Italian apple production.

Result: The structured retrieval and constrained synthesis design successfully mitigated hallucination risk while preserving cross-domain diversity. The proof-of-concept demonstrated AI-assisted, evidence-grounded interpretation supporting implementation-oriented decision-making beyond conventional LCA studies.

Conclusion: The framework enables more disciplined translation of LCA impact results into strategic pathways and opens new avenues for advanced AI tools in LCA, particularly for technologies deployable at scale. It represents a meaningful step toward structured, uncertainty-aware LCA interpretation.

Abstract: The interpretation phase of life cycle assessment often lacks structured mechanisms for translating quantified improvement opportunities addressing environmental hotspots into actionable strategic pathways under technological, social, and policy uncertainty. To overcome this limitation, this study introduces a perspective-conditioned retrieval-augmented generation framework for LCA interpretation, where a multi-perspective retrieval and controlled synthesis is incorporated in the artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted LCA. To operationalise large language models in LCA interpretation, a perspective fusion RAG architecture was developed, covering academic, industry, public discourse, and European union (EU) funding datasets. Our approach comprises three steps: (1) a scenario anchor defining system boundaries and decarbonization targets, (2) a set of perspective-specific micro-queries with constrained retrieval, and (3) a neutral synthesis step integrating only ledger-stored outputs without further retrieval. The framework is demonstrated through a hydrogen-enabled diesel reduction use case in an Italian apple production facility using GPT-5 nano as the reasoning model. Overall, the structured retrieval and constrained synthesis are designed to mitigate the risk of hallucination while preserving cross-domain diversity. The approach presented can support more disciplined translation of impact results into strategic pathways and opens up new avenues for the use of advanced AI tools in LCA studies, particularly those focused on technologies that could be deployed at scale. This proof-of-concept demonstrates how AI-assisted, evidence-grounded interpretation can support implementation-oriented decision-making beyond conventional LCA studies.

</details>


### [310] [TAVR-VLM: Risk-Conditioned Causal Grounding for Hallucination-Resistant Report Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26874)
*Zhixiang Lu,Xiwei Liu,Sifan Song,Changkai Ji,Anh Nguyen,Jionglong Su,Imran Razzak,Jinfeng Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TAVR-VLM proposes a Risk-Conditioned Causal Grounding Attention (R-CGA) mechanism that creates a "Risk → Region → Word" structural pathway to reduce diagnostic hallucinations in multimodal LLMs for TAVR planning. Evaluated on a 1,482-patient cohort, it achieves state-of-the-art performance (AUROC 0.896, CIDEr 0.936) while cutting hallucination rate to 8.1%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal LLMs applied to TAVR planning suffer from diagnostic hallucinations—generated text that lacks anatomical grounding—severely impeding their adoption in high-stakes clinical decision-making. There is a need for a framework that enforces structural, causally-grounded alignment between visual features and textual outputs.

Method: The proposed TAVR-VLM framework introduces Risk-Conditioned Causal Grounding Attention (R-CGA), which compresses multimodal inputs into a causal risk bottleneck to produce a purified global risk mask. During autoregressive generation, a support-projected causal consistency objective constrains token-level grounding strictly within this risk-defined support mask, enforcing a structural "Risk → Region → Word" pathway.

Result: On the M³TAVR dataset (1,482 patients), TAVR-VLM achieves AUROC of 0.896, CIDEr of 0.936, and reduces hallucination rate to 8.1%, establishing new state-of-the-art results across these metrics.

Conclusion: TAVR-VLM demonstrates that enforcing a causal structural grounding pathway significantly mitigates diagnostic hallucinations in surgical multimodal AI, improving both accuracy and interpretability for evidence-based TAVR planning.

Abstract: Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement (TAVR) planning requires meticulous multimodal reasoning. However, adapting Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to this high-stakes domain is severely impeded by diagnostic hallucinations, where generated text lacks anatomical grounding. To address this, TAVR-VLM is introduced: a novel framework featuring Risk-Conditioned Causal Grounding Attention (R-CGA) that instantiates a model-internal ``Risk $\rightarrow$ Region $\rightarrow$ Word'' structural grounding pathway. R-CGA compresses multimodal inputs into a causal risk bottleneck, purifying dense visual features into a global risk mask. During autoregressive generation, a support-projected causal consistency objective constrains token-level grounding within the risk-defined support mask. Evaluated on $\text{M}^3\text{TAVR}$, a comprehensive 1,482-patient cohort, TAVR-VLM establishes a new state-of-the-art. It achieves an AUROC of 0.896, boosts CIDEr to 0.936, and drastically reduces the hallucination rate to 8.1\%, thereby improving interpretability for evidence-based surgical AI.

</details>


### [311] [A Pipeline for Generating Longitudinal Synthetic Clinical Notes Using Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26879)
*William Poulett*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A modular synthetic clinical notes pipeline generates longitudinal patient records with internal consistency, writing style variation, and clinical detail. A dataset of 70 synthetic patients (20–50 notes each) is released at multiple validation levels to support clinical AI development without real patient data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real clinical documentation is highly sensitive, restricting access for AI development and evaluation. Synthetic data can circumvent privacy risks, but requires high fidelity, longitudinal consistency, and realistic variation to be useful for training summarisation, coding, and decision support models.

Method: A modular three-stage pipeline: (1) structured patient generation, (2) semi-structured patient journey simulation, (3) unstructured clinical note generation via large language models. Internal consistency across longitudinal records is prioritized. LLM-based validation and augmentation mechanisms enhance faithfulness, realism, and diversity.

Result: A released dataset comprising 70 synthetic patients, each with 20–50 clinical notes spanning full hospital journeys. The dataset is offered at multiple validation tiers, allowing users to trade off realism against scalability for their specific use case.

Conclusion: The synthetic clinical notes pipeline and dataset provide a privacy-preserving alternative to real clinical data, enabling development of summarisation tools, coding models, and clinical decision support systems without reliance on sensitive patient records.

Abstract: Synthetic data is increasingly used to enable the development and evaluation of AI systems in domains where access to real-world data is restricted. In healthcare, clinical documentation presents particular challenges due to its sensitivity. This work introduces a synthetic clinical notes pipeline and dataset designed to support the development of clinical AI tools while avoiding the privacy risks associated with real patient data. The dataset is generated using a modular pipeline that combines structured patient generation, semi-structured patient journey simulation, and unstructured clinical note generation using large language models. The pipeline is designed to prioritise internal consistency across longitudinal patient records, while also capturing variation in writing style, note structure, and clinical detail. Additional mechanisms, including LLM-based validation and augmentation steps, are used to improve faithfulness, realism, and diversity of the generated notes. We release a dataset of 70 synthetic patients, each associated with 20-50 clinical notes spanning a full hospital journey. The dataset is provided at multiple levels of validation, enabling users to balance realism and scalability depending on their use case. This dataset supports the development, testing, and evaluation of clinical AI systems, including summarisation tools, coding models, and decision support systems, without reliance on real patient data.

</details>


### [312] [Generative Retrieval via Diffusion Transformer with Metric-Ordered Sequence Training and Hybrid-Policy Preference Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26899)
*Chenghao Liu,Yu Zhang,Zhongtao Jiang,Kun Xu,Zhenwei An,Renzhi Wang,Zhao Wang,Jiachen Zhang,Yuxiao Zhang,Kun Xu,Songfang Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper formalizes "pattern-preserving attribute retrieval" — retrieving items that both match a target attribute and stay within a fine-grained pattern defined by a seed set. The authors propose MO-DiT+HPPO, a staged framework combining metric-ordered continuation pretraining and hybrid-pool preference optimization, demonstrating significant improvements across multiple domain-split evaluations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard embedding-based retrieval maximizes similarity to a query, but real-world production settings often require items that satisfy a target attribute *while preserving a specific pattern* expressed by seed examples. Averaging seeds preserves the pattern but yields low-attribute items; global attribute retrieval drifts to unrelated patterns. This tension between pattern fidelity and attribute relevance motivates a new formalization and solution.

Method: The paper proposes **MO-DiT+HPPO**, a staged framework: (1) raw-sequence pretraining, (2) **multi-domain metric-ordered continuation pretraining** that converts sparse online retrieval labels into in-pattern trajectories ordered from low to high predicted attribute density — teaching a single Diffusion Transformer (DiT) the metric-improvement direction across domains, (3) tail-centroid fine-tuning, and (4) **HPPO (Hybrid-Pool Preference Optimization)** which aligns generated query distributions with the true online objective by labeling a hybrid candidate pool with the online intersection metric and applying reference-anchored preference optimization. A **Pareto pair filter** retains only winner pairs that do not degrade same-pattern purity.

Result: Across four attribute domains under item- and pattern-holdout protocols, metric-ordered DiT improves the intersection metric over a pretrained generative retriever, and HPPO yields further gains — achieving significant improvements on seven of eight domain-split cells with a marginal tie on the hardest split. Metric-predictor validation, order ablations, CPT/SFT comparisons, and candidate-policy ablations confirm the source of gains.

Conclusion: The staged MO-DiT+HPPO framework effectively resolves the tension between pattern preservation and attribute retrieval, with metric-ordered training providing the core directional signal and HPPO fine-tuning aligning the model with the true online objective. The Pareto filter is critical for maintaining pattern purity while improving attribute metrics.

Abstract: Embedding-based retrieval ranks items by their similarity to a query in a shared vector space and usually aims to return the highest-scoring items. In many production settings this is not what is wanted: given a seed set that expresses a fine-grained pattern, one needs more items that both satisfy a target attribute and stay within that pattern. We formalize this as pattern-preserving attribute retrieval.
