The two goals pull against each other: averaging the seeds preserves the pattern but stays in a low-attribute region, while global attribute retrieval drifts to unrelated patterns. We approach the task with continuous generative retrieval, where a model reads a sequence of item embeddings and generates query embeddings for nearest-neighbor search. We propose MO-DiT+HPPO, a staged framework with raw-sequence pretraining, multi-domain metric-ordered continuation pretraining, tail-centroid fine-tuning, and HPPO. Metric-ordered training turns sparse online retrieval labels into in-pattern trajectories ordered from low to high predicted attribute density, teaching one model the metric-improvement direction across domains. HPPO aligns the generated query distribution with the true online objective by labeling a hybrid candidate pool with the online intersection metric and applying reference-anchored preference optimization. A Pareto pair filter keeps only winner pairs that do not lower same-pattern purity, raising the attribute metric without sacrificing the pattern. Across four attribute domains under item- and pattern-holdout protocols, metric-ordered DiT improves the intersection metric over a pretrained generative retriever, and HPPO improves it further, with significant gains on seven of eight domain-split cells and a marginal tie on the hardest split. Metric-predictor validation, order ablations, CPT/SFT comparisons, and a candidate-policy ablation show where the gains come from.

</details>


### [313] [Learning to Recover Task Experts from a Multi-Task Merged Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26902)
*Jinwook Jung,Taegyu Kim,Kumju Jo,Sungyong Baik*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ReTeX is a framework that recovers task-specific expert performance from a single merged checkpoint by predicting additive offsets that undo parameter interference. It uses SVD subspace signatures for task identification without a router, achieving >95% expert recovery in vision/NLP and enabling emergent adaptive interpolation for OOD tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Static model merging suffers from parameter interference that degrades individual task performance, while dynamic merging requires costly storage and loading of redundant expert components at inference. The authors seek a method that recovers task-expert performance from a single merged model without these overheads.

Method: ReTeX models parameter interference as affine transformations approximated by additive offsets. It proposes: (1) a parameter offset predictor that recovers task experts from the merged checkpoint by predicting and applying these offsets; (2) a router-free task identifier based on SVD subspace signatures pre-computed offline — at inference, it assigns an input to the task whose subspace yields the smallest projection residual. Together, these enable recovery of task-specific performance without storing multiple expert copies.

Result: ReTeX recovers over 95% of individual-expert performance in both vision and NLP domains. It significantly improves generalization to unseen tasks. The parameter offset prediction also enables emergent adaptive interpolation of expert knowledge for out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks.

Conclusion: Parameter interference in merging can be effectively modeled as additive offsets that are predictable. ReTeX provides a storage-efficient alternative to dynamic merging, recovering near-expert performance from a single checkpoint while generalizing to unseen tasks through emergent interpolation. Code is publicly available.

Abstract: Multi-task model merging aims to consolidate several task-specific experts into a unified model, yet static merging consistently suffers from parameter interference. While dynamic merging models aim to bridge this gap, many works rely on the costly storage and loading of redundant expert components at inference. In this work, from the perspective of task expert, we view parameter interference as parameter perturbation introduced to each expert during merging process. We show that such parameter perturbations can be modeled as affine transformation, which can be approximated as additive offsets. Motivated by these, we propose Recover Task eXpert (ReTeX), a framework that predicts those offsets, in order to undo parameter interference and recover task-expert performance from a single merged checkpoint. To recover the appropriate expert when task identity is unknown, we introduce a router-free task identifier based on SVD subspace signatures computed offline before inference. At inference, the identifier selects the task whose subspace yields the smallest projection residual for a given input. As a result, ReTeX recovers over 95% of individual-expert performance in both vision and NLP domains, while significantly improving generalization to unseen tasks. Crucially, we also show that the parameter offset prediction leads to emergent adaptive interpolation of expert knowledge for out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks. ReTeX adaptively interpolates seen expert knowledge to handle unseen tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/BAIKLAB/ReTeX

</details>


### [314] [Diagnosing Task Insensitivity in Language Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26918)
*Jingyu Liu,Xiaopeng Wu,Kehan Chen,Chuan Yu,Yong Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs acting as agents suffer from OOD generalization failures due to task insensitivity—they over-rely on spurious patterns from training and ignore task instructions. The authors propose Task-Perturbed NLL Optimization, a contrastive regularizer that enforces action dependence on task tokens, improving task sensitivity and OOD generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs deployed as long-horizon agents exhibit weak out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. The authors identify a specific failure mode: task insensitivity, where models default to learned action patterns even when task instructions are semantically corrupted or replaced, ignoring the actual task at hand.

Method: The paper first diagnoses the problem by showing (1) models continue with original-task actions under semantically corrupted instructions, and (2) attention drifts away from task tokens toward local observations during training. The proposed remedy, Task-Perturbed NLL Optimization, is a lightweight contrastive regularizer that explicitly penalizes the model when its action predictions are insensitive to perturbations of the task description, thereby enforcing dependence on the task instruction.

Result: Extensive evaluations demonstrate that the proposed regularizer improves task sensitivity and OOD generalization, while also preserving more stable attention allocation to task tokens during training.

Conclusion: Task insensitivity is a key bottleneck for OOD generalization in LLM agents, arising from an optimization bias toward shortcut features. The proposed contrastive regularizer effectively mitigates this, yielding more task-sensitive, generalizable agents.

Abstract: Large language models can serve as capable long-horizon agents, but their out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization remains weak. We identify a key source of this failure as task insensitivity: when faced with similar but distinct tasks, models might apply patterns learned during training and fail to solve the task at hand. We show that models often continue with actions aligned with the original task even when the instruction is semantically corrupted and cannot be directly answered. We further find that, when we replace the task description in a trained prompt with another similar but distinct task, the model may still output the same action. This behavior is accompanied by a consistent training-time attention drift away from task tokens and toward local observations, suggesting an optimization bias toward shortcuts. To mitigate this problem, we propose Task-Perturbed NLL Optimization, a lightweight contrastive regularizer that explicitly encourages action dependence on the task instruction. Extensive evaluations show that our intervention improves task sensitivity and OOD generalization while preserving more stable attention to task tokens.

</details>


### [315] [Where Do CoT Training Gains Land in LLM based Agents?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26935)
*Jingyu Liu,Zhiwen Wang,Yuxin Jing,Huanyu Zhou,Yong Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CoT training improves models' direct action prediction from prompts just as much as it improves reasoning-based action, suggesting CoT's benefit is not primarily from faithfulness but from general policy improvement; masking action tokens during training enhances out-of-domain generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work shows verbalized chain-of-thought (CoT) is often unfaithful — it reflects post-hoc rationalization rather than genuine reasoning. This raises the question: is CoT training actually improving the model's ability to reason through actions, or is it simply improving its ability to predict actions directly from the prompt?

Method: The authors compare "prompt actions" (predicting action without CoT) against "CoT actions" (predicting action with CoT) across training checkpoints. They measure how action quality evolves, whether the relative advantage of CoT over prompt actions changes, and how often later checkpoints revise actions in response to CoT. They also experiment with selectively masking action-token supervision on a fraction of training examples.

Result: Prompt-action quality improves substantially across checkpoints. The relative advantage of CoT over prompt actions remains stable, indicating CoT training does not widen CoT's advantage but instead improves prompt-action quality. Later checkpoints are less likely to revise actions based on CoT, showing increased reliance on the prompt. Masking action-token supervision improves out-of-domain generalization.

Conclusion: CoT training primarily improves the model's ability to directly predict actions from prompts rather than enhancing the faithfulness or causal role of CoT reasoning. This insight can be leveraged — by masking action supervision — to improve generalization.

Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is widely used in language-model agents, but prior work has shown that verbalized CoT is not always faithful and may instead reflect post-hoc reasoning, which means the model already knows the answer before reasoning. We therefore ask what CoT training is actually improving: is the model getting better at changing its action through generated reasoning, or is it getting better at predicting the action directly from the prompt? We study this question by comparing \emph{prompt actions} (predicting action without CoT) with CoT actions (predicting action with CoT). Across checkpoints, prompt-action quality improves substantially. While interacting with the environment, the relative advantage of CoT actions over prompt actions remains similar, showing that CoT training does not widen the advantage of CoT reasoning, and it helps to improve the quality of prompt actions. We further find that later checkpoints are less likely to revise the action in response to CoT, suggesting greater reliance on the prompt. Motivated by these patterns, we selectively mask action-token supervision on a fraction of training examples. This intervention improves out-of-domain generalization.

</details>


### [316] [Look-Before-Move: Narrative-Grounded World Visual Attention in Dynamic 3D Story Worlds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26964)
*Jiaming Bian,Bingliang Li,Yuehao Wu,Pichao Wang,Zhi Wang,Hailan Ma,Huadong Mo,Zhenhong Sun*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces "Look-Before-Move," a camera planning framework for dynamic 3D story worlds that separates observation specification from motion execution. It formulates Narrative-Grounded World Visual Attention, where an embodied observer decides what to observe, how to compose it, and how to shift attention under narrative intent and physical constraints. The framework uses a Semantic Observation Contract, Monte Carlo Viewpoint Search, and Semantic Trajectory Grounding. A new benchmark (StoryBlender-based, 50 stories, 457 scenes, 1585 shots) demonstrates improvements in subject perception, intent consistency, and trajectory quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As embodied AI and world models operate in dynamic 3D environments, visual perception must advance beyond passive interpretation of given observations toward active decision-making about what to observe. Current camera planning lacks the ability to organize visual attention — deciding what evidence to acquire — before executing motion, especially under narrative intent and physical 3D constraints.

Method: The Look-Before-Move framework operates in three stages: (1) Semantic Observation Contract — converts directorial/narrative intent into executable visual constraints; (2) Monte Carlo Viewpoint Search — finds narrative-compliant and geometrically feasible viewpoints; (3) Semantic Trajectory Grounding — connects selected viewpoints into continuous, collision-aware, temporally coherent camera motion. The framework is evaluated on a newly constructed Dynamic 3D Story World Benchmark (StoryBlender) with 50 stories, 457 scenes, and 1585 shots featuring animated characters and executable 3D environments.

Result: The proposed framework demonstrates improved subject perception, intent consistency, and trajectory quality over representative baselines, validating the importance of organizing visual attention prior to generating camera motion.

Conclusion: Separating observation specification from motion execution — thinking about what to observe before deciding how to move — is critical for camera planning in dynamic 3D story worlds. The Look-Before-Move paradigm effectively bridges narrative intent with geometrically feasible camera control.

Abstract: As embodied AI and world models increasingly operate in dynamic 3D environments, visual perception must move beyond passively interpreting given observations toward actively deciding what to observe. We study this problem through camera planning in dynamic 3D story worlds, where the camera must not only generate smooth motion, but also decide what visual evidence should be acquired before it moves. We formulate this capability as Narrative-Grounded World Visual Attention, where the camera acts as an embodied observer that determines what to observe, how to compose the observation, and how to shift attention over time under narrative intent and physical 3D constraints. To realize this capability, we propose Look-Before-Move, a camera planning framework that separates observation specification from motion execution. It first builds a Semantic Observation Contract to convert directorial intent into executable visual constraints, then performs Monte Carlo Viewpoint Search to find narrative-compliant and geometrically feasible viewpoints, and finally applies Semantic Trajectory Grounding to connect selected viewpoints into continuous, collision-aware, and temporally coherent camera motion. We further construct a dynamic 3D Story World Benchmark based on StoryBlender, covering 50 stories, 457 scenes, and 1585 shots with animated characters, semantic scene configurations, and executable 3D environments. Experiments show that our framework improves subject perception, intent consistency, and trajectory quality over representative baselines, demonstrating the importance of organizing visual attention before generating camera motion.

</details>


### [317] [Einstein World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26969)
*Munachiso Samuel Nwadike,Zangir Iklassov,Ali Mekky,Zayd M. Kawakibi Zuhri,Kentaro Inui*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces Einstein World Models (EWMs), a framework that augments LLM reasoning by integrating visual-temporal simulations (rollouts) into the reasoning trace, enabling models to perform visual thought experiments beyond text-only reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors question whether complex reasoning requires the ability to visualize counterfactual scenarios beyond direct experience. They investigate whether equipping LLMs with a visual imagination mechanism — generating inspectable visual rollouts as intermediate reasoning steps — can enhance reasoning capabilities that language alone may not adequately support.

Method: EWMs extend LLM tool-calling capabilities into visual thought experiments. Within an EWM, the LLM invokes a "world-module" (distinct from a world model) to produce short visual-temporal rollouts of scenes under consideration. These rollouts serve not as final answers but as inspectable hypotheses that inform subsequent reasoning steps within the trace.

Result: The paper proposes a blueprint architecture rather than presenting empirical results. The framework conceptually extends tool-calling paradigms (e.g., web search, code execution) into visual simulation, positioning visual rollouts as intermediate reasoning artifacts that complement language-based reasoning.

Conclusion: Visualising counterfactual events can complement language as a mechanism for complex thought. EWMs provide a structured way to integrate visual-temporal simulations into LLM reasoning pipelines, treating them as inspectable hypotheses that support downstream reasoning, thereby extending LLM capabilities into the domain of visual thought experiments.

Abstract: Does intelligence require the ability to reason about phenomena beyond direct experience? It is natural to suspect that some complex thought cannot be captured through language alone. However, of particular concern to this work, is whether visualising counterfactual events can complement language as a mechanism for complex thought. We ask whether LLMs can be trained to utilise such visualisation mechanisms, in a way that benefits their reasoning abilities. Motivated by this question, we propose Einstein World Models. EWMs are a blueprint for LLM-based reasoning systems that place visual-temporal rollouts inside the reasoning trace, allowing them to reason in ways that text alone may not support well. In an EWM, the LLM calls a world-module (not to be confused with a world model), to produce short rollouts of scenes under consideration. The returned rollout is treated not as the answer, but as an inspectable hypothesis that can support later reasoning. Einstein World Models extend the capability of LLMs for tool calling (such as web search or code execution), into the domain of visual thought experiments.

</details>


### [318] [Adaptive Utility driven Resource Orchestration for Resilient AI (AURORA-AI)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27005)
*Rahul Umesh Mhapsekar,Ilias Cherkaoui,Lizy Abraham,Indrakshi Dey*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AURORA-AI is a closed-loop resource orchestration framework that uses Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman control, Lyapunov stability monitoring, and fairness-aware composite utility to adaptively allocate compute across heterogeneous AI models under non-stationary conditions, outperforming five baselines (Static, Round Robin, Greedy, LinUCB, PPO) in recovery speed, utility, fairness, and stability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern AI deployments face non-stationary computational, demographic, and operational conditions where static resource allocation degrades both predictive performance and human-centric properties (fairness, explainability). Existing controllers lack a unified framework that jointly optimizes performance, fairness, cost, latency, robustness, and interpretability under disruptions such as demographic bias shocks, concept drift, and black-swan events.

Method: AURORA-AI integrates three components: (1) Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) feedback control for optimal dynamic resource allocation, (2) Lyapunov-based stability monitoring to ensure system resilience, and (3) a fairness-aware composite utility function that jointly weights predictive performance, demographic parity, cost, latency, robustness, and interpretability. The framework continuously redistributes computational budget across a population of heterogeneous AI models in a closed loop. Evaluation uses stress-rich discrete-time simulation injecting demographic bias shocks, gradual concept drift, and abrupt black-swan disruptions, compared against Static, Round Robin, Greedy, LinUCB, and PPO-based deep RL agents.

Result: AURORA-AI achieves immediate recovery from black-swan events (vs. 88 time steps for Static, 22 for PPO), lifts the alpha-quantile by 29% and the super-quantile by 25%, simultaneously reduces both mean and maximum demographic parity gap, and increases the fraction of Lyapunov-stable operating steps.

Conclusion: Fairness-aware adaptive orchestration grounded in stability theory provides a practical and theoretically sound path toward resilient, human-centric AI deployment under dynamic, disruptive conditions.

Abstract: Modern AI systems are increasingly deployed under non-stationary computational, demographic, and operational conditions in which static resource allocation strategies degrade both predictive performance and human-centric properties such as fairness and explainability. This paper presents AURORA-AI, an Adaptive Utility-driven Resource Orchestration framework for Resilient AI that unifies Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman feedback control, Lyapunov-based stability monitoring, and a fairness-aware composite utility into a single closed-loop policy.The framework continuously redistributes computational budget across a population of heterogeneous AI models so that the global utility, defined jointly over predictive performance, demographic parity, cost, latency, robustness, and interpretability, remains maximised under disruption. The framework is evaluated in a stress-rich discrete-time simulation that concurrently injects demographic bias shocks, gradual concept drift, and abrupt black-swan disruptions, and is compared against five established controllers including Static, Round Robin, Greedy, LinUCB, and a deep reinforcement-learning agent based on Proximal Policy Optimisation. AURORA-AI achieves immediate recovery from the black-swan event compared to eighty-eight time steps for the Static baseline and twenty-two for Proximal Policy Optimisation, lifts the alpha-quantile and the super-quantile by twenty-nine and twenty-five percent respectively, simultaneously reduces the mean and maximum demographic parity gap, and increases the fraction of Lyapunov-stable operating steps. These results indicate that fairness-aware adaptive orchestration grounded in stability theory is a practical and theoretically motivated path toward resilient human-centric AI deployment.

</details>


### [319] [How to evaluate clustering with ground truth?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27061)
*Pasi Fränti*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Reviews external cluster validity indexes, focusing on set-matching measures. Recommends Centroid Index (CI) for intuitive cluster-level evaluation, Pair-set Index (PSI) for normalized point-level scores unbiased by cluster size, and clustering accuracy (ACC) when all points should contribute equally.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide guidance on selecting among external cluster validity indexes when ground truth is available, given the variety of existing measures with different properties and biases.

Method: Comparative review and analysis of common external validity indexes, organized around set-matching-based measures, examining their properties at both cluster-level and point-level granularity.

Result: CI is identified as the preferred cluster-level measure due to its intuitiveness and explainability. For point-level evaluation, PSI offers normalized scoring unbiased by cluster sizes, while ACC and other set-matching measures are suitable when equal weighting of all points is desired.

Conclusion: The choice of external validity index should be guided by the evaluation granularity needed (cluster-level vs. point-level) and whether normalization or equal point contribution is prioritized.

Abstract: External indexes can be used for cluster evaluation when ground truth is available. We review the most common external validity indexes focusing on set-matching-based measures. We recommend centroid index (CI), because it is an intuitive cluster-level measure with an explainable result. If we need a more fine-tuned, point-level measure, there are more choices. Pair-set index (PSI) provides a normalized score which is not biased by cluster sizes. If all points should matter equally, then clustering accuracy (ACC) or any other set-matching measure is suitable.

</details>


### [320] [Joint Learning of Experiential Rules and Policies for Large Language Model Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27136)
*Shicheng Ye,Chao Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: JERP jointly updates a long-term experiential-rule pool and the policy from the same interaction trajectories, keeping rules aligned with the evolving policy while gradually absorbing stable behaviors into the model for improved LLM agent performance on interactive tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches separate experiential knowledge use: external rule prompting (interpretable but drifts from evolving policy) vs. parameter updating via trajectories (broad improvement but limited local correction in sparse-reward settings). A unified method that couples both is needed.

Method: JERP maintains a long-term experiential-rule pool and a policy, both updated from the same interaction trajectories. At decision time, task-relevant rules are retrieved and provided alongside interaction history. Post-episode, trajectories optimize the policy and revise the rule pool by comparing current rollouts against reference successful trajectories.

Result: Experiments on AlfWorld and WebShop demonstrate consistent gains in decision performance for complex interactive tasks.

Conclusion: Coupling rule-pool revision with policy optimization from shared trajectories keeps experiential knowledge aligned with the evolving policy, enabling both stable behavior absorption into the model and effective local corrections.

Abstract: For LLM agents in multi-step interactive environments, a key challenge is to make effective use of accumulated interaction experience. Existing work has typically separated two uses of such experience: keeping it outside the model as natural-language rules for later prompting, or using trajectories and feedback to update the model parameters. The former is easy to interpret but can fall out of sync with the evolving policy; the latter improves the policy more broadly but provides only limited correction for local mistakes in sparse-reward settings. We present Joint Learning of Experiential Rules and Policies for LLM Agents (JERP), which updates a long-term experiential-rule pool and the policy from the same interaction trajectories. At decision time, JERP retrieves task-relevant rules and conditions the agent on them together with the interaction history. After each episode, it uses the collected trajectories both to optimize the policy and to revise the rule pool by comparing current rollouts with reference successful trajectories. This coupling keeps the rule pool aligned with the evolving policy while allowing stable and effective behaviors to be gradually absorbed into the model itself. Experiments on AlfWorld and WebShop show that JERP yields consistent gains in decision performance for complex interactive tasks.

</details>


### [321] [OpenRCA 2.0: From Outcome Labels to Causal Process Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27154)
*Aoyang Fang,Yifan Yang,Jin'ao Shang,Qisheng Lu,Junjielung Xu,Rui Wang,Songhan Zhang,Yuzhong Zhang,Boxi Yu,Pinjia He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PAVE introduces a step-wise labeling protocol using fault injection interventions to reconstruct causal propagation paths for RCA. This yields OpenRCA 2.0, the first cross-system RCA benchmark with step-wise causal annotations. Evaluation of 11 LLMs reveals that while 76% identify at least one correct root-cause service, only 61.5% ground it in a verified causal path — a failure mode hidden by outcome-only evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RCA datasets label only the final root cause without annotating the causal propagation path from cause to observed symptom, reducing RCA to naive pattern matching. This gap prevents rigorous evaluation of LLM agentic capabilities such as long-context understanding, multi-step reasoning, and tool use that true RCA demands.

Method: PAVE is a step-wise labeling protocol that uses known interventions from fault injection to perform forward verification — reasoning from cause to effect — to reconstruct causal propagation paths. This protocol is applied to create OpenRCA 2.0, a benchmark with 500 instances featuring step-wise causal annotations for LLM-based RCA agents.

Result: Across 11 frontier LLMs, exact root-cause set recovery averages only 20.7%. Relaxing criteria reveals ungrounded diagnosis: 76.0% of cases identify at least one correct root-cause service, but only 61.5% ground that identification in a verified causal propagation path to the observed symptom.

Conclusion: Outcome-only evaluation masks the ungrounded diagnosis failure mode. Step-wise causal ground truth is essential for developing and evaluating trustworthy LLM-based RCA agents, as it exposes the gap between identifying a root cause and actually reasoning through the causal chain.

Abstract: Root cause analysis (RCA) poses a holistic test of LLM agentic capabilities, such as long-context understanding, multi-step reasoning, and tool use. However, existing datasets suffer from a fundamental gap: they label only the root cause, not the propagation path connecting it to the observed symptom, which largely simplifies the task to naive pattern matching. To support rigorous evaluation, we introduce PAVE, a step-wise labeling protocol that leverages known interventions from fault injection to reconstruct causal propagation paths. The mechanism is forward verification: reasoning from cause to effect rather than inferring backward from symptoms. Applying PAVE yields OpenRCA 2.0 (500 instances), the first cross-system RCA benchmark with step-wise causal annotations for LLM agents. Across 11 frontier LLMs, recovering the exact root-cause set succeeds in only 20.7% of cases on average. To locate where this difficulty lies, we relax the criterion and find what we call the ungrounded diagnosis: agents identify at least one correct root-cause service in 76.0% of cases, but ground that service in a verified causal propagation path to the observed symptom in only 61.5%. Outcome-only evaluation hides this failure mode; step-wise causal ground truth is the missing piece for trustworthy LLM-based RCA agents.

</details>


### [322] [TOPS: First-Principles Visual Token Pruning via Constructing Token Optimal Preservation Sets for Efficient MLLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27161)
*Tinghao Wang,Yichen Guo,Rui Huang,Zheng Lu,Qizhe Zhang,Chenxi Li,Yuan Zhang,Jiajun Cao,Zhirong Shen,Yaosong Du,Guangyan Gan,Wenya Wang,Lin William Cong,Shanghang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes TOPS, a training-free visual token pruning method for multimodal LLMs grounded in an information-theoretic framework that balances task relevance, information coverage, and semantic diversity. TOPS removes up to 77.8% of visual tokens while maintaining or even improving model performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MLLMs suffer from heavy computational overhead due to the large number of visual tokens. Existing pruning methods are suboptimal: attention-based approaches retain redundant tokens, diversity-based methods ignore user instructions, and hybrid methods lack a principled formulation of the pruning objective.

Method: The authors formulate visual token pruning as constructing Token Optimal Preservation Sets (TOPS) using a top-down information-theoretic analysis. They derive three principles: (1) Task Relevance — tokens must be relevant to the user instruction; (2) Information Coverage — selected tokens should collectively cover the information content; and (3) Semantic Diversity — tokens should be semantically non-redundant. Based on these, TOPS is implemented as a training-free, model-agnostic module applicable to various MLLMs.

Result: Experiments across 7 MLLM backbones and 14 benchmarks show TOPS outperforms prior pruning methods. On LLaVA-NeXT, TOPS removes 77.8% of visual tokens while preserving 100.0% and 100.6% performance on the 7B and 13B models respectively, and can even mitigate hallucination.

Conclusion: Principled visual token pruning via TOPS not only achieves substantial efficiency gains without performance degradation but also suggests that removing redundant visual tokens can reduce hallucination, inspiring future lightweight MLLM architectures.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved strong multimodal reasoning capabilities, but their efficiency is limited by the large number of visual tokens, which introduces substantial computational overhead. Visual token pruning offers a natural solution, yet existing methods are imperfect: attention-based criteria tend to retain redundant tokens, while diversity-based criteria are often agnostic to user instructions. Even methods that combine multiple criteria still lack a principled formulation of the intrinsic objective of token pruning. In this paper, we revisit visual token pruning from a first-principles perspective and formulate it as constructing Token Optimal Preservation Sets. Through a top-down information-theoretic analysis, we identify three fundamental principles for effective token selection: Task Relevance, Information Coverage, and Semantic Diversity. Based on these principles, we propose TOPS, a training-free and model-agnostic pruning module that can be applied to various MLLMs. Extensive experiments on 7 MLLM backbones and 14 benchmarks demonstrate that TOPS outperforms prior methods under diverse pruning settings. Notably, on LLaVA-NeXT, TOPS removes 77.8% of visual tokens while preserving 100.0% and 100.6% performance on its 7B and 13B models, respectively, suggesting that pruning redundant visual tokens can sometimes mitigate hallucination and inspire future lightweight MLLM design.

</details>


### [323] [A Process Harness for Uplifting Legacy Workflows to Agentic BPM: Design and Realization in CUGA FLO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27188)
*Fabiana Fournier,Lior Limonad*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces the "process harness," a mechanism that wraps an agentic, policy-governed layer around existing deterministic workflow engines, enabling AI-driven reasoning and adaptation without replacing the underlying BPM infrastructure. Formalized via the Task-Decision-Flow (TDF) model and implemented as CUGA FLO.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Legacy workflow engines are deterministic and structurally compliant but lack the flexibility, reasoning, and adaptability offered by LLM-based agents. Rather than replacing these engines entirely—which is costly and risky—the authors seek a way to uplift existing BPM systems with agentic capabilities while preserving the engine's structural authority and imperative compliance.

Method: Proposes the process harness concept: a policy-governed agentic layer around a deterministic workflow engine that intercepts designated control points. Formalizes this through the Task-Decision-Flow (TDF) model with three agent types—TaskAgent (knowledge-intensive tasks), DecisionAgent (per-case gateway routing), and FlowAgent (runtime flow adaptation via hooks)—each governed by explicit policies from the process FRAME. The approach is implemented in CUGA FLO and demonstrated on a loan approval workflow.

Result: The CUGA FLO implementation demonstrates the process harness on a loan approval workflow, exercising all three agent types and hook-driven regulatory override. The approach successfully reconciles imperative requirements (deterministic structural compliance) with normative requirements (policy-framed agentic autonomy at designated control points).

Conclusion: The process harness enables a pragmatic, incremental path to Agentic BPM by augmenting rather than replacing existing workflow engines. It uniquely balances structural compliance (imperative) with agentic flexibility (normative), making it suitable for regulated enterprise environments that require both deterministic process guarantees and adaptive, reasoning-driven decision-making.

Abstract: We introduce the process harness, a new mechanism for uplifting legacy workflows into Agentic Business Process Management (Agentic BPM) without replacing the underlying workflow engine. A process harness places a policy-governed agentic layer around a deterministic workflow engine, intercepting designated control points to contribute reasoning, adaptation, and oversight while the engine retains structural authority over the process. To define the process harness rigorously, we develop the Task-Decision-Flow (TDF) model, specifying both its data schema and its execution semantics. TDF decomposes LLM reasoning across three policy-governed agent types: a TaskAgent for knowledge-intensive task execution, a DecisionAgent for per-case gateway routing, and a FlowAgent that governs runtime flow adaptation through a principled hook mechanism. Each agent reasons within an explicit policy drawn from the process FRAME, the aggregate policy set governing all LLM calls in the system. We then present CUGA FLO as the design and implementation realization of the TDF model, and demonstrate it on a loan approval workflow that exercises all three agent types and hook-driven regulatory override. The process harness uniquely reconciles imperative requirements, realized through deterministic workflow execution that enforces structural compliance, with normative requirements, realized through policy-framed agentic autonomy invoked at designated control points wherever the process demands it.

</details>


### [324] [Vulnerability of Natural Language Classifiers to Evolutionary Generated Adversarial Text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27215)
*Manjinder Singh,Alexander E. I. Brownlee,Mohamed Elawady*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GAversary is a black-box adversarial attack using a genetic algorithm with GloVe embeddings for word replacement mutations. It achieves substantially stronger attack success than BAE and A2T (e.g., reducing accuracy from 76.8% to 5.8% vs. BAE's 27.6%) at the cost of perturbing ~2× more words and slightly lower semantic similarity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing NLP adversarial attacks either require white-box access to model internals or produce suboptimal results. The authors aim to develop a stronger black-box attack that requires only logit outputs while maintaining semantic similarity, using evolutionary optimization to find more effective adversarial perturbations.

Method: GAversary is a hybrid genetic algorithm operating in a black-box setting (only logit outputs needed). Its key innovation is using GloVe embeddings as the mutation operator to propose semantically similar word replacements. The GA evolves a population of adversarial examples through selection, crossover, and mutation to maximize misclassification while preserving semantic similarity.

Result: On benchmark datasets, GAversary dramatically reduced target model accuracy — in the best case from 76.8% to 5.8%, far surpassing BAE (27.6%) and A2T. The trade-off includes perturbing roughly twice as many words, slightly lower semantic similarity scores, and approximately a 5% increase in runtime compared to the baselines.

Conclusion: GAversary demonstrates that black-box genetic algorithms augmented with embedding-based mutations can produce significantly stronger adversarial attacks than existing methods, establishing a new effectiveness ceiling for black-box NLP attacks, albeit with modest trade-offs in perturbation rate and similarity.

Abstract: Deep learning models have achieved impressive performance across various fields but remain vulnerable to adversarial inputs, particularly in NLP, where such attacks can have significant real-world consequences. Adversarial attacks often involve small, semantically similar token replacements to fool NLP models, and recent methods have become more precise by targeting specific vulnerable words, often by exploiting some level of access to the model's internal structure. This paper proposes GAversary, a hybrid Genetic Algorithm (GA) to generate adversarial attacks on natural language models. The GA is able to treat the target model as a black box, requiring only the logit value output by the model to guide the search. GAversary differs from GAs previously proposed for this problem by using GloVe embeddings to propose word replacements (the mutation operator) to improve the semantic similarity of the adversarial examples. GAversary is applied to several benchmark data sets and well-known target models. GAversary is able to substantially reduce the target model's accuracy on test data compared to the BAE and A2T attacks compared against (in the best case, reducing a 76.8% accuracy to 5.8%, compared to BAE's 27.6%). The trade-off is that GAversary perturbs just under twice as many words as the other two methods, with a slightly lower semantic similarity to the original text and around a 5% increase in run-time.

</details>


### [325] [Ask, Don't Judge: Binary Questions for Interpretable LLM Evaluation and Self-Improvement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27226)
*Sangwoo Cho,Kushal Chawla,Pengshan Cai,Zefang Liu,Chenyang Zhu,Shi-Xiong Zhang,Sambit Sahu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BINEVAL decomposes LLM evaluation into atomic binary questions, aggregates them into multi-dimensional scores, and uses the transparent question-level feedback for both interpretable evaluation and iterative prompt optimization, matching or outperforming strong baselines across multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM output evaluation suffers from three key bottlenecks: human evaluation is expensive and slow, lexical metrics correlate poorly with human judgments on open-ended generation, and holistic LLM judges produce opaque scores that are hard to debug and diagnose.

Method: BINEVAL uses a two-stage framework: (1) a meta-prompt generates fine-grained, atomic binary questions from the evaluation task prompt, and (2) an LLM answers these questions independently for each candidate output. The binary verdicts are then aggregated into interpretable, multi-dimensional scores with calibrated overall scores. The resulting question-level feedback is transparent and directly usable for prompt improvement via iterative optimization.

Result: On SummEval, Topical-Chat, and QAGS, BINEVAL matches or outperforms UniEval and G-Eval, with especially strong results on factual consistency (QAGS). It better matches human score distributions, avoids ceiling effects common in prior LLM judges, and improves discrimination between borderline and flawed outputs. The question-level feedback also supports iterative prompt optimization, improving evaluator prompts on summarization and generation prompts on IFBench under both self-update and cross-model update settings.

Conclusion: BINEVAL provides a task-agnostic, training-free, and interpretable evaluation framework that combines strong empirical correlation with human judgments and practical value for diagnostic analysis and prompt optimization.

Abstract: Evaluating LLM outputs remains a major bottleneck in NLP: human evaluation is expensive and slow, lexical metrics correlate poorly with human judgments on open-ended generation, and holistic LLM judges often produce opaque scores that are hard to debug. We propose BINEVAL, a framework that decomposes evaluation criteria into atomic binary questions and aggregates the resulting verdicts into interpretable, multi-dimensional scores. Given a task prompt, a meta-prompt generates fine-grained evaluation questions, and an LLM answers them independently for each output, yielding transparent question-level feedback together with calibrated overall scores. This decomposition makes evaluation easier to inspect, easier to diagnose, and directly usable for prompt improvement. Across SummEval, Topical-Chat, and QAGS, BINEVAL matches or outperforms strong baselines including UniEval and G-Eval, with especially strong results on factual consistency benchmarks such as QAGS. Beyond competitive correlation with human judgments, BINEVAL better matches human score distributions and avoids the ceiling effects common in prior LLM judges, leading to better discrimination between borderline and clearly flawed outputs. We further show that the same question-level feedback supports iterative prompt optimization, improving evaluator prompts on summarization and generation prompts on IFBench under both self-update and cross-model update settings. Overall, BINEVAL provides a task-agnostic, training-free, and interpretable evaluation framework that combines strong empirical performance with practical diagnostic and optimization value.

</details>


### [326] [EO-WM: A Physically Informed World Model for Probabilistic Earth Observation Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27277)
*Junwei Luo,Shuai Yuan,Zhenya Yang,Yansheng Li,Zhe Liu,Hengshuang Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EO-WM is a video diffusion transformer for multispectral Earth observation forecasting that uses a physically informed conditioning framework (climatological baseline, weather anomalies, cumulative stress signals) to better capture weather-driven vegetation dynamics. It introduces two new benchmarks (Extreme Summer, Seasonal Matched-Pair) for evaluating weather-response fidelity, achieving meaningful improvements in NDVI decline prediction and directional hit rate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing EO forecasting methods either collapse uncertainty into deterministic predictions or treat weather as undifferentiated conditioning signals. Current benchmarks also overemphasize pixel-level reconstruction accuracy rather than testing whether forecasts respond correctly to changed weather forcing. The authors aim to reframe EO forecasting as a partially observed, weather-driven world modeling problem that explicitly handles sparse observations, unobserved land-surface states, and weather-conditioned uncertainty.

Method: The authors propose EO-WM, a video diffusion transformer with a three-component physically informed conditioning framework: (1) a climatological baseline pathway, (2) a weather anomaly pathway (separated from baseline via distinct conditioning branches), and (3) cumulative physical stress signals that accumulate anomalous forcing over time to capture sustained heat/drought stress. The model treats EO forecasting as conditional video generation where weather serves as the conditioning signal driving land-surface dynamics.

Result: EO-WM achieves a relative 5.63% reduction in NDVI decline amplitude error and a relative 7.80% improvement in directional hit rate compared to baselines, while maintaining competitive performance on standard pixel-level metrics (e.g., MSE, SSIM). The Extreme Summer Benchmark tests severity-aware vegetation degradation prediction under extreme heat/drought, and the Seasonal Matched-Pair Benchmark evaluates whether forecasts produce the correct differential response when weather forcing is altered for the same location.

Conclusion: Explicitly separating baseline climatology from weather anomalies and modeling cumulative stress improves a diffusion-based EO forecasting model's sensitivity to weather forcing. The proposed diagnostic benchmarks reveal behavior that standard pixel-level metrics miss, and the open-source release aims to spur further work on causality-aware EO forecasting.

Abstract: Earth Observation (EO) forecasting aims to predict future Earth surface dynamics from satellite observations under changing meteorological conditions. In this paper, we view this task as a partially observed, weather-driven world modeling problem, in which weather acts as a conditioning signal, while forecasting remains uncertain due to sparse observations and unobserved land-surface states. However, existing methods do not fully capture this setting: deterministic models collapse uncertainty into a single future prediction, while diffusion-based methods typically treat weather variables as undifferentiated conditioning signals, and existing benchmarks focus mainly on reconstruction accuracy rather than whether forecasts respond correctly to changed weather forcing.We introduce EO-WM, a video diffusion transformer for multispectral EO forecasting. EO-WM incorporates a physically informed conditioning framework that represents meteorological forcing through a climatological baseline, weather anomalies, and cumulative physical stress signals. Specifically, it separates baseline and anomaly through distinct conditioning pathways, and accumulates anomalous forcing over time to capture sustained heat and drought stress. To evaluate weather-response behavior beyond standard metrics, we introduce two diagnostic benchmarks: an Extreme Summer Benchmark for severity-aware prediction of vegetation degradation under extreme weather, and a Seasonal Matched-Pair Benchmark for testing response fidelity under changed weather forcing. Experiments show that EO-WM reduces the error in predicted Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) decline amplitude by a relative 5.63% and improves directional hit rate by a relative 7.80%, while remaining competitive on standard pixel-level metrics. The benchmarks and model will be made open-source at https://github.com/Luo-Z13/EO-WM.

</details>


### [327] [Simulation-based inference for rapid Bayesian parameter estimation in epidemiological models: a comparison with MCMC](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27286)
*Alina Bazarova,Johann Fredrik Jadebeck,Henrik Zunker,Carolina J. Klett-Tammen,Torben Heinsohn,Wolfgang Wiechert,Katharina Noeh,Stefan Kesselheim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper compares simulation-based inference (SBI) using neural posterior estimation against traditional MCMC for Bayesian calibration of a mechanistic SECIR epidemiological model. Using German COVID-19 ICU occupancy data, SBI achieves comparable posterior accuracy while dramatically reducing runtime—from ~1000s to ~60–70s for 31-day windows and from >19,000s to ~157s for a 201-day reconstruction—demonstrating SBI as a scalable solution for near-real-time epidemiological inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MCMC-based Bayesian calibration of mechanistic epidemiological models is computationally prohibitive for high-dimensional, nonlinear systems, especially when repeated near-real-time inference is required for outbreak monitoring. There is a need for faster, scalable alternatives that preserve posterior accuracy.

Method: The authors applied simulation-based inference with neural posterior estimation to a mechanistic SECIR (Susceptible-Exposed-Carrier-Infected-Recovered) model. They calibrated the model using COVID-19 ICU occupancy data from Germany (2020), testing across multiple epidemic phases using both 31-day inference windows and a challenging 201-day reconstruction problem with multiple transmission change points. Posterior agreement was evaluated via Wasserstein distances, Kullback-Leibler divergences, and posterior predictive checks, with runtime comparisons between SBI (CPU+GPU) and MCMC (CPU-only).

Result: For 31-day windows, SBI posteriors showed strong agreement with MCMC and accurately reproduced ICU trajectories. In the 201-day setting, SBI preserved dominant posterior structure despite increased uncertainty. SBI reduced runtime from ~1000s (MCMC) to ~60–70s for 31-day problems, and from >19,000s (MCMC) to ~157s for the 201-day problem, all while maintaining comparable predictive performance.

Conclusion: SBI with neural posterior estimation provides a rapid, computationally efficient, and scalable framework for Bayesian calibration of mechanistic epidemiological models, making it well-suited for repeated near-real-time inference and rapid outbreak analysis without sacrificing posterior accuracy.

Abstract: Mechanistic epidemiological models are widely used to support infectious disease forecasting and public-health decision making. Bayesian calibration of such models is commonly performed using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), which can become computationally expensive for high-dimensional nonlinear systems and repeated near-real-time analyses. Here, we investigate simulation-based inference (SBI) using neural posterior estimation as a scalable alternative for Bayesian calibration of a mechanistic SECIR epidemiological model using COVID-19 intensive care unit (ICU) occupancy data from Germany during 2020. We compared SBI and MCMC across multiple epidemic phases using both 31-day inference windows and a substantially more challenging 201-day reconstruction problem involving multiple transmission change points. Posterior agreement was evaluated quantitatively using Wasserstein distances and Kullback-Leibler divergences together with posterior predictive checks. Across the 31-day windows, SBI recovered posterior distributions in strong agreement with MCMC while accurately reproducing observed ICU trajectories. In the 201-day setting, SBI preserved the dominant posterior structure despite increased uncertainty. SBI, by combining CPU and GPU resources, substantially reduced computational runtime compared with MCMC, which was restricted to running on CPUs. Whereas MCMC required approximately 1000 seconds for the 31-day inference problems, SBI achieved comparable posterior and predictive performance in approximately 60-70 seconds on a single GPU. For the 201-day inference problem, SBI required an average of 157 seconds, while the MCMC runs took over 19,000 seconds. Our results demonstrate that SBI provides a rapid and computationally efficient framework for Bayesian calibration of mechanistic epidemiological models, supporting repeated near-real-time inference and rapid outbreak analysis.

</details>


### [328] [Prompt Injection in Automated Résumé Screening with Large Language Models: Single and Multi-Injection Settings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27287)
*Preet Baxi,Jiannan Xu,Jane Yi Jiang,Stefanus Jasin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Prompt injection in LLM-based résumé screening reliably boosts rankings when manipulation is rare and candidate quality is homogeneous, but its effectiveness collapses as injection becomes widespread. In heterogeneous pools, injection can occasionally enable lower-quality candidates to outrank higher-quality ones, raising fairness concerns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs are increasingly deployed for automated job applicant screening, candidates have incentives to strategically manipulate these systems. The authors investigate the vulnerability of LLM-based résumé screening to prompt injection — subtle, non-qualification-adding text designed to bias model evaluations — and examine how this threat varies with prevalence and candidate quality distribution.

Method: Controlled experiments manipulating (1) the prevalence of prompt injection among candidates, (2) the homogeneity vs. heterogeneity of candidate quality, and (3) the presence of prompt injection text in résumés. Rankings are evaluated under different experimental conditions to measure injection effectiveness and fairness impacts.

Result: Prompt injection reliably improves rankings when résumé quality is homogeneous and few candidates inject. Effectiveness rapidly diminishes as injection becomes widespread, collapsing at high prevalence. Under heterogeneous quality, injection is less effective on average but can occasionally let lower-quality candidates outrank higher-quality ones.

Conclusion: LLM-based résumé screening is most vulnerable to prompt injection when manipulation is rare and candidate quality differences are small. The findings highlight both the practical limits of injection attacks and the fairness risks they pose when quality varies across candidates.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to screen and rank job applicants, creating incentives for candidates to strategically manipulate algorithmic hiring systems. We study prompt injection in automated résumé screening, defined as subtle self-promotional text that introduces no new qualifications but is designed to influence LLM evaluations. Using controlled experiments, we show that prompt injection reliably improves applicant rankings when résumé quality is homogeneous and few candidates inject. However, its effectiveness rapidly diminishes as more candidates inject, collapsing when manipulation becomes widespread. When candidate quality is heterogeneous, prompt injection is less effective on average, but can occasionally allow lower-quality candidates to outrank higher-quality ones, raising fairness concerns. Overall, LLM-based screening is most vulnerable when manipulation is rare and candidate quality differences are small. Code and resources are publicly available at: https://github.com/preetb1199/Prompt_Injection_ACL26

</details>


### [329] [When Does Combining Language Models Help? A Co-Failure Ceiling on Routing, Voting, and Mixture-of-Agents Across 67 Frontier Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27288)
*Josef Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Multi-model LLM systems (routing, voting, cascades, etc.) improve accuracy, but gains are fundamentally capped by the "all-wrong rate" β — how often every model fails on the same query. Unlike standard pairwise error correlation ρ, β cannot be inferred from marginals and pairwise correlations alone. The authors provide a Clopper-Pearson bound for finite-sample certification of maximum achievable gain. Empirically, across 67 models, the all-wrong tail is substantially underestimated by Gaussian copula models; co-failure is linked to answer format rather than subject domain; and gains derive from models failing on different queries, not from adding more models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The field routinely reports average pairwise error correlation (ρ) as a diagnostic for ensemble diversity, but this quantity is insufficient: it cannot identify the all-wrong rate β, which is the true upper bound on accuracy for any policy whose output is a single model's answer. The authors aim to establish β as the correct metric and provide tools to bound it before training a router or ensemble.

Method: The authors formally derive that for any single-answer selection policy, accuracy ≤ 1 − β (the all-wrong rate). They use a Clopper-Pearson confidence bound to give finite-sample certificates on β. Empirically, they evaluate 67 models from 21 providers on open-ended mathematics, execution-graded code, and GPQA-Diamond questions (in both multiple-choice and free-response formats). They fit a tetrachoric-calibrated single-factor Gaussian copula model to test whether it adequately prices the all-wrong tail, and compare heterogeneous low-ρ ensembles against high-ρ Self-MoA ensembles.

Result: The Gaussian copula model underprices β by a factor of ~2.5 on open-ended mathematics (observed β=0.052 vs. predicted 0.023; 90% CI [1.7, 3.4]; k=17). On execution-graded code, β=0.079. GPQA-Diamond free-response yields β=0.127 (five-judge panel, κ 0.73–0.92), implicating answer format as a co-failure source. Low-ρ heterogeneous ensembles outperform high-ρ Self-MoA at matched quality. On checkable tasks, combining models rarely beats the single best model without strong query-level routing signals. Gains come from models failing on different questions, not model count.

Conclusion: β (the all-wrong rate) is the fundamental accuracy ceiling for single-answer multi-model policies and should be reported alongside ρ. Pairwise correlation is insufficient for diagnosing ensemble potential. Finite-sample Clopper-Pearson bounds on β provide a pre-training certificate. Co-failure is driven by answer format, and diversity of failure patterns — not model count — drives gains.

Abstract: Multi-model LLM systems such as routing, voting, cascades, fusion, and mixture-of-agents are used to beat single-model accuracy. We show that their gain is capped by a quantity the field rarely reports. For any policy whose output is one member model answer, accuracy cannot exceed one minus beta, where beta is the rate at which every model is wrong on the same query. In contrast, the usual diagnostic, average pairwise error correlation rho, cannot identify beta: error laws with identical marginals and pairwise correlations can have different all-wrong rates. A Clopper-Pearson bound on beta gives a finite-sample certificate on the largest gain any router, vote, or cascade could deliver before training a router.
  Across 67 models from 21 providers, a tetrachoric-calibrated single-factor model still underprices the all-wrong tail: on open-ended mathematics, observed beta is 0.052 versus 0.023 under the full 67-model Gaussian copula, about 2.5 times underpricing, with 90 percent CI 1.7 to 3.4 and k equals 17. The effect recurs on execution-graded code, where beta is 0.079. Re-asking the same GPQA-Diamond questions in free-response rather than multiple-choice form reopens the tail, with beta 0.127 and a five-judge panel with kappa 0.73 to 0.92, locating co-failure in answer format rather than subject. At matched quality, low-rho heterogeneous ensembles beat high-rho Self-MoA, but on checkable tasks in our pool, combining models rarely beats the single best model without a strong query-level routing signal. Gains come from models failing on different questions, not from adding more models.

</details>


### [330] [Language-Based Digital Twins for Elderly Cognitive Assistance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27334)
*Mohammad Mehdi Hosseini,Mohammad H. Mahoor,Hiroko H. Dodge*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a language-based digital twin framework using LLMs to simulate elderly conversational behavior for MCI detection. A multi-head cVAE evaluates fidelity and predicts cognitive scores, with experiments on I-CONECT showing performance comparable to real data and superior to GPT baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Early detection of Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) is challenging, and language/conversational patterns offer a non-invasive biomarker. Current approaches lack personalized, continuous monitoring tools that can model individual cognitive trajectories through speech.

Method: A digital twin framework built on LLMs that mimics elderly conversational behavior using stylometric cues and contextual metadata. A multi-head conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) jointly evaluates reconstruction quality and predicts Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores for cognitive consistency.

Result: On the I-CONECT dataset, the digital twin preserves identity-specific characteristics. Reconstruction errors and MoCA prediction errors are comparable to real data, and the approach outperforms baseline GPT-generated responses.

Conclusion: Language-based digital twins represent a scalable, non-invasive approach for personalized and continuous cognitive health monitoring, with promising fidelity and clinical relevance for MCI detection.

Abstract: Digital twins have emerged as a promising paradigm for personalized healthcare, enabling modeling of individual behavior and health trajectories. In cognitive health, early detection of Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) remains challenging, where language and conversational patterns serve as non-invasive biomarkers. In this work, we propose a language-based digital twin framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to mimic the conversational behavior of elderly individuals by incorporating stylometric cues and contextual metadata. To evaluate fidelity and cognitive consistency, we introduce a multi-head conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) that jointly measures reconstruction quality and predicts cognitive scores. Experiments on the I-CONECT dataset show that the digital twin preserves identity-specific characteristics and achieves reconstruction and MoCA prediction errors comparable to real data, while outperforming baseline GPT-generated responses. These results highlight the potential of language-based digital twins as a scalable and non-invasive approach for personalized and continuous cognitive health monitoring.
